nodes.label: Comments on artifacts
nodes.rationale: Comments let a user pin notes to specific parts of an artifact instead of describing a location in prose. A comment is created by selecting content in an artifact and clicking Comment, then typing the note and pressing Enter or clicking Save.

nodes.label: Describing a location in prose
nodes.rationale: The alternative comments replace: telling Claude in prose which part of an artifact you mean, rather than pinning the note to that part directly.

nodes.label: Commentable artifact surfaces
nodes.rationale: Comments can be attached by selecting text in a Markdown, plain-text, LaTeX, or code file; selecting text in a PDF; clicking a point on an image or figure; or clicking an element in a rendered HTML report with Comment mode on.

nodes.label: Comment mode on rendered HTML reports
nodes.rationale: A rendered HTML report is not commented on by text selection: you turn on Comment and then click an element in the report.

nodes.label: Comments on session transcripts
nodes.rationale: Besides artifact files, images and HTML reports, session transcripts can also be commented on.

nodes.label: Non-commentable artifact types
nodes.rationale: Tables and other artifact types outside the supported set cannot be commented on at all.

nodes.label: Leaving a comment
nodes.rationale: Select content in an artifact and click Comment, type the comment and press Enter (or click Save); Shift+Enter inserts a new line instead of saving.

nodes.label: Highlighted badge and numbered pin
nodes.rationale: A saved comment renders as a highlighted badge on text or a numbered pin on images; hovering reads it and clicking offers Edit or Delete.

nodes.label: Sending comments to Claude
nodes.rationale: Saving a comment does not send it to Claude; comments travel with the user's next message, which separates authoring a comment from delivering it.

nodes.label: Pending comments and batching
nodes.rationale: Pending comments appear above the message box and are sent with the next message, so several comments can be batched and sent together or sent one at a time.

nodes.label: What Claude receives per comment
nodes.rationale: Claude receives each comment with its filename, the quoted selection (or the marked image), and the user's note — which is what pins the note to a location without prose description.

nodes.label: Sent comments become message cards
nodes.rationale: Once sent, comments leave the artifact and appear as cards on the message — the comment no longer lives on the artifact it was pinned to.

nodes.label: No threads, no resolve state
nodes.rationale: Comments have neither threads nor a resolve state, so there is no ongoing conversation attached to a comment after it is sent.

nodes.label: Comment on the new version to revise again
nodes.rationale: To revise an artifact again after Claude has updated it, the user comments on the new version — iteration proceeds version by version rather than by continuing an existing comment.

nodes.label: 1,000-character comment cap
nodes.rationale: Comment text is capped at 1,000 characters.

nodes.label: Comments excluded from downloads and Files
nodes.rationale: Comments are not included in downloads of an artifact and do not appear in Files, so they exist only inside the conversation surface.

nodes.label: Custom connector
nodes.rationale: A custom connector adds any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server to Claude, either as a Remote connector (an HTTPS web server) or as a Local command (a program running on your own computer).

nodes.label: Add connector flow
nodes.rationale: Connectors are added under Settings > Connectors > Add connector, where you choose Remote or Local command and enter a Name restricted to lowercase letters, digits and hyphens.

nodes.label: Remote connector
nodes.rationale: A Remote connector points at an MCP server hosted as an HTTPS web server; adding one requires entering the server URL.

nodes.label: Local command connector
nodes.rationale: A Local command connector runs an MCP server as a program on your own computer; adding one requires entering the command to run.

nodes.label: Remote advanced settings
nodes.rationale: For a Remote connector, Advanced settings covers the transport (SSE or Streamable HTTP), OAuth client settings, and the Headers helper command.

nodes.label: SSE or Streamable HTTP transport
nodes.rationale: A Remote connector's transport is chosen between SSE and Streamable HTTP in Advanced settings.

nodes.label: Local advanced settings
nodes.rationale: For a Local command connector, Advanced settings covers the command's arguments and its environment variables.

nodes.label: Connectors Directory
nodes.rationale: Browse Connectors Directory, offered in the Add connector flow, opens the public directory of connectors.

nodes.label: Provider sign-in for remote servers
nodes.rationale: Remote servers that require login take the user through the provider's own sign-in page during connection.

nodes.label: Organization admin policy on custom connectors
nodes.rationale: On Team and Enterprise plans, custom connectors can be added and used only if the organization allows them; the admin controls page documents this setting.

nodes.label: Disabled-connector state
nodes.rationale: When an organization disallows custom connectors, the Remote and Local command options are grayed with an admin-disabled note; connectors added earlier stay listed but grayed and unusable by Claude, and they work again if the organization turns custom connectors back on.

nodes.label: Ask each time default
nodes.rationale: Every tool exposed by a custom connector starts at the Ask each time permission level, so the first behaviour of a newly added connector is per-call approval.

nodes.label: Per-tool Always allow or Block
nodes.rationale: On a connector's page, individual tools can be set to Always allow or Block under Tools, overriding the Ask each time default per tool.

nodes.label: Skip approvals
nodes.rationale: Skip approvals can be turned on for a whole connector; it disables the per-call approval card for every tool on that connector, so the documentation warns it should be used only with connectors from trusted developers.

nodes.label: Trust-the-developer warning
nodes.rationale: An explicit warning states that only connectors from developers you trust should be used, because turning off per-call approval removes the last per-invocation check on that connector's tools.

nodes.label: Local connector sandbox
nodes.rationale: Local-command connectors run inside the sandbox with the same network limits that apply to Claude's code, and each is given a per-connector writable directory.

nodes.label: Unencrypted local env vars
nodes.rationale: Environment variables for local connectors are stored unencrypted in a configuration file readable only by your account, so high-value secrets should not be placed there.

nodes.label: Remote compute clusters
nodes.rationale: Claude Science lets you connect a machine reachable over SSH — a lab workstation with a GPU or an HPC login node — so Claude can run jobs on it. The feature covers adding the host, probing it, submitting jobs, and reading host-specific instructions.

nodes.label: SSH host connection
nodes.rationale: An SSH host is a remote machine registered with Claude Science so Claude can reach it over SSH. Connecting a host is what makes remote job execution — on a GPU workstation or an existing HPC cluster — possible.

nodes.label: Existing ~/.ssh/config reuse
nodes.rationale: Claude Science uses your existing `~/.ssh/config`: the address, user, port, and any `ProxyJump` for a host come from that file rather than being re-entered.

nodes.label: Key or ssh-agent authentication
nodes.rationale: Authentication to a remote host uses your own SSH key or `ssh-agent`; no separate credential mechanism is introduced.

nodes.label: Nothing installed on the host
nodes.rationale: Claude Science installs nothing on the remote host itself, so connecting a workstation or HPC login node requires no agent or daemon deployment there.

nodes.label: Org-level SSH host disablement
nodes.rationale: On Team and Enterprise plans an organization can turn SSH hosts off via the admin controls, which removes the **Add SSH host** action.

nodes.label: Behavior when SSH hosts are turned off
nodes.rationale: When an org disables SSH hosts, previously added hosts stay listed but refuse new commands and file transfers; a job already running can still be stopped and its results collected.

nodes.label: Adding a host
nodes.rationale: A host is added under **Settings > Compute > SSH hosts > Add SSH host**: choose or type an alias, optionally add notes, optionally set Advanced overrides, then click **Add**.

nodes.label: SSH config host alias
nodes.rationale: The host is identified by an alias chosen or typed from `~/.ssh/config`; its address, user, port, and `ProxyJump` are then resolved from that config entry.

nodes.label: Host notes
nodes.rationale: Optional notes about a host — partition, account code, module loads, whether software can be installed — are read by Claude before the first job, and probe results are saved as editable notes on the host's detail page.

nodes.label: Advanced user/port/identity overrides
nodes.rationale: Under **Advanced**, the **User**, **Port**, or **Identity file** inherited from `~/.ssh/config` can optionally be overridden when adding a host.

nodes.label: Read-only host probe
nodes.rationale: Adding a host runs a read-only probe of the machine; it can be re-run later with the **Probe** action on the host's detail page.

nodes.label: Probe inventory of host capabilities
nodes.rationale: The probe records CPUs, memory, GPUs, CUDA driver, presence of conda/modules/Apptainer, scratch directories, and whether `sbatch` exists; results are saved as editable notes.

nodes.label: SLURM partition discovery
nodes.rationale: On SLURM clusters the read-only probe additionally reads the cluster's partitions.

nodes.label: Remote job execution
nodes.rationale: Claude runs jobs on a connected host — as detached processes on a workstation or through `sbatch` on a SLURM cluster — with the job script and inputs copied to a job directory under the scratch directory.

nodes.label: Detached-process jobs on workstations
nodes.rationale: Workstations run jobs as detached processes rather than through a scheduler.

nodes.label: sbatch submission on SLURM clusters
nodes.rationale: SLURM clusters receive jobs via `sbatch`, which is why the probe checks whether `sbatch` exists and reads partitions.

nodes.label: Jobs survive connection loss
nodes.rationale: Jobs launched on a remote host survive loss of the SSH connection — both the detached-process and `sbatch` paths keep running.

nodes.label: Scratch directory
nodes.rationale: The scratch directory is set on the host's detail page and is where job directories are created; for SLURM it must be on a shared filesystem.

nodes.label: Concurrent job limit
nodes.rationale: A per-host **Concurrent job limit**, defaulting to 100, caps how many jobs may run at once and is configured on the host's detail page.

nodes.label: Run-this-job approval card
nodes.rationale: When Claude proposes a remote job, a **Run this job on `<host>`?** card shows the command and script for the user to approve before anything runs.

nodes.label: Approval scopes
nodes.rationale: A remote-job approval is granted at one of four scopes: **Once**, **This conversation**, **This project**, or **Global**.

nodes.label: Job directory staging
nodes.rationale: On approval, the job script and its inputs are copied to a job directory created under the host's scratch directory.

nodes.label: Remote jobs run outside the sandbox
nodes.rationale: A warning states that remote jobs run outside the sandbox, as your user on the host, with access to everything your account can read and write there.

nodes.label: 30-minute default job timeout
nodes.rationale: The default job timeout is 30 minutes; longer work must be flagged to Claude before the job is submitted.

nodes.label: Output pull-back into the session
nodes.rationale: When a job finishes its outputs are pulled back into the session automatically.

nodes.label: ~100 MB file-size threshold
nodes.rationale: Files over the size threshold — about 100 MB by default — are not transferred back; they stay on the host and Claude records their paths instead.

nodes.label: Host Details document
nodes.rationale: The Details document on a host's detail page holds host-specific instructions — how environments are activated, where data and packages live, the cluster's scheduling conventions — which Claude reads, updates as it works, and the user can edit at any time.

nodes.label: Claude Science beta admin-control gap
nodes.rationale: Claude Science is in beta, and some admin controls that govern other Claude products do not yet govern it. This page enumerates exactly which controls do not apply.

nodes.label: Admin controls reference page
nodes.rationale: The Admin controls page (/docs/claude-science/admin-controls) carries the complete per-setting table and describes the controls on the Organization settings > Claude Science page itself.

nodes.label: Audit log does not cover Claude Science
nodes.rationale: Claude Science does not write events to the organization audit log, so audit-log-based monitoring sees nothing from it.

nodes.label: Compliance API (Enterprise)
nodes.rationale: For Enterprise organizations with the Compliance API enabled, settings changes and read-only session transcripts are available through the Compliance API instead of the audit log; Claude Science session coverage there is itself in beta.

nodes.label: Organization data export excludes local data
nodes.rationale: The organization data export does not include data stored on members' computers, so a Claude Science member's local conversations and artifacts are absent from it.

nodes.label: Claude Science stores data on members' computers
nodes.rationale: Claude Science keeps conversations and artifacts on members' computers rather than on Anthropic's servers. Server-side org controls cannot reach that local storage.

nodes.label: Custom Data Retention window does not reach local data
nodes.rationale: The Custom Data Retention auto-delete window applies to conversations, projects, and artifacts stored on Anthropic's servers; it does not reach Claude Science data kept on members' computers. It does apply to session transcripts returned by the Compliance API.

nodes.label: No local-deletion signal to Anthropic
nodes.rationale: When a member deletes local Claude Science data, Anthropic is not notified, so the matching server-side records are not dropped early. Each expires under its own retention period instead.

nodes.label: Server-side records: model-call log and session transcript
nodes.rationale: The server-side records matching a Claude Science session are the model-call log and, for Enterprise organizations with the Compliance API enabled, the session transcript. Each expires under its own retention period.

nodes.label: Connector allowlist does not filter custom connectors
nodes.rationale: The organization's connector allowlist applies only to Directory connectors the organization publishes; it does not filter the custom connectors a member adds in the app.

nodes.label: Org-wide custom connector off switch
nodes.rationale: The only available lever over member-added custom connectors is turning custom connectors off for the whole organization — there is no per-connector filtering.

nodes.label: Organization settings > Claude Science page
nodes.rationale: The Claude Science controls for connectors, skills, and the sandbox domain allowlist live on the Organization settings > Claude Science page, separate from the connector allowlist and from the code execution network allowlist used for claude.ai chat.

nodes.label: Sandbox domain allowlist
nodes.rationale: Claude Science's sandbox domain allowlist is configured on the Organization settings > Claude Science page and is distinct from the code execution network allowlist that governs claude.ai chat.

nodes.label: Session-duration setting covers sign-in only
nodes.rationale: The organization's session-duration setting limits only the browser sign-in step; it does not bound how long a signed-in Claude Science member stays active.

nodes.label: App holds its own token after sign-in
nodes.rationale: After a member signs in, the Claude Science app holds its own token and stays signed in beyond the organization's session-duration window.

nodes.label: Turning Claude Science off for the organization
nodes.rationale: Turning Claude Science off for the organization stops a signed-in member within a few minutes, which is the available lever despite the app's independent token.

nodes.label: Offboarding does not wipe local data
nodes.rationale: Removing a member from the organization revokes their ability to sign in but does not wipe Claude Science data already on their computer.

nodes.label: Device management software for local data
nodes.rationale: Organizations are told to use their device management software to handle local Claude Science data at offboarding, since removal from the organization leaves that data in place.

nodes.label: Claude for Government changelog
nodes.rationale: Release notes for Claude for Government, published as dated Update entries. The captured window covers five releases from 2026.08.24.1 through 2026.08.28.1, each listing Admin Console fixes, accessibility work, and new configuration settings.

nodes.label: Release 2026.08.28.1
nodes.rationale: The 2026.08.28.1 release improved screen reader and keyboard support in the Admin Console, darkened the sign-in page's main button for readability, added the 'Restart deadline for configuration changes' setting, and added a search box to the Config page.

nodes.label: Release 2026.08.26.1
nodes.rationale: The 2026.08.26.1 release fixed the session idle timeout counting from sign-in rather than last activity, added further Admin Console screen reader support, raised the idle timeout ceiling to 96 hours, and introduced per-group connector management.

nodes.label: Release 2026.08.25.2
nodes.rationale: The 2026.08.25.2 release fixed plugin and marketplace uploads failing with 'Something went wrong' for all but the smallest zip files, and added text alternatives to the Analytics page charts.

nodes.label: Release 2026.08.25.1
nodes.rationale: The 2026.08.25.1 release contained a single fix: the 'By product' table on the Analytics page had been counting Claude for Microsoft 365 activity as 'Unknown'.

nodes.label: Release 2026.08.24.1
nodes.rationale: The 2026.08.24.1 release fixed Admin Console pages cutting off content at high zoom or in narrow windows, and added two Claude Desktop telemetry settings under Config > Compliance and telemetry.

nodes.label: Admin Console
nodes.rationale: The Admin Console is the administrative web surface for Claude for Government, containing the Config pages, the Analytics page, key and seat management, and the setup wizards. Nearly every change in this changelog window touches it.

nodes.label: Admin Console screen reader and keyboard support
nodes.rationale: Accessibility work spanning two releases: actions such as revoking a key or saving seats now announce their result and return keyboard focus to the control used; dialog options, repeated buttons and usage meters get distinct announced names; every page has its own browser title; and setup wizards move focus to the new step's heading.

nodes.label: Sign-in page button contrast and link-result announcement
nodes.rationale: The main button on the sign-in pages was changed to a dark button with a white label so it is easier to read, and the page opened by an emailed sign-in link now announces its result to screen readers.

nodes.label: Restart deadline for configuration changes
nodes.rationale: A setting under Config > Compliance and telemetry that sets how long members can keep working after a settings change before Claude Desktop requires the restart that applies it. It takes effect only on Claude Desktop 1.40609.0 or later.

nodes.label: Claude Desktop 1.40609.0
nodes.rationale: The minimum Claude Desktop version at which the 'Restart deadline for configuration changes' setting takes effect. On earlier desktop builds the setting is inert.

nodes.label: Config page setting search box
nodes.rationale: A search box added to the Config page that finds a setting by its name or description and navigates directly to it.

nodes.label: Session idle timeout setting
nodes.rationale: A tenant setting that signs members out after a period of inactivity, defaulting to 24 hours. The 24-hour default was unchanged by the 2026.08.26.1 release, which altered both how the timeout is counted and how high it can be set.

nodes.label: Idle timeout counted from last activity
nodes.rationale: Fix for members on the default 24-hour session idle timeout being signed out a day after signing in even when they had kept using Claude. The timeout now counts from a member's last activity rather than from sign-in.

nodes.label: 96-hour idle timeout ceiling
nodes.rationale: A tenant admin can now set the session idle timeout as high as 96 hours (5,760 minutes), with larger values refused. A value above 24 hours saved before this release had been ignored and now applies.

nodes.label: Per-group connector management
nodes.rationale: Connector management was added to the Group configuration pages, so tenant admins and organization owners can add, override, or remove connectors for one directory group instead of only for the whole tenant or organization.

nodes.label: Compliance API activity feed
nodes.rationale: The Compliance API feed records administrative activity types. Group-level connector changes appear there as new activity types, making per-group overrides auditable.

nodes.label: Plugin and marketplace zip upload fix
nodes.rationale: Fix for adding a plugin or marketplace under Config > Integrations > Plugins failing with 'Something went wrong' for all but the smallest zip files.

nodes.label: Admin Console Analytics page
nodes.rationale: The Admin Console's Analytics page renders usage charts and a 'By product' breakdown table. Two consecutive releases changed it: one fixed product attribution, the next made its charts readable by screen readers.

nodes.label: Chart text alternatives
nodes.rationale: Text alternatives added to the Analytics page charts: screen readers announce each chart by name and can read its plotted values as a table.

nodes.label: 'By product' table attribution fix
nodes.rationale: Fix for the 'By product' table on the Analytics page counting Claude for Microsoft 365 activity as 'Unknown' instead of attributing it to that product.

nodes.label: Claude for Microsoft 365 activity
nodes.rationale: Usage originating from Claude for Microsoft 365, a product whose activity the Analytics 'By product' table failed to attribute, reporting it as 'Unknown' until the 2026.08.25.1 release.

nodes.label: High-zoom and narrow-window reflow fix
nodes.rationale: Fix for Admin Console pages cutting off setting names, values, and buttons at high browser zoom or in narrow windows; content now wraps instead of scrolling sideways.

nodes.label: Application event level (Claude Desktop)
nodes.rationale: A Config > Compliance and telemetry setting that chooses how much of Claude Desktop's application event log is sent to the organization's telemetry collector.

nodes.label: Telemetry resource attributes (Claude Desktop)
nodes.rationale: A Config > Compliance and telemetry setting that adds the organization's own labels to every telemetry record emitted by Claude Desktop.

nodes.label: Config > Compliance and telemetry
nodes.rationale: The Admin Console configuration section that holds compliance and telemetry settings, including the restart deadline, the Claude Desktop application event level, and telemetry resource attributes.

nodes.label: Tenant admin
nodes.rationale: The administrative role that configures tenant-wide behaviour: it sets the session idle timeout (now up to 96 hours) and, alongside organization owners, manages connectors per directory group.

nodes.label: Claude Desktop
nodes.rationale: The desktop client governed by these Admin Console settings: it enforces the restart deadline after a configuration change, and emits the application event log and telemetry records the two 2026.08.24.1 settings control.

nodes.label: Additional resources page
nodes.rationale: The 'Additional resources' page collects learning resources and documentation formats optimized for AI ingestion. It is organized into two card groups: 'Learning resources' for humans building with Claude, and 'Resources for AI ingestion' for machine consumption.

nodes.label: Learning resources section
nodes.rationale: A three-column card group listing five entry points for learning to build with Claude: Quickstarts, Courses, Cookbook, Use case guides, and the Glossary.

nodes.label: Quickstarts
nodes.rationale: Quickstarts are deployable applications built with the API, published at github.com/anthropics/anthropic-quickstarts.

nodes.label: Courses
nodes.rationale: Courses are step-by-step lessons on building with Claude, hosted at academy.claude.com/courses.

nodes.label: Cookbook
nodes.rationale: The Cookbook at platform.claude.com/cookbook provides replicable code samples and implementations.

nodes.label: Use case guides
nodes.rationale: Use case guides are in-depth production guides for building common use cases with Claude, indexed at /docs/en/about-claude/use-case-guides/overview.

nodes.label: Glossary
nodes.rationale: The Glossary defines key terms and concepts for working with Claude and language models, at /docs/en/about-claude/glossary.

nodes.label: Resources for AI ingestion
nodes.rationale: A two-column card group of documentation formats optimized for consumption by a model rather than a human reader: the API primer for Claude ingestion and llms.txt.

nodes.label: API primer for Claude ingestion
nodes.rationale: The API primer at /docs/en/claude_api_primer is a concise API guide written specifically to be ingested by Claude rather than read by a person.

nodes.label: llms.txt
nodes.rationale: llms.txt, served at platform.claude.com/llms.txt, is an LLM-optimized index of the documentation.

nodes.label: Claude model migration guides index
nodes.rationale: A hub page titled 'Migration guides' that collects guides for migrating to the latest Claude models from previous Claude versions. It carries no migration steps itself; it is a link index plus a 'Get help' section.

nodes.label: Migrating to Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1
nodes.rationale: The listed migration guide covering both Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, at /docs/en/models/fable-5-1/migration-guide. It is the only entry in the index that pairs two model names in one guide alongside the Fable 5 / Mythos 5 entry.

nodes.label: Migrating to Claude Mythos 5 and Claude Fable 5
nodes.rationale: The listed migration guide covering Claude Mythos 5 and Claude Fable 5, at /docs/en/models/fable-5/migration-guide. It is the predecessor generation to the Fable 5.1 / Mythos 5.1 guide listed above it.

nodes.label: Migrating to Claude Opus 5
nodes.rationale: The listed migration guide for Claude Opus 5, at /docs/en/models/opus-5/migration-guide.

nodes.label: Migrating to Claude Sonnet 5
nodes.rationale: The listed migration guide for Claude Sonnet 5, at /docs/en/models/sonnet-5/migration-guide.

nodes.label: Migrating to Claude Haiku 4.5
nodes.rationale: The listed migration guide for Claude Haiku 4.5, at /docs/en/models/haiku-4-5/migration-guide. It is the only entry for a 4.x model, so the index spans generations rather than only the current one.

nodes.label: Get help section
nodes.rationale: The page's second half, naming four escalation routes when a migration runs into trouble: the API documentation, the model capabilities overview, the API release notes, and contacting support.

nodes.label: API documentation (detailed specifications)
nodes.rationale: The API overview docs, recommended for detailed specifications during a migration.

nodes.label: Model capabilities overview
nodes.rationale: The models overview page, recommended for performance comparisons between models — the input to choosing which model to migrate to.

nodes.label: API release notes
nodes.rationale: The API release notes page, recommended for reviewing API updates that may affect a migration.

nodes.label: Contact support during migration
nodes.rationale: The final escalation route: contact support if any issues are encountered during migration. It is the only route that is a human channel rather than a document.

nodes.label: Skills for enterprise guide
nodes.rationale: Governance guidance for enterprise admins and architects who must govern Agent Skills across an organization: how to vet, evaluate, deploy and manage Skills at scale. Authoring guidance lives in best practices and architecture in the Skills overview.

nodes.label: Two distinct vetting questions
nodes.rationale: Deploying Skills in an enterprise requires answering two separate questions: are Skills safe in general (platform-level security, covered in the overview's security considerations), and how do I vet this specific Skill (the risk assessment plus review checklist).

nodes.label: Risk tier assessment
nodes.rationale: Before approving a Skill for deployment, evaluate it against a fixed table of risk indicators, each graded High or Medium concern. The indicators cover code execution, instruction manipulation, MCP references, network access, hardcoded credentials, filesystem scope and tool invocations.

nodes.label: Risk indicator: code execution
nodes.rationale: Scripts in the Skill directory (*.py, *.sh, *.js) are a High concern because scripts run with full environment access.

nodes.label: Risk indicator: instruction manipulation
nodes.rationale: Directives that tell Claude to ignore safety rules, hide actions from users, or alter behavior conditionally are a High concern because they can bypass security controls.

nodes.label: Risk indicator: MCP server references
nodes.rationale: Instructions referencing MCP tools in the form ServerName:tool_name are a High concern because they extend the Skill's access beyond the Skill itself.

nodes.label: Risk indicator: network access patterns
nodes.rationale: URLs, API endpoints, and fetch/curl/requests calls are a High concern because they are a potential data exfiltration vector.

nodes.label: Risk indicator: hardcoded credentials
nodes.rationale: API keys, tokens or passwords inside Skill files or scripts are a High concern: the secrets end up exposed in Git history and in the context window. Credentials should come from environment variables or secure credential stores instead.

nodes.label: Risk indicator: filesystem access scope
nodes.rationale: Paths outside the Skill directory, broad glob patterns and path traversal ('../') are a Medium concern because the Skill may access unintended data.

nodes.label: Risk indicator: tool invocations
nodes.rationale: Instructions directing Claude to use bash, file operations or other tools are a Medium concern; review what operations are actually performed. Combined risk is higher when a Skill uses file-read and network tools together.

nodes.label: Skill review checklist
nodes.rationale: An eight-step manual audit to complete before deploying any third-party or internal Skill: read all directory content, run scripts sandboxed to verify behavior matches purpose, check for adversarial instructions, check for network calls, verify no hardcoded credentials, enumerate the tools and commands invoked, confirm redirect destinations, and verify no data-exfiltration patterns.

nodes.label: Never deploy untrusted Skills unaudited
nodes.rationale: A malicious Skill can direct Claude to execute arbitrary code, access sensitive files, or transmit data externally, so Skills from untrusted sources must never be deployed without a full audit. Skill installation deserves the same rigor as installing software on production systems.

nodes.label: Skill and plugin security scanning
nodes.rationale: Claude Enterprise organizations can turn on automated scanning of custom Skills in claude.ai and Claude Cowork; after it is enabled, Skills uploaded or edited there are scanned for hidden code execution, data exfiltration, or tampering with Claude's safeguards. A Skill that fails or has an unfinished scan is blocked; one that passes with a warning stays usable behind a caution notice.

nodes.label: Scanning does not cover the Claude API
nodes.rationale: Skills uploaded through the Skills API (/v1/skills), including from the Claude Console, are not scanned, so API deployments must rely on the manual review checklist and on version pinning instead.

nodes.label: Scanning exclusions
nodes.rationale: Scanning does not apply to Skills already in the organization when it was turned on, nor to organizations with certain data-handling configurations such as customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK), zero data retention (ZDR), or HIPAA readiness.

nodes.label: Evaluation before deployment
nodes.rationale: Skills can degrade agent performance if they trigger incorrectly, conflict with other Skills, or give poor instructions, so evaluation must be required before any production deployment, with approval gates on five named dimensions.

nodes.label: Evaluation dimension: triggering accuracy
nodes.rationale: Measures whether the Skill activates for the right queries and stays inactive for unrelated ones. Example failure: the Skill triggers on every mention of a spreadsheet even when the user only wants to discuss data.

nodes.label: Evaluation dimension: isolation behavior
nodes.rationale: Measures whether the Skill works correctly on its own. Example failure: the Skill references files that do not exist in its directory.

nodes.label: Evaluation dimension: coexistence
nodes.rationale: Measures whether adding this Skill degrades other Skills. Example failure: the new Skill's description is too broad and steals triggers from existing Skills.

nodes.label: Evaluation dimension: instruction following
nodes.rationale: Measures whether Claude follows the Skill's instructions accurately. Example failure: Claude skips validation steps or uses the wrong libraries.

nodes.label: Evaluation dimension: output quality
nodes.rationale: Measures whether the Skill produces correct, useful results. Example failure: generated reports have formatting errors or missing data.

nodes.label: Evaluation suite requirements
nodes.rationale: Skill authors must submit evaluation suites of 3-5 representative queries per Skill covering cases where the Skill should trigger, should not trigger, and ambiguous edge cases, tested across every model the organization uses (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus) because Skill effectiveness varies by model.

nodes.label: Evaluation results signal lifecycle actions
nodes.rationale: Declining trigger accuracy means updating the description or instructions; coexistence conflicts mean consolidating overlapping Skills or narrowing descriptions; consistently low output quality means rewriting instructions or adding validation steps; persistent failures across updates mean deprecating the Skill.

nodes.label: Skill lifecycle management
nodes.rationale: A six-stage lifecycle for organizational Skills: Plan, Create and review, Test, Deploy, Monitor, and Iterate or deprecate.

nodes.label: Lifecycle step: Plan
nodes.rationale: Identify workflows that are repetitive, error-prone, or need specialized knowledge, map them to organizational roles, and decide which are candidates for Skills.

nodes.label: Lifecycle step: Create and review
nodes.rationale: The author follows best practices; a security review using the review checklist and an evaluation suite are both required before approval; and separation of duties is established so Skill authors are never their own reviewers.

nodes.label: Lifecycle step: Test
nodes.rationale: Require evaluations both in isolation (the Skill alone) and alongside existing Skills (coexistence testing), verifying triggering accuracy, output quality and absence of regressions across the active Skill set before production approval.

nodes.label: Lifecycle step: Deploy
nodes.rationale: Upload through the Skills API for workspace-wide access, then document the Skill in the internal registry with its purpose, owner and version.

nodes.label: Lifecycle step: Monitor
nodes.rationale: Track usage patterns and user feedback and rerun evaluations periodically to detect drift or regressions as workflows and models evolve. Usage analytics are not currently available through the Skills API, so application-level logging must record which Skills are included in requests.

nodes.label: Lifecycle step: Iterate or deprecate
nodes.rationale: The full evaluation suite must pass before any new version is promoted; Skills are updated when workflows change or scores decline, and deprecated when evaluations consistently fail or the workflow is retired.

nodes.label: Recall limits on simultaneous Skills
nodes.rationale: Each Skill's name and description compete for attention in the system prompt, so with too many Skills active Claude may pick the wrong Skill or miss relevant ones. Limit how many are loaded simultaneously, measure recall accuracy with the evaluation suite as Skills are added, and stop adding when performance degrades.

nodes.label: API cap of 20 Skills per request
nodes.rationale: API requests support a maximum of 20 Skills each. A role needing more than one request supports should either consolidate narrow Skills into broader ones or route requests to different Skill sets based on task type.

nodes.label: Start specific, consolidate later
nodes.rationale: Teams should start with narrow, workflow-specific Skills rather than broad multipurpose ones and consolidate into role-based bundles as organizational patterns emerge — merging only when the consolidated Skill's evaluations confirm performance equivalent to the individual Skills it replaces. Example: formatting-sales-reports, querying-pipeline-data and updating-crm-records become sales-operations.

nodes.label: Consistent naming conventions
nodes.rationale: Organizations should use consistent Skill naming conventions across teams; the formatting guidance itself lives in the naming conventions section of the best-practices doc.

nodes.label: Internal Skill registry
nodes.rationale: Maintain a registry entry per Skill recording its purpose (which workflow it supports), owner (team or individual responsible for maintenance), current deployed version, dependencies (MCP servers, packages, external services), and evaluation status (last evaluation date and results).

nodes.label: Role-based Skill bundles
nodes.rationale: Group Skills by organizational role so each user's active set stays focused — sales gets CRM operations, pipeline reporting and proposal generation; engineering gets code review, deployment workflows and incident response; finance gets report generation, data validation and audit preparation. A bundle should contain only what that role's daily workflows need.

nodes.label: Skill directories in Git
nodes.rationale: Store Skill directories in Git for history tracking, code review through pull requests, and rollback capability; each Skill directory containing SKILL.md and bundled files maps naturally onto a Git-tracked folder, and Git is the single source of truth for Skill files.

nodes.label: API-based distribution
nodes.rationale: The Skills API provides workspace-scoped distribution: a Skill uploaded through the API is available to every member of that workspace, with upload, versioning and management endpoints documented in the Skills API guide.

nodes.label: Versioning strategy
nodes.rationale: Four-part version discipline covering production pinning, development on latest, a rollback plan, and integrity verification of reviewed Skills.

nodes.label: Pin production Skills to specific versions
nodes.rationale: Production requests must pin Skills to specific versions, run the full evaluation suite before promoting a new version, and treat every update as a new deployment requiring a full security review.

nodes.label: Omitting version silently changes production
nodes.rationale: If the `version` field is omitted, requests use the latest version, so a new version uploaded by anyone in the workspace immediately changes what production agents run.

nodes.label: Development and testing on latest
nodes.rationale: Development and testing environments should use latest versions in order to validate changes before promoting them to production.

nodes.label: Rollback plan
nodes.rationale: Keep the previous Skill version as a fallback and revert to the last known-good version immediately if a new version fails evaluations in production.

nodes.label: Integrity verification of reviewed Skills
nodes.rationale: Compute checksums of reviewed Skills and verify them at deployment time, and use signed commits in the Skill repository to establish provenance.

nodes.label: Custom Skills do not sync across surfaces
nodes.rationale: Skills uploaded to the API are not available on claude.ai or in Claude Code, and vice versa; each surface requires separate uploads and management, so an organization deploying across surfaces must implement its own synchronization process.

nodes.label: Routine fire endpoint
nodes.rationale: POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/claude_code/routines/{routine_id}/fire is the HTTP entry point that starts a new run of an existing Claude Code routine and returns the resulting session ID and URL. It is the on-demand trigger for a routine, callable by any authenticated system over HTTP.

nodes.label: Routine (saved configuration)
nodes.rationale: A routine is a saved configuration on Claude Code on the web: a prompt, one or more repositories, and connectors, packaged so it can run unattended on a schedule, in response to GitHub events, or when called over HTTP.

nodes.label: Claude Code on the web
nodes.rationale: Claude Code on the web runs Claude Code sessions on Anthropic-managed cloud infrastructure at claude.ai/code. It is the surface that hosts routines and the sessions this endpoint creates.

nodes.label: Experimental API stability contract
nodes.rationale: The endpoint is experimental: request and response shapes, rate limits, and token semantics might change. Breaking changes ship behind new dated beta header versions, and the two previous header versions continue to work so callers have time to migrate.

nodes.label: anthropic-beta experimental-cc-routine-2026-04-01
nodes.rationale: Every request must include the header `anthropic-beta: experimental-cc-routine-2026-04-01`. Requests without it return 400 invalid_request_error.

nodes.label: anthropic-version header
nodes.rationale: The `anthropic-version` header is required and carries the API version, for example `2023-06-01`. `Content-Type: application/json` is required whenever a body is present.

nodes.label: Per-routine bearer token
nodes.rationale: Authentication is `Authorization: Bearer <token>` using a per-routine token prefixed `sk-ant-oat01-`, created in the Claude Code web UI rather than a Claude API key. A missing token, or one that does not match the routine, returns 401 authentication_error.

nodes.label: Token generation in the web UI
nodes.rationale: A token is generated by opening the routine for editing, clicking Add another trigger under Select a trigger, choosing API, then clicking Generate token in the modal. The token is shown once and cannot be retrieved later; the modal also shows the full fire URL.

nodes.label: Token rotation and revocation
nodes.rationale: Tokens are generated and revoked from the routine's API trigger settings at claude.ai/code/routines. There is no public API for token management, and generating a new token revokes the previous one.

nodes.label: Single-routine token scope
nodes.rationale: The bearer token is scoped to a single routine and grants no read access. A compromised token can only trigger that one routine; it gives no access to other routines and none to account data.

nodes.label: Plan and entitlement requirement
nodes.rationale: Calling the endpoint requires a claude.ai account on a Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise plan with Claude Code on the web enabled. An account or organization without access receives 403 permission_error.

nodes.label: Differences from the Claude Platform
nodes.rationale: The endpoint belongs to the Claude Code product surface and diverges from the Claude Platform APIs along authentication, token scope, SDK support, billing, path namespace, and stability.

nodes.label: Claude Platform APIs
nodes.rationale: The Claude Platform APIs authenticate with an `x-api-key` Claude API key from the Claude Console, carry workspace-level token scope, are available in all client SDKs, bill against Claude Platform usage, live under the `/v1/...` namespace, and are stable or standard beta.

nodes.label: /v1/claude_code path namespace
nodes.rationale: Claude Code product-surface endpoints live under the `/v1/claude_code/...` path namespace, distinct from the Claude Platform's `/v1/...`.

nodes.label: Subscription-usage billing
nodes.rationale: Runs triggered through this endpoint bill as Claude Code subscription usage on claude.ai, not as Claude Platform usage. Organizations with extra usage enabled continue past the included allowance on metered overage.

nodes.label: routine_id path parameter (trig_ prefix)
nodes.rationale: `routine_id` is the routine's string identifier in the URL path. Despite the parameter name, its value is prefixed `trig_` rather than `routine_`, and it appears in the URL shown by the API-trigger modal.

nodes.label: Optional text body field
nodes.rationale: The optional `text` string carries initial context for the run — an alert body, a failing log line, a git diff — up to 65,536 characters. It is freeform and not parsed, so structured payloads arrive as a literal string, and unknown body fields are ignored.

nodes.label: routine_fire response
nodes.rationale: A successful call returns 200 OK with `type` always `routine_fire`, `claude_code_session_id` for the session created, and `claude_code_session_url` linking to that session on claude.ai for watching the run, reviewing changes, or continuing the conversation.

nodes.label: Fire-and-return semantics
nodes.rationale: The request returns as soon as the session is created. It does not stream session output and does not wait for the session to complete.

nodes.label: Standard Anthropic error envelope
nodes.rationale: Errors use the standard Anthropic error envelope: a top-level `type: "error"` with a nested `error` object carrying its own `type` (such as `not_found_error`) and a `message` string.

nodes.label: Error status codes and causes
nodes.rationale: 400 invalid_request_error covers a missing or invalid beta header, `text` over 65,536 characters, or a paused routine; 401 authentication_error a missing or mismatched token; 403 permission_error a lack of account access; 404 not_found_error a nonexistent routine; 429 rate_limit_error a run or usage limit; 500 api_error an unexpected server error to retry with exponential backoff; 503 overloaded_error a temporary overload.

nodes.label: 503 instead of the Platform's 529
nodes.rationale: For the `overloaded_error` type the Claude Platform returns HTTP 529, but this endpoint returns 503 — a status-code divergence a shared client would otherwise mishandle.

nodes.label: Daily run allowance and usage limits
nodes.rationale: Routine runs count against a per-account daily allowance that varies by plan, and the resulting sessions draw down the same Claude Code subscription usage as interactive sessions. Reaching either limit returns 429 rate_limit_error with a `Retry-After` header showing when the window resets; remaining daily runs are visible at claude.ai/code/routines.

nodes.label: No idempotency key
nodes.rationale: Each successful request creates a new session and there is no idempotency key. A webhook caller that retries therefore creates multiple sessions.

nodes.label: No SDK support
nodes.rationale: The endpoint is not in the Anthropic SDKs, because its token model differs from API key authentication and typical callers such as CI jobs and alerting webhooks send the request directly.

nodes.label: Typical callers
nodes.rationale: Typical callers are alerting systems, CI pipelines, and internal tools that need to start a Claude Code session programmatically. Most integrations store the fire URL and the token as secrets and call the endpoint directly.

nodes.label: GitHub Actions CI-failure trigger
nodes.rationale: The documented GitHub Actions step runs on `if: failure()`, reads ROUTINE_FIRE_URL and ROUTINE_FIRE_TOKEN from repository secrets, and curls the endpoint with a `text` body naming the failing workflow, run id, and ref.

nodes.label: Predictable HTTP error code format
nodes.rationale: The Claude API follows a predictable HTTP error code format in which each status code maps to a named error type (400 invalid_request_error, 401 authentication_error, 402 billing_error, 403 permission_error, 404 not_found_error, 409 conflict_error, 413 request_too_large, 429 rate_limit_error, 500 api_error, 504 timeout_error, 529 overloaded_error).

nodes.label: 400 invalid_request_error
nodes.rationale: A 400 invalid_request_error signals an issue with the format or content of the request, and is also used for other 4XX codes not listed separately. The API additionally returns 400 when usage reaches an organization or workspace spend limit you set, except limits on the Claude Code workspace, which can return 429 instead.

nodes.label: 401 authentication_error
nodes.rationale: A 401 authentication_error means the API key is malformed, revoked, or expired. On Claude Platform on AWS the same status can instead indicate a problem with AWS credentials or the SigV4 signature.

nodes.label: 402 billing_error
nodes.rationale: A 402 billing_error means there is an issue with billing or payment information; check payment details in the Claude Console, or in AWS Marketplace when using Claude Platform on AWS.

nodes.label: 403 permission_error
nodes.rationale: A 403 permission_error means the API key lacks permission for the specified resource; the fix is to check the organization's access and workspace settings in the Claude Console.

nodes.label: 404 not_found_error
nodes.rationale: A 404 not_found_error means the requested resource was not found; check the endpoint path and any resource IDs in the request URL.

nodes.label: 409 conflict_error
nodes.rationale: A 409 conflict_error means the request conflicts with a resource's current state, for example a concurrent modification or a uniqueness violation. Resolve the conflict, then retry the request.

nodes.label: 413 request_too_large
nodes.rationale: A 413 request_too_large means the request exceeds the maximum allowed number of bytes for the endpoint; the per-endpoint maximums are listed under Request size limits.

nodes.label: 429 rate_limit_error
nodes.rationale: A 429 rate_limit_error means the organization hit a rate limit, reached its usage tier's monthly spend cap, or reached a spend limit on the Claude Code workspace. A tier spend-cap 429 carries no retry-after header and keeps failing until access resumes.

nodes.label: 500 api_error
nodes.rationale: A 500 api_error is an unexpected error internal to Anthropic's systems. Retry with exponential backoff, and if it persists contact support with the request ID.

nodes.label: 504 timeout_error
nodes.rationale: A 504 timeout_error means the request timed out while processing. The documented remedy is the streaming Messages API for long-running requests, with further options under Long requests.

nodes.label: 529 overloaded_error
nodes.rationale: A 529 overloaded_error means the API is temporarily overloaded; it can occur when the API experiences high traffic across all users, independent of one organization's usage.

nodes.label: Acceleration limits on sharp usage increases
nodes.rationale: In rare cases an organization with a sharp increase in usage can see 429 errors caused by acceleration limits on the API. Ramping traffic up gradually and keeping usage patterns consistent avoids hitting them.

nodes.label: SDK automatic retry with exponential backoff
nodes.rationale: The official SDKs automatically retry transient failures — connection errors, rate limits, and 5xx server errors — with exponential backoff, twice by default. Each SDK client accepts a maximum-retries option to reconfigure or disable this behavior.

nodes.label: retry-after header
nodes.rationale: The retry-after header tells a client when to retry; SDK retry logic honors it when present. Its absence is diagnostic: a usage-tier spend-cap 429 has no retry-after header, which is how that case is recognized.

nodes.label: Mid-stream SSE errors after a 200
nodes.rationale: When receiving a streaming response over server-sent events, an error can occur after the API has already returned a 200. In that case error handling does not follow the standard HTTP-status mechanisms; the shape is documented under streaming error events.

nodes.label: Request size limits
nodes.rationale: The API enforces a maximum request size per endpoint type, and exceeding it yields a 413 request_too_large. The limits differ sharply by endpoint rather than being one global cap.

nodes.label: 32 MB limit: Messages and Token Counting APIs
nodes.rationale: Both the Messages API and the Token Counting API cap a single request at 32 MB.

nodes.label: 256 MB limit: Batch API
nodes.rationale: The Batch API accepts a maximum request size of 256 MB, eight times the Messages API limit.

nodes.label: 500 MB limit: Files API
nodes.rationale: The Files API accepts the largest requests of any endpoint type, at a maximum of 500 MB.

nodes.label: Cloudflare returns 413 before the API servers
nodes.rationale: On the direct Claude API, Cloudflare returns the 413 request_too_large error before the request ever reaches the API servers, so an oversized request is rejected at the edge.

nodes.label: JSON error response shape
nodes.rationale: The API always returns errors as JSON with a top-level error object that always includes a type and a message value, plus a sibling request_id field for tracking and debugging.

nodes.label: Error type values may expand under the versioning policy
nodes.rationale: In accordance with the API versioning policy, the values inside error objects may expand and the set of type values can grow over time, so clients must not treat the current list as closed.

nodes.label: SDK typed exceptions instead of raw JSON
nodes.rationale: The official SDKs raise typed exceptions rather than returning raw JSON, with class names and namespaces differing by language (anthropic.NotFoundError in Python, Anthropic::Errors::NotFoundError in Ruby, com.anthropic.errors.NotFoundException in Java). Catch the typed classes, most specific first, rather than string-matching messages.

nodes.label: Go's single *anthropic.Error value
nodes.rationale: The Go SDK is the exception to per-status exception classes: every error surfaces as a single *anthropic.Error value and the caller branches on its StatusCode.

nodes.label: request-id header
nodes.rationale: Every API response includes a unique request-id header, for example req_018EeWyXxfu5pfWkrYcMdjWG. Including that ID when contacting support is what lets a specific request be located quickly.

nodes.label: Two request IDs on Claude Platform on AWS
nodes.rationale: On Claude Platform on AWS a response carries two IDs: the AWS request ID (x-amzn-requestid, primary and indexed in CloudTrail) and the Anthropic request ID (request-id, secondary). Use the AWS ID for CloudTrail lookups and the Anthropic ID for Anthropic support tickets.

nodes.label: SDK accessors for the request ID and other headers
nodes.rationale: Python and TypeScript expose the request ID as a _request_id property on top-level response objects; C#, Go, Java and PHP expose it through raw-response accessors and Ruby through middleware. The same mechanisms — with_raw_response in Python, .withResponse() in TypeScript — also read other response headers such as anthropic-organization-id and anthropic-workspace-id.

nodes.label: Long-request guidance: stream or batch
nodes.rationale: For long-running requests, especially those over 10 minutes, use the streaming Messages API or the Message Batches API, and avoid setting a large max_tokens on a non-streaming call.

nodes.label: Networks drop idle connections
nodes.rationale: Some networks drop idle connections after a variable period, which can make a long non-streaming request fail or time out without ever receiving a response from Anthropic. Networks also differ in reliability, so the risk is not uniform.

nodes.label: TCP socket keep-alive
nodes.rationale: A direct API integration can set a TCP socket keep-alive to reduce the impact of idle-connection timeouts on some networks.

nodes.label: Message Batches API polling
nodes.rationale: The Message Batches API manages the risk of network issues by letting a client poll for results instead of requiring an uninterrupted network connection for the life of the request.

nodes.label: SDK 10-minute non-streaming validation
nodes.rationale: The SDKs validate that a non-streaming Messages API request is not expected to exceed a 10-minute timeout, and they also set a socket option for TCP keep-alive.

nodes.label: SDK stream accumulation into a final Message
nodes.rationale: If a caller does not need incremental events, the SDKs can consume the stream and return the complete Message object, identical to what a non-streaming call returns — via get_final_message, finalMessage, MessageAccumulator, Aggregate, or accumulated_message depending on language.

nodes.label: Common validation errors
nodes.rationale: A catalogue of frequently hit request-validation failures, most of which surface as a 400 invalid_request_error whose message names the unsupported parameter or the offending content-block position.

nodes.label: Assistant prefill not supported
nodes.rationale: Claude 4.6 and later models and Claude Mythos Preview do not support prefilling assistant messages; a request whose last message is a prefilled assistant message returns a 400 invalid_request_error saying the conversation must end with a user message.

nodes.label: Structured outputs and output_config.format
nodes.rationale: Where prefill is unavailable, the documented substitutes are structured outputs on models that support them, system prompt instructions, or output_config.format. Structured outputs are also the recommended route when the response itself must be in a fixed JSON shape.

nodes.label: Thinking blocks cannot be modified
nodes.rationale: If the most recent assistant message contains thinking or redacted_thinking blocks that were edited, reordered, filtered out, or reconstructed before being sent back, the request returns a 400 invalid_request_error whose message begins with the offending block's position, such as messages.1.content.0.

nodes.label: Pass every thinking block back unchanged with tool use
nodes.rationale: With tool use, every thinking and redacted_thinking block from the assistant turn must be passed back exactly as received, including blocks whose thinking field is empty. An application that filters content blocks by type before resending must include both thinking and redacted_thinking.

nodes.label: Extended thinking removed in Claude 4.7+
nodes.rationale: Claude 4.7 and later models removed extended thinking, so sending thinking: {"type": "enabled"} returns a 400 invalid_request_error directing the caller to thinking.type.adaptive plus output_config.effort instead.

nodes.label: Adaptive thinking rejected on Claude 4.5 and earlier
nodes.rationale: Models that support only extended thinking — Claude 4.5 and earlier — reject thinking: {"type": "adaptive"} with a 400 invalid_request_error; those models require thinking: {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": N}.

nodes.label: Thinking cannot be disabled on Fable 5.x and Mythos
nodes.rationale: On Claude Fable 5.1, Mythos 5.1, Fable 5, Mythos 5 and Mythos Preview thinking is always on, and thinking: {"type": "disabled"} returns a 400. On the Fable/Mythos 5 and 5.1 models the error message's own suggestion of thinking.type.enabled is ALSO rejected — omitting the thinking parameter entirely is what works, running with adaptive thinking.

nodes.label: display: omitted to hide thinking content
nodes.rationale: To keep thinking content out of responses on models where thinking cannot be turned off, set display: "omitted" on the thinking configuration rather than trying to disable thinking.

nodes.label: Forced tool use unsupported on Fable 5.1 / Mythos 5.1
nodes.rationale: Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 do not support forced tool use: tool_choice of type "any" or "tool" returns a 400 invalid_request_error, including on the token counting endpoint. Only tool_choice "auto" (the default) and "none" are accepted.

nodes.label: Strict tool use with tool_choice auto
nodes.rationale: Where forced tool use is unavailable, the documented substitute is tool_choice auto combined with strict tool use, which keeps tool inputs schema-valid without forcing a tool call.

nodes.label: Thinking block bound to a different conversation
nodes.rationale: On Claude Fable 5.1 a replayed thinking block is accepted only while the system prompt, tools and preceding messages are unchanged. For accounts created on or after 2026-08-31, or when thinking.block_binding.prefix_mismatch_behavior is "error", a block whose earlier history changed is rejected with a 400 naming the first failing block's position; with "drop_block" the API drops the block and the request succeeds. Keeping history append-only avoids it, and a block from a model the target model cannot read is dropped rather than rejected.

nodes.label: thinking-binding-controls-2026-08-01 beta header
nodes.rationale: Sending thinking.block_binding without the thinking-binding-controls-2026-08-01 beta header returns a 400 whose message ends in 'block_binding: Extra inputs are not permitted'; the fix is to add the header or remove the field. The header is what unlocks prefix_mismatch_behavior: "drop_block".

nodes.label: Outbound web identity federation disabled on AWS
nodes.rationale: If every request to Claude Platform on AWS returns 'Outbound web identity federation is disabled for your account', run aws iam enable-outbound-web-identity-federation once per AWS account.

nodes.label: Two types of limits
nodes.rationale: The Claude API imposes two distinct kinds of limits: spend limits, which cap the maximum monthly cost an organization can incur, and rate limits, which cap the number of API requests over a defined period. Both exist to mitigate misuse and manage capacity.

nodes.label: Spend limit
nodes.rationale: A spend limit sets the maximum monthly cost an organization can incur for API usage. Each of the Start, Build and Scale tiers carries a monthly spend cap, viewable and adjustable on the Billing page of the Claude Console.

nodes.label: Rate limit
nodes.rationale: A rate limit sets the maximum number of API requests an organization can make over a defined period of time. Limits are designed to prevent API abuse while minimizing impact on common customer usage patterns, and are enforced at the organization level.

nodes.label: Usage tier
nodes.rationale: Limits are defined by usage tier. Organizations are placed on a tier automatically based on usage history and account standing and can move to a higher tier over time as they use the API; the tier and current limits are visible on the Rate limits page in the Claude Console.

nodes.label: Evaluation tier
nodes.rationale: New organizations and organizations with limited usage history may start in the Evaluation tier, whose limits fall below the standard published limits while account history is established. These starting limits are an anti-fraud and anti-abuse measure and increase automatically as usage history builds.

nodes.label: Token bucket algorithm
nodes.rationale: The API uses the token bucket algorithm for rate limiting: capacity is continuously replenished up to the maximum limit rather than being reset at fixed intervals.

nodes.label: Sub-interval burst enforcement
nodes.rationale: Limits may be enforced over shorter intervals than the stated period: a 60 requests-per-minute limit might be enforced as 1 request per second, so short bursts can exceed the limit and trigger rate limit errors.

nodes.label: Organization-level enforcement
nodes.rationale: The API enforces service-configured limits at the organization level; organizations may additionally set user-configurable limits for their workspaces. Organization-wide limits always apply even if workspace limits add up to more.

nodes.label: Limits are maximums, not guaranteed minimums
nodes.rationale: All documented limits represent maximum allowed usage, not guaranteed minimums. They exist to reduce unintentional overspend and to ensure fair distribution of resources among users.

nodes.label: Monthly spend caps by tier
nodes.rationale: Monthly spend caps by usage tier: Start $500 USD, Build $1,000 USD, Scale $200,000 USD. The cap is the maximum an organization can spend on the API in a calendar month.

nodes.label: Custom tier
nodes.rationale: Organizations on the Custom tier have no monthly spend cap; their limits are arranged with their account team. For rate limits above the Scale tier, customers contact sales through the Rate limits page in the Claude Console.

nodes.label: Reaching the spend cap (HTTP 429)
nodes.rationale: Once the tier spend cap is reached, API usage pauses until 00:00 UTC on the first day of the next month unless a higher limit is requested sooner. While paused, requests return HTTP 429 with error type rate_limit_error and no retry-after header, so retries (including SDK automatic retries) fail until access resumes.

nodes.label: enforced_spend_limit_reached error code
nodes.rationale: On the Messages API, a spend-cap 429 carries error.details.error_code of enforced_spend_limit_reached. This field is how callers distinguish a spend-cap response from an ordinary rate limit response, since both use error type rate_limit_error.

nodes.label: Self-set spend limit
nodes.rationale: An organization can set its own spend limit below its tier cap via Settings > Billing > Spend limits > Adjust limit; the value cannot exceed the current tier cap. When usage reaches a self-set limit, requests return HTTP 400 with error type invalid_request_error and a message beginning 'You have reached your specified API usage limits' (or the workspace variant), stating when access resumes.

nodes.label: Claude Code workspace limit
nodes.rationale: Limits on the Claude Code workspace are checked separately: Claude Code requests over that workspace's limit can instead receive an HTTP 429 that carries a retry-after header, rather than the 400 returned for other self-set spend limits.

nodes.label: Messages API rate limits (RPM/ITPM/OTPM)
nodes.rationale: Messages API rate limits are measured in requests per minute (RPM), input tokens per minute (ITPM) and output tokens per minute (OTPM) for each model class. Exceeding any of them returns a 429 error naming which limit was exceeded, along with a retry-after header indicating how long to wait.

nodes.label: Acceleration limits
nodes.rationale: 429 errors can also result from acceleration limits, which fire when an organization's usage increases sharply. The documented avoidance strategy is to ramp traffic up gradually and maintain consistent usage patterns.

nodes.label: Cache-aware ITPM
nodes.rationale: Unlike providers that use a combined TPM limit covering all cached and uncached input and output tokens, for most Claude models only uncached input tokens count toward ITPM, making the effective limit higher than it appears. ITPM is estimated at the start of each request and adjusted during the request to reflect actual input tokens used.

nodes.label: Which token fields count toward ITPM
nodes.rationale: input_tokens (tokens after the last cache breakpoint) and cache_creation_input_tokens (tokens being written to cache) count toward ITPM; cache_read_input_tokens (tokens read from cache) do not count for most models. Example: with a 2,000,000 ITPM limit and an 80% cache hit rate, roughly 10,000,000 total input tokens per minute can be processed.

nodes.label: Total input tokens formula
nodes.rationale: total_input_tokens = cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens. Because input_tokens only covers tokens after the last cache breakpoint, a 200k-token cached document plus a 50-token question reports input_tokens: 50 even though total input is 200,050 tokens.

nodes.label: Prompt caching as throughput strategy
nodes.rationale: Caching repeated content — system instructions and prompts, large context documents, tool definitions and conversation history — substantially increases actual throughput without raising rate limits, and cached input is billed at the cache read rate, a fraction of the base input price.

nodes.label: Claude Haiku 3.5 cache-read exception
nodes.rationale: Claude Haiku 3.5 (footnote 4 in the tier tables, retired except on Bedrock and Google Cloud) also counts cache_read_input_tokens toward its ITPM rate limit, unlike all other models.

nodes.label: OTPM evaluated in real time
nodes.rationale: OTPM rate limits are evaluated in real time as output tokens are produced, counting only the tokens actually generated. The max_tokens parameter does not factor into OTPM calculations, so there is no rate limit downside to setting a higher max_tokens.

nodes.label: Per-model rate limits
nodes.rationale: Rate limits are applied separately for each model, so different models can be used up to their respective limits simultaneously. Current limits and behavior are visible on the Rate limits page in the Claude Console.

nodes.label: inference_geo shares one limit pool
nodes.rationale: Rate limits are currently shared across all inference_geo values: requests with inference_geo 'us' and inference_geo 'global' draw from the same rate limit pool.

nodes.label: Start tier Messages API limits
nodes.rationale: Start tier: Claude Fable 5.x is 1,000 RPM / 500,000 ITPM / 100,000 OTPM; Opus 5, Opus 4.x, Sonnet 5, Sonnet 4.x and Haiku 4.5 are each 1,000 RPM / 2,000,000 ITPM / 400,000 OTPM; Haiku 3.5 is 1,000 RPM / 100,000 ITPM / 20,000 OTPM.

nodes.label: Build tier Messages API limits
nodes.rationale: Build tier: Claude Fable 5.x is 2,000 RPM / 1,500,000 ITPM / 300,000 OTPM; Opus 5, Opus 4.x, Sonnet 5, Sonnet 4.x and Haiku 4.5 are each 5,000 RPM / 5,000,000 ITPM / 1,000,000 OTPM; Haiku 3.5 is 2,000 RPM / 200,000 ITPM / 40,000 OTPM.

nodes.label: Scale tier Messages API limits
nodes.rationale: Scale tier: Claude Fable 5.x is 4,000 RPM / 4,000,000 ITPM / 800,000 OTPM; Opus 5, Opus 4.x, Sonnet 5, Sonnet 4.x and Haiku 4.5 are each 10,000 RPM / 10,000,000 ITPM / 2,000,000 OTPM; Haiku 3.5 is 4,000 RPM / 400,000 ITPM / 80,000 OTPM.

nodes.label: Fable combined rate limit bucket
nodes.rationale: The Fable rate limit is a total limit applying to combined traffic across Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Fable 5. Claude Mythos 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5 share a separate combined limit on the same terms.

nodes.label: Opus 4.x combined rate limit bucket
nodes.rationale: The Opus 4.x rate limit is a total limit applying to combined traffic across Claude Opus 4.8, 4.7, 4.6 and 4.5. Claude Opus 5 has a separate rate limit and is not part of this combined bucket.

nodes.label: Sonnet 4.x combined rate limit bucket
nodes.rationale: The Sonnet 4.x rate limit is a total limit applying to combined traffic across Sonnet 4.6 and Sonnet 4.5. Claude Sonnet 5 has a separate rate limit and is not part of this combined bucket.

nodes.label: Message Batches API limits
nodes.rationale: The Message Batches API has its own rate limits shared across all models: an RPM limit to all API endpoints, a cap on batch requests in the processing queue, and a cap per batch. Start is 1,000 RPM / 200,000 queued / 100,000 per batch; Build 2,000 / 300,000 / 100,000; Scale 4,000 / 500,000 / 100,000. A batch request counts as queued until it is successfully processed by the model.

nodes.label: Managed Agents rate limits
nodes.rationale: Claude Managed Agents endpoints are rate-limited per organization and separately from the Messages API: create endpoints (agents, sessions, environments) allow 300 requests per minute, and read endpoints (retrieve, list, stream) allow 1,200 requests per minute.

nodes.label: Files API rate limit
nodes.rationale: Files API requests have their own per-organization limit, shared across upload, list, retrieve, download and delete operations and separate from the Messages API limits; the current value is published in the Files API documentation.

nodes.label: Fast mode rate limits
nodes.rationale: Fast mode (research preview) with speed: 'fast' on Claude Opus 5 or Opus 4.8 has dedicated rate limits separate from standard Opus limits; exceeding them returns a 429 with a retry-after header, and the response carries anthropic-fast-* headers reporting fast mode limit status. Fast mode errors on Opus 4.7 and runs at standard speed on Opus 4.6.

nodes.label: Console Usage page rate limit charts
nodes.rationale: The Claude Console Usage page provides two rate limit charts per limit (for example per model): a Rate Limit - Input Tokens chart showing hourly maximum uncached ITPM, the current ITPM limit and the input token cache rate, and a Rate Limit - Output Tokens chart showing hourly maximum OTPM and the current OTPM limit. They are used to see headroom, spot peak use, decide what limits to request and improve caching rates.

nodes.label: Requesting higher limits
nodes.rationale: Higher rate limits or a higher monthly spend cap are requested with the 'Request rate limit increase' control on the Rate limits page in the Claude Console; Anthropic support can also raise limits, and urgent needs go through Anthropic support. Moving to a higher tier restores access after a spend cap pause.

nodes.label: Lower limits for Workspaces
nodes.rationale: Custom spend and rate limits can be set per Workspace to protect an Organization from overuse. Example: with an Organization limit of 40,000 ITPM and 8,000 OTPM, one Workspace might be capped at 30,000 ITPM, leaving the remaining tokens per minute available to other Workspaces.

nodes.label: Workspace limit rules
nodes.rationale: Limits cannot be set on the default Workspace; unset Workspace limits match the Organization limit; Workspace limits are set per limiter type (RPM, ITPM, OTPM); and Organization-wide limits always apply even if Workspace limits sum to more.

nodes.label: Rate Limits API
nodes.rationale: The Rate Limits API reads the configured organization and workspace rate limits programmatically, as an alternative to inspecting the Rate limits page in the Claude Console.

nodes.label: Rate limit response headers
nodes.rationale: API responses include headers reporting the enforced limit, current usage and reset time: anthropic-ratelimit-{requests,tokens,input-tokens,output-tokens}-{limit,remaining,reset}. Remaining token counts are rounded to the nearest thousand and reset times are given in RFC 3339 format.

nodes.label: retry-after header
nodes.rationale: The retry-after header gives the number of seconds to wait before retrying; earlier retries fail. It is not sent with the spend-cap 429, which is what makes that response un-retryable until the cap period ends.

nodes.label: Token headers report the most restrictive limit
nodes.rationale: The anthropic-ratelimit-tokens-* headers display values for the most restrictive limit currently in effect — for example the Workspace per-minute token limit if that is what was exceeded; where Workspace limits do not apply they return total tokens remaining (input plus output). The anthropic-workspace-id response header identifies which Workspace a request counted against.

nodes.label: Priority Tier headers
nodes.rationale: Priority Tier customers additionally receive anthropic-priority-input-tokens-{limit,remaining,reset} and anthropic-priority-output-tokens-{limit,remaining,reset} headers, reporting the Priority Tier token allowance, remaining tokens rounded to the nearest thousand, and RFC 3339 replenishment time.

nodes.label: Claude Platform on AWS deviations
nodes.rationale: The documented rate limits apply to Claude Platform on AWS, but billing runs through AWS Marketplace rather than Anthropic credit purchases, organizations are placed on the Start tier and do not move between usage tiers automatically, the 'Request rate limit increase' flow is unavailable (higher limits go through an account representative or Anthropic support), and per-workspace rate limit configuration and fast mode are not available. The same monthly spend caps apply and requests stop at the cap in the same way.

nodes.label: Anthropic service tiers
nodes.rationale: Anthropic offers three service tiers — Priority, Standard, and Batch — which let an application balance availability, performance, and predictable costs against its needs.

nodes.label: Priority Tier
nodes.rationale: Priority Tier is available only to organizations with an existing capacity commitment. The API prioritizes requests in this tier over all other requests, with prioritized computational resources.

nodes.label: Standard Tier
nodes.rationale: Standard is the default service tier for all API requests and the default tier for both piloting and scaling everyday use cases. The API prioritizes standard requests alongside all other requests with best-effort availability.

nodes.label: Batch tier
nodes.rationale: Batch is the tier best suited to asynchronous workflows that can wait, or that benefit from running outside an organization's normal capacity.

nodes.label: Priority Tier no longer purchasable
nodes.rationale: Priority Tier capacity commitments are no longer available for purchase. Organizations with an existing commitment may continue using Priority Tier through their contract end date; anyone needing guaranteed capacity is directed to contact sales.

nodes.label: "Server overloaded" errors
nodes.rationale: "Server overloaded" HTTP errors are the failure mode that peak-time contention produces; prioritizing a request above all others is what minimizes them.

nodes.label: How requests get assigned tiers
nodes.rationale: Anthropic assigns a request to Priority Tier when the organization has sufficient Priority Tier capacity in both input tokens per minute and output tokens per minute. Otherwise the request proceeds at standard tier.

nodes.label: Input-token capacity burndown
nodes.rationale: Input usage is counted against Priority Tier capacity at type-specific rates: all ordinary input tokens draw 1 token per token, while cache reads, cache writes, and US-only inference draw at their own multipliers.

nodes.label: Output-token capacity burndown
nodes.rationale: Output usage draws 1 token per token against Priority Tier capacity, except for US-only inference on Claude 4.6 and later models, which draws 1.1 tokens per token.

nodes.label: Cache-read burndown rate (0.1x)
nodes.rationale: Cache reads count as 0.1 tokens per token read from the cache when drawing down Priority Tier input capacity.
