nodes.label: Cache-write burndown rates (1.25x / 2.00x)
nodes.rationale: Cache writes count as 1.25 tokens per token for a 5 minute TTL, and 2.00 tokens per token for a 1 hour TTL, against Priority Tier input capacity.

nodes.label: US-only inference burndown (1.1x)
nodes.rationale: For US-only inference requests (`inference_geo: "us"`) on Claude 4.6 and later models, both input and output tokens count as 1.1 tokens per token against Priority Tier capacity.

nodes.label: Burndown rates reflect relative pricing
nodes.rationale: The burndown rates are a restatement of the relative pricing of each token type: US-only inference is priced at 1.1x on Claude 4.6 and later models, so each such token draws down 1.1 tokens of Priority Tier capacity.

nodes.label: Priority requests also draw regular rate limits
nodes.rationale: A request assigned to Priority Tier pulls from both Priority Tier capacity and the regular rate limits; if servicing it would exceed the rate limits, the request is declined.

nodes.label: Automatic fallback to standard tier
nodes.rationale: Requests beyond an organization's committed capacity automatically fall back to standard tier rather than failing; the same applies whenever the Priority Tier conditions are not met.

nodes.label: `service_tier` request parameter
nodes.rationale: The `service_tier` parameter on a Messages request controls which service tiers may be used for that request; it is settable from cURL, the `ant` CLI, and every official SDK (Python, TypeScript, C#, Go, Java, PHP, Ruby).

nodes.label: `service_tier: "auto"`
nodes.rationale: `"auto"` is the default value of `service_tier`: it uses Priority Tier capacity if available and falls back to the organization's other capacity if not.

nodes.label: `service_tier: "standard_only"`
nodes.rationale: `"standard_only"` restricts a request to standard tier capacity only — useful when a caller deliberately does not want to spend Priority Tier capacity on it.

nodes.label: `usage.service_tier` response field
nodes.rationale: The response `usage` object includes a `service_tier` field (e.g. `"priority"`) alongside the token counts, which is how a caller determines which service tier was actually assigned to the request.

nodes.label: `anthropic-priority-*` response headers
nodes.rationale: Requesting `service_tier="auto"` against a model with a Priority Tier commitment returns headers giving the priority input/output token limit, remaining amount, and reset time; the mere presence of these headers detects that a request was eligible for Priority Tier even when it was over the limit.

nodes.label: Components of a Priority Tier commitment
nodes.rationale: A Priority Tier commitment consists of a number of input tokens per minute, a number of output tokens per minute, a commitment duration of 1, 3, 6, or 12 months, and a specific model version.

nodes.label: 99.5% uptime target
nodes.rationale: Priority Tier targets 99.5% uptime with prioritized computational resources — the availability guarantee an existing commitment buys.

nodes.label: Models excluded from Priority Tier
nodes.rationale: Priority Tier is supported on all available Claude models except Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Mythos 5, Claude Mythos Preview, Claude Opus 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.

nodes.label: Admin deployment decision map
nodes.rationale: The page is an ordered decision map for administrators deploying Claude Code across an organization: choose an API provider, decide how settings reach devices, decide what to enforce, set up usage visibility, and review data handling. Each decision links to the section below and to its reference page. SSO, SCIM provisioning and seat assignment are out of scope here — they are configured at the Claude account level.

nodes.label: Managed settings precedence
nodes.rationale: Claude Code enforces organization policy through managed settings that take precedence over local developer configuration, apart from a few security-sensitive exceptions. The settings control which tools, commands, servers and network destinations Claude can reach.

nodes.label: Choose your API provider
nodes.rationale: Claude Code connects to Claude through one of several API providers. The choice affects billing, authentication, which compliance posture the organization inherits, and which Claude Code features developers can use.

nodes.label: Claude for Teams / Enterprise provider
nodes.rationale: Choose Claude for Teams / Enterprise when you want Claude Code and claude.ai under one per-seat subscription with no infrastructure to run. The page names this the default recommendation.

nodes.label: Claude Console provider
nodes.rationale: Choose Claude Console when the organization is API-first or wants pay-as-you-go billing. Console organizations get a different analytics and spend-control surface than Teams / Enterprise plans.

nodes.label: Amazon Bedrock provider
nodes.rationale: Choose Amazon Bedrock when you want to inherit existing AWS compliance controls and billing. Bedrock deployments expose spend through AWS Cost Explorer and do not receive organization-level model controls.

nodes.label: Google Cloud's Agent Platform provider
nodes.rationale: Choose Google Cloud's Agent Platform when you want to inherit existing GCP compliance controls and billing. Spend is exposed through GCP Billing rather than Anthropic's own dashboards.

nodes.label: Microsoft Foundry provider
nodes.rationale: Choose Microsoft Foundry when you want to inherit existing Azure compliance controls and billing. Spend is exposed through Azure Cost Management.

nodes.label: Features requiring a claude.ai account
nodes.rationale: Claude Code on the web, Routines, Code Review, Remote Control and the Chrome extension are not available through Console API keys or cloud-provider credentials alone. Organizations deploying on Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Microsoft Foundry must plan whether developers also need Claude for Teams or Enterprise seats.

nodes.label: Proxy and firewall requirements
nodes.rationale: The proxy and firewall requirements documented in Network configuration apply regardless of which API provider the organization chooses.

nodes.label: LLM gateway
nodes.rationale: An LLM gateway gives a single endpoint in front of multiple providers and centralized request logging. It is the alternative to a Claude apps gateway when you need to route traffic by data sensitivity or record request-level logs.

nodes.label: Claude apps gateway
nodes.rationale: A self-hosted Claude apps gateway serves three admin jobs at once: it delivers server-managed settings for gateway sign-ins on cloud-provider deployments, it enforces per-user spend limits, and it records a per-request audit log carrying IdP identity.

nodes.label: Decide how settings reach devices
nodes.rationale: Managed settings define organization policy, and Claude Code checks four delivery sources in priority order: server-managed (highest), plist/registry policy, file-based managed settings, then the Windows user registry (lowest). Policy can be delivered from the Claude admin console, an MDM system, or a file on disk.

nodes.label: Server-managed settings
nodes.rationale: Server-managed settings are delivered from the claude.ai admin console, or from a self-hosted Claude apps gateway for gateway sign-ins. They are the highest-priority managed source, work on all platforms, and need no endpoint infrastructure to deploy; delivery through the admin console requires a Claude for Teams or Enterprise plan.

nodes.label: Startup fetch and hourly refresh
nodes.rationale: Claude Code fetches server-managed settings at startup and refreshes them hourly during the session, so policy changes reach running sessions without a restart.

nodes.label: plist / HKLM registry policy
nodes.rationale: The high-priority OS-level channel is the macOS `com.anthropic.claudecode` plist and the Windows `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\ClaudeCode` registry key. It works with any provider and resists tampering because writing it requires admin privileges.

nodes.label: File-based managed settings
nodes.rationale: The medium-priority channel is a `managed-settings.json` on disk: `/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/` on macOS, `/etc/claude-code/` on Linux and WSL, and `C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\` on Windows. It works on all platforms.

nodes.label: Windows user registry (HKCU)
nodes.rationale: `HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\ClaudeCode` is the lowest-priority managed source and Windows-only. Because it is writable without elevation, the page says to treat it as a convenience default rather than an enforcement channel.

nodes.label: Admin-privilege tamper resistance
nodes.rationale: A managed source is only an enforcement channel if a developer cannot rewrite it. Requiring administrator privileges to write is what separates the plist / HKLM sources (and the Program Files file) from the user-writable HKCU key.

nodes.label: Mixed-provider delivery fallback
nodes.rationale: If an organization mixes providers, configure server-managed settings for claude.ai users plus a file-based or plist/registry fallback so users on other providers still receive managed policy. Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry deployments can otherwise get remote delivery only by running a Claude apps gateway.

nodes.label: Array merge versus value replacement
nodes.rationale: Array settings such as `permissions.allow` and `permissions.deny` merge entries from all sources, so developers can extend managed lists but never remove from them. For `fallbackModel`, `availableModels` and `modelPicker` the managed value replaces lower layers instead of merging.

nodes.label: WSL sessions in Claude Code Desktop
nodes.rationale: On Windows, Claude Code Desktop can run sessions inside a WSL 2 distribution. The Claude Code process runs inside the distribution, so it resolves managed settings through the WSL discovery path — by default only the Linux file path at `/etc/claude-code` — and Windows-only sources do not reach it.

nodes.label: disableWslSessions policy value
nodes.rationale: Claude Desktop turns WSL sessions off by default on devices it detects as organization-managed, for example when `C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json` exists. To re-enable them, set `disableWslSessions` under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Claude` to the REG_SZ string `false` or REG_DWORD `0` (Claude Desktop v1.19367.0 or later); an HKCU value does not work, and Desktop reads the policy each time a session starts so no app restart is needed.

nodes.label: wslInheritsWindowsSettings
nodes.rationale: Setting `wslInheritsWindowsSettings: true` in one of the admin-only Windows sources — the HKLM registry or the `C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode` file — extends Windows managed policy to WSL sessions on the same machine, which otherwise read only `/etc/claude-code`.

nodes.label: wslPolicyGate denial log
nodes.rationale: When a device still refuses WSL sessions, Help > Troubleshooting > Show Logs in Explorer saves a copy of the log folder to Downloads; searching `main.log` for `[wslPolicyGate] denying WSL session` names the reason in parentheses, such as `(cli-file-present)`. With the .exe installer the live file is at `%APPDATA%\Claude\logs\main.log`.

nodes.label: WSL endpoint-detection blind spot
nodes.rationale: Processes inside the WSL 2 utility VM are not visible to Windows-side endpoint detection sensors, so observing in-distro process and file activity requires a Linux sensor from the EDR vendor running inside the distribution. Claude Code's OpenTelemetry tool-execution telemetry is emitted identically for WSL and native sessions.

nodes.label: Decide what to enforce
nodes.rationale: Managed settings can lock down tools, sandbox execution, restrict MCP servers and plugin sources, and control which hooks run. The page enumerates each control surface together with the setting keys that drive it.

nodes.label: Permission rules
nodes.rationale: `permissions.allow` and `permissions.deny` allow, ask, or deny specific tools and commands. They operate at the tool layer, not the OS layer.

nodes.label: Permission lockdown
nodes.rationale: `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly` makes only managed permission rules apply, and `permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode` disables `--dangerously-skip-permissions`.

nodes.label: Starting permission mode
nodes.rationale: `permissions.defaultMode` chooses the permission mode developers' terminal sessions start in instead of the built-in default, and `permissions.disableAutoMode` removes auto mode. The VS Code extension reads a `defaultMode` only on Pro, Max and Team plans.

nodes.label: Sandboxing
nodes.rationale: `sandbox.enabled` and `sandbox.network.allowedDomains` provide OS-level filesystem and network isolation with domain allowlists — enforcement below the tool layer, so it binds arbitrary child processes as well as Claude's own tools.

nodes.label: Managed policy CLAUDE.md
nodes.rationale: A CLAUDE.md deployed at the managed policy path carries org-wide instructions that load in every session and cannot be excluded by developers.

nodes.label: MCP server control
nodes.rationale: `allowedMcpServers`, `deniedMcpServers`, `allowManagedMcpServersOnly`, or a deployed `managed-mcp.json` file restrict which MCP servers users can add or connect to, or deploy a fixed set.

nodes.label: Plugin marketplace control
nodes.rationale: `strictKnownMarketplaces`, `blockedMarketplaces`, `disableSideloadFlags`, `disableCommandPluginSources` and `pluginSuggestionMarketplaces` restrict which marketplace sources users can add and install from, reject the CLI flags that sideload plugins/agents/MCP servers for a single run, block `command` plugin sources, and allowlist which marketplaces' plugins can be suggested.

nodes.label: Customization lockdown
nodes.rationale: `strictPluginOnlyCustomization` blocks skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers from user and project sources, so they can only arrive through plugins or managed settings.

nodes.label: Hook restrictions
nodes.rationale: `allowManagedHooksOnly` restricts which hooks run and `allowedHttpHookUrls` restricts HTTP hook URLs; the settings reference lists the full effect list of what runs under `allowManagedHooksOnly`.

nodes.label: Login enforcement
nodes.rationale: `forceLoginMethod` and `forceLoginOrgUUID` restrict login to a specific method or Anthropic organization across the VS Code extension, Agent SDK, `claude setup-token` and `/install-github-app`; the terminal login screen pre-selects the method without enforcing it. Organization verification applies to claude.ai logins only, not Console logins or gateway sign-in, and before v2.1.212 only terminal logins applied either key. When set, sessions authenticated by `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` or `apiKeyHelper` are blocked at startup, while cloud-provider sessions are unaffected.

nodes.label: Disable agent view
nodes.rationale: `disableAgentView` turns off `claude agents`, `--bg`, `/background`, and the on-demand background-session supervisor.

nodes.label: Corporate launcher (processWrapper)
nodes.rationale: `processWrapper` prefixes the background-agent supervisor, its workers, and the other covered background processes with a required corporate launcher — offered as the alternative to turning agent view off entirely.

nodes.label: availableModels model restrictions
nodes.rationale: `availableModels` filters which models appear in the picker; adding `enforceAvailableModels` also constrains the auto-selected default model. This settings-based path is the one that works on cloud providers, alongside the `model` key in managed settings for a default.

nodes.label: minimumVersion version floor
nodes.rationale: `minimumVersion` prevents auto-update from installing below an org-wide minimum. It blocks downgrades only.

nodes.label: Required version range
nodes.rationale: `requiredMinimumVersion` and `requiredMaximumVersion` make Claude Code refuse to start at all when the running version falls outside an org-approved range — stronger than `minimumVersion`, which only blocks downgrades.

nodes.label: Telemetry opt-out
nodes.rationale: Setting `env` with `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC` to `1` turns off Anthropic-bound usage metrics, error reports and surveys on every device; the data-usage page lists per-category variables.

nodes.label: Organization-level model controls
nodes.rationale: Organizations whose members authenticate through claude.ai or the Anthropic API can govern models without deploying settings: organization model restrictions disable individual models, an organization default model sets which model new sessions start on, and organization effort limits cap effort per role. All three require a Claude Enterprise plan, restrictions and effort limits are enforced server-side, enforcement is available only to a limited set of organizations, and none of them reach Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, or Claude Platform on AWS.

nodes.label: Cloud environments admin surface
nodes.rationale: Claude Code on the web has its own admin surface: on the Cloud environments page in admin settings, Owners create organization-shared environments that set the network access level, environment variables and setup script for members' cloud sessions, and choose the organization's default environment separately.

nodes.label: Tool-layer denial does not stop Bash egress
nodes.rationale: Permission rules and sandboxing cover different layers: denying WebFetch blocks Claude's fetch tool, but if Bash is allowed, `curl` and `wget` can still reach any URL. That gap is the reason a network allowlist enforced at the OS level is needed.

nodes.label: Set up usage visibility
nodes.rationale: Monitoring is chosen by what the organization needs to report on. Dashboards, APIs and spend controls differ between Claude for Teams / Enterprise plans and Claude Console organizations, so the availability column must be checked before planning reporting around a capability.

nodes.label: OpenTelemetry usage monitoring
nodes.rationale: Usage monitoring is an OpenTelemetry export of sessions, tools and tokens, and it is the one visibility capability available on all providers.

nodes.label: Analytics dashboard
nodes.rationale: The analytics dashboard gives adoption and contribution metrics with a leaderboard on Teams / Enterprise (claude.ai/analytics) and per-user usage and spend metrics on Console (platform.claude.com/claude-code).

nodes.label: Programmatic usage reporting APIs
nodes.rationale: Per-user usage and cost data is available over an API: the Enterprise Analytics API for Enterprise plans and the Claude Code Analytics API for Console organizations.

nodes.label: Spend and rate controls
nodes.rationale: Spend limits and rate limits live in admin settings for Teams / Enterprise and in workspace limits for Console; on third-party clouds they come from cloud budget controls or from a Claude apps gateway with per-user spend limits.

nodes.label: Teams / Enterprise spend report
nodes.rationale: On Teams and Enterprise, per-user usage and spend numbers come from the spend report in the organization's analytics settings, not from the analytics dashboard. Cloud providers instead expose spend through AWS Cost Explorer, GCP Billing or Azure Cost Management.

nodes.label: Review data handling
nodes.rationale: The data-handling decision covers retention and compliance posture, which is determined by the chosen API provider. It spans the data usage policy, Zero Data Retention, and the security architecture.

nodes.label: No model training on customer code
nodes.rationale: On Team, Enterprise, Claude API and cloud provider plans, Anthropic does not train models on the organization's code or prompts.

nodes.label: Data usage policy
nodes.rationale: The data usage reference states what Anthropic collects, how long it is retained, and what is never used for training.

nodes.label: Zero Data Retention (ZDR)
nodes.rationale: Zero Data Retention means nothing is stored after the request completes. It is available to qualified accounts on Claude for Enterprise.

nodes.label: Security architecture
nodes.rationale: The Security reference covers the network model, encryption, authentication and audit trail, and carries the threat model the enforcement controls on this page defend against.

nodes.label: Request-level audit logging
nodes.rationale: Request-level audit logging, or routing traffic by data sensitivity, requires placing a gateway between developers and the provider — a self-hosted Claude apps gateway records a per-request audit log carrying IdP identity, or another LLM gateway can be used.

nodes.label: Verify and onboard
nodes.rationale: After configuring managed settings, an administrator verifies enforcement on a developer machine and then hands developers onboarding and troubleshooting resources.

nodes.label: /status Setting sources line
nodes.rationale: Running `/status` inside Claude Code shows a `Setting sources` line reading `Enterprise managed settings` followed by the source that won in parentheses. It names only the managed source Claude Code selected, so a session receiving server-managed keys reports `(remote)` and cannot confirm whether a Windows flag arrived; `(HKLM)` confirms a registry deployment, and `(file)` confirms a Windows file deployment only when the distribution has no managed file of its own.

nodes.label: Developer onboarding resources
nodes.rationale: Administrators share the Quickstart (first-session walkthrough), Common workflows (everyday patterns such as code review, refactoring and debugging), and the Anthropic Academy courses Claude 101 and Claude Code in Action.

nodes.label: Login troubleshooting fixes
nodes.rationale: The most common login fixes are: run `/logout` then `/login` to switch accounts, run `claude update` if the enterprise auth option is missing, and restart the terminal after updating.

nodes.label: "Not added to your organization yet" seat error
nodes.rationale: If a developer sees "You haven't been added to your organization yet," their seat does not include Claude Code access and must be updated in the admin console — a seat problem, not a login problem.

nodes.label: Advisor tool
nodes.rationale: The advisor tool lets Claude consult a second, typically stronger model at key moments during a task — before committing to an approach, when stuck on a recurring error, or before declaring a task complete. The advisor returns guidance that Claude applies before continuing. It is experimental, and behavior, pricing and availability may change.

nodes.label: Server-side execution as a server tool
nodes.rationale: The advisor runs server-side on Anthropic's infrastructure as a server tool, available to both subscription and API-billed accounts. The user chooses which model acts as the advisor, and Claude decides when to call it.

nodes.label: Anthropic API only
nodes.rationale: The advisor requires the Anthropic API and is not available on Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry, because it is a server-executed tool.

nodes.label: LLM gateway availability is conditional
nodes.rationale: Through an LLM gateway configured with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, advisor availability depends on whether the gateway forwards the request intact to the Anthropic API.

nodes.label: Advisor receives the full conversation
nodes.rationale: The advisor always receives the full conversation, including every tool call and result. There is no partial or filtered view; the advisor reads the whole transcript on each consultation.

nodes.label: Model-driven consultation timing
nodes.rationale: Claude decides when to call the advisor: it tends to consult before committing to an approach, when an error keeps recurring, and before declaring a task done, but the timing is model-driven rather than rule-based. A user can request a consultation in the prompt, e.g. 'consult the advisor before you continue'.

nodes.label: No setting caps or forces advisor calls
nodes.rationale: There is no setting to cap or force advisor calls. To make Claude consult more or less often during a task, the only lever is saying so in the instructions.

nodes.label: Fit: long multi-step tasks
nodes.rationale: The advisor fits long, multi-step tasks where most turns are routine but plan quality determines the outcome — large refactors, debugging sessions where an error keeps recurring, and tasks to be independently checked before Claude declares them done.

nodes.label: Poor fit: short tasks and uniformly hard work
nodes.rationale: The advisor adds less value on short tasks where there is little to plan, or on work where every turn needs the strongest model. For those, switching the main model is the recommended alternative.

nodes.label: /advisor command
nodes.rationale: Running /advisor without arguments opens a picker of available advisor models; passing a model directly (e.g. `/advisor opus`) sets it. The command confirms with 'Advisor set to' followed by the model name.

nodes.label: advisorModel setting
nodes.rationale: The `advisorModel` key in the settings file (e.g. {"advisorModel": "opus"}) configures a persistent default advisor without opening a session. A selection made via /advisor is saved here and persists across sessions.

nodes.label: --advisor launch flag
nodes.rationale: `claude --advisor opus` sets the advisor for a single session without changing the saved setting; Claude Code uses the flag instead of the advisorModel setting for that session. The flag is not listed in `claude --help`.

nodes.label: Launch-time error conditions for --advisor
nodes.rationale: Claude Code exits with an error at launch if the session's main model doesn't support the advisor, the requested model (such as Haiku) can't act as an advisor, the organization's availableModels allowlist excludes it, or Fable was requested while the account still requires usage-credits consent.

nodes.label: Background sessions start without the advisor
nodes.rationale: If a background session is started with --advisor and any launch error condition applies, Claude Code starts the session without the advisor instead of exiting.

nodes.label: Advisor must be at least as capable
nodes.rationale: The governing rule for model pairing: the advisor must be at least as capable as the main model. Models ranked equally capable (e.g. Sonnet 5 and Opus 4.6) may advise each other.

nodes.label: Accepted main-model / advisor pairings
nodes.rationale: Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.6 accept Fable/Opus/Sonnet; Sonnet 5 and Opus 4.6 accept Fable/Opus/Sonnet 5 (a Sonnet 4.6 advisor is rejected); Opus 4.7 or later accepts Fable and Opus 4.7 or later only; Fable 5.1 or Fable 5 accept Fable 5.1 or the same Fable version, rejecting any Opus or Sonnet advisor and rejecting a Fable 5 advisor for a Fable 5.1 main.

nodes.label: Haiku can call but not act as advisor
nodes.rationale: Haiku 4.5 can call the advisor but cannot act as one; requesting Haiku as the advisor is one of the launch-time error conditions.

nodes.label: Model aliases resolve to built-in defaults
nodes.rationale: The advisor can be set as `fable`, `opus`, or `sonnet`; these aliases resolve to Claude Code's built-in default version for each model family and advance with new Claude Code releases. A full model ID such as `claude-opus-5` can be passed instead.

nodes.label: Subagents inherit the advisor
nodes.rationale: Subagents inherit the configured advisor and apply the same pairing check against their own model. A subagent whose own model satisfies the pairing may still use the advisor even when the main model's requests do not carry it.

nodes.label: Pre-request pairing validation
nodes.rationale: Claude Code validates the pairing before sending a request. If the advisor is less capable than the main model, or either model is unrecognized, the advisor is not attached to the main model's requests; the /advisor output and a notification report this.

nodes.label: Fable as the advisor
nodes.rationale: Fable is an accepted advisor for every listed main model and is the only advisor family a Fable main model accepts. On some plans Fable usage bills to usage credits, and Fable as the advisor bills the same way.

nodes.label: One-time Fable usage-credits consent
nodes.rationale: Where an account requires the one-time consent to bill Fable usage to usage credits, Claude Code does not save or apply Fable as the advisor until it is accepted: /advisor fable points to /model fable, `claude --advisor fable` exits at launch, a background session starts without the advisor, and an already-saved Fable advisorModel sends requests without the advisor. Consent is granted by running /model fable and choosing to continue on Fable.

nodes.label: Fable advisor version requirements
nodes.rationale: Fable 5.1 requires Claude Code v2.1.255 or later and Fable 5 requires v2.1.170 or later, plus Fable access.

nodes.label: availableModels organization allowlist
nodes.rationale: Claude Code does not invoke a saved advisor that the organization's availableModels allowlist excludes; the remedy is to pick an allowed model with /advisor. A launch with --advisor naming an excluded model exits with an error.

nodes.label: Common cost/capability pairings
nodes.rationale: Illustrative pairings: Sonnet main + Opus advisor (escalate planning and completion checks); Sonnet main + Fable advisor (Fable only at decision points); Haiku main + Opus advisor (lowest-cost main with strong planning); Opus main + Opus advisor (an independent second Opus for high-stakes work); Fable main + Fable advisor (highest capability); Sonnet main + Sonnet advisor (a lower-cost second opinion).

nodes.label: Advising transcript line: Reviewed or Declined
nodes.rationale: During a call the transcript shows an `Advising` line with the advisor model name. On return it reports either Reviewed (the advisor reviewed the conversation; press Ctrl+O to read readable guidance) or Declined ('Advisor declined to advise on this request'; Ctrl+O shows any reason given).

nodes.label: Claude surfaces conflicts with advisor guidance
nodes.rationale: Claude generally follows the advisor's guidance but adapts when its own evidence contradicts a specific claim: if a recommended step fails when tried, or file contents contradict the advice, Claude surfaces the conflict rather than following the guidance unconditionally.

nodes.label: Advisor token cost
nodes.rationale: Each advisor call has the advisor model read the conversation, consuming tokens at the advisor model's rates on top of main-model usage. With API billing you pay the advisor's input and output rates; on subscription plans advisor usage counts toward plan usage limits, except a Fable advisor which bills to usage credits on plans where Fable usage does.

nodes.label: Cheaper than running the stronger model throughout
nodes.rationale: Because Claude calls the advisor at decision points rather than on every turn, pairing a faster main model with a stronger advisor typically costs less than running the stronger model throughout.

nodes.label: Advisor usage in /usage session totals
nodes.rationale: Advisor usage counts toward the session totals shown by /usage; how advisor tokens are reported in API responses is covered by the Claude API advisor-tool usage-and-billing documentation.

nodes.label: Toggling the advisor preserves the prompt cache
nodes.rationale: Enabling or disabling the advisor mid-session does not invalidate the main model's prompt cache. Unlike changing model or effort level, toggling /advisor keeps the cached prefix intact, and the advisor's returned guidance is cached as part of the transcript on later turns.

nodes.label: The advisor's own read is never cached
nodes.rationale: The advisor model's own read of the conversation is not cached: each advisor call processes the full transcript anew, with no reuse between calls.

nodes.label: Advisor requirements set
nodes.rationale: The advisor tool requires all three of: Anthropic API only (it is a server-executed tool), a supported main model, and feature-flag fetching being enabled. All three must hold; none is sufficient alone.

nodes.label: Supported main models
nodes.rationale: The advisor requires a supported main model: Fable, Opus 4.6 or later, Sonnet 4.6 or later, or Haiku 4.5. Claude Code still saves an advisor the current main model doesn't support, and that advisor activates after switching to a compatible main model with /model.

nodes.label: Feature-flag fetching requirement
nodes.rationale: Claude Code turns the advisor on through a feature flag it fetches from Anthropic. In a session where a variable that turns flag fetching off is set — such as DISABLE_TELEMETRY — the advisor stays off.

nodes.label: /advisor off
nodes.rationale: Running `/advisor off`, or choosing 'No advisor' in the /advisor picker, stops using the advisor and clears the saved advisorModel.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ADVISOR_TOOL
nodes.rationale: Setting CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ADVISOR_TOOL=1 disables the advisor tool entirely: the /advisor command becomes unavailable, any configured advisorModel is ignored, and the --advisor flag is accepted but has no effect.

nodes.label: Comparison of ways to combine model strengths
nodes.rationale: The advisor is one of several ways to combine model strengths; the choice is made on WHEN the stronger model should run and HOW that run starts. The alternatives compared are opusplan, subagents with `model` set, and /model.

nodes.label: opusplan as an alternative
nodes.rationale: With opusplan the stronger model runs during plan mode when allowed by availableModels, then switches to Sonnet for execution; it starts when the user enters plan mode, rather than being called mid-task by Claude.

nodes.label: Subagents with model set as an alternative
nodes.rationale: A subagent with `model` set runs the stronger model for the entire delegated subtask, and starts when Claude delegates or the user invokes the subagent — a whole-subtask scope rather than the advisor's decision-point scope.

nodes.label: /model switch as an alternative
nodes.rationale: Switching with /model makes the stronger model run from the next request onward, started by the user rather than by Claude — the recommended option when every turn needs the strongest model.

nodes.label: Agent SDK hooks
nodes.rationale: Hooks are callback functions that run your code in response to agent events, such as a tool being called, a session starting, or execution stopping. They let you intercept and customize agent behavior at key execution points.

nodes.label: What hooks let you do
nodes.rationale: The doc enumerates five things hooks enable: blocking dangerous operations, logging and auditing tool calls, transforming inputs and outputs, requiring human approval for sensitive actions, and tracking session lifecycle.

nodes.label: Block dangerous operations
nodes.rationale: Hooks can block dangerous operations before they execute, such as destructive shell commands or unauthorized file access. The table lists 'block dangerous shell commands' as the example use case for PreToolUse.

nodes.label: Log and audit tool calls
nodes.rationale: Hooks can log and audit every tool call for compliance, debugging, or analytics; the PostToolUse row names 'log all file changes to audit trail' as its example use case.

nodes.label: Transform inputs and outputs
nodes.rationale: Hooks can transform inputs and outputs to sanitize data, inject credentials, or redirect file paths before an operation runs or before Claude sees a result.

nodes.label: Require human approval
nodes.rationale: Hooks can require human approval for sensitive actions such as database writes or API calls, by returning a permission decision that asks the user rather than allowing outright.

nodes.label: Track session lifecycle
nodes.rationale: Hooks can track session lifecycle to manage state, clean up resources, or send notifications — for example saving session state before exit or cleaning up temporary resources at session end.

nodes.label: How hooks work (five-step flow)
nodes.rationale: Hook execution proceeds in five ordered stages: an event fires, the SDK collects registered hooks for that event, matchers filter which hooks run, the matching callbacks execute, and each callback returns a decision object.

nodes.label: Step 1: an event fires
nodes.rationale: Something happens during agent execution and the SDK fires an event: a tool is about to be called (PreToolUse), a tool returned a result (PostToolUse), a subagent started or stopped, the agent is idle, or execution finished.

nodes.label: Step 2: the SDK collects registered hooks
nodes.rationale: The SDK checks for hooks registered for that event type, including callback hooks passed in options.hooks and shell command hooks from settings files when the corresponding settingSources / setting_sources entry is enabled, which it is for default query() options.

nodes.label: Step 3: matchers filter which hooks run
nodes.rationale: If a hook has a matcher pattern (like "Write|Edit"), the SDK tests it against the event's target, for example the tool name. Hooks without a matcher run for every event of that type.

nodes.label: Step 4: callback functions execute
nodes.rationale: Each matching hook's callback function receives input about what is happening: the tool name, its arguments, the session ID, and other event-specific details.

nodes.label: Step 5: your callback returns a decision
nodes.rationale: After performing any operations (logging, API calls, validation), the callback returns an output object telling the agent what to do: allow the operation, block it, modify the input, or inject context into the conversation.

nodes.label: settingSources / setting_sources
nodes.rationale: settingSources (TypeScript) / setting_sources (Python) controls whether shell command hooks defined in settings files such as .claude/settings.json are loaded into an SDK session; setting it to ["project"] loads .claude/settings.json including its hooks.

nodes.label: The hooks option shape
nodes.rationale: Hooks are configured in the hooks field of agent options (ClaudeAgentOptions in Python, the options object in TypeScript): a dictionary/object whose keys are hook event names and whose values are arrays of matchers, each holding an optional filter pattern and the callback functions.

nodes.label: matcher field
nodes.rationale: matcher is an optional string pattern matched against the event's filter field, following the same rules as matchers in settings files. For tool hooks it is the tool name (Bash, Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep, WebFetch, Agent and others); for other events it matches a different field, such as the notification type.

nodes.label: Matchers match names, not arguments
nodes.rationale: Matchers only match tool names, not file paths or other arguments. To filter by file path you must inspect tool_input.file_path inside the hook body and return {} early for paths you do not care about.

nodes.label: MCP tool matcher pattern
nodes.rationale: MCP tools are named mcp__<server>__<action>, where <server> is the key used in the mcpServers configuration, so a regex matcher of ^mcp__ targets every MCP tool at once.

nodes.label: Omitting the matcher
nodes.rationale: Omitting the matcher runs the callbacks for every occurrence of the event — useful on purpose for logging every tool call, but an over-broad empty matcher is also a listed cause of a tool being blocked unexpectedly.

nodes.label: HookMatcher timeout field
nodes.rationale: The timeout field on a HookMatcher sets the callback's timeout in seconds. When omitted, Claude Code applies the event's default timeout, and SDK callbacks follow the command hook defaults.

nodes.label: Hook callback arguments
nodes.rationale: Every hook callback receives exactly three arguments: the typed input data object, the tool use ID, and a context argument.

nodes.label: Hook input data
nodes.rationale: The first callback argument is a typed object of event details whose shape differs per hook type — PreToolUseHookInput carries tool_name and tool_input, NotificationHookInput carries message. In TypeScript it is typed as the base HookInput and usually cast to the specific type.

nodes.label: Shared input fields
nodes.rationale: All hook inputs share three fields regardless of event type: session_id, cwd, and hook_event_name.

nodes.label: agent_id and agent_type
nodes.rationale: agent_id and agent_type are populated when a hook fires inside a subagent. In TypeScript they sit on the base hook input and are available to all hook types; in Python they are optional on PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure and PermissionRequest, and required on SubagentStart and SubagentStop.

nodes.label: Tool use ID argument
nodes.rationale: The second callback argument (str | None in Python, string | undefined in TypeScript) is the tool use ID, which correlates PreToolUse and PostToolUse events belonging to the same tool call.

nodes.label: Callback context and AbortSignal
nodes.rationale: The third callback argument is context: in TypeScript it carries a signal property (an AbortSignal) for cancellation, which should be passed to fetch so a request cancels when the hook times out. In Python this argument is reserved for future use.

nodes.label: Hook callback output object
nodes.rationale: A callback returns an object with two categories of fields — top-level fields accepted on every event, and hookSpecificOutput controlling the current operation. Returning {} allows the operation unchanged; the format is the same JSON output format used by Claude Code shell command hooks.

nodes.label: Top-level output fields
nodes.rationale: Top-level output fields are accepted on every event: systemMessage shows a message to the user, and continue (continue_ in Python) determines whether the agent keeps running after the hook. Some events discard them or deliver them elsewhere.

nodes.label: hookSpecificOutput
nodes.rationale: hookSpecificOutput is the nested object that controls the current operation; the fields set inside it depend on the hook event type, and it should include hookEventName to identify which hook type the output is for.

nodes.label: permissionDecision
nodes.rationale: For PreToolUse hooks, permissionDecision inside hookSpecificOutput takes one of "allow", "deny", "ask", or "defer" and decides whether the tool call proceeds, is blocked, is shown to the user, or is postponed.

nodes.label: permissionDecisionReason
nodes.rationale: permissionDecisionReason tells the model why a decision was made — for a deny it explains the block so the model avoids retrying — and logging what reason each hook returns is the recommended way to debug an unexpectedly blocked tool.

nodes.label: updatedInput
nodes.rationale: updatedInput, set inside hookSpecificOutput on a PreToolUse hook, replaces the tool's arguments. Pair it with 'allow' to auto-approve or 'ask' to show the user; omitting permissionDecision still applies the modified input through normal permission evaluation. Always return a new object rather than mutating tool_input.

nodes.label: The defer decision
nodes.rationale: Returning permissionDecision "defer" ends the query so the tool call can be resumed later. With 'defer', any updatedInput you also returned is ignored.

nodes.label: additionalContext
nodes.rationale: For PostToolUse hooks, additionalContext appends information to the tool result. It is also the documented way to pass context to the model, in contrast to systemMessage which addresses the user.

nodes.label: updatedToolOutput
nodes.rationale: updatedToolOutput replaces a tool's output before Claude sees it and works for any tool in both SDKs. The older updatedMCPToolOutput field replaces MCP tool output only and is deprecated.

nodes.label: classifierContext
nodes.rationale: In the TypeScript SDK a PostToolUse callback can return classifierContext, a short note about the tool call's result for the auto mode permission classifier. Because the callback runs in your own process, the classifier may weigh a relayed user statement as user intent. It requires TypeScript Agent SDK v0.3.236 or later.

nodes.label: Permission decision precedence
nodes.rationale: When multiple hooks or permission rules apply, deny takes priority over defer, which takes priority over ask, which takes priority over allow. If any hook returns deny, the operation is blocked regardless of the other hooks.

nodes.label: Asynchronous hook output
nodes.rationale: Returning { async: true, asyncTimeout: <ms> } (async_ in Python, to avoid the reserved keyword) signals async mode: the agent proceeds immediately without waiting for the hook to finish, with asyncTimeout an optional millisecond bound on the background operation.

nodes.label: Async output cannot influence the operation
nodes.rationale: Async outputs cannot block, modify, or inject context into the operation, because the agent has already moved on. They are only appropriate for side effects such as logging, metrics, or notifications.

nodes.label: Available hook events
nodes.rationale: The SDK exposes hooks for many stages of agent execution — tool calls, prompts, compaction, model switches, permissions, session and worktree lifecycle, tasks, MCP elicitation, config and file changes — each row naming the trigger, per-SDK availability, and an example use case.

nodes.label: Python vs TypeScript hook parity gap
nodes.rationale: Some hooks are available in both SDKs while many are TypeScript-only: PostToolBatch, UserPromptExpansion, MessageDisplay, StopFailure, PostCompact, PreModelSwitch, PostModelSwitch, PermissionDenied, SessionStart, SessionEnd, Setup, TeammateIdle, TaskCreated, TaskCompleted, Elicitation, ElicitationResult, ConfigChange, InstructionsLoaded, WorktreeCreate, WorktreeRemove, CwdChanged, FileChanged and DirectoryAdded are listed 'No' for Python.

nodes.label: PreToolUse event
nodes.rationale: PreToolUse fires on a tool call request in both SDKs and can block or modify it. Its input includes tool_name and tool_input, and its hookSpecificOutput carries permissionDecision, permissionDecisionReason and updatedInput.

nodes.label: PostToolUse event
nodes.rationale: PostToolUse fires on a tool execution result in both SDKs; the companion PostToolUseFailure fires on a tool execution failure. PostToolUse output can append additionalContext or replace the result with updatedToolOutput.

nodes.label: SubagentStart and SubagentStop
nodes.rationale: SubagentStart fires on subagent initialization (tracking parallel task spawning) and SubagentStop on subagent completion (aggregating results); both exist in Python and TypeScript, and SubagentStop input exposes agent_id, agent_transcript_path and stop_hook_active.

nodes.label: Notification event in SDK sessions
nodes.rationale: In SDK sessions Claude Code runs Notification hooks only for permission_prompt (after a permission request has waited about six seconds on canUseTool; requires TS SDK v0.3.233+ or Python v0.2.139+), elicitation_complete and elicitation_response. Types like idle_prompt, auth_success and elicitation_dialog come from interactive UI that SDK sessions do not run.

nodes.label: SessionStart/SessionEnd unavailable in Python callbacks
nodes.rationale: SessionStart and SessionEnd can be registered as SDK callback hooks in TypeScript but not in Python, whose HookEvent type omits them. In Python they are only available as shell command hooks in settings files, or initialization can be triggered off the first message from client.receive_response().

nodes.label: Default hook timeouts
nodes.rationale: Default per-event timeouts are 600 seconds for most events, 30 seconds for UserPromptSubmit, PreModelSwitch and PostModelSwitch, and 10 seconds for MessageDisplay. SessionEnd callbacks run during shutdown under a shorter budget, 1.5 seconds by default.

nodes.label: What happens when a callback times out
nodes.rationale: A timed-out callback is cancelled and treated as a failed hook: its output is discarded and the session continues rather than hanging. PreToolUse skips the tool call and reports the timeout to Claude (an explicit deny from another hook wins); PostToolUse keeps the result; UserPromptSubmit and UserPromptExpansion block the prompt because they can act as policy gates; Stop/SubagentStop warn and stop normally; PreModelSwitch blocks the switch; other events log and continue.

nodes.label: Example: block writes to .env
nodes.rationale: The introductory example registers a PreToolUse hook with a "Write|Edit" matcher, inspects tool_input.file_path, and returns permissionDecision "deny" with reason "Cannot modify .env files" when the file name is .env; Claude's final response then explains it cannot create .env files.

nodes.label: Example: redirect writes into /sandbox
nodes.rationale: This example intercepts Write tool calls and returns updatedInput with file_path prefixed by /sandbox plus permissionDecision 'allow' to auto-approve the rewrite. To confirm it, use a writable prefix such as ./sandbox or /tmp/sandbox (macOS forbids a root-level /sandbox) and check the path named in the tool result.

nodes.label: Example: block /etc writes with an explanation
nodes.rationale: This example blocks writes whose file_path starts with /etc and explains why to both audiences at once: permissionDecision 'deny' stops the call, permissionDecisionReason tells the model so it avoids retrying, and a top-level systemMessage shows the user what happened.

nodes.label: Example: auto-approve read-only tools
nodes.rationale: This example returns permissionDecision 'allow' for Read, Glob and Grep so read-only filesystem tools run without user confirmation, while every other tool stays subject to normal permission checks.

nodes.label: Multiple hooks run in parallel
nodes.rationale: When an event fires, all matching hooks run in parallel and the most restrictive permission result applies — a single deny blocks the tool call whatever the others return. Completion order is non-deterministic, so each hook must act independently rather than assume another has already run.

nodes.label: Example: multi-tool matchers
nodes.rationale: One PreToolUse registration can carry matchers of different scope: a pipe-separated exact list "Write|Edit|NotebookEdit" for file-modification tools, a regex "^mcp__" for every MCP tool, and an omitted matcher for a global logger that sees every tool call.

nodes.label: HTTP requests from hooks
nodes.rationale: Hooks can perform asynchronous operations such as HTTP requests, but errors must be caught inside the hook because an unhandled exception can interrupt the agent. The webhook example runs the blocking call via asyncio.to_thread in Python, passes the AbortSignal to fetch in TypeScript, and never re-throws.

nodes.label: Example: forward notifications to Slack
nodes.rationale: A matcher-less Notification hook POSTs each notification's message field, prefixed with 'Agent status:', to a Slack incoming webhook URL, then returns {} because Notification hooks do not modify agent behavior.

nodes.label: Troubleshooting: hook not firing
nodes.rationale: Causes of a hook not firing: a wrongly-cased event name (PreToolUse, not preToolUse), a matcher that does not match the tool name exactly, registration under the wrong event key, and non-tool events whose matchers test other fields — Stop ignores matchers entirely.

nodes.label: max_turns can skip hooks
nodes.rationale: Hooks may not fire when the agent hits the max_turns limit, because the session ends before the hooks can execute.

nodes.label: Troubleshooting: modified input not applied
nodes.rationale: When a modified input is ignored, check that updatedInput sits inside hookSpecificOutput rather than at the top level, that it is not paired with permissionDecision 'defer' (which drops it), and that hookEventName is included.

nodes.label: Recursive hook loops with subagents
nodes.rationale: A UserPromptSubmit hook that spawns subagents can loop infinitely if those subagents trigger the same hook. Prevent it by checking for a subagent indicator in the hook input, tracking subagent state in a shared variable, or scoping hooks to the top-level agent session only.

nodes.label: Multiplying subagent permission prompts
nodes.rationale: When spawning multiple subagents, each may request permissions separately for its own tool calls. Avoid repeated prompts with PreToolUse hooks that auto-approve specific tools, or with permission rules, which subagents inherit from the parent conversation.

nodes.label: Troubleshooting: systemMessage not appearing
nodes.rationale: systemMessage addresses the user, not the model. On Claude Code v2.1.227+ it can surface in the message stream as an SDKInformationalMessage depending on the event; before that, only SessionStart and Setup hooks surfaced output there, with everything else visible only via includeHookEvents lifecycle events.

nodes.label: Agent SDK subprocess model
nodes.rationale: Calling query() makes the Agent SDK spawn a separate `claude` CLI process and talk to it over stdio; that subprocess owns the shell, the working directory, and the JSONL session transcripts on local disk. Every hosting decision on this page follows from this, because hosting the SDK is not like hosting a stateless API wrapper.

nodes.label: One session maps to one subprocess
nodes.rationale: One agent session maps to one subprocess, so N concurrent sessions means N subprocesses, each with its own process tree and transcript file. By default they all inherit the application's working directory.

nodes.label: Per-session cwd option
nodes.rationale: When sessions need separate filesystems, pass a distinct `cwd` in the options of each session's query() call (`options: { cwd: "/work/session-a" }` in TypeScript, `ClaudeAgentOptions(cwd=...)` in Python). Without it every session inherits the application's working directory.

nodes.label: Agent state on local disk
nodes.rationale: Three kinds of agent state live on the container filesystem by default: session transcripts, CLAUDE.md memory files, and working-directory artifacts. None of them survive a container restart, a scale-down, or a move to a different node.

nodes.label: Session transcripts on disk
nodes.rationale: JSONL session transcripts default to `~/.claude/projects/`, or the `projects/` directory under `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` when that variable is set.

nodes.label: CLAUDE.md memory files
nodes.rationale: CLAUDE.md memory files live at `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` for the user tier and in the session's working directory for the project tier. In a shared multi-tenant container these filesystem-loaded files can leak one tenant's context into another tenant's session.

nodes.label: Working-directory artifacts
nodes.rationale: Files the agent creates live in the session's working directory. They are not covered by a SessionStore and need their own storage strategy, such as a mounted volume or an object-store sync.

nodes.label: SessionStore adapter
nodes.rationale: A SessionStore adapter mirrors session transcripts to durable storage so they survive a restart, scale-down, or node move. Reference implementations exist for S3, Redis, and Postgres, plus a conformance suite for custom adapters.

nodes.label: SessionStore covers transcripts only
nodes.rationale: SessionStore mirrors transcripts only — not CLAUDE.md memory files and not other working-directory artifacts. Those must be handled with a shared volume or a separate sync.

nodes.label: Dual-write: mirror, not replacement
nodes.rationale: The subprocess writes to local disk first and the SDK forwards a copy of each batch to the store. A fresh session's local transcript outlives the run, but a run resumed from the store deletes its local copy at the end, so the store then holds the only durable copy.

nodes.label: mirror_error system message
nodes.rationale: When the SDK cannot deliver a batch to the store it drops the batch, emits a `{ type: "system", subtype: "mirror_error" }` message, and continues the query. Alert on these messages if store durability matters, because mirror writes are best-effort.

nodes.label: Managed Agents as the hosted alternative
nodes.rationale: If you do not need infrastructure control, custom isolation, or your own data plane, Managed Agents is a hosted REST API where Anthropic runs the agent and the sandbox: the application sends events and streams back results with no hosting infrastructure to operate.

nodes.label: Hosting cookbook deployment targets
nodes.rationale: The claude-cookbooks hosting notebook carries deployable Dockerfiles and Kubernetes manifests for local Docker, Modal, and Kubernetes. It answers where the container runs, which is a separate decision from which session pattern to use.

nodes.label: The four session patterns
nodes.rationale: Four patterns — ephemeral, long-running, hybrid, and multi-agent container — cover session lifecycle: how long a container lives relative to the sessions it serves. You choose a session pattern here and a deployment target from the cookbook.

nodes.label: Ephemeral sessions pattern
nodes.rationale: Create a container for each user task and destroy it when the task completes; best for one-off tasks such as bug investigation and fix, invoice and receipt extraction, document translation, and media transformation. The user may still interact with the AI while the task runs, but the container is destroyed once it completes.

nodes.label: One-shot TASK_PROMPT entrypoint
nodes.rationale: The ephemeral container runs a one-shot entrypoint that reads the task from the `TASK_PROMPT` environment variable, calls the SDK, and exits. It prints each message, including a result message whose subtype is `success`; hitting the turn limit yields `error_max_turns` and then raises, so wrap the loop in a try block if the container must exit cleanly.

nodes.label: maxTurns as the only turn bound
nodes.rationale: `maxTurns` in TypeScript or `max_turns` in Python bounds how many tool-use round trips an agent takes before stopping, and the same option in a subagent's AgentDefinition caps that subagent. It is the available substitute for the wall-clock timeouts the SDK does not provide.

nodes.label: Long-running sessions pattern
nodes.rationale: Persistent container instances, often hosting multiple SDK processes each, serve ongoing work such as an email triage agent, a per-user site builder served through container ports, or a Slack chat bot. The container exposes an HTTP or WebSocket endpoint and maps each active session to a long-lived query, so it must be sized to hold the maximum number of concurrent sessions in memory.

nodes.label: streamInput, startup and ClaudeSDKClient
nodes.rationale: In TypeScript, `streamInput()` adds turns to an active session and `startup()` pre-warms subprocesses ahead of incoming traffic; in Python, `ClaudeSDKClient` holds a session open across turns. These are the APIs that keep a session and its subprocess alive between requests.

nodes.label: Hybrid sessions pattern
nodes.rationale: Ephemeral containers hydrate from a SessionStore on startup and persist updates back, spinning down while idle and back up when the user returns — best for sessions that span many interactions but sit idle between them, such as a personal project manager, paused deep research, or a support agent loading ticket history. It hinges on resuming a session by ID with a shared store attached, and the provider's idle timeout should be tuned to how often users return.

nodes.label: Multi-agent container pattern
nodes.rationale: Run multiple SDK subprocesses inside one container, best for agents that must collaborate closely such as multi-agent simulations in a shared environment. Each agent needs its own working directory so they do not overwrite each other's files, and settings loading must be isolated so per-agent CLAUDE.md files do not leak across agents.

nodes.label: Container-based sandboxing
nodes.rationale: Running the SDK inside a sandboxed container gives process isolation, resource limits, network control, and an ephemeral filesystem. Self-hosted options include Docker, gVisor, and Firecracker.

nodes.label: Sandbox provider selection criteria
nodes.rationale: Choosing a sandbox provider means answering five questions: who runs the sandbox (as-a-service vs self-hosted), cold-start latency (ephemeral patterns need sub-second starts), whether persistent storage is offered, the pricing model (per-second suits bursty ephemeral work, hourly suits long-running sessions), and networking support for custom egress rules, outbound proxies, and private VPC peering.

nodes.label: Container runtime dependencies
nodes.rationale: The container needs the SDK's language runtime — Python 3.10+ for the Python SDK or Node.js 18+ for the TypeScript SDK. Both SDKs bundle a native Claude Code binary for most installs, so the spawned CLI needs no separate Node.js install.

nodes.label: Bundled CLI pinned to the SDK version
nodes.rationale: The bundled binary is pinned to the SDK package version, so updating the SDK is how you update the CLI. The SDK follows semver: take patch releases continuously, and review the TypeScript or Python changelog before taking a minor.

nodes.label: 1 GiB / 5 GiB / 1 CPU starting point
nodes.rationale: 1 GiB RAM, 5 GiB disk, and 1 CPU per agent is a reasonable starting point for a freshly started instance. Memory usage grows with session length and tool activity, so size for the session lengths and concurrency you actually need rather than the idle baseline — the 1 GiB figure is a floor, not a ceiling.

nodes.label: Outbound network and egress proxy
nodes.rationale: The SDK needs outbound HTTPS to api.anthropic.com, or the provider's regional endpoint on Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud's Agent Platform, plus access to any MCP servers or external tools the agents use. For production, route outbound traffic through an egress proxy that enforces domain allowlists, injects credentials, and logs requests.

nodes.label: Inbound port terminates at your app, not the subprocess
nodes.rationale: For inbound traffic you expose an HTTP or WebSocket port on the container; your application handles client requests on that port and calls the SDK internally. The `claude` subprocess itself does not listen on the network.

nodes.label: OpenTelemetry from the environment
nodes.rationale: Agent SDK agents are long-lived processes spawning tool calls across many API round-trips, so without telemetry you cannot see which tools ran, how long they took, or where a session stalled. The SDK inherits OpenTelemetry configuration from the environment, so setting OTEL variables (CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1, OTLP exporters and endpoint) at the container or orchestrator level makes every query() call export spans, metrics, and log events.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA is traces-only
nodes.rationale: `CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA=1` is required only for traces; omit it if you export metrics and logs alone.

nodes.label: Prompt text excluded from exports by default
nodes.rationale: Prompt text and tool inputs are not included in telemetry exports by default; including them requires explicit opt-in flags documented under controlling sensitive data in exports.

nodes.label: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the subprocess environment
nodes.rationale: The subprocess reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from its environment; supply it from a secret manager, or set `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` to route model calls through a proxy that injects the key outside the container.

nodes.label: Authenticate at a gateway, not in the agent
nodes.rationale: Put authentication at a gateway in front of the agent container. The agent should receive pre-authenticated requests and should not be the component that validates user tokens.

nodes.label: Inject tool credentials at the proxy
nodes.rationale: Keep tool credentials out of the agent environment: route outbound calls through a proxy that injects API keys after the request leaves the container. The agent makes the call; the proxy adds the credential.

nodes.label: Agents-per-host formula
nodes.rationale: Because each session runs in its own subprocess, concurrency on a host is bounded by how many subprocesses its RAM can hold: agents per host = (host RAM - overhead) / (per-session RAM ceiling).

nodes.label: Measure the per-session RAM ceiling
nodes.rationale: Measure the per-session ceiling by running a representative session to your target length under your expected tool load and recording peak RSS, rather than assuming the documented starting point.

nodes.label: Pin sessions by consistent hashing on sessionId
nodes.rationale: For long-running sessions, run a pool of containers behind a load balancer and pin each session to one container using consistent hashing on `sessionId`. A pinned session keeps hitting the same container — and therefore the same running subprocess — until it is evicted or the container restarts.

nodes.label: Token cost dominates infrastructure cost
nodes.rationale: Anthropic token cost typically dominates container infrastructure cost by an order of magnitude or more: a minimally provisioned container runs roughly $0.05 per hour while a single long agent session can spend dollars in tokens.

nodes.label: Multi-tenant isolation in a shared container
nodes.rationale: Default SDK behaviour reads settings and CLAUDE.md memory files from the filesystem, so a shared container serving multiple tenants needs explicit isolation: empty setting sources, disabled auto memory, a per-tenant config directory, a per-tenant working directory, and per-tenant egress rules applied together.

nodes.label: settingSources: [] skips filesystem settings
nodes.rationale: Passing `settingSources: []` in TypeScript or `setting_sources=[]` in Python skips user, project, and local settings loading for that query.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1
nodes.rationale: Auto memory at `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/` loads into the system prompt regardless of settingSources, so `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1` must be set in `env` as a separate control. Other inputs also load unconditionally, documented under what settingSources does not control.

nodes.label: Per-tenant CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR
nodes.rationale: Point `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` at a per-tenant directory so tenants do not share the global `~/.claude.json` config. When each config directory serves one working directory and no SessionStore is shared across tenants, `CLAUDE_CODE_PROJECT_DIR_NAME` can also be set to keep transcript paths short — requiring TypeScript Agent SDK v0.3.234+ or Python Agent SDK v0.2.140+.

nodes.label: Per-tenant working directory
nodes.rationale: Use a per-tenant working directory and pass `cwd` explicitly on every query() call; construct the tenant directory and config directory so each tenant gets a path no other tenant can read.

nodes.label: Per-tenant egress rules at the proxy
nodes.rationale: Apply per-tenant egress rules at the proxy — distinct outbound IPs, credentials, or domain allowlists — so a compromised tenant cannot exfiltrate data via another tenant's outbound policy.

nodes.label: env replaces in TypeScript, merges in Python
nodes.rationale: In TypeScript, `env` replaces the subprocess environment, so `...process.env` must be spread to keep inherited variables like PATH and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. In Python, `env` is merged on top of the inherited environment.

nodes.label: Cross-tenant context leak
nodes.rationale: In a shared container serving multiple tenants, filesystem-loaded settings and CLAUDE.md memory files can leak one tenant's context into another tenant's session. It is the failure the multi-tenant isolation options exist to prevent.

nodes.label: No top-level session timeout
nodes.rationale: A session does not time out on its own — there is no top-level session timeout. The documented remedy is to bound tool-use round trips with maxTurns / max_turns.

nodes.label: Memory growth over long sessions
nodes.rationale: Memory usage grows over long sessions, which is a known limitation to design around when planning host capacity.

nodes.label: Wide subagent fanouts hit rate limits
nodes.rationale: Large parallel-subagent fanouts can hit rate limits, a known limitation of the deployment design.

nodes.label: No per-subagent wall-clock deadline
nodes.rationale: There is no per-subagent wall-clock deadline. For background subagents only, `CLAUDE_ASYNC_AGENT_STALL_TIMEOUT_MS` sets a stall watchdog that fires when a `run_in_background` subagent stops producing output — it is not a total-runtime deadline.

nodes.label: Cap session length or recycle subprocesses
nodes.rationale: The documented response to memory growth over long sessions is to cap session length or recycle subprocesses periodically, sized against the scaling-and-concurrency numbers.

nodes.label: Batch subagent dispatch
nodes.rationale: Break work into smaller batches rather than issuing one wide dispatch, so a parallel-subagent fanout does not hit rate limits.

nodes.label: Deployment failure triage
nodes.rationale: The troubleshooting section covers the case where an agent that works on your machine fails in a deployed service, naming three failure shapes: the CLI not found at service start, the CLI present but unable to launch, and the Claude Code process exiting mid-run.

nodes.label: CLI not found at service start
nodes.rationale: In Python, a container or service manager runs the application with a different PATH than your shell, so a locally working install is invisible to the process. In TypeScript, the image build skipped the SDK's optional dependencies, or `pathToClaudeCodeExecutable` points at a file that does not exist in the image.

nodes.label: CLI present but will not launch
nodes.rationale: Claude Code cannot start from a binary that does not match the container's architecture or libc, or from a file that lost its execute permission during the image build.

nodes.label: Claude Code process exits mid-run
nodes.rationale: When the Claude Code process exits mid-run, the error the application receives depends on the SDK language and on whether the CLI reported an error result first; the CLI process exit troubleshooting entries cover each message.

nodes.label: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
nodes.rationale: MCP is an open standard for connecting AI agents to external tools and data sources, letting an agent query databases and integrate with APIs like Slack and GitHub without writing custom tool implementations.

nodes.label: MCP server
nodes.rationale: An MCP server exposes external tools to the agent. It can run as a local process, connect over HTTP, or execute directly in-process within the SDK application.

nodes.label: mcpServers option
nodes.rationale: Servers can be configured in code by passing them in the `mcpServers` option to `query()` (`mcp_servers` in Python). Claude Code registers the servers passed there at startup.

nodes.label: .mcp.json config file
nodes.rationale: A `.mcp.json` file at the project root declares servers under an `mcpServers` key, using the same fields as the in-code form. Servers loaded from settings files commonly show `pending` at init because Claude Code only waits 2 seconds for them when `options.mcpServers` is absent.

nodes.label: project setting source
nodes.rationale: `.mcp.json` is picked up only when the `project` setting source is enabled — the default for `query()` options. If `settingSources` is set explicitly, `"project"` must be included for the file to load.

nodes.label: MCP connection timing
nodes.rationale: Whether a server delays the first turn depends on its type: a stdio server, or an HTTP/SSE server with no cached tool list, blocks the first turn until it connects; a remote server with a cached tool list and an in-process SDK server never delay it.

nodes.label: MCP_TIMEOUT
nodes.rationale: `MCP_TIMEOUT` sets the first-turn connection wait, 30 seconds by default; the connection fails at that deadline. It is raised in milliseconds when a server needs more startup time.

nodes.label: cached remote tool list
nodes.rationale: Claude Code can save a remote server's tool list from a previous connection. Those cached tools are available from the first turn with no wait; the server itself connects on its first tool call, and that deferred connect has its own timeout.

nodes.label: MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING
nodes.rationale: Setting `MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING` to `0` blocks startup itself — a phase earlier than the first-turn wait, before the init message is sent — on the whole connection batch. Servers still pending at the cap keep connecting in the background.

nodes.label: MCP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS
nodes.rationale: Claude Code caps the blocking startup wait at 5 seconds by default; `MCP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS` adjusts that cap, in milliseconds.

nodes.label: alwaysLoad: true
nodes.rationale: `alwaysLoad: true` on a server's config makes its tools available at their full schemas on the first turn, exempt from tool-search deferral. Claude Code waits at startup for that server's tools, capped at the same deadline, while other servers keep connecting in the background.

nodes.label: system init message
nodes.rationale: Claude Code emits a `system` message with subtype `init` at the start of each query, carrying each MCP server's connection status at the moment it is emitted, plus the `tools` array.

nodes.label: MCP server status field
nodes.rationale: The per-server `status` field can be `"pending"`, `"connected"`, `"failed"`, `"needs-auth"`, or `"disabled"`. Checking for `"failed"` or `"needs-auth"` detects servers that will not be usable.

nodes.label: pending is not a failure
nodes.rationale: `"pending"` at init must not be read as a failure: it can mean the server has not connected yet, that its tool list was served from the cache with the connection made on first use, or that the connection deadline expired (which reports `pending` or `failed` depending on timing).

nodes.label: allowedTools
nodes.rationale: MCP tools require explicit permission: without it Claude sees the tools but cannot call them. `allowedTools` auto-approves named tools or whole servers so no permission prompt is raised.

nodes.label: mcp__server__tool naming
nodes.rationale: MCP tools follow the pattern `mcp__<server-name>__<tool-name>`; a `list_issues` tool on a server named `github` becomes `mcp__github__list_issues`. The `mcp__` prefix is also how MCP tools are identified in the init `tools` array and in `tool_use` blocks.

nodes.label: wildcard tool pattern
nodes.rationale: A `*` wildcard such as `mcp__github__*` allows every tool from one server without listing each individually, while `mcp__db__query` grants a single tool.

nodes.label: permissionMode acceptEdits
nodes.rationale: `permissionMode: "acceptEdits"` does NOT auto-approve MCP tools — it covers only file edits and filesystem Bash commands — so it cannot substitute for `allowedTools` when granting MCP access.

nodes.label: permissionMode bypassPermissions
nodes.rationale: `permissionMode: "bypassPermissions"` does auto-approve MCP tools but also disables most other safety prompts, which is broader than necessary; a wildcard in `allowedTools` grants exactly the intended server and nothing more.

nodes.label: MCP transport types
nodes.rationale: Transport is chosen from what the server's docs supply: a command to run means stdio, a URL means HTTP or SSE, and tools built in your own code mean an SDK MCP server.

nodes.label: stdio transport
nodes.rationale: stdio servers are local processes communicating over stdin/stdout, configured with a `command` and `args` (e.g. `npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem <dir>`). They always block the first turn until they connect.

nodes.label: HTTP/SSE transport
nodes.rationale: HTTP and SSE transports serve cloud-hosted MCP servers and remote APIs, configured with `type` (`"http"` or `"sse"`), a `url`, and optional `headers`.

nodes.label: streamable-http alias
nodes.rationale: In `.mcp.json` and other JSON config files, `"streamable-http"` is accepted as an alias for `"http"`. The SDKs' `McpHttpServerConfig` type declares only `"http"`, so code-passed servers must use `"http"`.

nodes.label: SDK (in-process) MCP server
nodes.rationale: An SDK MCP server defines custom tools directly in application code instead of running a separate process. It never delays the first turn, and one registered by an `initialize` control request begins connecting as soon as Claude Code processes that request. In TypeScript its tool-call limit is set by passing `timeout` to `createSdkMcpServer()`.

nodes.label: MCP tool search
nodes.rationale: Tool search withholds tool definitions from context and loads only the ones Claude needs for each turn. It is enabled by default.

nodes.label: tool definitions consume context
nodes.rationale: With many MCP tools configured, their definitions can consume a significant portion of the context window — the cost that tool search exists to remove.

nodes.label: env field credentials
nodes.rationale: Most MCP servers need authentication; the `env` field of a server's config passes API keys, tokens and other credentials to the server process.

nodes.label: HTTP auth headers
nodes.rationale: For HTTP and SSE servers, authentication is passed as `headers` in the server configuration, typically `Authorization: Bearer <token>` sourced from an environment variable.

nodes.label: ${VAR} expansion in config
nodes.rationale: In `.mcp.json`, the `${API_KEY}` / `${API_TOKEN}` syntax expands environment variables at runtime, so the secret itself never has to be written into the config file.

nodes.label: OAuth 2.1 authentication
nodes.rationale: The MCP specification supports OAuth 2.1, but the SDK never opens a browser or runs an interactive OAuth flow: when a server returns an authorization challenge with no stored token, the run continues without that server's tools. The application must complete the OAuth flow itself and pass the resulting access token in the server's headers.

nodes.label: needs-auth status
nodes.rationale: A server that returned an authorization challenge reports status `needs-auth`; the init message may still show `pending` for it, so confirming that credentials are needed requires a later status poll.

nodes.label: mcpServerStatus() / get_mcp_status()
nodes.rationale: Because the init message is only a snapshot, updated per-server statuses come from polling `mcpServerStatus()` in the TypeScript SDK or `ClaudeSDKClient.get_mcp_status()` in Python later in the session.

nodes.label: automatic reconnection
nodes.rationale: When a remote server's connection drops mid-session, Claude Code moves it back to `"pending"` while reconnecting — with no configuration change on the caller's side. After five failed reconnection attempts the server reports `"failed"`, or `"needs-auth"` if it needs authorizing again.

nodes.label: reconnectMcpServer()
nodes.rationale: To retry a connection manually after automatic reconnection has given up, call `reconnectMcpServer()` in TypeScript or `ClaudeSDKClient.reconnect_mcp_server()` in Python.

nodes.label: tools array discovery
nodes.rationale: Filtering the init message's `tools` array for names starting with `mcp__` lists the available MCP tools — but only for servers that connected within the first-turn wait plus those with a cached tool list; tools of any other server are absent.

nodes.label: GitHub MCP issues example
