nodes.rationale: Teammates inherit the lead's effort level; in split-pane mode this applies from v2.1.186, since earlier versions did not pass the lead's session effort to split-pane teammates. Because effort follows the lead, /effort typed while viewing a teammate still applies to that teammate's later turns, unlike /model and /fast.

nodes.label: Subagent definitions as teammate roles
nodes.rationale: A teammate can be spawned from a subagent type in any scope (project, user, plugin, CLI-defined), letting a role such as security-reviewer be defined once and reused as both subagent and teammate. Claude Code applies the definition's tools (adding SendMessage and the Task tools for in-process teammates) and model; the body is appended to the default system prompt in-process but replaces it in split panes; skills are never applied; mcpServers apply only to split-pane teammates.

nodes.label: Teammates planning before implementing
nodes.rationale: For complex or risky work, switch the lead into plan mode before asking for a teammate: a teammate spawned while the lead is in plan mode works in read-only plan mode until its plan is ready, then exits plan mode and implements once approved.

nodes.label: Automatic teammate plan approval
nodes.rationale: When a teammate finishes planning it sends a plan approval request to the lead, and Claude Code approves it in the lead's session as soon as it arrives, without the lead or the user reviewing it. This is the designed exception to teammate permission prompts; the teammate's subsequent edits and commands still go through permission prompts.

nodes.label: Teammate permission inheritance
nodes.rationale: Teammates start with the lead's permission settings — if the lead runs with --dangerously-skip-permissions, so do all teammates. Individual teammate modes can be changed after spawning, but per-teammate modes cannot be set at spawn time.

nodes.label: Teammate permission prompts surface in the lead
nodes.rationale: Teammate permission requests bubble up to the lead session and must be approved there by the user, which can create friction; pre-approving common operations in permission settings before spawning teammates reduces the interruptions.

nodes.label: Inter-agent message trust boundary
nodes.rationale: When one agent sends another a message over SendMessage, Claude Code tells the receiving agent it came from another Claude session, not from the user. A teammate cannot approve a permission prompt or supply consent on the user's behalf, and a teammate denied an action cannot relay it to another teammate to bypass the check; the same rules apply to messages from the user's other sessions.

nodes.label: Auto-mode message classifier
nodes.rationale: In auto mode the classifier applies two checks to messages between agents: it treats an approval claim relayed from another agent as untrusted input rather than user confirmation, and it reviews every message — plain or structured protocol messages such as shutdown requests and plan approval responses — before delivery, with blocked messages never reaching the recipient.

nodes.label: Per-teammate context isolation
nodes.rationale: Each teammate has its own context window and, when spawned, loads the same project context as a regular session — CLAUDE.md, MCP servers, and skills — plus the lead's spawn prompt. The lead's conversation history does not carry over.

nodes.label: Put task detail in the spawn prompt
nodes.rationale: Because teammates do not inherit the lead's conversation history, the spawn prompt must carry task-specific detail — the files to review, the focus areas, the stack facts, and the reporting format — for the teammate to work usefully.

nodes.label: Idle and failure notifications
nodes.rationale: When a teammate finishes and stops it automatically notifies the lead and includes its final answer in the notification; a teammate whose turn ends on an API error notifies the lead that it failed and includes the error text.

nodes.label: Teammate-to-teammate messaging
nodes.rationale: Teammates message each other directly by name — this self-coordination is what distinguishes teams from subagents, which only return results to their caller. Messages address one recipient at a time, so reaching everyone means sending one message per recipient.

nodes.label: Agent panel
nodes.rationale: The lead's terminal lists teammates in the agent panel below the prompt input: up/down arrows select a teammate, Enter opens its transcript to message it directly, and Escape clears the selection or interrupts the viewed teammate's turn. Subagents appear in the same panel as teammates, so the panel alone does not confirm that a team formed.

nodes.label: Idle row hiding and collapsing
nodes.rationale: As of v2.1.199 an idle teammate's row stays visible while any agent is still working; once every agent is idle, idle rows hide after 30 seconds and reappear on the teammate's next turn, with the teammate still running and addressable while hidden. When more than three teammates are idle, the surplus rows collapse into one counting row such as '2 idle agents', expandable with Enter.

nodes.label: Teammates not appearing
nodes.rationale: When teammates seem absent: a row that disappeared after sitting idle has been hidden, not stopped, and messaging the teammate by name brings it back; the task may not have been complex enough for Claude to spawn a team at all; and for split panes, tmux must be on PATH or it2 installed with the iTerm2 Python API enabled.

nodes.label: A named subagent launches as a teammate
nodes.rationale: Claude launches a teammate whenever it calls the Agent tool with a name while agent teams are enabled, and it is not asked to confirm. Because Claude names ordinary subagents on its own so it can message them later, teams can form during delegation the user never framed as team work.

nodes.label: Turning agent teams off
nodes.rationale: Setting CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS to 0 makes named subagents launch as subagents again, with no new session needed: Claude Code reapplies settings-file env values on save and rereads the variable each time it spawns a subagent. Claude may still name subagents afterwards, and the name keeps working as a SendMessage address.

nodes.label: Settings precedence over the teams flag
nodes.rationale: A user settings.json value of 0 overrides a shell export, but higher-precedence sources still win: project settings, local settings, and a --settings payload apply after user settings, and managed settings apply after every other source — an organization enabling agent teams there requires an administrator to change it.

nodes.label: Interactive-session requirement
nodes.rationale: Spawning teammates requires an interactive session. In non-interactive mode with the -p flag, including Agent SDK sessions, Claude does not spawn teammates and a named subagent runs as an ordinary subagent even with agent teams enabled.

nodes.label: Task dependencies
nodes.rationale: Tasks can depend on other tasks: a pending task with unresolved dependencies cannot be claimed until those dependencies complete. Claude Code manages this automatically — completing a task unblocks the tasks that depended on it with no action from the user.

nodes.label: Task tool availability
nodes.rationale: The shared task list is only available to agents that have the Task tools (TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskList, TaskUpdate). Agents without them coordinate through messages instead, and only sessions with the Task tools can see task status and claim available work.

nodes.label: File locking on task claims
nodes.rationale: Task claiming uses file locking to prevent race conditions when multiple teammates try to claim the same task simultaneously.

nodes.label: Teammate shutdown request
nodes.rationale: To end a teammate gracefully, ask the lead to shut it down by name; the lead sends a shutdown request that the teammate can approve, exiting gracefully, or reject with an explanation. The team's shared directories are cleaned up automatically at session end, so there is no separate cleanup step.

nodes.label: Team hooks as quality gates
nodes.rationale: Three hooks enforce rules on team work, each using exit code 2 to send feedback: TeammateIdle runs when a teammate is about to go idle and keeps it working; TaskCreated runs when a task is being created and can prevent creation; TaskCompleted runs when a task is being marked complete and can prevent completion.

nodes.label: Session-derived team name
nodes.rationale: Teams and tasks are stored locally under a session-derived name: the literal 'session-' followed by the first eight characters of the session ID. Claude Code generates the config and task directories automatically at session startup and updates them as teammates join, go idle, or leave.

nodes.label: Team config file
nodes.rationale: The team config lives at ~/.claude/teams/{team-name}/config.json, holds runtime state such as session IDs and tmux pane IDs, and is removed when the session ends. It must not be hand-edited or pre-authored because the next state update overwrites it; its members array names each member and agent ID so teammates can discover each other, and there is no project-level equivalent (a .claude/teams/teams.json in a project is an ordinary file).

nodes.label: Task list persistence
nodes.rationale: The task list directory at ~/.claude/tasks/{team-name}/ persists locally and is never uploaded, so resumed sessions keep their tasks — unlike the team config directory, which is deleted at session end.

nodes.label: cleanupPeriodDays retention
nodes.rationale: Retention of the persisted task list is governed by the same cleanupPeriodDays setting that controls session transcripts, following the standard retention sweep rules for the .claude directory.

nodes.label: Mailbox entry validation
nodes.rationale: Claude Code validates every entry when it reads a mailbox file: entries that do not match the message format are reported as errors and removed, while the valid messages are still delivered. Before v2.1.207 a single malformed entry caused a repeated error every second and blocked delivery for that mailbox until the file was deleted by hand.

nodes.label: Send confirmed only on a successful write
nodes.rationale: A message is reported as sent only when the write to the recipient's mailbox file succeeds, for plain text and structured protocol messages alike. If the write fails — a full disk, an unwritable mailbox directory — the sending agent gets an error and nothing is sent.

nodes.label: Removed TeamCreate/TeamDelete tools
nodes.rationale: Before v2.1.178 a team had to be created and named first via the TeamCreate and TeamDelete tools; both no longer exist. Spawning a teammate now needs no setup step and cleanup is automatic, the Agent tool's team_name input is accepted but ignored, and the team_name field in TaskCreated, TaskCompleted and TeammateIdle hook payloads carries the session-derived name and is deprecated.

nodes.label: subagentPromptCacheTtl for teammates
nodes.rationale: An in-process teammate's requests fall outside the main conversation's cache TTL bucket, so its prompt cache holds for five minutes by default, including on a Claude subscription. Setting subagentPromptCacheTtl to 1h extends it, though the API bills 1-hour cache writes at a higher rate.

nodes.label: Team size guidance
nodes.rationale: There is no hard limit on teammates, but token costs scale linearly, coordination overhead grows, and returns diminish. Start with 3-5 teammates for most workflows — even 15 independent tasks are a good fit for 3 teammates — and scale up only when simultaneous work genuinely helps; three focused teammates often outperform five scattered ones.

nodes.label: Coordination overhead
nodes.rationale: Agent teams add coordination overhead: more teammates means more communication, more task coordination, and more potential for conflicts. Teams work best when teammates operate independently; sequential tasks, same-file edits, and dependency-heavy work are better served by a single session or subagents.

nodes.label: Task sizing
nodes.rationale: Tasks that are too small cost more in coordination than they return; tasks that are too large let teammates work too long without check-ins and raise the risk of wasted effort. The right size is a self-contained unit with a clear deliverable — a function, a test file, a review — with roughly 5-6 tasks per teammate.

nodes.label: File conflict risk
nodes.rationale: Two teammates editing the same file leads to overwrites, so work must be broken up such that each teammate owns a different set of files.

nodes.label: Wasted-effort risk
nodes.rationale: Letting a team run unattended for too long, or giving teammates tasks too large to check in on, increases the risk that parallel work goes in an unproductive direction and has to be discarded.

nodes.label: Monitor and steer
nodes.rationale: The recommended practice is to check in on teammates' progress, redirect approaches that are not working, and synthesize findings as they arrive rather than only at the end.

nodes.label: Parallel code review use case
nodes.rationale: A single reviewer gravitates toward one class of issue at a time, so splitting review criteria into independent lenses — security, performance, test coverage — gives each thorough attention simultaneously. Each reviewer works the same PR through a different filter and the lead synthesizes across all three.

nodes.label: Competing-hypotheses investigation use case
nodes.rationale: When a root cause is unclear, spawn several teammates on different hypotheses and instruct them to argue like a scientific debate, each trying to disprove the others' theories. The theory that survives multiple independent adversarial investigators is much more likely to be the actual root cause.

nodes.label: Anchoring in sequential investigation
nodes.rationale: Sequential investigation suffers from anchoring: a single agent tends to find one plausible explanation and stop looking, and once one theory has been explored, subsequent investigation is biased toward it.

nodes.label: Agents stopping early
nodes.rationale: Teammates may stop after errors instead of recovering; the remedy is to open the teammate's output and give it more instructions, or spawn a replacement. The lead can also stop early, deciding the team is finished before all tasks are complete, in which case it should be told to keep going.

nodes.label: Talking to a teammate directly
nodes.rationale: Any teammate can be messaged directly to add instructions, ask follow-ups, or redirect its approach — arrow keys plus Enter in-process (x stops it, Ctrl+T toggles the task list), or clicking its pane in split mode. While viewing an in-process teammate, plain text and skills go to that teammate but built-in commands still run in the lead's session, and a teammate's model and fast mode are fixed at spawn so /model and /fast only change the lead (with a notice shown as of v2.1.199).

nodes.label: Limitation: no session resumption for in-process teammates
nodes.rationale: /resume and /rewind do not restore in-process teammates. After resuming, the lead may try to message teammates that no longer exist, and the fix is to tell it to spawn new ones.

nodes.label: Limitation: one team per session
nodes.rationale: A session has exactly one team, scoped to that session; additional named teams cannot be created and a team cannot be shared across sessions.

nodes.label: Limitation: no nested teams
nodes.rationale: Teammates cannot spawn their own teammates; only the lead can manage the team.

nodes.label: Limitation: the lead is fixed
nodes.rationale: The main session is the lead for its entire lifetime: a teammate cannot be promoted to lead and leadership cannot be transferred.

nodes.label: Limitation: no background subagents from in-process teammates
nodes.rationale: An in-process teammate's own subagents run in the foreground because a teammate's background work cannot outlive the lead's process. Claude Code errors when a teammate spawns a subagent whose definition sets background: true, and a run_in_background: true request either errors or runs silently in the foreground.

nodes.label: Limitation: task status can lag
nodes.rationale: Teammates sometimes fail to mark tasks completed, which blocks the tasks that depend on them. When a task looks stuck, check whether the work is actually done and update the status manually or tell the lead to nudge the teammate.

nodes.label: Limitation: shutdown can be slow
nodes.rationale: Teammates finish their current request or tool call before shutting down, so a graceful shutdown can take time.

nodes.label: Agent view
nodes.rationale: Agent view, opened with `claude agents`, is one screen listing every background Claude Code session grouped by state: what is running, what needs input, and what is done. It takes over the full terminal, shows pinned and needs-input sessions at the top, and is in research preview so its interface and shortcuts may change.

nodes.label: Background session
nodes.rationale: A background session is a full Claude Code conversation that keeps running without a terminal attached. Claude Code treats every session listed in agent view as a background session whether or not you are attached; `/status` reports Session kind as background job attached or unattended.

nodes.label: Dispatch input
nodes.rationale: The input at the bottom of agent view. Typing a prompt and pressing Enter starts a new background session; every prompt starts its own new session rather than following up on an existing one. Typing can also filter the list, and a few commands such as /exit, /model and /login run in agent view itself.

nodes.label: Dispatch from agent view
nodes.rationale: Dispatching from agent view starts a background session named automatically by a Haiku-class model from the prompt. Prefixes control the start: a leading subagent name or @name runs that subagent as the main agent, @repo targets a repository, /command dispatches a skill or command, and a leading ! runs a shell job instead.

nodes.label: Session row
nodes.rationale: Each session appears as a row showing its name, current activity summary, and its age counted from when the session was created; a finished session's age freezes at how long the run took. The name is tinted with the color set by /color in that session.

nodes.label: Session state
nodes.rationale: A row's icon color and animation encode state: Working (animated), Needs input (yellow), Idle (dimmed), Completed (green), Failed (red) and Stopped (grey). Needs input covers questions, permission decisions, sandbox prompts, MCP elicitation, and commands that require an attached terminal.

nodes.label: Process shape icon
nodes.rationale: Separately from state color, the icon shape reports the underlying process: a star shape means the process is alive and replies immediately, a dot means the process exited but replying or attaching restarts it from where it left off, and another shape marks a /loop session sleeping between iterations with a run count and countdown.

nodes.label: Row summary
nodes.rationale: The one-line summary in each row tells you what the session is doing, needs, or produced without opening the transcript. While a session works the text refreshes at most every 15 seconds from the session's own output with no model request, and a model-written summary is produced at each turn end and rewritten every few minutes during long turns.

nodes.label: Haiku-class summarizer
nodes.rationale: Row summaries and automatic session names are written by a Haiku-class model as one short request through your normal provider, billed under the same data usage terms as the session. On a provider or gateway with no Haiku-class model configured the request falls back to the session's main model; ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL chooses one.

nodes.label: Pull request label
nodes.rationale: When a session opens or works on a pull request, Claude Code adds a linked label at the row's right edge, written as #1234 for a pull request and !1234 for a GitLab merge request, colored by status: yellow waiting on checks or review, green passing with no blocking review, purple merged, grey draft or closed. Multiple links collapse to a count such as 3 PRs.

nodes.label: Peek panel
nodes.rationale: Pressing Space on a selected row opens the peek panel, which shows the sentence the row truncates - the exact question for a blocked session, the result for a finished one, the full status sentence for a working one - plus linked pull requests and a waiting time. You can type a reply and press Enter, pick a numbered choice, press Tab for a suggested reply, or prefix ! to send a Bash command.

nodes.label: Attach to a session
nodes.rationale: Pressing Enter or the right arrow on a row attaches: agent view is replaced by the full interactive session and Claude posts a recap of what happened while you were away. Attached sessions always render in fullscreen mode because a background session has no terminal scrollback, and detaching with the left arrow, Ctrl+Z, /exit or double Ctrl+C never stops the session.

nodes.label: Left-arrow background/detach gesture
nodes.rationale: Pressing the left arrow on an empty prompt backgrounds a foreground session and opens agent view with its row selected, or detaches an attached session. It waits about ten seconds for a running tool, refuses while unsent text is in the input, and can be turned off with the leftArrowOpensAgents setting.

nodes.label: /background (/bg)
nodes.rationale: Running /background or its alias /bg moves the current conversation into a background session and frees the terminal; a trailing prompt gives one more instruction and an in-progress response continues in the background session. Exiting a session with background work running offers Move to background and exit instead of quitting.

nodes.label: /fork
nodes.rationale: Running /fork copies the current conversation into a new background session while the original keeps running, carrying over the model, permission mode, effort level, and directories or do-not-ask-again grants added during the session. After the fork the two conversations are independent unless cross-session messaging is enabled.

nodes.label: Work that carries over when backgrounding
nodes.rationale: Backgrounding starts a fresh process that resumes the saved conversation and moves in-flight work with it: background shell commands, backgrounded subagents, dynamic workflows, /loop scheduled tasks and automatic artifact comment replies keep running there. Work whose state lives only in the process, such as a monitor, is stopped instead.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_DISABLE_ADOPT
nodes.rationale: Setting the CLAUDE_DISABLE_ADOPT=1 environment variable stops in-flight work instead of carrying it into the backgrounded session; Claude Code then asks you to confirm before backgrounding.

nodes.label: Background this session? dialog
nodes.rationale: When backgrounding would stop, restart, or leave work running unattended - work that cannot move such as a monitor, a dynamic workflow with running subagents that would restart from the beginning, or automatic artifact replies - Claude Code shows the Background this session? dialog so you can confirm or choose Stay.

nodes.label: claude --bg
nodes.rationale: Passing --bg or --background starts a session that goes straight to the background with the prompt as a positional argument; combining it with -p or --print is rejected before any session is created. After backgrounding, Claude prints the session's short ID and the agents, attach, logs and stop commands, and --name sets the display name.

nodes.label: --agent on a background session
nodes.rationale: Combining --agent with --bg runs a defined subagent as the session's main agent. An unmatched name fails the launch with an --agent not found error, and on later resume or restart Claude Code restores the agent's system prompt and tool restrictions, searching the session's own trusted directory first.

nodes.label: Shell job (--exec or ! prefix)
nodes.rationale: Passing --exec, or typing ! as the first character of the dispatch input, runs a shell command as a PTY-backed background job instead of a Claude session, so no model is invoked and no output is sent to any session. Its captured output stays in memory and the row cleans up about five minutes after the command exits.

nodes.label: Worktree isolation of file edits
nodes.rationale: Every background session starts in your working directory and, before editing files, Claude moves it into an isolated git worktree under .claude/worktrees/ so parallel sessions read the same checkout but each writes to its own. Claude skips the worktree when already inside a linked worktree, when the target file is inside one, outside a git repository with no hook, or for writes outside the working directory.

nodes.label: worktree.bgIsolation setting
nodes.rationale: Setting worktree.bgIsolation to none in a project's .claude/settings.json turns off worktree isolation for that repository, so background sessions edit the working copy directly without moving into a worktree first.

nodes.label: WorktreeCreate hook
nodes.rationale: Configuring a WorktreeCreate hook lets Claude isolate edits the same way outside git, for a different version control system. When the hook fails in a non-git directory Claude skips isolation and edits in place, while inside a git repository Claude Code blocks writes to the shared checkout until the session moves into a worktree.

nodes.label: Preserve-the-work instruction
nodes.rationale: When a background session has made code changes in a worktree Claude entered, Claude Code instructs Claude to preserve the work before finishing so it survives deleting the session: commit without asking and push when there is a remote, open a draft pull request when the task calls for it, never push to main or force-push or merge, and defer to your own git instructions.

nodes.label: Deleting a session
nodes.rationale: Deleting with Ctrl+X twice in agent view, or with claude rm, removes the session from the list while the conversation transcript stays on your machine through claude --resume. Agent view removes a Claude-created worktree including uncommitted changes, whereas claude rm keeps a worktree that has uncommitted changes.

nodes.label: Kept cases that refuse a delete
nodes.rationale: Neither agent view nor claude rm removes a worktree holding commits Claude Code cannot confirm are saved elsewhere, or one another running session is using or has locked; the worktree and session are kept and the reason named, showing as not deleted on the row. Commits on a remote, or on the local default branch checked out in the main checkout, do not block the delete.

nodes.label: /resume picker in the dispatch input
nodes.rationale: On Claude Code v2.1.212 or later a bare /resume in the dispatch input opens a picker of the repository's past sessions, newest first and including ones deleted from the list, and Enter resumes the selected session as a background session that rejoins the list. A targeted, --cwd-scoped, safe-mode, or flag-launched view shows an attach to a session to run it hint instead.

nodes.label: Session filters
nodes.rationale: Typing in the dispatch input filters instead of dispatching: a:<name> shows sessions running the named agent, s:<state> shows sessions in a state (s:blocked covers everything waiting on you), a #number or pull/merge request URL shows the session working on it, and any other URL matches the session whose first prompt contained it.

nodes.label: Agent view keyboard shortcuts
nodes.rationale: Pressing ? lists every shortcut. Arrows move between rows, Enter attaches or dispatches, Space toggles the peek panel, Ctrl+S switches grouping, Ctrl+T pins, Ctrl+R renames, Ctrl+G opens the prompt in $EDITOR, Ctrl+X stops and deletes, Shift+arrows reorder, and Esc closes the panel, clears the input or exits.

nodes.label: Grouping and ordering the list
nodes.rationale: Agent view groups sessions with Ready for review and Needs input above Working and Completed; the group names are not one-to-one with states, since a session moves to Ready for review when it has an open pull request and Completed collects finished, failed and stopped sessions. Ctrl+S switches to grouping by directory and the choice persists across runs.

nodes.label: Pinning a session
nodes.rationale: Pressing Ctrl+T pins a session to the top of its group and keeps its process running while idle. A pinned session is exempt from the supervisor's idle stop, and when the host runs low on memory the supervisor stops idle non-pinned sessions first.

nodes.label: Idle session process stop
nodes.rationale: Once a session has finished and sat unattached for about an hour, the supervisor stops its process to free resources; the transcript and state stay on disk and the next attach or reply starts a fresh process from where it left off. When every session has finished and no terminal is connected the supervisor itself exits.

nodes.label: The supervisor process
nodes.rationale: Background sessions are hosted by a per-user supervisor process, separate from your terminal and from agent view, that starts automatically the first time you background a session or open agent view. It authenticates with the same stored credentials as interactive sessions and makes no network connections beyond the model API.

nodes.label: Pre-warmed worker
nodes.rationale: The supervisor keeps one pre-warmed worker process ready so a dispatch starts without a cold-launch delay: on dispatch it assigns that worker, applies the session's directory, settings and credentials, then starts a replacement. If no healthy pre-warmed worker is available it launches a fresh process instead.

nodes.label: Unexpected-exit restart safeguards
nodes.rationale: The supervisor restarts a session whose process exits unexpectedly, with three safeguards: a session already recorded done, failed or stopped is not restarted unless an undelivered reply is waiting; ending a backgrounded session's process yourself marks it stopped rather than restarting it; and a restarted session is told it was restarted so it can re-verify time-sensitive context.

nodes.label: Background-work handoff across process restarts
nodes.rationale: Background work the session started at the top level is handed off when its process is stopped, restarted or updated, including on Windows: a finished shell command is reported with its output, a dynamic workflow resumes with running subagents starting over, and a background subagent resumes from its own transcript. Work living only inside the process stops with it.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BG_EXIT_HANDOFF
nodes.rationale: Setting CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BG_EXIT_HANDOFF to 1 stops all of a session's background work along with its process instead of handing it off to the next process.

nodes.label: Auto-update restart of the supervisor
nodes.rationale: The supervisor watches the installed Claude Code binary on disk - a local file watch, not a network check - and restarts into the new version after the auto-updater replaces it; detached background sessions keep running and the new supervisor reconnects. It then restarts remaining idle sessions onto the new version a few at a time, and never moves a session onto an older version.

nodes.label: Where session state is stored
nodes.rationale: Session state lives under the Claude Code config directory, or CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR when set, which runs a separate supervisor instance: ~/.claude/daemon.log holds the supervisor log, daemon/roster.json the list of running sessions used to reconnect, jobs/<id>/state.json the per-session state, and jobs/<id>/tmp/ a scratch directory removed when the session is deleted.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_JOB_DIR
nodes.rationale: Each background session has CLAUDE_JOB_DIR set to its ~/.claude/jobs/<id> directory, so shell commands the session runs can write temporary files to $CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp without colliding with parallel sessions and without prompting for write permission.

nodes.label: Shell session-management commands
nodes.rationale: Every background session has a short ID, its directory name under ~/.claude/jobs/, usable from the shell: claude agents opens the view, attach opens a session in the terminal, logs prints recent output, stop ends it, respawn restarts it (or --all for every running session), rm removes it, and claude daemon status or stop --any manages the supervisor.

nodes.label: claude agents --json
nodes.rationale: claude agents --json prints active sessions as a JSON array and exits, with --all adding completed background sessions and --cwd limiting the list. Entries always carry cwd, kind and startedAt, add id and state for background sessions, pid and status while the process is alive, waitingFor when blocked, and sessionId and name when set.

nodes.label: Dispatch defaults
nodes.rationale: Passing --permission-mode, --model, --effort or --agent when opening agent view sets defaults for every session dispatched from it, shown in the footer below the dispatch input. --agent falls back to the agent setting or the built-in catch-all claude agent, and --restricted (v2.1.248 or later) starts every dispatched session in restricted mode.

nodes.label: Permission mode inheritance
nodes.rationale: A background session's permission mode depends on how it started: backgrounding with /bg or the left arrow keeps the mode the session was in, dispatching from an agent view opened with the left arrow inherits the originating session's mode, and dispatching from a shell-started claude agents or claude --bg starts the way a new session in that directory would unless dispatch defaults say otherwise.

nodes.label: Bypass-permissions disclaimer
nodes.rationale: Claude Code refuses claude --bg --permission-mode bypassPermissions until you have accepted the bypass disclaimer by running claude --dangerously-skip-permissions once interactively, since that mode lets an unwatched session act without approval. Passing the flags to claude agents shows the same disclaimer.

nodes.label: bypassPermissions in background sessions
nodes.rationale: bypassPermissions lets a session act without approval. Carrying --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions through backgrounding keeps the mode reachable in the Shift+Tab cycle without granting anything new, and a session launched in bypassPermissions stays in it across a supervisor restart.

nodes.label: What persists across supervisor restarts
nodes.rationale: The permission mode, model and effort chosen for a background session, plus the configuration flags it carries and a name set with /rename or Ctrl+R, all persist when the supervisor stops and restarts its process. Effort taken from settings rather than a flag is re-read from settings.json at each process start.

nodes.label: Dispatch model and its override
nodes.rationale: The model in the agent view header is the dispatch default, taken from the model setting in user settings. --model when opening agent view overrides it for the run, and typing /model <name> in the dispatch input sets a session-scoped override marked (session) in the header without writing to settings; /model default clears it.

nodes.label: Configuration flag pass-through
nodes.rationale: Agent view accepts the same configuration flags as claude - --settings, --add-dir, --plugin-dir, --mcp-config, --strict-mcp-config - applying --settings and --plugin-dir to itself and passing every configuration flag through to dispatched sessions. Flags repeat once per value, and --add-dir or --mcp-config placed before agents breaks claude agents --json.

nodes.label: Gateway endpoint forwarding
nodes.rationale: A background session does not inherit a gateway ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL from the shell that started the supervisor; a project's settings env block is the durable way to point sessions at an LLM gateway. A gateway exported in the dispatching shell reaches the worker only when the supervisor captured the same gateway environment and the session is dispatched into that directory or is your own backgrounded session.

nodes.label: --cwd list scoping
nodes.rationale: By default agent view lists every background session across all your projects. Passing --cwd narrows the list to sessions started under that directory, still including a session that moved into a worktree under that path; interactive sessions in other terminals do not appear until backgrounded, and subagents and teammates are never separate rows.

nodes.label: Dispatching to a specific directory
nodes.rationale: A new session runs in the directory agent view was opened from. To target another, open claude agents there, mention a child repository or registered in-tree worktree with @repo (directories with spaces and worktrees added outside the repository are not listed), or cd and run claude --bg. When grouped by directory, dispatching targets the selected row's directory.

nodes.label: Agent view notifications
nodes.rationale: While agent view is open Claude Code sends a notification through the configured preferredNotifChannel when a local background session starts needing input, finishes, or fails, and fires the Notification hook with the agent_needs_input or agent_completed type. Scheduled /loop sessions notify only when they need input, and the terminal tab title shows the awaiting-input count.

nodes.label: Turning agent view off
nodes.rationale: Setting disableAgentView to true, or the CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AGENT_VIEW environment variable, turns off background agents and agent view entirely; administrators can enforce it through managed settings. With it off, /fork keeps the older forked-subagent behavior and /subtask is unavailable.

nodes.label: Quota consumption of parallel sessions
nodes.rationale: Background sessions consume your subscription usage the same as interactive sessions, so running ten agents in parallel uses quota roughly ten times as fast as running one. Each dispatched session uses quota independently, which is the reason to check the limitations before dispatching many at once.

nodes.label: Sleep preservation and wake reconnection
nodes.rationale: Sleep alone does not stop sessions: they are preserved across sleep, their processes resume on wake and the supervisor reconnects instead of treating the gap as idle. A session that was mid-response when the machine slept can come back unresponsive, and opening it makes the supervisor restart its process and continue the interrupted response.

nodes.label: Failed or stopped after shutdown
nodes.rationale: Shutting down or restarting the machine stops running background sessions. A session waiting on input stays under Needs input; any other session that last progressed within 48 hours shows as failed and restarts on attach or reply, while past 48 hours it shows as stopped with ended while the background service was off and needs a second Enter to resume.

nodes.label: claude daemon stop --any --keep-workers
nodes.rationale: When attaching, peeking or claude logs reports that the background service did not respond, the supervisor has likely stalled; stopping it lets the next claude agents start a fresh one. Passing --keep-workers leaves background sessions running so the new supervisor reconnects to them, while without it the command ends those sessions too.

nodes.label: Could not resolve authentication method
nodes.rationale: A background dispatch failing with Could not resolve authentication method while interactive sessions authenticate normally means no stored credential was available to the supervisor process itself, since the supervisor supplies a fresh credential snapshot when it assigns a pre-warmed worker. Confirm /login or an API key, then stop the supervisor so the next start reads your credentials.

nodes.label: macOS protected-folder access
nodes.rationale: On macOS the background session host runs as its own process and requests access to protected folders separately from your terminal, so a session can report Operation not permitted reading ~/Desktop, ~/Documents or ~/Downloads. Grant access under Privacy and Security > Files and Folders; the native installer's entry persists across updates while Homebrew or npm entries show the binary path.

nodes.label: macOS local-network permission
nodes.rationale: On macOS 15 and later the system blocks a process from reaching local-network devices until permission is granted, so a LAN-targeting command can fail with connect: no route to host in a background session even when it works in a foreground terminal. The first such command triggers the Local Network prompt; granting it once restores parity.

nodes.label: Conversation already open elsewhere
nodes.rationale: Two processes cannot write to the same transcript, so Claude Code refuses to start a stopped session whose saved conversation is already open in another live process: a terminal resume shows Open in a terminal and Can't open - this session is running in another terminal, while another non-interactive process shows that the conversation is already open. A reply typed with the refused attempt is saved for the next start.

nodes.label: No saved transcript
nodes.rationale: A stopped session backgrounded from another conversation and stopped before its first response finished has nothing to resume, because until then the conversation lives only in the session it came from; claude attach refuses with This session has no saved transcript. Agent view offers a second Enter to restart the session fresh, and the original conversation stays intact.

nodes.label: Terminal host died or stopped responding
nodes.rationale: The supervisor runs each background session's terminal in its own host process and offers a restart when it dies or stops responding, with the conversation saved and resumed. On Linux and WSL it polls every few seconds and marks the session failed; an open producing no output for about ten seconds ends with a restart offer, and a shell-command row is never restarted because that would run the command again.

nodes.label: possibly low memory note
nodes.rationale: When a background session's process exits before it finishes starting and the host reports low memory, the row's status adds possibly low memory - free some up and retry. The note is a hypothesis, added only when the process exited silently without writing an error and without a signal; a process that did write an error shows that error instead.

nodes.label: Research preview status and limitations
nodes.rationale: Agent view is in research preview: the interface and keyboard shortcuts may change, sessions are local to your machine and stop if it shuts down, quota is consumed per session, and Claude-created worktrees are deleted with the session in agent view unless a kept case applies.

nodes.label: Version history of agent view
nodes.rationale: The page carries a version-history table from v2.1.139, where agent view was introduced as a research preview, through v2.1.251, recording when each flag and behavior arrived - --cwd at v2.1.141, the configuration flags at v2.1.142, worktree.bgIsolation at v2.1.143, --agent at v2.1.157, the dispatch /model override at v2.1.172, /fork as a background copy at v2.1.212, and gateway forwarding for cloud providers at v2.1.251. Older versions reject unsupported flags with an unknown option error.

nodes.label: Voice dictation in agent view inputs
nodes.rationale: With voice dictation enabled, holding or tapping the push-to-talk key while the peek panel's reply input is focused dictates a reply instead of typing it, and the same works in the dispatch input at the bottom of agent view.

nodes.label: Task list moves with the conversation
nodes.rationale: Claude's task list moves to the background session together with the conversation when you background it, so the checklist is intact when you return to that row; agent view also keeps the row you pressed the left arrow from bold and undimmed so you can tell which session you came from.

nodes.label: Claude Code on Amazon Bedrock
nodes.rationale: Claude Code can run against Amazon Bedrock as a third-party model platform, configured either through an interactive login wizard or through environment variables for CI and scripted enterprise rollouts.

nodes.label: Bedrock prerequisites
nodes.rationale: Before configuring Claude Code with Amazon Bedrock you need an AWS account with Bedrock access enabled, access to the desired Claude models (for example Claude Sonnet 4.6), appropriate IAM permissions, and optionally the AWS CLI if no other credential mechanism exists.

nodes.label: /setup-bedrock sign-in wizard
nodes.rationale: The login wizard, reachable by choosing 3rd-party platform then Amazon Bedrock at the login prompt or by running /setup-bedrock, asks how you authenticate to AWS, asks for a region, verifies which Claude models the account can invoke, lets you pin them, and writes the result to the env block of the user settings file (~/.claude/settings.json, or $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/settings.json).

nodes.label: Manual environment-variable setup
nodes.rationale: The manual path configures Amazon Bedrock through environment variables instead of the wizard — submit use case details, configure AWS credentials, set CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK, and pin model versions — and is the recommended route for CI or a scripted enterprise rollout to a team.

nodes.label: Use case details submission
nodes.rationale: Before invoking an Anthropic model for the first time you must submit use case details once per AWS account: select an Anthropic model from the Bedrock console Model catalog and complete the use case form. Access is granted immediately after submission.

nodes.label: PutUseCaseForModelAccess for AWS Organizations
nodes.rationale: With AWS Organizations the use case form can be submitted once from the management account via the PutUseCaseForModelAccess API, which requires the bedrock:PutUseCaseForModelAccess IAM permission; approval then extends to child accounts automatically.

nodes.label: AWS default credential provider chain
nodes.rationale: Claude Code uses the default AWS SDK credential chain, which can be fed by aws configure, static access-key environment variables, an SSO profile (AWS_PROFILE after aws sso login), or AWS Management Console credentials via aws login. Role credentials for an SSO profile are requested from the IAM Identity Center region named by the profile's sso_region, which need not match the Bedrock region.

nodes.label: AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK API key
nodes.rationale: Amazon Bedrock API keys, exported as AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK, provide a simpler authentication method without full AWS credentials; they do not go through the default provider chain and so are excluded from Claude Code's credential cache.

nodes.label: Credential caching
nodes.rationale: Claude Code resolves the AWS default credential provider chain once and keeps the credentials in memory, reusing them until five minutes before expiry or for one hour when they carry no expiration; a credential error from the API clears the cache and the retry resolves fresh credentials. Requires v2.1.207 or later.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_AWS_CRED_CACHE
nodes.rationale: Setting CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_AWS_CRED_CACHE=1 makes Claude Code resolve the AWS credential chain on every request instead of reusing cached credentials.

nodes.label: Credential chain resolve timeout
nodes.rationale: Each resolve of the credential chain times out after 60 seconds; a stalled step such as a credential_process helper waiting for unreachable input fails the request with 'AWS default-chain credential resolve timed out'. CLAUDE_CODE_AWS_CHAIN_RESOLVE_TIMEOUT_MS raises the limit for legitimately slow interactive sign-ins. Before v2.1.207 a stalled resolution waited indefinitely.

nodes.label: Advanced credential configuration
nodes.rationale: Claude Code supports automatic credential refresh for AWS SSO and corporate identity providers through two settings-file entries, awsAuthRefresh and awsCredentialExport, which have different trigger conditions.

nodes.label: awsAuthRefresh setting
nodes.rationale: awsAuthRefresh runs a command (for example `aws sso login --profile myprofile`) only when Claude Code detects expired credentials, then retries the request. It suits commands that modify the .aws directory; its output is shown to the user but interactive input is not supported.

nodes.label: awsCredentialExport setting
nodes.rationale: awsCredentialExport runs at session start and on each credential reload even when chain credentials are still valid, and is for cases where you cannot modify .aws and must return credentials directly. Its output is captured silently and must be JSON with a Credentials object; since v2.1.181 the flat `aws configure export-credentials --format process` shape is also accepted, and since v2.1.176 a valid ISO 8601 Expiration caches until five minutes before that time.

nodes.label: STS GetCallerIdentity pre-check
nodes.rationale: Before running the awsAuthRefresh command Claude Code makes an STS GetCallerIdentity call to confirm the credentials really are expired and skips the command when they still work; the check honors HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY. Before v2.1.239 it was sent directly and hung at startup on proxy-only networks.

nodes.label: SSO authentication loop behind a proxy
nodes.rationale: When a corporate VPN or TLS-inspection proxy interrupts the SSO browser flow, Claude Code reads the interrupted connection as an authentication failure, re-runs awsAuthRefresh and loops, spawning browser tabs repeatedly. The fix is to remove awsAuthRefresh and run `aws sso login` manually before starting Claude Code.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK
nodes.rationale: Exporting CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1 enables the Amazon Bedrock integration; ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_BASE_URL optionally overrides the Bedrock endpoint URL for custom endpoints or gateways. Until CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK is set, the /setup-bedrock command is hidden from the command menu and must be typed in full.

nodes.label: AWS region resolution order
nodes.rationale: As of v2.1.172 Claude Code resolves the region as AWS_REGION, then AWS_DEFAULT_REGION, then the active profile's region (shared credentials file before shared config file), then us-east-1; a value not shaped like a region name (containing a slash, dot, or space) is treated as unset. The active profile is AWS_PROFILE or `default`, and /status shows the resolved region and its source.

nodes.label: ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL_AWS_REGION
nodes.rationale: ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL_AWS_REGION overrides the AWS region used for the small/fast (Haiku-class) model on both Bedrock and Mantle; on Bedrock it has no effect unless ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL or the deprecated ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL is set.

nodes.label: Bedrock feature limitations
nodes.rationale: On Amazon Bedrock the /logout command is unavailable because authentication is handled through AWS credentials, and the WebSearch tool is not available. Settings files can hold environment variables such as AWS_PROFILE that you do not want leaked to other processes.

nodes.label: Pinning model versions
nodes.rationale: Deployments to multiple users should pin specific Bedrock model IDs with ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL, ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL and ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL so administrators control when users move to a new model; the example IDs use the `us.` cross-region inference profile prefix, and GovCloud uses `us-gov.`.

nodes.label: Built-in default models and aliases
nodes.rationale: With no pinning variables set, the primary model is Opus 5 (e.g. us.anthropic.claude-opus-5) and the small/fast model is Sonnet 4.5; the `opus` alias resolves to Opus 5 and `sonnet` to Sonnet 4.5. On v2.1.207–v2.1.218 the primary default was Opus 4.8, and before v2.1.207 it was Sonnet 4.5 with `opus` resolving to Opus 4.6.

nodes.label: ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL
nodes.rationale: Setting ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL to a model ID available in the account is what makes background tasks use a Haiku-class model on Amazon Bedrock, and is also the precondition for ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL_AWS_REGION having any effect there.

nodes.label: Background-task model selection
nodes.rationale: Background tasks such as session title generation normally use the small/fast model, but on Amazon Bedrock they use the default Sonnet model because Haiku may not be enabled in every account or region. Selecting a primary model via --model, ANTHROPIC_MODEL, the `model` setting, or ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL makes background tasks use that model, and setting ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL without ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL counts as such a selection.

nodes.label: Opus default billing risk
nodes.rationale: Because Opus models cost more per token than Sonnet, a deployment that does not pin a primary model is billed at the Opus rate once it updates to v2.1.207 or later; setting ANTHROPIC_MODEL to Sonnet 4.5's full model ID keeps Sonnet, and a deployment steering ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL without ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL keeps its steered Sonnet as the default.

nodes.label: modelOverrides setting
nodes.rationale: The ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_*_MODEL variables configure one inference profile per model family; to expose several versions of the same family in the /model picker, each routed to its own application inference profile ARN, use the modelOverrides map in the settings file. The mapping also applies to IDs passed via --model or ANTHROPIC_MODEL (since v2.1.200), and unmapped versions fall back to the built-in Bedrock ID or a profile discovered at startup.

nodes.label: Startup model checks
nodes.rationale: At startup with Bedrock configured, Claude Code verifies that the models it intends to use are accessible; if a pinned version is older than the current default and the newer one is invokable it prompts to update the pin, writing the new ID to user settings and restarting, and remembers a decline until the next default change. Pins pointing at an application inference profile ARN are skipped as administrator-managed.

nodes.label: Unpinned model fallback
nodes.rationale: When no model is pinned and the current default is unavailable in the account, Claude Code falls back for the current session and shows a notice — trying earlier versions of the default first and, for an Opus default with no available Opus version, the default Sonnet model. The fallback is not persisted. A version selected via --model/ANTHROPIC_MODEL/the model setting acts as the session's pinned default and skips the check with no fallback notice; plain aliases and unrecognized IDs such as ARNs do not act as pins.

nodes.label: Cross-region inference profile prefixes
nodes.rationale: On the Bedrock Invoke API, Claude Code resolves its built-in default models to cross-region inference profile IDs whose prefix is derived from the resolved AWS region: us-gov-* to `us-gov.`, us-* to `us.`, eu-* to `eu.`, ap-* to `apac.`, and all other regions to `global.`.

nodes.label: ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_REGION_PREFIX
nodes.rationale: ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_REGION_PREFIX (values us, eu, apac, jp, au, global; requires v2.1.224+) chooses the prefix Claude Code tries first while keeping the built-in default models. The preferred prefix is a preference, not a guarantee: with profile discovery available Claude Code tries the preferred-prefix profile, then any matching profile, then the built-in ID with the preferred prefix; without discovery it applies the prefix unchecked and requests fail with a 400 if such profiles are not enabled.

nodes.label: GovCloud prefix override
nodes.rationale: Claude Code ignores ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_REGION_PREFIX in AWS GovCloud regions, always using `us-gov.` — the only prefix that routes within the GovCloud partition — and also falls back to the region-derived prefix when the variable holds an invalid value.

nodes.label: Inference profile discovery
nodes.rationale: When Claude Code can list the inference profiles in the account it checks profile availability before applying a prefix and can discover matching profiles at startup; when profile discovery is unavailable it applies the preferred prefix blind.

nodes.label: Required IAM policy
nodes.rationale: The IAM policy for Claude Code allows bedrock:InvokeModel, bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream, bedrock:ListInferenceProfiles and bedrock:GetInferenceProfile on inference-profile, application-inference-profile and foundation-model ARNs, plus aws-marketplace:ViewSubscriptions and Subscribe conditioned on aws:CalledViaLast being bedrock.amazonaws.com. Resources may be narrowed to specific inference profile ARNs.

nodes.label: bedrock:GetInferenceProfile permission
nodes.rationale: bedrock:GetInferenceProfile lets Claude Code resolve an application inference profile ARN to its backing foundation model so it can choose the correct request shape. Without it Claude Code recovers by retrying once with the alternate shape, costing an extra round-trip per new model — most often in AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK deployments whose token policy is narrower than a full IAM role.

nodes.label: Dedicated AWS account recommendation
nodes.rationale: The docs recommend creating a dedicated AWS account for Claude Code to simplify cost tracking and access control.

nodes.label: 1M token context window on Bedrock
nodes.rationale: Claude Sonnet 5, Opus 4.6 and later, and Sonnet 4.6 support the 1M token context window on Amazon Bedrock. Sonnet 5 always runs with the 1M window on both the Invoke API and Mantle with no [1m] variant; for the other Invoke-API models the extended window is enabled by selecting a 1M variant, either through the setup wizard or by appending [1m] to a manually pinned model ID.

nodes.label: Bedrock service tiers
nodes.rationale: ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_SERVICE_TIER set to default, flex or priority trades cost against latency and is sent as the X-Amzn-Bedrock-Service-Tier header on each request; tier availability varies by model and region, and reserved capacity instead uses a provisioned throughput ARN as the model ID.

nodes.label: AWS Bedrock Guardrails
nodes.rationale: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails implement content filtering for Claude Code: create and publish a Guardrail, then pass X-Amzn-Bedrock-GuardrailIdentifier and X-Amzn-Bedrock-GuardrailVersion via ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS in the settings file, enabling Cross-Region inference on the Guardrail when using cross-region inference profiles. Headers delivered through a Claude apps gateway policy count as settings that need approval.

nodes.label: Prompt caching on Bedrock
nodes.rationale: DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING=1 turns prompt caching off and ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H=1 requests a 1-hour cache TTL instead of the 5-minute default, billed at a higher rate. Prompt caching may not be available in all Bedrock regions — cache token counts staying at zero is the signal to check AWS's supported models and regions.

nodes.label: Bedrock Invoke API
nodes.rationale: Claude Code talks to Amazon Bedrock through the Invoke API (InvokeModelWithResponseStream) and does not support the Converse API; models are addressed by inference profile ID, which is also the remedy for an 'on-demand throughput isn't supported' error.

nodes.label: Mantle endpoint
nodes.rationale: Mantle is an Amazon Bedrock endpoint that serves Claude models through the native Anthropic API shape rather than the Bedrock Invoke API, using the same AWS credentials, IAM permissions and awsAuthRefresh configuration. /status shows the provider as 'Amazon Bedrock (Mantle)' when it is active.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_USE_MANTLE
nodes.rationale: CLAUDE_CODE_USE_MANTLE=1 routes requests to the Mantle endpoint, whose URL Claude Code constructs from the AWS region (resolved with the same precedence as Bedrock as of v2.1.172); ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_MANTLE_BASE_URL overrides that URL for a custom endpoint or gateway.

nodes.label: Mantle model IDs
nodes.rationale: Mantle model IDs are prefixed with `anthropic.` and carry no version suffix, for example anthropic.claude-sonnet-5 or anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5; availability depends on what the organization has been granted, with additional IDs listed in AWS onboarding materials. Mantle has its own lineup, so Bedrock inference profile IDs such as us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6 do not work there.

nodes.label: Running Mantle alongside the Invoke API
nodes.rationale: Setting both CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK and CLAUDE_CODE_USE_MANTLE lets one session call both endpoints: model IDs matching the Mantle format go to Mantle and all others to the Bedrock Invoke API. With both active /status shows 'Amazon Bedrock + Amazon Bedrock (Mantle)'.

nodes.label: availableModels picker setting
nodes.rationale: Listing a Mantle model ID in availableModels surfaces it in the /model picker as a custom option routed to Mantle, and simultaneously restricts the picker to the listed entries; because the Mantle ID and the bare alias resolve to the same family the merge keeps only the more specific entry, so version prefixes or full IDs must also be listed to stay selectable.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_MANTLE_AUTH
nodes.rationale: When a centralized LLM gateway injects AWS credentials server-side, CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_MANTLE_AUTH=1 disables client-side authentication so Claude Code sends Mantle requests without SigV4 signatures or x-api-key headers, paired with ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_MANTLE_BASE_URL pointing at the gateway.

nodes.label: Streaming content-type through a gateway
nodes.rationale: Bedrock streams InvokeModelWithResponseStream responses as a binary event stream with Content-Type application/vnd.amazon.eventstream, and a gateway must forward the body and headers unmodified. A rewritten Content-Type (commonly text/event-stream) makes Claude Code reject the response with an error beginning 'Bedrock streaming response has content-type'; a dropped header makes it assume the event stream, and a gateway that both drops the header and re-emits SSE forces a slower non-streaming path.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BEDROCK_CONTENT_TYPE_DEFAULT
nodes.rationale: Setting CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BEDROCK_CONTENT_TYPE_DEFAULT=1 makes Claude Code read the body as server-sent events, restoring streaming when a gateway both drops the Content-Type header and re-emits the stream as SSE. A gateway that converts the stream to SSE is no longer serving the Bedrock API and should instead be connected as an LLM gateway via ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL.

nodes.label: Zero token counts in /context
nodes.rationale: /context counts per-tool-group tokens by sending tool schemas to the Bedrock count-tokens API; before v2.1.196 Bedrock rejected that request because the schemas carried unaccepted fields, so every tool group showed 0 tokens while other rows such as messages and memory files were unaffected. Updating to v2.1.196 or later fixes it.

nodes.label: Mantle endpoint errors
nodes.rationale: If /status does not show 'Amazon Bedrock (Mantle)' the variable is not reaching the process; a 403 with valid credentials means the AWS account has not been granted access to the requested model; and a 400 naming the model ID means that model is not served on Mantle, so a Mantle-format ID or dual-endpoint mode is required.

nodes.label: Region troubleshooting
nodes.rationale: For region issues, check model availability with `aws bedrock list-inference-profiles --region your-region`, switch to a supported region via AWS_REGION, or use inference profiles for cross-region access.

nodes.label: Bedrock troubleshooting
nodes.rationale: The troubleshooting section collects the known Bedrock failure modes: SSO authentication loops behind corporate proxies, region and throughput errors, streaming failures behind a gateway, zero token counts in /context, and Mantle endpoint errors.

nodes.label: Claude Code artifact
nodes.rationale: An artifact is a live, interactive web page that Claude Code publishes from a session to a private URL on claude.ai. It is opened in a browser and updates in place as the session continues, and it can be kept private, shared with an organization, or published to a public link.

nodes.label: When to use an artifact
nodes.rationale: Use an artifact when terminal text is the wrong medium: output easier to look at and interact with than to read line by line. Examples given are walking a reviewer through a PR with annotated diffs, rendering a dashboard from data the session pulled, laying out options side by side, keeping an investigation timeline during a long task, and sending a teammate a link instead of pasting output into Slack.

nodes.label: What an artifact is not
nodes.rationale: An artifact is a capture of work: one self-contained page with no backend, so it cannot store form input or serve multiple routes, and its only path to outside data at view time is calling MCP connectors. A hosted internal tool with a backend should be deployed on your own infrastructure instead.

nodes.label: Creating an artifact
nodes.rationale: Claude may publish an artifact on its own when the output suits a page, or the user can ask for one by naming the feature or describing the visual output in plain language. After the first publish Claude prints the URL and the browser opens to the new page; Ctrl+] reopens the most recent artifact from the terminal.

nodes.label: Page written to a temporary file outside the project
nodes.rationale: Unless the user names a location, Claude writes the page to an HTML or Markdown file in a temporary directory outside the project, then publishes that file.

nodes.label: Publishing goes through the session's permission mode
nodes.rationale: Publishing a new artifact is gated by the session's permission mode, which decides whether the user is prompted before the page is uploaded to claude.ai.

nodes.label: Auto mode publishes via a classifier
nodes.rationale: In Auto mode the classifier reviews the publish instead of prompting the user, so Claude can publish a page without the user seeing a prompt. Which mode sessions start in depends on the plan.

nodes.label: Manual and Accept edits modes prompt for permission
nodes.rationale: In Manual and Accept edits modes Claude Code asks for permission, naming the file, that it uploads to claude.ai (Anthropic's servers) to host as a titled page private to the user until shared; the user selects Yes to publish.

nodes.label: Cases where Claude asks again after the first approval
nodes.rationale: After one approval Claude Code republishes without asking, but asks again when Claude declares a runtime capability such as connector calls, when the artifact has since been shared publicly, or when it has been shared with specific people or the organization with the latest version chosen as the version viewers see.

nodes.label: Artifact title and tab emoji
nodes.rationale: Claude picks the artifact's title and an emoji for its browser-tab icon; both appear in the claude.ai gallery and in shared links, so a specific title or icon must be requested in the prompt.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_ARTIFACT_AUTO_OPEN
nodes.rationale: Setting CLAUDE_CODE_ARTIFACT_AUTO_OPEN=0 in the environment stops the browser from opening automatically when a new artifact is published.

nodes.label: A local HTML file with no link means artifacts are not enabled
nodes.rationale: If Claude responds that it cannot publish, or writes a local HTML file without returning a link, the artifact tool is not enabled for that session and the Availability requirements should be checked.

nodes.label: Updating an artifact
nodes.rationale: Asking Claude to revise the page (or letting a long-running task republish as it progresses) makes Claude edit the underlying file and publish again to the same URL. Anyone with the page open sees the update in place.

nodes.label: Each publish becomes a version
nodes.rationale: Every publish becomes a version of the artifact, and the Share control in the page header lets the author choose which version viewers see.

nodes.label: Updating from a different session needs the URL
nodes.rationale: To update an artifact from a different session you must give Claude its URL or attach it with /artifacts; without either, a new session creates a new artifact instead of updating the existing one.

nodes.label: /artifacts command
nodes.rationale: /artifacts lists every artifact you own and every artifact shared with you; o opens one in the browser, c copies its link, and Enter attaches it to the current session (before v2.1.216 Enter opened it instead). The list is read from the claude.ai account, so it survives a new session or /clear, and requires Claude Code v2.1.208 or later.

nodes.label: Share control in the page header
nodes.rationale: A new artifact is visible only to its author; sharing is done by opening the artifact in a browser and using the Share control in the page header, which also links to the author's gallery.

nodes.label: Artifact gallery at claude.ai/code/artifacts
nodes.rationale: The gallery at claude.ai/code/artifacts lists every artifact the user has created, and is linked from the artifact page header.

nodes.label: Publisher attribution to viewers
nodes.rationale: On an artifact shared within the organization the publisher's name appears in the title menu, and on a public artifact it appears in the header for signed-in viewers in the same organization. A viewer who is not signed in or is outside the organization sees the label 'Content is user-generated and unverified.' instead.

nodes.label: Sharing within your organization
nodes.rationale: On Team and Enterprise plans an author can grant access to specific people in the organization or to everyone in it; viewers sign in to claude.ai as members of that organization to see the page.

nodes.label: Public link sharing
nodes.rationale: A public link can be opened by anyone on the internet with no claude.ai sign-in. On Pro and Max plans a public link is the only way to share an artifact; on Team and Enterprise plans public sharing is off until an Owner enables it for the organization.

nodes.label: Editor role on a shared artifact
nodes.rationale: People you share with are viewers by default and cannot change the page; on Team and Enterprise plans you can switch a person's role from viewer to editor in the share dialog. An editor publishes new versions by giving Claude the URL or attaching it from /artifacts, and everyone with the page open sees each update live.

nodes.label: Comments on an artifact
nodes.rationale: Only an artifact shared within your organization takes comments; the people you share it with can leave comment threads on the page and Claude can read and reply to them. Requires Claude Code v2.1.221 or later and a Team or Enterprise plan.

nodes.label: Thread activation for Claude
nodes.rationale: Someone who can edit the artifact activates a thread by sending a comment with Send to Claude or mentioning @claude in it. Claude can reply to or resolve only an activated thread; other threads stay open until a person resolves them on the page, and viewers see each reply attributed to Claude via the author.

nodes.label: When Claude cannot read comments
nodes.rationale: If Claude says it cannot read comments, check three things: that Claude Code is v2.1.221 or later; that this is not the first session since installing or upgrading from before v2.1.221 (start a new session and ask again); and that feature-flag fetching has not been turned off.

nodes.label: Claude replying to comments on its own
nodes.rationale: After a session publishes an artifact, Claude Code watches it for comments for as long as the session runs; a sent comment reaches the session immediately and Claude can read the thread and reply without being asked. Requires v2.1.228 or later, and no watching happens if feature-flag fetching is off. If the comment-delivery service becomes unavailable, Claude Code retries for a while and then stops watching.

nodes.label: Permission mode decides the auto-reply behaviour
nodes.rationale: The permission mode decides what happens when a sent comment arrives: Claude replies on its own (showing 'Auto-replied to comment thread' or 'Auto-edited Artifact'), waits for approval to read then to post (showing 'Comments are waiting on Artifact'), or pauses entirely in plan mode until the user leaves plan mode and asks.

nodes.label: 60 sent comments per hour per artifact
nodes.rationale: Claude stops replying on its own to an artifact after it handles 60 sent comments or thread activations on that artifact within an hour; the user sees 'Comments are waiting on Artifact' once, and Claude resumes as that hour's comments age out.

nodes.label: Three ways to stop automatic replies
nodes.rationale: Ctrl+C once at an idle prompt pauses replying on every watched artifact until the next message; stopping the task in /tasks stops replies on that artifact until replies are resumed there, surviving both a republish and a later session resume; and pressing Ctrl+X Ctrl+K twice within 3 seconds stops replies on every artifact for the rest of the session, undoable only by restarting, not by asking Claude to resume.

nodes.label: /tasks lists watched artifacts
nodes.rationale: Running /tasks shows each artifact the session is watching, listed as a live-updates task, and is where an individual artifact's automatic replies can be stopped.

nodes.label: Public sharing turns comments off
nodes.rationale: Viewers cannot comment on a publicly shared artifact; the page reads 'Comments aren't available while this Artifact is shared publicly.' An artifact that already has comment threads must have those threads deleted before it can be switched to a public link.

nodes.label: MCP connector calls from a published page
nodes.rationale: An artifact can call MCP connectors each time someone views it, so the page shows current data rather than a snapshot from the building session. Available on Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise plans and requires Claude Code v2.1.209 or later; on earlier versions the page ships with whatever data the session gathered.

nodes.label: Declared connector allowlist
nodes.rationale: Claude declares which connectors the page may call as part of publishing, and the page cannot call connectors outside that declaration. Only connectors from the author's claude.ai account qualify.

nodes.label: Local MCP servers cannot be called by the published page
nodes.rationale: Local MCP servers configured in Claude Code, such as those from .mcp.json, can supply data while Claude builds the page, but the published page cannot call them.

nodes.label: Connector calls run on the viewer's account
nodes.rationale: A published page's connector call uses the account of the person viewing the page, not the publisher's, so two people opening the same dashboard can see different data. The page never sees anyone's credentials; claude.ai makes the calls on the page's behalf.

nodes.label: Each viewer approves connector access
nodes.rationale: claude.ai asks each viewer for permission before the page's first connector call. A viewer who declines, or who has not connected a connector the page uses, still sees the page but without its live sections; a denial lasts for that page load and reloading brings the ask back.

nodes.label: Viewer-triggered connector actions with side effects
nodes.rationale: A page can offer controls that invoke connector tools with side effects, such as posting a message or updating an issue, and the action goes through the account of whoever selects the control.

nodes.label: Live data fetch and browser-side caching
nodes.rationale: The page fetches data when it loads and can refresh on an interval or from a refresh control. Responses are cached in the viewer's browser, so a reopened page renders from the cached responses immediately and then updates with fresh results.

nodes.label: Fallback message naming the required connector
nodes.rationale: When planning to share a connector-backed page, ask Claude to include a fallback message in each live section naming the connector it needs, so a viewer missing that connection sees what to connect instead of an empty section.

nodes.label: A connector-backed artifact cannot be public
nodes.rationale: An artifact that calls connectors cannot be shared to a public link on any plan. On Team and Enterprise plans it can be kept private or shared within the organization; on Pro and Max, where public is the only sharing route, it stays private to the author.

nodes.label: Empty live sections for a viewer
nodes.rationale: When a connector-backed page renders but its live sections stay empty for a viewer, the causes to work through are: the viewer has not connected the connector (connectors are per-account; add one under Settings > Connectors and reload), the viewer declined the permission ask, or connector calls are turned off for the organization.

nodes.label: What you can build
nodes.rationale: An artifact is a single HTML page, so anything expressible in HTML, CSS and inline JavaScript is in scope; the documented recurring patterns are walking through a change, comparing alternatives, tuning with interactive controls, bringing a result back to the session, and tracking work in progress.

nodes.label: Pattern: walk through a change
nodes.rationale: Ask for a page that renders a diff or design change with annotations beside the relevant lines, colour-coded by severity, so reviewers read the reasoning next to the code instead of reconstructing it from a description.

nodes.label: Pattern: compare alternatives
nodes.rationale: Ask for several variants on one page — layouts, copy, API shapes, or implementation plans — laid out as a grid with a one-line tradeoff under each, so they can be evaluated against one another.

nodes.label: Pattern: tune with interactive controls
nodes.rationale: Ask for sliders, toggles or input fields bound to the thing being adjusted — for example easing curve, duration and delay on a transition, with the animation shown live — so values can be explored directly instead of described.

nodes.label: Pattern: bring the result back to the session
nodes.rationale: An artifact can act as a lightweight editor for a decision handed back to Claude: ask for an export control (such as a 'Copy as prompt' button on a draggable triage board) that produces text to paste into the terminal, so interacting with the page flows back into the session.

nodes.label: Pattern: track work in progress
nodes.rationale: Ask Claude to keep an artifact current while a long task runs — for example turning a migration plan into a checklist that is ticked off as items complete, with a note for anything skipped — so anyone with the link can follow along without reading the terminal.

nodes.label: Built-in artifact design skill
nodes.rationale: Claude applies a built-in design skill when building an artifact, so pages get a deliberate palette, typography and layout without extra prompting; it also looks for an existing design system in the project first. Requires Claude Code v2.1.182 or later.

nodes.label: Design token precedence: prompt > design system > Claude
nodes.rationale: Design tokens are the named colour, typography and spacing values a design system reuses; recording them where Claude can find them (CLAUDE.md or a theme file) keeps artifacts on brand. Claude treats the project's design system as higher precedence than its own choices, and the prompt as higher precedence than both.

nodes.label: Google Fonts is the only external font source
