nodes.rationale: The SSRF guard rejects loopback destinations unless CLAUDE_GATEWAY_ALLOW_LOOPBACK=1 is set in the gateway's environment: a loopback OIDC issuer such as http://localhost:8081 is rejected, and an http://localhost OTLP destination passes config validation but has every export blocked with ECONNREFUSED_SSRF. It also applies on the proxied IdP path.

nodes.label: oidc.form_action_origins
nodes.rationale: Additional origins for the /device page's Content-Security-Policy form-action directive. The gateway already allows 'self' and the discovered authorization_endpoint origin, but Chrome enforces form-action against the entire redirect chain, so every origin an authorization request may redirect through (Azure AD federated to ADFS, hub-spoke Okta, an SSO interceptor) must be listed.

nodes.label: session section
nodes.rationale: A required section shaping the bearer tokens the gateway mints after sign-in: jwt_secret, at least 32 bytes of entropy signing the gateway's HS256 bearer tokens, and ttl_hours, the token lifetime.

nodes.label: jwt_secret rotation via secret array
nodes.rationale: jwt_secret accepts a single string or an array for rotation: index 0 signs and all entries verify. To rotate, prepend a new secret, wait ttl_hours, then drop the old one.

nodes.label: session.ttl_hours
nodes.rationale: Gateway bearer token lifetime, default 1 hour; the CLI silently refreshes before expiry when the IdP issues refresh tokens. A shorter lifetime deprovisions faster, a longer one makes fewer IdP round-trips, and where offline_access is unavailable it should be raised to 8 or 12 to avoid hourly browser logins. It also bounds how quickly a group-membership change takes effect.

nodes.label: store section (PostgreSQL)
nodes.rationale: A required section pointing the gateway at its PostgreSQL database, which holds device grants and rate-limit counters. The gateway runs its own schema migrations at boot and on upgrade, so the role needs rights to create and alter tables; password belongs in store.password rather than the URL, and max_connections defaults to a conservative 5 per replica.

nodes.label: Device-grant rendezvous
nodes.rationale: The device-grant rendezvous, where the browser callback writes and the polling CLI reads, needs cross-replica state — which is why postgres_url is required rather than optional.

nodes.label: upstreams section
nodes.rationale: A required, ordered list saying where inference goes — Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry. The gateway forwards to the first upstream that resolves the requested model. Cloud provider clients are built once at startup and their SDKs refresh credentials internally, so rotating cloud credentials needs no restart.

nodes.label: Failover status codes
nodes.rationale: 5xx, 429, 401, 403, 404, timeouts and missing-endpoint 501 fail over to the next upstream; other 4xx does not, because those errors are attributable to the request rather than the upstream. 429 is per-upstream capacity so provisioned throughput overflows to on-demand, and 404 is per-upstream model availability. Failover on 404 requires gateway v2.1.198 or later.

nodes.label: Upstream error-response selection
nodes.rationale: A non-failover status returns that upstream's own response and no further upstreams are tried. When every attempted upstream failed in a failover-eligible way, the gateway returns the last 429, else in order the last 401/403, the last 404, the last 501, and otherwise its own 502 `all upstreams failed (N attempted)` where N counts every entry including skipped ones.

nodes.label: capability_rejected: error tokens
nodes.rationale: Cloud upstream error text can name account IDs, role ARNs and project IDs, so the gateway records the full text in the operational log and shows the developer either the upstream's message (400/413 in Anthropic's standard envelope) or a capability_rejected: token — for example Bedrock's `Input is too long for requested model.` becomes `capability_rejected: prompt_too_long`, on which Claude Code compacts automatically. Requires gateway v2.1.233 or later.

nodes.label: provider: anthropic upstream
nodes.rationale: The minimal Anthropic upstream takes an API key from the Claude Console (auth.api_key, sent as x-api-key) or an OAuth bearer (auth.oauth_token, sent as Authorization: Bearer). Both static forms are read once at startup, so a bearer is refreshed by remounting the secret and restarting; base_url defaults to https://api.anthropic.com.

nodes.label: Workload Identity Federation auth
nodes.rationale: Instead of a static key or bearer, the Anthropic upstream can use federation_rule_id, organization_id and identity_token_file: the gateway exchanges the mounted workload OIDC JWT for a short-lived bearer and refreshes it automatically. The token file is re-read on every exchange, so rotated projected tokens are picked up without a restart.

nodes.label: forward_user_identity headers
nodes.rationale: Setting forward_user_identity: true on an anthropic upstream whose base_url is a proxy you operate makes the gateway add x-litellm-end-user-id, x-claude-gateway-user-id (the IdP sub) and x-claude-gateway-user-email so the proxy can attribute spend per developer. If the base_url is the Anthropic API the gateway refuses to start; requires Claude Code v2.1.233 or later.

nodes.label: provider: bedrock upstream
nodes.rationale: An Amazon Bedrock upstream takes a region and either an empty auth block (the AWS default credential chain: env vars, ~/.aws/credentials, ECS task role, EC2 metadata, or IRSA on EKS), explicit AWS keys, or aws_bearer_token. Explicit credentials must be complete or boot fails (since v2.1.207), and the principal needs bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream on both inference-profile and foundation-model ARNs.

nodes.label: provider: anthropicAws (Claude Platform on AWS)
nodes.rationale: Claude Platform on AWS serves the first-party Anthropic API on AWS infrastructure at aws-external-anthropic.<region>.api.aws, using first-party model IDs, honoring anthropic-beta headers and serving count_tokens, so no Bedrock-specific translation applies. It requires region and workspace_id, authenticates by API key or SigV4 (api_key wins when both are set), runs in a separate AWS account from Bedrock so a Bedrock-scoped IAM role does not authorize it, and needs Claude Code v2.1.198 or later.

nodes.label: provider: vertex (Google Cloud Agent Platform)
nodes.rationale: A vertex upstream takes region and project_id, and an empty auth block uses Application Default Credentials (GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS, GCE metadata, or GKE Workload Identity); service-account JSON key files are supported but discouraged and the field takes a path, not contents. Setting region: global lets Google route each request to an available region instead of pinning one, and the service account needs roles/aiplatform.user.

nodes.label: provider: foundry (Microsoft Foundry)
nodes.rationale: A foundry upstream derives its endpoint from resource: and authenticates preferably with use_azure_ad: true through DefaultAzureCredential (Managed Identity on AKS, ACI or App Service, the Azure CLI, or environment credentials); API keys work but are project-wide and do not rotate automatically. The identity needs the Azure AI User or Cognitive Services User role.

nodes.label: Multiple named upstreams
nodes.rationale: The same provider can appear more than once with a distinct name:, covering different regions, different accounts via different credential chains, provisioned throughput versus on-demand, and cross-provider fallback. Failing over between cloud providers, or to the direct Anthropic API, changes which agreement, geography and other terms govern the request.

nodes.label: Model-scoped routing
nodes.rationale: Only a custom model id — one that is not a built-in Claude model — skips upstreams absent from its upstream_model map. The gateway tries built-in models on every upstream in order and uses the provider's default ID where the map has no entry, so for built-in models the map changes which ID an upstream receives rather than whether it is tried.

nodes.label: models section
nodes.rationale: An optional admin-curated model list served at /v1/models and used to translate model IDs per upstream. It is required for non-US Amazon Bedrock regions, Bedrock provisioned-throughput ARNs, and Microsoft Foundry deployment names. Each key under upstream_model must match a configured upstream's name (which defaults to the provider name) or boot fails.

nodes.label: auto_include_builtin_models
nodes.rationale: A top-level flag deciding whether the built-in Claude catalog is exposed alongside the curated models list; false exposes only the configured list. With it true, Bedrock cross-region inference profiles route automatically, and region-pinned deployments still need an explicit models block.

nodes.label: admin section (spend limits)
nodes.rationale: The optional admin block enables /v1/organizations/spend_limits, which mirrors Anthropic's public Admin API, and per-developer spend enforcement on /v1/messages. It carries named write_keys and read_keys (attributable in the audit log as admin-key:<id>), admin_groups for human admins via the gateway JWT, blocked_message, retention settings, and group_limit_mode (min default, or max).

nodes.label: enforcement.fail_closed_on_error
nodes.rationale: Default false: spend enforcement fails open on a Postgres outage so inference stays up. Setting true fails closed — over-cap developers are blocked, but so is everyone else if the store is unreachable — and requires an admin block, without which the gateway refuses to start.

nodes.label: pricing section
nodes.rationale: Tells the spend meter what to charge instead of USD list price so caps and /effective reflect contracted rates; amounts stay in USD and remain an estimate, not an invoice. multiplier (default 1, greater than 0 and at most 1) scales every metered amount, and overrides give per-upstream, per-model input/output/cache_read/cache_write rates in USD per million tokens. Requires Claude Code v2.1.227 or later and an admin block.

nodes.label: Pricing override matching precedence
nodes.rationale: An override row replaces list price for requests its named upstream serves for that model, including the higher fast-mode rate. Where rows overlap the meter picks the most specific — the exact model string sent upstream, then the exact ID the client sent, then the built-in model name. An unknown upstream name fails boot, as do two rows for one upstream naming the same model; web-search requests stay at the $0.01 list price with the multiplier still applied.

nodes.label: managed section (role-based policies)
nodes.rationale: Defines role-based access policies keyed on IdP groups or email domain, evaluated in order with the first match selected and merged onto the match: {} catch-all base, served per-user at GET /managed/settings with ETag/304 caching. The gateway keeps no user directory and has no SCIM endpoint: it authorizes each request from the IdP token's claims, so lifecycle management stays in the IdP.

nodes.label: Policy merge rules by key type
nodes.rationale: Allow-lists (availableModels, permissions.allow) are fully replaced by a specific policy; deny-lists and hook arrays (permissions.deny/ask, disabledMcpjsonServers, deniedMcpServers, blockedMarketplaces, every hooks event array) take the union of base and policy so an org-wide deny or audit hook cannot be dropped by a per-role override; record-typed keys (env, modelOverrides, skillOverrides) shallow-merge.

nodes.label: Matcher values that stop the gateway at boot
nodes.rationale: At boot the gateway checks every policy's match block and the admin_groups list, and stops with a field-naming error on an empty groups list, an empty entry in groups or admin_groups, an empty email_domain, or an email_domain containing @, whitespace or a comma. Before v2.1.232 these values started the gateway and silently matched everyone, no one, or only a user whose claim contained an empty entry.

nodes.label: Policy cli block (managed-settings document)
nodes.rationale: Each cli value is a complete Claude Code managed-settings.json document expressed as YAML, applied at the managed tier above user and project settings. The gateway validates it against the schema bundled with its own installed version, so an unrecognized top-level key fails boot and a key from a newer CLI release requires upgrading the gateway first; env, pluginConfigs and keys nested under permissions stay deliberately open. The key was formerly named settings, still accepted as an alias.

nodes.label: availableModels server-side enforcement
nodes.rationale: availableModels is enforced server-side at /v1/messages as well as by the CLI, so a denied model returns 400 regardless of what the client sends and a patched client cannot bypass it. The gateway also validates the model value itself: missing or empty returns `model is required` (v2.1.228+) and a non-string returns `model must be a string` (v2.1.221+).

nodes.label: Client security approval dialog
nodes.rationale: Because managed settings arrive over the network, the CLI shows a security approval dialog before applying hooks, approval-requiring env variables, shell-execution settings such as apiKeyHelper and statusLine, sandbox binary and traffic-intercepting settings, and managed CLAUDE.md content. It protects the developer's machine from a compromised or hostile gateway, not the organization from the developer; a declining developer exits the session, and a non-interactive -p run applies the settings for that run only without recording approval.

nodes.label: Claude Desktop overlay (desktop block)
nodes.rationale: The same gateway serves Claude Desktop when its bootstrapUrl points at <listen.public_url>/user/bootstrap, but /user/bootstrap returns 404 unless the matching policy carries a desktop key (v2.1.203+). The gateway derives the model list, disabled tools and egress allowlist from the policy's cli block, fills unset keys from the match: {} base, keeps the base's restriction for disabledBuiltinTools and builtinToolPolicy, and replaces arrays and nested objects such as banner whole.

nodes.label: mcpServers rejected in a cli policy
nodes.rationale: At boot the gateway rejects mcpServers inside a policy's cli block, so MCP servers cannot be distributed per group to Claude Code clients; deploy them via the file-based managed-mcp.json on each device. Claude Desktop's managedMcpServers setting can be delivered through a policy's desktop block with v2.1.232 or later.

nodes.label: Precedence with other managed sources
nodes.rationale: When a device also has an MDM-delivered policy or a local managed-settings.json, gateway-delivered settings rank first, and a policyHelper configured locally runs only when the gateway delivers no settings. Gateway policies apply to every Claude Code invocation on the machine including claude -p runs and Agent SDK sessions; if the gateway is unreachable at startup, signed-in sessions exit with an error rather than running without their policy.

nodes.label: telemetry section (OTLP forwarding)
nodes.rationale: The CLI sends OTLP-over-HTTP metrics, logs and optional traces to the gateway, which relays them verbatim to each forward_to destination with its configured headers. Each destination URL must be https:// apart from a loopback collector, both protobuf and JSON encodings are relayed, and the CLI stamps each export with user.id, user.email and user.groups from the gateway-issued JWT so per-developer attribution needs no developer configuration.

nodes.label: Per-signal opt-in and signal sensitivity
nodes.rationale: Each forward_to destination opts into metrics, logs and traces independently, defaulting to metrics only. Metrics are aggregate counters such as token counts, request counts and latency, while logs and traces can carry full bash commands, tool inputs and file paths — anything Claude Code does on a developer's machine — so they should be enabled only on destinations whose access controls and retention warrant that data.

nodes.label: Six pushed OTEL environment variables
nodes.rationale: Configuring telemetry.forward_to together with listen.public_url turns telemetry on and pushes six variables to every connected client through /managed/settings: CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1, OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER, OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER and OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER set to otlp, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT built from public_url, and OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=http/protobuf. Traces additionally need CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA=1, which the gateway does not push.

nodes.label: HTTP tuning blocks
nodes.rationale: Four optional top-level blocks tune the HTTP surface with defaults that suit most deployments: access_control (allow_cidrs/deny_cidrs, deny checked first, default-deny when allow_cidrs is non-empty, /healthz and /readyz exempt), limits (max_request_bytes 32 MiB returning 413, plus optional header-size 431 and URL-length 414 caps), timeouts, and rate_limits.

nodes.label: timeouts.upstream_ttfb_ms
nodes.rationale: Maximum wait for the upstream's response headers (time to first byte), default 120000 ms; the response body then streams with no wall-clock cap. It applies to the direct Anthropic upstream path, while every other provider is bounded by its provider SDK's own timeout.

nodes.label: Device sign-in rate limits
nodes.rationale: rate_limits.device_authorization defaults to 30 requests per 600 seconds per IP on the unauthenticated device-authorization endpoint, and device_verify to 10 per 600 seconds on user_code submissions at /device. These limits apply only to the device-grant sign-in flow, not to /v1/messages inference, and should be raised for a large org behind a shared egress IP or NAT.

nodes.label: Client-side login keys (forceLoginGatewayUrl)
nodes.rationale: Developer machines are pointed at the gateway separately through each device's managed-settings.json — forceLoginMethod: gateway, forceLoginGatewayUrl and parentSettingsBehavior: merge — because the gateway cannot push the keys that tell the client where it is. These keys are honored only from a managed source (managed-settings.json, the macOS plist, the Windows HKLM registry, or a policy helper); a developer's own settings.json has no effect.

nodes.label: Four-step production deployment order
nodes.rationale: A production Claude apps gateway deployment follows four ordered steps: set up the identity provider, deploy the gateway container, set up operations (logs, probes, rotation, upgrades), and review the security posture. The first two are where choices are made; the last two are reference material consulted once the gateway is running.

nodes.label: Private-network-only gateway address
nodes.rationale: Claude Code only connects to a gateway whose address is private. This is a deliberate security guard, because a trusted gateway can push settings that run commands on developer machines; the gateway must sit behind an internal load balancer or VPN with a hostname resolving only to private IPs.

nodes.label: Confidential OIDC client registration
nodes.rationale: Register a confidential OAuth/OpenID Connect web application in the IdP with the single redirect URI https://<gateway>/oauth/callback, and assign it to the users or groups who should have gateway access.

nodes.label: Three IdP requirements
nodes.rationale: Any OIDC-compliant IdP works if it serves /.well-known/openid-configuration (over HTTPS in production), supports the authorization-code flow, and returns email plus optionally groups in the id_token or from the userinfo endpoint with oidc.userinfo_fallback: true. Private PKI is handled with oidc.ca_cert_pem.

nodes.label: PKCE on the authorization-code flow
nodes.rationale: PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) is on by default for the gateway's authorization-code exchange with the IdP, so an intercepted authorization code is useless. It can be disabled with oidc.use_pkce: false for IdPs that do not support it.

nodes.label: Okta org server needs userinfo_fallback
nodes.rationale: Okta's org authorization server returns a thin id_token that omits email and groups, so oidc.userinfo_fallback: true is required when it is the issuer; a custom authorization server emits them directly and needs no fallback. Okta emits groups only when the groups scope is requested and the app's claim filter allows it — userinfo_fallback cannot fill a claim the IdP was never asked for.

nodes.label: Entra emits group Object IDs
nodes.rationale: With Microsoft Entra ID the issuer is https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/v2.0, and Entra emits group Object IDs rather than names, so policy matching must use GUIDs in managed.policies.match.groups or App Roles for readable names. A tenant emitting roles instead of groups needs oidc.groups_claim: roles.

nodes.label: Google Workspace group lookup
nodes.rationale: Google's id_token carries no groups, so group-based allowed_groups or managed.policies require oidc.google_groups, which reads each user's groups through the Admin SDK Directory API with a domain-wide-delegated service account; otherwise gate on oidc.allowed_email_domains. Google also ignores offline_access, so refresh tokens need oidc.extra_auth_params: { access_type: offline, prompt: consent }.

nodes.label: Refresh tokens drive renewal and deprovisioning
nodes.rationale: Refresh tokens let the gateway renew a developer's session silently without a browser round trip, and they drive deprovisioning: when the IdP disables a user, the next refresh fails and the session ends within ttl_hours. The gateway requests offline_access by default; without refresh tokens the gateway still works but developers must re-run the browser login.

nodes.label: session.ttl_hours tradeoff
nodes.rationale: Raising session.ttl_hours to 8 or 12 keeps developers from re-logging in hourly when the IdP cannot issue refresh tokens, but the tradeoff is deprovisioning latency: without refresh tokens a disabled user keeps access until the longer TTL elapses.

nodes.label: Stateless binary coordinating through Postgres
nodes.rationale: The gateway is a single stateless Linux binary that coordinates through Postgres, so it deploys like any other stateless service — kept inside the network, reachable over HTTPS by developers and the IdP, and treated like any service holding a production credential.

nodes.label: No separate license or per-seat fee
nodes.rationale: The gateway carries no separate license or per-seat fee: it is part of the claude binary, so the cost is inference against the existing commitment plus the compute it runs on.

nodes.label: Gateway does not enforce sole model route
nodes.rationale: The gateway does not enforce that the only route to a model goes through it — a developer with their own credential can still call the provider directly. Closing that path is a network policy decision, such as blocking egress to api.anthropic.com except from the gateway.

nodes.label: skipWebFetchPreflight for blocked egress
nodes.rationale: Blocking developer egress to api.anthropic.com also breaks the WebFetch domain safety check, which each developer machine calls directly; setting skipWebFetchPreflight: true in the managed policy disables that check so the block does not break WebFetch.

nodes.label: Multiple gateways, one issuer each
nodes.rationale: Each gateway is a separate deployment with its own config, and the CLI stores trust and credentials per gateway hostname, so teams can use different gateways without conflict. Serving multiple OIDC issuers requires running separate instances.

nodes.label: Serverless constraints
nodes.rationale: Cloud Run works if min-instances is set to 1 to avoid a cold OIDC discovery, but Lambda and Cloud Functions do not work at all because the gateway is a long-running HTTP server.

nodes.label: listen.trusted_proxies and X-Forwarded-For
nodes.rationale: Every production topology puts an L7 proxy (Ingress, Cloud Run front end, ALB) in front of plain-HTTP replicas, so listen.trusted_proxies must name the proxy's source ranges for the gateway to read client IPs from X-Forwarded-For — and the header is honored only when the TCP peer is trusted. Without it every request appears to come from the proxy's IP, collapsing per-IP rate limits into one bucket and recording the proxy's IP in audit events.

nodes.label: SSE keepalive ping and proxy idle timeout
nodes.rationale: On every upstream except provider: anthropic the gateway writes an SSE ping after roughly 15 seconds of stream silence, while on provider: anthropic it passes the response through unchanged including the API's own pings. The proxy's idle timeout must exceed that keepalive interval; a default such as an ALB's 60 seconds suffices, and gateways older than v2.1.229 sent nothing at all during quiet periods.

nodes.label: Building the pinned container image
nodes.rationale: Operators build their own image around the native claude binary from a standard Claude Code release: download the Linux build for the image architecture from a pinned release, verify it against the release's GPG-signed manifest.json, and copy it into the build context. Mirror the release into an internal registry if builds cannot reach the release host, and pin the version the fleet runs.

nodes.label: glibc-based base image
nodes.rationale: The glibc build's only dynamic dependencies are glibc libraries, so a glibc-based image is the straightforward choice; musl-based images need the linux-x64-musl or linux-arm64-musl build plus additional packages.

nodes.label: Writable state directory via CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR
nodes.rationale: The gateway runs as any user, but minimal images have no writable home, so CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR must point at a writable path such as /tmp/.claude.

nodes.label: Container command and listen port
nodes.rationale: The container command is `claude gateway --config /etc/claude/gateway.yaml`, with the config file mounted read-only and secrets supplied as environment variables; the gateway listens on listen.port, default 8080.

nodes.label: Kubernetes Deployment shape
nodes.rationale: On Kubernetes the gateway runs as a plain Deployment: config from a ConfigMap and secrets from a Secret (referenced in YAML via ${file:/path/to/secret} or as environment variables), TLS terminated at the Ingress with listen.public_url set to the Ingress hostname, and readiness/liveness probes pointed at GET /readyz and GET /healthz.

nodes.label: Prefer platform workload identity over static keys
nodes.rationale: Upstream credentials should come from the platform's workload identity rather than static keys; a cross-cloud pairing such as an Amazon Bedrock upstream running on GKE instead sets explicit credentials in the upstream's auth block.

nodes.label: Cloud Run service configuration
nodes.rationale: On Cloud Run, leave listen.port at 8080 (matching Cloud Run's default PORT) or set port: ${PORT}, set public_url to the externally reachable origin, mount the config as a secret volume, and set min-instances: 1 to avoid a cold OIDC discovery on the first request.

nodes.label: public_url must be a private origin
nodes.rationale: In production public_url is normally an internal load balancer's hostname, because /login rejects public addresses and a *.run.app URL resolves to one — so the Cloud Run URL alone works only for a curl or browser smoke test. The exception is a network where *.run.app resolves privately through Private Service Connect and a Cloud DNS private zone.

nodes.label: Pushing the gateway URL via managed settings
nodes.rationale: Once the gateway serves, forceLoginMethod, forceLoginGatewayUrl and parentSettingsBehavior: "merge" must be pushed to each developer machine through managed settings — by MDM or by writing the per-OS managed-settings.json. Without this, /login shows the standard account picker with no gateway option.

nodes.label: Audit event stream
nodes.rationale: One of two stderr streams: single-line JSON per security-relevant event — config.load, session.mint, session.refresh, device.*, auth.denied, access.denied, inference, managed.serve, desktop_bootstrap.*, spend.blocked, and admin.* events. Fields vary: mint/refresh carry sub, email and client_ip; denial events carry the reason and client IP; admin.denied records the reason without the presented key material.

nodes.label: Operational logs and CLAUDE_GATEWAY_LOG_LEVEL
nodes.rationale: The second stderr stream is human-readable [gateway]-prefixed lines for boot, warnings and upstream errors, with verbosity set by CLAUDE_GATEWAY_LOG_LEVEL (debug/info/warn/error, default info). At debug the gateway logs claim NAMES and not values, so email_claim and groups_claim can be diagnosed without logging PII; the level never affects audit events, which are always emitted.

nodes.label: /healthz liveness and /readyz readiness
nodes.rationale: The gateway serves GET /healthz as a liveness probe and GET /readyz as a readiness probe, where /readyz additionally verifies the store is reachable. Both endpoints are exempt from access_control.allow_cidrs so probes keep working on a locked-down listener.

nodes.label: OAuth discovery document as boot check
nodes.rationale: /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server returns 200 only after config load, OIDC discovery, upstream client construction and Postgres migration have all succeeded, so it doubles as an end-to-end boot check.

nodes.label: Postgres outage behavior
nodes.rationale: If Postgres goes down the gateway keeps serving signed-in developers — bearer tokens validate locally against the JWT secret and refreshes do not touch the store — while new sign-ins fail because the device flow and its rate-limit counters live in Postgres. Spend-limit enforcement fails open by default during the outage and can be flipped to fail closed.

nodes.label: Readiness probe choice during a store outage
nodes.rationale: During a Postgres outage /readyz reports not-ready, so orchestrators gating traffic on readiness pull every replica at once and even servable inference fails at the load balancer; /healthz keeps passing so replicas are not restarted. Pointing readiness at /healthz instead keeps signed-in developers working, at the cost of new sign-ins failing against a replica that still reports ready.

nodes.label: IdP outage behavior
nodes.rationale: If the IdP goes down, existing sessions keep working until ttl_hours elapses while new logins and refreshes fail; a longer ttl_hours is advised for IdPs with frequent maintenance windows.

nodes.label: Three-step JWT secret rotation
nodes.rationale: Rotate the signing secret in three steps so existing sessions survive: generate a new secret and prepend it to the session.jwt_secret array, roll the deployment so new tokens sign with the new secret while old ones still verify, then after ttl_hours plus a margin remove the old secret and roll again.

nodes.label: No per-session revocation
nodes.rationale: Bearer tokens validate locally against the JWT secret, so there is no per-session revocation. Replacing the secret outright, without keeping the old one in the array, invalidates every outstanding session at once; individual offboarding is done by deprovisioning the user in the IdP, whose session then ends within ttl_hours.

nodes.label: Postgres store: five tables plus migrations
nodes.rationale: The gateway holds five data tables — kv (device grants with a 10-minute TTL and rate-limit counters), spend, spend_limits, admin_audit and principal_emails — plus a _migrations table, all created by boot-time migrations. Its database role therefore needs rights to create and alter tables, so it should point at a database or schema dedicated to the gateway to keep that grant narrow.

nodes.label: TTL loop and retention sweeps
nodes.rationale: A 30-second loop expires kv rows past their TTL and an hourly sweep enforces the retention windows on the spend tables — admin.spend_retention_months default 13, admin.audit_retention_days default 365, admin.identity_retention_days default 90 — so nothing grows without bound. Without spend limits configured, only kv is written.

nodes.label: principal_emails holds the only PII
nodes.rationale: principal_emails stores each principal's last-seen email, display name and IdP groups and is the only table containing PII; erasing a departed developer immediately means DELETE FROM principal_emails WHERE principal = '<sub>', since spend and admin_audit rows reference only the pseudonymous OIDC sub.

nodes.label: Self-migrating upgrades under an advisory lock
nodes.rationale: Replicas are stateless so a rolling restart is safe at any time, and the gateway runs schema migrations at boot, meaning deploying the new binary self-migrates the database. Concurrent replicas serialize on a Postgres advisory lock so only one applies each migration.

nodes.label: Rollback safety and config-key validation
nodes.rationale: Migrations are append-only, so rolling back to a prior binary that knows fewer migrations is safe — it ignores the extra rows. Rollback also re-validates the YAML against the older binary's schema, so a config that adopted a key introduced by the newer release fails boot on the older one and the new key must be removed first.

nodes.label: Pinned version means operator-owned patching
nodes.rationale: Because the gateway's version is pinned in the operator's own image, fixes in new Claude Code releases — including security fixes — reach the deployment only when the pin is updated and redeployed, so the gateway belongs in the same patching cadence as other services holding production credentials.

nodes.label: Data flow table
nodes.rationale: Inference flows CLI to gateway to the operator's upstream and reaches Anthropic only if the Anthropic API is a configured upstream; telemetry goes to the operator's collector, identity flows IdP to gateway to JWT to CLI, managed settings flow from the gateway YAML to the CLI, and the audit log goes from gateway stderr to the operator's aggregator — none of the latter four are ever sent to Anthropic by the gateway.

nodes.label: Threat model: untrusted developer laptops
nodes.rationale: The gateway sits inside the network perimeter, but individual developer laptops are not treated as trusted. The design accounts for that in three ways: short-lived JWTs instead of raw upstream keys, device-verification hardening, and an SSRF guard on outbound requests.

nodes.label: RFC 8628 device grant protections
nodes.rationale: The CLI-to-gateway leg uses the RFC 8628 device grant so developers hold short-lived JWTs rather than raw upstream keys, and the device-verification page enforces same-origin POST plus a per-IP rate limit per RFC 8628 §5.1.

nodes.label: SSRF guard on outbound requests
nodes.rationale: Outbound requests pass through an SSRF guard that resolves DNS, blocks link-local, cloud-metadata and loopback addresses by default, and pins the connection to the resolved IP, so operator-influenced URLs such as the IdP and OTLP destinations cannot be redirected to metadata endpoints. RFC 1918 ranges are deliberately allowed; CLAUDE_GATEWAY_ALLOW_LOOPBACK=1 relaxes the loopback block for every operator-configured URL and also skips the boot-time metadata-reachability warning.

nodes.label: Two out-of-scope threats
nodes.rationale: A compromised gateway host and a malicious OIDC provider are explicitly out of scope because they are the operator's infrastructure to secure: the host both holds the upstream credential and distributes managed settings to every developer (comparable to MDM control), and the provider signs the id_tokens the gateway trusts so it can assert any identity.

nodes.label: user_code entropy and expiry
nodes.rationale: The user_code typed into the /device verification page is 8 characters from a 20-character alphabet — 20^8, about 2.56×10^10 combinations — and it expires after 10 minutes, which is the brute-force resistance argument.

nodes.label: Per-IP rate limits on sign-in only
nodes.rationale: The gateway applies per-IP rate limits on the device-grant endpoints, configurable via rate_limits; they should be raised when many developers sign in from one shared corporate NAT address, and they apply only to the sign-in flow, never to inference.

nodes.label: Compliance posture answers
nodes.rationale: The security section collects the answers a compliance questionnaire asks: data residency, host-process traffic, client analytics, error reporting, client machines, survey ratings, transcript sharing, client updates, TLS, and vulnerability disclosure.

nodes.label: Data residency answer
nodes.rationale: The gateway's own data plane sends nothing to Anthropic unless the Anthropic API is a configured upstream, in which case the existing data-handling agreement applies to the inference path; telemetry, audit, identity and settings go only to operator-configured destinations.

nodes.label: Host-process traffic before v2.1.227
nodes.rationale: The host process is the Claude Code CLI; `claude gateway` runs under the same third-party rules as Bedrock and Google Agent Platform deployments and sends nothing to Anthropic. Before v2.1.227 it sent startup telemetry (disabled by CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1) and one credential-free HEAD request to /api/hello whose response it ignored, so blocking it at the firewall was harmless.

nodes.label: Client analytics disabled while gateway-signed-in
nodes.rationale: The CLI disables its own usage analytics, error reporting and Anthropic-bound survey rating uploads while signed in to a gateway, but before the first sign-in it still sends startup events — even on machines whose managed settings force gateway sign-in — so DISABLE_TELEMETRY must be delivered in the same client-side managed settings. Error reporting is also off whenever model requests go to any non-first-party endpoint.

nodes.label: Transcript sharing writes a local bundle
nodes.rationale: Choosing Yes on a survey's transcript-share prompt writes a local file under ~/.claude/feedback-bundles/ instead of uploading anything to Anthropic. Separately, update checks are independent of gateway traffic: DISABLE_UPDATES stops laptops fetching releases, while DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER stops only background updates.

nodes.label: TLS posture
nodes.rationale: public_url must be served over HTTPS in production, either from the gateway's own listen.tls or from a TLS-terminating ingress in front of plain-HTTP replicas, with listen.public_url set either way — the gateway itself does not refuse plain HTTP. The IdP must serve HTTPS, Postgres supports ?sslmode=require, and Strict-Transport-Security is set at the ingress.

nodes.label: CLI TLS fingerprint pinning
nodes.rationale: Claude Code pins the gateway's certificate fingerprint at first connect, so replicas behind one address serving different certificates — or TLS interception on the path — end the session with `Cloud gateway sign-in was not completed` and a mismatch naming the hostname and the first 16 characters of both fingerprints. The fix is to serve one certificate for the hostname, typically by terminating TLS once at the ingress.

nodes.label: IMDSv2 hop limit blocks Bedrock credentials
nodes.rationale: On EC2, IMDSv2's default hop limit of 1 blocks the instance-metadata request from inside the container, so every Bedrock request returns 502 with `Could not load credentials from any providers` while boot and /readyz still pass — the AWS SDK resolves instance credentials on the first request, not at client construction. Raising the hop limit to 2 fixes it, but ECS task roles avoid the change entirely.

nodes.label: Chrome form-action CSP over the redirect chain
nodes.rationale: Chrome enforces the form-action CSP directive against the entire redirect chain, so an IdP that redirects onward to a non-allowlisted second host blocks the Approve button in Chrome while Safari and Firefox work; each additional origin in the chain must be added to oidc.form_action_origins.

nodes.label: response_mode=query for the callback
nodes.rationale: The gateway explicitly requests response_mode=query so the callback is a plain redirect; an IdP returning the code via response_mode=form_post auto-submits it cross-origin, which Chrome blocks under a strict CSP and which Safari allows but the callback then fails because it reads only the query string.

nodes.label: public_url mismatch behind an ALB
nodes.rationale: Login that works locally but fails behind an ALB is caused by public_url still naming the local or inner http:// origin, so the IdP receives the wrong redirect_uri; listen.public_url must be the external https:// origin and <public_url>/oauth/callback must be registered with the IdP.

nodes.label: id_token missing email claim
nodes.rationale: `token exchange failed …: id_token missing email claim` means the IdP does not include email in the id_token by default; the rejection fires only when allowed_email_domains is set, since without it a missing email mints a session with no email. Fixes are IdP-side claim configuration, or oidc.userinfo_fallback: true when the IdP serves email only from userinfo.

nodes.label: Symptom-cause-fix troubleshooting matrix
nodes.rationale: Troubleshooting is keyed on the observed error in a symptom/cause/fix table covering login, boot, IdP, proxy and TLS failures. Reporting a problem requires the gateway's stderr, the redacted gateway.yaml, the version (shown at / and in the x-cc-gateway-version header), and for login issues a --debug-file capture — all of which carry identities and hook/MCP output and must be redacted before public posting.

nodes.label: Gateway resolves to a public address
nodes.rationale: `/login` refuses a gateway hostname that resolves to at least one public IP, because Claude Code checks every resolved address and requires all of them to be private. A common cause is a dual-stack name — including AWS internal dual-stack load balancers, which return public-range AAAA records — fixed by dropping the public-range record or serving a separate internal-only DNS name.

nodes.label: HTTP proxy on a public network blocks login
nodes.rationale: If HTTPS_PROXY or HTTP_PROXY applies to the gateway host and the proxy hostname resolves to a public address, /login refuses; a proxy resolving only to private addresses is allowed. The remedy is adding the gateway host to NO_PROXY — the message names the exact entry — or using a privately-resolving proxy. An unresolvable proxy or gateway hostname usually means the machine is off the corporate network or VPN.

nodes.label: Claude apps gateway
nodes.rationale: A self-hosted service that sits between developers' Claude Code clients and the model provider. Developers sign in with the corporate IdP instead of holding API keys or cloud credentials; the gateway holds the upstream credential, enforces model access and managed settings by IdP group, and relays usage telemetry to the organization's own observability stack.

nodes.label: Shipped in the claude binary
nodes.rationale: The gateway is included in the `claude` binary, so the same executable that runs Claude Code on a laptop runs the gateway server with `claude gateway --config gateway.yaml`. It is Anthropic's own gateway, tested alongside each Claude Code release, so it forwards the headers and request fields Claude Code sends without operators maintaining a separate allowlist.

nodes.label: SSO sign-in with short-lived bearer tokens
nodes.rationale: Developers authenticate with corporate SSO and receive short-lived bearer tokens rather than holding credentials, so offboarding happens in the IdP: deprovision a user and their gateway access expires within the session lifetime, one hour by default.

nodes.label: Upstream credential stays in your infrastructure
nodes.rationale: The upstream API key or cloud credential lives only in the organization's own infrastructure; developers never hold it. Requests to the model go through the gateway using the organization's upstream credential.

nodes.label: session.ttl_hours
nodes.rationale: The `session` block sets a JWT secret and `ttl_hours`, one hour by default. The TTL also bounds revocation latency on IdP deprovision: sessions refresh silently before expiry, and a failed refresh after deprovisioning prompts a re-login.

nodes.label: Per-IdP-group access control
nodes.rationale: IdP groups map to model allowlists and managed settings policies. The gateway enforces model access server-side, rejecting requests for non-granted models, and selects each group's managed settings policy, which the CLI applies at the managed settings tier, so a developer cannot override what their policy locks.

nodes.label: Managed settings delivery
nodes.rationale: The gateway delivers managed settings to signed-in clients itself, taking the place of server-managed settings from the claude.ai admin console.

nodes.label: OTLP telemetry fan-out
nodes.rationale: Each configured destination receives OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) metrics with token counts, model, user identity, and latency by default, with logs and traces as per-destination opt-ins. Exports are identity-stamped and both protobuf and JSON encodings are supported.

nodes.label: Upstream routing and per-provider translation
nodes.rationale: Clients speak the Anthropic Messages API to the gateway, and the gateway translates for each upstream with failover between them. Regions, providers, or failover order can change without developers noticing or reconfiguring.

nodes.label: Supported model upstreams
nodes.rationale: Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, and the Anthropic API are supported upstreams, with multiple upstreams and failover. The Bedrock upstream uses the `bedrock-runtime` endpoint and the AWS default credential chain; Bedrock's Mantle endpoint is not a supported upstream, and the Claude Platform on AWS upstream needs Claude Code v2.1.198 or later on the server.

nodes.label: Data plane sends nothing to Anthropic
nodes.rationale: The gateway's own data plane sends nothing to Anthropic infrastructure unless the Anthropic API is a configured upstream. The organization controls where telemetry, audit logs, managed settings, and developers' IdP identity go, and the gateway sends none of them to Anthropic.

nodes.label: Claude Enterprise as the alternative
nodes.rationale: The gateway is designed for organizations that must, or prefer to, route inference through their own cloud provider, for example to meet data residency requirements. Without that requirement, and wanting features such as SCIM provisioning or Claude Code on web and mobile, Claude Enterprise may be a better fit.

nodes.label: Other LLM gateway implementations
nodes.rationale: If an organization already runs an LLM gateway or API gateway that meets its needs, it should keep using it; the Other LLM gateways page covers configuring Claude Code against it.

nodes.label: GET /protocol contract
nodes.rationale: A running Claude apps gateway serves a superset of the documented gateway protocol contract at `GET /protocol`, adding the gateway-specific endpoints for SSO sign-in, managed settings delivery, and telemetry. It can be fetched with curl from any deployed gateway.

nodes.label: Protocol compatibility policy
nodes.rationale: Breaking changes to the gateway protocol are announced in advance, but indefinite backwards compatibility is not guaranteed.

nodes.label: Private-network-only address requirement
nodes.rationale: At `/login` Claude Code requires the gateway's hostname or IP to resolve only to private addresses (RFC 1918, link-local, CGNAT 100.64.0.0/10, IPv6 ULA fc00::/7, or loopback). The check runs on each resolved IP, so any public address rejects the URL; a corporate HTTPS proxy must also resolve privately or the gateway host must be added to NO_PROXY.

nodes.label: A trusted gateway can push settings that run commands
nodes.rationale: The stated threat behind the private-address guard: a gateway a client trusts can push settings that run commands on developer machines, so Claude Code only connects to a gateway whose address is private.

nodes.label: Claude Code v2.1.195 or later
nodes.rationale: The `claude gateway` subcommand and the gateway sign-in flow ship in v2.1.195; both the gateway server machine and each developer machine must be on that version or later. Claude Platform on AWS needs v2.1.198+, Claude Desktop support v2.1.203+, and the `chatTabEnabled` policy key v2.1.227+, all on the gateway server.

nodes.label: OIDC identity provider
nodes.rationale: Any OIDC-compliant IdP works (Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, Keycloak, Dex, PingFederate); the gateway runs standard OIDC discovery and the authorization-code flow against it. SAML and LDAP are not supported, and only one issuer per gateway is supported.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL 14 or later
nodes.rationale: Postgres backs the device sign-in flow, where the browser callback writes and the polling CLI reads, plus rate-limit counters. Without spend limits it stores a few KB of short-lived auth state; with spend limits it also holds durable spend, audit, and identity tables that should be backed up. The gateway runs its own schema migrations at boot, so the role needs DDL rights.

nodes.label: HTTPS reachability and public_url
nodes.rationale: The gateway must be reachable over https from developer laptops and from the sign-in browser, and serves the device-verification page on the same listener. Either provide a cert via `listen.tls` or run behind a TLS-terminating ingress, setting `listen.public_url` to the external origin in both cases; plain http is accepted only on loopback hosts.

nodes.label: Linux-only server runtime
nodes.rationale: The gateway server runs only on the native Linux binary. macOS works for local development, and Windows is not supported as a server platform.

nodes.label: gateway.yaml minimal config
nodes.rationale: The minimal configuration has five sections — `listen`, `oidc`, `session`, `store`, and `upstreams` — and every other field has a default. Per-group RBAC and managed settings (`managed.policies`), telemetry fan-out (`telemetry`), and multi-upstream failover or provisioned-throughput ARNs (`models`) are added afterwards.

nodes.label: ${ENV_VAR} secret expansion
nodes.rationale: Secrets in gateway.yaml are read via ${ENV_VAR} expansion — the OIDC client secret, the JWT secret, and the Postgres URL — so the config file itself can live in version control.

nodes.label: auto_include_builtin_models catalog
nodes.rationale: Models are translated per upstream automatically: the built-in catalog maps ids such as claude-opus-4-8 to us.anthropic.claude-opus-4-8 for every Bedrock-supported Claude model. Setting `auto_include_builtin_models: false` and adding a `models:` list exposes only specific models.

nodes.label: Amazon Bedrock IAM and use-case form
nodes.rationale: The Bedrock upstream needs an AWS principal with bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream on both the inference-profile/us.anthropic.* ARNs and the underlying foundation-model/anthropic.* ARNs, plus Anthropic's one-time use case form for the account. Credentials should come from IRSA on EKS, an ECS task role, or an EC2 instance profile rather than static keys.

nodes.label: Docker Compose quickstart deployment
nodes.rationale: The quickstart builds a container image around the `claude` binary and runs it alongside Postgres with Docker Compose, mounting gateway.yaml read-only and passing secrets as environment variables. With an existing TLS-terminating ingress, Compose can be skipped and the binary run directly with `claude gateway --config gateway.yaml`.

nodes.label: Fail-closed boot sequence
nodes.rationale: Boot is fail-closed for the config, the Postgres connection with a 5-second timeout, OIDC discovery, and upstream client construction: if any is unreachable or misconfigured the gateway exits with an error rather than serving traffic in a degraded state. The last stderr line names the problem — unreachable Postgres, a role without DDL permission, a bad OIDC discovery document, or a config schema violation with the offending field path.

nodes.label: Boot does not validate the inference path
nodes.rationale: A successful boot does not validate the inference path, because Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud Agent Platform instance credentials resolve on the first request rather than at boot.

nodes.label: Boot log and audit event format
nodes.rationale: Log lines use the format `[gateway] <timestamp> <level> <message>` on stderr and audit events are single-line JSON with an `evt` field. A fresh database prints one `migration N applied` line per schema migration and an already-migrated one prints none; a healthy boot ends with `claude gateway listening on`.

nodes.label: Three-check auth surface verification
nodes.rationale: Three checks confirm the gateway can authenticate a real user: fetch /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server (boot complete and config valid), POST /oauth/device_authorization (device flow works and Postgres is writable), and open verification_uri_complete in a browser (the IdP leg). The first failing check localises the fault, and an IdP bounce-back is diagnosed from the audit log, which records every auth rejection with its reason.

nodes.label: OAuth device authorization flow
nodes.rationale: The gateway advertises device_authorization_endpoint and token_endpoint with grant types urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code and refresh_token. A device authorization returns device_code, user_code, verification_uri, verification_uri_complete, expires_in and interval, and the verification URI is built from public_url.

nodes.label: IdP OAuth client registration
nodes.rationale: Step one is registering an OIDC web application in the IdP with the redirect URI https://claude-gateway.<domain>/oauth/callback, matching the value set as listen.public_url, and noting the client_id and client_secret. The gateway builds the IdP redirect_uri from public_url, so a local Compose setup needs a second redirect URI for localhost.

nodes.label: forceLoginMethod and forceLoginGatewayUrl
nodes.rationale: Setting forceLoginMethod to "gateway" and forceLoginGatewayUrl to the gateway's public_url in the per-OS managed settings file opens /login directly on the Cloud gateway screen with the URL filled in. These login keys belong in the file pushed to machines via MDM, not in the gateway's managed.policies[].cli block, which only reaches already-connected clients.

nodes.label: Developer /login gateway sign-in
nodes.rationale: Developers connect from their own laptops with one browser sign-in using their corporate work account: run /login, press Enter on the Cloud gateway screen, and complete the browser sign-in. Once signed in, the model picker shows the developer's availableModels allowlist, managed settings apply at startup and refresh hourly, and telemetry routes to the organization's collector.

nodes.label: TLS leaf certificate pinning
nodes.rationale: The CLI fingerprints the gateway's TLS leaf certificate on first connect and pins it per hostname; the /login prompt shows the first 16 characters as lowercase hex with no colons, so admins should publish the expected SHA-256 fingerprint alongside the URL. Certificate rotation re-prompts every developer, so rotations should be treated as planned events.

nodes.label: Approval memory keyed to the pinned certificate
nodes.rationale: If the gateway policy includes settings that need approval, the developer sees the security approval dialog again after accepting a new certificate, because Claude Code keys approval memory to the pinned certificate.

nodes.label: No claude.ai account, API key, or subscription needed
nodes.rationale: Developers need no claude.ai account, API key, or subscription, because model requests go through the gateway on the organization's upstream credential.

nodes.label: Developers cannot configure the gateway themselves
nodes.rationale: A developer cannot set the gateway up manually: the login picker has no gateway option, forceLoginGatewayUrl is ignored in a developer's own settings files, and forceLoginMethod alone without a URL leaves the developer at a "Contact your IT administrator" message.

nodes.label: /user/bootstrap policy for Claude Desktop sessions
nodes.rationale: Claude Desktop runs its Cowork, Code, and optional Chat tabs on embedded Claude Code sessions and passes them policy built from the configuration the gateway serves at /user/bootstrap: the model allowlist, disabled tools, and the egress allowlist derived from the matched policy's `cli` block, plus the `desktop` overlay. Other `cli` keys such as hooks, `env`, and scoped permission rules reach only clients that sign in through /login.

nodes.label: parentSettingsBehavior: merge opt-in
nodes.rationale: Settings passed by a launching process are parent settings, and Claude Code ignores them on any machine with an admin-deployed managed source unless the source that delivers the policy sets parentSettingsBehavior: "merge". Claude Code reads the key only from the selected source, so it must be mirrored — as the whole snippet — into any client-side source that outranks the managed-settings file.

nodes.label: Which machines need the merge opt-in
nodes.rationale: Machines that only run Claude Desktop need the opt-in, because the egress allowlist reaches embedded sessions only as parent settings and without it those sessions run unrestricted with no warning. Machines where developers sign in through /login do not need it, and policyHelper fleets cannot use it because Claude Code never merges parent settings there.

nodes.label: resolveSettings() policyOrigin check
nodes.rationale: On a machine that only runs Claude Desktop, calling the Agent SDK's resolveSettings() and reading policyOrigin on the managed entry names the selected client-side source — plist, hklm, or file — which is the source that must carry the snippet. The gateway's cli block never counts as the selected source for embedded Desktop sessions, since they do not fetch gateway policy.

nodes.label: Any launching host can supply parent settings
nodes.rationale: Once parentSettingsBehavior: "merge" is deployed, any host process that launches Claude Code can supply parent settings — not only Claude Desktop, but also an Agent SDK application or an IDE extension.

nodes.label: Restrictive-key filter on parent settings
nodes.rationale: Claude Code filters parent settings against an allowlist of restrictive keys, but some allowed keys can grant access rather than restrict it: without the allowManaged*Only locks, host-supplied permission allow rules and sandbox allowlists still apply. The policy's deny and ask rules stay in force either way, since they are evaluated before any allow rule.

nodes.label: Stripped forwarding of sandbox.credentials
nodes.rationale: Parent-supplied sandbox.credentials entries are forwarded in stripped form: deny entries keep only path or name plus mode; file entries with mode: mask become a sentinel-only whole-file mask with an empty injectHosts and all structured-masking fields dropped; envVars mask entries are not forwarded at all; and awsPairs/sigv4 are restriction-only, with a parent sigv4 block pinning streaming, presigned and sigv4a to deny.

nodes.label: The five allowManaged*Only locks
nodes.rationale: To keep parent settings as close to restriction-only as the filter supports, deploy all five locks — allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly, allowManagedMcpServersOnly, allowManagedHooksOnly, sandbox.network.allowManagedDomainsOnly and sandbox.filesystem.allowManagedReadPathsOnly — plus the allowlists they govern, in the same sources as the merge opt-in.

nodes.label: Lock behavior across managed sources
nodes.rationale: Setting one lock does not restrict the others. From an admin source below the winner the two sandbox locks still apply, and allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly still blocks parent-supplied allow rules and additionalDirectories; the hooks and MCP locks need the winning source by default. Under the managedSourcesBehavior merge opt-in the strictest value any source sets applies, and on policyHelper fleets the locks are read from the helper's output alone.

nodes.label: Locks ignore the developer's own entries
nodes.rationale: Each lock makes Claude Code ignore the developer's own entries for that setting, so the organization's allowlists must sit next to the locks. Locking network domains with an empty managed domain list blocks all sandboxed outbound traffic; locking MCP servers with no managed or parent-supplied allowedMcpServers loads every server deniedMcpServers does not block; and allowRead entries only re-allow paths inside denyRead regions.

nodes.label: Four settings the locks do not cover
nodes.rationale: Four parent-supplied settings pass the filter even with all five locks set: forceLoginOrgUUID, allowedMcpServers and availableModels are honored when the highest-priority (or winning) admin source does not set them, so the admin value must be set there; and strictPluginOnlyCustomization passes regardless of any lock, making Claude Code ignore the developer's own customization including protective hooks.

nodes.label: Connecting Claude Desktop
nodes.rationale: Claude Desktop connects through a different MDM key: set bootstrapUrl in its managed configuration to <listen.public_url>/user/bootstrap and opt the user's policy in with a `desktop` key, requiring Claude Code v2.1.203+ on the server. Desktop signs the developer in through the same IdP browser SSO step and then fetches its configuration from the gateway instead of from Anthropic, with model access and policy following the same per-group rules as the CLI.

nodes.label: CLI and Desktop sessions are separate
nodes.rationale: A developer who uses both the CLI and Claude Desktop signs in to each separately; the gateway session is not shared between them. Claude Desktop reads the gateway URL from its own managed configuration and signs in with its own flow, separate from the forceLoginMethod and forceLoginGatewayUrl keys.

nodes.label: No service-token flow for CI pipelines
nodes.rationale: There is no service-token flow for unattended pipelines. Gateway sign-in always runs the browser device flow, so a CI job with no developer to approve the sign-in cannot authenticate; those workloads must be configured against the provider directly.

nodes.label: All sessions on a signed-in machine use the gateway session
nodes.rationale: Once a developer has signed in, every Claude Code session on that machine uses the gateway session — including non-interactive `claude -p` runs and sessions started by the Agent SDK — and Claude Code applies the gateway policy to each of them.

nodes.label: Remote and headless sign-in over SSH
nodes.rationale: The device flow separates the polling CLI from the approving browser, so a remote development box with no display still works: the developer runs /login over SSH on the remote machine and opens the verification link in the browser on their laptop.

nodes.label: Server-side model access enforcement
nodes.rationale: Requests for models the policy does not grant return 400, and the /model picker is filtered to the policy's availableModels allowlist. Setting enforceAvailableModels: true makes the Default option resolve to a model inside availableModels; without it, Default stays selectable and is rejected at request time when that model is not granted.

nodes.label: Telemetry destination override on gateway sessions
nodes.rationale: In sessions signed in through /login the CLI sends its OTLP/HTTP exports to the gateway regardless of any locally set OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, and the gateway relays them to telemetry.forward_to destinations. Embedded Claude Desktop sessions instead export to the configured endpoint, and the session token is attached only when that endpoint is the gateway. With no destination configured for a signal, the gateway accepts and discards it.

nodes.label: The gateway token is the session's only credential
nodes.rationale: While signed in to a gateway, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, apiKeyHelper, Anthropic profiles, and any earlier claude.ai login are ignored, so developers do not need to log out of claude.ai first.

nodes.label: Startup apply plus hourly policy poll
nodes.rationale: Locked keys cannot be overridden locally. The CLI applies the policy at startup and applies changes on each hourly poll, apart from the changes that only take effect at the next launch.

nodes.label: Signed-in sessions exit when the gateway is unreachable
nodes.rationale: Signed-in sessions exit at startup with an error after about 10 seconds when the gateway is unreachable, rather than starting without their settings.

nodes.label: Deprovisioning expires the session
nodes.rationale: A session whose user is disabled in the IdP expires within ttl_hours, when the next silent refresh fails and the developer is prompted to re-login.

nodes.label: What the organization can see
nodes.rationale: Usage telemetry carries the developer's identity, token counts, model, and latency to the organization's collector, and the gateway does not log or store prompt or completion content. Whether richer telemetry such as logs and traces — which can include commands and file paths — is collected is the organization's per-destination choice.

nodes.label: Availability and limitations matrix
nodes.rationale: A table records which Claude Code features work through the gateway and what the gateway server itself supports, giving the alternative in the Notes column wherever something is unsupported.

nodes.label: anthropic-beta header forwarding
nodes.rationale: The gateway delivers the anthropic-beta values the CLI sends to every upstream, so operators do not maintain a beta allowlist. For Amazon Bedrock, which ignores the header, the gateway moves the values into the request body's anthropic_beta field; other upstreams receive the header as sent.

nodes.label: Server-side web search disabled
nodes.rationale: Server-side web search is not available: the CLI cannot see which upstream provider the gateway routes to, so it cannot verify web search support and disables WebSearch on gateway sessions.

nodes.label: Remote Control not available
nodes.rationale: Remote Control is not available through the gateway; the CLI shows an error naming the gateway, since Remote Control requires the Anthropic API.

nodes.label: Prompt caching limited to the 5-minute TTL
nodes.rationale: Standard prompt caching is available — the gateway forwards cache_control breakpoints to every upstream and the CLI marks the system context it appends mid-conversation for caching. The 1-hour cache TTL is not available: the CLI omits the extended-cache-ttl beta because not every reachable upstream supports it, so gateway sessions use the 5-minute TTL.

nodes.label: First-party-only optimizations disabled
nodes.rationale: First-party-only optimizations such as global cache scope and token-efficient tools are not available; the CLI does not enable them on gateway sessions.

nodes.label: OTLP/gRPC not supported
nodes.rationale: The gateway supports OTLP over HTTP only; OTLP/gRPC is not supported.

nodes.label: One OIDC issuer per gateway
nodes.rationale: Multi-tenant operation with multiple OIDC issuers is not supported: one issuer per gateway, so separate instances must be run. SAML, LDAP and other non-OIDC auth are likewise unsupported and need an OIDC bridge in front.

nodes.label: No admin UI and no Helm chart
nodes.rationale: There is no admin UI — configuration is the YAML file and changing it means redeploying — and no Helm chart, since the gateway runs as a standard stateless Kubernetes Deployment.

nodes.label: Per-user and per-group spend limits
nodes.rationale: Per-user and per-group spend limits are available, putting caps on individual developers or groups so a runaway workload cannot consume the whole commitment. Enabling them makes Postgres hold durable spend, audit, and identity tables that should be backed up.

nodes.label: Auto mode on gateway sessions
nodes.rationale: Auto mode is available and follows the third-party provider rules: only models eligible on third-party providers can use it. Before v2.1.207, auto mode on gateway sessions required setting CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_AUTO_MODE=1, deliverable through the managed policy's env block.

nodes.label: Claude Code on the web
nodes.rationale: Claude Code on the web runs tasks on Anthropic-managed cloud infrastructure at claude.ai/code, or on an organization's self-hosted environment when routed there. Sessions persist even if the browser is closed and can be monitored from the Claude mobile app.

nodes.label: Research preview availability
nodes.rationale: Claude Code on the web is in research preview for Pro, Max, and Team users, and for Enterprise users with premium seats or Chat + Claude Code seats.

nodes.label: Cloud session
nodes.rationale: A cloud session is the unit of work in Claude Code on the web: it runs in an isolated VM, persists across browser closes, appears in the sidebar at claude.ai/code, and can be reviewed, shared, archived, or deleted.

nodes.label: Cloud environment
nodes.rationale: Every cloud session runs in a cloud environment — the saved configuration that controls network access, environment variables, and setup scripts.

nodes.label: Default environment
nodes.rationale: If no environment exists yet, onboarding sets up a Default environment with Trusted network access — either creating it automatically or prompting the user to create it, depending on the plan.

nodes.label: Environments apply across every surface
nodes.rationale: The same environments apply wherever a cloud session starts: the web, the terminal, Claude Tag, routines, and the mobile and Desktop apps. Claude Tag channel sessions use organization-level environments only — shared or self-hosted.

nodes.label: Self-hosted environment
nodes.rationale: Sessions an organization routes to a self-hosted environment run on the organization's own infrastructure, where isolation, egress restriction, and git credentials are the deployment's responsibility, and no Anthropic-managed API credentials exist.

nodes.label: GitHub authentication options
nodes.rationale: Cloud sessions need access to GitHub repositories to clone code and push branches. Access can be granted in two ways — authorizing the Claude GitHub App, or running /web-setup — and either method works.

nodes.label: Claude GitHub App authorization
nodes.rationale: Authorizing the Claude GitHub App during web onboarding grants repository access; it is best for browser onboarding and for teams that want Auto-fix. Installing the App on a repository enables PR webhooks but is not a session-level access control.

nodes.label: /web-setup token sync
nodes.rationale: Running /web-setup in the terminal syncs the local gh CLI token to the Claude account, granting cloud sessions repository access. It suits individual developers who already use gh.

nodes.label: Session access spans the whole connected account
nodes.rationale: With either authentication method, a cloud session can access any repository the connecting GitHub account can see — not just repositories the Claude GitHub App is installed on. To restrict reach, restrict access on GitHub itself, for example by limiting team or repository membership.

nodes.label: Quick web setup organization toggle
nodes.rationale: Quick web setup is an organization setting that lets members connect GitHub with /web-setup, skips the GitHub App install prompt during browser onboarding, and has onboarding create the Default environment. It is off by default on Team and Enterprise plans, which hides /web-setup; an Owner enables it in Admin settings > Claude Code.

nodes.label: Zero Data Retention blocks cloud features
nodes.rationale: Organizations with Zero Data Retention enabled cannot use /web-setup or other cloud session features.

nodes.label: Moving tasks between web and terminal
nodes.rationale: Handoff workflows require the Claude Code CLI signed in to the same claude.ai account. New cloud sessions can be started from the terminal, and running cloud sessions pulled into the terminal to continue locally.

nodes.label: CLI handoff is one-way
nodes.rationale: From the CLI, session handoff is one-way: cloud sessions can be pulled into the terminal with --teleport, but an existing terminal session cannot be pushed to the web. Only the Desktop app's 'Continue in' menu can send a local session to the web.

nodes.label: --cloud flag
nodes.rationale: `claude --cloud "<task>"` creates a new cloud session on claude.ai. The cloud VM clones the current directory's GitHub remote at the current branch — not the local checkout — so local commits must be pushed first; it works with one repository at a time.

nodes.label: --remote deprecated alias
nodes.rationale: The older --remote spelling still works as a deprecated alias for --cloud.

nodes.label: Live provisioning checklist and queued input
nodes.rationale: While the cloud container starts, the CLI shows a live checklist of setup steps such as cloning the repository and running the setup script, and it queues messages typed during provisioning, sending them once the session is ready.

nodes.label: Plan locally, execute remotely
nodes.rationale: For complex tasks, start Claude in plan mode (`claude --permission-mode plan`) to collaborate on an approach without editing source, then save, commit and push the plan so the cloud VM can clone it, and start a cloud session to execute it autonomously.

nodes.label: Parallel cloud tasks
nodes.rationale: Each --cloud command creates its own independent cloud session, so multiple tasks can be started and run simultaneously in separate sessions.

nodes.label: /tasks session monitor
nodes.rationale: `/tasks` in the Claude Code CLI checks progress of background cloud sessions; pressing `t` from that list teleports into one. Sessions can also be opened on claude.ai or the mobile app to interact directly.

nodes.label: Local repository bundle upload
nodes.rationale: When `claude --cloud` runs from a repository not connected to GitHub, Claude Code bundles the local repository and uploads it to the cloud session, including full history across all branches plus uncommitted changes to tracked files. The fallback activates automatically when GitHub access is unavailable.

nodes.label: Credential-like files excluded from bundles
nodes.rationale: On macOS, Linux, and WSL, uncommitted changes to files named like credentials or keys (.env, Terraform *.tfvars, id_rsa, *.pem) are left out of the upload and named; the session starts with the committed version or without the file. In a linked worktree or submodule layout those changes are uploaded and named instead.

nodes.label: Bundle size and content limits
nodes.rationale: A bundled repository must be a git repository with at least one commit and under 100 MB; larger repositories fall back to bundling only the current branch, then to a single squashed snapshot, failing only if that is still too large. Untracked files are excluded, and bundle-created sessions cannot push back to a remote without GitHub authentication.

nodes.label: CCR_FORCE_BUNDLE=1
nodes.rationale: Setting CCR_FORCE_BUNDLE=1 forces the local-bundle upload path even when GitHub is connected.

nodes.label: Send follow-ups from the CLI
nodes.rationale: `claude -p "your message" --cloud <session-id>` posts one message into a running cloud session and exits without waiting for a reply. It authenticates with Anthropic account credentials, sends no local session state, works from any logged-in machine and shell, and accepts the message on stdin.

nodes.label: Accepted session ID forms
nodes.rationale: For <session-id>, pass the bare ID such as session_... or cse_..., or the session's claude.ai/code/<id> URL with or without scheme or query string. The ID is found in the session list at claude.ai/code.

nodes.label: --output-format json result shape
nodes.rationale: `--output-format json` returns {ok, session_id, url} on success or {ok: false, session_id, error} on a failed send. Configuration errors such as an unsupported provider or disabled org policy print to stderr without JSON, and stream-json is not supported with --cloud <session-id>.

nodes.label: Third-party providers cannot use cloud sessions
nodes.rationale: --cloud requires an Anthropic account and is unavailable when Claude Code is configured for Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or another third-party provider. An LLM gateway configured only through ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL does not count as a third-party provider, but claude auth login is still required.

nodes.label: allow_remote_sessions organization policy
nodes.rationale: The organization's allow_remote_sessions policy must be enabled for cloud sessions; an Owner turns it on in the Claude Code admin settings. When off, sends fail with 'Cloud sessions are disabled by your organization's policy.'

nodes.label: Unverifiable policy fails closed
nodes.rationale: If Claude Code cannot fetch the organization's cloud-session policy it refuses the send rather than assuming cloud sessions are allowed, reporting 'Couldn't verify your organization's policy for cloud sessions.'

nodes.label: --teleport
nodes.rationale: Teleport pulls a cloud session into the terminal: Claude verifies the correct repository, fetches and checks out the cloud session's branch, and loads the full conversation history. It requires claude.ai subscription authentication rather than an API key.

nodes.label: Teleport entry points
nodes.rationale: A session can be teleported via `claude --teleport` (picker) or `claude --teleport <session-id>`, `/teleport` or `/tp` inside a CLI session, pressing `t` in /tasks, 'Open in > Terminal' from the web session menu, or `/teleport` inside the cloud session (requires Claude Code v2.1.223 or later there).

nodes.label: Teleport requirements
nodes.rationale: Teleport checks four requirements before resuming: a clean git state (it prompts to stash), a checkout of the same repository and not a fork, a branch that was pushed to the remote, and authentication to the same claude.ai account used in the cloud session.

nodes.label: Teleport yields a separate local copy
nodes.rationale: The terminal gets its own copy of a teleported session: new work there stays local and does not appear in the cloud session on claude.ai or the mobile app.

nodes.label: --resume (local history)
nodes.rationale: --resume reopens a conversation from this machine's local history and does not list cloud sessions, whereas --teleport pulls a cloud session and its branch.

nodes.label: Remote Control
nodes.rationale: --remote-control exposes a LOCAL CLI session for monitoring from the web and is unrelated to --cloud, which creates cloud sessions. Starting /remote-control in a teleported local session is how steering from a phone continues.

nodes.label: Slash commands in cloud sessions
nodes.rationale: Cloud sessions support built-in commands that produce text output; terminal-only commands such as /plugin or /resume are unavailable. Picker commands (/model, /effort, /fast, /color, /rename) take the value as an argument and need v2.1.205+, /config opens settings and ignores key=value, /compact and /context work, and /clear does not.

nodes.label: Web-set auto-compact override
nodes.rationale: Claude Code on the web sets CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE in cloud sessions itself so compaction triggers partway through the auto-compact window; that value overrides one added in environment variables.
