nodes.rationale: After the main conversation's first API response, the Session block gains a `Prompt cache (main)` line summarizing request count, share of input tokens served from cache, misses, expected rebuilds, and warm/cold state. Its counts come from the API response cache token fields, so it works on every provider and gateway; it covers the main conversation only, not subagents, and requires v2.1.251 or later.

nodes.label: Cache miss definition (5% and 2,000 tokens)
nodes.rationale: Claude Code counts a request as a cache miss when it re-processed more than 5% and at least 2,000 tokens of what it could have read from cache. The miss report shows the time of the last miss and how many tokens those requests wrote back to the cache.

nodes.label: Expected cache rebuild
nodes.rationale: When Claude Code itself rewrote the conversation — by compaction or by clearing old tool results from context — it counts the resulting miss as an 'expected rebuild' rather than a miss. This part of the line appears only after at least one expected rebuild has happened.

nodes.label: Warm or cold cache state
nodes.rationale: The warm/cold segment reports whether the cached prefix is still within its cache lifetime and which TTL is in effect; when cold it shows how long the session has been idle, and when no response reported cache tokens the line ends with `no prompt caching reported by the API`.

nodes.label: statusline prompt_cache object
nodes.rationale: Status line scripts can read the same prompt-cache numbers programmatically from the `prompt_cache` object exposed to statusline scripts.

nodes.label: Plan usage breakdown
nodes.rationale: On a Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise plan, `/usage` shows a breakdown of what counts against plan limits — attribution, behavior flags, and loop rows — toggled between the last 24 hours and last 7 days with `d` or `w`.

nodes.label: Usage attribution by skill, subagent, plugin, MCP server
nodes.rationale: The breakdown attributes recent usage to skills, subagents, plugins, and individual MCP servers as percentages of the total. An MCP server's share counts only requests that consumed one of its tool results; before v2.1.222 every request after one MCP call was attributed to that server, overstating its share.

nodes.label: Behavior flags at the 10% threshold
nodes.rationale: Behaviors such as long context or cache misses are flagged in the `/usage` breakdown when one accounts for 10% or more of recent usage, each shown with a tip to reduce it.

nodes.label: Loops rows for scheduled tasks
nodes.rationale: The breakdown lists a row per heaviest `/loop` or other scheduled task, ordered by total tokens, reporting fire frequency, run count, total and per-run tokens, and last run. Rows are keyed by the task's prompt, so a loop stopped and re-created stays one row; requires v2.1.242 or later.

nodes.label: Figures computed from local session history
nodes.rationale: The plan usage breakdown figures are approximate and computed from local session history on this machine, so usage from other devices or from claude.ai is not included.

nodes.label: VS Code Account & usage dialog
nodes.rationale: In the VS Code extension the attribution shares and behavior flags appear in the Account & usage dialog with a Day/Week toggle, but without the Loops rows; requires v2.1.174 or later.

nodes.label: Usage-credits row in /usage
nodes.rationale: While usage credits are on, `/usage` shows a usage-credits row: on Pro and Max, month-to-date spend against a monthly limit (or `Unlimited` with no figure when none is set); on Team and Enterprise, the member's own spend against any limit that applies to them, excluding org-wide limits. It appears as soon as credits are on and shows 0% until first spend.

nodes.label: Last-known usage on a failed request
nodes.rationale: When the plan-limits request fails — usually a rate-limited usage endpoint — `/usage` shows the last bars loaded on this machine within the past 60 minutes plus a `Showing last-known usage` note, with `r` to retry. With no recent snapshot it reports the rate limit and offers the same retry.

nodes.label: /insights usage-pattern report
nodes.rationale: `/insights` analyzes recent local sessions and writes an HTML report on how you work — topics, friction points such as misunderstood requests or buggy code, and suggestions — rather than how many tokens you used. One run analyzes up to 200 previously unseen sessions, skips very short ones, and runs on any plan and provider with its tokens counting against your plan or API usage.

nodes.label: Insights report storage and cleanup
nodes.rationale: The latest report is written to `~/.claude/usage-data/report.html` with a timestamped copy of each run kept alongside it, and reports are deleted at startup on the same `cleanupPeriodDays` schedule as other session data (30 days by default).

nodes.label: Usage credits
nodes.rationale: Usage credits are extra paid usage that lets a subscriber keep working past their plan's usage limit, controlled with spend limits at the individual, group, or organization level.

nodes.label: /usage-credits command
nodes.rationale: `/usage-credits` manages usage credits after signing in with a claude.ai subscription through `/login`; it is unavailable with API key authentication. Its behavior is role-dependent: Pro/Max opens Settings > Usage, a Team/Enterprise member with billing access opens Admin settings > Usage, and a member without billing access sends a request to admins.

nodes.label: Usage-credit request to admins
nodes.rationale: A Team or Enterprise member without billing access confirms, then sends a request to org admins; the confirmation appears only in interactive sessions, so `-p` non-interactive mode and Remote Control send nothing and tell the user to run it interactively. A pending request blocks duplicates until an admin dismisses it (before v2.1.222 a dismissed request also blocked new ones).

nodes.label: In-CLI spend-limit raise prompt
nodes.rationale: On Pro and Max plans, reaching the spend limit while usage credits remain available prompts the user to raise or remove the limit without leaving the CLI; a server rejection surfaces the 'Could not update your spend limit' error.

nodes.label: Organization access paths determine cost controls
nodes.rationale: Which cost controls an organization has depends on how it accesses Claude Code: a Claude for Teams/Enterprise plan (seat allowance), the Claude Console (billed per token), or a cloud provider (billed per token to the cloud account). When sign-in methods are mixed, each developer is metered by the one they authenticated with.

nodes.label: Claude for Teams and Enterprise
nodes.rationale: On Claude for Teams and Enterprise plans the cost controls live in the claude.ai admin console rather than the Claude Console: spend report, adoption analytics, seat-allowance ceiling with optional usage credits and spend limits, and per-user reporting.

nodes.label: Per-seat allowance
nodes.rationale: Each Teams/Enterprise member's Claude Code usage draws from a per-seat allowance that resets on a rolling five-hour window and a weekly window, shared with Claude chat and Cowork and sized by the member's seat tier (Standard or Premium). Usage inside the allowance is not metered in dollars, and the allowance is the default spend ceiling.

nodes.label: Spend report in org analytics
nodes.rationale: The org-analytics spend report shows estimated spend per user and per model with CSV export, updated daily. It covers usage-credit spend and appears only once usage credits are turned on.

nodes.label: Adoption analytics dashboard
nodes.rationale: The claude.ai analytics dashboard shows daily active users, sessions, and contribution metrics with CSV export of contribution data — an adoption view rather than a spend view.

nodes.label: Enterprise Analytics API
nodes.rationale: On the Enterprise plan, the Enterprise Analytics API returns per-user usage and cost reports across Claude surfaces including Claude Code; a Primary Owner creates a key with the `read:analytics` scope. On Teams, the equivalent is the spend report CSV.

nodes.label: Claude Console workspaces
nodes.rationale: API organizations manage Claude Code spend through Console workspaces: workspace spend limits cap total Claude Code spend, and the Console provides cost and usage reporting.

nodes.label: Auto-created 'Claude Code' workspace
nodes.rationale: First authenticating Claude Code with a Claude Console account automatically creates a workspace called 'Claude Code' that centralizes cost tracking for all org Claude Code usage. API keys cannot be created for it; it exists exclusively for Claude Code authentication and usage.

nodes.label: Workspace rate limit protects other workloads
nodes.rationale: For organizations with custom rate limits, Claude Code traffic in the auto-created workspace counts toward the organization's overall API rate limits; setting a workspace rate limit on its Limits page caps Claude Code's share and protects other production workloads.

nodes.label: Console dashboard and Claude Code Analytics API
nodes.rationale: The Console dashboard shows spend and accepted lines per member, and the Claude Code Analytics API returns the same daily per-user metrics programmatically using an Admin API key.

nodes.label: TPM/RPM per-user recommendations by team size
nodes.rationale: Recommended per-user TPM/RPM decreases as team size grows (200k-300k TPM at 1-5 users down to 10k-15k at 500+), because fewer users run Claude Code concurrently in larger organizations. The limits apply at the organization level, so individuals can temporarily exceed their calculated share; unusually concurrent scenarios such as live training need higher allocations.

nodes.label: Cloud-provider billing (Bedrock, Google Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry)
nodes.rationale: On Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry, Claude Code is billed per token to the cloud account and spend controls live in the cloud provider's billing console. Claude Code sends no metrics from the cloud back to Anthropic, so the Anthropic analytics dashboards and Claude Code Analytics API do not cover this usage.

nodes.label: OpenTelemetry metrics export
nodes.rationale: OpenTelemetry export works on every setup and is the only option that streams per-user token and cost metrics into an organization's own observability stack in near real time, giving per-user token counts, costs, and tool activity regardless of provider.

nodes.label: Claude apps gateway
nodes.rationale: A self-hosted Claude apps gateway provides per-user usage attribution, OTLP metrics with token counts, and per-user spend limits on cloud providers.

nodes.label: LLM gateway spend tracking (LiteLLM)
nodes.rationale: Routing all Claude Code traffic through an LLM gateway proxy tracks spend per key; several large enterprises reported using LiteLLM, an open-source tool that tracks spend by key. It is unaffiliated with Anthropic and has not been audited for security.

nodes.label: Diagnosing which ceiling a developer hit
nodes.rationale: Developers bring limit questions to their admin, and four situations mean different things: a seat-based usage window, a gateway spend limit, a context/auto-compact warning (not a usage limit at all), and unexpectedly high spend on an API or cloud plan.

nodes.label: Session or weekly usage-window limit
nodes.rationale: 'You've hit your session limit' or 'weekly limit' is a seat-based usage window on a subscription plan, shared across all models, so switching models with `/model` cannot restore access. The message states when the window resets.

nodes.label: Model-specific limit (Opus or Sonnet)
nodes.rationale: After a model-specific message such as 'You've hit your Opus limit' or 'You've hit your Sonnet limit', switching to a model outside that family with `/model` does keep the developer working — unlike the shared session or weekly window.

nodes.label: Wait and continue after a usage-limit reset
nodes.rationale: On v2.1.234 or later, Claude Code can wait and continue an interrupted task automatically after a usage limit resets, either on its own or picked from `/rate-limit-options`. Fleet-wide, `autoContinueAtUsageLimit` in managed settings controls whether it starts that wait by itself.

nodes.label: Gateway spend-limit block
nodes.rationale: A spend-limit message from a self-hosted Claude apps gateway means the developer passed a spend cap the admin set; the gateway blocks their requests until the period resets or the cap is raised.

nodes.label: Context / auto-compact warning is not a usage limit
nodes.rationale: A context or auto-compact warning is not a usage limit: the conversation has grown close to the session's auto-compact window, the threshold at which Claude Code summarizes older history to free space. The remedy is context reduction, not more quota.

nodes.label: Unexpectedly high API or cloud spend
nodes.rationale: Unexpectedly high spend on an API or cloud-provider plan usually traces to long sessions that were never cleared or to Opus left as the default model; the highest-impact habits are clearing between unrelated tasks and matching the model to the job.

nodes.label: Agent team token costs
nodes.rationale: Agent teams spawn multiple Claude Code instances, each with its own context window, so token usage scales with the number of active teammates and how long each one runs; each active teammate keeps consuming tokens until it exits or the session ends.

nodes.label: Agent team cost practices
nodes.rationale: To keep agent team costs manageable: use Sonnet for teammates, keep teams small (usage is roughly proportional to team size), keep spawn prompts focused since everything in them adds to context from the start, shut teammates down when their work is done, and keep team tasks small and self-contained.

nodes.label: Agent teams disabled by default
nodes.rationale: Agent teams are disabled by default; enabling them requires setting `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1` in settings.json or the environment.

nodes.label: Agent teams use ~7x tokens in plan mode
nodes.rationale: Agent teams use approximately 7x more tokens than standard sessions when teammates run in plan mode, because each teammate maintains its own context window and runs as a separate Claude instance.

nodes.label: Token costs scale with context size
nodes.rationale: Token costs scale with context size — the more context Claude processes, the more tokens are consumed — which makes every cost-reduction strategy in the doc a strategy for keeping context small and per-message cost down.

nodes.label: Prompt caching
nodes.rationale: Claude Code automatically optimizes cost through prompt caching, which reduces the cost of repeated content such as system prompts by re-reading history at the cached token rate.

nodes.label: Auto-compaction
nodes.rationale: Auto-compaction summarizes conversation history when the session approaches its context limit, automatically holding context — and therefore cost — down without user action.

nodes.label: Clear between unrelated tasks
nodes.rationale: Use `/clear` to start fresh when switching to unrelated work, because stale context wastes tokens on every subsequent message. `/rename` before clearing makes the session easy to find again with `/resume`.

nodes.label: Custom compaction instructions
nodes.rationale: `/compact Focus on code samples and API usage` tells Claude what to preserve during summarization, and a `# Compact instructions` section in CLAUDE.md customizes it persistently. In a fresh session `/compact` prints `Not enough messages to compact.`

nodes.label: Choose the right model
nodes.rationale: Sonnet handles most coding tasks well and costs less than Opus, so Opus should be reserved for complex architectural decisions or multi-step reasoning. Switch mid-session with `/model`, set a default in `/config`, and specify `model: haiku` for simple subagent tasks.

nodes.label: Reduce MCP server overhead
nodes.rationale: MCP tool definitions are deferred by default, so only tool names and server instructions enter context until a specific tool is used. `/context` shows what is consuming space, and `/mcp` lists configured servers so unused ones can be disabled.

nodes.label: Prefer CLI tools over MCP servers
nodes.rationale: CLI tools such as `gh`, `aws`, `gcloud`, and `sentry-cli` remain more context-efficient than MCP servers because they add no per-tool listing to context; Claude can run them directly as commands.

nodes.label: Code intelligence plugins for typed languages
nodes.rationale: Code intelligence plugins give Claude precise symbol navigation instead of text search, so one 'go to definition' call replaces a grep plus reads of several candidate files. Installed language servers also report type errors automatically after edits, catching mistakes without running a compiler.

nodes.label: Offload preprocessing to hooks
nodes.rationale: Custom hooks can preprocess data before Claude sees it — instead of Claude reading a 10,000-line log to find errors, a hook greps for `ERROR` and returns only matching lines, cutting context from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds.

nodes.label: Skills supply domain knowledge on demand
nodes.rationale: A skill can give Claude domain knowledge so it does not have to explore: a 'codebase-overview' skill describing architecture, key directories, and naming conventions delivers that context on invocation instead of spending tokens reading multiple files.

nodes.label: PreToolUse test-output filtering hook
nodes.rationale: A worked example: a PreToolUse hook matching `Bash` rewrites test-runner commands (`npm test`, `pytest`, `go test`) to pipe through `grep -A 5 -E '(FAIL|ERROR|error:)' | head -100`, returning `updatedInput` with `permissionDecision: allow`. Verify with `/hooks`, or run with `claude --debug-file` and look for the `modified tool input keys` line.

nodes.label: Move CLAUDE.md instructions into skills
nodes.rationale: CLAUDE.md is loaded into context at session start, so workflow-specific instructions in it cost tokens even during unrelated work. Skills load on demand only when invoked; the doc's target is to keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines of essentials.

nodes.label: Adjust extended thinking
nodes.rationale: Extended thinking is on by default and its tokens are billed as output tokens, with default budgets of tens of thousands of tokens per request. Reduce cost on simple tasks by lowering the effort level with `/effort` or `/model`, disabling thinking in `/config`, or setting `MAX_THINKING_TOKENS` on fixed-budget models. Adaptive-reasoning models ignore nonzero budgets, and Fable models always use extended thinking.

nodes.label: Delegate verbose operations to subagents
nodes.rationale: Running tests, fetching documentation, or processing log files consumes significant context; delegating them to subagents keeps the verbose output in the subagent's context while only a summary returns to the main conversation.

nodes.label: Write specific prompts
nodes.rationale: Vague requests like 'improve this codebase' trigger broad scanning; a specific request such as 'add input validation to the login function in auth.ts' lets Claude work with minimal file reads.

nodes.label: Habits for complex work
nodes.rationale: Four habits avoid tokens wasted going down the wrong path: use plan mode (Shift+Tab) before implementation to get approval on an approach; course-correct early with Escape, `/rewind`, or double-Escape to a checkpoint; give verification targets such as test cases, screenshots, or expected output; and test incrementally, one file at a time.

nodes.label: Background token usage
nodes.rationale: Claude Code uses tokens for background functionality even when idle — conversation summarization for `claude --resume`, and commands like `/usage` that generate status requests — typically under $0.04 per session.

nodes.label: Why usage climbs in a long session
nodes.rationale: A session open for hours can consume far more plan limit than the user's activity suggests, for a small set of identified reasons: long context, cache misses, scheduled tasks, cross-session messages, goal check-ins, active agent teammates, and compaction itself.

nodes.label: Long context sent with every request
nodes.rationale: Claude Code sends the full conversation with every request, and each tool use sends another request carrying that batch of tool results. With prompt caching that history is re-read at the cached token rate, so even a one-line question in a day-old session draws usage for the whole conversation.

nodes.label: Cache miss after an idle break
nodes.rationale: The first message after a break longer than the cache lifetime misses the cache and reprocesses the full context. The lifetime is one hour on a subscription, drops to five minutes once drawing on usage credits, and is five minutes by default on an API key or cloud provider; the one-hour TTL can be chosen explicitly. On Pro and Max, resuming a large session after a long break offers to resume from a summary.

nodes.label: Scheduled tasks fire while idle
nodes.rationale: A scheduled task fires on its interval even while the session is idle, sending the full context each time.

nodes.label: Cross-session messages start idle turns
nodes.rationale: Claude Code delivers a message from another of your sessions as a new turn when this session sits idle, sending the full context each time. Setting `crossSessionInbound` to `hold` holds inbound messages instead of delivering them.

nodes.label: Idle goal check-ins
nodes.rationale: While background work keeps an active goal waiting, Claude Code asks Claude to check on that work even when idle, starting a new turn that sends the full context — at most three idle check-ins per goal between prompts (uncapped before v2.1.246, and requiring v2.1.236 or later). `CLAUDE_CODE_GOAL_CHECKIN_MINUTES=0` turns check-ins off.

nodes.label: Compaction is itself a large request
nodes.rationale: `/compact` reads the conversation it summarizes, so compacting a large context is itself a large request. When continuity is not needed, `/clear` costs nothing.

nodes.label: Enterprise consumption planning guide
nodes.rationale: The Claude Enterprise consumption guide is the planning reference for admins: it explains how consumption differs across Claude chat, Claude Code, and Cowork and gives per-user dollar starting points. Budget more for a coding seat than a chat seat, since each Claude Code turn carries file contents, tool calls, and multi-step reasoning — one debugging session can exceed a day of chat.

nodes.label: Version checks and billing support channels
nodes.rationale: Claude Code updates regularly and those updates can change how features work, including cost reporting, so `claude --version` is the first check when behavior differs from the docs. Account-specific billing questions go through the in-product messenger — claude.ai for subscription plans, platform.claude.com for Console/API billing.

nodes.label: Claude Code data training policy
nodes.rationale: Anthropic's policy governing whether data sent to Claude Code may be used to train future models. It splits by account class: consumer accounts get a per-user choice, while commercial accounts are excluded from generative-model training unless they opt in.

nodes.label: Consumer training choice (Free, Pro, Max)
nodes.rationale: Free, Pro and Max users choose whether their data may be used to improve future Claude models. When the setting is on, Anthropic trains new models with data from those accounts, including data produced by using Claude Code from them. The preference can be changed at any time at claude.ai/settings/data-privacy-controls.

nodes.label: Commercial no-training policy
nodes.rationale: Team and Enterprise plans, API, third-party platforms and Claude Gov keep existing policies: Anthropic does not train generative models on code or prompts sent to Claude Code under commercial terms, unless the customer has chosen to provide their data for model improvement.

nodes.label: Development Partner Program
nodes.rationale: An explicit opt-in through which an organization admin can supply materials for Anthropic to train on. It is available only for the Anthropic first-party API, and not for Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud's Agent Platform users.

nodes.label: /feedback command (and /bug, /share)
nodes.rationale: Running /feedback sends a copy of the conversation history, including code, to Anthropic, which may use it to improve products and services. /bug and /share submit through the same path.

nodes.label: Five-year feedback transcript retention
nodes.rationale: Transcripts shared via /feedback, or via /bug and /share which report through the same path, are retained for 5 years.

nodes.label: Claude-drafted feedback
nodes.rationale: Claude can draft a feedback report and queue it locally for the user to review; Claude Code sends nothing until the user chooses to send the draft. A sent draft uses the same submission path and retention as other /feedback reports, and includes the transcript only if the user chose to include it on the draft's review screen.

nodes.label: Session quality survey
nodes.rationale: The "How is Claude doing this session?" prompt records only the rating, including when "Dismiss" is selected. No conversation transcripts, inputs, outputs or other session data are collected as part of the rating prompt itself; it is a simple product satisfaction metric.

nodes.label: Transcript-share follow-up prompt
nodes.rationale: A separate optional step after the rating asking whether Anthropic may look at the session transcript. "Yes" uploads the conversation transcript, subagent transcripts and the raw session log file, retained up to 6 months; "No" declines; "Don't ask again" suppresses it in future sessions. Nothing is uploaded unless Yes is explicitly selected, and responses never affect data training preferences or train models.

nodes.label: Pre-upload secret redaction
nodes.rationale: Known API key and token patterns are redacted before a shared transcript is uploaded or written to a local archive. Source code, file contents and other conversation content are uploaded as-is.

nodes.label: Local feedback bundle archive
nodes.rationale: On Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, signed-in Claude apps gateway sessions, or with no Anthropic credentials configured, the same payload is written to ~/.claude/feedback-bundles/ instead of being uploaded. Nothing leaves the machine until the user forwards that file.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FEEDBACK_SURVEY
nodes.rationale: Setting CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FEEDBACK_SURVEY=1 disables session quality surveys. The survey is also disabled when DISABLE_TELEMETRY, DO_NOT_TRACK or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC is set.

nodes.label: feedbackSurveyRate setting
nodes.rationale: A settings-file probability between 0 and 1 that controls how often the session quality survey appears, for users who want to reduce frequency rather than disable the survey outright.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FEEDBACK_SURVEY_FOR_OTEL
nodes.rationale: Organizations that block nonessential traffic but capture survey responses through their own OpenTelemetry collector can set CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FEEDBACK_SURVEY_FOR_OTEL=1 to re-enable the survey. Ratings then log to the configured collector only; the transcript-share follow-up and all other Anthropic-bound feedback traffic stay disabled.

nodes.label: Claude Code data retention
nodes.rationale: Anthropic retains Claude Code data based on account type and preferences, with separate consumer and commercial tiers plus a local on-disk cache. Full terms live in the Commercial Terms of Service, Consumer Terms and Privacy Policy.

nodes.label: Consumer retention: 5 years or 30 days
nodes.rationale: Free, Pro and Max users who allow data use for model improvement get a 5-year retention period supporting model development and safety improvements; users who do not allow it get 30 days.

nodes.label: Commercial retention: 30-day standard
nodes.rationale: Team, Enterprise and API users have a standard 30-day retention period.

nodes.label: Zero data retention (ZDR)
nodes.rationale: ZDR is available to qualified accounts for Claude Code on Claude for Enterprise. It is not included in the standard Enterprise plan and is enabled per organization by the account team after confirming eligibility; it also removes server-side persistence on the Anthropic API.

nodes.label: Local plaintext transcript cache
nodes.rationale: Claude Code clients store session transcripts locally in plaintext under ~/.claude/projects/ for 30 days by default, to enable session resumption.

nodes.label: cleanupPeriodDays
nodes.rationale: The setting that adjusts the local transcript cache retention period away from its 30-day default.

nodes.label: Desktop/Cowork cleanup exemption
nodes.rationale: Transcripts of sessions started or most recently continued in Claude Desktop or Cowork are exempt by default from the local 30-day cleanup limit.

nodes.label: Web session deletion
nodes.rationale: Individual Claude Code on the web sessions can be deleted at any time; deleting a session permanently removes that session's event data.

nodes.label: Data access overview
nodes.rationale: For first-party users, what is logged is documented separately for local and remote Claude Code. For remote Claude Code, Claude accesses only the repository where the session was initiated, not other connected repositories.

nodes.label: Remote Control data flow
nodes.rationale: Remote Control sessions follow the local data flow because all execution happens on the user's machine; while connected, the session transcript is also stored on Anthropic servers to sync the conversation across devices.

nodes.label: Local data flow over TLS 1.2+
nodes.rationale: Claude Code runs locally and sends all user prompts and model outputs over the network to reach the LLM, encrypted in transit via TLS 1.2 or later. It is compatible with most popular VPNs and LLM proxies.

nodes.label: Encryption at rest by model provider
nodes.rationale: Encryption at rest is determined by the model provider rather than by Claude Code itself; the doc tabulates the guarantee for each supported provider.

nodes.label: Anthropic API encryption at rest
nodes.rationale: The Anthropic API uses infrastructure-level disk encryption (AES-256); Zero Data Retention can be enabled for no server-side persistence.

nodes.label: Amazon Bedrock encryption at rest
nodes.rationale: Amazon Bedrock provides AES-256 encryption with AWS-managed keys, with customer-managed keys available via AWS KMS.

nodes.label: Google Cloud Agent Platform encryption at rest
nodes.rationale: Google Cloud's Agent Platform uses Google-managed encryption keys, with CMEK available.

nodes.label: Microsoft Foundry encryption at rest
nodes.rationale: Microsoft Foundry depends on the deployment's hosting option: Hosted on Azure keeps prompts and completions within Azure, egressing only usage metadata and content flagged by Anthropic's safety systems, while Hosted on Anthropic routes requests to Anthropic infrastructure with AES-256 disk encryption.

nodes.label: Cloud execution in Anthropic-managed VMs
nodes.rationale: Claude Code on the web runs sessions in Anthropic-managed virtual machines by default: the repository is cloned to an isolated VM, and prompts, code changes and outputs follow the same data policies and retention as local Claude Code usage.

nodes.label: Self-hosted execution environments
nodes.rationale: Sessions an organization routes to a self-hosted environment run on infrastructure the organization controls, with a separate reference describing what stays on those machines and what still goes to Anthropic.

nodes.label: GitHub credential proxy
nodes.rationale: In Anthropic-hosted cloud sessions, GitHub authentication is handled through a secure proxy so the user's GitHub credentials never enter the sandbox.

nodes.label: Outbound security proxy
nodes.rationale: All outbound traffic from an Anthropic-hosted cloud session goes through a security proxy for audit logging and abuse prevention.

nodes.label: Operational telemetry services
nodes.rationale: Claude Code sends two kinds of operational telemetry — usage metrics and error reports — each of which can be turned off individually, or all at once via the nonessential-traffic switch.

nodes.label: Usage metrics (DISABLE_TELEMETRY)
nodes.rationale: Metrics cover latency, reliability and usage patterns and are sent to Anthropic and to third-party logging infrastructure over TLS. They never include code, prompts or file paths; DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 opts out.

nodes.label: Error reports (DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING)
nodes.rationale: Error messages and stack traces from Claude Code's own internals are sent to a third-party error tracking service over TLS, with known patterns of secrets, file paths, email addresses and other personal information redacted before anything leaves the machine. DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING=1 opts out.

nodes.label: Error reporting eligibility conditions
nodes.rationale: Error reporting is on only when all four hold: the user signs in with a Claude Pro or Max subscription, runs Claude Code v2.1.198 or later, connects directly to the Claude API, and the organization has no zero data retention or HIPAA agreement.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC
nodes.rationale: A single switch that disables all non-essential traffic at once — metrics, error reports and surveys — but does not affect the WebFetch domain safety check or official plugin marketplace auto-install, each of which has its own opt-out.

nodes.label: Feature-flag evaluation
nodes.rationale: Setting DISABLE_TELEMETRY or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC also disables the feature-flag evaluation that Remote Control depends on; DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING does not.

nodes.label: Feedback history scope selection
nodes.rationale: Before submitting from the feedback dialog the user chooses how much history to include: the current session only (the default), or also other sessions from the same project over the last 24 hours or 7 days.

nodes.label: Feedback storage in Google Cloud Storage
nodes.rationale: Feedback data is encrypted in transit via TLS and stored in Google Cloud Storage, which encrypts stored data at rest by default. Optionally, a GitHub issue is created in the public repository.

nodes.label: DISABLE_FEEDBACK_COMMAND
nodes.rationale: Setting the DISABLE_FEEDBACK_COMMAND environment variable to 1 opts out of sending /feedback reports to Anthropic.

nodes.label: Default behaviors by API provider
nodes.rationale: A matrix stating that error reporting, telemetry and bug reporting default off on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry and Claude Platform on AWS, while defaulting on for the Claude API; session quality surveys and the WebFetch domain safety check are exceptions that run regardless of provider.

nodes.label: Claude apps gateway session defaults
nodes.rationale: On a signed-in Claude apps gateway session, usage analytics, error reporting and survey ratings to Anthropic are disabled by the gateway credential itself, with no setting to re-enable them.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_PROVIDER_MANAGED_BY_HOST
nodes.rationale: When a host platform sets CLAUDE_CODE_PROVIDER_MANAGED_BY_HOST, metrics default to on for Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry and Claude Platform on AWS and follow the standard DISABLE_TELEMETRY opt-out; error reporting and /feedback reports remain off by default there.

nodes.label: WebFetch domain safety check
nodes.rationale: Before fetching a URL, WebFetch sends only the requested hostname to api.anthropic.com to check it against an Anthropic-maintained safety blocklist — not the full URL, path or page contents. A passing hostname is cached five minutes; a blocked or failed one is re-checked on the next request. If a network blocks api.anthropic.com, WebFetch requests fail until the domain is allowlisted or the preflight is skipped.

nodes.label: skipWebFetchPreflight setting
nodes.rationale: Setting skipWebFetchPreflight: true in settings disables the domain safety check, so WebFetch retrieves any URL without consulting the blocklist — the doc recommends combining it with WebFetch permission rules to restrict reachable domains.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_OFFICIAL_MARKETPLACE_AUTOINSTALL
nodes.rationale: The dedicated opt-out for official plugin marketplace auto-install, which the nonessential-traffic switch does not cover.

nodes.label: Environment variables in settings.json
nodes.rationale: All of the data-usage environment variables can be checked into settings.json, per the settings reference, so an organization's opt-out posture travels with the repository or machine configuration.

nodes.label: Config debugging premise
nodes.rationale: When Claude ignores an instruction or a configured feature does not appear, the cause is usually that the file did not load, loaded from a different location than expected, or was overridden by another file. Debugging therefore means inspecting what Claude Code actually loaded, rather than assuming a bug.

nodes.label: /context
nodes.rationale: /context shows everything occupying the context window for the current session, broken down by system prompt, system tools, MCP tools, custom subagents with the source each loaded from, memory files, skills, and conversation messages. It is the first command to run, to confirm whether CLAUDE.md, rules, or skill descriptions are present at all.

nodes.label: Bundled skills appear only in /context
nodes.rationale: The skills section of /context also includes bundled skills, which /skills does not list. A skill missing from /skills is therefore not proof that no such skill loaded.

nodes.label: /memory
nodes.rationale: /memory shows memory file locations across user and project scopes, with the option to open each in an editor, plus access to the auto memory folder and the auto memory toggle.

nodes.label: /skills
nodes.rationale: /skills lists available skills from project, user, and plugin sources, and shows a badge per skill — a "user-only" label means Claude will not trigger it on its own.

nodes.label: /hooks
nodes.rationale: /hooks lists every hook registered for the current session, grouped by event, and shows the active hook configurations. A hook that does not appear there is not being read at all.

nodes.label: /mcp
nodes.rationale: /mcp shows every configured MCP server, its connection status, and whether it has been approved for the current project. It also offers the Reconnect action for a server that connected but returned no tools.

nodes.label: /permissions
nodes.rationale: /permissions shows the resolved allow and deny rules currently in effect, after all scopes have merged.

nodes.label: /doctor
nodes.rationale: /doctor is an in-session setup checkup covering installation health, invalid settings files, unused extensions, duplicate subagent names in the same directory, and checked-in CLAUDE.md content Claude can derive from the codebase — proposing fixes and asking before applying them.

nodes.label: /debug [issue]
nodes.rationale: /debug [issue] enables debug logging for the session and prompts Claude to diagnose the issue using the log output and settings paths.

nodes.label: /status
nodes.rationale: /status shows which settings sources are active, including whether managed settings are in effect. It is the check to run when a problem survives even a clean configuration directory.

nodes.label: claude doctor (terminal)
nodes.rationale: Running `claude doctor` from the terminal prints read-only installation and settings diagnostics without starting a session, and is how invalid settings files are found. It also reports settings validation failures and lists a managed-settings key that was dropped.

nodes.label: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md loads on demand
nodes.rationale: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files do not load at session start; they load on demand when Claude reads a file in that directory with the Read tool — not at launch, and not when writing or creating files there. Their absence from a /context breakdown is therefore expected, not a fault.

nodes.label: Loaded but not followed
nodes.rationale: If /context confirms the file loaded but Claude still is not following a particular instruction, the issue is how the instruction is written rather than whether it loaded. CLAUDE.md works well for guidance you would give a new teammate: project conventions, build commands, and where files belong.

nodes.label: What lowers instruction adherence
nodes.rationale: Adherence drops when an instruction is vague enough to interpret multiple ways, when two files give conflicting direction, or when the file has grown long enough that individual rules get less attention.

nodes.label: Guidance vs enforcement
nodes.rationale: CLAUDE.md and permissions solve different problems: CLAUDE.md tells Claude how the project works so it makes good decisions, while permissions and hooks enforce limits regardless of what Claude decides. Use CLAUDE.md for "we do it this way here" and permissions or hooks for security boundaries and anything that must never happen, where a guarantee is needed instead of guidance.

nodes.label: Settings scope precedence
nodes.rationale: Settings merge across managed, user, project, and local scopes: managed settings apply first when present, and among the rest the closer scope overrides the broader one in the order local, then project, then user. When a setting does not seem to apply, the value is usually being overridden by another scope.

nodes.label: Flags and env vars as an override layer
nodes.rationale: Some settings can also be set by command-line flags or environment variables, which act as another override layer on top of the scope merge — so an environment variable is a common reason a configured value appears to be ignored.

nodes.label: settings.local.json overrides settings.json
nodes.rationale: A settings.json value that seems ignored is often set again in settings.local.json: settings.local.json overrides settings.json, and both override ~/.claude/settings.json.

nodes.label: ~/.claude.json is app state, not settings
nodes.rationale: Permissions, hooks, or env set globally are ignored when they were added to ~/.claude.json, which holds app state and UI toggles. Those keys belong in ~/.claude/settings.json — two different files.

nodes.label: Project MCP servers need one-time approval
nodes.rationale: Project-scoped servers in .mcp.json require a one-time approval; if the prompt was dismissed the server stays disabled until it is approved from /mcp. A correctly defined server can therefore provide no tools at all.

nodes.label: Relative paths break MCP server startup
nodes.rationale: A server that fails to start shows as failed in /mcp, and relative file paths in `command` or `args` are a frequent cause: they resolve against the directory Claude Code was launched from, not the location of .mcp.json. Use absolute paths for local scripts; executables on PATH such as npx or uvx work as-is.

nodes.label: Connected server listing zero tools
nodes.rationale: A server shown as connected but listing zero tools has started successfully but is not returning a tool list. The first remedy is Reconnect from /mcp.

nodes.label: claude --debug=mcp and the debug log
nodes.rationale: If an MCP server's tool count stays at zero after a reconnect, run `claude --debug=mcp` and read the server's stderr in the debug log at ~/.claude/debug/<session-id>.txt.

nodes.label: .mcp.json location and mcpServers key
nodes.rationale: Project MCP config goes at the repository root as .mcp.json — not inside .claude/ — with servers under the `mcpServers` key. Servers placed under a top-level `servers` key, as in VS Code's mcp.json, never load.

nodes.label: settings.json does not read mcpServers
nodes.rationale: MCP servers added under an `mcpServers` key in settings.json never appear, because settings.json does not read that key. Define project servers in .mcp.json at the repository root, or run `claude mcp add --scope user` for user-scoped servers.

nodes.label: Per-server env in .mcp.json
nodes.rationale: An MCP server starts without expected environment variables when its config entry does not set them and they are absent from the environment Claude Code passes to stdio servers — its own environment, minus the variables it strips from subprocesses. Setting per-server `env` inside the server's .mcp.json entry does not depend on the launch environment or workspace trust.

nodes.label: Hooks live under the hooks key in settings.json
nodes.rationale: There is no standalone hooks file for project or user config: hooks must be defined under the "hooks" key in a settings file. A hook that does not appear in /hooks is not being read. Only plugins load a separate hooks/hooks.json.

nodes.label: Matcher separator and the v2.1.191 boundary
nodes.rationale: The `matcher` field is a single string that uses `|` to match multiple tool names, e.g. "Edit|Write". From v2.1.191 a `,` is an equivalent list separator, but earlier versions evaluated a comma as a literal regex character so "Edit,Write" matched nothing — use `|`, or upgrade.

nodes.label: Misspelled tool name matches nothing
nodes.rationale: A misspelled tool name produces a matcher that matches nothing, so the hook fails silently — it is registered and visible, but never fires.

nodes.label: Matcher matching is case-sensitive
nodes.rationale: A lowercase matcher value such as "bash" never fires, because matching is case-sensitive and tool names are capitalized: Bash, Edit, Write, Read.

nodes.label: Array matcher is a schema error
nodes.rationale: Giving `matcher` a JSON array instead of a string is a schema error: Claude Code shows a settings error notice and rejects the whole user, project, or local settings file, `claude doctor` reports the validation failure, and no hook from that file appears in /hooks.

nodes.label: Managed settings drop the whole hooks key
nodes.rationale: In managed settings, an invalid array matcher makes Claude Code drop the entire `hooks` key from the file that contains it, so none of that file's hooks apply. The file's other settings still apply, and `claude doctor` lists the dropped key.

nodes.label: settings.json edits apply without restart
nodes.rationale: Edits to settings.json take effect in the running session after a brief file-stability delay, so no restart is needed. If /hooks still shows the old definition a few seconds after saving, run /hooks again to refresh the view.

nodes.label: claude --debug traces hook evaluation
nodes.rationale: When /hooks shows the hook but it still does not fire, start a session with `claude --debug` and trigger the tool call: the debug log records each event, which matchers were checked, and the hook's exit code and output.

nodes.label: SessionEnd hook for cleanup
nodes.rationale: Cleanup logic that never runs at session end usually means no SessionEnd hook is configured; add one in settings.json.

nodes.label: claude --safe-mode
nodes.rationale: `claude --safe-mode` launches a session with all customizations disabled — CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins, hooks, MCP servers, and custom commands and agents — while authentication, model selection, built-in tools, and permissions work normally. If the problem disappears, one of those surfaces is the cause.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR clean session
nodes.rationale: If the problem persists in safe mode, or the settings themselves are suspect, point CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR at an empty directory to bypass everything under ~/.claude and launch from a directory with no .claude folder, .mcp.json, or CLAUDE.md (e.g. `cd /tmp && CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=/tmp/claude-clean claude`). The first-run setup screens confirm the clean directory is in effect; later launches skip them because onboarding state is saved there.

nodes.label: Managed settings survive isolation
nodes.rationale: Organization-managed configuration is not disabled by isolation: safe mode still applies managed hooks and settings policy, and a clean configuration directory still reads MDM profiles, registry policy, and managed-settings.json from locations outside the config directory, refetching server-managed settings once it has credentials. Managed plugins, skills, CLAUDE.md, and MCP servers are turned off in safe mode.

nodes.label: Reintroduce configuration one file at a time
nodes.rationale: If the problem disappears in the clean session, the cause is somewhere in the real ~/.claude or project .claude files: reintroduce them one at a time, by copying files into the temporary directory or by launching from the project, to find which one is responsible.

nodes.label: Skills need a folder with SKILL.md
nodes.rationale: A skill does not appear in /skills when its file sits at .claude/skills/name.md instead of in a folder; the required layout is .claude/skills/name/SKILL.md.

nodes.label: disable-model-invocation and description mismatch
nodes.rationale: A skill listed in /skills that Claude never invokes either has `disable-model-invocation: true` in its frontmatter — shown as a "user-only" badge — or its description does not match how the request is phrased.

nodes.label: Subagents and CLAUDE.md
nodes.rationale: The built-in Explore and Plan agents skip CLAUDE.md, while custom subagents load it the same way the main conversation does. For Explore or Plan, restate the instruction in the delegating prompt; for a custom subagent, put critical instructions in the agent file body, which becomes the agent's system prompt.

nodes.label: Prefix deny rules match the literal command string
nodes.rationale: A `Bash(rm *)` deny rule does not block `/bin/rm` or `find -delete`, because prefix rules match the literal command string rather than the underlying executable. Add explicit patterns for each variant, or use a PreToolUse hook or the sandbox for a hard guarantee.

nodes.label: Install and login problems are out of scope
nodes.rationale: This guide covers configuration that did not take effect; installation, authentication, and connectivity problems (command not found, PATH, login) belong to the separate Troubleshoot installation and login page, and performance, hangs, and search issues to Troubleshooting.

nodes.label: Claude Desktop application
nodes.rationale: The Claude Desktop app has three tabs: Chat for conversations, Cowork for Dispatch and longer agentic work, and Code for software development. It ships as a universal macOS build, a Windows x64 or ARM64 installer, and a Linux beta distributed via apt or .deb.

nodes.label: Code tab
nodes.rationale: The Code tab is the software-development surface of the desktop app and the subject of this reference page. On Windows it requires Git for Windows to be installed before the tab will work.

nodes.label: Session
nodes.rationale: In the Code tab each conversation is a session with its own chat history, project folder, and code changes, independent of any other session. The sidebar lists sessions and lets several run in parallel.

nodes.label: Four pre-send session settings
nodes.rationale: Before sending the first message you configure four things in the prompt area: environment (Local, Cloud, SSH, or WSL), project folder, model, and permission mode. Model and permission mode can be changed during the session.

nodes.label: Permission modes
nodes.rationale: Permission modes control how much autonomy Claude has in a session: whether it asks before editing files, running commands, or both. They are switchable at any time from the mode selector next to the send button; earlier versions labeled them Ask permissions, Auto accept edits, and Plan mode.

nodes.label: Manual mode (default)
nodes.rationale: Manual mode (settings key `default`) makes Claude ask before editing files or running commands; you see a diff and can accept or reject each change.

nodes.label: Accept edits mode
nodes.rationale: Accept edits (`acceptEdits`) auto-accepts file edits and common filesystem commands such as mkdir, touch, and mv, but still asks before other terminal commands.

nodes.label: Plan mode
nodes.rationale: Plan mode (`plan`) lets Claude read files and run commands to explore, then propose a plan without editing source. The documented best practice is to start complex tasks in Plan, then switch to Accept edits or Manual to execute the approved plan. Unlike other modes, a Plan selection applies to the current session only rather than being remembered per folder.

nodes.label: Auto mode
nodes.rationale: Auto mode (`auto`) executes all actions with background safety classifiers that verify alignment with your request, reducing permission prompts while keeping oversight. It appears in the selector when available and has no separate Settings toggle.

nodes.label: Bypass permissions mode
nodes.rationale: Bypass permissions (`bypassPermissions`) runs without prompts except for actions no mode auto-approves, safety-classifier flags on external sites, and desktop actions such as archiving a session where Claude always asks. It is equivalent to the CLI's --dangerously-skip-permissions, is enabled in Settings on Pro and Max but only by organization policy on Team and Enterprise, is unavailable in cloud sessions, and should be used only in sandboxed containers or VMs.

nodes.label: permissions.defaultMode and per-folder memory
nodes.rationale: Adding `permissions.defaultMode` to a settings file sets the default mode for new local sessions, and the desktop app reads the same settings files as the CLI. A mode picked in the selector is remembered per folder and takes precedence over defaultMode for that folder, except Plan.

nodes.label: Auto mode availability requirements
nodes.rationale: Auto mode is available to all users on the Anthropic API and requires Claude Opus 4.6 or later, Sonnet 4.6 or later, or a Fable model. Enterprise deployments routing Desktop to Google Cloud's Agent Platform also get auto mode by default.

nodes.label: Permission modes in cloud sessions
nodes.rationale: Cloud sessions support Accept edits, Plan, and Auto only. Accept edits corresponds to `default` mode there because cloud sessions pre-approve file edits, so the selector shows Accept edits instead of Manual; Bypass permissions is not available, including in self-hosted environments.

nodes.label: Browser pane
nodes.rationale: The Browser pane is a tabbed browser inside the session, opened with Cmd+Shift+B (Ctrl+Shift+B on Windows) or the Views menu. It hosts app previews, opens static HTML, PDF, image, and video files from the project, and uses a clean browser profile separate from your personal browser.

nodes.label: App preview and self-verification
nodes.rationale: Claude can start a dev server and open it in the Browser pane to verify its own changes — taking screenshots, inspecting the DOM, clicking elements, filling forms, and fixing what it finds. This works for frontend apps and backend servers alike, and servers can be started, stopped, or configured from the session toolbar's server dropdown, with cookies and local storage optionally persisted across restarts.

nodes.label: autoVerify
nodes.rationale: When autoVerify is enabled Claude verifies code changes automatically after every edit — screenshots, error checks, and confirmation the change works — before completing its response. It is on by default and can be disabled per project with "autoVerify": false in .claude/launch.json or from the server dropdown; preview tools remain available when it is off.

nodes.label: .claude/launch.json
nodes.rationale: Claude auto-detects the dev server setup and stores it in .claude/launch.json at the root of the folder chosen when starting the session; the file supports JSON with comments and can hold multiple configurations (e.g. a frontend and an API). Because preview uses that folder as its working directory, subfolders with their own dev servers are not detected automatically.

nodes.label: launch.json configuration fields
nodes.rationale: Each configurations entry accepts name, runtimeExecutable, runtimeArgs, port (default 3000), cwd, env, autoPort, program, args, and url. runtimeExecutable+runtimeArgs starts a server through a package manager while program+args runs a standalone script with node; env must not hold secrets because the file is committed to the repo.

nodes.label: autoPort port-conflict handling
nodes.rationale: autoPort:true makes Claude pick a free port, autoPort:false fails with an error when the port is taken (for OAuth callbacks or CORS allowlists that need an exact port), and unset makes Claude ask once and save the answer. When Claude picks a different port it passes it to the server via the PORT environment variable.

nodes.label: Preview url field and its localhost rule
nodes.rationale: The url field overrides the default http://localhost:<port> preview address for HTTPS servers, *.localhost subdomains, and redirect sign-in flows. For security a localhost url must be just the origin — no path or query, and the port must match the entry's port — and a violating value is reported as a configuration error naming the url and the fix; setting url with no command attaches the preview to a server you already run.

nodes.label: Browsing external sites
nodes.rationale: The Browser pane can open documentation, issue trackers, and any other site next to the running app, including popup sign-in flows such as Google OAuth. Claude reads and interacts with external pages using the same tools it uses to verify your app, but under two extra safety checks.

nodes.label: Safety classifiers and domain allowlist on external pages
nodes.rationale: Safety classifiers — the same ones auto mode uses — review Claude's write actions on external pages such as clicking and typing in every permission mode, and a flagged action produces a permission prompt regardless of mode. In modes other than Auto and Bypass permissions, a domain allowlist check also runs before Claude navigates to a new site.

nodes.label: Per-site action approval
nodes.rationale: The first time Claude acts on an external site a permission card offers Allow once, Always allow, or Deny; Always allow saves the approval for that site on your device and each site, including subdomains, needs its own. Local dev servers and project files need no approval, and even on an approved site Claude will not purchase items, create accounts, or bypass CAPTCHAs without your input.

nodes.label: Claude in Chrome extension
nodes.rationale: The Claude in Chrome extension shares your browser's login state, so it is the right tool when you want Claude to act as you in logged-in sessions; the Browser pane's clean profile is for building and testing your app and sites that do not need your identity. Both share the same safety model, and the Browser follows the same organizational site allowlist and blocklist controls as the extension.

nodes.label: browserExternalPageTools and disableBrowserExternalNavigation
nodes.rationale: browserExternalPageTools set to "disabled" removes Claude's tools on external pages while users can still navigate there; disableBrowserExternalNavigation set to the JSON boolean true blocks all external navigation for both users and Claude, including allowlisted sites, while leaving localhost previews and file previews working.

nodes.label: Diff view with line comments
nodes.rationale: A diff stats indicator such as +12 -1 opens a file-by-file diff viewer. Clicking any line opens a comment box, and comments on multiple lines are submitted together with Cmd+Enter (Ctrl+Enter on Windows); Claude then makes the requested changes, which appear as a new diff.

nodes.label: Review code in the diff view
nodes.rationale: The Review code button asks Claude to evaluate the current diffs before you commit, leaving comments in the diff view. It focuses on high-signal issues — compile errors, definite logic errors, security vulnerabilities, obvious bugs — and deliberately does not flag style, formatting, pre-existing issues, or anything a linter would catch.

nodes.label: Pull request CI monitoring
nodes.rationale: After a pull request is opened a CI status bar appears in the session; Claude Code uses the GitHub CLI to poll check results and surface failures, and sends a desktop notification when CI finishes.

nodes.label: Auto-fix and Auto-merge toggles
nodes.rationale: Auto-fix makes Claude attempt to fix failing CI checks by reading the failure output and iterating; Auto-merge makes Claude merge the PR once all checks pass, using the squash method. Auto-merge must first be enabled in the GitHub repository settings or Claude cannot merge.

nodes.label: GitHub CLI requirement
nodes.rationale: PR monitoring requires the GitHub CLI (gh) to be installed and authenticated on your machine; if gh is not installed, Desktop prompts you to install it the first time you try to create a PR.

nodes.label: Draggable pane layout
nodes.rationale: The Code tab is built around panes arrangeable in any layout — chat, diff, browser, terminal, file, plan, tasks, subagent, plus the iOS Simulator on macOS. Panes are dragged by header to reposition and by edge to resize; Cmd+\ (Ctrl+\) closes the focused pane. The pane layout, terminal, file editor, and view modes require Claude Desktop v1.2581.0 or later.

nodes.label: Integrated terminal pane
nodes.rationale: The integrated terminal (Ctrl+` or the Views menu) opens in the session's working directory and shares Claude's environment, so commands like npm test or git status see the same files Claude is editing. It is available in local sessions only.

nodes.label: File pane editor
nodes.rationale: Clicking a file path in chat or the diff viewer opens it in the file pane for spot edits, with a warning and override/discard choice if the file changed on disk. It is available in local and SSH sessions only; for cloud sessions you ask Claude to make the change. HTML, PDF, image, and video paths open in the Browser pane instead, and right-click offers Attach as context, Open in an installed editor, Show in Finder/Explorer, and Copy path.

nodes.label: Tasks pane
nodes.rationale: The tasks pane shows background work running inside the current session — subagents, background shell commands, and dynamic workflows — and clicking an entry shows its output in the subagent pane or stops it.

nodes.label: Transcript view modes
nodes.rationale: Three view modes control transcript detail: Normal (tool calls collapsed into summaries with full text responses), Verbose (every tool call, file read, and intermediate step), and Summary (only final responses and the changes made). Ctrl+O cycles them; Verbose is for debugging why Claude acted, Summary for scanning many parallel sessions.

nodes.label: Code tab keyboard shortcuts
nodes.rationale: Cmd+/ (Ctrl+/) lists all Code tab shortcuts, which include Cmd+N new session, Cmd+W close, Ctrl+Tab session cycling, Esc to stop, Cmd+Shift+D/B/S for diff, Browser and element select, Cmd+; side chat, and Cmd+Shift+M/I/E for the mode, model and effort menus. Terminal-based interactive-mode shortcuts such as Shift+Tab do not apply in Desktop.

nodes.label: Usage ring
nodes.rationale: The usage ring next to the model picker shows current context window usage and plan usage for the period. Context usage is per session, while plan usage is shared across all Claude Code surfaces.

nodes.label: Automatic compaction
nodes.rationale: When context fills up Claude automatically summarizes the conversation and continues working; typing /compact triggers that summarization earlier to free context space.

nodes.label: Computer use
nodes.rationale: Computer use lets Claude open apps and control the screen for GUI-only work. It is a research preview on macOS and Windows requiring a Pro or Max plan, is off by default, needs Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions on macOS, and — unlike the sandboxed Bash tool — runs on your actual desktop, so the trust boundary differs even though Claude checks each action and flags on-screen prompt injection.

nodes.label: Most-precise-tool-first ladder
nodes.rationale: Claude tries the most precise tool first: a connector for a service, Bash for a shell command, Claude in Chrome for browser work, the iOS Simulator pane for iOS apps, and computer use only when none of those apply. Computer use is the broadest and slowest, reserved for things nothing else can reach such as native apps, hardware control panels, and proprietary tools without an API.

nodes.label: Per-app access tiers
nodes.rationale: App approvals are prompted per app and carry a fixed tier by category: View only (browsers, trading platforms), Click only (terminals, IDEs), and Full control (everything else). Approvals last the session — 30 minutes in Dispatch-spawned sessions — apps with broad reach show an extra warning, and Denied apps can be listed in Settings to reject them without prompting.

nodes.label: iOS Simulator pane
nodes.rationale: For running and testing iOS apps Desktop opens a dedicated iOS Simulator pane on macOS instead of controlling the screen, and the pane works without enabling computer use. Administrators can set disableMobileSimulatorTools to true to remove Claude's device control and capture tools while leaving the pane usable for the user's own taps.

nodes.label: Parallel sessions in the sidebar
nodes.rationale: New sessions (Cmd+N) run in parallel and are cycled with Ctrl+Tab; Cmd-clicking a sidebar session opens it in a second pane so two sessions are visible at once. The sidebar filters by status, project, or environment and groups by project, and the app sends an OS notification when a session finishes a task you are not viewing.

nodes.label: Git worktree session isolation
nodes.rationale: For Git repositories each session gets its own isolated copy of the project using Git worktrees, so changes in one session do not affect others until committed. Worktrees live in <project-root>/.claude/worktrees/ by default with a configurable location and branch prefix, and a .worktreeinclude file pulls gitignored files such as .env into new worktrees.

nodes.label: Git requirement for session isolation
nodes.rationale: Session isolation requires Git; most Macs include it, and on Windows Git is required for the Code tab to work at all, so Git for Windows must be installed and the app restarted. A repository needing Git LFS also fails until Git LFS is installed and git lfs install has been run.

nodes.label: Auto-archive after PR merge or close
nodes.rationale: Turning on "Auto-archive after PR merge or close" in Settings makes a session archive itself when its pull request merges or closes, removing the worktree. It applies only to local sessions that have finished running; otherwise you archive manually from the sidebar's archive icon.

nodes.label: Side chat (/btw)
nodes.rationale: A side chat (Cmd+; or /btw) asks a question that reads the session's context up to that point but adds nothing back to the main conversation, so the session is not steered off course. Side chats work in local, SSH, and WSL sessions and are not saved to disk, so they cannot be reopened after the app closes.

nodes.label: Working across sessions
nodes.rationale: Claude can list other Code tab sessions, read what each has been doing, message between them, and rename or archive them in response to plain-language requests. It sees only sessions the desktop app runs itself — local, SSH, and WSL — never cloud sessions, terminal CLI sessions, VS Code extension sessions, or the session asking; by default the 20 most recently active, skipping archived ones.

nodes.label: Four cross-session safety behaviors
nodes.rationale: Claude Code applies four safety behaviors across sessions: it always asks before archiving a session, even in Auto and Bypass permissions; it neither sends from nor delivers to an unwatched session such as a scheduled-task run; it checks each message against the receiving session's inbound controls, dropping it when crossSessionInbound is refuse and reporting the refusal; and it quotes each incoming message attributed to its sending session while the receiving session's own permission settings still govern any action taken.

nodes.label: Cloud sessions
nodes.rationale: Cloud sessions run on Anthropic-managed infrastructure and continue after the app closes or the computer shuts down, for large refactors, test suites, and migrations; usage counts toward subscription plan limits with no separate compute charges. They alone support multiple repositories, each with its own branch selector, and can be monitored from claude.ai/code or the mobile app.

nodes.label: Continue in another surface
nodes.rationale: The Continue in menu moves a session elsewhere: to Claude Code on the Web, where Desktop pushes the branch, generates a conversation summary, and creates a cloud session with the full context (requiring a clean working tree, unavailable for SSH sessions), or to a supported IDE opened at the current working directory.

nodes.label: Sessions from Dispatch
nodes.rationale: Dispatch is a persistent conversation in the Cowork tab that can spawn a Code session either on request or on its own judgment; bug fixes, dependency updates, test runs, and PRs route to Code while research, document editing, and spreadsheet work stay in Cowork. Such sessions appear in the sidebar with a Dispatch badge, push-notify your phone, and require a Pro or Max plan.

nodes.label: Customize configuration (connectors, skills, plugins)
nodes.rationale: Clicking Customize in the sidebar manages connectors, skills, and plugins in one place. The Cowork tab sources its skills, plugins, and connectors from this Customize configuration, which syncs through your claude.ai account rather than from the CLI's ~/.claude directory.

nodes.label: Connectors
nodes.rationale: Connectors are MCP servers with a graphical setup flow — Google Calendar, Slack, GitHub, Linear, Notion and more — added from the + button in local and SSH sessions before or during a session. The + button is unavailable in cloud and WSL sessions, where routines configure connectors at creation time instead.

nodes.label: MCP servers in Desktop
nodes.rationale: MCP servers configured in ~/.claude.json or .mcp.json work in both the CLI and Desktop; integrations not offered as connectors are added manually through settings files. In local and SSH sessions the desktop app delivers each user's connected claude.ai connectors to Claude Code directly, so no MCP setting or managed-mcp.json reaches them.

nodes.label: claude_desktop_config.json precedence
nodes.rationale: The Desktop app loads MCP servers from claude_desktop_config.json into local Code tab sessions alongside ~/.claude.json and .mcp.json, and on a name collision the Code tab connects once using the claude_desktop_config.json definition. When user-scope ~/.claude.json and .mcp.json define the same stdio server name the Code tab uses the ~/.claude.json one, departing from the CLI scope hierarchy; the standalone CLI never reads claude_desktop_config.json.

nodes.label: Skills in Desktop sessions
nodes.rationale: Skills load automatically when relevant or are invoked by typing / in the prompt box, covering built-in commands, custom skills, project skills, and plugin skills. Personal skills in ~/.claude/skills/ apply to local sessions, an SSH session reads that path from the remote host's home directory, and cloud sessions instead load the skills enabled for your claude.ai account.

nodes.label: Plugins in Desktop
nodes.rationale: Plugins package skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers, and LSP configurations and can be installed from the desktop app without the terminal, scoped to user, project, or local-only. The plugin browser is unavailable in cloud sessions and desktop-installed plugins do not carry there — a cloud session needs the plugin declared in the repository's enabledPlugins or enabled for the claude.ai account as a synced plugin; plugins are unavailable in WSL sessions.

nodes.label: Environment configuration
nodes.rationale: The environment chosen when starting a session determines where Claude executes and how you connect: Local on your machine, Cloud on Anthropic-managed infrastructure, SSH on a remote machine you manage, or WSL inside a WSL 2 distribution on Windows using its Linux toolchain and native paths.

nodes.label: Local sessions and shell environment inheritance
nodes.rationale: The desktop app does not always inherit your full shell environment: launched from the Dock or Finder on macOS it reads ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc only to extract PATH and a fixed set of Claude Code variables, and on Windows it inherits user and system variables but never reads PowerShell profiles.

nodes.label: Local environment editor
nodes.rationale: Hovering Local in the environment dropdown and clicking the gear opens the local environment editor; variables saved there are stored encrypted on your machine and apply to every local session and preview server. Variables added to the env key of ~/.claude/settings.json instead reach Claude sessions only, not dev servers — which is why secrets for a dev server belong in this editor rather than launch.json.

nodes.label: Extended thinking and adaptive reasoning controls
nodes.rationale: Extended thinking is on by default; on the Anthropic API setting MAX_THINKING_TOKENS to 0 turns it off, which has no effect on Fable models that always think, and Claude Code then sends effort high to models such as Opus 5 that reject the higher level with thinking off. On adaptive-reasoning models non-zero MAX_THINKING_TOKENS values are ignored, and only Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 accept CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ADAPTIVE_THINKING=1 for a fixed budget.

nodes.label: disableDesktopLocalSessions
nodes.rationale: Administrators can set disableDesktopLocalSessions to the JSON boolean true, read from managed settings only and requiring Claude Desktop v1.37937.0 or later, to turn off Code sessions that run on the device. Local stays visible but grayed out with a tooltip, WSL is grayed the same way on Windows, and new sessions default to the first configured SSH connection.

nodes.label: SSH sessions
nodes.rationale: An SSH session runs Claude Code on a remote Linux or macOS machine — cloud VMs, dev containers, or hardware-specific servers — with the desktop app as the interface. A connection is defined by Name, SSH Host, SSH Port (default 22), and Identity File; Desktop installs Claude Code on the remote machine automatically on first connect, and SSH sessions support permission modes, connectors, plugins, and MCP servers.

nodes.label: sshConfigs pre-configured connections
nodes.rationale: Administrators distribute SSH connections by adding sshConfigs to a managed settings file; each entry requires id, name, and sshHost with optional sshPort and sshIdentityFile. Managed connections appear automatically in each user's environment dropdown and are marked managed so users can select but not edit or delete them; users may also add sshConfigs to their own ~/.claude/settings.json.

nodes.label: sshHostAllowlist
nodes.rationale: sshHostAllowlist restricts Desktop's SSH sessions to hosts whose resolved hostname matches a case-insensitive pattern, checked after ~/.ssh/config resolution via ssh -G so aliases and ProxyJump entries pass when the resolved HostName matches; an empty array disables SSH sessions entirely. It is read from managed settings only, honored only by the Desktop app, does not restrict ssh run through the Bash tool, and governs connection targets rather than network egress.

nodes.label: Enterprise configuration
nodes.rationale: Organizations on Team or Enterprise plans manage desktop app behavior through three mechanisms: admin console controls, managed settings files, and device management policies.

nodes.label: Admin console controls
nodes.rationale: The admin settings console toggles Code in the desktop, Code in the web, Remote Control, and Disable Bypass permissions mode for an organization.

nodes.label: Managed settings keys for Desktop
nodes.rationale: Managed settings override project and user settings for Desktop sessions and can be deployed in a file or pushed through the admin console. The documented keys are permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode, disableAutoMode, autoMode, browserExternalPageTools, disableMobileSimulatorTools, disableBrowserExternalNavigation, sshConfigs, sshHostAllowlist, disableDesktopLocalSessions, and managedMcpServers.

nodes.label: managedMcpServers
nodes.rationale: managedMcpServers pushes MCP server configurations to all users and exists only in third-party (3P) Desktop deployments. Each entry sets a transport of http, sse, or stdio plus connection details and an optional toolPolicy map restricting which tools users may invoke, delivered by managed settings file, MDM, or a Claude apps gateway policy's desktop block (which needs Claude Code v2.1.232 or later on the gateway server) because 3P deployments receive no admin-console settings.

nodes.label: Which managed settings reach which session
nodes.rationale: Reach depends on where the session runs: local sessions read a deployed file and also admin-console pushes on Anthropic's API with an eligible login or key; cloud sessions receive server-managed settings only, since device-deployed files never reach Anthropic-managed VMs (a self-hosted runner image's file does apply); SSH sessions read the remote host's file while Desktop reads sshConfigs, sshHostAllowlist, and disableDesktopLocalSessions locally; and Cowork sessions never fetch admin-console settings.

nodes.label: MDM and group policy
nodes.rationale: IT teams manage the desktop app through MDM on macOS via the com.anthropic.claudefordesktop preference domain (Jamf, Kandji) or Windows group policy at the registry key SOFTWARE\Policies\Claude. Policies include enabling or disabling the Claude Code feature, controlling auto-updates, and setting a custom deployment URL.

nodes.label: Network access requirements
nodes.rationale: Desktop loads application code and user content from Anthropic CDN hosts over HTTPS on port 443 unless a custom OTLP, gateway, or MCP port is configured; a wildcard list and a narrower explicit host list are both given, with some dynamically generated subdomains that must stay wildcards. Under IP allowlisting, bridge.claudeusercontent.com must egress through the same proxy address as claude.ai and api.anthropic.com, or Claude in Chrome and other bridge features stop working while the rest of the app keeps running.

nodes.label: Artifact font and library CDN hosts
nodes.rationale: Artifacts optionally request fonts.googleapis.com and fonts.gstatic.com — blocking them only falls back to other typefaces — and load JavaScript libraries solely from cdnjs.cloudflare.com, cdn.jsdelivr.net, cdn.tailwindcss.com, and code.jquery.com. A blocked library has no fallback, so both classes should be blocked with a fast rejection rather than a silent drop that hangs until timeout.

nodes.label: Authentication and SSO
nodes.rationale: Enterprise organizations can require SSO for all users, with SAML configuration covered in the SSO setup article and OIDC in the Claude Enterprise Administrator Guide.

nodes.label: Data handling by session type
nodes.rationale: Claude Code processes code locally in local sessions and on Anthropic-managed infrastructure in cloud sessions, unless routed to a self-hosted environment.
