Cloud sessions, including self-hosted ones, send conversations and code context to Anthropic's API, while local and SSH sessions send them to whichever model provider the deployment configures — Anthropic's API by default.

nodes.label: Enterprise deployment channels
nodes.rationale: Desktop is distributed to fleets via MDM on macOS using the .dmg installer (Jamf, Kandji) and via the MSIX package on Windows, which supports silent installation.

nodes.label: Desktop and CLI parity
nodes.rationale: Desktop runs the same underlying engine as the CLI with a graphical interface; both can run simultaneously on the same machine and project, keeping separate session history while sharing configuration and project memory via CLAUDE.md. Use Desktop for parallel sessions, pane arrangement, and visual review; use the CLI for scripting, automation, or a terminal workflow.

nodes.label: /desktop handoff command
nodes.rationale: Running /desktop in the terminal saves the CLI session, opens it in the desktop app, and exits the CLI. It is available on macOS and x64 Windows with a Claude subscription login, and not with API key authentication or on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry.

nodes.label: Configuration shared between Desktop and CLI
nodes.rationale: Desktop and the CLI read the same configuration: CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md project memory, MCP servers in ~/.claude.json or .mcp.json, hooks and skills defined in settings, permission rules and other settings in ~/.claude.json and ~/.claude/settings.json, and the same set of available models.

nodes.label: CLI flag equivalents in Desktop
nodes.rationale: Desktop maps common CLI flags to UI: --model and ANTHROPIC_MODEL to the model dropdown, --resume/--continue to clicking a sidebar session, --permission-mode to the mode selector, --add-dir to the + repo button in cloud sessions, --verbose to Verbose view mode, and MAX_THINKING_TOKENS to the local environment editor. --allowedTools/--disallowedTools have no per-session equivalent (settings-file permission rules still apply) and --print/--output-format are unavailable because Desktop is interactive only.

nodes.label: What is not available in Desktop
nodes.rationale: Desktop lacks third-party providers by default (Anthropic's API unless routed through a gateway or a 3P deployment), Computer Use on the Linux beta, inline code suggestions, and agent teams — which are CLI-only, with dynamic workflows and cross-session messaging as the in-Desktop substitutes. Terminal-dialog commands behave differently: /permissions replies that it isn't available in this environment, and /config opens Settings while ignoring any argument.

nodes.label: Desktop-specific troubleshooting
nodes.rationale: The page's troubleshooting section covers app-specific failures: 403/authentication errors fixed most often by signing out and back in, blank or stuck launch screens, "Failed to load session" from a missing folder or uninstalled Git LFS, PATH problems that hide npm or node, Git and Git LFS errors, Windows MCP server failures, and quit/install issues. Runtime API errors such as 500, 529, 429, or Prompt is too long are identical across CLI, desktop, and web and live in the Error reference instead.

nodes.label: "Branch doesn't exist yet" after a cloud session
nodes.rationale: Cloud sessions can create branches that do not exist locally; clicking the branch name in the session toolbar copies it so you can git fetch origin <branch-name> and git checkout it.

nodes.label: Local scheduled task (Desktop)
nodes.rationale: A local scheduled task starts a new Claude Code session automatically at a chosen time and frequency for recurring work such as daily code reviews, dependency audits, or morning briefings. It runs on your machine with direct access to local files and tools, but only fires while the Desktop app is open and the computer is awake.

nodes.label: Desktop Routines page
nodes.rationale: The Desktop app's Routines page, reached from the Code tab sidebar or its More menu, is where both local scheduled tasks and remote routines are created; clicking New routine and choosing Local starts a local task.

nodes.label: Remote routine (cloud)
nodes.rationale: A remote routine runs in the cloud (Anthropic-managed by default) even when your computer is off, needs no open session, and can also fire on API calls or GitHub events. It has no access to local files (it works from a fresh clone), runs autonomously without permission prompts, and its minimum interval is one hour.

nodes.label: /loop session-scoped scheduling
nodes.rationale: /loop schedules recurring work inside an existing CLI session on your machine: it requires an open session, inherits that session's MCP servers and permission prompts, is restored on --resume if unexpired, and is recommended for quick polling during a session.

nodes.label: Three scheduling options compared
nodes.rationale: Claude Code offers three ways to schedule recurring or one-off work — Cloud routines, Desktop local tasks, and /loop — compared across where they run, whether the machine or an open session is required, persistence across restarts, local file access, MCP server configuration, permission prompts, and minimum interval.

nodes.label: One-minute minimum interval
nodes.rationale: Desktop local tasks and /loop both support a minimum interval of 1 minute, while cloud routines are limited to a minimum interval of 1 hour.

nodes.label: Isolated Git worktree toggle
nodes.rationale: Enabling the worktree toggle when creating a task gives each run its own isolated Git worktree, the same way parallel Desktop sessions work.

nodes.label: Runs against current working-directory state
nodes.rationale: By default a scheduled task runs against whatever state the working directory is in at fire time, including uncommitted changes — so an in-progress edit is visible to the run unless isolation is enabled.

nodes.label: Desktop 1.1.5368 requirement
nodes.rationale: Local scheduled tasks are not available on Claude Desktop versions before 1.1.5368.

nodes.label: Task configuration fields
nodes.rationale: A local task is configured with Name (converted to lowercase kebab-case, used as the on-disk folder name, must be unique), Description (shown in the task list), Instructions (written like any prompt-box message, with pickers for permission mode, model, working folder and worktree), and Schedule.

nodes.label: Trusted folder required to save
nodes.rationale: A folder must be selected before a task can be saved, and if that folder has not been trusted yet Desktop prompts you to trust it before saving.

nodes.label: Create and manage tasks in plain language
nodes.rationale: Tasks can be created, listed, edited and paused by asking Claude in any Desktop session — for example 'set up a daily code review that runs every morning at 9am' (recurring), 'remind me at 3pm tomorrow to check the deploy' (a one-time task that disables itself after firing), or 'pause my dependency-audit task'. Deletion is the exception and must use the Delete button on the task's detail page.

nodes.label: Schedule presets
nodes.rationale: The Schedule control offers Manual (no schedule, only Run now), Hourly, Daily (time picker defaulting to 9:00 AM local), Weekdays (Daily minus Saturday and Sunday), and Weekly (time picker plus day picker).

nodes.label: Custom schedules by asking Claude
nodes.rationale: Intervals the picker does not offer — every 15 minutes, the first of each month, or a single run at a specific future time — are set by asking Claude in plain language in any Desktop session, e.g. 'schedule a task to run all the tests every 6 hours.'

nodes.label: Per-minute schedule check
nodes.rationale: While the app is open, Desktop checks the schedule every minute and starts a fresh session when a task is due, independent of any manual sessions the user has open.

nodes.label: Deterministic stagger delay
nodes.rationale: Each task is given a small delay of a few minutes after its scheduled time to stagger API traffic; the delay is deterministic, so the same task always starts at the same offset.

nodes.label: Scheduled session in the sidebar
nodes.rationale: When a task fires you get a desktop notification and a new session appears under a Scheduled section in the sidebar; opening it shows what Claude did, lets you review changes, or answer permission prompts. Claude can edit files, run commands, create commits and open pull requests exactly as in a session you start yourself.

nodes.label: No inter-session messaging
nodes.rationale: A scheduled session cannot send or receive messages between desktop sessions through the desktop app's session surface, unlike the cross-session messaging available to manually started sessions.

nodes.label: Sleeping machine skips runs
nodes.rationale: Tasks only run while the Desktop app is running and the computer is awake; if the computer sleeps through a scheduled time, that run is skipped.

nodes.label: Keep computer awake setting
nodes.rationale: Enabling 'Keep computer awake' in Settings under Desktop app → General prevents idle-sleep so scheduled runs are not skipped. It does not help when the laptop lid is closed, which still puts the machine to sleep.

nodes.label: Single catch-up run for missed times
nodes.rationale: On app start or machine wake, Desktop checks whether each task missed runs in the last seven days and starts exactly one catch-up run for the most recently missed time, discarding anything older — a daily task that missed six days runs once. A notification is shown when a catch-up run starts.

nodes.label: Time guardrails in the prompt
nodes.rationale: Because a catch-up run can fire long after its scheduled time (a 9am task might run at 11pm), timing-sensitive prompts should carry their own guardrails, e.g. 'Only review today's commits. If it's after 5pm, skip the review and just post a summary of what was missed.'

nodes.label: Per-task permission mode
nodes.rationale: Each scheduled task carries its own permission mode, set when the task is created or edited — one of the ways Desktop tasks differ from cloud routines, which run autonomously with no permission prompts.

nodes.label: settings.json allow rules apply
nodes.rationale: Allow rules from ~/.claude/settings.json also apply to scheduled task sessions, in addition to the task's own permission mode.

nodes.label: Manual-mode permission stall
nodes.rationale: If a task runs in Manual mode and needs a tool it lacks permission for, the run stalls until the user approves it; the session stays open in the sidebar so the approval can be given later.

nodes.label: Saved always-allow approvals
nodes.rationale: Selecting 'always allow' for each permission prompt during a Run now makes future runs of that task auto-approve the same tools without prompting; these saved approvals can be reviewed and revoked from the task's detail page.

nodes.label: requiresUserInteraction MCP tools
nodes.rationale: MCP tools marked requiresUserInteraction prompt on every call and offer no always-allow option, so runs that call them stall every time.

nodes.label: Run now
nodes.rationale: Run now starts the task immediately without waiting for the next scheduled time; it is the only way a Manual-schedule task fires, and the recommended way to surface and pre-approve permission prompts right after creating a task.

nodes.label: Task detail page
nodes.rationale: Clicking a task in the Routines list of the Code tab opens its detail page, which offers Run now, an Active/Paused status toggle, Edit (instructions, schedule, folder and other settings), run history, an Always allowed permissions panel, and Delete.

nodes.label: Run history with skip reasons
nodes.rationale: The history lists every past run including skipped ones; hovering a skipped entry shows why — the computer was asleep, the previous run was still in progress, or other scheduled tasks were already running — and Show more loads older entries.

nodes.label: Delete task and on-disk files
nodes.rationale: Delete removes the task and archives all sessions it created; an 'Also delete files on disk' checkbox in the confirmation dialog additionally removes the task's SKILL.md and associated data from ~/.claude/scheduled-tasks/.

nodes.label: update_scheduled_task MCP tool
nodes.rationale: A running scheduled task can modify its own schedule or prompt from inside its session using the update_scheduled_task MCP tool — for example rescheduling a code review to run earlier once it detects that a release branch has been created.

nodes.label: Task SKILL.md on disk
nodes.rationale: A task's prompt lives at ~/.claude/scheduled-tasks/<task-name>/SKILL.md, using YAML frontmatter for name and description with the prompt as the body; edits take effect on the next run. Schedule, folder, model and enabled state are NOT stored in this file.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR location
nodes.rationale: Scheduled-task files normally live under ~/.claude/, but move under CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR when that environment variable is set.

nodes.label: Claude Desktop app
nodes.rationale: The Claude Desktop app has three tabs: Chat for conversations, Cowork for Dispatch and longer agentic work, and Code for software development. Downloads exist for macOS (universal), Windows x64 and ARM64, and Linux (beta) via apt or .deb.

nodes.label: Code tab
nodes.rationale: The Code tab is the desktop app's software-development surface and the subject of this reference page. On Windows it requires Git for Windows installed before it will work, and the app must be restarted after installing it.

nodes.label: Session
nodes.rationale: In the Code tab each conversation is a session with its own chat history, project folder, and code changes, independent of every other session. The sidebar lists sessions and lets several run in parallel; each tracks its own context and changes.

nodes.label: Four pre-send session settings
nodes.rationale: Before the first message you configure four things in the prompt area: environment (where Claude runs), project folder, model, and permission mode. Model and permission mode can be changed mid-session; environment and folder are chosen up front.

nodes.label: Environment configuration
nodes.rationale: The environment picked when starting a session determines where Claude executes and how you connect: Local, Cloud, SSH, or (on Windows) WSL. Feature availability — @mention, terminal, file pane, connectors, plugins, permission modes — varies by environment.

nodes.label: Local session environment
nodes.rationale: Local sessions run on your machine with direct file access. The app does not inherit your full shell environment: on macOS it reads the shell profile only to extract PATH and a fixed set of Claude Code variables; on Windows it inherits user and system variables but never reads PowerShell profiles.

nodes.label: Cloud session environment
nodes.rationale: Cloud sessions run on Anthropic-managed infrastructure and continue after you close the app or shut down the computer; usage counts toward subscription plan limits with no separate compute charges. They can be monitored from claude.ai/code or the mobile app, and support custom cloud environments with their own network access levels and variables.

nodes.label: SSH session environment
nodes.rationale: An SSH session runs Claude Code on a remote Linux or macOS machine while the desktop app is the interface; Desktop installs Claude Code there automatically on first connect. A connection is defined by Name, SSH Host, SSH Port (default 22), and Identity File, and SSH sessions support permission modes, connectors, plugins, and MCP servers.

nodes.label: WSL session environment
nodes.rationale: On Windows a session can run inside a WSL 2 distribution using its Linux toolchain and native paths. WSL sessions lack @mention, the + button for connectors and plugins, side chats and plugins generally, and their availability on managed devices is governed separately from local sessions.

nodes.label: Permission modes
nodes.rationale: Permission modes control how much autonomy Claude has — whether it asks before editing files, running commands, or both — and are switched at any time from the mode selector next to the send button. A mode picked in the selector is remembered per folder and outranks defaultMode, except Plan which applies to the current session only. The CLI-only dontAsk mode is unavailable in Desktop.

nodes.label: Manual mode (default)
nodes.rationale: Manual mode, settings key `default`, makes Claude ask before editing files or running commands; you see a diff and accept or reject each change. It was formerly labeled 'Ask permissions'.

nodes.label: Accept edits mode
nodes.rationale: Accept edits (`acceptEdits`) auto-accepts file edits and common filesystem commands such as mkdir, touch and mv, while still asking before other terminal commands. In cloud sessions it corresponds to `default` mode, because cloud sessions pre-approve file edits and therefore show Accept edits instead of Manual.

nodes.label: Plan mode
nodes.rationale: Plan mode (`plan`) lets Claude read files and run commands to explore, then propose a plan without editing source code. The documented best practice is to start complex tasks in Plan and switch to Accept edits or Manual once the approach is approved.

nodes.label: Auto mode
nodes.rationale: Auto mode (`auto`) executes all actions with background safety classifiers that verify alignment with your request, reducing permission prompts while keeping oversight. It appears in the selector only when available and has no separate Settings toggle.

nodes.label: Bypass permissions mode
nodes.rationale: Bypass permissions (`bypassPermissions`) runs without prompts except for actions no mode auto-approves, safety classifiers on external sites, and desktop actions Claude always asks about such as archiving a session. It is equivalent to --dangerously-skip-permissions, is enabled in Settings on Pro/Max but by organization policy on Team/Enterprise, is unavailable in cloud sessions, and should only be used in sandboxed containers or VMs.

nodes.label: Auto mode availability requirements
nodes.rationale: Auto mode is available to all users on the Anthropic API and requires Claude Opus 4.6 or later, Sonnet 4.6 or later, or a Fable model. It is also available by default in Enterprise deployments routed to Google Cloud's Agent Platform, and admins can remove it with the disableAutoMode managed setting.

nodes.label: permissions.defaultMode
nodes.rationale: Adding `permissions.defaultMode` to a settings file sets the default permission mode for new local sessions; the desktop app reads the same settings files as the CLI. A per-folder selector choice takes precedence over it.

nodes.label: Prompt box
nodes.rationale: Typing and pressing Enter sends work to Claude; you can redirect at any point by pressing stop to interrupt or by sending a correction that Claude reads as soon as the current action completes. The + button beside it exposes file attachments, skills, connectors, and plugins.

nodes.label: @mention and file attachments
nodes.rationale: Two ways to bring in external context: typing `@` plus a filename adds a file to the conversation (unavailable in cloud and WSL sessions), and images, PDFs and other files can be attached or dragged into the prompt. Attachments are useful for bug screenshots, mockups, and reference documents.

nodes.label: Browser pane
nodes.rationale: The Browser pane is a tabbed browser inside the Code tab, opened with Cmd+Shift+B (Ctrl+Shift+B on Windows) or the Views menu. It hosts running-app previews and can also open static HTML files, PDFs, images and videos from the project when their path is clicked in chat. It uses a clean browser profile with none of your saved logins or history.

nodes.label: App preview and self-verification
nodes.rationale: Claude can start a dev server and open it in the Browser pane to verify its own changes, for frontend apps and backend servers alike — taking screenshots, inspecting the DOM, clicking elements, filling forms, testing API endpoints and reading server logs. Servers are started, stopped and configured from the server dropdown, and 'Persist sessions' keeps cookies and local storage across restarts.

nodes.label: autoVerify
nodes.rationale: With autoVerify enabled — the default — Claude automatically verifies code changes after editing files, taking screenshots, checking for errors, and confirming the change works before completing its response. It is disabled per project with "autoVerify": false in .claude/launch.json or from the server dropdown; preview tools remain available on demand when it is off.

nodes.label: .claude/launch.json
nodes.rationale: Claude detects the dev server setup and stores it in .claude/launch.json at the root of the folder selected when the session started; preview uses that folder as its working directory, so subfolders with their own servers are not auto-detected. The file is JSON-with-comments, holds a `version` and a `configurations` array, and can define several servers (e.g. a frontend and an API) for one project.

nodes.label: launch.json configuration fields
nodes.rationale: Each configurations entry accepts name, runtimeExecutable, runtimeArgs, port (default 3000), cwd (supports ${workspaceFolder}), env, autoPort, program, args, and url. Secrets must not go in `env` because the file is committed to the repo; use the local environment editor instead.

nodes.label: autoPort port-conflict handling
nodes.rationale: autoPort decides what happens when the preferred port is taken: true finds a free port automatically, false fails with an error (for servers that need an exact port such as OAuth callbacks or CORS allowlists), and unset makes Claude ask once and save the answer. When Claude picks a different port it passes it to the server via the PORT environment variable.

nodes.label: url field and localhost restrictions
nodes.rationale: Setting `url` makes the preview open an address other than http://localhost:<port>, for HTTPS servers, *.localhost subdomains, or sign-in redirects. A localhost url must be just the origin with no path or query and a port matching the entry, otherwise it is reported as a configuration error; other addresses prompt for permission the first time. Providing `url` with no command attaches the preview to a server you already run.

nodes.label: program vs runtimeExecutable
nodes.rationale: Use runtimeExecutable with runtimeArgs to start a dev server through a package manager (npm + ["run","dev"] runs `npm run dev`); use program when you have a standalone script to run with node directly ("server.js" runs `node server.js`), passing extra flags via args.

nodes.label: Browsing external sites
nodes.rationale: The Browser pane can open documentation, issue trackers and any other site next to the running app, including popup sign-in flows such as Google OAuth. Claude reads and interacts with external pages using the same tools it uses to verify your app, but subject to two extra safety checks.

nodes.label: External-page safety checks
nodes.rationale: Safety classifiers — the same ones Auto mode uses — review Claude's write actions such as clicking and typing on external pages in every permission mode, and produce a permission prompt regardless of mode when they flag an action. In modes other than Auto and Bypass permissions, a domain allowlist check also runs before navigating to a new site.

nodes.label: Per-site action approval
nodes.rationale: The first time Claude acts on an external site a permission card offers Allow once, Always allow (saved per site on your device and revocable in Settings), or Deny; each site including each subdomain needs its own approval. Local dev servers and project files need no approval, so auto-verify keeps working without prompts, and even on approved sites Claude will not purchase, create accounts, or bypass CAPTCHAs without your input.

nodes.label: Claude in Chrome extension
nodes.rationale: The Chrome extension shares your browser's login state, so it is the right tool when you want Claude to act as you in logged-in sessions; the Browser pane's clean profile is for building and testing your app and for sites that do not need your identity. Both share the same safety model and the same admin site allowlist/blocklist controls.

nodes.label: browserExternalPageTools and disableBrowserExternalNavigation
nodes.rationale: Two managed settings scope external browsing differently: browserExternalPageTools set to "disabled" lets users still navigate to external sites while removing Claude's ability to read or act on them, and disableBrowserExternalNavigation set to the JSON boolean true blocks all external navigation for users and Claude alike, including allowlisted sites, while leaving localhost previews working.

nodes.label: Diff view and inline comments
nodes.rationale: A diff stats indicator such as `+12 -1` opens a viewer with a file list on the left and changes on the right, for reviewing modifications file by file before opening a pull request. Clicking a line opens a comment box; multiple comments are submitted together with Cmd+Enter (Ctrl+Enter on Windows), and Claude's response arrives as a new reviewable diff.

nodes.label: Review code action
nodes.rationale: 'Review code' in the diff view's top-right toolbar asks Claude to evaluate the current diffs before committing, leaving comments in the diff view that you can answer or ask it to revise. The review targets high-signal issues — compile errors, definite logic errors, security vulnerabilities, obvious bugs — and deliberately skips style, formatting, pre-existing issues, and anything a linter would catch.

nodes.label: PR status monitoring, auto-fix and auto-merge
nodes.rationale: After a PR is opened a CI status bar appears and Claude Code polls check results with the GitHub CLI. Auto-fix makes Claude read failure output and iterate on failing checks; Auto-merge squash-merges once all checks pass, but only if auto-merge is already enabled in the GitHub repository settings. A desktop notification fires when CI finishes.

nodes.label: GitHub CLI prerequisite
nodes.rationale: PR monitoring requires the GitHub CLI (`gh`) installed and authenticated on the machine; if it is missing, Desktop prompts you to install it the first time you try to create a PR.

nodes.label: Auto-archive after PR merge or close
nodes.rationale: Turning on 'Auto-archive after PR merge or close' in Settings → Claude Code makes a session archive itself once its pull request merges or closes; it applies only to local sessions that have finished running. Archiving is also what removes a session's worktree.

nodes.label: Drag-and-drop pane layout
nodes.rationale: The Code tab is built around arrangeable panes — chat, diff, browser, terminal, file, plan, tasks, subagent, plus the iOS Simulator on macOS. Panes are repositioned by dragging their header, resized by dragging an edge, closed with Cmd+\ (Ctrl+\ on Windows), and opened from the Views menu.

nodes.label: Desktop v1.2581.0 requirement
nodes.rationale: The pane layout, integrated terminal, file editor and view modes require Claude Desktop v1.2581.0 or later; update via Claude → Check for Updates on macOS or Help → Check for Updates on Windows.

nodes.label: Integrated terminal
nodes.rationale: The terminal pane, opened from Views or with Ctrl+`, starts in the session's working directory and shares Claude's environment, so `npm test` or `git status` sees the same files Claude is editing. Extra tabs open with + or by right-clicking a folder in chat; it is available in local sessions only.

nodes.label: File pane editor
nodes.rationale: Clicking a file path in chat or the diff viewer opens it in the file pane for spot edits saved back to disk (HTML, PDF, image and video paths go to the Browser pane instead). If the file changed on disk since opening, the pane warns and offers override or discard. Available in local and SSH sessions; in cloud sessions you ask Claude to make the change.

nodes.label: File context menu
nodes.rationale: Right-clicking a file path in chat, the diff viewer, or the file pane offers Attach as context (adds the file to the next prompt), Open in (VS Code, Cursor, Zed), Show in Finder/Explorer, and Copy path.

nodes.label: Transcript view modes
nodes.rationale: Three view modes control transcript detail: Normal (tool calls collapsed into summaries with full text responses), Verbose (every tool call, file read and intermediate step), and Summary (only final responses and the changes made). Switch from the Transcript view dropdown or cycle with Ctrl+O; Verbose is for debugging why Claude acted, Summary for scanning many parallel sessions.

nodes.label: Code tab keyboard shortcuts
nodes.rationale: Cmd+/ (Ctrl+/ on Windows) lists all shortcuts. Documented bindings include Cmd+N new session, Cmd+W close, Ctrl+Tab session cycling, Esc stop, Cmd+Shift+D diff, Cmd+Shift+B Browser, Ctrl+` terminal, Cmd+\ close pane, Cmd+; side chat, Ctrl+O view modes, and Cmd+Shift+M/I/E for the mode, model and effort menus. They apply only to the Code tab — terminal interactive-mode shortcuts such as Shift+Tab do not.

nodes.label: Usage ring
nodes.rationale: The usage ring next to the model picker shows current context-window usage and plan usage for the period. Context usage is per session, while plan usage is shared across all your Claude Code surfaces.

nodes.label: Automatic context compaction
nodes.rationale: When context fills up Claude automatically summarizes the conversation and continues working; typing `/compact` triggers that summarization earlier to free context space.

nodes.label: Computer use
nodes.rationale: Computer use lets Claude open apps and control your screen for GUI-only or CLI-less tools. It is a research preview on macOS and Windows requiring a Pro or Max plan (not Team or Enterprise) with the app running, and unlike the sandboxed Bash tool it runs on your actual desktop, so the trust boundary differs even though Claude checks each action and flags on-screen prompt injection.

nodes.label: Tool precedence before computer use
nodes.rationale: Computer use is the broadest and slowest option, so Claude tries the most precise tool first: a connector for the service, then Bash for shell commands, then Claude in Chrome for browser work, then the iOS Simulator pane for iOS apps, and only then screen control — reserved for native apps, hardware control panels, and proprietary tools with no API.

nodes.label: Enabling computer use
nodes.rationale: Computer use is off by default and enabled in three steps: update and restart the app, turn on the Computer use toggle in Settings > General under Desktop app, and on macOS grant Accessibility (click, type, scroll) and Screen Recording (see the screen) permissions. On Windows the toggle alone completes setup.

nodes.label: Per-app access tiers
nodes.rationale: App approval is per session and shows a fixed tier set by app category: View only (screenshots only) for browsers and trading platforms, Click only (click and scroll, no typing or shortcuts) for terminals and IDEs, and Full control for everything else. Broad-reach apps show an extra warning, Denied apps are rejected without prompting, and hidden windows are restored when Claude finishes unless that setting is off.

nodes.label: iOS Simulator pane
nodes.rationale: For running and testing iOS apps Desktop opens a dedicated iOS Simulator pane on macOS instead of controlling the screen, and that pane works without computer use enabled. Admins can set disableMobileSimulatorTools to block Claude's device control and capture tools while leaving the pane usable for the user's own taps.

nodes.label: Parallel sessions with Git worktree isolation
nodes.rationale: New sessions (+ New session or Cmd+N) run tasks in parallel, and for Git repositories each session gets its own isolated copy of the project via Git worktrees so changes do not affect other sessions until committed. Cmd-clicking a sidebar session opens a second pane for viewing two at once, and the sidebar can filter by status, project or environment.

nodes.label: Git prerequisite for session isolation
nodes.rationale: Session isolation requires Git; most Macs include it (check with `git --version`), and on Windows Git is required for the Code tab to work at all, so Git for Windows must be installed and the app restarted.

nodes.label: Worktree location and .worktreeinclude
nodes.rationale: Worktrees live in <project-root>/.claude/worktrees/ by default, changeable under 'Worktree location' in Settings → Claude Code, with an optional branch prefix prepended to every worktree branch name. A .worktreeinclude file in the project root copies gitignored files such as .env into new worktrees.

nodes.label: Side chat (/btw)
nodes.rationale: A side chat, opened with Cmd+; (Ctrl+; on Windows) or by typing /btw, asks a question that reads the session's context up to that point without adding anything back to the main conversation. Side chats are available in local, SSH and WSL sessions and are never saved to disk, so they cannot be reopened after closing the app.

nodes.label: Tasks pane
nodes.rationale: The tasks pane shows background work running inside the current session — subagents, background shell commands, and dynamic workflows — and clicking an entry shows its output in the subagent pane or stops it.

nodes.label: Work across sessions
nodes.rationale: Claude can list other Code tab sessions, read what each has been doing, message between them, and rename or archive them on request. It sees only sessions the desktop app itself runs — local, SSH and WSL — never cloud sessions or terminal-CLI/VS Code sessions, never the session you are asking from, and by default only the 20 most recently active, skipping archived ones.

nodes.label: Cross-session safety behaviors
nodes.rationale: Four safety behaviors apply: Claude asks before archiving any session in every permission mode including Auto and Bypass; it cannot send or deliver cross-session messages for an unwatched session such as a scheduled-task run; each message is checked against the receiving session's inbound controls, with crossSessionInbound set to refuse dropping it; and every incoming message is quoted and attributed to its sending session while the receiver's own permission settings still govern any action.

nodes.label: Multi-repository cloud sessions
nodes.rationale: After selecting a cloud environment, the + button next to the repo pill adds additional repositories to the session, each with its own branch selector — useful for tasks spanning codebases, such as updating a shared library and its consumers.

nodes.label: Continue in another surface
nodes.rationale: The 'Continue in' menu moves a session elsewhere: to Claude Code on the Web, where Desktop pushes the branch, generates a conversation summary and creates a cloud session with full context (requires a clean working tree, unavailable for SSH sessions), or to a supported IDE opened at the current working directory.

nodes.label: Sessions from Dispatch
nodes.rationale: Dispatch is a persistent conversation in the Cowork tab that can spawn a Code session either on request or by deciding a task is development work — bug fixes, dependency updates, tests, opening PRs — while research, document and spreadsheet work stays in Cowork. The session appears in the Code sidebar with a Dispatch badge and pushes a phone notification when it finishes or needs approval; Dispatch requires Pro or Max and is unavailable on Team and Enterprise.

nodes.label: Customize configuration hub
nodes.rationale: Clicking Customize in the sidebar manages connectors, skills and plugins in one place. The Cowork tab sources its skills, plugins and connectors from this Customize configuration, which syncs through your claude.ai account rather than from the CLI's ~/.claude directory.

nodes.label: Connectors
nodes.rationale: Connectors add integrations such as Google Calendar, Slack, GitHub, Linear and Notion from the + button in local and SSH sessions, before or during a session, letting Claude read calendars, send messages and create issues. The + button is absent in cloud and WSL sessions, where routines configure connectors at creation time instead.

nodes.label: MCP servers in Desktop
nodes.rationale: Connectors are MCP servers with a graphical setup flow; integrations not listed there are added by configuring MCP servers manually in settings files, and custom connectors can be built on remote MCP. Desktop and the CLI share MCP servers configured in ~/.claude.json or .mcp.json.

nodes.label: Skills and slash commands in Desktop
nodes.rationale: Claude loads skills automatically when relevant, or you invoke one by typing / or picking Slash commands from the + button — covering built-in commands, custom skills, project skills and plugin skills. Personal skills in ~/.claude/skills/ apply to local sessions, an SSH session reads that path on the remote host, and cloud sessions load the skills enabled for your claude.ai account.

nodes.label: Plugins in Desktop
nodes.rationale: Plugins bundle skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers and LSP configurations and are installed from the desktop app's plugin browser in local and SSH sessions, scoped to user, project or local-only. The browser is unavailable in cloud sessions and plugins installed from the app do not reach them: declare the plugin in the repository's .claude/settings.json enabledPlugins, or enable it for your claude.ai account as a synced plugin. Plugins are unavailable in WSL sessions.

nodes.label: Local environment editor
nodes.rationale: Hovering Local in the environment dropdown and clicking the gear opens the local environment editor; variables saved there are stored encrypted on the machine and apply to every local session and preview server. Variables in ~/.claude/settings.json's `env` key reach Claude sessions only, not dev servers — which is why secrets belong here rather than in the committed launch.json.

nodes.label: Extended thinking and effort variables
nodes.rationale: Extended thinking is on by default; on the Anthropic API MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=0 turns it off (no effect on Fable models, which always think), and with thinking off Claude Code sends effort `high` to models that reject the other combination, such as Opus 5. On adaptive-reasoning models non-zero MAX_THINKING_TOKENS values are ignored; Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 accept CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ADAPTIVE_THINKING=1 for a fixed budget, while Fable models, Sonnet 5 and Opus 4.7+ have no fixed-budget mode.

nodes.label: disableDesktopLocalSessions
nodes.rationale: Set to the JSON boolean true in managed settings only (Desktop v1.37937.0+), disableDesktopLocalSessions turns off Code sessions that run on the device. Local stays visible but grayed out with an explanatory tooltip, WSL is grayed the same way on Windows, new sessions default to the first configured SSH connection, and continuing an existing local session reports that local sessions are unavailable.

nodes.label: sshConfigs
nodes.rationale: Administrators distribute SSH connections by adding sshConfigs to a managed settings file; each entry requires id, name and sshHost, with optional sshPort and sshIdentityFile. Managed connections appear automatically in every user's environment dropdown and are selectable but not editable or deletable; users may also put sshConfigs in their own ~/.claude/settings.json, which is where dialog-added connections are stored.

nodes.label: sshHostAllowlist
nodes.rationale: sshHostAllowlist limits Desktop SSH sessions to hosts whose resolved hostname matches a case-insensitive pattern (`*` matches any host, `*.example.com` matches the domain and subdomains, anything else is exact); an empty array disables SSH sessions. The check runs after ~/.ssh/config resolution via `ssh -G`, it is read from managed settings only, and only the Desktop app honors it — it does not restrict `ssh` run through the Bash tool nor network egress.

nodes.label: Enterprise configuration
nodes.rationale: Organizations on Team or Enterprise plans manage desktop app behavior through three mechanisms: admin console controls, managed settings files, and device management policies — plus network, data-handling, authentication and deployment requirements documented alongside them.

nodes.label: Admin console controls
nodes.rationale: The admin settings console exposes four toggles: Code in the desktop, Code in the web, Remote Control, and Disable Bypass permissions mode.

nodes.label: Managed settings keys
nodes.rationale: Managed settings override project and user settings for Desktop sessions and can be deployed as a file or pushed through the admin console. The documented keys are permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode, disableAutoMode, autoMode, browserExternalPageTools, disableMobileSimulatorTools, disableBrowserExternalNavigation, sshConfigs, sshHostAllowlist, disableDesktopLocalSessions, and managedMcpServers (third-party deployments only).

nodes.label: Which managed settings reach which session
nodes.rationale: Reach depends on where the session runs: local sessions read a deployed file and, on eligible logins, remotely pushed settings; cloud sessions receive server-managed settings only, since device files cannot reach Anthropic-managed VMs; SSH sessions read the remote host's file while Desktop itself reads sshConfigs, sshHostAllowlist and disableDesktopLocalSessions locally; Cowork sessions never fetch admin-console settings and remote Cowork receives neither. Connectors are delivered directly to Claude Code, so no MCP setting or managed-mcp.json governs them.

nodes.label: Device management policies
nodes.rationale: IT teams manage the app through MDM on macOS via the com.anthropic.claudefordesktop preference domain (Jamf, Kandji) or Windows group policy at SOFTWARE\Policies\Claude. Policies include enabling or disabling the Claude Code feature, controlling auto-updates, and setting a custom deployment URL.

nodes.label: Network access requirements
nodes.rationale: Desktop loads code and user content from Anthropic CDN hosts (anthropic.com, claude.ai, claude.com, claude.app and their wildcards, plus *.claudeusercontent.com and *.claudemcpcontent.com), over HTTPS on port 443 unless a custom OTLP, gateway or MCP port is configured. A narrower explicit host list is offered to reduce wildcards; bridge.claudeusercontent.com must egress through an allowlisted address when IP allowlisting is enabled, or Claude in Chrome and other bridge features stop working.

nodes.label: Artifact font and library CDNs
nodes.rationale: An artifact may request fonts.googleapis.com and fonts.gstatic.com — optional, with fallback typefaces if blocked — and JavaScript libraries from cdnjs.cloudflare.com, cdn.jsdelivr.net, cdn.tailwindcss.com and code.jquery.com and no other external host. A blocked library has no fallback, so both classes should be blocked with a fast rejection rather than a silent drop.

nodes.label: Data handling by session type
nodes.rationale: Code is processed locally in local sessions or on Anthropic-managed infrastructure in cloud sessions, unless the organization routes them to a self-hosted environment. Cloud sessions send conversations and code context to Anthropic's API; local and SSH sessions send them to whichever model provider the deployment configures, Anthropic's API by default.

nodes.label: Enterprise deployment and SSO
nodes.rationale: Desktop is distributed via MDM with the .dmg on macOS (Jamf, Kandji) and via the MSIX package on Windows, which supports silent installation. Enterprise organizations can require SSO for all users, with SAML setup documented in support and OIDC in the Enterprise Administrator Guide.

nodes.label: Desktop vs CLI
nodes.rationale: Desktop runs the same underlying engine as the CLI with a graphical interface, and both can run simultaneously on the same machine and project; each keeps separate session history while sharing configuration and project memory via CLAUDE.md. Use Desktop for parallel sessions, pane layout and visual review; use the CLI for scripting, automation, or a terminal workflow.

nodes.label: /desktop handoff command
nodes.rationale: Running `/desktop` in the terminal saves the CLI session, opens it in the desktop app and exits the CLI. It is available on macOS and x64 Windows when signed in with a Claude subscription, and not with API key authentication or on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry.

nodes.label: CLI flag equivalents
nodes.rationale: Common CLI flags map to UI affordances: --model and ANTHROPIC_MODEL to the model dropdown, --resume/--continue to clicking a sidebar session, --permission-mode to the mode selector, --dangerously-skip-permissions to Bypass permissions, --add-dir to the + repo button in cloud sessions, --verbose to Verbose view mode, and MAX_THINKING_TOKENS to the local environment editor. --allowedTools/--disallowedTools have no per-session equivalent, and --print/--output-format are unavailable because Desktop is interactive only.

nodes.label: Shared configuration files
nodes.rationale: Desktop and CLI read the same files, so setup carries over: CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md, MCP servers in ~/.claude.json or .mcp.json, hooks and skills defined in settings, and settings in ~/.claude.json and ~/.claude/settings.json including permission rules and allowed tools. The same models are available in both.

nodes.label: claude_desktop_config.json precedence
nodes.rationale: The Desktop app loads MCP servers from claude_desktop_config.json into local Code tab sessions alongside ~/.claude.json and .mcp.json, and on a name collision the Code tab connects once using the claude_desktop_config.json definition. For stdio servers re-delivered to the embedded CLI, a name defined at the top level of ~/.claude.json wins over .mcp.json — departing from the CLI scope hierarchy. The standalone CLI never reads claude_desktop_config.json; `claude mcp add-from-claude-desktop` imports those servers.

nodes.label: CLI/Desktop feature comparison
nodes.rationale: Point-by-point: the CLI has all permission modes including dontAsk, third-party providers, settings-file MCP, the /plugin command, --worktree isolation, separate terminals, cron-based recurrence, and scripting; Desktop has Manual/Accept edits/Plan/Auto (Bypass once enabled), Anthropic's API by default, a Connectors and plugin-manager UI, autocompleting @mention, image and PDF attachments, automatic worktrees, sidebar tabs, scheduled tasks, app and screen control, the iOS Simulator pane, and Dispatch — with no scripting or automation.

nodes.label: What Desktop does not support
nodes.rationale: Desktop omits third-party providers by default (gateway and 3P routing documented separately), Computer Use on Linux beta, inline autocomplete-style code suggestions, and agent teams — for which dynamic workflows or cross-session messaging substitute. Terminal-dialog commands behave differently: argument-less ones such as /permissions reply "isn't available in this environment", and /config opens Settings while ignoring any text after it.

nodes.label: Desktop troubleshooting
nodes.rationale: The troubleshooting section covers only desktop-specific issues — version checking, blank or stuck launch screens, 'Failed to load session', tools missing from PATH, Git/Git LFS errors, Windows MCP server failures, quitting problems, and Windows install quirks. Runtime API errors such as 500, 529, 429 or 'Prompt is too long' behave identically across CLI, desktop and web and are documented in the error reference.

nodes.label: 403 and authentication errors
nodes.rationale: For Error 403: Forbidden or other authentication failures in the Code tab: sign out and back in (the most common fix), verify an active paid Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise subscription, fully quit and reopen the app if the CLI works but Desktop does not, and check internet and proxy settings.

nodes.label: Git and Git LFS errors
nodes.rationale: 'Git is required' on Windows means installing Git for Windows and restarting the app; 'Git LFS is required by this repository but is not installed' means installing Git LFS, running `git lfs install`, and restarting. A repository needing uninstalled Git LFS is also one cause of 'Failed to load session'.

nodes.label: Branch doesn't exist yet
nodes.rationale: Cloud sessions can create branches that do not exist on the local machine; copy the branch name from the session toolbar, then `git fetch origin <branch-name>` and `git checkout <branch-name>` to work with it locally.

nodes.label: Claude Code plugin system
nodes.rationale: Plugins extend Claude Code with skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers. A plugin's detail view enumerates the components it contributes: commands, skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers, and LSP servers.

nodes.label: Plugin marketplace
nodes.rationale: A marketplace is a catalog of plugins that someone else has created and shared, letting users discover and install extensions without building them. Marketplaces are backed by a .claude-plugin/marketplace.json file in a repo, a local directory, or a hosted URL.

nodes.label: Two-step marketplace flow
nodes.rationale: Using a marketplace is a two-step process: first add the marketplace, which registers the catalog with Claude Code and installs nothing, then browse the catalog and install the individual plugins you want.

nodes.label: /plugin marketplace add
nodes.rationale: `/plugin marketplace add` registers a catalog from a GitHub owner/repo shorthand, a git URL, a local path, or a remote marketplace.json URL. `/plugin market` is an accepted shortcut for `/plugin marketplace`, and `rm` for `remove`.

nodes.label: /plugin install plugin@marketplace
nodes.rationale: `/plugin install plugin-name@marketplace-name` opens that plugin's details, where you choose an installation scope. The same choices appear from the Discover tab by pressing Enter on a plugin.

nodes.label: Official Anthropic marketplace
nodes.rationale: Claude Code adds `claude-plugins-official` automatically the first time it starts interactively; if a network block or a marketplace policy prevented that, add it with `/plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-official`. It is curated by Anthropic and inclusion is at Anthropic's discretion.

nodes.label: Community marketplace
nodes.rationale: `anthropics/claude-plugins-community` hosts third-party plugins that passed Anthropic's automated validation and safety screening, installed under the marketplace name `claude-community`. Unlike the official marketplace it must be added manually, and the in-app submission forms add plugins here rather than to the official catalog.

nodes.label: Demo plugins marketplace
nodes.rationale: Anthropic maintains a demo marketplace (`claude-code-plugins`) in the anthropics/claude-code repository with example plugins showing what the plugin system can do. It must be added manually with `/plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-code`.

nodes.label: Commit-SHA pinning of community plugins
nodes.rationale: Each plugin in the community marketplace catalog is pinned to a specific commit SHA, so an install resolves to a reviewed revision rather than to whatever the upstream repository currently holds.

nodes.label: /plugin panel and its four tabs
nodes.rationale: `/plugin` opens an interactive terminal panel with four tabs cycled by Tab / Shift+Tab: Discover (browse plugins from all marketplaces), Installed (view and manage), Marketplaces (add, remove, update), and Errors (plugin loading errors).

nodes.label: Plugin details pane
nodes.rationale: Selecting a plugin shows a details pane with what it contains and what it costs: a Context cost estimate, a Last updated date, and a Will install section. Plugins from local or custom marketplaces may supply none of that data.

nodes.label: Context cost estimate
nodes.rationale: The details pane shows a Context cost estimate: how many tokens the plugin adds to the context window on every turn. For plugins from local or custom marketplaces the row may be absent because the marketplace does not supply the data.

nodes.label: Will install section
nodes.rationale: A Will install section lists the plugin's commands, agents, skills, hooks, and MCP and LSP servers so the user can review exactly what is added before installing. When the marketplace does not supply it, the section reads 'Components will be discovered at installation'.

nodes.label: Suggested-for-this-directory pinning
nodes.rationale: When an administrator allowlists a marketplace via the `pluginSuggestionMarketplaces` managed setting, plugins marked relevant to the current working directory are pinned at the top of the Discover tab with a 'suggested for this directory' label.

nodes.label: Code intelligence (LSP) plugins
nodes.rationale: Code intelligence plugins configure Language Server Protocol connections and enable Claude Code's built-in LSP tool, giving Claude jump-to-definition, find-references, and immediate type errors after edits. Users can also create their own LSP plugin for other languages.

nodes.label: Language server binary requirement
nodes.rationale: The plugin does not install the language server for you: each code intelligence plugin requires its own binary (clangd, csharp-ls, gopls, jdtls, kotlin-language-server, lua-language-server, intelephense, pyright-langserver, rust-analyzer, sourcekit-lsp, typescript-language-server). If a server is already installed, Claude may prompt to install the matching plugin.

nodes.label: Automatic diagnostics
nodes.rationale: After every file edit Claude makes, the language server reports errors and warnings back, so Claude sees type errors, missing imports, and syntax issues without running a compiler or linter, and fixes an error it introduced in the same turn. Press Ctrl+O to read the diagnostics yourself.

nodes.label: LSP code navigation
nodes.rationale: With a language server Claude can jump to definitions, find references, get hover type info, list symbols, find implementations, and trace call hierarchies — more precise than grep-based search, though availability varies by language and environment.

nodes.label: No plugin language servers in cloud sessions
nodes.rationale: In cloud sessions Claude Code does not start plugin language servers, so Claude does not get the LSP tool there. Cloud sessions also require declaring plugins under `enabledPlugins` in .claude/settings.json rather than using the interactive panel.

nodes.label: Executable not found in $PATH
nodes.rationale: `Executable not found in $PATH` in the /plugin Errors tab after installing a code intelligence plugin means the required language server binary is missing and must be installed.

nodes.label: External integration plugins
nodes.rationale: These plugins bundle pre-configured MCP servers so Claude connects to external services without manual setup: github and gitlab for source control; atlassian, asana, linear and notion for project management; figma for design; vercel, firebase and supabase for infrastructure; slack for communication; sentry for monitoring.

nodes.label: security-guidance plugin
nodes.rationale: The `security-guidance` plugin reviews each change Claude makes for common vulnerabilities and instructs Claude to fix what it finds in the same session; project-specific rules can be added.

nodes.label: Development workflow plugins
nodes.rationale: Official plugins adding skills and agents for common development tasks: commit-commands (git commit, push, PR creation), pr-review-toolkit (agents for reviewing pull requests), agent-sdk-dev (building with the Claude Agent SDK), and plugin-dev (creating your own plugins).

nodes.label: Output style plugins
nodes.rationale: Plugins that customize how Claude responds: explanatory-output-style gives educational insights about implementation choices, learning-output-style provides an interactive learning mode for skill building.

nodes.label: Marketplace source types
nodes.rationale: A marketplace can be added from four kinds of source: GitHub repositories in owner/repo format, any git repository URL (GitLab, Bitbucket, self-hosted), local directories or direct paths to marketplace.json, and remote URLs to hosted marketplace.json files.

nodes.label: owner/repo GitHub shorthand
nodes.rationale: A GitHub repository containing a `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` file is added with the `owner/repo` shorthand, where owner is the GitHub username or organization and repo the repository name — e.g. `anthropics/claude-code`.

nodes.label: Git URL marketplace source
nodes.rationale: A marketplace on any git host is added by full URL, over HTTPS or SSH. Claude Code clones an SSH address whether or not it ends in .git, and clones gitlab.com URLs with nested subgroups such as https://gitlab.com/group/subgroup/project.

nodes.label: Host-dependent .git suffix rules
nodes.rationale: For an https:// URL the .git suffix rule depends on the host: github.com and gitlab.com are recognized with or without it (gitlab.com without the suffix needs v2.1.232+, earlier versions read it as a direct marketplace.json link); Azure DevOps paths containing /_git/ must omit it or the clone fails; every other host, including self-managed GitLab, must include it.

nodes.label: Required https:// prefix
nodes.rationale: Claude Code v2.1.196 and later reject a host typed without the https:// prefix (e.g. gitlab.com/company/plugins.git) as an invalid GitHub owner/repo shorthand and tell you to add the prefix; earlier versions misread it as a GitHub repository path and failed at clone time.

nodes.label: Branch or tag ref pinning
nodes.rationale: To add a specific branch or tag of a git marketplace, append `#` followed by the ref, e.g. `/plugin marketplace add https://gitlab.com/company/plugins.git#v1.0.0`.

nodes.label: Local path marketplace source
nodes.rationale: A local directory containing `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` can be added (`/plugin marketplace add ./my-marketplace`), as can a direct path to a marketplace.json file.

nodes.label: Remote marketplace.json URL
nodes.rationale: A hosted marketplace.json can be added directly by URL. URL-based marketplaces have limitations compared with git-based ones, notably 'path not found' errors for plugins that use relative paths.

nodes.label: extraKnownMarketplaces setting
nodes.rationale: `extraKnownMarketplaces` in .claude/settings.json declares marketplaces by source (e.g. a github repo). Claude Code clones a git entry whether or not its URL ends in .git, and administrators can set `"autoUpdate": true` per entry in managed settings.

nodes.label: Installation scopes
nodes.rationale: Every install picks a scope: User scope installs for yourself across all projects, Project scope installs for all collaborators and adds the plugin to .claude/settings.json, and Local scope installs for yourself in this repository only without sharing.

nodes.label: Managed scope plugins
nodes.rationale: Plugins with managed scope are installed by administrators via managed settings and cannot be modified by the user.

nodes.label: claude plugin shell commands
nodes.rationale: `claude plugin install` installs without an interactive step, to user scope unless `--scope` is passed, and `--yes` accepts a command-source plugin's displayed command. Because it does not run in a session, its plugins load at the next start or on /reload-plugins; `claude plugin details` prints a plugin's component inventory and the shell commands are the scripting path that never opens the panel.

nodes.label: Catalog refresh on a named install
nodes.rationale: Installing `plugin-name@marketplace-name` makes Claude Code refresh that marketplace before the catalog lookup, even if auto-update or DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER is set. A plugin-name-only install in a session refreshes only background-updated marketplaces and only after a lookup miss, while `claude plugin install plugin-name` reads cached catalogs without refreshing. Before v2.1.232 no refresh happened before the lookup.

nodes.label: Conditions that skip the refresh
nodes.rationale: Claude Code skips the pre-install refresh when the marketplace was not added from GitHub, another git host or a remote URL; when a seed directory supplies it; when it was refreshed within the last 30 seconds; when CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC is set; or when managed settings block the marketplace, in which case the install is refused outright.

nodes.label: Cached-catalog fallback on refresh failure
nodes.rationale: If the refresh before a named install fails — for example because you are offline — Claude Code looks the plugin up in the cached catalog anyway; `claude plugin install` reports `marketplace not refreshed` in its success message and `/plugin install` shows the failure above the details or in the not-found message.

nodes.label: Install summary
nodes.rationale: The install summary states whether the plugin is active in the current session: `Plugin is now active.` means Claude Code activated it as part of the install; `Run /reload-plugins to activate.` means it is not active yet; a load failure is reported in the summary with detail in the Errors tab.

nodes.label: Session activation of an installed plugin
nodes.rationale: Installing a plugin does not always make it live in the running session: activation is skipped when it would invalidate the prompt cache or when the activation attempt failed. Before v2.1.221 no install took effect in the current session until /reload-plugins or a restart.

nodes.label: /reload-plugins
nodes.rationale: `/reload-plugins` applies plugin enables, disables and pending installs without restarting, reloading all active plugins and printing counts of plugins, skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers and LSP servers. Before v2.1.246 the skills count included only commands/ entries, so a plugin's SKILL.md skills could reload while the summary reported 0 skills.

nodes.label: Prompt cache invalidation guard
nodes.rationale: When a reload would invalidate the prompt cache, /reload-plugins warns and skips until it is rerun with `--force`; the same guard is why an install may leave a plugin inactive until an explicit reload.

nodes.label: Token cost of reloading plugins
nodes.rationale: Reloading has a token cost on the next request: newly loaded components announce themselves in appended content while existing history still reads from the prompt cache. A plugin providing MCP servers costs more when its tools are not deferred by tool search, because the change invalidates the cache and the next request re-reads the whole conversation.

nodes.label: Plugins execute arbitrary code
nodes.rationale: Plugins and marketplaces are highly trusted components that can execute arbitrary code on your machine with your user privileges, so only plugins and marketplaces from trusted sources should be installed or added.

nodes.label: Trust-before-install warning
nodes.rationale: Anthropic does not control what MCP servers, files, or other software a plugin includes and cannot verify that they work as intended, so users must satisfy themselves a plugin is trustworthy — checking its homepage — before installing.

nodes.label: Managed marketplace restrictions
nodes.rationale: Organizations can restrict which marketplaces users may add via managed marketplace restrictions; a blocked marketplace also causes Claude Code to refuse the install, and such a policy can be why the official marketplace was never auto-added.

nodes.label: Installed tab management
nodes.rationale: The Installed tab lists plugins grouped by scope and sorted problems-first: load errors and unresolved dependencies at the top, then favorites, with disabled plugins folded behind a collapsed header. Press f to favorite, type to filter by name or description, Enter to open a detail view and enable, disable, or uninstall.

nodes.label: Uninstall scope prompt
nodes.rationale: Uninstalling a plugin that a project's .claude/settings.json enables prompts for the scope meant: disable it for yourself alone, writing an override to .claude/settings.local.json while leaving it installed for the project, or uninstall it for everyone by removing it from the shared .claude/settings.json.

nodes.label: Not used recently detection
nodes.rationale: Claude Code groups self-installed marketplace plugins unused for at least two weeks across at least 10 sessions under a 'Not used recently' header with a Last used line, so users can drop plugins still paying startup and context cost. Organization-managed plugins, --plugin-dir plugins, and plugins contributing a theme, output style, monitor or workflow are never listed.

nodes.label: LSP activity counts as plugin use
nodes.rationale: A plugin's language server counts as used when it delivers diagnostics or answers a navigation request, so an active LSP plugin is not listed as unused. Before v2.1.203 that activity could not be counted and LSP plugins were exempt entirely; the first session on a counting version resets the usage record of each LSP plugin with no recorded use.

nodes.label: strictKnownMarketplaces
nodes.rationale: When an organization restricts marketplaces with the `strictKnownMarketplaces` setting, both the 'Not used recently' header and the 'Last used' line are hidden.

nodes.label: Direct plugin management commands
nodes.rationale: `/plugin list` (with --enabled/--disabled), `/plugin disable`, `/plugin enable` and `/plugin uninstall` manage plugins directly; the disable/enable/uninstall forms open the plugin panel to apply the change and leave it open, so Esc is needed before typing another command.

nodes.label: Marketplace-entry name vs plugin.json name
nodes.rationale: In plugin-name@marketplace-name identifiers, plugin-name is the name in the marketplace entry, which can differ from the name in the plugin's own plugin.json. As of v2.1.195 the interface and the enable/disable commands accept either name; earlier versions reported `already disabled` and left such a plugin enabled.

nodes.label: Marketplace list/update/remove commands
nodes.rationale: Marketplaces are managed from the Marketplaces tab or with direct commands: `/plugin marketplace list` shows all configured marketplaces, `/plugin marketplace update <name>` refreshes its plugin listings, and `/plugin marketplace remove <name>` removes it.

nodes.label: Removing a marketplace uninstalls its plugins
nodes.rationale: Removing a marketplace will uninstall any plugins that were installed from it — the removal is not catalog-only.

nodes.label: Marketplace and plugin auto-update
nodes.rationale: Claude Code can refresh marketplace data and update installed plugins on disk in the background after startup, with a random delay of up to ten minutes so the running session keeps its launch versions. claude-plugins-official and most official Anthropic marketplaces default to auto-update on; third-party and local development marketplaces default to off, and it is toggled per marketplace from the Marketplaces tab.

nodes.label: headersHelper plugins excluded from auto-update
nodes.rationale: Auto-update leaves out a plugin whose marketplace entry declares a `headersHelper`: Claude Code neither runs the command nor downloads the archive on that path, and instead lists the plugin in the /plugin Errors tab so it can be updated from its own view.

nodes.label: command-source plugin update cadence
nodes.rationale: Plugins with a `command` source update on their own cadence, independent of the marketplace auto-update setting and of DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER: Claude Code re-runs the command once per session and installs the output as a new plugin version when its hash has changed.

nodes.label: DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER
nodes.rationale: Setting the `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER` environment variable disables automatic updates both for Claude Code itself and for plugins fetched from marketplaces; command-source plugins still follow their own once-per-session re-resolve.

nodes.label: FORCE_AUTOUPDATE_PLUGINS
nodes.rationale: Setting `FORCE_AUTOUPDATE_PLUGINS=1` alongside `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER=1` keeps plugin auto-updates enabled while Claude Code's own auto-updates stay off.

nodes.label: Team marketplaces via project settings
nodes.rationale: Team admins configure automatic marketplace installation for a project by adding `extraKnownMarketplaces` (and `enabledPlugins`) to the project's .claude/settings.json; Claude Code then adds those marketplaces without a further prompt.

nodes.label: Repository folder trust
nodes.rationale: A project's configured marketplaces are only added once the team member trusts the repository folder — folder trust is the gate that precedes any project-declared marketplace being registered.

nodes.label: External-source plugins are not auto-installed
nodes.rationale: As of v2.1.195, adding a marketplace does not install plugins that come from an external source on any path that loads plugins: a plugin enabled only by the project's .claude/settings.json and sourced from e.g. a GitHub repo or npm package stays uninstalled, reported as not installed with the `claude plugin install` command to run.

nodes.label: Declared plugin dependencies
nodes.rationale: When a plugin declares dependencies, the install output lists which dependencies were auto-installed alongside it; unresolved dependencies push a plugin to the top of the Installed tab.

nodes.label: /plugin command not recognized
nodes.rationale: An 'unknown command' response, or /plugin not appearing at all, means the installed Claude Code is too old or the environment does not support the interactive panel.

nodes.label: Version check and update remedy
nodes.rationale: Run `claude --version` to see what is installed, update via `brew upgrade claude-code` (or claude-code@latest), `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code@latest`, or re-running the native installer, then restart the terminal and run claude again.

nodes.label: Alternatives when /plugin is unavailable
nodes.rationale: If Claude replies that /plugin is not available in this environment, use the plugin browser in the Claude desktop app, or declare the plugin under `enabledPlugins` in .claude/settings.json for cloud sessions.

nodes.label: Plugin skills not appearing
nodes.rationale: A common failure is that a plugin's skills do not appear after installation, even though the plugin itself installed; plugin skills are namespaced by plugin name, e.g. commit-commands provides /commit-commands:commit.

nodes.label: Clear the plugin cache
nodes.rationale: If plugin skills do not appear, clear the cache with `rm -rf ~/.claude/plugins/cache`, restart Claude Code, and reinstall the plugin.

nodes.label: Code intelligence troubleshooting
nodes.rationale: Three named failure modes: a language server not starting (verify the binary is installed and on $PATH, check the Errors tab); high memory usage from servers like rust-analyzer and pyright on large projects (disable the plugin and rely on Claude's built-in search); and false-positive unresolved-import diagnostics in monorepos with a misconfigured workspace, which do not affect Claude's ability to edit code.

nodes.label: Environment variables reference
nodes.rationale: Environment variables can control Claude Code behavior such as model selection, authentication, request routing, and feature toggles. Many of the same behaviors can also be configured through a settings file field, a CLI flag, or an in-session command like /model.

nodes.label: Setting a variable in the shell
nodes.rationale: A variable exported in the shell before launching `claude` lasts for that terminal session; adding the export to ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, [Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable or `setx` makes it persist. The assignment prints nothing on success, so the doc recommends echoing the variable in the same shell to confirm it is set.

nodes.label: Setting variables under the settings `env` key
nodes.rationale: Variables added under the `env` key of a settings.json apply every time `claude` runs, read directly from the file regardless of how claude was launched. A running session picks up new and changed values when the file is saved, except for features that read their variables once at startup such as OpenTelemetry monitoring; removing a variable does not unset it until the next launch.

nodes.label: Which settings file an env block applies to
nodes.rationale: ~/.claude/settings.json applies to you in every project, .claude/settings.json to everyone in the project and is checked into source control, .claude/settings.local.json to you in that project only, and managed settings to everyone in the organization as deployed by an admin.

nodes.label: Variable-versus-setting precedence is per key
nodes.rationale: Some behaviors have both an environment variable and a dedicated settings key, and which one Claude Code reads first differs per key. For ANTHROPIC_MODEL and CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_CONNECT_IDE the variable is read first and the `model` or `autoConnectIde` setting is used only when the variable is unset.

nodes.label: Settings `env` overrides the shell value
nodes.rationale: When the same variable is set in both the shell and a settings file `env` block, the settings file value applies: Claude Code writes each `env` entry into the process environment, replacing the value inherited from the shell. Between settings files, `env` values follow settings precedence, so a managed entry overrides user or project settings.

nodes.label: Empty string as the only way to unset
nodes.rationale: A settings file can set a variable but cannot remove one, so to override a variable you cannot unset — such as a stale CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX exported by a shell profile you do not control — set it to an empty string in the `env` block. Claude Code treats the empty value as unset for provider selection, though subprocesses still inherit the empty value.

nodes.label: Interaction with CLI flags and slash commands
nodes.rationale: How an environment variable interacts with CLI flags and in-session commands varies per feature: --model and /model override ANTHROPIC_MODEL, while CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL overrides --effort and /effort. Each variable's row states the precedence or links to the page documenting it.

nodes.label: Shell values read at startup, settings values reapplied live
nodes.rationale: Claude Code reads shell environment variables at startup, so changes to them take effect the next time you launch claude. Variables set under the `env` key in settings files are reapplied to a running session when the file changes, with the startup-only exception for features that read their variables once.

nodes.label: Numeric value spellings
nodes.rationale: Numeric variables such as timeouts, token budgets, and retry counts accept scientific notation and digit-separator spellings in addition to plain digits, except where a variable's row notes it takes plain digits only — Claude Code reads `2e3` as 2000 and `64_000` as 64000. Before v2.1.211 these spellings could silently set a much smaller value, such as `1e6` setting a timeout to 1.

nodes.label: On/off value convention
nodes.rationale: For variables that turn a behavior on or off, `1` or `true` turns it on and `0` or `false` turns it off, in any casing.

nodes.label: Presence-only variables
nodes.rationale: Some variables read only whether you set them at all, so any non-empty value including `0` turns the behavior on and you turn it off by unsetting or emptying the variable. The doc names six: CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC, DISABLE_TELEMETRY, DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING, CLAUDE_CODE_TMUX_TRUECOLOR, FALLBACK_FOR_ALL_PRIMARY_MODELS and IS_DEMO.

nodes.label: FORCE_HYPERLINK parses a number, not a boolean
nodes.rationale: FORCE_HYPERLINK enables clickable OSC 8 hyperlinks when the terminal supports them but is not auto-detected, and only `0` turns them off because Claude Code parses the value as a number rather than a Boolean — so `false`, `no` or `off` enable hyperlinks. The footer PR or merge-request badge renders as a hyperlink even without detected support unless you set `0`.

nodes.label: Feature-flag fetching
nodes.rationale: Claude Code turns some features on through feature flags it fetches from Anthropic, and it skips that fetch in sessions that set DISABLE_GROWTHBOOK, DISABLE_TELEMETRY, DO_NOT_TRACK or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC, in third-party-provider sessions unless a host sets CLAUDE_CODE_PROVIDER_MANAGED_BY_HOST, and in Claude apps gateway sessions.

nodes.label: Features unavailable without flag fetching
nodes.rationale: With fetching off you cannot start sessions in auto mode by default on Pro/Max/Team, use Remote Control, message sessions beyond this machine, run `claude import`, use the advisor tool, read or reply to artifact comments, or get the v2 MCP client runtime and its protocol probe without setting MCP_SDK_GENERATION and MCP_PROTOCOL_NEGOTIATION; Claude-drafted feedback and the Windows PowerShell-by-default behavior are also flag-gated.

nodes.label: First session after an install or upgrade
nodes.rationale: In the first session after installing Claude Code or upgrading to a version that adds a feature, a flag-gated feature can be missing and the session can start in Manual mode on a plan that otherwise starts in auto mode; the flags are fetched during that session so both are present next time.

nodes.label: Standard OpenTelemetry exporter variables
nodes.rationale: Standard OpenTelemetry exporter variables — OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER, OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS, OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL, OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES and signal-specific variants — are also supported alongside the Claude Code-specific ones.

nodes.label: Variables ignored in project and local settings
nodes.rationale: A group of variables is honored only from the shell, user settings or managed settings and is ignored in project and local settings: BETA_TRACING_ENDPOINT, ENABLE_BETA_TRACING_DETAILED, CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, CLAUDE_CODE_TMPDIR and OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES are each documented that way. CLAUDE_CODE_PROJECT_DIR_NAME and CLAUDE_CODE_RESTRICTED are read only from the launching environment, never a settings `env` block.

nodes.label: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
nodes.rationale: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is sent as the X-Api-Key header and, when set, is used instead of a Claude Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise subscription even while logged in. In non-interactive mode (-p) it is always used when present; interactively you approve it once before it overrides the subscription, and `unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` returns to the subscription.

nodes.label: ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN
nodes.rationale: ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN supplies a custom value for the Authorization header, and the value you set is prefixed with `Bearer `.

nodes.label: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL
nodes.rationale: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL overrides the API endpoint to route requests through a proxy or gateway. Pointing it at a non-first-party host disables MCP tool search by default (set ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true if the proxy forwards tool_reference blocks), and as of v2.1.196 Remote Control is disabled when it points anywhere other than api.anthropic.com.

nodes.label: Provider selection switches
nodes.rationale: A family of on/off variables selects the model provider: CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK (Amazon Bedrock), CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX (Google Cloud's Agent Platform), CLAUDE_CODE_USE_FOUNDRY (Microsoft Foundry), CLAUDE_CODE_USE_MANTLE (the Bedrock Mantle endpoint) and CLAUDE_CODE_USE_ANTHROPIC_AWS (Claude Platform on AWS).

nodes.label: Provider endpoint URL overrides
