nodes.rationale: Three related failures about the model string itself: `There's an issue with the selected model` when the configured name is unrecognized or the account lacks access, `Model "…" is not a recognized model id` produced locally at switch time with a did-you-mean hint, and a server-side `Claude Code <version> does not support this model` requiring an update. The local recognition check runs only on the Anthropic API; other providers define their own model names and any string is passed through.

nodes.label: Plan and organization model restrictions
nodes.rationale: A model can be blocked by the subscription plan (`Claude Opus is not available with the Claude Pro plan`, cleared by `/logout` then `/login` after an upgrade, because the stored token reflects the plan at sign-in) or by an organization admin or an `availableModels` allowlist, in which case Claude Code substitutes an allowed model and continues. A family alias such as `opus` resolves to the newest permitted version of that family rather than being rejected outright.

nodes.label: Thinking and effort configuration rejections
nodes.rationale: Three rejections from the thinking/effort configuration: a CLI older than the model's minimum sending `thinking.type.enabled` the model no longer accepts, an effort level above `high` with extended thinking turned off, and a thinking budget larger than the output limit so no room remains for the answer (`max_tokens must be greater than thinking.budget_tokens`, seen mainly on Bedrock and Google Cloud's Agent Platform).

nodes.label: Tool use or thinking block mismatch
nodes.rationale: The conversation history reached the API in an inconsistent state, usually after an interrupted tool call or a turn edited mid-stream: the sequence of `tool_use`, `tool_result` and `thinking` blocks no longer matches what the API expects. All three message variants mean the same thing, and `/rewind` steps back to a checkpoint before the corrupted turn.

nodes.label: Unsupported tool content removed
nodes.rationale: When connected directly to the Anthropic API, Claude Code removes tool content the API does not accept from a loaded or previewed saved session and leaves a placeholder line. Such content reaches a session file when something other than the Anthropic API answered in the API's format, typically a third-party proxy translating another provider's tool calls; the removal happens only on a direct Anthropic API connection.

nodes.label: Usage Policy refusal
nodes.rationale: The API declined to respond because content in the conversation triggered a Usage Policy check, and the message names the model that declined plus a Request ID to quote to support. The check evaluates the full conversation rather than the latest prompt, so a new message in the same session — or reopening it with `--continue`/`--resume` — usually re-triggers the same refusal.

nodes.label: Safety measures flagged a cybersecurity topic
nodes.rationale: The model's server-side safeguards flagged conversation content as a cybersecurity topic, with a message naming the model and linking to the Cyber Verification Program, which grants access for legitimate cybersecurity work. On Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry the same flag produces the Usage Policy refusal message instead.

nodes.label: Installation errors section
nodes.rationale: Errors that appear while installing or updating Claude Code, from the install script, `claude install`, or `claude update`. `command not found`, PATH, permission, and TLS problems during setup are covered by the separate Troubleshoot installation and login page.

nodes.label: Installation was killed before it could finish
nodes.rationale: The install script reports when the `claude install` step is terminated by a signal. On Linux, exit code 137 means SIGKILL, usually the kernel out-of-memory killer on a low-memory host, and the script says Claude Code needs roughly 512MB of free memory. Any other fatal signal, and 137 on macOS, prints the exit code without the out-of-memory explanation.

nodes.label: The connection dropped while downloading the update
nodes.rationale: The connection to the download server closed while the binary was being fetched and the retries did not recover; Claude Code retries a dropped, stalled, or checksum-failing download up to three attempts, but never retries a completed HTTP error such as a 404. A download that stays connected but exceeds the 10-minute total deadline fails with `Download timed out` and is not retried, because a connection that slow will not finish on an immediate retry.

nodes.label: Command-line errors section
nodes.rationale: Errors from the `claude` command line and its subcommands, from a command name submitted at the prompt, and from commands such as `/security-review` that gather context by running shell commands before their prompt runs, including errors from `/tui`, which relaunches the CLI.

nodes.label: CLI flag and argument validation refusals
nodes.rationale: Startup refusals that exit 1 rather than running with a broken configuration: `--bg` combined with `--print` (which would create an unattachable job), an invalid `--agents` value checked in order and stopping at the first failing check, a `--json-schema` value that is not parseable JSON, not an object, or fails schema compilation, a `--settings` file over 2 MiB or not a regular file, a cloud session requested from a `--restricted` session, and a global flag placed before the `remote-control` verb that would not carry over to the sessions it starts.

nodes.label: The current directory no longer exists
nodes.rationale: `claude` was started from a directory deleted or moved after the shell entered it, such as a worktree another shell removed, so Claude Code cannot read its working directory and exits with code 1 before starting the session in both interactive and non-interactive mode. A different read failure, such as a permissions change, names the error code instead (`Can't read the current directory (EACCES)`).

nodes.label: Workspace trust gates settings and helpers
nodes.rationale: Several refusals trace to a folder having no saved workspace trust: `claude remote-control` exits 1 because it cannot show the trust dialog itself, project `permissions.allow` rules and `additionalDirectories` entries are ignored with a count in the warning, and an MCP server's `headersHelper` is skipped so the server connects on its static headers alone. Home-directory trust is never saved, so accepting the dialog there cannot satisfy these checks.

nodes.label: claude import unavailable or config unreadable
nodes.rationale: `claude import` exits 1 in two situations: the import flow is off in this build, because the feature flag has not been fetched yet, because the session runs on a third-party provider where flags are never fetched, or because telemetry/flag-fetching was disabled; and `~/.claude.json` cannot be parsed, where the subcommand does not show the recovery dialog an interactive session would.

nodes.label: MCP server setup and connection refusals
nodes.rationale: Configuration-time MCP failures: a server from Claude Desktop whose name uses characters `claude mcp` disallows (the import continues for the others), a server URL pointing at an Anthropic-hosted connector host whose sign-in works only through claude.ai, an MCP server whose `headersHelper`-minted `Authorization` header the server rejected with 401/403 (with no OAuth fallback, because the helper supplies Authorization), and a `--permission-prompt-tool` naming a tool that was not among the connected MCP tools when a permission decision was first needed.

nodes.label: Injected dynamic-context command failures
nodes.rationale: `/security-review` diffs against `origin/HEAD`, and when that ref does not exist the git commands that gather the diff fail and the review stops before it starts; the quoted command varies because several git commands run at once and whichever fails first is reported. The same shape applies to any skill that injects dynamic context, with two sibling strings that fire before the command runs: a failed permission check (injected commands never prompt) and a skill demanding bash on a machine without Git Bash.

nodes.label: Missing or whitespace-only prompt
nodes.rationale: Bare `claude` needs stdout to be a terminal, so a redirected stdout or a non-terminal console runs non-interactively and reports `Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print` even without the flag. Separately, a prompt made entirely of whitespace is refused before it is sent, because the API rejects messages with no visible text.

nodes.label: Unknown command
nodes.rationale: A submitted `/` name matched no command in this session, so Claude Code reports the name and suggests the closest command or alias the menu lists. The cause is usually a typo, a command whose requirement (platform, plan, authentication method, or organization policy) is not met in this session, or a plugin or MCP command that is not installed or connected. Prompts whose first word after the `/` starts with punctuation or is a path are sent to Claude as normal messages.

nodes.label: Ultrareview refuses before the cloud session starts
nodes.rationale: `/code-review ultra` and `claude ultrareview` refuse a review before spending a free run or billing usage credits when: the diff exceeds the file and line limits, `git merge-base` finds no shared commit with the base branch, the checkout has no branches to bundle, no GitHub account is connected to the Claude account, the connected GitHub account cannot see the repository, or the GitHub App preflight failed transiently while the repo bundle upload also failed.

nodes.label: Resume failures
nodes.rationale: Two distinct resume failures that both exit 1: Claude Code could not read or process the saved transcript for the selected session, so it ends the process rather than continue partially loaded; and no saved transcript matched the passed session ID, whose causes include a mistyped ID, a transcript deleted by the 30-day retention sweep, a session that ran on a different machine, or duplicate copies of a project directory carrying the same ID.

nodes.label: Cannot switch renderers in this session
nodes.rationale: Switching renderers restarts the Claude Code process, so `/tui` is declined when background work would be abandoned by the restart, or when the session holds restrictions the restarted process cannot be given — launch flags such as `--system-prompt` or a `--tools` allowlist, session-scoped deny or ask permission rules, ask rules with no command-line form, and rules or added directories a command line cannot carry intact.

nodes.label: /terminal-setup left your Zed keymap unchanged
nodes.rationale: `/terminal-setup` in Zed could not complete the keymap update and left the file as it was, naming the cause on the first line — unreadable file, a file that does not parse as an array of keybinding blocks, a failed `.bak` backup, or a merged result that did not verify — and ending with the keybinding block to add by hand.

nodes.label: Plugin errors section
nodes.rationale: Errors from plugin and marketplace configuration. Plugin problems that do not produce one of these messages, such as a marketplace URL that does not load or a plugin that installs but does not appear, belong to the separate plugin troubleshooting page.

nodes.label: Marketplace registration and registry failures
nodes.rationale: Two marketplace-level failures: a marketplace registered under a name reserved for official Anthropic marketplaces but sourced from a non-`anthropics` repository, re-checked on every load so the marketplace and its installed plugins stop loading; and a `~/.claude/plugins/known_marketplaces.json` registry that is unreadable or invalid JSON (`Failed to load marketplace configuration`) or valid JSON not matching the registry schema (`Marketplace configuration file is corrupted`). A missing registry file is not a failure.

nodes.label: Plugin command references user_config in a shell command
nodes.rationale: A plugin hook, monitor, or MCP `headersHelper` command references `${user_config.KEY}` where the substituted string would be passed to a shell, so a configured value containing `$(...)`, backticks, or `;` would run as code. Claude Code refuses to start the component rather than substitute, and the check runs on the command template, so the error appears even with no value configured yet.

nodes.label: Plugin archive integrity check failed
nodes.rationale: A marketplace entry using an `archive` source with a `sha256` pin downloaded a file whose digest does not match, so Claude Code refuses the install and nothing changes in the plugin cache. The three possible causes are the file at the URL changing after the pin was computed, a wrong digest entered by the author, and a URL serving a different file than was pinned.

nodes.label: Path escapes plugin directory
nodes.rationale: A component path declared in a plugin's `plugin.json` or its marketplace entry resolves outside the plugin's own directory, so Claude Code drops that path and loads the rest of the plugin; the component name in the message names the declaring field. Sharing files between plugins in one marketplace is done with a symlink inside the plugin directory.

nodes.label: Tool errors section
nodes.rationale: Errors from Claude's built-in tools. Claude corrects most of them on its own; the first two need a change from the user, because they come from a subagent definition or a permission rule the user controls.

nodes.label: Agent would be spawned with zero tools
nodes.rationale: Every entry in a subagent's `tools` list failed to match a usable tool, so Claude Code refused to launch it rather than run a subagent that cannot act. The message groups entries by cause: unrecognized names, tools subagents cannot use (background subagents keep a smaller set), and valid entries matching no tool in this session. Omitting the `tools` field entirely, or leaving the list empty, never triggers the refusal.

nodes.label: File is covered by a Read deny rule
nodes.rationale: Edit or Write was called on a path matched by a `Read` deny rule, including creating a new file there. Both tools change content Claude has to be able to read back, so Claude Code refuses before any file access. NotebookEdit is not covered by `Read` deny rules, so an `Edit` deny rule for the same path is needed to block it too.

nodes.label: subagent_type is required
nodes.rationale: Claude called the Agent tool without a `subagent_type` in a session with no general-purpose subagent to fall back on, which happens when `CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_DISABLE_BUILTIN_AGENTS=1` is set in non-interactive mode or when the main-thread agent's `tools: Agent(...)` allowlist leaves out `general-purpose`. The message lists the subagents the session does have, so Claude can retry with one.

nodes.label: Memory index is over its read limit
nodes.rationale: A write left the auto-memory index `MEMORY.md` over a read limit of 200 lines or 25KB. The write succeeded, but only the first 200 lines or 25KB loads at session start, so entries past the limit are silently dropped on every read. YAML frontmatter and block-level HTML comments are stripped before loading and excluded from the measurement, and the error is delivered to Claude after the write rather than shown as a terminal banner.

nodes.label: pkill pattern matches the Claude Code process
nodes.rationale: A `pkill` command in a Bash tool call used a pattern, typically with `-f`, matching the Claude Code process itself. Claude Code tests the pattern with `pgrep` first and refuses when its own process ID is in the result, rather than letting the command end the session. The check runs on Linux only; on macOS `pkill` runs unmodified.

nodes.label: Failed to write to a teammate's inbox
nodes.rationale: Claude Code could not write a message to a teammate's mailbox file under `~/.claude/teams/{team}/inboxes/`, so the recipient received nothing — from a full disk, an unwritable directory, or another agent holding the inbox lock too long. Structured agent-team protocol messages fail the same way and name the undelivered message, and three of them carry their own consequence, such as a plan approval request that leaves the teammate in plan mode until a resubmission succeeds.

nodes.label: Cross-session message size and rate limits
nodes.rationale: A cross-session message to another session on the same machine is refused when the serialized message exceeds 1,048,576 characters, and when a rapid burst reaches what the receiving session's inbox accepts. In both cases the receiving session gets nothing and the refusal appears in the sending session's tool result rather than as a terminal banner; resending the same oversized text fails the same way.

nodes.label: Refusing to send a cross-session message
nodes.rationale: Before writing a cross-session message, Claude Code checks that the target session's inbox socket is the endpoint the message was addressed to, and refuses when a check fails: a symlink at the socket path, a target that cannot be inspected, a process that is not the addressed session, an unreadable endpoint identity or owner, an endpoint owned by another user, or a different process holding a reused process id.

nodes.label: Refusing to read, write, or search a path
nodes.rationale: Claude Code checks a path's permission rules and then confirms that resolution again when the tool opens the file or starts the search, refusing the operation when it cannot confirm the path still leads to the approved location. Reasons include a symlink replaced between check and use, a changed parent-directory resolution, a symlink at the approved write location, an unopenable search root, an expired permission record under many concurrent file operations, and ripgrep resolvable only by name on PATH.

nodes.label: Background session errors section
nodes.rationale: Background sessions run without an interactive terminal of their own, so commands that need one behave differently there. These messages appear in a background session's transcript, in the terminal that attaches to one, in the session or shell that dispatched it, or — for the worktree-guard entries — in any session isolated in a worktree.

nodes.label: Commands refused in a background session
nodes.rationale: Commands that open an interactive dialog cannot do so while no terminal is attached, so `/install-github-app`, the `/mcp` settings list, and the MCP menu's authentication actions respond with a message and the session appears under Needs input in agent view. Non-panel forms such as `/mcp enable|disable|reconnect <server>` still work without attaching.

nodes.label: Worktree-isolation path guard blocks a write or command
nodes.rationale: The worktree-isolation guard resolves symlinks before checking that a write or a command's working directory does not reach the shared checkout, and blocks the operation when resolution fails or when the path names a network location. Two messages: a spelling that cannot be safely resolved (a symlink storing a raw dot segment, a network-share or device-namespace shape, an unreadable ancestor), and a network-shaped path such as a UNC share or `/net` automount while the checkout is local — which isolating the session cannot unblock.

nodes.label: Refusals when opening a stopped background session
nodes.rationale: Three refusals to open a stopped background session rather than silently start a blank one or re-run its original prompt: the session has no saved transcript because it was stopped before its first response finished, its saved conversation is already open in another live Claude Code process, and its saved conversation has been removed by transcript cleanup. Each names its recovery — `claude respawn <id>`, using the process that holds the conversation, or `claude rm <id>`.

nodes.label: Worktree has commits that are not pushed anywhere
nodes.rationale: Deleting a background session whose worktree holds commits Claude Code cannot confirm are saved elsewhere keeps the worktree and the session row instead of destroying the commits, printing the kept path and the reason. A `Ctrl+X` double-press in agent view consents to discarding uncommitted changes but not commits, so it is refused there too; commits on a remote, or on the local default branch checked out in the main checkout, do not block the delete.

nodes.label: Background session host process failures
nodes.rationale: Three ways a background session's process stops being reachable: its terminal host process died while the service still held the connection (the conversation is saved and Enter restarts it), the service accepted the open but no output arrived for about ten seconds so the attempt ended, and another process stopped the session while a respawn was in flight. A row running a shell command is never restarted automatically, because a restart would run the command again.

nodes.label: Session agent no longer available
nodes.rationale: A resumed session was running a custom agent that Claude Code could not find, searching the session's original directory first (when that workspace is trusted) and then the resume directory. The session still resumes but with the default tools and system prompt, so the agent's tool restrictions no longer apply, and because the fallback is not saved the warning repeats on every resume until the agent is re-created or named with `--agent`.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_PROCESS_WRAPPER launcher errors
nodes.rationale: `CLAUDE_CODE_PROCESS_WRAPPER` is set to a value that cannot be used, so Claude Code refuses to start the affected process rather than run it without the launcher. A launcher that starts but exits without replacing itself reports that it `must exec, not daemonize`, and a launcher problem that prevents reaching the background service is reported as the reason inside `Couldn't reach the background service (...)`.

nodes.label: Background service failed to start or become reachable
nodes.rationale: Three failures starting the supervisor process that hosts background sessions: `EUNKNOWN` on Windows, usually a software restriction policy such as Group Policy or AppLocker blocking the program; `EACCES` (or `ENOENT`/`ENOEXEC`/`EPERM`) on an npm installation while `npm install -g` is replacing the binary, which Claude Code waits up to ten seconds and retries through; and a service process that exited before accepting connections, reported with its exit code and first error line.

nodes.label: Wrapper and IDE errors section
nodes.rationale: These errors come from the program that launched Claude Code — an IDE extension or an Agent SDK application — rather than from Claude Code itself, which is why they are the one group on this page that is not surface-uniform.

nodes.label: Claude Code process exited with code N
nodes.rationale: The underlying `claude` process exited non-zero, and the exit code alone does not say what failed: the real error is in the process's own output, which the wrapper appends when it captured any and otherwise keeps in its logs. Running `claude` in a terminal in the same project usually reproduces the failure with its real message.

nodes.label: Could not locate the Claude CLI on PATH
nodes.rationale: The VS Code extension refuses to launch Claude Code on Windows when the integrated terminal's shell is PowerShell and it cannot find the installed `claude` on PATH, because launching by name there would run a `claude` from the open folder instead of the installed CLI. The PATH entry must be a user or system environment variable rather than a PowerShell profile edit, and VS Code must be restarted, since it reads PATH at startup.

nodes.label: Restored the code, but skipped files
nodes.rationale: A `/rewind` code restore skipped tracked paths rather than writing or deleting through them, because a path is or became a symlink, hard link, or other non-regular file, its directory changed since the checkpoint, or its backup could not be safely read. Skipped paths keep their current contents, and the message gives only a count — the debug log names each path as the restore runs.

nodes.label: Session saving warnings section
nodes.rationale: Warnings shown on a persistent line below the input box when Claude Code is not saving the session transcript. The session keeps working either way; the warnings say the session may be missing from `--resume` later.

nodes.label: Transcript writes are failing
nodes.rationale: Writes to the transcript file are failing, and the message names the cause with the underlying error code such as `ENOSPC`. The warning appears on the first failure for conditions that do not clear on their own — full disk, exceeded quota, read-only filesystem, over-length path, or a POSIX permission error — and only after repeated failures spanning at least a minute for everything else, including Windows permission errors an antivirus scan can cause transiently.

nodes.label: Transcript saving is off
nodes.rationale: Two notices that the session writes no transcript: `CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY` was set, an intentional opt-out for ephemeral scripted sessions that can also arrive through a shell profile or wrapper; and an inherited `CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION` marker, which Claude Code sets in the subprocesses it spawns so nested sessions do not fill the `--resume` list, but which can leak through a long-lived intermediary such as a terminal or launcher.

nodes.label: Configuration warnings section
nodes.rationale: Claude Code writes most of these messages to stderr rather than into the conversation, and most of them at startup; an entry says so when its message appears elsewhere, such as the debug log or a startup notice in the conversation view, or at another time, such as at request time.

nodes.label: Fullscreen renderer start failures
nodes.rationale: A previous fullscreen session on this machine exited before it finished starting, so Claude Code starts on the classic renderer and prints a notice; repeated failures turn fullscreen off on that machine until `/tui fullscreen` is run again. A separate message reports that Claude Code exited after an unrecoverable interface error, adding a second sentence only when the error happened while the fullscreen renderer was starting.

nodes.label: Agent descriptions are over the 15.0k-token limit
nodes.rationale: The combined descriptions of the user's non-built-in subagents exceed 15,000 estimated tokens, counting each agent's name plus its `description` frontmatter. This is a startup notice in the conversation view rather than stderr, and Claude Code loads every agent whether or not the total is over the limit, so the warning does not change what loads.

nodes.label: Remote managed settings failed to load
nodes.rationale: A session eligible for server-managed settings could not fetch them, and the parenthesized cause names what failed (`network error`, `request timed out`, `authentication rejected (401)`). The rest of the line says which policy the session runs on: `using cached policy` from an earlier successful fetch, minus the withheld environment variables, or `no remote policy applied` with no cache.

nodes.label: Permission rules weaker or more inert than intended
nodes.rationale: Two startup warnings that keep the rule and change nothing: a `Write`, `NotebookEdit`, `MultiEdit`, or `Glob` path rule that file permission checks never consult, because they check against `Edit` and `Read` rules only; and a `Bash` allow rule whose `*` precedes the word that determines which command it is, so it also approves any options inserted at that position — for git, options such as `-c` and `--exec-path` can run arbitrary commands. Each warning names the rule's source in parentheses.

nodes.label: crossSessionInbound must be one of accept, hold, refuse
nodes.rationale: A settings file set `crossSessionInbound` to an unrecognized value such as the typo `"reject"`. In a user, project, local, or `--settings` file the value is ignored and cross-session messages are held for approval while it is present; in managed settings Claude Code treats the unrecognized value as `refuse`, the most restrictive value, until an administrator fixes it.

nodes.label: The 200K limit isn't enforced
nodes.rationale: `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT=1` normally holds sessions on 1M-context models to a 200K window through auto-compaction, but no compaction threshold caps this session at or below 200K. The two configurations that defeat the enforcement are an unrecognized model ID combined with disabled unknown-model window enforcement or a raised assumed window, and a `context-1m` beta still requested through `ANTHROPIC_BETAS` or `--betas`.

nodes.label: Unrecognized model ID on a request
nodes.rationale: Claude Code sent a request for a model ID this version does not recognize with no `modelOverrides` entry mapping it, and still sends the request unchanged rather than exiting or switching models. It writes a machine-readable `[claude-code:unrecognized_model]` prefix followed by a one-line JSON object carrying at least `model` and `query_source`, once per model string per process, to stderr in `-p` mode and to the debug log otherwise.

nodes.label: Responses seem lower quality than usual
nodes.rationale: When answers seem less capable but no error is shown, the cause is usually conversation state rather than the model: Claude Code does not silently change model versions, and switches to a fallback only via a configured `--fallback-model`, a Bedrock or Google Cloud startup check, or automatic model fallback on Fable 5.1, Fable 5 and Opus 5. The checks are model selection, effort level, context pressure, and stale instructions; rewinding beats correcting in-thread, because a wrong attempt left in context anchors later answers.

nodes.label: Report an error
nodes.rationale: For anything the page does not cover, `/feedback` sends the transcript and a description to Anthropic and offers a prefilled GitHub issue, `claude doctor` gives a read-only diagnostic of the installation and `/doctor` runs the in-session checkup, status.claude.com shows active incidents, and the claude-code GitHub issues are searchable. On third-party providers, or with no Anthropic credentials, `/feedback` saves a local archive instead of sending.

nodes.label: Fast mode
nodes.rationale: Fast mode is a high-speed configuration for Claude Opus that makes the model up to 2.5x faster at a higher cost per token. It is toggled on with /fast when speed matters for interactive work like rapid iteration or live debugging, and off when cost matters more than latency.

nodes.label: Not a different model, a different API configuration
nodes.rationale: Fast mode is not a different model: it runs Claude Opus with a different API configuration that prioritizes speed over cost efficiency, so quality and capabilities are identical and only response latency changes.

nodes.label: Supported models: Opus 5 and Opus 4.8
nodes.rationale: Fast mode is supported on Opus 5 and Opus 4.8 only. It is not available on Sonnet, Haiku, or any other model.

nodes.label: Opus 4.7 fast mode removal
nodes.rationale: Fast mode for Opus 4.7 was deprecated on June 25, 2026 and removed on July 24, 2026. Claude Code now treats Opus 4.7 like any other model without fast mode support, so switching to it turns fast mode off.

nodes.label: /fast command
nodes.rationale: In the CLI, typing /fast and pressing Tab toggles fast mode on or off, and running /fast again reports whether fast mode is currently on. It is also the command used to re-enable fast mode after a cooldown or a credits-exhausted shutoff.

nodes.label: fastMode setting
nodes.rationale: Setting "fastMode": true in the user settings file turns fast mode on. The VS Code extension follows this setting and offers a Toggle fast mode command whenever the selected model supports fast mode.

nodes.label: Fast mode in non-interactive mode
nodes.rationale: In non-interactive mode with the -p flag, /fast works only in a session launched with fast mode in its --settings value, for example claude -p --settings '{"fastMode": true}'. The toggle then applies to that session only and is not saved as the default; any other non-interactive session reports that fast mode is not available.

nodes.label: Fast mode persists across sessions by default
nodes.rationale: By default, fast mode turned on in an interactive session persists across sessions as a saved preference, and a new session starts from that saved preference.

nodes.label: Toggling mid-turn
nodes.rationale: /fast can be run while Claude is working and Claude Code toggles fast mode without waiting for the turn to end. The running turn finishes at its original speed, so the speed change takes effect from the next turn; if the toggle also switches models, the new model is used from the next request in that turn.

nodes.label: Enabling fast mode switches to Opus
nodes.rationale: If the current model does not support fast mode, enabling fast mode makes Claude Code switch to Opus. Disabling fast mode again leaves the session on Opus; changing model afterwards requires /model.

nodes.label: Fast mode ON indicators
nodes.rationale: Enabling fast mode shows a "Fast mode ON" confirmation and a small lightning icon next to the prompt while fast mode is active. The same ON/OFF confirmation appears whenever a model switch turns fast mode on or off.

nodes.label: Fast mode default model by CLI version
nodes.rationale: Opus 5 is the fast mode default in Claude Code v2.1.219 and later. Before that, fast mode defaulted to Opus 4.8 on v2.1.154 through v2.1.218, and to Opus 4.7 on v2.1.142 through v2.1.153.

nodes.label: Switching away turns fast mode off
nodes.rationale: When the user switches to a model that does not support fast mode, Claude Code turns fast mode off. This includes Opus 4.7; before v2.1.221 fast mode stayed on after such a switch and the API rejected the requests.

nodes.label: Switching back restores fast mode
nodes.rationale: Switching back to a supported Opus model turns fast mode on again when the saved fast mode preference is on. A model switch never turns fast mode on when the saved preference is off, and it does not turn it on under per-session opt-in either — /fast must be run.

nodes.label: Remote Control status resend
nodes.rationale: Claude Code resends the session's fast mode status to devices connected through Remote Control after a model switch, a reconnection, or a failed availability check. Model switches made from a Remote Control device produce the same ON/OFF confirmations as /model or /config model=<model>.

nodes.label: Fast mode pricing
nodes.rationale: Fast mode costs $10 per MTok input and $50 per MTok output on both Opus 5 and Opus 4.8, which is higher than standard Opus pricing. That pricing is flat across the full 1M token context window.

nodes.label: First enable reprices the whole conversation context
nodes.rationale: The first time fast mode is enabled in a conversation, the user pays the full fast mode uncached input token price for the entire conversation context, so the cost grows the deeper into a conversation it is enabled. The charge applies once per conversation, so toggling off and on again later does not repeat it.

nodes.label: Enable at the start of a session
nodes.rationale: For the best cost efficiency, fast mode should be enabled at the start of a session rather than switched on mid-conversation, because enabling it later reprices a larger accumulated context.

nodes.label: Check the login method with /status
nodes.rationale: Where fast mode spend appears depends on how the user signed in, so /status is run first: a Login method row such as "Claude Max account" means a Claude subscription, while an API key row means requests bill to a Claude Console organization.

nodes.label: Pro and Max spend visibility
nodes.rationale: On Pro and Max, fast mode is paid from usage credits and the spend is shown in the Usage credits section of Settings > Usage on claude.ai. That figure includes fast mode but does not break it out separately.

nodes.label: Team and Enterprise spend visibility
nodes.rationale: On Team and Enterprise, the organization pays for a user's fast mode usage from its usage credits. An individual sees their own usage-credits spend with /usage, while the organization's view is documented under Claude for Teams and Enterprise.

nodes.label: Console spend: Group by Speed
nodes.rationale: A Claude Console organization pays for fast mode with the rest of its API usage. On the Console Usage and Cost pages, selecting "Speed (Research Preview)" in the Group by menu separates fast mode from standard-speed usage, and that option appears only when the selected date range includes fast mode usage.

nodes.label: When fast mode is the right choice
nodes.rationale: Fast mode is best for interactive work where response latency matters more than cost: rapid iteration on code changes, live debugging sessions, and time-sensitive work with tight deadlines.

nodes.label: When standard mode is better
nodes.rationale: Standard mode is better for long autonomous tasks where speed matters less, for batch processing or CI/CD pipelines, and for cost-sensitive workloads.

nodes.label: Fast mode versus effort level
nodes.rationale: Fast mode and effort level both affect response speed but differently: fast mode keeps the same model quality at lower latency and higher cost, while a lower effort level reduces thinking time and may lower quality on complex tasks. The two can be combined for maximum speed on straightforward tasks.

nodes.label: Requirement: Anthropic API or subscription only
nodes.rationale: Fast mode is available only through the Anthropic Console API and for Claude subscription plans using usage credits. It is not available on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, or Claude Platform on AWS.

nodes.label: Requirement: usage credits turned on
nodes.rationale: On Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise plans the account must have usage credits turned on, which allows billing beyond the plan's included usage; until then /fast shows "Fast mode requires usage credits · /usage-credits to turn them on". Fast mode usage draws directly from usage credits even when plan usage remains.

nodes.label: Requirement: paid Console organization
nodes.rationale: Claude Console accounts do not use usage credits; the organization pays for fast mode per token with the rest of its API usage. On the Console's free Evaluation plan /fast shows "Fast mode unavailable during evaluation. Please purchase credits.", cleared by purchasing credits in Console billing settings.

nodes.label: Requirement: Owner enablement for Team and Enterprise
nodes.rationale: Fast mode is disabled by default for Team and Enterprise organizations and an Owner must explicitly enable it before users can access it. Until then /fast reports "Fast mode has been disabled by your organization."

nodes.label: availableModels allowlist interaction
nodes.rationale: If an organization's availableModels allowlist excludes the fast-mode Opus model, /fast is refused with "is not in your organization's allowed models". The exception is a session already running on an allowed Opus model that supports fast mode, where /fast enables fast mode on the current model instead of switching models.

nodes.label: Console organization enablement and provisioning
nodes.rationale: For Console API customers an admin enables fast mode in Claude Code preferences, and because fast mode is a research preview the organization must also have fast mode access provisioned (via an account manager or the waitlist). Without provisioned access the API rejects each fast mode request with a 429 that Claude Code treats as a fast mode rate limit, and unlike a real cooldown the rejections continue until access is provisioned.

nodes.label: Claude AI Team/Enterprise enablement
nodes.rationale: For Claude AI Team and Enterprise organizations, an Owner enables fast mode at Admin Settings > Claude Code on claude.ai.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FAST_MODE
nodes.rationale: Setting CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FAST_MODE=1 is another option for disabling fast mode entirely, documented alongside the other Claude Code environment variables.

nodes.label: Fast mode availability check
nodes.rationale: Before offering fast mode, Claude Code checks the organization's fast mode availability with a request sent directly to api.anthropic.com. The check does not follow ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL but does use a configured HTTP proxy, and a check that succeeded in the past keeps working from its cached result.

nodes.label: Connectivity failure of the availability check
nodes.rationale: When the availability check fails, /fast reports "Fast mode unavailable due to network connectivity issues" and requests run at standard speed even though the organization has fast mode enabled. The same message appears on an open network when the check reaches api.anthropic.com but presents a gateway-issued credential (from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or an apiKeyHelper) that Anthropic rejects.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_FAST_MODE_NETWORK_ERRORS
nodes.rationale: CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_FAST_MODE_NETWORK_ERRORS=1 treats a failed availability check as available while still honoring a "disabled by your organization" response. It is the fix when the network refuses the connection or Anthropic rejects a gateway credential, and it does not apply to configurations that produce a disabled response.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_FAST_MODE_ORG_CHECK
nodes.rationale: CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_FAST_MODE_ORG_CHECK=1 skips the availability check entirely. It is the fix when the network intercepts the request rather than refusing it, and it is the remedy for both the bearer-token-only session and the intercepting-proxy block page.

nodes.label: ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN-only session skips the check
nodes.rationale: A session authenticating with ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN alone never sends the availability check: without a claude.ai login, an Anthropic API key, or a cached successful check, Claude Code treats fast mode as disabled by the organization. Allowlisting direct egress does not help this case because no request is sent.

nodes.label: TLS-inspecting proxy block page read as disabled
nodes.rationale: A proxy that intercepts the availability check and answers with its own page — for example a TLS-inspecting proxy returning an HTTP 200 block page — is read as a response saying the organization has fast mode disabled, rather than as a connectivity failure.

nodes.label: Skip variables affect only the client-side check
nodes.rationale: The skip variables affect only the client-side availability check. When an organization genuinely has fast mode disabled, the API rejects fast mode requests whether or not the variables are set.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC suppresses the check
nodes.rationale: Setting CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC also suppresses the availability check; without a previously cached successful check, /fast reports "Fast mode is currently unavailable". Both skip variables restore fast mode in that configuration too.

nodes.label: fastModePerSessionOptIn
nodes.rationale: Setting fastModePerSessionOptIn to true in any settings file makes each session start with fast mode off and requires users to enable it explicitly with /fast. Team and Enterprise Owners can deploy it organization-wide through server-managed settings; the user's preference is still saved, so removing the setting restores persistent behavior.

nodes.label: Cost control for concurrent sessions
nodes.rationale: Per-session opt-in is useful for controlling costs in organizations where users run multiple concurrent sessions, since a persistent fast mode preference would otherwise apply to every one of them.

nodes.label: Separate fast mode rate limits
nodes.rationale: Fast mode has rate limits separate from standard Opus, and all supported Opus models share one fast mode rate limit pool. On hitting the limit, fast mode automatically falls back to standard speed, the lightning icon turns gray to indicate cooldown, work continues at standard speed and pricing, and fast mode automatically re-enables when the cooldown expires.

nodes.label: Running out of usage credits mid-session
nodes.rationale: If usage credits run out mid-session, Claude Code retries each rejected fast mode request at standard speed and pricing with no cooldown. Interactive sessions show "Fast mode disabled · usage credits exhausted" and turn fast mode off for the rest of the session without changing the saved preference, while non-interactive --output-format stream-json sessions and the Agent SDK emit the same text as a system message with subtype notification once per turn and keep fast mode on (Claude Code v2.1.221 or later).

nodes.label: Research preview status
nodes.rationale: Fast mode is a research preview feature: the feature may change based on feedback, availability and pricing are subject to change, and the underlying API configuration may evolve. Issues and feedback go through the usual Anthropic support channels.

nodes.label: Feature availability matrix
nodes.rationale: The document compares which Claude Code features are available across Anthropic subscription plans, the Anthropic Console, Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry. Its baseline claim is that the Claude Code CLI and everything that runs locally work on every provider; only server-backed features vary.

nodes.label: Availability table legend
nodes.rationale: In the availability tables, a check mark means available, a cross means not available, and "See note" links to a footnote describing partial support. A qualifier after a check mark narrows availability to that subset, and "Admin-enabled" means the feature is off until an organization admin turns it on.

nodes.label: Authentication determines reachable features
nodes.rationale: How you authenticate determines which features Claude Code can reach, so each provider is a column in the availability tables. Readers are told to find their column by how they signed in or which CLAUDE_CODE_USE_* environment variable they set.

nodes.label: Claude subscription authentication
nodes.rationale: The Claude subscription column covers signing in with a claude.ai account on the Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise plan. It is the only authentication method that reaches the subscription-only feature set, and within it the plan tier decides further availability.

nodes.label: Anthropic Console authentication
nodes.rationale: The Anthropic Console column covers authenticating with an Anthropic API key, or signing in to a Console account without one. Everything in the varies-by-provider table is available except that fast mode requires provisioned access, and server-managed settings are available when the API key belongs to a Team or Enterprise organization.

nodes.label: Amazon Bedrock provider
nodes.rationale: Amazon Bedrock means using Claude models from the Bedrock model catalog with CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK set. It is the most restricted column: no subscription features, no web search, fast mode, Advisor, Channels, analytics dashboard, server-managed settings, or the /design-sync and /import commands.

nodes.label: Mantle endpoint
nodes.rationale: The Mantle endpoint, selected with CLAUDE_CODE_USE_MANTLE, is explicitly covered by the Amazon Bedrock column of the availability tables rather than being a separate provider.

nodes.label: Claude Platform on AWS
nodes.rationale: Claude Platform on AWS means Claude was bought through AWS Marketplace but Claude Code still calls the Anthropic API, with CLAUDE_CODE_USE_ANTHROPIC_AWS set. It gets web search and Zero Data Retention for qualified accounts, but loses fast mode, Advisor, Channels, GitHub Actions, analytics, server-managed settings, and /design-sync and /import.

nodes.label: Google Cloud's Agent Platform
nodes.rationale: Google Cloud's Agent Platform is Google-operated and selected with CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX. Web search works there only on Claude 4 models and later, auto mode is limited to Sonnet 5, Opus 4.7 or later and the Fable models, and tool search is unsupported on models earlier than the Claude 4.5 generation.

nodes.label: Microsoft Foundry
nodes.rationale: Microsoft Foundry is Anthropic-operated and selected with CLAUDE_CODE_USE_FOUNDRY. Web search and tool search depend on the hosting option — web search works only on Anthropic-hosted deployments and tool search is unsupported on Azure-hosted ones — and GitLab CI/CD is unavailable while GitHub Actions works.

nodes.label: Features available on every provider
nodes.rationale: The CLI and Agent SDK, VS Code and JetBrains extensions, subagents, hooks, commands, skills, CLAUDE.md memory, plugins, MCP servers, checkpoints, sandboxing, Workflows, OpenTelemetry metrics, and the managed settings file work on every provider. Three of them — MCP servers, subagents, and commands — carry provider-specific differences.

nodes.label: claude.ai MCP connector gating
nodes.rationale: MCP servers work on every provider, but connectors imported from claude.ai load only when a claude.ai subscription is the active authentication method. Switching authentication therefore silently drops those connectors.

nodes.label: MCP tool search availability
nodes.rationale: Tool search is off by default when ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL points to a non-first-party host. It is also unsupported on Google Cloud's Agent Platform models earlier than the Claude 4.5 generation, and on Microsoft Foundry deployments hosted on Azure.

nodes.label: Explore subagent model inheritance
nodes.rationale: The built-in Explore subagent caps its inherited model at Opus when running on the Claude API, but inherits the main conversation's model directly on any other provider, including Claude Platform on AWS.

nodes.label: Slash commands that vary by provider
nodes.rationale: /design-sync and /import (including its `claude import` subcommand form) are unavailable on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, and Claude Platform on AWS. /voice requires a claude.ai account, and /list-agents with its /peers alias exists only in sessions where cross-session messaging is enabled.

nodes.label: Features requiring a Claude subscription
nodes.rationale: Claude Code on the web, mobile, Slack, Desktop, Routines (/schedule), Ultrareview, Code Review (Team and Enterprise), Remote Control, the Chrome extension, computer use (Pro and Max), Artifacts, and voice dictation all require signing in with a claude.ai account. None is reachable with an Anthropic Console API key or from a third-party provider.

nodes.label: Claude Code Desktop partial exception
nodes.rationale: Desktop is the partial exception to the subscription-only rule: gateway routing can be configured in the app or by an administrator, Enterprise deployments can route Desktop to Google Cloud's Agent Platform or a gateway via managed settings, and Claude Desktop on 3P runs the Code tab on Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, or a self-hosted LLM gateway.

nodes.label: Web search availability
nodes.rationale: Web search runs in the local CLI but needs a server-side capability: it is available on Claude subscriptions, the Anthropic Console, and Claude Platform on AWS; absent on Amazon Bedrock; limited to Claude 4 models and later on Google Cloud's Agent Platform; and limited to Anthropic-hosted deployments on Microsoft Foundry.

nodes.label: Fast mode availability
nodes.rationale: Fast mode is available on Claude subscriptions — owner-enabled on Team and Enterprise — and on provisioned Anthropic Console organizations. It is unavailable on Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry.

nodes.label: Auto mode availability
nodes.rationale: Auto mode is fully available on Claude subscriptions, the Anthropic Console, and Claude Platform on AWS. On Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry it supports only Claude Sonnet 5, Opus 4.7 or later, and the Fable models, and the built-in starting permission mode on those providers is Manual.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_AUTO_MODE version window
nodes.rationale: In Claude Code v2.1.158 through v2.1.206, auto mode on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry also required setting CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_AUTO_MODE=1. Version v2.1.207 removed that requirement.

nodes.label: Advisor availability
nodes.rationale: The Advisor is available only on Claude subscriptions and the Anthropic Console; it is unavailable on all four third-party provider columns. It is called out as an Anthropic-only feature that works behind an LLM gateway only if the gateway forwards requests intact to the Anthropic API.

nodes.label: Cross-session messaging availability
nodes.rationale: Cross-session messaging works on every provider but is same-machine only under API-key authentication and on all four third-party providers. It requires v2.1.224 or later on macOS and Linux (including WSL 2), v2.1.234 on native Windows, and v2.1.248 on the third-party providers.

nodes.label: Remote Control as the cross-machine gate
nodes.rationale: Claude can find Claude Code on the web sessions and sessions on other machines only from a session connected to Remote Control, which itself needs a claude.ai sign-in. Remote Control is also one of the features Claude Code turns off whenever ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL points away from api.anthropic.com.

nodes.label: Channels availability
nodes.rationale: Channels are available on Claude subscriptions and the Anthropic Console and unavailable on all four third-party providers. On the plan axis they are automatic on Pro and Max but admin-enabled on Team and Enterprise.

nodes.label: GitHub Actions availability
nodes.rationale: GitHub Actions works on Claude subscriptions, the Anthropic Console, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry, but not on Claude Platform on AWS. It is one of the recommended substitutes for cloud sessions where Routines are unavailable.

nodes.label: GitLab CI/CD availability
nodes.rationale: GitLab CI/CD works on every column except Microsoft Foundry, which makes it the complement of GitHub Actions: it is the recommended cloud-session substitute on Claude Platform on AWS, where GitHub Actions is unavailable.

nodes.label: Analytics dashboard and API
nodes.rationale: The analytics dashboard is available to Team and Enterprise claude.ai plans and the API to Enterprise; on the Anthropic Console the dashboard and API are available but contribution metrics require a claude.ai Team or Enterprise organization. No third-party provider offers analytics.

nodes.label: Server-managed settings
nodes.rationale: Server-managed settings are available to Team and Enterprise organizations on both Claude subscriptions and the Anthropic Console, and on no third-party provider. They are also among the features Claude Code disables whenever ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL points at a non-Anthropic host.

nodes.label: Zero Data Retention availability
nodes.rationale: Zero Data Retention is offered to qualified Enterprise accounts on a Claude subscription and to qualified Anthropic Console and Claude Platform on AWS accounts. On Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry it is subject to your agreement with the cloud provider, and it is not part of the standard Enterprise plan — it requires separate enablement by Anthropic.

nodes.label: LLM gateway availability rule
nodes.rationale: When you authenticate through an LLM gateway, feature availability matches the underlying provider the gateway forwards to — except for the features Claude Code itself turns off. Anthropic-only features such as the Advisor work only if the gateway forwards requests intact to the Anthropic API.

nodes.label: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL feature shutoff
nodes.rationale: Whenever ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL points at a host other than api.anthropic.com, Claude Code turns off features such as Remote Control and server-managed settings regardless of what the gateway forwards, and tool search defaults to off. This is a client-side shutoff, independent of the upstream provider's capabilities.

nodes.label: Third-party telemetry off by default
nodes.rationale: On Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, and Claude Platform on AWS, error reporting and telemetry to Anthropic are off by default. The data-usage page documents what traffic still reaches Anthropic and how to opt out.

nodes.label: Documented substitutes for missing features
nodes.rationale: Each provider tab names substitutes for what it lacks: /loop instead of /schedule for scheduling, GitHub Actions or GitLab CI/CD instead of cloud sessions, and on Amazon Bedrock the WebFetch tool with a specific URL instead of web search.

nodes.label: Availability by subscription plan
nodes.rationale: A second axis applies only to claude.ai sign-ins: the Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise table. It is explicitly stated not to apply if you authenticate through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, or an Anthropic Console API key.

nodes.label: Admin-enabled plan features
nodes.rationale: Some plan-tier entries read Admin-enabled rather than a check mark: Remote Control and Channels on Team and Enterprise, and Artifacts on Enterprise. The feature is present but off until an organization admin turns it on.

nodes.label: Enterprise-only plan features
nodes.rationale: The Enterprise plan is the only tier with the Enterprise Analytics API, SCIM, the Compliance API, and Zero Data Retention. Claude Code on the web on Enterprise additionally requires a premium seat or a Chat + Claude Code seat.

nodes.label: Model availability is a separate axis
nodes.rationale: Which Claude models and context-window sizes exist per provider and region is documented elsewhere (Model configuration and the Models overview), not in this feature matrix.

nodes.label: Model capabilities vs Claude Code features
nodes.rationale: Vision, PDF input, and extended thinking are model capabilities rather than Claude Code features, so they work on every provider that offers the model. They are deliberately excluded from the provider availability tables.

nodes.label: Prompt caching parity
nodes.rationale: Prompt caching works the same way on most providers; on Amazon Bedrock its support varies by model. It is documented alongside model availability rather than in the feature tables.

nodes.label: Claude Code extension layer
nodes.rationale: The extension layer is the set of features you add on top of Claude Code's built-in tools to customize what Claude knows, connect it to external services, and automate workflows: CLAUDE.md, skills, code intelligence, MCP, subagents, dynamic workflows, cross-session messaging, hooks, plugins and marketplaces. Each extension plugs into a different part of the agentic loop.

nodes.label: Built-in tools
nodes.rationale: Claude Code combines a model that reasons about code with built-in tools for file operations, search, execution and web access. The doc states these built-in tools cover most coding tasks, so the extension layer is what you add beyond them.

nodes.label: CLAUDE.md
nodes.rationale: CLAUDE.md adds persistent context that Claude sees every session; its full content loads at session start and is present in every request. It is the place for project conventions, build commands, project structure and 'always do X' / 'never do X' rules, and it is the recommended first extension for new users.

nodes.label: Keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines
nodes.rationale: The doc's rule of thumb is to keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines; if it grows, move reference content into skills (which load on demand) or split it into .claude/rules/ files. Running /doctor produces trim proposals for a checked-in CLAUDE.md.

nodes.label: CLAUDE.md files are additive
nodes.rationale: When CLAUDE.md exists at multiple levels (managed, user, project, nested subdirectories) the files are additive: all levels contribute content to context simultaneously. Files from the working directory and above load at launch, subdirectories load as Claude works in them, and conflicts are reconciled by Claude's judgment with more specific instructions typically winning.

nodes.label: .claude/rules/ files
nodes.rationale: Rules files in .claude/rules/ load every session, or only when matching files are opened if they carry `paths` frontmatter. They exist to keep CLAUDE.md focused and are best for language-specific or directory-specific guidelines, saving context relative to always-on CLAUDE.md content.

nodes.label: Skills
nodes.rationale: A skill is a markdown file containing knowledge, workflows or instructions; the doc calls it the most flexible extension. Skills can be invoked with a command like /deploy or loaded automatically by Claude when relevant, and can run in the current conversation or in isolated context via subagents or `context: fork`.

nodes.label: Reference skills vs action skills
nodes.rationale: Skills come in two shapes: reference skills provide knowledge Claude uses throughout a session (such as an API style guide), while action skills tell Claude to do something specific (such as a /deploy skill that runs a deployment workflow).

nodes.label: Bundled skills
nodes.rationale: Claude Code ships bundled skills such as /code-review, /batch and /debug that work out of the box, in addition to the skills a user or plugin author creates.

nodes.label: disable-model-invocation frontmatter
nodes.rationale: Setting `disable-model-invocation: true` in a skill's frontmatter hides that skill from Claude entirely until the user invokes it manually; nothing loads until invocation, giving the skill zero context cost. The doc recommends it for skills with side effects so only the user triggers them.

nodes.label: skillOverrides setting
nodes.rationale: For a skill you did not write, the `skillOverrides` setting achieves the same visibility change as `disable-model-invocation: true` without editing the skill's own file.

nodes.label: Skill override priority
nodes.rationale: Skills override by name across levels: when the same skill name exists at multiple levels, one definition wins by priority managed > user > project. Plugin skills are namespaced so they do not enter this contest.

nodes.label: Code intelligence (LSP)
nodes.rationale: Code intelligence connects Claude to a language server for symbol-level navigation and live type errors. It loads diagnostics after file edits and symbol locations on lookup, and the LSP tool stays inactive until a code intelligence plugin for the language is installed.

nodes.label: MCP (Model Context Protocol)
nodes.rationale: MCP is the protocol that connects Claude to external services and tools, providing purpose-built tools and data access with connection and authentication handled by the server. At session start it loads tool names and server instructions; full JSON schemas stay deferred until a specific tool is needed.

nodes.label: MCP tool search
nodes.rationale: MCP tool search is on by default, which keeps idle MCP tools consuming minimal context. /mcp shows each server's connection status and /context all shows how many tokens each loaded MCP tool uses.

nodes.label: MCP scope precedence
nodes.rationale: MCP servers override by name with the precedence local > project > user, so a server defined at a narrower scope replaces the same-named one defined more broadly.

nodes.label: Subagents
nodes.rationale: Subagents are isolated workers that run their own loop in a separate context window with their own input and output tokens, returning only a summary to the conversation that spawned them. They suit tasks that read many files, parallel work and specialized workers, and keep intermediate output out of the main session.

nodes.label: Subagent skills preloading
nodes.rationale: In a subagent, skills do not load on demand: the skills listed in the subagent's `skills:` field are fully preloaded into its context at launch. Subagents can still discover and invoke unlisted project, user and plugin skills through the Skill tool.

nodes.label: Subagent scope priority
nodes.rationale: Subagents override by name with the precedence managed > CLI flag > project > user > plugin, a different order from the one that governs skills.

nodes.label: Forking the current conversation
nodes.rationale: A fork is a subagent variant in which Claude Code loads the parent's conversation so far, system prompt and tools instead of a fresh isolated context. A skill can also run in isolated context using `context: fork`.

nodes.label: Dynamic workflows
nodes.rationale: A dynamic workflow is a script Claude writes that runs many subagents in the background and returns one result. Use it when a job outgrows a handful of subagents or when you want findings cross-checked before you see them — a codebase-wide audit, a large migration, or a plan drafted from several angles.

nodes.label: Cross-session messaging
nodes.rationale: Cross-session messaging lets Claude deliver a message from one of your sessions to another, for sessions you run yourself that need each other's findings mid-task — for example one session warning another that a change it made breaks what the other is building on.

nodes.label: Hooks
nodes.rationale: A hook runs a shell command, HTTP request, MCP tool call, LLM prompt or subagent when Claude Code reaches a lifecycle event. Hooks execute outside the main conversation, load nothing by default, and are best for automation that must run on every matching event: linting after edits, blocking unsafe commands, logging, notifications.

nodes.label: Hook lifecycle events
nodes.rationale: Hooks fire at specific lifecycle events — tool execution (such as PreToolUse and PostToolUse), session boundaries (such as SessionStart), prompt submission, permission requests and compaction.

nodes.label: Hook determinism
nodes.rationale: A hook always fires on its event: the trigger is guaranteed. A skill, by contrast, is instructions Claude interprets, so its outcome can vary. Determinism is the axis on which the doc separates the two.

nodes.label: Put guardrails in hooks
nodes.rationale: An instruction like 'never edit .env' written in CLAUDE.md or a skill is a request, not a guarantee; a PreToolUse hook that blocks the edit is enforcement. The doc's rule is that if a rule must hold every time, it must be a hook rather than a prompt instruction.

nodes.label: Hook output lands in context
nodes.rationale: Hooks cost zero context unless they return output; when they do, that output is added as messages to the conversation. A PostToolUse hook running a linter feeds its results back as text Claude reads, which a /fix-lint skill can then tell Claude how to resolve.

nodes.label: Hooks merge across levels
nodes.rationale: Unlike skills, subagents and MCP servers, hooks do not override by name: all registered hooks fire for their matching events regardless of which level or source registered them.

nodes.label: Plugins
nodes.rationale: Plugins are the packaging layer: a plugin bundles skills, hooks, subagents and MCP servers into a single installable unit. Use one when the same setup must be reused across multiple repositories or distributed to others.

nodes.label: Plugin skill namespacing
nodes.rationale: Plugin skills are namespaced (for example /my-plugin:review) so that multiple plugins can coexist without their skill names colliding.

nodes.label: Plugin marketplaces
nodes.rationale: Marketplaces host and distribute collections of plugins; together with plugins they form the packaging and distribution layer for the other extension features.

nodes.label: Artifacts
nodes.rationale: An artifact publishes session output as a private, interactive web page, for output you want to see or share visually rather than as terminal text — for example an incident timeline that updates as Claude investigates.

nodes.label: Build your setup over time
nodes.rationale: You do not need to configure everything up front: each feature has a recognizable trigger, and most teams add them in roughly a fixed order as those triggers appear. The same triggers also tell you when to update what you already have — a repeated mistake is a CLAUDE.md edit, a workflow you keep tweaking by hand is a skill needing another revision.

nodes.label: How features layer
nodes.rationale: Features can be defined user-wide, per-project, via plugins, or through managed policies, and they resolve differently when the same feature exists at several levels: CLAUDE.md files are additive, skills/subagents/MCP servers override by name with per-feature priority orders, and hooks merge.

nodes.label: Feature combination patterns
nodes.rationale: Real setups combine extensions because each solves a different problem — CLAUDE.md always-on context, skills on-demand knowledge and workflows, MCP external connections, subagents isolation, hooks automation. The doc names four recurring combination patterns.

nodes.label: Pattern: Skill + MCP
nodes.rationale: MCP provides the connection while a skill teaches Claude how to use it well — for example MCP connects to your database and a skill documents your schema and query patterns.

nodes.label: Pattern: Skill + Subagent
nodes.rationale: A skill spawns subagents for parallel work — for example an /audit skill that kicks off security, performance and style subagents that each work in isolated context.

nodes.label: Pattern: CLAUDE.md + Skills
nodes.rationale: CLAUDE.md holds the always-on rules while skills hold reference material loaded on demand — for example CLAUDE.md says 'follow our API conventions' and a skill contains the full API style guide.

nodes.label: Pattern: Hook + MCP
nodes.rationale: A hook triggers external actions through MCP — for example a post-edit hook that sends a Slack notification when Claude modifies critical files.

nodes.label: Context costs of extensions
nodes.rationale: Every feature added consumes some of Claude's context. Too much can fill the context window and can also add noise that makes Claude less effective — skills may not trigger correctly, or Claude may lose track of conventions — so each feature's loading strategy and cost is a design trade-off.

nodes.label: Gateway (proxy between Claude Code and a provider)
nodes.rationale: A gateway is a proxy an organization runs between Claude Code and a model provider: Claude Code sends its API traffic to the gateway instead of directly to the provider, and the gateway forwards it using a credential the organization holds. Developers authenticate to the gateway rather than holding provider credentials.

nodes.label: Centralized auth, usage tracking, budgets and audit logging
nodes.rationale: Because developers authenticate to the gateway rather than holding provider credentials, authentication, usage tracking, budgets, and audit logging all happen in one place the organization controls. This centralization is the stated reason to run a gateway at all.

nodes.label: Gateway request flow
nodes.rationale: Each developer's Claude Code sends requests to the gateway's address and authenticates with a gateway-issued credential; the gateway authenticates the developer, applies the configured access and budget rules, and forwards the request to the provider with the organization's credential.

nodes.label: Developer credential
nodes.rationale: Each developer holds their own credential, issued by the gateway. It authenticates them to the gateway and identifies them in usage tracking.

nodes.label: Provider credential
nodes.rationale: The gateway holds one credential for the organization's provider account, shared by all forwarded traffic. Every request forwarded under it is charged to the account behind it.

nodes.label: Upstream model providers
nodes.rationale: The provider a gateway forwards to can be Anthropic's API or a cloud provider such as Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry. The gateway's configuration decides which one.

nodes.label: Changing provider without touching developer machines
nodes.rationale: With Claude apps gateway, or any other gateway that exposes a single Anthropic-format endpoint, changing the upstream provider does not require touching developer machines.

nodes.label: Claude apps gateway
nodes.rationale: Claude apps gateway is Anthropic's own self-hosted gateway, shipped inside the `claude` binary, so an organization need not adopt a separate gateway product. It routes to Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry, or the Anthropic API as the upstream.

nodes.label: Other (third-party) LLM gateways
nodes.rationale: An organization that already runs an LLM gateway or API gateway can point Claude Code at it instead of adopting Claude apps gateway. The separate 'Other LLM gateways' page carries the admin rollout checklist, what such a gateway must implement, and how to configure Claude Code for it.

nodes.label: Browser SSO sign-in via corporate IdP (/login)
nodes.rationale: Developers sign in to a Claude apps gateway with their corporate identity provider through `/login`. The sign-in is a browser SSO step, and there is no service-token flow.

nodes.label: Model access and managed settings enforced by IdP group
nodes.rationale: Claude apps gateway enforces model access and managed settings per identity-provider group, so policy follows the developer's IdP membership rather than their machine.

nodes.label: OTLP usage metrics to your own observability stack
nodes.rationale: Claude apps gateway emits OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) usage metrics to the organization's own observability stack.

nodes.label: Keeping forwarding rules current with each release
nodes.rationale: A separately maintained gateway needs its forwarding rules updated as the headers and request fields Claude Code sends change with each release. Claude apps gateway is built, tested and released alongside the CLI, so it already forwards those headers and fields and there is no list to keep current.

nodes.label: CI pipelines cannot authenticate through the gateway
nodes.rationale: Because sign-in is a browser SSO step with no service-token flow, a CI pipeline with no developer present to approve the sign-in cannot authenticate through Claude apps gateway; those pipelines must be configured against the provider directly.

nodes.label: Agent SDK and `claude -p` sessions on a signed-in machine
nodes.rationale: Agent SDK sessions and `claude -p` runs on a machine where a developer has already signed in use that machine's gateway session and are governed by its policies.

nodes.label: No endorsement, and no non-Claude models through any gateway
nodes.rationale: Anthropic does not endorse, maintain, or audit other gateway products, and does not support routing Claude Code to non-Claude models through any gateway.

nodes.label: Gateway traffic is billed at API rates, not to a subscription
nodes.rationale: When developers connect through a gateway with a gateway credential, usage is billed to the organization's provider account at API rates and their claude.ai subscriptions are neither used nor charged; the gateway credential turns off subscription login for that session.

nodes.label: ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN
nodes.rationale: Setting ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN for a gateway you run supplies the gateway credential and turns off subscription login for that session, so the traffic bills to the account behind the gateway's provider credential.

nodes.label: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL alone keeps the subscription active
nodes.rationale: The exception to gateway billing is setting only ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL with no gateway credential: requests still route through the gateway, but a saved claude.ai login stays the active credential, so the subscription's usage limits and billing apply.

nodes.label: Things configured separately from the gateway
nodes.rationale: A gateway routes model API requests only; several things an admin might expect it to handle are configured elsewhere — model selection, non-gateway network traffic, client telemetry and its destinations, and corporate HTTP proxies.

nodes.label: Model selection (/model and model env vars)
nodes.rationale: Which model answers is chosen with the `/model` command or the model environment variables, not by the gateway: the gateway decides where requests go, not which model the developer selects.

nodes.label: Per-group availableModels allowlist
nodes.rationale: Claude apps gateway can bound the model choice with a per-group `availableModels` allowlist, but the developer still picks within that bound.

nodes.label: Non-gateway traffic: version checks and downloads
nodes.rationale: Claude Code sends version checks and downloads directly to Anthropic, separate from the gateway path, so the network still needs egress to the required domains — or set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC to turn off the optional streams.

nodes.label: Client analytics disabled on Claude apps gateway sign-in
nodes.rationale: Claude Code disables its Anthropic-bound client analytics when a session signs in to a Claude apps gateway. Analytics sent before that sign-in are not covered by it.

nodes.label: DISABLE_TELEMETRY in client-side managed settings
nodes.rationale: To keep pre-sign-in startup analytics off as well, deliver DISABLE_TELEMETRY through the client-side managed settings on each device.

nodes.label: Client telemetry on other gateways depends on the provider
nodes.rationale: On a non-Anthropic gateway, whether Claude Code sends the optional client telemetry stream depends on the provider; the telemetry defaults table in the data-usage docs covers each case.

nodes.label: Telemetry destinations depend on how the session signed in
nodes.rationale: Where Claude Code sends a gateway session's telemetry depends on how that session signed in; the Claude apps gateway page's 'What's enforced on developers' section states where each kind of session's exports go.

nodes.label: Corporate HTTP proxy (HTTPS_PROXY)
nodes.rationale: An HTTPS_PROXY sits between Claude Code and every server it talks to, including the gateway, so a network that requires a proxy must configure the proxy in addition to the gateway.

nodes.label: Sign-in check that the proxy host is on a private network
nodes.rationale: For a self-hosted Claude apps gateway, sign-in checks that the proxy host is also on a private network before proceeding.

nodes.label: NO_PROXY exemption for the gateway host
nodes.rationale: If the proxy host is not on a private network, add the gateway host to NO_PROXY so the CLI connects to the gateway directly instead of through the proxy.

nodes.label: Claude Code glossary
nodes.rationale: The glossary defines Claude Code terminology, with each entry linking to the page that covers the concept in depth. Model-level concepts such as tokens, temperature and RAG live in the separate platform glossary, and Claude Desktop terms such as desktop extension, MCPB and DXT live in the Claude Help Center.

nodes.label: Agent teams
nodes.rationale: Agent teams are multiple independent Claude Code sessions coordinated by a team lead, sharing a task list and peer-to-peer messaging. Each teammate has its own context window and can be interacted with directly, unlike a subagent that reports only to its parent. The feature is experimental and disabled by default.

nodes.label: Agentic coding
