nodes.rationale: When an OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_* variable is set in managed settings, Claude Code removes conflicting developer-set variables at startup and logs a warning visible with --debug: a generic endpoint removes every developer per-signal endpoint, a generic protocol removes per-signal protocols, and a credential removes the per-signal credential plus every developer endpoint. This changes where telemetry is delivered, not what is collected.

nodes.label: Exporter selectors follow per-key precedence
nodes.rationale: OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER, OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER and the beta OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER are NOT force-removed by managed settings; a developer can still disable a signal or switch it to the console exporter, so administrators must set the selectors in managed settings too if they need them locked.

nodes.label: OTEL_* is not passed to subprocesses
nodes.rationale: Claude Code does not pass OTEL_* environment variables to the subprocesses it spawns, including the Bash tool, hooks, MCP servers and language servers, so an instrumented application run through Bash must be given the exporter variables directly.

nodes.label: Launcher-provided endpoints pin the destination
nodes.rationale: When the desktop app or a self-hosted environment runner launches Claude Code and names an OTLP endpoint in the environment it provides, the launcher's telemetry variables remove developer-set variables exactly as managed settings do, while variables the launcher itself set are kept. Requires v2.1.251 or later.

nodes.label: BETA_TRACING_ENDPOINT
nodes.rationale: With detailed beta tracing active, Claude Code exports logs and traces to BETA_TRACING_ENDPOINT instead of through the logs and traces exporters, so it is removed whenever managed settings decide either signal's destination. A metrics-only endpoint or credential does not remove it; before v2.1.251 a developer-set value redirected those signals even when managed settings pinned the collector.

nodes.label: mTLS client-certificate configuration
nodes.rationale: How client certificates are configured depends on the protocol in use for that signal: http/protobuf and http/json use CLAUDE_CODE_CLIENT_CERT / CLAUDE_CODE_CLIENT_KEY with NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS for the CA, while grpc uses OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_CLIENT_KEY / OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_CLIENT_CERTIFICATE with OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_CERTIFICATE.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_OTEL_CONTENT_MAX_LENGTH
nodes.rationale: Caps content-bearing attributes (model responses, tool content, system prompts, raw API bodies) at 61440 UTF-16 code units (60 KB) by default, sized for backends that cap attribute values at 64 KB. A lower OpenTelemetry SDK attribute limit wins, so the [TRUNCATED ...] marker stays within it. Requires v2.1.214 or later.

nodes.label: OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS
nodes.rationale: Disabled by default; only prompt LENGTH is recorded. Setting it to 1 includes verbatim prompt content on the user_prompt event and the interaction span's user_prompt attribute, which is otherwise <REDACTED>.

nodes.label: OTEL_LOG_ASSISTANT_RESPONSES
nodes.rationale: Controls whether assistant response text appears on assistant_response events (default disabled, requires v2.1.193+). When unset it falls back to the value of OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS, so it must be set explicitly to 0 to keep responses redacted while prompt logging is on.

nodes.label: OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS
nodes.rationale: Disabled by default; enabling it logs tool parameters and input arguments — Bash commands, MCP server and tool names, skill names, user-authored workflow names and tool input — plus custom/plugin/MCP command names on user_prompt events, and un-redacts third-party plugin and skill names.

nodes.label: OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT
nodes.rationale: Disabled by default; enabling it records tool input and output bodies as span events (a tool.output event on claude_code.tool), truncated at the content limit per attribute. It requires tracing to be active and can surface raw file contents from Read results and Bash output.

nodes.label: OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES
nodes.rationale: Emits the full Anthropic Messages API request and response JSON as api_request_body / api_response_body events. Bodies carry the entire conversation history, so enabling it implies consent to everything the prompt, tool-details and tool-content flags would reveal; =1 gives truncated inline bodies and file:<dir> writes untruncated bodies to disk with a body_ref pointer. Extended-thinking content is always redacted.

nodes.label: Metrics temporality preference
nodes.rationale: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_TEMPORALITY_PREFERENCE defaults to `delta`; set it to `cumulative` when the metrics backend expects cumulative temporality.

nodes.label: Metrics cardinality control
nodes.rationale: OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_SESSION_ID, _VERSION, _ACCOUNT_UUID, _ENTRYPOINT and _RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES decide which attributes are attached to metric datapoints. Lower cardinality generally means better performance and lower storage cost but less granular analysis.

nodes.label: Content-Length on HTTP OTLP exports
nodes.rationale: For the http/protobuf and http/json protocols Claude Code sends each export request with a Content-Length header. Between v2.1.191 and v2.1.212 it used chunked transfer encoding, which Azure Monitor and other length-requiring endpoints rejected with 411 or 400 errors.

nodes.label: Distributed tracing (beta)
nodes.rationale: Tracing exports spans linking each user prompt to the API requests and tool executions it triggers, so a full request is viewable as one trace. It is off by default and requires both CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 and CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA=1, reusing the common OTLP endpoint, protocol, headers and mTLS configuration.

nodes.label: Span hierarchy
nodes.rationale: Each user prompt starts a claude_code.interaction root span whose children are claude_code.llm_request, claude_code.hook and claude_code.tool. A tool span has two children of its own — blocked_on_user for the permission wait and execution for the tool body — and an Agent/Task subagent's API and tool spans nest under the parent tool span.

nodes.label: Span attributes and status
nodes.rationale: Every span carries the standard attributes plus a span.type attribute matching its name. The llm_request, tool.execution and hook spans set OpenTelemetry status ERROR when they record a failure; all other spans end with status UNSET.

nodes.label: claude_code.hook span
nodes.rationale: The hook span appears only under DETAILED beta tracing, which requires ENABLE_BETA_TRACING_DETAILED=1 plus BETA_TRACING_ENDPOINT set in the shell, user settings or managed settings — both are ignored in project and local settings, and CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA alone does not produce it. Interactive CLI sessions additionally need the organization allowlisted; SDK and -p sessions do not.

nodes.label: Outbound W3C traceparent propagation
nodes.rationale: With tracing active, Bash and PowerShell subprocesses inherit a TRACEPARENT variable carrying the active tool execution span's context, and model requests plus outbound HTTP MCP requests carry a traceparent header with the API's traceresponse recorded as a span link. It is sent only when ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is unset or points at the Anthropic API, unless CLAUDE_CODE_PROPAGATE_TRACEPARENT=1 is set.

nodes.label: Inbound trace context in SDK and -p sessions
nodes.rationale: In Agent SDK and non-interactive -p sessions Claude Code reads TRACEPARENT and TRACESTATE from its own environment so its interaction span becomes a child of the caller's trace; interactive sessions deliberately ignore inbound TRACEPARENT to avoid inheriting ambient CI or container values. The same context also stamps trace_id/span_id onto OTLP event records even with no traces exporter configured.

nodes.label: Deferred tool calls rejoin the original trace
nodes.rationale: When a PreToolUse hook defers a tool call, Claude Code saves the deferring turn's trace context; when the session resumes and the tool re-runs, the tool's spans join that earlier turn's trace as children of its claude_code.interaction span.

nodes.label: otelHeadersHelper dynamic headers
nodes.rationale: For enterprises needing dynamic authentication, the `otelHeadersHelper` setting names an executable or shell command that must print valid JSON of string header key-value pairs. It applies only to http/protobuf and http/json; with grpc only the static headers variables are used, and failures are reported in /status, the debug log and stderr under -p.

nodes.label: Headers helper refresh interval
nodes.rationale: The headers helper script runs at startup and periodically thereafter to support token refresh, every 29 minutes by default, tunable via CLAUDE_CODE_OTEL_HEADERS_HELPER_DEBOUNCE_MS (default 1740000 ms).

nodes.label: OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES multi-team support
nodes.rationale: Custom key=value attributes such as department, team.id and cost_center are attached to every metric datapoint and event record in addition to the OTLP resource block, enabling per-team filtering, cost-center tracking and team dashboards. Custom keys never override standard attributes: on a collision the built-in value wins.

nodes.label: OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES formatting rules
nodes.rationale: The variable takes strictly comma-separated key=value pairs of US-ASCII characters excluding control characters, whitespace, double quotes, commas, semicolons and backslashes; spaces are invalid and must be replaced with underscores/camelCase or percent-encoded. Wrapping a value in quotes does not escape a space — the quotes become part of the literal value.

nodes.label: Standard attributes on all metrics and events
nodes.rationale: Every metric and event carries session.id, app.version, app.entrypoint, organization.id, user.account_uuid, user.account_id, user.id, user.email, terminal.type and the OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES keys. user.id is a random anonymous identifier generated on first run and persisted in ~/.claude.json, containing no personal information and not derived from the Claude account.

nodes.label: Claude apps gateway identity stamping
nodes.rationale: On a Claude apps gateway session the CLI stamps exports with the authenticated IdP identity: user.id is the IdP subject rather than an installation identifier, user.email is the signed-in email, user.groups carries IdP group membership, and identity.source is gateway-oidc. Gateway identity is applied last, so user.* and identity.* keys set via OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES are ignored.

nodes.label: Event-only attributes
nodes.rationale: prompt.id, workspace.host_paths, workflow.run_id and workflow.name are attached to events but never to metrics, because on metrics they would cause unbounded cardinality.

nodes.label: Exported metrics catalog
nodes.rationale: Claude Code exports eight metrics: session.count, lines_of_code.count, pull_request.count, commit.count, cost.usage (USD), token.usage (tokens), code_edit_tool.decision and active_time.total (s). Count metrics carry no OpenTelemetry unit string.

nodes.label: Prometheus-only exports omit units
nodes.rationale: When prometheus is the ONLY exporter listed in OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER, Claude Code omits the USD, tokens and s units so the scrape stays valid Prometheus text format; metric names are unchanged and combined configurations such as otlp,prometheus keep the units. Before v2.1.216 the scrape included OpenMetrics-only # UNIT lines some scrapers rejected.

nodes.label: Session counter metric
nodes.rationale: claude_code.session.count is incremented at the start of each session and carries start_type of fresh, resume, continue or agents_view. The agents_view value identifies the `claude agents` dashboard process — a local UI launch rather than a conversational session — so dashboards can filter it out.

nodes.label: Lines of code counter metric
nodes.rationale: claude_code.lines_of_code.count is incremented when code is added or removed, carrying type (added/removed) and, from v2.1.172, the model identifier that made the change.

nodes.label: Cost counter metric
nodes.rationale: claude_code.cost.usage is incremented after each API request and carries model, query_source (main/subagent/auxiliary), speed, effort, and the attribution set agent.name, skill.name, plugin.name, marketplace.name, mcp_server.name and mcp_tool.name. It is the metric used to attribute spend to specific skills, plugins or subagent types.

nodes.label: Token counter metric
nodes.rationale: claude_code.token.usage is incremented after each API request with type of input, output, cacheRead or cacheCreation, plus model, query_source, speed, effort and the same skill/plugin/agent/MCP attribution attributes defined on the cost counter.

nodes.label: Code edit tool decision counter
nodes.rationale: claude_code.code_edit_tool.decision is incremented when a user accepts or rejects Edit, Write or NotebookEdit usage, carrying tool_name, decision, the decision source, and the programming language of the edited file (unknown for unrecognized extensions).

nodes.label: Active time counter metric
nodes.rationale: claude_code.active_time.total tracks time actively spent using Claude Code, excluding idle time, with type 'user' for keyboard interactions and 'cli' for tool execution and AI response generation.

nodes.label: Third-party name redaction policy
nodes.rationale: Built-in, bundled and official-marketplace skill, plugin, agent and workflow names appear verbatim, while user-authored and third-party names are replaced with placeholders such as custom, custom_skill or third-party unless OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 is set. This protects third-party names from appearing in logs by default.

nodes.label: plugin_id_hash
nodes.rationale: A deterministic hash of the plugin name and marketplace, sent only to the configured exporter, that lets a fleet count distinct third-party plugins without recording their names. For plugins synced from claude.ai the hash uses the marketplace name claude.ai reports, or 'synced' otherwise.

nodes.label: Exported events catalog
nodes.rationale: Claude Code exports its event stream via the OpenTelemetry logs/events protocol whenever OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER is configured. Every event carries the standard attributes plus event.name, an ISO 8601 event.timestamp and event.sequence, a monotonically increasing counter ordering events within a session.

nodes.label: Event correlation attributes
nodes.rationale: prompt.id is a UUID v4 linking every event produced while processing one user prompt; message.uuid matches the transcript entry (v2.1.214+); client_request_id is the client-generated x-client-request-id that pairs a request with its response even for timeouts that never produced a server request_id.

nodes.label: Transcript joins are version-specific
nodes.rationale: message.uuid, request_id and tool_use_id each match a field in the session transcript, but the transcript entry format is internal to Claude Code and changes between versions, so a pipeline joining on those fields can break on any release and the joins must be treated as version-specific rather than a stable contract.

nodes.label: claude_code.user_prompt event
nodes.rationale: Logged when a user submits a prompt, carrying prompt_length, the redacted-by-default prompt, message.uuid, command_name and command_source. Built-in and bundled command names emit as-is while custom, plugin and MCP command names collapse to custom or mcp unless OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1.

nodes.label: claude_code.assistant_response event
nodes.rationale: Logged after each API request returning text content (v2.1.193+), covering only the response's text blocks — thinking and tool-use blocks are excluded. It carries response_length, the redacted-by-default response, model, request_id, message.uuid and query_source.

nodes.label: claude_code.tool_result event
nodes.rationale: Logged when a tool completes execution and never for a rejected call. It carries tool_name, tool_use_id, success, duration_ms, error_type, decision_type (always accept), decision_source, tool_input_size_bytes, tool_result_size_bytes and mcp_server_scope, plus tool_parameters and tool_input when OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1.

nodes.label: claude_code.tool_decision event
nodes.rationale: Logged when a tool permission decision is made, carrying tool_name, tool_use_id, decision, tool_source (builtin, mcp, or sdk_host_builtin_mcp) and source. It is the only place a REJECTED call is recorded, and with OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 its tool_parameters shows which command was rejected.

nodes.label: Permission decision source values
nodes.rationale: source is one of config (decided automatically from settings, flags, permission mode or an inherently safe tool — and also when a permission-prompt request itself fails), hook, user_permanent, user_temporary, user_abort or user_reject. In the interactive CLI a saved rule's later matches emit config, whereas SDK and -p sessions re-emit user_permanent/user_temporary.

nodes.label: claude_code.api_request event
nodes.rationale: Logged for each API request to Claude with model, cost_usd, cost_usd_micros, duration_ms, input/output/cache_read/cache_creation tokens, request_id, client_request_id, speed, query_source, effort and the skill/plugin/agent/MCP attribution attributes.

nodes.label: claude_code.api_error event
nodes.rationale: Logged when an API request to Claude fails, carrying error, status_code (absent for non-HTTP errors), duration_ms, attempt (total attempts including the initial request), request_id, client_request_id, speed, query_source and effort.

nodes.label: claude_code.api_refusal event
nodes.rationale: Logged when a request returns stop_reason 'refusal'. Because refusals arrive on a successful response stream rather than as an HTTP error, api_error does not fire for them. It carries server_fallback_hop, has_category, has_explanation, and — only with OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 — the category value (cyber, bio, frontier_llm, reasoning_extraction).

nodes.label: api_request_body and api_response_body events
nodes.rationale: Emitted only when OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES is set: one request-body event per attempt (so retries each produce their own) and one response-body event per successful response. Each carries body or body_ref, body_length, body_truncated, model and query_source.

nodes.label: claude_code.permission_mode_changed event
nodes.rationale: Logged when the permission mode changes, carrying from_mode, to_mode and trigger (shift_tab, exit_plan_mode, auto_gate_denied or auto_opt_in; absent for SDK or bridge transitions). It is the signal a SIEM uses to detect permission-mode escalation.

nodes.label: claude_code.auth event
nodes.rationale: Logged when /login or /logout completes, carrying action, success, auth_method, a categorical error_category and status_code. The raw error message is never included.

nodes.label: claude_code.mcp_server_connection event
nodes.rationale: Logged when an MCP server connects, disconnects or fails, carrying status, transport_type, server_scope, duration_ms, error_code, is_plugin, plugin_id_hash and plugin.name. server_name and the full error message appear only with OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1.

nodes.label: claude_code.internal_error event
nodes.rationale: Logged when Claude Code catches an unexpected internal error, recording only the error class name and an errno-style code — never the message or stack trace. It is not emitted against Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Microsoft Foundry, or when DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING is set.

nodes.label: claude_code.plugin_installed event
nodes.rationale: Logged when a plugin finishes installing from either the `claude plugin install` CLI command or the interactive /plugin UI, carrying marketplace.is_official, install.trigger (cli or ui), plugin.name, plugin.version and marketplace.name.

nodes.label: claude_code.plugin_loaded event
nodes.rationale: Logged once per enabled plugin at session start to inventory which plugins are active across a fleet, carrying plugin.name, marketplace.name, plugin.version, plugin.scope, enabled_via, plugin_id_hash, has_hooks, has_mcp, host_owned_mcp, the skill/command/agent path counts and safe_mode.

nodes.label: claude_code.skill_activated event
nodes.rationale: Logged when a skill is invoked, whether Claude calls it through the Skill tool or a user runs it as a / command, carrying skill.name, invocation_trigger (user-slash, claude-proactive or nested-skill), skill.source, skill.kind and the owning plugin and marketplace names.

nodes.label: claude_code.at_mention event
nodes.rationale: Logged when Claude Code resolves an @-mention, carrying mention_type (file, directory, agent, mcp_resource or peer) and success. Not every mention emits one: early-exit paths such as permission denials, oversized files, PDF reference attachments and directory listing failures return without logging.

nodes.label: claude_code.api_retries_exhausted event
nodes.rationale: Logged once when an API request fails after more than one attempt, alongside the final api_error event, carrying model, the final error, status_code, total_attempts, total_retry_duration_ms and speed.

nodes.label: claude_code.hook_registered event
nodes.rationale: Logged once per configured hook at session start to inventory active hooks across a fleet, carrying hook_event, hook_type (command, prompt, mcp_tool, http or agent), hook_source, safe_mode, and — with OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 — hook_matcher, plus plugin.name and plugin_id_hash for plugin hooks.

nodes.label: Hook execution start and complete events
nodes.rationale: hook_execution_start fires when hooks begin for a hook event and hook_execution_complete when they all finish, the latter reporting num_hooks, num_success, num_blocking, num_non_blocking_error, num_cancelled and total_duration_ms. hook_definitions appears only when BOTH detailed beta tracing and OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 are enabled.

nodes.label: claude_code.hook_plugin_metrics event
nodes.rationale: Logged when an official-marketplace plugin hook emits per-invocation metrics — third-party marketplace plugins and user-configured hooks cannot emit it. It carries plugin_id in <name>@<marketplace> form, hook_event, and up to 20 plugin-emitted boolean or numeric keys matching ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,39}$.

nodes.label: claude_code.compaction event
nodes.rationale: Logged when conversation compaction completes, carrying trigger (auto or manual), success, duration_ms, pre_tokens, post_tokens, error, and precompute_reuse — which on manual /compact records whether the background-prepared summary was reused (hit) or why it was not (miss_custom_instructions, miss_hook, miss_not_ready).

nodes.label: claude_code.subagent_completed event
nodes.rationale: Logged when a subagent returns its result, carrying agent_type, agent.source, is_built_in, is_async, total_tokens, total_tool_uses, duration_ms, model, final_model and model_swapped. total_tokens covers only the FINAL request's footprint, not a sum across the run, so token and cost rollups must use the counters filtered to query_source 'subagent'.

nodes.label: claude_code.feedback_survey event
nodes.rationale: Logged when a session quality survey is shown or answered, carrying event_type (appeared, responded, transcript_prompt_appeared), appearance_id linking one survey instance, survey_type, response, and enabled_via_override — a boolean confirming CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FEEDBACK_SURVEY_FOR_OTEL is applied across a fleet.

nodes.label: claude_code.retention_sweep event
nodes.rationale: Logged once per run of the retention cleanup sweep that deletes transcripts and application data older than cleanupPeriodDays. It runs at most once per session in the background, is delayed at least 10 minutes if any session on the machine swept in the last 24 hours, and is skipped entirely under `claude -p --bare`. Requires v2.1.227 or later.

nodes.label: Retention sweep skip reasons
nodes.rationale: When Claude Code cannot safely determine the retention period it pauses the sweep and reports result 'skipped' with a skip_reason of user_source_disabled, settings_unknowable or settings_invalid_key_set. A managed cleanupPeriodDays pins the period so the sweep still runs even when a lower-priority settings file is broken.

nodes.label: Retention sweep counters are floors
nodes.rationale: The deletion counters are present only when result is 'complete'. artifacts_deleted counts a whole removed directory tree as one item, files_retained_fresh is counted only by per-file sweeps, and files_past_cutoff above zero means files outlived retention while zero is NOT proof none did, because a failed directory removal counts toward error_count instead.

nodes.label: Cost metrics are approximations
nodes.rationale: Cost metrics are approximations; official billing data comes from the API provider — Claude Console, Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud's Agent Platform — rather than from telemetry.

nodes.label: Streaming usage counted exactly once
nodes.rationale: Claude Code counts each streaming response toward the cost and token metrics exactly once, including when a gateway or proxy behind ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL streams usage progressively across multiple frames. Before v2.1.214 such multi-frame streams inflated cost.usage and token.usage by roughly one extra full request per extra frame.

nodes.label: Per-model commit breakdown requires a join
nodes.rationale: Because one session can span multiple models, per-model breakdowns of commits can only be approximated by joining against the token or cost metrics on session.id, filtered to query_source 'main' so auxiliary and subagent requests do not attribute the session's commits to a model that did not make them.

nodes.label: Detecting retry exhaustion
nodes.rationale: Claude Code retries failed requests internally and emits one api_error only after giving up, so that event is the terminal signal. attempt equals one more than the effective retry limit — 11 by default and never more than 16 unless CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG is set — while a lower value indicates a non-retryable error such as a 400.

nodes.label: OpenTelemetry events as audit data
nodes.rationale: OpenTelemetry events are the audit data source for Claude Code activity: every event carries identity attributes tying tool calls, MCP activity and permission decisions back to the triggering user, and the OTLP logs exporter can deliver them to any SIEM with an OTLP receiver or to a Collector that forwards to one.

nodes.label: Attributing actions to users
nodes.rationale: MCP tool calls, Bash commands and file edits are attributed to the developer who started the session; Claude Code does not act under a separate service account. With a direct API key or on Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Microsoft Foundry there is no Claude account, so only user.id and session.id are populated and identity must be attached manually via OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES.

nodes.label: Auditing MCP activity
nodes.rationale: Full MCP call detail requires the logs exporter plus OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1, after which mcp_server_connection, tool_result and tool_decision carry server name, tool name and call arguments. Without the flag those events keep scope, tool_source, is_plugin and plugin_id_hash but redact tool_name to the literal 'mcp_tool' for user-configured servers and omit argument content.

nodes.label: Mapping security signals to events
nodes.rationale: Detection rules map a signal to an event and attributes: tool_decision for allow/deny, permission_mode_changed for escalation, hook_execution_complete for a policy hook block, auth for login failures, mcp_server_connection for server failures, plugin_installed for plugin provenance, and tool_result/tool_decision with tool details for commands run and files touched.

nodes.label: Claude Code emits the raw event stream only
nodes.rationale: Anomaly detection, baselining, correlation across sessions and alerting are the responsibility of the SIEM or observability backend; Claude Code emits the raw event stream and nothing more.

nodes.label: Sending events to a SIEM
nodes.rationale: Point OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_LOGS_ENDPOINT at the SIEM's OTLP receiver or a Collector that forwards to its native ingest API. The documented managed-settings example exports events only, with OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 for MCP and Bash auditing, and is confirmed by looking for claude_code.user_prompt in the SIEM.

nodes.label: Backend choice determines possible analyses
nodes.rationale: Time series databases suit rate calculations, columnar stores suit complex queries and unique-user analysis, log aggregation systems suit full-text event search, and distributed tracing systems suit span visualization and latency analysis. DAU/WAU/MAU reporting needs a backend with efficient unique-value queries.

nodes.label: Service resource attributes
nodes.rationale: All exports carry service.name — claude-code for terminal sessions and claude-code-desktop for sessions started from the Claude Desktop Code tab — plus service.version, os.type, os.version, host.arch, an optional wsl.version, and the meter name com.anthropic.claude_code. Dashboards filtering on service.name = claude-code must add claude-code-desktop to also capture Code tab telemetry.

nodes.label: Security and privacy posture
nodes.rationale: OpenTelemetry export to your backend is opt-in and requires explicit configuration; raw file contents and code snippets are never included in metrics or events, and all OTEL data goes only to the endpoint you configure, never to Anthropic. user.email is included when authenticated via OAuth, so organizations concerned about it must filter or redact it in the backend.

nodes.label: Claude Code ROI Measurement Guide
nodes.rationale: A separate repository, anthropics/claude-code-monitoring-guide, provides ready-to-use Docker Compose configurations, Prometheus and OpenTelemetry setups, and templates for productivity reports integrated with tools like Linear.

nodes.label: Monitoring on Amazon Bedrock
nodes.rationale: Detailed usage-monitoring guidance for Claude Code on Amazon Bedrock lives in the aws-solutions-library-samples guidance-for-claude-code-with-amazon-bedrock repository's MONITORING.md, outside this page.

nodes.label: Claude Code
nodes.rationale: Claude Code is an agentic, AI-powered coding tool that reads your codebase, edits files, runs commands, and integrates with your development tools. It understands an entire codebase and can work across multiple files and tools to build features, fix bugs, and automate development tasks.

nodes.label: Claude Code surfaces
nodes.rationale: Claude Code runs on several surfaces: the terminal, IDE extensions, a desktop app, and the web. Most surfaces require a Claude subscription or an Anthropic Console account.

nodes.label: Terminal CLI surface
nodes.rationale: The full-featured CLI for working with Claude Code directly in the terminal: edit files, run commands, and manage an entire project from the command line. After installing, you `cd` into a project and run `claude`.

nodes.label: VS Code extension surface
nodes.rationale: The VS Code extension provides inline diffs, @-mentions, plan review, and conversation history directly in the editor. It installs for VS Code or Cursor, or from the Extensions view, and is opened via the Command Palette.

nodes.label: Desktop app surface
nodes.rationale: A standalone app for running Claude Code outside an IDE or terminal: review diffs visually, run multiple sessions side by side, schedule recurring tasks, and kick off cloud sessions. Available for macOS, Windows x64/ARM64, and in beta on Ubuntu/Debian via apt.

nodes.label: Web surface
nodes.rationale: Claude Code runs in the browser at claude.ai/code with no local setup, for kicking off long-running tasks, working on repos you do not have locally, or running multiple tasks in parallel. Available on desktop browsers and via the Claude app for iOS and Android.

nodes.label: JetBrains plugin surface
nodes.rationale: A plugin for IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, and other JetBrains IDEs with interactive diff viewing and selection context sharing. It is installed from the JetBrains Marketplace and requires the Claude Code CLI to be installed separately.

nodes.label: Claude mobile app
nodes.rationale: The Claude app for iOS and Android runs Claude Code on the web surface from a phone, and is a destination for continuing a task started locally (`claude --cloud`).

nodes.label: Shared Claude Code engine
nodes.rationale: Each surface connects to the same underlying Claude Code engine, so a repo's CLAUDE.md files, settings, and MCP servers work identically across all of them.

nodes.label: Native install script
nodes.rationale: The recommended install method: `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash` on macOS/Linux/WSL, `irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex` in Windows PowerShell, and an install.cmd download in Windows CMD. Shell-mismatch errors (`&&` not a valid statement separator, `irm` not recognized) tell you which Windows shell you are actually in.

nodes.label: Background auto-update
nodes.rationale: Native installations automatically update in the background to keep the user on the latest version.

nodes.label: Homebrew cask install
nodes.rationale: `brew install --cask claude-code` installs via Homebrew, which offers two casks: `claude-code` tracks the stable channel (typically about a week behind, skipping releases with major regressions) and `claude-code@latest` tracks the latest channel and receives new versions as soon as they ship.

nodes.label: WinGet install
nodes.rationale: `winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode` installs Claude Code on Windows via WinGet.

nodes.label: Linux package-manager install
nodes.rationale: Claude Code can also be installed with apt, dnf, or apk on Debian, Fedora, RHEL, and Alpine.

nodes.label: Manual update requirement
nodes.rationale: Package-manager installations do not auto-update: Homebrew users must run `brew upgrade claude-code` (or `claude-code@latest`) and WinGet users `winget upgrade Anthropic.ClaudeCode` periodically to get the latest features and security fixes.

nodes.label: Git for Windows
nodes.rationale: Git for Windows is recommended on native Windows installs. WSL setups do not need it.

nodes.label: Windows shell tool selection
nodes.rationale: On native Windows, Claude Code uses the Bash tool when Git for Windows is installed; if it is not installed, Claude Code falls back to PowerShell as the shell tool.

nodes.label: First-use login prompt
nodes.rationale: Running `claude` for the first time prompts the user to log in before any work begins.

nodes.label: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY approval path
nodes.rationale: If the `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` environment variable is set, Claude Code skips the login prompt and instead asks the user to approve the key.

nodes.label: Subscription / Console account requirement
nodes.rationale: Most surfaces require a Claude subscription or an Anthropic Console account; the desktop app requires a paid subscription, and both `claude --teleport` and the `/desktop` handoff require a claude.ai subscription.

nodes.label: Third-party provider support
nodes.rationale: The Terminal CLI, VS Code, and JetBrains surfaces also support third-party providers, an alternative to a Claude subscription or Console account.

nodes.label: Automating deferred chores
nodes.rationale: Claude Code handles tedious tasks: writing tests for untested code, fixing lint errors across a project, resolving merge conflicts, updating dependencies, and writing release notes — e.g. `claude "write tests for the auth module, run them, and fix any failures"`.

nodes.label: Feature building and bug fixing
nodes.rationale: Described in plain language, Claude Code plans the approach, writes code across multiple files, and verifies it works. For bugs, it traces the issue through the codebase from an error message or symptom, identifies the root cause, and implements a fix.

nodes.label: Git commits and pull requests
nodes.rationale: Claude Code works directly with git: it stages changes, writes commit messages, creates branches, and opens pull requests, e.g. `claude "commit my changes with a descriptive message"`.

nodes.label: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
nodes.rationale: MCP is an open standard for connecting AI tools to external data sources. Through MCP, Claude Code can read design docs in Google Drive, update Jira tickets, pull data from Slack, or use custom tooling.

nodes.label: Instructions, skills, and hooks customization
nodes.rationale: Claude Code is customized through three mechanisms grouped together in the docs: persistent instructions (CLAUDE.md plus auto memory), packaged repeatable workflows (skills), and shell commands run around Claude Code actions (hooks).

nodes.label: CLAUDE.md project instructions
nodes.rationale: CLAUDE.md is a markdown file added to a project root that Claude Code reads at the start of every session; it carries coding standards, architecture decisions, preferred libraries, and review checklists.

nodes.label: Auto memory
nodes.rationale: Claude also builds auto memory as it works, saving learnings across sessions without the user writing anything — in contrast to CLAUDE.md, which the user authors.

nodes.label: Skills
nodes.rationale: Skills package repeatable workflows that a team can share, invoked like `/review-pr` or `/deploy-staging`.

nodes.label: Hooks
nodes.rationale: Hooks run shell commands before or after Claude Code actions — for example auto-formatting after every file edit, or running lint before a commit.

nodes.label: Parallel sub-agents
nodes.rationale: Multiple Claude Code agents can be spawned to work on different parts of a task simultaneously, with a lead agent that coordinates the work, assigns subtasks, and merges results.

nodes.label: Background agents (agent view)
nodes.rationale: Background agents run several full Claude Code sessions in parallel and let the user watch them all from one screen.

nodes.label: Agent SDK
nodes.rationale: For fully custom workflows, the Agent SDK lets developers build their own agents powered by Claude Code's tools and capabilities, with full control over orchestration, tool access, and permissions.

nodes.label: CLI composability and scripting
nodes.rationale: Claude Code is composable and follows the Unix philosophy: logs can be piped into it, it can run in CI, and it chains with other tools via `claude -p` — e.g. `tail -200 app.log | claude -p "Slack me if you see any anomalies"` or `git diff main --name-only | claude -p "review these changed files for security issues"`.

nodes.label: Scheduled recurring tasks
nodes.rationale: Claude can run on a schedule to automate repeating work: morning PR reviews, overnight CI failure analysis, weekly dependency audits, or syncing docs after PRs merge. Three mechanisms serve this: Routines, Desktop scheduled tasks, and `/loop`.

nodes.label: Routines (cloud schedules)
nodes.rationale: Routines run in the cloud, so they keep running even when the user's computer is off. They can also trigger on API calls or GitHub events, and are created from the web, the Desktop app, or by running `/schedule` in the CLI.

nodes.label: Desktop scheduled tasks
nodes.rationale: Desktop scheduled tasks run on the user's own machine, with direct access to local files and tools.

nodes.label: /loop in-session repetition
nodes.rationale: `/loop` repeats a prompt within a CLI session for quick polling — the lightest of the three scheduling mechanisms, bounded to the current session.

nodes.label: Session portability across surfaces
nodes.rationale: Sessions are not tied to a single surface: work can be moved between terminal, desktop, web, phone, and team chat as the user's context changes.

nodes.label: Remote Control
nodes.rationale: Remote Control lets a user step away from their desk and keep working on a local session from a phone or any browser — the recommended option for continuing a local session from another device.

nodes.label: Dispatch
nodes.rationale: Dispatch accepts a task messaged from a phone and creates a Desktop session the user can then open.

nodes.label: claude --teleport
nodes.rationale: A long-running task kicked off on the web or the Claude mobile app can be pulled into the terminal with `claude --teleport`. Teleport requires a claude.ai subscription.

nodes.label: /desktop handoff
nodes.rationale: Running `/desktop` continues the current terminal session in the Desktop app, where diffs can be reviewed visually. The handoff requires a claude.ai subscription and is available on macOS and x64 Windows.

nodes.label: Slack integration
nodes.rationale: Tasks can be routed from team chat: mentioning `@Claude` in Slack with a bug report returns a pull request.

nodes.label: Channels
nodes.rationale: Channels is the option for pushing events from Telegram, Discord, iMessage, or a user's own webhooks into a Claude Code session.

nodes.label: GitHub Actions integration
nodes.rationale: In CI, GitHub Actions is one of the two named ways to automate code review and issue triage with Claude Code.

nodes.label: GitLab CI/CD integration
nodes.rationale: GitLab CI/CD is the other named CI path for automating code review and issue triage with Claude Code.

nodes.label: GitHub Code Review
nodes.rationale: GitHub Code Review is the named option for getting automatic code review on every pull request.

nodes.label: Chrome integration
nodes.rationale: The Chrome integration is the named option for debugging live web applications with Claude Code.

nodes.label: Automated code review and triage
nodes.rationale: Automating PR review and issue triage is a named use case, served by GitHub Actions or GitLab CI/CD in CI, and by GitHub Code Review for automatic review on every PR.

nodes.label: Dynamic workflows
nodes.rationale: The 'A harness for every task' article describes how the Claude Code team uses dynamic workflows to orchestrate many subagents at once; it is listed as a next step after installation.

nodes.label: Permission mode
nodes.rationale: A permission mode sets which actions Claude can take in a session without asking the user first. Modes set the baseline, on top of which permission rules (allow/ask/deny) are layered; a running session's mode can be changed at any time via the CLI Shift+Tab cycle, the VS Code mode indicator, or the Desktop mode selector.

nodes.label: Manual mode (config value `default`)
nodes.rationale: The mode that reviews every action: only reads run without asking, and Claude stops before most file edits, shell commands, and network access. Its config value is `default` (what hooks and SDK integrations use) while the UI label is Manual; the CLI accepts `manual` as an alias from v2.1.200 onward, and the status bar shows `⏸ manual mode on`.

nodes.label: acceptEdits mode
nodes.rationale: acceptEdits lets Claude create and edit files in the working directory without prompting, and also auto-approves the common filesystem Bash commands `mkdir`, `touch`, `rm`, `rmdir`, `mv`, `cp`, and `sed` (including behind safe env prefixes like `LANG=C` or wrappers like `timeout`/`nice`/`nohup`). Auto-approval applies only inside the working directory or `additionalDirectories`; everything else still prompts.

nodes.label: Plan mode
nodes.rationale: Plan mode tells Claude to research and propose changes without making them: it reads files, runs exploratory shell commands, and writes a plan, but edits stay blocked until the plan is approved — except in sessions where bypass permissions are available, where the blocks are not enforced. Enter it with Shift+Tab, a `/plan` prompt prefix, or `claude --permission-mode plan`.

nodes.label: Auto mode
nodes.rationale: Auto mode lets Claude execute without routine permission prompts because a separate classifier model reviews actions before they run instead of the user. It is the built-in starting permission mode on Pro, Max, and Team plans, and it nudges Claude to keep working rather than stopping for clarifying questions. The docs warn it reduces prompts but does not guarantee safety.

nodes.label: dontAsk mode
nodes.rationale: In dontAsk mode Claude Code auto-denies every tool call that would otherwise prompt, so the session never waits for input: only `permissions.allow` matches, built-in read-only Bash commands, and PreToolUse-hook-approved calls run. It is intended for CI pipelines and restricted environments with a pre-defined allowlist, and it never appears in the Shift+Tab cycle — it must be set with `--permission-mode dontAsk`.

nodes.label: bypassPermissions mode
nodes.rationale: bypassPermissions disables permission prompts and safety checks so tool calls execute immediately, including writes to protected paths; `--dangerously-skip-permissions` is equivalent. It cannot be entered from a session that did not start with it enabled, offers no protection against prompt injection, and is documented for isolated containers, VMs, or dev containers only.

nodes.label: Auto-mode classifier model
nodes.rationale: The classifier is a separate model that reviews actions before they run in auto mode, blocking anything that escalates beyond the user's request, targets unrecognized infrastructure, or appears driven by hostile content Claude read. It also reviews SendMessage traffic to other agents (v2.1.222+) and `rm`/`rmdir` removals targeting critical paths, including removals hidden inside command or process substitution.

nodes.label: Auto mode availability requirements
nodes.rationale: Auto mode requires all of: any plan; the organization not setting `permissions.disableAutoMode` to "disable"; a supported model (Opus 4.6+/Sonnet 4.6+/a Fable model on the Anthropic API and Claude Platform on AWS, but only Sonnet 5, Opus 4.7+ and Fable models on Bedrock, Agent Platform, Foundry and gateway sessions — Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, Haiku and claude-3 are unsupported everywhere); and a supported provider. Anthropic can also turn it off server-side, and a session that got that answer keeps auto mode off until it ends.

nodes.label: Protected paths
nodes.rationale: A small set of paths whose writes are never auto-approved except in bypassPermissions and in planning sessions with bypass available: directories such as `.git`, `.vscode`, `.idea`, `.husky`, `.cargo`, `.devcontainer`, `.yarn`, `.mvn` and `.claude` (except `.claude/worktrees`), plus files like `.gitconfig`, shell rc files, `.npmrc`, `.bazelrc`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, `.mcp.json` and `.claude.json`. Per mode: prompted in default/acceptEdits, classifier-routed in auto, denied in dontAsk, allowed in bypassPermissions.

nodes.label: Critical paths circuit breaker
nodes.rationale: Claude Code never lets an allow rule or a PreToolUse hook returning "allow" approve an `rm`/`rmdir` targeting a critical path — the filesystem root, any top-level directory, the home directory, Windows drive roots, the working directory and its parents, and globs under additional working directories. A glob directly under a shell variable (`rm -rf "$DIR"/*`) counts because an empty variable makes it a root removal, and hiding it in `$(...)`, backticks, or `<(...)` does not skip the check.

nodes.label: Remove-Item PowerShell check
nodes.rationale: With the PowerShell tool enabled, `Remove-Item` gets its own check separate from the `rm` critical-path list, first matching case winning: system paths are denied in every mode without asking; wildcards (a bare `*`, or any target ending in `/*` or `\*`, including `$dir/*`) are denied in every mode before the classifier ever sees them; and `-Recurse` on the working directory or a parent follows the ordinary per-mode outcome, with bypassPermissions skipping the check.

nodes.label: Actions no mode auto-approves
nodes.rationale: Five classes are never auto-approved in any mode, including bypassPermissions: tools matched by an explicit ask rule; connector tools an organization set to `ask`; tools requiring user interaction (`AskUserQuestion` and MCP tools marked `requiresUserInteraction`); `rm`/`rmdir` removals targeting a critical path; and the cross-session messaging safeguards.

nodes.label: Permission rules (allow / ask / deny)
nodes.rationale: Permission rules layer on top of the mode baseline to pre-approve or block specific tools, and they resolve first in the classifier's decision order. Deny rules block in every mode including bypassPermissions; allow rules have no effect in bypassPermissions; and deny/ask rules do not apply to `EndConversation` as long as Claude has at least one other callable tool.

nodes.label: Deny rules
nodes.rationale: Deny rules block in every permission mode, including bypassPermissions, and a matching deny rule still blocks a critical-path removal outright. Because they are stored configuration rather than transcript text, the docs recommend a deny rule over a stated conversational boundary when a hard guarantee is needed.

nodes.label: Ask rules
nodes.rationale: An explicit ask rule forces a permission prompt in every mode, including auto and bypassPermissions and for critical-path removals. Ask rules that match on a command's content, such as `Bash(git push *)`, fall back to a permission prompt rather than reaching the classifier, and Claude Code does not offer the switch-to-auto-mode option on prompts an ask rule or a hook forced.

nodes.label: Which mode a session starts in
nodes.rationale: A new terminal session takes its permission mode from the first of three that applies: the `--permission-mode` flag (or `--dangerously-skip-permissions`), `permissions.defaultMode` in a settings file, then the built-in default. If the selected mode is `auto` but auto mode is unavailable to the session, Claude Code starts in Manual instead.

nodes.label: permissions.defaultMode setting
nodes.rationale: `permissions.defaultMode` pins the starting permission mode per machine (`~/.claude/settings.json`), per project (`.claude/settings.json`), or per organization (managed settings), with ordinary settings precedence deciding between them. One value is special-cased: an `"auto"` value in `.claude/settings.json` or `.claude/settings.local.json` does not take effect, and Claude Code then falls back to the built-in default rather than to a `defaultMode` from `~/.claude/settings.json`.

nodes.label: Built-in starting permission mode table
nodes.rationale: The built-in default is `auto` only for a Pro, Max, or Team plan in a terminal or the VS Code extension; it is `default` when any settings file disables auto mode, when feature-flag fetching is off, in the first session after an install or upgrade, under `claude -p` or the Agent SDK, on Bedrock/Agent Platform/Foundry/Claude Platform on AWS/gateway sessions, and on Enterprise plans or a Console API key. The `auto` built-in requires v2.1.228+ (v2.1.233+ on native Windows).

nodes.label: permissions.disableAutoMode
nodes.rationale: Setting `permissions.disableAutoMode` to "disable" in managed settings removes auto mode from the organization: `auto` leaves the Shift+Tab cycle and a session started with `--permission-mode auto` starts in Manual instead. From v2.1.251 a session already running in auto mode leaves it once the setting reaches that session from an admin-deployed source, showing `auto mode disabled by settings`; before that a running session kept auto mode until it ended.

nodes.label: CLI Shift+Tab mode cycle
nodes.rationale: In the CLI, Shift+Tab cycles `default` → `acceptEdits` → `plan` → back to `default` (from `auto`, the first press switches to `default`). Optional modes slot in after `plan`, `bypassPermissions` first and `auto` last: `auto` appears when available and switches without a confirmation prompt, `bypassPermissions` appears only when the session was started with an enabling flag or setting, and `dontAsk` never appears at all.

nodes.label: VS Code extension mode selection
nodes.rationale: The VS Code extension switches modes via the indicator under the prompt box (labels: Manual, Edit automatically, Plan, Auto, Bypass permissions) and starts each conversation from its own four-item list: `claudeCode.initialPermissionMode`, then the last sticky pick (Manual/Edit automatically/Auto only), then `defaultMode` from managed or user settings on Pro/Max/Team with feature flags, then the built-in default. It never reads a project's `.claude/settings.json` for the starting mode, and `claudeCode.initialPermissionMode` does not accept `auto`.

nodes.label: Desktop app mode selector
nodes.rationale: In the desktop app's Code tab a mode selector sits next to the send button; Auto appears when auto mode is available and Bypass permissions requires the Allow bypass permissions mode toggle on Pro and Max (organization policy controls it on Team and Enterprise). A mode picked there is remembered per folder and outranks `defaultMode` for that folder, except Plan which applies to the current session only. The Cowork tab has its own separate permission modes.

nodes.label: Web, mobile and Remote Control mode dropdown
nodes.rationale: On claude.ai/code and mobile, which modes the dropdown offers depends on where the session runs: cloud sessions offer Accept edits (which corresponds to `default`, because cloud sessions pre-approve file edits regardless of mode), Plan, and Auto, with Bypass permissions unavailable; Remote Control sessions on a local machine offer Manual, Accept edits, and Plan, and never report bypassPermissions to claude.ai. Remote Control requires the local machine to be signed in with a claude.ai account — API keys are not supported.

nodes.label: Cloud sessions ignore dontAsk and bypassPermissions from settings
nodes.rationale: Claude Code on the web does not honor `defaultMode: "bypassPermissions"` or `"dontAsk"` from settings files, so a repository's checked-in settings cannot start a cloud session in either mode. The setting is ignored silently and the session starts in the mode shown in the dropdown; cloud sessions do still honor `defaultMode: "acceptEdits"`.

nodes.label: Review and approve a plan
nodes.rationale: When the plan is ready Claude offers three choices: approve and use auto mode (labelled "Yes, auto-accept edits" when auto mode is unavailable, or a switch to BYPASS PERMISSIONS when the session started with bypass enabled), approve and manually review each edit, or keep planning. Approving exits plan mode into the mode the chosen option names; Ctrl+G opens the proposed plan in the default editor first, and accepting a plan also generates a session title.

nodes.label: useAutoModeDuringPlan
nodes.rationale: When auto mode is available and `useAutoModeDuringPlan` is on — the default — the classifier reviews shell commands during planning instead of prompting the user, running approved commands and blocking rejected ones. Otherwise commands outside the built-in read-only set prompt, even with the sandbox's auto-allow mode enabled; v2.1.212 through v2.1.217 prompted for every such command regardless of auto-mode availability.

nodes.label: Classifier decision order
nodes.rationale: Every action follows a fixed order, first match winning: (1) allow/ask/deny rules resolve immediately, except that protected-path writes and (v2.1.218+) critical-path removals route to the classifier anyway and `requiresUserInteraction`/org-`ask` connector tools prompt directly; (2) read-only actions and working-directory edits auto-approve except protected-path writes; (3) everything else goes to the classifier; (4) a block returns a reason to Claude, usually the fixed text `Blocked by classifier` from v2.1.208.

nodes.label: What the classifier blocks by default
nodes.rationale: The default block list covers `curl | bash`-style download-and-execute, exfiltration to external endpoints, production deploys and migrations, mass cloud-storage deletion, IAM/repo permission grants, force push, irreversible destruction of pre-session files, history-discarding git commands (`reset --hard`, `clean -fd`, `stash drop`), amending a pushed or non-session commit, and `terraform`/`pulumi`/`cdk` destroys. Later versions add secret-manager writes, unapproved PR merges, production feature-flag changes, tunnels and reverse shells, credential printing, registry re-pointing, transcript writes (v2.1.205+), and unresolvable `rm -rf "$VAR"` deletes.

nodes.label: What the classifier allows by default
nodes.rationale: Allowed without a prompt: local file operations in the working directory, installing dependencies declared in lock files or manifests, reading `.env` and sending credentials to their matching API, read-only HTTP, and pushing to any branch of the repository being worked in including the default branch (v2.1.211+; deploy-marked branches such as `production` or `gh-pages` are judged on their own terms). v2.1.195+ also allows deleting jobs Claude created that session, security-related code review, inter-agent messages, and data flow to trusted infrastructure listed in `environment`.

nodes.label: Trusted working directory and session-start remotes
nodes.rationale: The classifier's trust boundary is the working directory plus the remotes configured for it when the session started; everything else is external until trusted infrastructure is configured. From v2.1.200, a remote added or repointed mid-session with `git remote add` or `git remote set-url` is not trusted — earlier versions trusted such remotes.

nodes.label: Boundaries stated in conversation
nodes.rationale: A boundary the user states in conversation ("don't push", "wait until I review before deploying") is a block signal the classifier honours even where the default rules would allow the action, and it stays in force until the user lifts it — Claude's own judgment that the condition was met does not. Boundaries are not stored as rules: the classifier re-reads them from the transcript each check, so context compaction can lose one.

nodes.label: When auto mode falls back
nodes.rationale: A blocked action is notified and listed under /permissions → Recently denied, where `r` retries it with manual approval. If the classifier blocks 3 times consecutively or 20 times in total — thresholds that are not configurable — auto mode pauses and prompting resumes; any allowed action resets the consecutive counter. Non-interactive `-p` runs without `--permission-prompt-tool` have no prompt to fall back to, so the action simply does not run and Claude keeps working.

nodes.label: Mode switch during a pending classifier check
nodes.rationale: If the permission mode changes while a classifier check is pending, Claude Code discards a verdict the new mode would not have requested rather than applying it: the user is prompted for approval instead, or the action is auto-denied in dontAsk mode.

nodes.label: Classifier review of subagents
nodes.rationale: The classifier checks subagent work at three points: the delegated task description before spawn (v2.1.178+), each of the subagent's actions under the same rules as the parent session with any `permissionMode` in the subagent's frontmatter ignored, and the full action history on return, prepending a security warning to the results if the return check flags a concern.

nodes.label: What the classifier sees
nodes.rationale: The classifier sees user messages, tool calls other than read-only lookups, and CLAUDE.md content; tool results are stripped, so hostile content in a file or web page cannot manipulate it directly. A PostToolUse hook's `classifierContext` field can annotate a result as application-provided context, and a separate server-side probe scans incoming tool results for suspicious content before Claude reads them.

nodes.label: git status pre-check before destructive commands
nodes.rationale: Before a command that would discard uncommitted work, such as `git reset --hard` or `rm -rf`, Claude Code runs `git status` itself and shows the classifier whether staged, modified, or untracked work is present — reporting untracked files even when the repository sets `status.showUntrackedFiles=no`.

nodes.label: Broad allow rules dropped on entering auto mode
nodes.rationale: Entering auto mode drops allow rules that grant arbitrary code execution — blanket `Bash(*)`/`PowerShell(*)`, wildcarded interpreters like `Bash(python*)`, package-manager run commands, `Agent` rules, and (from v2.1.236) `Monitor` rules, since Monitor commands run through the shell. Narrow rules such as `Bash(npm test)` stay in effect, and the dropped rules are restored on leaving auto mode.

nodes.label: Sandbox network verdict caching
nodes.rationale: From v2.1.198 the classifier reuses its verdict per network host and port instead of re-running on every connection: an allow is reused until new content enters the conversation; a context-window-overflow deny is reused (v2.1.234+) until new content arrives or compaction shrinks what the classifier reads; an evaluated deny lasts the turn interactively and the whole run in non-interactive and Agent SDK sessions. Changing the permission mode or rules drops all cached verdicts.

nodes.label: Classifier cost and latency
nodes.rationale: The classifier runs on Claude Sonnet 5 by default rather than the `/model` selection, unless Anthropic configures a classifier model server-side or the session model is Sonnet 4.6 / `availableModels` excludes Sonnet 5, in which case it uses the session's model or an Opus model for Fable sessions. The session's first auto-mode request validates that default and then fixes it for the session. On Enterprise and API-billed accounts classifier calls count toward token usage, and each check adds a round-trip before execution.

nodes.label: Bash sandbox and isolation boundaries
nodes.rationale: Permission modes decide whether Claude asks before an action; the Bash sandbox and outer isolation boundaries decide what an action can reach once it runs. The sandbox's auto-allow mode (macOS, Linux, WSL2) is the way to cut prompts without a classifier, deny rules and content-matching ask rules still applying; sandbox network access requests are routed through the classifier rather than allowed by default.

nodes.label: Common setups table
nodes.rationale: The docs pair each goal with a starting configuration and the isolation it needs: review everything → Manual with no isolation; fewer prompts without a classifier → Manual plus the Bash sandbox in auto-allow; explore first → plan mode; hands-off → auto mode (a sandbox or container adding defense in depth); CI with an exact allowlist → `-p … --permission-mode dontAsk --allowedTools …`; fully unattended → `--dangerously-skip-permissions` inside a required container, VM, or sandbox runtime, run as a non-root user.

nodes.label: Root/sudo refusal for bypassPermissions
nodes.rationale: On Linux and macOS Claude Code refuses to start in bypassPermissions as root or under `sudo`, printing "--dangerously-skip-permissions cannot be used with root/sudo privileges for security reasons". The check is skipped automatically inside a recognized sandbox, and the documented way to run autonomously in a container is the dev container configuration, which runs as a non-root user.

nodes.label: One-time bypassPermissions acceptance dialog
nodes.rationale: The first interactive session started with bypassPermissions shows a warning dialog asking the user to accept responsibility for actions taken without permission checks; the acceptance is saved to user settings so the dialog appears once, and declining exits Claude Code. Non-interactive mode shows no dialog, and a `--bg` background session is refused until the dialog has been accepted interactively.

nodes.label: --restricted flag
nodes.rationale: A session started with `--restricted` (v2.1.248+) refuses bypassPermissions outright, and in such a session the classifier cannot approve protected-path writes.

nodes.label: Cross-session messaging safeguards
nodes.rationale: Two cross-session messaging safeguards survive even bypassPermissions (and plan sessions with bypass available): the `isolatePeerMachines` approval prompt for messages to sessions beyond this machine, and — when no `crossSessionInbound` value applies — holding an inbound message from another of the user's sessions for approval, delivering without asking only when the sending session identifies itself as also bypassing prompts. Held messages are re-evaluated against the inbound rules when the mode changes.

nodes.label: First-run auto mode notice and defaultMode prompt
nodes.rationale: The first time the built-in default starts a session in auto mode, Claude Code shows a one-time notice linking to this page — at the top of the terminal session, or as a dismissible card on the VS Code new-conversation screen. Separately, on Pro/Max/Team, if `~/.claude/settings.json` sets a non-`auto` `defaultMode` and no other file sets one, Claude Code asks once whether to change the setting to auto mode and leaves it unchanged if declined.

nodes.label: Yes, and switch to auto mode (Bash prompt option)
nodes.rationale: In Manual and acceptEdits modes, when auto mode is available, a Bash command's permission prompt gains a "Yes, and switch to auto mode" option that approves the command and switches the session to auto mode (v2.1.247+). PowerShell tool prompts do not offer it, and neither do prompts forced by an ask rule or a hook, because auto mode would still show those prompts.

nodes.label: Tiered permission system
nodes.rationale: Claude Code uses a tiered permission system to balance power and safety: each tool type has its own approval requirement in Manual mode, and its own behavior for 'Yes, and don't ask again'. Permission modes change which of these tiers actually ask you.

nodes.label: Read-only tool tier
nodes.rationale: File reads and Grep require no approval within the working directory and additional directories, so there is no 'don't ask again' behavior to save.

nodes.label: Bash command tier
nodes.rationale: Shell execution requires approval except for a built-in set of read-only commands, and an approval saved with 'don't ask again' persists permanently per repository and command.

nodes.label: File modification tier
nodes.rationale: Editing or writing files always requires approval, and a file-modification approval lasts only until the session ends rather than being written to a settings file.

nodes.label: Web fetch and web search tier
nodes.rationale: WebFetch requires approval except for a built-in set of preapproved documentation domains and saves permanently per repository and domain; WebSearch always requires approval and saves permanently per repository.

nodes.label: Where a saved approval is written
nodes.rationale: A permanently saved approval is written to .claude/settings.local.json at the root of the git repository and applies to future sessions anywhere in that repository, including subdirectories and worktrees. Outside a git repository, or on Windows, Claude Code does not use the repository root and saves the rule elsewhere.

nodes.label: Worktree resolution of saved rules (v2.1.211)
nodes.rationale: The repository root is resolved through worktrees to the main checkout. Before v2.1.211 the rule was always saved in the starting directory, so an approval granted in a worktree or subdirectory did not apply to the rest of the repository; rules saved that way still apply where they were saved.

nodes.label: Prompts that offer only one-time approval
nodes.rationale: Claude Code offers 'don't ask again' or session-long options only when the prompt can show everything they would allow, so a saved rule covers only what its option named. The options are omitted when the command or edit is too large to show, when the label cannot fit all covered commands or paths, or when the starting directory cannot be safely shortened.

nodes.label: Ctrl+E command explanation
nodes.rationale: On a Bash or PowerShell prompt, Ctrl+E shows a model-generated explanation of what the command does, why Claude is running it, and what could go wrong, labeled Low, Med or High risk. The command is sent to the model only when you press Ctrl+E, showing it does not run the command, and permissionExplainerEnabled: false in ~/.claude.json turns the shortcut off.

nodes.label: Comment attached to a permission answer
nodes.rationale: On most prompts (Bash, PowerShell, file, MCP) pressing Tab on Yes or No opens a comment field; WebFetch and browser prompts and the session-long or rule-saving options do not take one. On Yes the comment is sent after the result; on No it is sent as the reason for denial and Claude continues, whereas a bare No from the main conversation stops the turn.

nodes.label: /permissions dialog
nodes.rationale: /permissions lists every permission rule and the settings.json file it comes from, and can be opened while Claude is working: a change applies from Claude's next tool call in the same turn (before v2.1.234 it was queued until the turn finished). When auto mode is available the dialog also has an Auto mode tab holding the classifier rules.

nodes.label: Allow rule
nodes.rationale: Allow rules let Claude Code use the specified tool without manual approval.

nodes.label: Ask rule
nodes.rationale: Ask rules prompt for confirmation whenever Claude Code tries to use the specified tool, and a matching ask rule prompts even when a more specific allow rule also matches the same call.

nodes.label: Deny rule
nodes.rationale: Deny rules prevent Claude Code from using the specified tool and are evaluated first, so no other rule or settings level can re-allow a denied call.

nodes.label: Deny-then-ask-then-allow precedence
nodes.rationale: Rules are evaluated in the fixed order deny, then ask, then allow; the first match in that order determines the outcome and rule specificity does not change the order.

nodes.label: A deny rule cannot carry allowlist exceptions
nodes.rationale: A broad deny such as Bash(aws *) blocks every matching call including ones that also match a narrower allow such as Bash(aws s3 ls), because specificity never overrides the deny-first order.

nodes.label: Bare-name deny removes the tool from context
nodes.rationale: A deny rule naming a bare tool such as Bash removes the tool from Claude's context entirely so Claude never sees it, while a scoped rule such as Bash(rm *) leaves the tool available and blocks only matching calls.

nodes.label: EndConversation exception
nodes.rationale: Bare-name removal applies to every tool except EndConversation: a deny rule cannot remove it while any other tool remains, and an ask rule never prompts for it. The same exception holds for bare-name glob rules and for PreToolUse hooks, which run for every tool except EndConversation.

nodes.label: Rules are enforced by Claude Code, not the model
nodes.rationale: Instructions in a prompt or CLAUDE.md shape what Claude tries to do but do not change what Claude Code allows; access is granted or revoked only through /permissions, permission rules, a permission mode, or a PreToolUse hook.

nodes.label: Permission modes
nodes.rationale: Claude Code supports several permission modes controlling how it approves tool calls; the mode a session starts in is set by defaultMode in the settings files.

nodes.label: default (Manual) mode
nodes.rationale: The default mode prompts for permission on first use of each tool. It is labeled Manual in the CLI, the VS Code and JetBrains extensions and the desktop app, and manual is accepted as an alias from Claude Code v2.1.200.

nodes.label: acceptEdits mode
nodes.rationale: acceptEdits automatically accepts file edits and common filesystem commands such as mkdir, touch, mv and cp for paths in the working directory or additionalDirectories.

nodes.label: plan mode
nodes.rationale: In plan mode Claude reads files and runs read-only shell commands to explore but does not edit source files; where auto mode is available, classifier-approved commands also run.

nodes.label: auto mode and its classifier
nodes.rationale: auto mode auto-approves tool calls with background safety checks that verify actions align with your request; a classifier reviews the actions instead of you, and its rules are editable from the Auto mode tab of /permissions.

nodes.label: dontAsk mode
nodes.rationale: dontAsk auto-denies tools unless pre-approved through /permissions or permissions.allow. AskUserQuestion, MCP tools marked requiresUserInteraction, and connector tools an organization set to ask are denied even when allowed.

nodes.label: bypassPermissions mode
nodes.rationale: bypassPermissions skips permission prompts except for the actions no mode auto-approves, including writes to protected paths such as .git and .claude; cross-session messaging safeguards still apply. It should only be used in isolated environments such as containers or VMs.

nodes.label: disableBypassPermissionsMode and disableAutoMode
nodes.rationale: Setting permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode or permissions.disableAutoMode to 'disable' in any settings file prevents those modes being used; they are most useful in managed settings where they cannot be overridden, though disableBypassPermissionsMode works from any scope and a user can lock themselves out with it.

nodes.label: Permission rule syntax
nodes.rationale: Permission rules follow the format Tool or Tool(specifier).

nodes.label: Bare tool name matches all uses
nodes.rationale: A tool name with no parentheses matches every use of that tool, so Bash matches all Bash commands and Read matches all file reads. Bash(*) is equivalent to Bash, and as a deny rule both forms remove the tool from Claude's context.

nodes.label: Specifiers for fine-grained control
nodes.rationale: A specifier in parentheses narrows a rule to specific uses: Bash(npm run build) matches that exact command, Read(./.env) that file, and WebFetch(domain:example.com) fetches to that host.

nodes.label: Match by input parameter
nodes.rationale: Deny and ask rules can match a top-level scalar input parameter on any built-in tool with Tool(param:value), such as Agent(model:opus) or Bash(run_in_background:true). Each rule names one parameter, nested fields are not matchable, * matches any character sequence, an omitted parameter never matches, and the value is compared against the literal input before normalization. Allow rules keep each tool's own specifier syntax because one safe parameter value would not establish the whole call is safe.

nodes.label: Primary content fields are not parameter-matchable
nodes.rationale: A tool's primary content field cannot be matched with param syntax: command for Bash and PowerShell, file_path for Read/Edit/Write, path for Grep and Glob, notebook_path for NotebookEdit, and url for WebFetch. A rule like Bash(command:rm *) would be bypassable by a compound command, so Claude Code ignores it and emits a startup warning; use Bash(rm *), Read(./path) or WebFetch(domain:host) instead.

nodes.label: Wildcard patterns in Bash rules
nodes.rationale: A * in a Bash rule matches any text including spaces so one rule covers a family of commands, while a rule with no * matches one exact command. A * may appear at the start, middle or end of the rule.

nodes.label: Put the * after the subcommand
nodes.rationale: Claude Code matches everything before the first * as written, so the words before it limit the rule: Bash(git log *) allows only git log commands while Bash(git *) allows every git command, including -c which makes git run a named program. Claude Code warns at startup about an allow rule whose * precedes the subcommand, such as Bash(git * main).

nodes.label: The three rules that decide a wildcard match
nodes.rationale: The * stands in for whatever text is in its place, including the program itself in Bash(* --version). A trailing * preceded by a space also matches the bare command, so Bash(ls *) matches ls, but only when that trailing * is the rule's only wildcard. The space before a trailing * is part of the rule: Bash(ls *) does not match lsof while Bash(ls*) does.

nodes.label: The :* trailing-wildcard suffix
nodes.rationale: Bash(ls:*) is an equivalent way to write Bash(ls *). The :* form is recognized only at the end of a pattern, so in Bash(git:* push) the colon is a literal character and matches nothing; the permission dialog writes the space-separated form when you save a command prefix.

nodes.label: Glob patterns in the tool-name position
nodes.rationale: Deny and ask rules accept glob patterns matching the full tool name, so "*" matches every tool and "mcp__*" every MCP tool across all servers. A tool matched by a bare-name glob deny is removed from Claude's context exactly as with a bare tool name.

nodes.label: Allow globs must be anchored to a named MCP server
nodes.rationale: Allow rules accept tool-name globs only after a literal mcp__<server>__ prefix whose server segment is glob-free, so mcp__puppeteer__* and mcp__github__get_* work while an unanchored allow glob such as "*", "B*" or "mcp__*" is skipped with a warning and auto-approves nothing.

nodes.label: Startup warning for a rule naming no known tool
nodes.rationale: A deny or ask rule whose tool name matches no known tool produces a startup warning to catch typos; tool names containing _ or * are exempt from the check.

nodes.label: Rules match canonical tool names only
nodes.rationale: The label shown in the transcript and permission dialog can differ from a tool's canonical name - the tool labeled Stop Task is canonically TaskStop - and permission rules and hook matchers match the canonical name only, so a rule written as Stop Task never matches.

nodes.label: Bash permission rules
nodes.rationale: Bash rules match the whole command text with * standing in for any text, and the surrounding section defines how compound commands, wrappers, read-only commands and redirections are matched.

nodes.label: Compound command splitting
nodes.rationale: Claude Code is aware of shell operators, so Bash(safe-cmd *) does not permit safe-cmd && other-cmd; the recognized separators are &&, ||, ;, |, |&, & and newlines and a rule must match each subcommand independently. When && or || has nothing after it the command is treated as unparseable and is not split for allow-rule matching, so Bash(npm *) does not approve it.

nodes.label: Approving a compound command saves per-subcommand rules
nodes.rationale: Approving a compound command with 'don't ask again' saves a separate rule for each subcommand that required approval rather than one rule for the whole string, so approving git status && npm test saves a rule for npm test. A cd into a subdirectory generates its own Read rule for that path, and at most 5 rules are saved for one compound command.

nodes.label: Wrappers stripped before matching
nodes.rationale: Before matching Bash rules Claude Code strips a fixed, non-configurable set of wrappers - timeout, time, nice, nohup, stdbuf, the shell builtins command and builtin, and zsh's noglob - so Bash(npm test *) also matches timeout 30 npm test. The query form command -v and zsh's nocorrect are not stripped. Bare xargs is stripped too, but only with no flags: xargs -n1 grep pattern is matched as an xargs command.

nodes.label: Leading environment assignments
nodes.rationale: A leading assignment of certain known-safe environment variables is stripped, so Bash(npm test *) matches NODE_ENV=test npm test. An allow rule will not match past an assignment of any other variable, while a deny or ask rule matches past any leading assignment, so a deny of Bash(rm *) still matches FOO=bar rm -rf tmp/.

nodes.label: Environment runners are not stripped
nodes.rationale: Development environment runners such as direnv exec, devbox run, mise exec, npx and docker exec are not in the wrapper list, so a rule like Bash(devbox run *) matches whatever follows run, including devbox run rm -rf .
