To approve work inside a runner, write one rule per inner command, such as Bash(devbox run npm test).

nodes.label: Exec wrappers cannot be prefix-approved
nodes.rationale: Exec wrappers such as watch, setsid, ionice and flock cannot be auto-approved by a prefix rule like Bash(watch *) and always prompt in Manual mode, and the same applies to find with -exec or -delete, which a Bash(find *) rule does not cover. Only an exact-match rule for the full command string approves such an invocation.

nodes.label: Built-in read-only Bash commands
nodes.rationale: Claude Code recognizes a built-in, non-configurable set of Bash commands as read-only and runs them without a prompt in every mode, including ls, cat, echo, pwd, head, tail, grep, find, wc, which, diff, stat, du, cd and read-only forms of git. Unquoted globs are permitted for commands whose every flag is read-only, and an ask or deny rule is the only way to make one of these prompt.

nodes.label: When a read-only command still prompts
nodes.rationale: In Manual mode a read-only command still prompts for: an unquoted glob on a command with write- or exec-capable flags such as find, sort, sed and git, since the glob could expand to a flag like -delete; docker pointed at another daemon via -H, --context, --url or --connection; file with -m/--magic-file or -f/--files-from; a Windows network (UNC) path, which could send Windows credentials to the host named; and any command the analysis cannot parse, including every command over 10,000 characters.

nodes.label: cd as a read-only command and its two exceptions
nodes.rationale: A cd into the working directory or an additional directory is read-only, and a compound such as cd packages/api && ls runs without a prompt when each part qualifies. Two combinations still prompt: cd with git, because running git in a new directory can execute that directory's hooks (a cd resolving to the current directory is a no-op and does not prompt), and cd with an output redirect whose target directory Claude Code cannot resolve after the cd, except a /dev/null target.

nodes.label: Argument-constraining Bash patterns are fragile
nodes.rationale: A pattern such as Bash(curl http://github.com/ *) intends to restrict curl to GitHub URLs but misses options before the URL, a different protocol, redirects to the host, a URL held in a variable, and extra spaces.

nodes.label: More reliable URL filtering
nodes.rationale: For reliable URL filtering, deny curl, wget and similar Bash network tools and use WebFetch with WebFetch(domain:...) allowances; validate URLs in a PreToolUse hook; or describe allowed patterns in CLAUDE.md, which shapes intent but enforces nothing and must be paired with one of the others. WebFetch alone does not prevent network access while Bash is allowed.

nodes.label: Output redirections are checked as file writes
nodes.rationale: Claude Code checks the target of >, >> or 2> as a file write against your Edit allow and deny rules, protected paths and the working directories, so a rule like Bash(git commit *) allows the command but not the target. A /dev/null target is not checked, and a target starting with ~ or containing a glob character needs approval.

nodes.label: PowerShell permission rules
nodes.rationale: PowerShell rules use the same shape as Bash rules: * matches at any position, the :* suffix equals a trailing space-star, and a bare PowerShell or PowerShell(*) matches every command.

nodes.label: PowerShell aliases and AST splitting
nodes.rationale: Common aliases are canonicalized before matching and matching is case-insensitive, so PowerShell(Get-ChildItem *) also matches gci, ls and dir. Claude Code parses the PowerShell AST and checks each subcommand independently, splitting on |, ; and, on PowerShell 7+, && and ||, and every subcommand must match for the compound command to be allowed.

nodes.label: Read and Edit rules
nodes.rationale: A Read deny rule for a path such as Read(./.env) or Read(./secrets/**) blocks Claude's file tools from reading it. Edit rules apply to all built-in tools that edit files, and Read rules are applied on a best-effort basis to Grep, Glob, @file mentions, and the selection and open-file context a connected IDE shares.

nodes.label: A Read deny also blocks Edit and Write
nodes.rationale: A Read deny rule also blocks the Edit and Write tools on the same path, including creating a new file there, requiring v2.1.208 or later on edits and v2.1.228 or later on writes. NotebookEdit is not covered, so an Edit deny rule is needed for paths no tool may change.

nodes.label: Only Edit(path) and Read(path) rules are consulted
nodes.rationale: Claude Code checks file permissions against Edit(path) and Read(path) rules only; a path rule written for Write, NotebookEdit, Glob or the legacy MultiEdit is accepted, never consulted, and warned about at startup, except a Glob rule passed in --allowedTools. Use Edit(docs/**) in place of Write/NotebookEdit/MultiEdit forms and Read(docs/**) in place of Glob(docs/**); a tool-name rule with no path, such as a deny for Write, still matches at the tool level.

nodes.label: Read and Edit denies reach recognized Bash file commands only
nodes.rationale: Read and Edit deny rules apply to Claude's built-in file tools and to file commands Claude Code recognizes in Bash such as cat, head, tail and sed, but not to arbitrary subprocesses that open files themselves, like a Python or Node script. OS-level enforcement across all processes requires enabling the sandbox.

nodes.label: The four path pattern anchors
nodes.rationale: Read and Edit rules use gitignore pattern syntax with four anchors: //path is absolute from the filesystem root, ~/path is home-relative, /path is relative to the settings source that defines it, and path or ./path is relative to the current directory. A single leading slash is therefore NOT an absolute path - /Users/alice/file anchors at the settings source, and //Users/alice/file is the absolute form.

nodes.label: Where a /path rule resolves per settings source
nodes.rationale: A /path pattern anchors at a directory associated with the settings source: the primary working directory for project settings, local settings, CLI flags and session rules; ~/.claude/path for user settings; and the file's own directory for a file passed with --settings. Local settings anchor at the session's primary working directory, not the repository root where the file is stored, so in a worktree a shared Edit(/src/**) matches that worktree's src/. A user-settings deny such as Read(/secrets/**) therefore blocks ~/.claude/secrets/**, not a project directory - use // or ~/ to reach every project.

nodes.label: Windows path normalization
nodes.rationale: On Windows paths are normalized to POSIX form before matching, so C:\Users\alice becomes /c/Users/alice; use //c/**/.env to match .env files anywhere on that drive and //**/.env to match across all drives.

nodes.label: Matching depth depends on pattern shape and rule type
nodes.rationale: Bare filenames follow gitignore semantics and match at any depth, so Read(.env) equals Read(**/.env). For a relative single-segment directory pattern the depth depends on rule type: as an allow rule Edit(src/**) matches only <cwd>/src, while as a deny or ask rule Read(secrets/**) matches a directory of that name at any depth. Every other shape matches at the same depth in every rule type - Edit(/src/**) only at its anchor, Edit(**/src/**) at any depth.

nodes.label: Generated path rules are escaped
nodes.rationale: When you approve a file path with 'don't ask again', Claude Code escapes gitignore pattern characters such as [, ] and * so the generated rule matches only the literal path approved; rules you write yourself are not escaped. Before v2.1.202 the path was saved unescaped, so a generated rule for a directory named [2024-06] Reports could fail to match itself or match sibling directories.

nodes.label: Symlinks are checked on both paths
nodes.rationale: When Claude accesses a symlink, permission rules check both the symlink path and its target: an allow rule applies only when both match, so a symlink inside an allowed directory pointing outside it still prompts, while a deny rule applies when either matches. Claude Code also re-confirms that an approved path still resolves to the location the permission check approved when the tool opens the file.

nodes.label: Grep and Glob search the resolved path directory
nodes.rationale: Grep and Glob search the directory their path argument resolves to, and Claude Code applies Read deny rules to that directory.

nodes.label: WebFetch domain rules
nodes.rationale: WebFetch rules use a domain: prefix matched case-insensitively against the requested URL's hostname, stripping a trailing dot from both sides. WebFetch(domain:*.example.com) matches any subdomain at any depth but not example.com itself, and wildcards in WebFetch rules require Claude Code v2.1.172 or later to match fetches.

nodes.label: A WebFetch wildcard cannot cross a dot
nodes.rationale: Except as a leading *. or a bare *, a wildcard matches only the text between two dots: WebFetch(domain:example.*) matches example.org but not example.evil.com, which keeps a trailing wildcard from matching domains an attacker could register.

nodes.label: Bare WebFetch versus WebFetch(domain:*)
nodes.rationale: Both cover every URL but behave differently, and only the domain: form also adds its domain to the sandbox's allowed or denied domain list. In allow, bare WebFetch fetches without prompting but leaves the sandbox allowlist unchanged, while WebFetch(domain:*) also lets sandboxed commands reach any host; in deny, bare WebFetch removes the tool entirely, while WebFetch(domain:*) keeps the tool, refuses each fetch, and blocks every host for sandboxed commands.

nodes.label: MCP permission rules
nodes.rationale: MCP rules name the server as configured, optionally followed by a tool: mcp__puppeteer matches any tool from that server, mcp__puppeteer__* does the same via wildcard, and mcp__puppeteer__puppeteer_navigate matches one tool. A parameter rule on an MCP tool must be passed with --disallowedTools, since Claude Code skips any mcp__ rule with parentheses found in a settings file and reports it in the invalid-settings dialog and in claude doctor.

nodes.label: Organization-set connector ask overrides allow rules
nodes.rationale: When an organization sets a claude.ai connector tool to ask and that setting reaches the session, allow rules for the tool have no effect: Claude Code prompts on every call even in auto and bypassPermissions modes, and denies it in dontAsk mode, which never prompts. Connector tools Claude Code fetches itself appear as mcp__claude_ai_<server>__<tool>.

nodes.label: Cowork routes Bash and WebFetch through MCP tools
nodes.rationale: In a Cowork session in the Claude Desktop app, shell commands run through mcp__workspace__bash and fetches through mcp__workspace__web_fetch rather than the built-in tools. Deny rules naming the whole Bash or WebFetch tool are applied to these Cowork tools, but allow rules never carry over.

nodes.label: Agent (subagent) rules
nodes.rationale: Agent(AgentName) rules control which subagents Claude may use - Agent(Explore), Agent(Plan) or a custom name - and are added to the deny array or passed with --disallowedTools to disable specific agents.

nodes.label: Cd rules
nodes.rationale: Cd rules control which directories the /cd command may move the session to. Cd is not model-invocable, so the rules apply only when you run /cd yourself; a bare Cd deny disables /cd entirely and a Cd(<path-pattern>) deny blocks matching targets, checking every spelling of the target including each symlink hop.

nodes.label: Any Cd allow rule switches /cd to allowlist mode
nodes.rationale: Adding any Cd allow rule makes the resolved target directory have to match one of your allow rules or /cd refuses; with no Cd rules configured /cd keeps its default behavior of prompting you to trust an unfamiliar directory.

nodes.label: Cd path matching differs from gitignore matching
nodes.rationale: Cd patterns share the //, ~/ and / anchors from Read and Edit rules, but matching is anchored to the whole directory path rather than gitignore-style: * matches exactly one path segment, ** matches across segments, and a trailing /** also matches its named root. So Cd(~/code/*) matches ~/code/app but not ~/code/app/src or ~/code.

nodes.label: PreToolUse hooks evaluate permissions at runtime
nodes.rationale: PreToolUse hooks are custom shell commands that run before the permission prompt for every tool except EndConversation, and their output can deny the tool call, force a prompt, or skip the prompt and let the call proceed.

nodes.label: Hook decisions do not bypass permission rules
nodes.rationale: Claude Code evaluates deny and ask rules regardless of what a PreToolUse hook returns: a matching deny blocks the call and a matching ask still prompts even when the hook returned allow or ask, preserving deny-first precedence including deny rules from managed settings. MCP tools marked requiresUserInteraction and organization-ask connector tools also still prompt after a hook returns allow.

nodes.label: A blocking hook outranks allow rules
nodes.rationale: A hook that exits with code 2 stops the tool call before permission rules are evaluated, so it blocks even when an allow rule would have let the call proceed. That is the documented way to run all Bash commands without prompts except a few: allow "Bash" and register a PreToolUse hook rejecting those specific commands.

nodes.label: Working directories and additional directories
nodes.rationale: Claude has access to files in the launch directory, which is the session's primary working directory until /cd moves it. Access is extended with the --add-dir CLI argument at startup, the /add-dir command during a session, or additionalDirectories in settings; files in additional directories become readable without prompts and their edit permissions follow the current permission mode. On macOS, a background session's host requests access to protected folders such as ~/Desktop, ~/Documents and ~/Downloads separately from the terminal.

nodes.label: Moving the session with /cd
nodes.rationale: /cd <path> moves the session to a new primary working directory, keeping the conversation, loading the new directory's CLAUDE.md and prompting for workspace trust if you have not worked there; it requires v2.1.169 or later and --resume then finds the session from the new directory.

nodes.label: What a /cd move activates and disconnects
nodes.rationale: After a move Claude Code applies the new directory's project settings, permission rules and hooks, its .mcp.json and local-scope MCP servers subject to the same approval as at startup, the plugins its settings enable plus its skills and subagents, and its env values layered on the previous ones. It disconnects the previous directory's project and local-scope MCP servers and newly disabled plugins' servers, takes additionalDirectories from the new settings while keeping --add-dir/-added ones, and keeps CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR pointing at the project root where the session started. Before v2.1.246 none of this applied until the session was resumed.

nodes.label: An additional directory grants file access, not configuration
nodes.rationale: Adding a directory extends where Claude can read and edit files but does not make it a full configuration root; most .claude/ configuration is not discovered from it. The few exceptions apply only to directories added with --add-dir or /add-dir (including the Agent SDK's additionalDirectories/add_dirs options, which pass through as --add-dir), while entries in permissions.additionalDirectories in a settings file grant file access only.

nodes.label: Configuration types loaded from an --add-dir directory
nodes.rationale: Skills in .claude/skills/ load with live reload; command files and subagents load without live reload, and a name collision resolves in favor of your project's command. From settings files only enabledPlugins and extraKnownMarketplaces are read, and CLAUDE.md, .claude/rules/ and CLAUDE.local.md load only when CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD=1 is set. These load through the project setting source, so excluding it with --setting-sources or settingSources drops them, and bare mode skips the commands and subagents.

nodes.label: Where each settings file is discovered
nodes.rationale: Output styles are discovered from the current working directory and its parents, ~/.claude/, and managed settings. Hooks and other .claude/settings.json keys load from the current working directory's .claude/ with no parent fallback, plus user and managed settings, while .claude/settings.local.json loads from the git repository root even when started in a subdirectory - except where Claude Code does not use the repository root, such as on Windows, and before v2.1.211. Agent SDK sessions load it from the working directory in all versions. Configuration is shared across projects via ~/.claude/, a plugin, or launching from the directory holding the .claude/ config.

nodes.label: Permissions versus sandboxing
nodes.rationale: Permissions and sandboxing are complementary layers: permissions control which tools Claude Code may use and which files or domains it may reach, applying to every tool except that a deny or ask rule cannot block EndConversation while other tools remain; sandboxing is OS-level enforcement of the Bash tool's filesystem and network access and applies only to Bash commands and their child processes.

nodes.label: Defense in depth across the two layers
nodes.rationale: Deny rules stop Claude from attempting a restricted access, while sandbox restrictions stop Bash commands from reaching resources outside the boundary even if a prompt injection bypasses Claude's decision-making. Filesystem restrictions merge sandbox.filesystem settings with Read and Edit deny rules, and network restrictions merge WebFetch(domain:...) rules with the sandbox's allowedDomains and deniedDomains lists.

nodes.label: autoAllowBashIfSandboxed substitutes for a whole-tool prompt
nodes.rationale: With sandboxing enabled and autoAllowBashIfSandboxed left at its default true, sandboxed Bash commands run without prompting even when permissions include a bare Bash ask rule or the equivalent Bash(*): the sandbox boundary substitutes for that whole-tool prompt. Content-scoped ask rules such as Bash(git push *), explicit deny rules, and rm or rmdir against a critical path still go through the regular flow, as do commands that cannot run sandboxed.

nodes.label: Plan mode skips the sandbox substitution
nodes.rationale: In plan mode Claude Code skips the autoAllowBashIfSandboxed substitution: without an ask rule the built-in read-only commands still run unprompted and any other shell command goes through the regular permission flow, and with a bare Bash ask rule every Bash command prompts including sandboxed read-only ones. Before v2.1.212 the substitution applied in plan mode too.

nodes.label: Managed settings
nodes.rationale: Administrators deploy managed settings that user and project settings cannot override, apart from a few security-sensitive keys. Some keys are managed-only, such as allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly, which limits permission rules to the managed source.

nodes.label: Settings precedence for permission rules
nodes.rationale: Permission rules follow the same settings precedence as all other settings, with managed settings highest: no other level, including command line arguments, can override a managed permission rule.

nodes.label: A deny at any level cannot be re-allowed
nodes.rationale: If a tool is denied at any level no other level can allow it: a managed deny cannot be overridden by --allowedTools, and --disallowedTools can add restrictions beyond managed settings. The same holds across scopes - a project deny blocks a user allow and a user deny blocks a project allow - because deny rules from any scope are evaluated before allow rules.

nodes.label: Embedder-supplied managed policy
nodes.rationale: Embedding hosts can supply additional managed policy through the SDK managedSettings option, including permission allow rules, unless the administrator sets the allowManaged*Only locks.

nodes.label: Project allow rules require workspace trust
nodes.rationale: permissions.allow rules and permissions.additionalDirectories in a project's .claude/settings.json grant capability, so Claude Code applies them only after you accept the workspace trust dialog for that folder, which lists the rules and directories first. deny and ask rules are unaffected because they only restrict.

nodes.label: How accepted trust is keyed and stored
nodes.rationale: In a repository the trust is keyed on the git repository root and covers the whole repository except any nested git repository such as a submodule, using the main checkout's root in a worktree. Outside a repository it is keyed on the starting directory and covers its subdirectories except nested repositories, and a session started in your home directory holds the trust for that session only without writing it to disk.

nodes.label: The trust dialog appears in interactive sessions only
nodes.rationale: Claude Code shows the trust dialog in interactive sessions only: a claude -p run or an SDK session never shows it, and trusting a parent folder does not count for the rules that require this exact folder.

nodes.label: When settings.local.json needs trust
nodes.rationale: A .claude/settings.local.json is normally your own file and its allow rules and additional directories apply without the trust step, but when the file is tracked in git or .claude is a symlink Claude Code treats it as repository-supplied and holds its rules until you trust the folder. Claude Code runs git to tell the two apart, and only once you have trusted the folder or are in a -p or SDK session, which counts as accepted.

nodes.label: The configuration-home exception
nodes.rationale: Started in your configuration home - your home directory, or a directory whose .claude subdirectory is set as CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR - Claude Code applies that folder's settings.local.json immediately without running git, unless it keeps local settings at a repository root instead. The exception skips only the trust step: ~/.claude/settings.local.json is still local scope and is read only in sessions started in the home directory itself, so cross-project rules belong in ~/.claude/settings.json.

nodes.label: What a repository supplies before you trust the folder
nodes.rationale: With only a parent folder trusted, hooks, env, helper commands and a skill's hooks and allowed-tools are used, while project allow rules and additionalDirectories are withheld until the dialog is accepted, subagent frontmatter hooks, @skills-dir plugins, extraKnownMarketplaces entries and inline subagent mcpServers are withheld with no dialog offered, .mcp.json servers prompt before connecting, and a headersHelper is not run. Under claude -p or the SDK the allow rules are withheld with a stderr warning while .mcp.json servers connect without asking. To trust a folder by hand, set projects["<path>"].hasTrustDialogAccepted to true in ~/.claude.json.

nodes.label: Precautions before running claude -p in an unfamiliar repository
nodes.rationale: Decide what the repository may run: pass --setting-sources user (or an SDK settingSources without project settings) so neither its settings files nor its .mcp.json are read; start with --bare so no hooks, skills, commands, subagents, plugins or .mcp.json servers load, noting env and helpers such as awsAuthRefresh still apply; pass --settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}' for that run, since setting it in user settings alone is overridden by project settings; and use disabledMcpjsonServers to reject a named server in every session type.

nodes.label: Claude Code plugin
nodes.rationale: A plugin is a self-contained directory of components that extends Claude Code with custom functionality. Its components are skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers, LSP servers, and monitors.

nodes.label: Plugin skills and commands
nodes.rationale: Plugins add skills that create /name shortcuts invokable by the user or by Claude. Skills live as directories with a SKILL.md under skills/, commands are flat markdown files under commands/, and both are discovered automatically when the plugin is installed.

nodes.label: Root SKILL.md single-skill plugin
nodes.rationale: A plugin with a SKILL.md at its root, no skills/ directory and no skills manifest field is loaded automatically as a single skill; no "skills": ["./"] entry is needed. The frontmatter name field controls the invocation name — without it Claude Code falls back to the install directory name, which for marketplace installs is a version string that changes on every update.

nodes.label: Boolean frontmatter value forms
nodes.rationale: In plugin skills and commands, Boolean frontmatter fields such as disable-model-invocation accept yes, no, on, off, 1 and 0 in any letter case in addition to true and false. Before v2.1.218 only true and false were recognized.

nodes.label: Plugin agents
nodes.rationale: Plugins can ship specialized subagents as markdown files in an agents/ directory. They appear in the @-mention typeahead under a scoped name such as my-plugin:code-reviewer once the plugin is enabled.

nodes.label: Supported plugin-agent frontmatter fields
nodes.rationale: Plugin agents support name, description, model, effort, maxTurns, tools, disallowedTools, skills, memory, background and isolation. The only valid isolation value is "worktree".

nodes.label: Fields banned from plugin agents
nodes.rationale: For security reasons hooks, mcpServers and permissionMode are not supported in the frontmatter of plugin-shipped agents.

nodes.label: Lenient loading of plugin agents
nodes.rationale: Claude Code loads a plugin agent even when its frontmatter has no name or does not parse: it names the agent after the file (agents/reviewer.md in my-plugin loads as my-plugin:reviewer) and, for unparsable frontmatter, uses "Agent from my-plugin plugin" as the description and ignores every field. By contrast a project, user or managed agent file in that state is skipped entirely.

nodes.label: claude plugin validate
nodes.rationale: claude plugin validate checks plugin.json, hooks/hooks.json and the frontmatter of skills, agents and commands in the plugin's default directories. For a plugin with a manifest pass the plugin directory; for one without a manifest pass the component directory (e.g. ./my-plugin/agents), which requires v2.1.233 or later.

nodes.label: --strict validation flag
nodes.rationale: Passing --strict to claude plugin validate treats warnings as errors, so CI can catch a misspelled field name or a field left over from another tool's manifest even though the plugin would still load at runtime.

nodes.label: Plugin hooks
nodes.rationale: Plugins can provide event handlers that respond to Claude Code events automatically, configured in hooks/hooks.json at the plugin root or inline in plugin.json as JSON with event matchers and actions.

nodes.label: Plugin hook lifecycle events
nodes.rationale: Plugin hooks respond to the same lifecycle events as user-defined hooks, including SessionStart, Setup, UserPromptSubmit, UserPromptExpansion, PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PermissionDenied, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, PostToolBatch, SubagentStart/Stop, TaskCreated/Completed, Stop, StopFailure, TeammateIdle, InstructionsLoaded, ConfigChange, CwdChanged, DirectoryAdded, FileChanged, WorktreeCreate/Remove, Pre/PostCompact, Pre/PostModelSwitch, Elicitation, ElicitationResult and SessionEnd.

nodes.label: Hook types
nodes.rationale: Five hook types exist: command (shell commands or scripts), http (POST the event JSON to a URL), mcp_tool (call a tool on a configured MCP server), prompt (evaluate a prompt with an LLM using the $ARGUMENTS placeholder) and agent (run an agentic verifier with tools).

nodes.label: Scoped names for hooks targeting a bundled MCP server
nodes.rationale: Hooks targeting the plugin's own bundled MCP server must use scoped names: tool matchers and if fields take mcp__plugin_<plugin-name>_<server-name>__<tool>, and an mcp_tool hook's server field takes plugin:<plugin-name>:<server-name>. A matcher written against the bare server key never fires.

nodes.label: Plugin-bundled MCP servers
nodes.rationale: Plugins can bundle Model Context Protocol servers to connect Claude Code with external tools and services, declared in a .mcp.json at the plugin root or inline in plugin.json using standard MCP server configuration.

nodes.label: Plugin MCP server integration behavior
nodes.rationale: Plugin MCP servers start automatically when the plugin is enabled, appear as standard MCP tools in Claude's toolkit, and can be configured independently of user MCP servers. Running /reload-plugins mid-session keeps the live connections of servers whose configuration is unchanged.

nodes.label: Plugin LSP servers
nodes.rationale: Plugins can provide Language Server Protocol servers that give Claude real-time code intelligence, configured in a .lsp.json at the plugin root or inline in plugin.json as a map of language-server names to configurations.

nodes.label: Required LSP config fields
nodes.rationale: An LSP server entry requires command (the LSP binary to execute, which must be in PATH) and extensionToLanguage (a map of file extensions to language identifiers). Claude Code skips a server missing either one, and the other configured servers still start.

nodes.label: Optional LSP config fields
nodes.rationale: Optional LSP fields are args, transport, env, initializationOptions, settings, workspaceFolder, startupTimeout, shutdownTimeout, restartOnCrash, maxRestarts and diagnostics. transport accepts socket but Claude Code runs every server over stdio, and diagnostics defaults to true, controlling whether diagnostics are pushed into Claude's context after edits.

nodes.label: restartOnCrash / shutdownTimeout version gate
nodes.rationale: restartOnCrash and shutdownTimeout require Claude Code v2.1.205 or later. Before that version the schema accepted both options but setting either caused Claude Code to skip that LSP server entirely at startup, with the reason visible only in claude --debug output.

nodes.label: First-registered LSP server wins an extension
nodes.rationale: When more than one enabled LSP server declares the same file extension, whether from one plugin or several, the first server registered handles those files and the others never start; the /plugin interface warns and names the plugin whose server is active. A skipped server does not claim its extensions, so another valid server still handles them.

nodes.label: LSP stdout is protocol-only
nodes.rationale: Claude Code reads a language server's stdout as protocol messages only, accepting headers up to 64 KiB and bodies up to 32 MiB. A server that exceeds either limit or writes non-protocol output to stdout is disconnected, and the disconnect counts as a crash for restartOnCrash and maxRestarts — so log output must go to stderr.

nodes.label: Language server binary installed separately
nodes.rationale: LSP plugins configure how Claude Code connects to a language server but do not include the server itself; the binary must be installed separately. The symptom of a missing binary is `Executable not found in $PATH` in the /plugin Errors tab.

nodes.label: Official LSP plugins
nodes.rationale: The official marketplace ships pyright-lsp (Pyright for Python), typescript-lsp (TypeScript Language Server) and rust-analyzer-lsp. Install the language server binary first, then install the plugin from the marketplace.

nodes.label: Plugin background monitors
nodes.rationale: A plugin can declare background monitors in monitors/monitors.json or experimental.monitors; each runs a shell command for the lifetime of the session and delivers every stdout line to Claude as a notification. They use the Monitor tool's mechanism, run only in interactive CLI sessions, run unsandboxed at the same trust level as hooks, and are not stopped when a plugin is disabled mid-session.

nodes.label: Monitor entry fields
nodes.rationale: A monitor requires name (unique within the plugin, preventing duplicate processes on reload), command (a persistent background process in the session working directory) and description. The optional when field is "always" by default or "on-skill-invoke:<skill-name>" to start the monitor the first time that skill is dispatched.

nodes.label: Monitor commands reject ${user_config.*}
nodes.rationale: A monitor command cannot reference ${user_config.*}: because the command runs through a shell, Claude Code rejects the monitor with an error instead of substituting the value. Monitor processes also do not receive CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_<KEY> variables, so the script must read the value from a config file it owns.

nodes.label: Plugin color themes
nodes.rationale: A plugin can ship color themes as JSON files in themes/, each with a base preset and a sparse overrides map of color tokens; they appear in /theme beside the built-in presets. Selecting one saves custom:<plugin-name>:<slug> in the user's config, and because plugin themes are read-only Ctrl+E copies the theme into ~/.claude/themes/ for editing.

nodes.label: Plugin installation scopes
nodes.rationale: Installing a plugin chooses a scope that determines where it is available and who else can use it: user (~/.claude/settings.json, the default), project (.claude/settings.json, shared via version control), local (.claude/settings.local.json, gitignored) and managed (read-only, update only).

nodes.label: Skills-directory plugins (@skills-dir)
nodes.rationale: Any folder under a skills directory containing a .claude-plugin/plugin.json is loaded on the next session as a plugin named <name>@skills-dir, with no marketplace and no install step. Unlike a copied marketplace install it is discovered in place rather than copied into the plugin cache, and it is removed by deleting the folder or running claude plugin disable <name>@skills-dir — there is no uninstall step.

nodes.label: Trust gate on project-scope skills-dir plugins
nodes.rationale: A project-scope plugin under <cwd>/.claude/skills/ comes from the repository rather than the user, so it loads only after the workspace trust dialog is accepted — trusting a parent folder or running with -p is not enough. Its MCP servers still need per-server approval, its LSP servers start only after the workspace is trusted, and its background monitors do not load at all. Personal-scope plugins under ~/.claude/skills/ have none of these restrictions.

nodes.label: Skills-dir plugins load only from the primary working directory
nodes.rationale: Project-scope @skills-dir plugins load only from the .claude/skills/ of the session's primary working directory; unlike plain skills and commands they do not walk up to the repository root, so launching from a subdirectory misses a plugin at the repo root. Launch from the repository root or move the session with /cd on v2.1.246 or later.

nodes.label: Editing and reloading a skills-directory plugin
nodes.rationale: Edits to a skill's SKILL.md take effect immediately in the current session, but changes to the plugin's other components — hooks/, .mcp.json, agents/, output-styles/ — do not; run /reload-plugins or restart Claude Code to pick those up.

nodes.label: Plugins synced from claude.ai
nodes.rationale: In Cowork and cloud sessions Claude Code downloads the plugins enabled for the user's claude.ai account into ~/.claude/plugins/synced/ and loads each as <name>@synced, with no marketplace and no install record; they are not loaded in the user's own terminal sessions. install/update/uninstall do not apply to them — removal happens by turning the plugin off for the claude.ai account. Before v2.1.239 they loaded as <name>@inline.

nodes.label: Synced plugin name collisions
nodes.rationale: When an enabled plugin from any other source — a marketplace install, a skills-directory plugin, or a --plugin-dir plugin — has the same name as a synced plugin, Claude Code loads that plugin and reports the synced copy as not loaded; disable your own copy to use the claude.ai one. Before v2.1.239 the synced copy won instead.

nodes.label: plugin.json manifest schema
nodes.rationale: .claude-plugin/plugin.json defines a plugin's metadata and configuration. The manifest is optional: without it Claude Code auto-discovers components in their default locations and derives the plugin name from the directory name. Use a manifest when metadata or custom component paths are needed.

nodes.label: name is the only required manifest field
nodes.rationale: If a manifest is included, name is the only required field: a unique kebab-case identifier with no spaces, control characters or bidirectional-formatting characters. It namespaces components (agent agent-creator in plugin-dev appears as plugin-dev:agent-creator), but when a marketplace entry lists the plugin under a different name, the marketplace entry name is what enabledPlugins and /plugin key on.

nodes.label: Unrecognized and wrong-typed manifest fields
nodes.rationale: Claude Code ignores unrecognized top-level manifest fields, so one plugin.json can double as a VS Code, Cursor, npm or MCPB/DXT manifest; validate reports them as warnings (suggesting a near-miss field name) and the plugin still loads. A recognized field with the wrong type usually fails the load — a string keywords is a load error — except experimental and metadata, where a non-object value is ignored with a warning.

nodes.label: Manifest metadata fields
nodes.rationale: Optional metadata fields include $schema (ignored at load time), displayName (UI name, falling back to name and never used for namespacing), version (pins the plugin so users update only on a bump; plugin.json wins over the marketplace entry), description, author, homepage, repository, license, keywords, metadata (free-form, never read by Claude Code) and defaultEnabled.

nodes.label: defaultEnabled
nodes.rationale: defaultEnabled: false ships a plugin that installs disabled, for plugins adding cost or scope a user should opt into. It is only the fallback: an entry in enabledPlugins at any settings scope persists across updates and takes precedence, as does a dependency requirement that writes true at install or enable time, and a marketplace entry's own defaultEnabled outranks the plugin.json value.

nodes.label: Component path manifest fields
nodes.rationale: The manifest can point components at custom paths: skills, commands, agents, workflows, hooks, mcpServers, outputStyles, lspServers, experimental.themes, experimental.monitors, userConfig, channels and dependencies.

nodes.label: Experimental components key
nodes.rationale: Components under the experimental key — themes and monitors — have a manifest schema that may change between releases while they stabilize. Declaring them at the top level still works but claude plugin validate warns, and a future release will require the experimental.* location.

nodes.label: userConfig
nodes.rationale: userConfig declares values Claude Code prompts for when the plugin is enabled, replacing hand-edited settings.json. Each option takes type (string, number, boolean, directory or file), title and description, plus optional sensitive, required, default, multiple and min/max. Values substitute as ${user_config.KEY} in MCP and LSP configs and hook commands, and reach hook processes as CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_<KEY>.

nodes.label: Shell-evaluated fields reject ${user_config.*}
nodes.rationale: Fields that run in a shell reject ${user_config.*}, because substituting a configured value into a shell command would let the shell run whatever the value contains; the component fails with an error instead. Shell-form hook commands should use exec form with args or read CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_<KEY>; monitor commands and MCP headersHelper must read the value from a config file. Before v2.1.207 these fields did substitute.

nodes.label: pluginConfigs settings sources
nodes.rationale: Non-sensitive userConfig values are stored under pluginConfigs in user settings; on macOS sensitive ones go to the Keychain (falling back to ~/.claude/.credentials.json), whose ~2 KB shared limit means keeping them small. Claude Code reads pluginConfigs only from user settings, --settings and managed settings, in that increasing order of precedence — a project's .claude/settings.json and settings.local.json are ignored, because a cloned repository could otherwise feed values into hook, MCP, LSP and monitor commands. enabledPlugins still honors project and local settings.

nodes.label: Plugin channels
nodes.rationale: The channels field declares message channels (Telegram, Slack, Discord style) that inject content into the conversation. Each channel's required server field must match a key in the plugin's mcpServers, and an optional per-channel userConfig, using the same schema as the top-level field, prompts for values such as bot tokens or owner IDs at enable time.

nodes.label: Replace-vs-add path behavior
nodes.rationale: Whether a custom path replaces or extends the default directory depends on the field: commands, agents, workflows, outputStyles, experimental.themes and experimental.monitors replace the default, while skills adds to the always-scanned skills/ (except for a marketplace entry whose source resolves to the marketplace root). Hooks, MCP servers and LSP servers have their own merge rules. When a default folder and its manifest key both exist, Claude Code warns about the ignored folder but still loads the plugin.

nodes.label: Relative path rules for manifest paths
nodes.rationale: All manifest paths must be relative to the plugin root and start with ./, except that the skills field also accepts "."; both "." and "./" denote the plugin root, and before v2.1.221 "." failed validation so "./" is the compatible spelling. Multiple paths may be given as arrays, components from custom paths keep the same naming and namespacing rules, and a skill path may point at a directory holding SKILL.md directly.

nodes.label: Plugin path environment variables
nodes.rationale: Three variables reference paths: ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} (the plugin's installation directory), ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} (a persistent directory surviving updates) and ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} (the project root). All three are exported to hook processes and MCP/LSP subprocesses; inline substitution happens in skill and agent content, hook and monitor commands, MCP stdio command/args/env, MCP http/sse/ws url/headers/headersHelper, and LSP command/args/env/workspaceFolder.

nodes.label: Persistent plugin data directory
nodes.rationale: ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} resolves to ~/.claude/plugins/data/{id}/ with non-alphanumeric characters in the plugin id replaced by -. It outlives any single plugin version, so an existence check alone cannot detect a dependency-manifest change; the recommended pattern diffs the bundled manifest against a copy in the data directory and reinstalls when they differ. It is deleted when the plugin is uninstalled from its last scope unless --keep-data is passed.

nodes.label: Plugin cache and file resolution
nodes.rationale: For security and verification, Claude Code copies marketplace plugins into ~/.claude/plugins/cache rather than using them in place, except command sources in link mode. Each installed version is a separate cache directory grouped by marketplace and plugin and named for the resolved version, with its own copy of the files and Node.js dependencies. Plugins can also be specified per-session with --plugin-dir or --plugin-url.

nodes.label: Orphaned version-directory sweep
nodes.rationale: On update or uninstall, Claude Code marks the previous version directory orphaned and removes it in a background sweep roughly 14 days later, so concurrent sessions holding the old version keep running; the sweep runs only while at least one plugin is installed. A symlinked development checkout in the cache is never orphaned or removed, and Glob and Grep skip orphaned version directories.

nodes.label: Automatic Node.js dependency install
nodes.rationale: When Claude Code copies a plugin into the cache it installs the plugin's own npm or Bun dependencies there, on install, on update, and at session start when an enabled plugin is not yet cached. The install runs only when the plugin root has both a package.json and a supported lockfile: bun.lock/bun.lockb use `bun install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts`, npm-shrinkwrap.json/package-lock.json use `npm ci --ignore-scripts`. yarn.lock and pnpm-lock.yaml are skipped because those managers support resolution-time hooks that bypass --ignore-scripts.

nodes.label: Constraints on the dependency install
nodes.rationale: The dependency install is constrained so no plugin or package code executes during it: frozen resolution (fail rather than re-resolve when package.json and the lockfile disagree), --ignore-scripts (no preinstall/install/postinstall), and a 60-second timeout after which the install is treated as failed. A failed or skipped install never blocks the plugin, cannot be disabled by any setting, and a timeout can leave a partial node_modules tree.

nodes.label: Path traversal limitations
nodes.rationale: Claude Code rejects a component path that resolves outside the plugin root, such as ../shared-utils, whether declared in plugin.json or in a marketplace entry, reporting a `path escapes plugin directory` error and loading the plugin without that component. It also does not copy files above the plugin root into the cache, so a script inside a copied plugin cannot read them either.

nodes.label: Sharing files within a marketplace via symlinks
nodes.rationale: How a symlink inside a plugin is handled at cache time depends on its target: within the plugin's own directory it is preserved as a relative symlink; elsewhere in the same marketplace it is dereferenced and the content copied (letting a meta-plugin's skills/ link to sibling plugins' skills); outside the marketplace it is skipped for security. For --plugin-dir, local-path and copy-mode command installs, only symlinks resolving within the plugin's own directory are preserved.

nodes.label: Standard plugin directory layout
nodes.rationale: A complete plugin holds .claude-plugin/plugin.json plus skills/, commands/, agents/, workflows/, output-styles/, themes/, monitors/, hooks/, bin/, settings.json, .mcp.json, .lsp.json and scripts/ at its root. The .claude-plugin/ directory contains only the manifest — every other directory must sit at the plugin root, and putting them inside .claude-plugin/ is why components go missing while the plugin still loads.

nodes.label: bin/ executables on PATH
nodes.rationale: Executables in a plugin's bin/ directory are added to the Bash tool's PATH and invokable as bare commands while the plugin is enabled. This directory cannot be included in a plugin distributed through claude.ai organization settings.

nodes.label: Plugin default settings.json
nodes.rationale: A settings.json at the plugin root supplies default configuration applied when the plugin is enabled, but only the agent and subagentStatusLine keys are supported.

nodes.label: A plugin's CLAUDE.md is not project context
nodes.rationale: A CLAUDE.md at the plugin root is not loaded as project context. Plugins contribute context through skills, agents and hooks, so instructions meant to reach Claude's context belong in a skill.

nodes.label: Default component file locations
nodes.rationale: Default locations are .claude-plugin/plugin.json (manifest), skills/, commands/ (flat markdown skills; new plugins should use skills/), agents/, workflows/, output-styles/, themes/, hooks/hooks.json, .mcp.json, .lsp.json, monitors/monitors.json, bin/ and settings.json. These are what Claude Code auto-discovers when no manifest overrides them.

nodes.label: claude plugin CLI
nodes.rationale: Claude Code provides non-interactive CLI commands for plugin management — init, install, uninstall, prune, enable, disable, update, list, details and tag — useful for scripting and automation.

nodes.label: claude plugin init
nodes.rationale: claude plugin init (alias new) scaffolds a plugin at ~/.claude/skills/<name>/ that loads on the next session as <name>@skills-dir with no install step. --with adds starter folders for skills, agents, hooks, mcp, lsp, output-style or channel; author defaults come from git config. Admins can block the skills-dir source via strictKnownMarketplaces or blockedMarketplaces, and init then fails before writing.

nodes.label: claude plugin install
nodes.rationale: claude plugin install <plugin|plugin@marketplace> installs from available marketplaces at a scope (--scope user, project or local; user by default), can set userConfig options with a repeatable --config key=value, and takes -y to accept a marketplace-declared command or headersHelper without the prompt. -y is required when stdin or stdout is not a TTY and has no effect inside a Claude Code session.

nodes.label: claude plugin uninstall
nodes.rationale: claude plugin uninstall (aliases remove, rm) removes a plugin at a scope; uninstalling from the last remaining scope also deletes its ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} directory unless --keep-data is passed. --prune additionally removes auto-installed dependencies no other plugin requires. The plugin-name@marketplace-name form uninstalls only that marketplace's copy — before v2.1.212 it could match a same-named plugin from a different marketplace.

nodes.label: claude plugin prune
nodes.rationale: claude plugin prune (alias autoremove) removes auto-installed plugin dependencies no installed plugin still requires; plugins installed directly are never touched. It lists orphaned dependencies and asks for confirmation, with --dry-run to preview and -y to skip the prompt (required when stdin or stdout is not a TTY).

nodes.label: claude plugin enable
nodes.rationale: claude plugin enable turns on a disabled plugin, and when the target is a marketplace install that declares dependencies it enables them transitively at the same scope. --scope is auto-detected from where the plugin is installed when omitted.

nodes.label: claude plugin disable
nodes.rationale: claude plugin disable turns a plugin off without uninstalling it. For a marketplace install it fails when another enabled plugin depends on it, and the error includes a chained command that disables every dependent first. -a/--all disables all enabled plugins and cannot be combined with --scope.

nodes.label: claude plugin update
nodes.rationale: claude plugin update updates a plugin at a scope (user, project, local or managed) and takes -y for marketplace-declared commands. A bare plugin name resolves against installed plugins; when installs from different marketplaces share the name Claude Code refuses and lists the qualified commands. Before v2.1.246 only the qualified form was accepted.

nodes.label: claude plugin list
nodes.rationale: claude plugin list prints installed plugins with version, source marketplace and enable status, with --json and --available (which requires --json). The in-session /plugin list covers marketplace installs only: skills-directory and synced plugins appear in claude plugin list but not inline, and --plugin-dir/--plugin-url plugins appear in claude plugin list only when the same flag precedes the subcommand.

nodes.label: claude plugin details and token cost
nodes.rationale: claude plugin details shows a plugin's component inventory (Skills — including commands — Agents, Hooks, MCP servers, LSP servers) and its projected token cost, split into always-on tokens added to every session by listing text and on-invoke tokens paid each time a component fires. The always-on total comes from the count_tokens API for the active model, per-component numbers are proportionally scaled, and a character-based estimate is the fallback when the API is unreachable.

nodes.label: claude plugin tag
nodes.rationale: claude plugin tag creates a release git tag for a plugin — the one in the current directory by default, or at a given path — with --push, --dry-run, --force, an annotation -m message where %s stands for the version, and --remote (default origin).

nodes.label: claude --debug for plugin loading
nodes.rationale: claude --debug shows which plugins are loading, errors in plugin manifests, skill/agent/hook registration and MCP server initialization. It is also where a skipped LSP server's reason and a failed dependency install's warning appear.

nodes.label: Common plugin failures and their causes
nodes.rationale: The documented failure modes are: a plugin not loading (invalid plugin.json — run claude plugin validate), skills not appearing (skills/ or commands/ wrongly placed inside .claude-plugin/), hooks not firing (script not executable — chmod +x, wrong-case event name, or a non-matching matcher), MCP server failures (missing ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}), path errors (absolute instead of ./-relative paths) and LSP `Executable not found in $PATH` (language server not installed).

nodes.label: Version as the plugin cache key
nodes.rationale: Claude Code uses a plugin's version as the cache key deciding whether an update is available, skipping the update when the computed version matches what is installed. For every source type except command it resolves the version from the first of: plugin.json's version, the marketplace entry's version, the git commit SHA (github, url, git-subdir and relative-path sources in a git-hosted marketplace), the SHA-256 digest shortened to 12 characters for archive sources, then `unknown` for npm sources or local directories outside a git repository.

nodes.label: command-source version derivation
nodes.rationale: For a command source Claude Code always derives the version from what the command produced: a 12-character content hash alone, or appended to plugin.json's version as <version>-<hash>. The marketplace entry's version is ignored, so changed hashed output yields a new version even when the authored version string is unchanged; in link mode the hash covers the printed directory's real path and top-level entries rather than file contents.

nodes.label: Three ways to version a plugin
nodes.rationale: Explicit version (set version in plugin.json) suits published plugins with stable release cycles — users update only on a bump, and pushing commits without one reports "already at the latest version". Commit-SHA version (omit version everywhere) suits internal plugins under active development — users update whenever the resolved commit changes. Digest version (an archive source with no version) updates on a changed sha256 pin, or on changed zip bytes when unpinned. Explicit versions should follow semantic versioning.

nodes.label: Prompt caching in Claude Code
nodes.rationale: Claude Code manages prompt caching automatically unless it is disabled. Without caching the API would reprocess the full history every turn; with caching it reuses what it already processed, bills the re-read at the cached token rate, and fully processes only what changed.

nodes.label: Exact prefix matching
nodes.rationale: The API caches by matching the start of each request — the prefix — against content it recently processed. The match is exact, so a change anywhere in the prefix recomputes everything after it. There is no per-file or per-segment caching.

nodes.label: Stable-first request layering
nodes.rationale: To get the most out of prefix matching, Claude Code orders each request so content that rarely changes between turns comes first: system prompt, then project context, then conversation.

nodes.label: System prompt layer
nodes.rationale: The first layer holds core instructions, tool definitions and output style. It changes when the set of loaded tool definitions changes or Claude Code is upgraded, and a change to it invalidates everything because all later content sits behind a different prefix.

nodes.label: Project context layer
nodes.rationale: The second layer holds CLAUDE.md, auto memory and unscoped rules. It changes when a session starts, or after /clear or /compact.

nodes.label: Conversation layer
nodes.rationale: The last layer holds your messages, Claude's responses and tool results, and changes every turn. A change confined to it leaves the system prompt and project context cached.

nodes.label: Model as part of the cache key
nodes.rationale: The model is not part of the prompt text but is part of the cache key: each model has its own cache, so switching models recomputes the entire request even when the content is identical.

nodes.label: Effort level as part of the cache key
nodes.rationale: Each effort level has its own cache for the same model, so changing effort mid-session recomputes the entire request. Like the model, it is not part of the prompt text and so does not appear in the layer table.

nodes.label: Actions that invalidate the cache
nodes.rationale: A named set of actions cause the next request to miss part or all of the cache, producing one slower and more expensive turn after which the new prefix is cached. Most are avoidable mid-task once you know they have a cost.

nodes.label: Actions that keep the cache
nodes.rationale: A second named set of actions either append to the end of the conversation or do not touch the request at all. Some of them, such as editing CLAUDE.md or changing output style, are also why a setting change waits for a restart to apply.

nodes.label: Where the cache lives
nodes.rationale: Caching happens server-side in whichever infrastructure serves the model: Anthropic's for an API key, Claude subscription or Claude Platform on AWS; the cloud provider's for Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud's Agent Platform; deployment-dependent for Microsoft Foundry; and wherever requests are forwarded for a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL or LLM gateway.

nodes.label: Gateway handling of cache_control markers
nodes.rationale: Through a gateway or base-URL override, what stays cached depends on how cache_control markers are handled: forwarded unchanged caches as at the provider's endpoint; a 400 naming cache_control makes Claude Code move the marker onto the last conversation message for the rest of the conversation; and silently removing the markers bills the entire conversation history as uncached input every turn.

nodes.label: Mid-conversation system context block
nodes.rationale: Claude Code appends system context mid-conversation, such as file-change notices, and marks that block for caching on every provider and connection. Bedrock (including its Mantle endpoint), Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry cache the block the same way the Claude API does.

nodes.label: Switching models
nodes.rationale: Switching with /model means the next request reads the entire conversation history with no cache hits, even though the content is identical, because each model has its own cache.

nodes.label: Warm-cache model switch confirmation
nodes.rationale: Claude Code asks you to confirm a terminal /model switch only while the cache is still warm — one cache TTL after the last request or response — and switches without asking once it has expired. Before v2.1.238 it did not check the TTL and asked even after expiry. A PreModelSwitch hook can require or skip the confirmation.

nodes.label: opusplan plan-mode model switch
nodes.rationale: The opusplan model setting resolves to Opus during plan mode and Sonnet during execution, so each plan-mode toggle is a model switch and starts a fresh cache.

nodes.label: Automatic model fallback
nodes.rationale: Automatic model fallback on Fable 5.1, Fable 5 and Opus 5 is also a model switch: when a safety classifier flags a request and the flagged category has a fallback model, Claude Code re-runs the request on that model and the session continues there.

nodes.label: Changing effort level
nodes.rationale: Switching with /effort means the next request reads the entire conversation history with no cache hits. When a change resolves to the level already in effect, such as setting the model's default explicitly, Claude Code keeps the cache and applies the change without asking.

nodes.label: Fast mode request header
nodes.rationale: Enabling fast mode adds a request header that is part of the cache key, so the first request sent with it reads the whole history uncached, billed at fast mode rates. The header is set once at turn start, the cost applies once per conversation, and turning fast mode off, falling back to standard speed after a rate limit, or turning it back on all keep the cache.

nodes.label: Connecting or disconnecting an MCP server
nodes.rationale: The cache invalidates when the set of tool definitions in the request changes between turns; whether an MCP server change does that depends on whether its tools are deferred or loaded into the prefix. Editing MCP config does not by itself change the cache — it takes effect only after a restart, which is when the server connects or disconnects.

nodes.label: Deferred MCP tools
nodes.rationale: Deferring tools via tool search is the default on supported models: a server connecting, disconnecting or changing its tool list only appends new content and does not disturb anything already cached.

nodes.label: Tools loaded into the prefix
nodes.rationale: When tool search is unavailable or disabled — older Google Cloud Agent Platform models, a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL gateway, an Azure-hosted Microsoft Foundry deployment that rejects tool search, an alwaysLoad server, or threshold-based loading — definitions sit in the prefix and any change to them invalidates the cache, including an unattended stdio exit, HTTP session expiry, automatic reconnection, or a dynamic tool update.

nodes.label: Advisor tool sits after the breakpoint
nodes.rationale: Toggling the advisor tool is an exception to the tool-definition rule: its definition sits after the cache breakpoint, so enabling or disabling /advisor keeps the cached prefix intact.

nodes.label: Enabling or disabling a plugin
nodes.rationale: What a plugin enable or disable costs depends on which component types the plugin provides. A plugin that provides MCP servers follows the MCP rules; enabling a code intelligence plugin gives Claude the LSP tool.

nodes.label: Plugin components that keep the cache
nodes.rationale: Claude Code never invalidates the cache for a plugin's skills, commands, agents, hooks, monitors or themes: it appends their content after the existing conversation, so the next request pays only for that content and reads everything before it from cache.

nodes.label: When plugin changes apply
nodes.rationale: A plugin change applies on /reload-plugins or a new session, and the cost lands on the first turn after it applies rather than at /plugin enable. Claude Code can also apply one itself for a command-source plugin, during an install from the /plugin interface, or when moving the session with /cd on v2.1.246+. A /reload-plugins that would trigger a full re-read is refused with a warning unless rerun with --force.

nodes.label: Disabling a plugin restores the earlier prefix
nodes.rationale: Disabling a plugin you enabled earlier in the session restores the previous request shape; if that prefix is still within its cache lifetime, the next request reads the older cache entry instead of rebuilding.

nodes.label: Denying an entire tool
nodes.rationale: A bare tool name such as Bash or WebFetch as a deny rule removes that tool from Claude's context entirely; because built-in tool definitions live in the system prompt layer, adding or removing such a rule mid-session invalidates the cache, applied on the next request whether set via /permissions or a settings file.

nodes.label: Scoped and non-deny permission rules keep the prefix
nodes.rationale: Only a deny rule matching in the tool-name position invalidates the cache. Scoped deny rules like Bash(rm *) and all allow and ask rules do not change which tools Claude sees — they are checked when Claude attempts a call — and an mcp__* glob leaves the cache intact when the matched tools are deferred.

nodes.label: Compacting the conversation
nodes.rationale: Compaction replaces message history with a summary, which by design invalidates the conversation layer since the new shorter history shares no prefix with the old one. The system prompt layer is reused and project context is reloaded from disk, cache-hitting only if CLAUDE.md and memory are unchanged since session start.

nodes.label: Compaction summarization request
nodes.rationale: To produce the summary Claude Code sends a separate request with the same system prompt, tools and history plus a summarization instruction. While the cache is warm it reads the prefix from cache, so a mid-session /compact costs a fraction of what the context size suggests; after a break longer than the cache lifetime it reprocesses the full history as uncached input, which is why /compact costs most when resuming an old session.

nodes.label: Upgrading Claude Code
nodes.rationale: A new version typically updates the system prompt or tool definitions, so the first request after an upgrade rebuilds the cache from the top. Auto-update downloads in the background but applies on next launch, never mid-session; DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER=1 controls when upgrades apply.

nodes.label: Resuming a session after an upgrade
nodes.rationale: Resuming a session after an upgrade reprocesses the entire conversation history with no cache hits, because the history now sits behind a different system prompt. The cost scales with conversation length, so the first turn back into a long session can be the most expensive request you send.

nodes.label: Editing files in your repository
nodes.rationale: File contents enter context only when Claude reads them, and reads append to the conversation. Editing a previously read file does not retroactively change the earlier read; Claude Code appends a <system-reminder> noting the change and Claude re-reads if needed.

nodes.label: Editing CLAUDE.md mid-session
nodes.rationale: Project-root and user-level CLAUDE.md files are read once at session start and held in memory. Editing them mid-session does not invalidate the cache, but the edit also does not apply — the new content loads on the next /clear, /compact or restart.

nodes.label: Nested CLAUDE.md and path-scoped rules
nodes.rationale: Nested CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories and rules with paths: frontmatter load later, when Claude first reads a matching file. Editing one before it loads does take effect; after it loads the content is part of conversation history, so a mid-session edit does not retroactively change it.

nodes.label: Changing output style
nodes.rationale: Output style is part of the system prompt, read once at session start. Changing it via /config or the outputStyle setting mid-session does not invalidate the cache, but the change also does not apply until the next /clear or restart.

nodes.label: Changing permission mode
nodes.rationale: Switching between permission modes, such as Manual to accept edits, changes neither the system prompt nor tool definitions, so mode changes are cache-safe.

nodes.label: Invoking skills and commands
nodes.rationale: Skills and commands inject their instructions as user messages at the point of invocation, so nothing earlier in the conversation changes. Plan mode and skill loading append their instructions as conversation messages for the same reason, leaving the cached prefix intact.

nodes.label: /recap
nodes.rationale: /recap generates a summary for display in the terminal. Unlike /compact it appends the summary as command output rather than replacing message history, so the cached prefix stays intact.

nodes.label: Rewinding the conversation
nodes.rationale: /rewind truncates the conversation back to an earlier turn whose remaining history is exactly what the cache was built from, so the next request hits the earlier cache entry — kept warm because every turn since read through that prefix. Restoring file checkpoints has no separate cache effect.

nodes.label: Cache lifetime and TTL
nodes.rationale: Cached prefixes expire after a period of inactivity and each cache hit resets the timer, so the cache stays warm while you keep working. After a long enough gap the next request recomputes the full input, which is why the first turn back after stepping away is noticeably slower.

nodes.label: Five-minute vs one-hour TTL trade-off
nodes.rationale: The API offers a five-minute TTL and a one-hour TTL. The hour keeps the cache warm through longer breaks but bills cache writes at a higher rate, so it helps for idle-and-return sessions and costs more on short bursts of work that never idle past five minutes.

nodes.label: Two fixed TTL request buckets
nodes.rationale: Claude Code decides the TTL per request and every request falls into one of two fixed buckets: the main conversation (interactive turns, -p runs, Agent SDK turns and inline helpers) and everything else (subagents, workflows, in-process teammates, forks, compaction and session titles).

nodes.label: Default TTL by billing type
nodes.rationale: On a Claude subscription within plan usage the main conversation defaults to one hour and everything else to five minutes except server-controlled helper requests, which get an hour. On usage credits, an API key or a cloud provider both buckets default to five minutes, and going over the plan limit drops the main conversation to the cheaper five-minute TTL.

nodes.label: promptCacheTtl and subagentPromptCacheTtl controls
nodes.rationale: You can set a TTL per bucket: promptCacheTtl or CLAUDE_CODE_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL for the main conversation, subagentPromptCacheTtl or CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL for everything else. Each accepts only 5m or 1h and all four require Claude Code v2.1.242 or later.

nodes.label: TTL precedence order
nodes.rationale: When several controls apply, Claude Code takes the first match: FORCE_PROMPT_CACHING_5M=1, then the bucket's environment variable, then the bucket's setting, then a subagent's experimental cacheTtl frontmatter (v2.1.248+, and a 1h there is ignored while the subscription is on usage credits), then ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H=1, then the bucket's default.

nodes.label: FORCE_PROMPT_CACHING_5M
nodes.rationale: FORCE_PROMPT_CACHING_5M=1 forces five minutes for both buckets and wins over every other TTL control. Set it when debugging cache behavior, comparing the two TTLs, or overriding a longer TTL set in managed settings.

nodes.label: Confirming which TTL cache writes used
nodes.rationale: Run claude -p "hello" --output-format json and read usage.cache_creation: one-hour cache writes are reported under ephemeral_1h_input_tokens and five-minute writes under ephemeral_5m_input_tokens. Through an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL gateway the one-hour request partly travels in the anthropic-beta header, which the gateway must forward unchanged.

nodes.label: Cache scoped to one machine and directory
nodes.rationale: In Claude Code the cache is effectively scoped to one machine and directory: the system prompt embeds working directory, platform, shell, OS version and auto memory paths, so sessions in different directories — including worktrees of the same repository — miss each other's cache. Parallel sessions in the same directory share a prefix; sequential ones share it only when the startup git status snapshot matches.

nodes.label: Broader API cache scope
nodes.rationale: The underlying API cache is broader: caches are isolated between organizations and, on some providers, between workspaces within an organization, and within those boundaries any two requests with the same model and prefix read the same cache. Agent SDK fleets can suppress per-machine system prompt sections to share the cache across machines.

nodes.label: Cache creation and read token fields
nodes.rationale: Cache performance shows up as two token counts on every response: cache_creation_input_tokens (written to cache, billed at the write rate) and cache_read_input_tokens (served from cache, billed at roughly 10% of the standard input rate). A high read-to-creation ratio means caching is working; persistently high creation means something is changing in the prefix.

nodes.label: /usage prompt cache statistics
nodes.rationale: For a per-session summary, /usage adds a Prompt cache (main) line to the Session block after the first response, showing hit ratio, miss count and whether the cache is warm right now. A statusline script can read the same numbers from the prompt_cache object; both require Claude Code v2.1.251 or later.

nodes.label: OpenTelemetry cache metrics
nodes.rationale: For visibility across an organization, the OpenTelemetry exporter reports cache read and creation tokens per user and session.

nodes.label: Subagents warm their own cache
nodes.rationale: A subagent starts its own conversation with its own system prompt and tool set, so its first request does not read the parent's cache and it warms one of its own across its turns. It falls outside the main-conversation TTL bucket, getting five minutes even on a subscription, and the parent's prefix stays intact because the call and result merely append.

nodes.label: Forks inherit the parent's cache
nodes.rationale: A fork, by contrast with a subagent, inherits the parent's system prompt, tools and conversation history exactly, so its first request reads the parent's cache.

nodes.label: Workflow fan-out prefix sharing
nodes.rationale: In a workflow fan-out of same-prefix agents, Claude Code briefly holds all but the first agent so their first requests can read the prefix the first agent cached.

nodes.label: Disabling prompt caching
nodes.rationale: Setting DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING=1 turns caching off for all models, with per-model variants DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_HAIKU, _SONNET, _OPUS and _FABLE. It is occasionally useful when debugging caching behavior with a specific model or provider; organization-wide policy goes in the env block of managed settings, and for normal use caching should stay enabled.

nodes.label: Claude Code Quickstart guide
nodes.rationale: An eight-step onboarding guide that takes a new user from installing Claude Code to using it for common development tasks in a few minutes. It covers install, login, first session, asking questions, making a code change, Git operations, bug fixes/features, and other workflows.

nodes.label: Prerequisites before you begin
nodes.rationale: Before starting you need an open terminal or command prompt, a code project to work with, and either a Claude subscription (Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise), a Claude Console account, or access through a supported cloud provider.

nodes.label: Terminal CLI scope of the guide
nodes.rationale: The quickstart explicitly covers the terminal CLI form of Claude Code, not the other surfaces it also ships on.

nodes.label: Other Claude Code interfaces
nodes.rationale: Beyond the terminal, Claude Code is available on the web, as a desktop app, in VS Code and JetBrains IDEs, in Slack, and in CI/CD via GitHub Actions and GitLab.

nodes.label: Native install (recommended)
nodes.rationale: The recommended install path: `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash` on macOS/Linux/WSL, `irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex` in Windows PowerShell, and a curl-based `install.cmd` invocation in Windows CMD.

nodes.label: Background auto-update of native installs
nodes.rationale: Native installations automatically update in the background to keep the user on the latest version; package-manager installs do not, and must be upgraded manually to get features and security fixes.

nodes.label: Telling PowerShell from CMD
nodes.rationale: `The token '&&' is not a valid statement separator` means you are in PowerShell, not CMD; `'irm' is not recognized` means you are in CMD, not PowerShell. The prompt shows `PS C:\` in PowerShell and `C:\` without `PS` in CMD.

nodes.label: Install failure troubleshooting path
nodes.rationale: If the install command fails with `syntax error near unexpected token '<'`, a 403, or another curl error, the Troubleshoot installation page matches the error to a fix and lists alternative install methods.

nodes.label: Git for Windows recommendation
nodes.rationale: Git for Windows is recommended on native Windows so Claude Code can use the Bash tool. WSL setups do not need it.

nodes.label: Shell tool selection on native Windows
nodes.rationale: On native Windows, Claude Code uses the Bash tool when Git for Windows is installed; if it is not installed, Claude Code falls back to PowerShell as the shell tool.

nodes.label: Homebrew cask install
nodes.rationale: `brew install --cask claude-code` installs Claude Code via Homebrew. Homebrew installs do not auto-update; `brew upgrade claude-code` (or `claude-code@latest`) is required to pick up new versions.

nodes.label: Homebrew stable vs latest casks
nodes.rationale: Homebrew offers two casks: `claude-code` tracks the stable release channel, typically about a week behind and skipping releases with major regressions, while `claude-code@latest` tracks the latest channel and receives new versions as soon as they ship.

nodes.label: WinGet install
nodes.rationale: `winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode` installs Claude Code on Windows. WinGet installs do not auto-update; run `winget upgrade Anthropic.ClaudeCode` periodically.

nodes.label: Linux package-manager installs
nodes.rationale: Claude Code can also be installed with apt, dnf, or apk on Debian, Fedora, RHEL, and Alpine.

nodes.label: claude --version install check
nodes.rationale: To confirm the installation worked, run `claude --version`; the command prints a version number followed by `(Claude Code)`.

nodes.label: Account requirement and first-use login
nodes.rationale: Claude Code requires an account to use. Starting an interactive session with the `claude` command prompts for login on first use.

nodes.label: Browser-based authentication
nodes.rationale: For Claude subscription or Console accounts, the user follows the prompts to complete authentication in the browser.

nodes.label: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY skips the login prompt
nodes.rationale: If the `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` environment variable is set, Claude Code skips the login prompt and instead asks the user to approve the key.

nodes.label: /login session command
nodes.rationale: Typing `/login` inside a running session switches accounts or re-authenticates. Where an organization runs a Claude apps gateway, `/login` opens directly on the Cloud gateway screen.

nodes.label: Supported account types
nodes.rationale: Login is supported with a Claude subscription plan, a Claude Console account, an enterprise cloud provider, or a self-hosted Claude apps gateway.

nodes.label: Claude subscription plans
nodes.rationale: Claude Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise subscriptions are the recommended way to log in to Claude Code.

nodes.label: Claude Console account
nodes.rationale: A Claude Console account gives API access with pre-paid credits and is one of the supported login paths.

nodes.label: Automatic Claude Code Console workspace
nodes.rationale: On first Console login, a "Claude Code" workspace is automatically created in the Console for centralized cost tracking.

nodes.label: Enterprise cloud provider access
nodes.rationale: Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry are the supported enterprise cloud providers for logging in to Claude Code.

nodes.label: Self-hosted Claude apps gateway
