nodes.rationale: An organization can run a self-hosted Claude apps gateway; the admin pre-configures the gateway URL and users sign in with corporate SSO from the Cloud gateway screen.

nodes.label: Stored credentials after login
nodes.rationale: Once logged in, credentials are stored so the user does not need to log in again; the Credential Management documentation covers the details.

nodes.label: Starting the first session in a project
nodes.rationale: A session is started by changing into any project directory and running `claude`; the working directory determines the project Claude Code operates on.

nodes.label: Session prompt header
nodes.rationale: The Claude Code prompt displays the version, the current model, and the working directory above it.

nodes.label: /help and /resume entry points
nodes.rationale: Inside a session, `/help` lists available commands and `/resume` continues a previous conversation.

nodes.label: Asking questions about the codebase
nodes.rationale: The recommended first use is understanding the codebase: asking what the project does, which technologies it uses, where the main entry point is, or to explain the folder structure. Claude can also be asked about its own capabilities.

nodes.label: Automatic project-file context
nodes.rationale: Claude Code reads project files as needed, so the user does not have to manually add context to the conversation.

nodes.label: First code change
nodes.rationale: Given a plain-language task such as adding a hello world function to the main file, Claude Code finds the appropriate file and shows the change; if it asks first, the user selects Yes to approve.

nodes.label: Permission modes
nodes.rationale: A session starts in a permission mode determined by plan, user settings, or organization policy, and the mode governs how much Claude Code does without asking.

nodes.label: Auto mode
nodes.rationale: Auto mode is the built-in starting permission mode for interactive terminal sessions on Pro, Max, and Team plans: a classifier reviews actions instead of the user, and Claude edits most files and runs most commands without asking.

nodes.label: Manual mode
nodes.rationale: On plans other than Pro, Max, and Team, Manual mode is the built-in starting permission mode.

nodes.label: Shift+Tab permission-mode switching
nodes.rationale: Pressing Shift+Tab at any time cycles the permission mode of the current session, regardless of which mode it started in.

nodes.label: Conversational Git operations
nodes.rationale: Claude Code makes Git operations conversational: asking what files changed, committing with a descriptive message, creating a branch, showing recent commits, and helping resolve merge conflicts.

nodes.label: Bug fixing and feature implementation
nodes.rationale: Claude is proficient at debugging and feature implementation; the user describes the desired feature or the observed bug in natural language rather than pointing at files.

nodes.label: What Claude Code does on an implementation request
nodes.rationale: For a bug fix or feature request Claude Code locates the relevant code, understands the context, implements a solution, and runs tests if available.

nodes.label: Other common workflows
nodes.rationale: Other everyday workflows include refactoring code (e.g. callbacks to async/await), writing unit tests, updating documentation such as a README, and reviewing changes to suggest improvements.

nodes.label: Essential shell commands
nodes.rationale: Shell commands run from the terminal to start or resume Claude Code: `claude` starts interactive mode, `claude "task"` starts it with an initial prompt, `claude -p "query"` runs a one-off query then exits, `claude -c` continues the most recent conversation in the current directory, and `claude -r` resumes a previous conversation.

nodes.label: Essential session commands
nodes.rationale: Session commands run inside Claude Code after it starts: `/clear` clears conversation history, `/help` shows available commands, and `/exit` (or Ctrl+D twice) exits Claude Code.

nodes.label: Pro tips for beginners
nodes.rationale: A set of beginner practices for getting better results: be specific, give step-by-step instructions, let Claude explore before changing, and use the interactive shortcuts. Talking to Claude like a helpful colleague — describing the goal — is the framing the guide recommends.

nodes.label: Be specific with requests
nodes.rationale: Instead of "fix the bug", state the symptom and the context: "fix the login bug where users see a blank screen after entering wrong credentials".

nodes.label: Use step-by-step instructions
nodes.rationale: Break complex tasks into numbered steps — e.g. create a database table, then an API endpoint, then the webpage that uses it — rather than giving one large request.

nodes.label: Let Claude explore first
nodes.rationale: Before making changes, let Claude understand the code — for example ask it to analyze the database schema before asking it to build something on top of that data.

nodes.label: Interactive shortcuts
nodes.rationale: Type `/` to see available commands and skills, use Tab for command completion, press the up arrow for command history, and press Shift+Tab to cycle permission modes.

nodes.label: What's next reading path
nodes.rationale: After the basics, the guide points to How Claude Code works (agentic loop and built-in tools), Best practices, Common workflows, and Extend Claude Code (CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks, MCP).

nodes.label: Getting help channels
nodes.rationale: Help comes from three places: `/help` or asking "how do I..." inside Claude Code, the rest of the documentation, and the Anthropic Discord community.

nodes.label: Remote Control
nodes.rationale: Remote Control connects claude.ai/code or the Claude iOS/Android app to a Claude Code session running on your own machine, so a task started at your desk can be picked up from a phone, tablet, or another browser. The web and mobile interfaces are a window into that local session, not a separate one.

nodes.label: Execution stays local
nodes.rationale: Claude keeps running locally for the whole Remote Control session, so code execution and filesystem access stay on your machine. Your filesystem, MCP servers, tools and project configuration all remain available, and typing `@` autocompletes file paths from your local project.

nodes.label: Subscription requirement
nodes.rationale: Remote Control is available on Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise plans; API keys are not supported. On Team and Enterprise it is off by default until an Owner enables the Remote Control toggle in Claude Code admin settings.

nodes.label: claude.ai login requirement
nodes.rationale: You must sign in through claude.ai with `/login` (or `claude auth login`). Without an eligible login, `claude remote-control` exits with an error, while `claude --remote-control` still starts an interactive session and shows a Remote Control failure notification shortly after launch. If ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set, unset it first.

nodes.label: Full-scope login token requirement
nodes.rationale: Long-lived tokens from `claude setup-token` or the CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN environment variable can only make model requests, so they cannot establish Remote Control sessions. The fix is `claude auth login` to obtain a full-scope session token.

nodes.label: api.anthropic.com endpoint requirement
nodes.rationale: Remote Control needs the session to talk to api.anthropic.com directly, because otherwise there is no claude.ai backend to pair with. It is unavailable on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry, when ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL points at another host such as an LLM gateway or proxy (enforced from v2.1.196), and behind an enterprise Claude apps gateway.

nodes.label: Feature-flag evaluation dependency
nodes.rationale: Remote Control availability depends on feature-flag evaluation, and DISABLE_TELEMETRY, DO_NOT_TRACK, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC and DISABLE_GROWTHBOOK each disable it. The variable must be unset in the shell environment or in a settings.json `env` block; before v2.1.154 this configuration produced the misleading 'not yet enabled for your account' message.

nodes.label: Workspace trust requirement
nodes.rationale: You must run `claude` in the project directory at least once to accept the workspace trust dialog before using Remote Control. The startup trust dialog never saves trust for a home directory, so Remote Control must be started from a project directory.

nodes.label: Remote Control eligibility checks
nodes.rationale: Claude Code runs a set of distinct eligibility checks before Remote Control starts — account entitlement, environment-variable conflicts, endpoint routing, reachability of the feature-flag service, and the organization's Remote Control setting — each producing its own error message. Eligibility is checked even before printing help, so `claude remote-control --help` errors when the account is ineligible.

nodes.label: claude doctor eligibility diagnosis
nodes.rationale: `claude doctor` reports which individual Remote Control eligibility check failed, which is how you tell an account-level refusal apart from an environment-variable conflict, an unreachable feature-flag service, or an organization policy.

nodes.label: Organization policy and disableRemoteControl
nodes.rationale: Two independent policies can block Remote Control: an IT administrator's `disableRemoteControl` in managed settings on the device, and the server-side organization-wide Remote Control toggle an Owner controls at claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-code, which is off by default on Team and Enterprise. The error message's own text says which one applies.

nodes.label: Server mode (claude remote-control)
nodes.rationale: Running `claude remote-control` in a project directory keeps a process running in the terminal as a server waiting for remote connections. It displays a session URL, shows a QR code when you press spacebar, and reports connection status and tool activity while a remote session is active.

nodes.label: Server-mode flags
nodes.rationale: Server mode accepts flags given after `remote-control`: `--name`, `--remote-control-session-name-prefix`, `-c/--continue`, `--session-id`, `--spawn`, `--capacity`, `--[no-]create-session-in-dir`, `--permission-mode`, `--debug-file`, `--verbose` and `--sandbox`/`--no-sandbox`. `--continue` and `--session-id` require v2.1.200 or later and are mutually exclusive with each other and with `--spawn`, `--capacity` and `--create-session-in-dir`.

nodes.label: --spawn session creation modes
nodes.rationale: `--spawn` chooses how the server creates sessions: `same-dir` (default, all sessions share the working directory and can conflict when editing the same files), `worktree` (each on-demand session gets its own git worktree, requiring a git repository), and `session` (single-session mode, set at startup only, rejecting additional connections). Pressing `w` at runtime toggles between same-dir and worktree.

nodes.label: --capacity concurrent session limit
nodes.rationale: `--capacity <N>` caps the number of concurrent sessions a server serves; the default is 32, and the flag cannot be combined with `--spawn=session`.

nodes.label: Global flags are not carried into spawned sessions
nodes.rationale: A global `claude` flag placed before `remote-control` (including one added by a wrapper script) is not carried over to the sessions the server creates. Claude Code allows it through only when dropping it cannot change what those sessions can do, such as `--verbose` or `--model`; for anything else, such as `--settings`, it refuses to start and names the flag to remove. Before v2.1.248 any option before `remote-control` caused an `unknown option` error on the flags after it.

nodes.label: Interactive mode (claude --remote-control)
nodes.rationale: `claude --remote-control` (alias `--rc`), optionally with a session name argument, starts a normal interactive terminal session with Remote Control enabled. Unlike server mode, you can type messages locally while the same session is also available remotely.

nodes.label: /remote-control from an existing session
nodes.rationale: Inside a running Claude Code session, `/remote-control` (or `/rc`), optionally with a name argument, starts a Remote Control session that carries over the current conversation history. The `--verbose`, `--sandbox` and `--no-sandbox` flags are not available with this command.

nodes.label: VS Code extension /remote-control
nodes.rationale: In the VS Code extension, typing `/remote-control` or `/rc` in the prompt box turns Remote Control on and shows a Remote Control indicator in the prompt-box footer; clicking it opens the session, and running the command again disconnects. Unlike the CLI it accepts no name argument and displays no QR code, deriving the title from conversation history or the first prompt.

nodes.label: /rc active status indicator and panel
nodes.rationale: An interactive terminal session shows a `/rc active` indicator in the footer while the connection is up (hidden if the terminal is too narrow); selecting it with the down arrow and Enter, or re-running `/remote-control`, opens a status panel with the session URL, a QR code, and a disconnect option that leaves the local session running. On failure the indicator switches to a persistent failure state carrying the reason.

nodes.label: Session taken over or ended elsewhere
nodes.rationale: When another device or Claude Code session took the session over, when you ended or archived it from another device or app, or when the server cannot find it, the failure reason says which and Claude Code deliberately omits its usual advice to run `/remote-control`. Reconnecting in those cases takes the session back or reopens an archived one, so the reason should be read before reconnecting.

nodes.label: Session URL reminders
nodes.rationale: While connected, Claude Code surfaces the session URL above the prompt box at two moments: a 'Still working' notification with a 'Check in from your phone' link when a turn exceeds a server-tuned threshold, and an 'Approve tool calls from your phone' notification after several permission prompts. They appear only a few times in total, cannot be configured or turned off, and each clears on its own.

nodes.label: Connecting from another device
nodes.rationale: An active session can be reached by opening its session URL in any browser, by scanning the QR code to open it in the Claude app, or by finding it by name in the session list at claude.ai/code or under Code in the mobile app, where Remote Control sessions show a computer icon with a green status dot. On connecting, the device shows subagents and workflows already running, and stopping one there stops that task on your machine.

nodes.label: Remote session title precedence
nodes.rationale: The remote session title is chosen in order: the name passed to `--name`, `--remote-control` or `/remote-control`; then a title set with `/rename`; then the last meaningful message in existing history; then an auto-generated name such as `myhost-graceful-unicorn` built from the hostname or `--remote-control-session-name-prefix`. Auto-generated titles match the conversation's language (or the `language` setting) on v2.1.176 or later.

nodes.label: Rename propagates back to the CLI
nodes.rationale: Renaming a session from claude.ai or the Claude app also updates the local title shown in `claude --resume`, the session name on the prompt bar, and the `claude agents` listing when the session runs in the background. Before v2.1.221 a remote rename updated only the title while the CLI kept its previous name; `/rename`, which runs in the CLI, set the name on any version.

nodes.label: What connected devices see
nodes.rationale: A connected device mirrors the terminal conversation as it happens, including compaction progress and `/clear` resets. Switching conversations with `/resume` does not send the switched-to conversation's title or earlier history to the device, though new messages flow both ways for whichever conversation is open, and a prompt sent mid-turn is queued and kept in the device's transcript.

nodes.label: Remote diff pane
nodes.rationale: When the session's directory is a git repository, a connected device's diff pane shows uncommitted changes: the device requests the diff over the connection and Claude Code computes it on your machine. With a clean working tree it instead serves the branch's changes since it diverged from the default branch. Before v2.1.247 the diff was reported only in sessions served by `claude remote-control`.

nodes.label: Model and effort control from a device
nodes.rationale: Picking a model from a connected device runs the local session on that model and is reflected in the terminal's `/model` picker, `/status` and `/config`; a pick from the device's model control lasts only for that session, while `/model <name>` sent from the device also sets the default for new sessions. Setting the effort level from the device applies to the session for that session only, is refused when CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL pins a level, and needs v2.1.234 or later on your machine.

nodes.label: Cross-session messaging over the same connection
nodes.rationale: The Remote Control connection also carries cross-session messages between your own sessions on different machines and from your Claude Code on the web sessions, routed through Anthropic servers like the rest of Remote Control traffic. This requires Claude Code v2.1.224 or later, and a terminal where Remote Control is off can neither see nor be reached by your sessions on other machines.

nodes.label: Forwarded dialogs expire
nodes.rationale: Permission prompts and AskUserQuestion questions stay open until answered, but other forwarded dialogs — such as the model-choice prompt after a safety refusal — wait five minutes by default and then close, continuing with the dialog's no-action default. `dialogExpiry` adjusts or disables that deadline (v2.1.224 or later); the mid-session Fable usage-credits consent prompt follows the same deadline but is shown only in the terminal and is never forwarded.

nodes.label: Auto-connect for all sessions (remoteControlAtStartup)
nodes.rationale: Remote Control activates only on an explicit `claude remote-control`, `claude --remote-control` or `/remote-control` unless auto-connect is on. The `/config` toggle 'Enable Remote Control for all sessions' takes true/false/default, and the settings-file equivalent is `remoteControlAtStartup`: a managed `true` outranks a user `false`, but a `false` in project or local settings still turns it off, while a `true` there is ignored so a checked-in file cannot enable it for everyone. Auto-connect signs in with your own claude.ai account and grants no one else access.

nodes.label: One remote session per interactive process
nodes.rationale: Outside server mode each Claude Code instance supports exactly one remote session at a time; running multiple instances gives each its own remote session. Running multiple concurrent sessions from a single process requires server mode.

nodes.label: Resuming sessions after stopping the server
nodes.rationale: Stopping `claude remote-control` with Ctrl+C makes its sessions stop responding remotely but does not archive them, provided no other server ran in that directory and `--no-create-session-in-dir` was not used. In the same directory, `claude remote-control` brings back every served session, `--continue` brings back only the one the server started with, and `--session-id <id>` brings back one by the URL segment between `/code/` and any `?`. These work for about four hours, and from v2.1.228 `--continue`/`--session-id` unarchive an archived session.

nodes.label: Resuming in a second terminal leaves Remote Control off
nodes.rationale: Resuming a conversation in a second terminal while the first still has Remote Control on prints a notice and leaves Remote Control off there rather than taking the session from the first terminal. While it is off, that terminal cannot see or be reached by your sessions on other machines; running `/remote-control` there moves Remote Control to it.

nodes.label: Conversation reconnection record
nodes.rationale: Each conversation carries a reconnection record naming the Remote Control session and the account that owned it, and that record decides whether and to which session `claude --resume`/`--continue` reconnects. Turning Remote Control off from the CLI status panel, VS Code, or an Agent SDK host removes the record unless the hosting app owns the claude.ai session; Claude Code before v2.1.227 did not record the account at all.

nodes.label: Resume outcomes
nodes.rationale: On resume, 'Couldn't reconnect to your Remote Control session' signals a possibly temporary failure; otherwise, if the server reports the recorded session gone, Claude Code starts a replacement without earlier messages when the record names your signed-in account, starts a new session silently when it names another account, and shows 'Previous session is unavailable' when the record has no account or the sign-in cannot be read. Behaviour differed before v2.1.232, v2.1.227 and v2.1.200.

nodes.label: "Previous session is unavailable"
nodes.rationale: This message means Claude Code could not bring back the previous Remote Control session and deliberately stopped rather than starting a new one, because the server reports a deleted session and one owned by another account identically. Running `/remote-control` starts a fresh session under the current login, and without restarting Claude Code first the conversation's earlier messages are left out of it.

nodes.label: Outbound-only connection model
nodes.rationale: The local session makes outbound HTTPS requests only and never opens inbound ports: it registers with the Anthropic API and polls for work, and the server routes messages between the web or mobile client and the local session over a streaming connection. All traffic goes through the Anthropic API over TLS using multiple short-lived credentials, each scoped to one purpose and expiring independently.

nodes.label: Transcript stored on Anthropic servers
nodes.rationale: While Remote Control is connected, the session transcript — your messages, Claude's responses and tool activity — is stored on Anthropic servers to keep the conversation in sync across devices and to let the session reconnect after a network drop. Execution and filesystem access still stay on your machine, and stored transcripts are retained under the Data usage policy.

nodes.label: disableRemoteControl setting
nodes.rationale: The `disableRemoteControl` setting turns Remote Control off entirely, and when applied through managed settings it disables Remote Control on that device independently of the organization-wide toggle and of how the user is signed in.

nodes.label: Zero Data Retention incompatibility
nodes.rationale: Organizations with compliance requirements such as Zero Data Retention cannot enable Remote Control; the admin panel's toggle is grayed out so an Owner cannot change it, and the error message's parenthetical names the incompatible configuration.

nodes.label: Trusted Devices
nodes.rationale: Trusted Devices is a beta, organization-wide Team/Enterprise setting requiring members to verify their device before viewing or steering Remote Control sessions from claude.ai, the mobile apps, or Claude Desktop. It ties access to a known device and a recent authentication rather than only a signed-in account, and applies solely to Remote Control — regular Claude chat, terminal Claude Code and API usage are unaffected.

nodes.label: Device enrollment
nodes.rationale: Each browser, phone or desktop app used for Remote Control enrolls its own credential, and enrollment is offered only shortly after a full sign-in so a device joins the trusted list as part of a real authentication rather than silently. Enrollment is a one-time step per device; unenrolled devices cannot view or steer Remote Control sessions, though regular Claude chat there is unaffected.

nodes.label: 18-hour recent sign-in and biometric step-up
nodes.rationale: Under Trusted Devices a member's sign-in must be no more than 18 hours old; rather than signing in daily, members confirm presence with Face ID, Touch ID, Windows Hello or a passkey, which refreshes the session immediately. A machine without a platform authenticator can use a hardware security key or sign in again instead.

nodes.label: Biometric data never leaves the device
nodes.rationale: Biometric checks run on the device through the operating system or browser, the same mechanism as passkey sign-in. Anthropic never receives or stores fingerprints, face data or any other biometric information; only the device's public key and basic metadata such as display name, platform and enrollment time are stored.

nodes.label: Enabling Trusted Devices
nodes.rationale: An Owner turns on 'Require trusted devices' under the Remote Control setting at claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-code. It applies to every member and to sessions started after enabling; sessions already running are not retroactively protected and continue without the device requirement until they end, and per-team or per-project scoping is not available.

nodes.label: Managing and revoking enrolled devices
nodes.rationale: Members review their enrolled devices — name, platform, enrollment date — in the Trusted devices section of claude.ai/settings/account, and removing one revokes its credential immediately while allowing re-enrollment after a fresh sign-in. Unused credentials expire on their own, and for a lost device where the member cannot sign in an admin can use 'Sign out everywhere' to revoke every session and enrolled device.

nodes.label: Terminal gets its credential automatically
nodes.rationale: The machine running Claude Code receives its own trusted-device credential automatically when the developer signs in to the CLI, so there is no separate enrollment step in the terminal. If the organization requires Trusted Devices and the machine is not enrolled, running `/login` performs the enrollment as part of sign-in.

nodes.label: Claude Code on the web
nodes.rationale: Claude Code on the web shares the claude.ai/code interface but executes in the cloud rather than on your machine. It suits kicking off a task with no local setup, working on a repo you have not cloned, or running multiple tasks in parallel, whereas Remote Control suits continuing in-progress local work from another device.

nodes.label: Choosing among away-from-terminal approaches
nodes.rationale: Claude Code offers several ways to work away from the terminal, differing in trigger, where Claude runs, and setup cost: Dispatch (Desktop, from the mobile app), Remote Control (your machine, CLI or VS Code), Channels (chat-app or server events), Slack (Anthropic cloud), self-hosted environments (your organization's infrastructure), and scheduled tasks (CLI, Desktop or cloud).

nodes.label: Mobile push notifications
nodes.rationale: When Remote Control is active, Claude can push notifications to your phone, typically when a long-running task finishes or a decision is needed, and you can request one in a prompt. Setup is: install the Claude app, sign in with the same account and organization, allow OS notifications, and enable 'Push when Claude decides' and/or 'Push when actions required' via `/config`. There is no per-event configuration beyond those two toggles.

nodes.label: Push suppression while you are present
nodes.rationale: Claude Code skips mobile pushes while you are typing in or focused on the connected terminal. From v2.1.181, setting CLAUDE_CLIENT_PRESENCE_FILE to a marker-file path extends that to any time you are at the machine — pushes are skipped while the file exists — so a screen-lock listener can create it on unlock and delete it on lock.

nodes.label: Reconnection and message queueing
nodes.rationale: If the laptop sleeps or the network drops, Claude Code reconnects automatically once the machine is back online, and while the connection rebuilds it queues messages, permission prompts and status updates from subagents and workflows, delivering them once the connection recovers.

nodes.label: HTTP 403 refusal handling
nodes.rationale: Once an interactive session is connected, Claude Code keeps retrying for up to three minutes when something between the machine and Anthropic's servers answers HTTP 403, as can happen after a VPN or network change. If the refusals persist it disconnects and the reason names what refused — a network edge, or a proxy, VPN or firewall on your own network.

nodes.label: Extended network outage behaviour
nodes.rationale: During a long outage on an awake machine the behaviour depends on the mode: server mode gives up after roughly 10 minutes and the `claude remote-control` process exits, requiring a fresh start, while an interactive session keeps working locally, retries for as long as the outage lasts, and reconnects on its own when the network returns.

nodes.label: Presence heartbeat failures
nodes.rationale: When only the session's presence heartbeats fail while the rest of the connection stays up, Claude Code re-registers the session for about 30 minutes and then disconnects with 'could not reach the Remote Control server for about 30 minutes'; running `/remote-control` reconnects.

nodes.label: Crashed sessions in server mode
nodes.rationale: If a session served by `claude remote-control` crashes, sending it a message from a connected device makes Claude Code serve it again; the server itself does not need restarting.

nodes.label: The local process must keep running
nodes.rationale: Remote Control runs as a local process, so closing the terminal, quitting VS Code, or otherwise stopping `claude` takes the session offline until it is brought back; unless Claude is mid-task, claude.ai and the app show it offline within seconds. Keeping a session alive on a remote machine after disconnecting from SSH requires `tmux` or `screen`.

nodes.label: Local-only vs remote-capable commands
nodes.rationale: Terminal-interface commands such as `/plugin` and `/resume` work only from the local CLI. From mobile and web you can use text-output commands (`/compact`, `/clear`, `/context`, `/usage`, `/exit`, `/usage-credits`, `/recap`, `/reload-plugins`), argument forms of `/model`, `/effort`, `/fast`, `/color`, `/rename` and `/autocompact` (v2.1.221), plus `/mcp` (v2.1.166) and `/config` (v2.1.181) with surface-specific behaviour; on Team and Enterprise, `/usage-credits` from mobile or web cannot send the admin request because its confirmation exists only in the CLI.

nodes.label: "Remote credentials fetch failed"
nodes.rationale: This error means Claude Code could not obtain a short-lived credential from the Anthropic API; `claude remote-control --verbose` shows the full error. Common causes are not being signed in, a firewall or proxy blocking outbound HTTPS on port 443, or an earlier session-creation failure. A stale login token is NOT a cause from v2.1.224 onward — Claude Code refreshes and retries on its own.

nodes.label: "Remote Control got an unexpected server response"
nodes.rationale: The server accepted the request but replied in a form this version of Claude Code could not read while creating the remote session or fetching its credentials. Retrying on the same version fails identically, so the fix is `claude update` followed by `/remote-control`. The message was added in v2.1.225.

nodes.label: Routine
nodes.rationale: A routine is a saved Claude Code configuration — a prompt, one or more repositories, and a set of connectors — packaged once and run automatically when a trigger matches. Routines are created and managed at claude.ai/code/routines, from the Desktop app, or from the CLI, and all three surfaces write to the same cloud account.

nodes.label: Research preview status
nodes.rationale: Routines are in research preview: behavior, limits, and the API surface may change. Several limits (GitHub webhook hourly caps, /fire request and response shapes) are explicitly called out as preview-era and subject to change.

nodes.label: Cloud execution infrastructure
nodes.rationale: Routines execute on Anthropic-managed cloud infrastructure, or on an organization's self-hosted environment when routed there, so they keep working when the user's laptop is closed. Each run creates a new session alongside the user's other sessions.

nodes.label: Trigger model
nodes.rationale: A routine starts when one of its triggers matches. Any combination of schedule, API, and GitHub triggers can be attached to the same routine and added or removed at any time from the Select a trigger section of the edit form — for example a PR review routine that runs nightly, fires from a deploy script, and reacts to every new PR.

nodes.label: Schedule trigger
nodes.rationale: A schedule trigger runs the routine on a recurring cadence — hourly, daily, weekdays, or weekly — or once at a specific future time. Times are entered in the user's local zone and converted automatically, so the routine runs at that wall-clock time regardless of where the cloud infrastructure sits.

nodes.label: API trigger
nodes.rationale: An API trigger gives a routine a dedicated HTTP endpoint that starts a new session when POSTed to with the routine's bearer token. It is used to wire Claude Code into alerting systems, deploy pipelines, and internal tools, and is added to an existing routine from the web — the CLI cannot create or revoke tokens.

nodes.label: GitHub trigger
nodes.rationale: A GitHub trigger starts a new session automatically when a matching event occurs on a connected repository, such as pull_request.opened or a merged PR in an SDK repo. It can be configured from the web UI or, on Claude Code v2.1.225 or later, from the CLI.

nodes.label: Plan availability
nodes.rationale: Routines are available on Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans. They are created and managed at claude.ai/code/routines or from the CLI with /schedule.

nodes.label: Organization Routines toggle
nodes.rationale: Team and Enterprise Owners can disable routines for all members with the Routines toggle at claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-code. When disabled, existing routines stop running and members cannot create new ones; on v2.1.227 or later the same toggle also hides /schedule in the CLI. It is a server-side setting that cannot be overridden locally.

nodes.label: Autonomous run session
nodes.rationale: Routines run autonomously as full Claude Code cloud sessions: there is no permission-mode picker and no approval prompts during a run. The session can run shell commands, use skills committed to the cloned repository, and call any connectors included in the routine.

nodes.label: Run reach is scoped by three inputs
nodes.rationale: What a routine can reach is determined by the repositories selected, the environment's network access and variables, and the connectors included. The documentation instructs scoping each of those to what the routine actually needs, since there are no approval prompts during a run.

nodes.label: Personal account ownership
nodes.rationale: Routines belong to an individual claude.ai account, are not shared with teammates, and count against that account's daily run allowance. Anything a routine does through the connected GitHub identity or connectors appears as the owner: commits and PRs carry their GitHub user, and connector actions use their linked accounts.

nodes.label: Routine prompt
nodes.rationale: The prompt is called the most important part of a routine: because the routine runs autonomously, the prompt must be self-contained and explicit about what to do and what success looks like. The prompt input includes a model selector, and Claude uses the selected model on every run.

nodes.label: Fired prompt is an assigned task, not consent
nodes.rationale: When a trigger fires, the session receives the routine's saved prompt as its assigned task rather than as untrusted content arriving mid-conversation. The trigger attests only that the prompt was stored ahead of time by an authorized session on the account, so the fired prompt is not live user input and cannot act as approval or consent for actions during the run; content fetched during the run keeps its normal handling. Before v2.1.213 the prompt was framed as an untrusted background notification and Claude could refuse to act on it.

nodes.label: Repository cloning per run
nodes.rationale: One or more GitHub repositories are added to a routine, and each is cloned at the start of every run starting from the repository's default branch unless the prompt specifies otherwise. Claude creates claude/-prefixed branches for its changes.

nodes.label: Branch push permission rules
nodes.rationale: Pushes to claude/-prefixed branches are always accepted. When the prompt directs Claude to push elsewhere, Claude Code checks the push first and rejects it if the branch is protected on GitHub, someone else has an open pull request from that branch, or the branch carries commits authored by someone other than the routine owner.

nodes.label: GitHub access for cloning
nodes.rationale: Routines need GitHub access to clone repositories. When a routine is created from the CLI with /schedule, Claude checks whether the account has GitHub access for the repository the command was run from and, if not, adds a setup note naming how to grant it.

nodes.label: Cloud environment
nodes.rationale: Each routine uses a cloud environment that controls network access, environment variables, and setup scripts, and the routine inherits the environment's network policy on every run. A changed policy applies from the next run.

nodes.label: Default Trusted network access
nodes.rationale: The Default environment uses Trusted network access, which allows only a default allowlist of package registries, cloud provider APIs, container registries, and common development domains through the session's network. Requests on that path to hosts outside the allowlist fail with 403 and x-deny-reason: host_not_allowed.

nodes.label: Custom and Full network access
nodes.rationale: To reach additional domains, the environment's Network access is changed to Custom and the domains entered under Allowed domains, optionally keeping the default allowlist alongside them; Full grants unrestricted access. The new policy applies from the next run.

nodes.label: Environment variables versus API credentials
nodes.rationale: Environment variables provide values Claude can use during each run, but they are visible to anyone who uses the environment, so keys for APIs Claude calls during a run should be stored as API credentials instead.

nodes.label: Cached setup script
nodes.rationale: An environment's setup script installs the dependencies and tools a routine needs. Its result is cached, so the script does not re-run on every session.

nodes.label: MCP connectors in a routine
nodes.rationale: Routines can use the account's connected MCP connectors to read from and write to external services during each run, for example reading a Slack channel and creating Linear issues. All currently connected connectors are included by default, and unneeded ones should be removed because Claude can use every tool from an included connector, including writes, without asking permission during a run.

nodes.label: Connector traffic bypasses the allowlist
nodes.rationale: MCP connector traffic is routed through Anthropic's servers rather than the session's network path, so connectors added to a routine work without adding their hosts to the environment's Allowed domains.

nodes.label: Local CLI MCP servers are not connectors
nodes.rationale: MCP servers added locally in the CLI with `claude mcp add` are stored on the user's machine rather than on the claude.ai account, so they do not appear in a routine's connectors list. To use one, add it as a connector at claude.ai/customize/connectors or declare it in a committed .mcp.json so it is part of the cloned repository.

nodes.label: Schedule presets and timezone conversion
nodes.rationale: The Select a trigger section offers preset frequencies — hourly, daily, weekdays, weekly. Times are entered in the user's local zone and converted automatically, and the same local-to-UTC conversion applies to one-off timestamps.

nodes.label: Schedule stagger
nodes.rationale: Runs may start a few minutes after the scheduled time due to stagger, and the offset is consistent for each routine.

nodes.label: Custom cron interval with a one-hour floor
nodes.rationale: For a custom interval such as every two hours or the first of each month, pick the closest preset in the form and then run `/schedule update` in the CLI to set a specific cron expression. The minimum interval is one hour; expressions that run more frequently are rejected.

nodes.label: One-off scheduled run
nodes.rationale: A one-off schedule fires the routine a single time at a specific timestamp — for a reminder, a post-rollout cleanup PR, or a follow-up when an upstream change lands. After it fires the routine auto-disables and the web UI marks it as Ran; running it again requires editing the routine and setting a new time. From the CLI the time can be described in natural language and Claude confirms the absolute timestamp before saving.

nodes.label: One-off runs are exempt from the daily cap
nodes.rationale: One-off runs do not count against the daily routine run cap. They still draw down regular subscription usage like any other session.

nodes.label: Per-routine endpoint and bearer token
nodes.rationale: Each routine gets its own URL and bearer token, generated only after the routine is saved because they depend on the routine ID. The token is scoped to triggering that routine only, and can be rotated or revoked from the same modal with Regenerate or Revoke.

nodes.label: Token is shown once
nodes.rationale: After clicking Generate token the token must be copied immediately: it is shown once and cannot be retrieved later, so it should be stored somewhere secure such as the alerting tool's secret store.

nodes.label: POST /fire request
nodes.rationale: A routine is triggered by POSTing to its /fire endpoint with the bearer token in the Authorization header. The body accepts an optional `text` field for run-specific context such as an alert body or a failing log; the value is freeform and is not parsed, so structured payloads arrive as a literal string. A wrong routine ID or token fails with a 401 authentication error.

nodes.label: routine-fire-payload wrapper
nodes.rationale: The `text` value does not reach the routine as a bare message: it arrives wrapped in a <routine-fire-payload> block that labels it as untrusted data and tells Claude not to follow instructions inside it unless the routine's own prompt says to. Because anyone holding the bearer token can send text, the wrapper makes fire text from a leaked token arrive labeled as data rather than as direct instructions.

nodes.label: Prompt must opt in to fire text
nodes.rationale: Because fire text is wrapped as untrusted data, a routine's saved prompt must opt in to acting on it — for example "Investigate the alert described in the routine-fire-payload block" — or the routine treats the text as inert context.

nodes.label: experimental-cc-routine-2026-04-01 beta header
nodes.rationale: The /fire endpoint ships under the `experimental-cc-routine-2026-04-01` beta header. Request and response shapes, rate limits, and token semantics may change during the research preview; breaking changes ship behind new dated beta header versions, and the two most recent previous header versions continue to work so callers have time to migrate.

nodes.label: Fire response with session URL
nodes.rationale: A successful /fire request returns JSON with type `routine_fire`, a `claude_code_session_id`, and a `claude_code_session_url`. Opening that URL in a browser shows the run in real time and allows reviewing changes or continuing the conversation manually.

nodes.label: /fire is claude.ai-only
nodes.rationale: The /fire endpoint is available to claude.ai users only and is not part of the Claude Platform API surface, although the full reference (error responses, validation rules, field limits) lives in the Claude Platform documentation.

nodes.label: Claude GitHub App installation requirement
nodes.rationale: The Claude GitHub App must be installed on the repository being subscribed to, whichever surface configures the trigger; the web UI prompts to install it, while the CLI path requires installing it from the GitHub App page first. Running /web-setup grants repository access for cloning but does not install the app and does not enable webhook delivery.

nodes.label: GitHub webhook hourly caps
nodes.rationale: During the research preview, GitHub webhook events are subject to per-routine and per-account hourly caps, and events beyond the limit are dropped until the window resets. Current limits are shown at claude.ai/code/routines.

nodes.label: One session per event, never reused
nodes.rationale: Claude Code does not reuse sessions across GitHub events, so two updates to the same pull request produce two independent sessions.

nodes.label: Supported GitHub event categories
nodes.rationale: GitHub triggers subscribe to two event categories: Pull request (opened, closed, assigned, labeled, synchronized, or otherwise updated) and Release (created, published, edited, or deleted). Within each category a specific action such as pull_request.opened can be picked, or all actions in the category.

nodes.label: Pull request filters
nodes.rationale: Filters narrow which pull requests start a session, and all filter conditions must match. Fields are author, title, body, base branch, head branch, labels, is draft, and is merged; each pairs with an operator: equals, contains, starts with, is one of, is not one of, or matches regex.

nodes.label: matches regex tests the whole field
nodes.rationale: The `matches regex` operator tests the entire field value rather than a substring: matching any title containing `hotfix` requires `.*hotfix.*`, since bare `hotfix` matches only a title that is exactly that. For literal substring matching, the `contains` operator is used instead.

nodes.label: Green run status is not task success
nodes.rationale: A green status in the run list means only that the session started and exited without an infrastructure error — not that the task in the prompt succeeded. Blocked network requests, missing connector tools, and task-level failures surface in the run transcript rather than in the status indicator.

nodes.label: Routine detail page
nodes.rationale: The detail page shows the routine's repositories, connectors, prompt, schedule, API tokens, GitHub triggers, and past runs. From it a run can be opened as a full session, the schedule paused or resumed via the Repeats toggle, the routine edited via the pencil icon, or deleted — deletion leaves past sessions in the session list.

nodes.label: Run now
nodes.rationale: Run now starts a run immediately without waiting for the next scheduled time, and can optionally supply run-specific text that reaches the routine the same way as the API trigger's `text` field — wrapped as an untrusted payload.

nodes.label: /schedule CLI creation
nodes.rationale: Running /schedule (alias /routines) in any session creates a scheduled routine conversationally, optionally from a description such as `/schedule daily PR review at 9am`. A successful start looks like a conversation with follow-up questions before saving; the CLI creates scheduled routines only — API triggers must be added on the web, while GitHub triggers work from either surface on v2.1.225 or later.

nodes.label: CLI routine management
nodes.rationale: `/schedule list` shows all routines, `/schedule update` changes one, and `/schedule run` triggers it immediately. Claude can also answer run-history questions, listing recent runs with status and links and reading a run's log to explain tool errors, permission denials, and the final result; that requires Claude Code v2.1.227 or later.

nodes.label: No next run time without a schedule
nodes.rationale: A routine with no schedule trigger — one started only by API calls or GitHub events — has no next run time, and the CLI shows none when Claude saves or updates it. Before v2.1.211 the CLI reported a next run time in the year 1 for such routines.

nodes.label: Daily routine run cap
nodes.rationale: Routines draw down subscription usage the same way interactive sessions do, and in addition have a daily cap on how many runs can start per account. Current consumption and remaining daily runs are shown at claude.ai/code/routines or claude.ai/settings/usage.

nodes.label: Usage credits and metered overage
nodes.rationale: When a routine hits the daily cap or the subscription usage limit, organizations with usage credits turned on can keep running routines on metered overage; without usage credits, additional runs are rejected until the window resets. On Team and Enterprise plans an admin enables credits for the organization.

nodes.label: /schedule returns Unknown command
nodes.rationale: The CLI hides /schedule when a requirement is unmet: authentication with a Console API key, an Anthropic profile or federation credential, or a cloud provider such as Bedrock, Google Cloud Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry; being inside a Claude Code on the web session; an organization policy disabling Claude Code on the web; or an Owner having turned routines off. Setting ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, or apiKeyHelper takes precedence over a claude.ai login and must be removed.

nodes.label: claude.ai subscription login requirement
nodes.rationale: /schedule requires a claude.ai subscription login; API accounts are not supported for routines. If Claude responds that authentication is needed, the CLI has no stored claude.ai login and the fix is to run /login, sign in, and retry.

nodes.label: Local Desktop scheduled task
nodes.rationale: In the Desktop app's New routine flow, choosing Cloud creates a routine while choosing Local instead creates a Desktop scheduled task, which runs on the user's own machine with access to local files rather than in the cloud.

nodes.label: Example routine use cases
nodes.rationale: Each documented example pairs a trigger type with unattended, repeatable work tied to a clear outcome: nightly backlog maintenance, API-triggered alert triage that opens a draft fix PR, bespoke code review on pull_request.opened, post-deploy verification, weekly docs-drift PRs, and a library port on merged PRs in a parallel SDK repository.

nodes.label: Sandboxed Bash tool
nodes.rationale: The Bash sandbox lets Claude run most shell commands without stopping to ask permission: instead of approving each command, you define which files and network domains commands can touch, and the operating system enforces that boundary for every Bash command and its child processes. It is built into Claude Code and isolates Bash subprocesses only.

nodes.label: /sandbox command panel
nodes.rationale: Running /sandbox opens a panel with three tabs — Mode (how sandboxed commands are approved), Overrides (the allowUnsandboxedCommands setting), and Config (the resolved sandbox settings) — plus a Dependencies tab on Linux when a package is missing. Selecting a mode saves it to the project's .claude/settings.local.json, which Claude Code adds to the global gitignore.

nodes.label: Platform support (macOS, Linux, WSL2)
nodes.rationale: The sandbox runs on macOS, Linux, and WSL2. Native Windows and WSL1 are not supported — WSL1 because bubblewrap needs kernel features only WSL2 provides — so Windows users must run Claude Code inside a WSL2 distribution or a container.

nodes.label: OS-level enforcement
nodes.rationale: The sandbox is enforced with operating-system security primitives rather than by inspecting the command string, so the boundary holds on the running process regardless of what the model chose to run and even if an allowed command does more than its name suggests.

nodes.label: Seatbelt (macOS enforcement)
nodes.rationale: On macOS the sandbox uses the built-in Seatbelt framework, so there is nothing to install. Seatbelt also causes known friction: Go-based CLIs such as gh, gcloud and terraform may fail TLS verification under it.

nodes.label: bubblewrap (Linux/WSL2 isolation)
nodes.rationale: bubblewrap is the unprivileged sandboxing tool that enforces filesystem isolation on Linux and WSL2, installed with the distribution package manager (apt-get/dnf install bubblewrap socat). In an unprivileged container it cannot mount a fresh /proc and fails with 'Can't mount proc on /newroot/proc: Operation not permitted'.

nodes.label: socat network relay
nodes.rationale: socat is the second required Linux/WSL2 package: the relay used to route network traffic through the sandbox proxy. When it is missing, the /sandbox Dependencies tab is the only tab shown until it is installed and Claude Code restarted.

nodes.label: Optional seccomp filter
nodes.rationale: The seccomp filter is optional and adds Unix domain socket blocking; it is installed with `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime`. Without it the sandbox cannot block a Unix socket at all — which is why, on WSL2, launching a Windows binary can only be blocked when the filter is present. When only this optional filter is missing, the Dependencies tab appears alongside the other tabs.

nodes.label: AppArmor bwrap userns profile (Ubuntu 24.04+)
nodes.rationale: On Ubuntu 24.04 and later the default AppArmor policy prevents bubblewrap from creating the user namespaces it needs. If `sysctl kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns` returns 1, install an /etc/apparmor.d/bwrap profile granting bwrap the `userns` capability and reload AppArmor; the profile applies only to bwrap itself, not to the commands it runs inside the sandbox.

nodes.label: WSL2 Windows-binary launches over a Unix socket
nodes.rationale: On WSL2, launching a Windows binary such as cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or anything under /mnt/c/ is handed to the Windows host over a Unix socket, so whether a sandboxed command can do it follows the sandbox's Unix-socket settings. Set allowAllUnixSockets to permit the launches, or add the command to excludedCommands to keep it out of the sandbox entirely.

nodes.label: Sandbox modes
nodes.rationale: Claude Code offers two sandbox modes, chosen on the /sandbox Mode tab. Both enforce identical filesystem and network restrictions; the only difference is whether sandboxed commands are auto-approved or still require explicit permission.

nodes.label: Auto-allow mode
nodes.rationale: In auto-allow mode Claude Code runs a sandboxable command inside the sandbox and approves it automatically, without asking. Commands that cannot be sandboxed fall back to the regular permission flow. It works independently of the permission mode setting, so sandboxed Bash commands that modify files within the boundaries execute without prompting even in Manual mode, where the file edit tools would prompt.

nodes.label: Regular permissions mode
nodes.rationale: In regular permissions mode all Bash commands go through the regular permission flow even when they are sandboxed. This provides more control at the cost of more approvals.

nodes.label: Rules auto-allow never skips
nodes.rationale: Even in auto-allow mode, explicit deny rules are always respected; rm/rmdir against a critical path still goes through the regular permission flow; and content-scoped ask rules such as Bash(git push *) still force a prompt. Only a bare `Bash` ask rule (or the equivalent `Bash(*)`) is skipped for commands that actually run sandboxed.

nodes.label: Plan mode is the auto-allow exception
nodes.rationale: Plan mode is the single exception to auto-allow's independence from permission modes: there auto-allow does not widen approvals, and a bare Bash ask rule is not skipped, so sandboxed commands — including read-only ones — still prompt. Before v2.1.212 the skip applied in plan mode too and auto-allow ran sandboxed commands there without a prompt.

nodes.label: Unsandboxed retry escape hatch
nodes.rationale: Claude Code reports sandbox violations in the blocked command's result, naming the denied path or host, so Claude can analyze the violation and may retry the command with the `dangerouslyDisableSandbox` parameter. The retry runs outside the sandbox and therefore goes through the regular permission flow; an ask rule for `Bash(dangerouslyDisableSandbox:true)` forces a prompt on every retry even in auto mode.

nodes.label: allowUnsandboxedCommands / Strict sandbox mode
nodes.rationale: Setting `"allowUnsandboxedCommands": false` — shown as Strict sandbox mode on the /sandbox Overrides tab — makes the `dangerouslyDisableSandbox` parameter completely ignored, so every command must either run sandboxed or be listed in excludedCommands.

nodes.label: excludedCommands
nodes.rationale: excludedCommands names commands that run outside the sandbox entirely — the documented remedy for docker, watchman-dependent jest, Go CLIs failing TLS under Seatbelt, and repeatedly failing git commands. It has no managed-only lockdown, so a developer can always append entries; administrators are told to keep the managed list narrow.

nodes.label: Session temp directory and $TMPDIR
nodes.rationale: The session temp directory is writable inside the sandbox by default and Claude Code points $TMPDIR at it for sandboxed commands, while unsandboxed commands inherit the shell's own $TMPDIR unchanged — so the two resolve $TMPDIR to different directories. To pass temporary files between them, write under the working directory instead.

nodes.label: Filesystem isolation layer
nodes.rationale: Filesystem isolation is one of the sandbox's two independent layers: it controls which paths sandboxed commands can read and write. Its restrictions are enforced at the OS level, so every command inside the sandbox and all of its child processes respect them.

nodes.label: Default write behavior
nodes.rationale: By default sandboxed commands may write to the current working directory and its subdirectories, any directories added with --add-dir, /add-dir, or permissions.additionalDirectories, and the session temp directory. They cannot modify files outside those — including shell configuration files such as ~/.bashrc and system binaries in /bin/ — without explicit permission.

nodes.label: Default read behavior
nodes.rationale: The default read policy grants read access to the entire computer except certain denied directories — which still allows reading credential files such as ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.ssh/. There is no built-in credential deny list, so only the files and variables explicitly listed are restricted.

nodes.label: sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite
nodes.rationale: sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite grants write access to specific paths outside the working directory (e.g. ["~/.kube", "/tmp/build"]) when subprocess tools such as kubectl, terraform or npm need it. The docs recommend it over excluding the tool from the sandbox entirely with excludedCommands. Edits to these lists apply to the running session.

nodes.label: denyRead / allowRead specificity
nodes.rationale: When read rules overlap, the more specific path wins: a narrow allowRead re-opens part of a denied region, while a denyRead — exact path or wildcard such as ~/**/.env — holds inside a wider allowRead, so a broad allow cannot silently re-expose a secret.

nodes.label: Sandbox path prefixes
nodes.rationale: Sandbox filesystem paths use standard conventions: `/` is absolute, `~/` resolves to the home directory, and `./` or no prefix resolves relative to the project root for project settings or to ~/.claude for user settings. The same '.' therefore means different directories depending on which settings file holds the configuration.

nodes.label: sandbox.filesystem.disabled
nodes.rationale: Setting sandbox.filesystem.disabled to true skips filesystem isolation while keeping network isolation, giving sandboxed commands unrestricted read and write access to the host filesystem with egress still confined to allowed domains. It is off by default and requires Claude Code v2.1.216 or later; with it on, a sandboxed command can write shell startup files, $PATH executables or ~/.claude/settings.json to widen its own access on the next run.

nodes.label: Which settings sources may set filesystem.disabled
nodes.rationale: Because turning filesystem isolation off widens what sandboxed commands can do, only user settings, managed settings and the --settings CLI flag may set it — a checked-out project's .claude/settings.json or settings.local.json cannot. When managed settings configure sandbox.filesystem at all, or list any credentials.files entry with mode deny, the key is pinned to managed settings alone.

nodes.label: Whether a managed credentials.files entry pins filesystem.disabled
nodes.rationale: An explicit `deny` entry pins filesystem.disabled, and so does a `mask` entry degraded to deny by validation, because validation rewrites it while settings load. A `mask` entry applied as a mask does not pin, and neither does one that falls back to deny at sandbox startup — the fallback happens after the pin check has already read the settings.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB
nodes.rationale: CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB strips credentials from all subprocesses regardless of sandboxing, unlike sandbox.credentials which affects sandboxed Bash commands only. When it is set, Claude Code also ignores filesystem.disabled from every source, including managed settings, and keeps filesystem isolation on.

nodes.label: sandbox.credentials
nodes.rationale: sandbox.credentials declares credential files and environment variables to protect from sandboxed commands, each entry naming a path or variable plus a mode. The dedicated block keeps credential rules grouped separately from general filesystem rules and requires Claude Code v2.1.187 or later; file paths follow the same prefix rules as sandbox.filesystem.*.

nodes.label: credentials mode: deny
nodes.rationale: With mode deny, listed file paths are blocked for reads inside the sandbox — the same restriction filesystem.denyRead applies, so it does not survive disabling filesystem isolation — and listed environment variables are unset before each sandboxed command runs, which is independent of the filesystem layer. Deny entries merge across every settings scope: any scope can add one and no scope can remove another's.

nodes.label: Credential masking
nodes.rationale: Masking goes further than deny: instead of blocking a credential, Claude Code shows sandboxed commands a sentinel placeholder and the sandbox proxy swaps in the real value on outbound requests to allowed hosts, so tools keep authenticating while the command and its logs never hold the real secret. When the same variable is listed with deny in any scope, deny takes precedence.

nodes.label: Masked environment variables
nodes.rationale: "mode": "mask" on an envVars entry (Claude Code v2.1.199+) protects a credential while keeping tools such as gh or npm working, which a deny entry would break by removing the variable entirely. The sandboxed command sees a per-session sentinel; substitution covers request headers and bodies.

nodes.label: Masked credential files
nodes.rationale: File entries accept "mode": "mask" from Claude Code v2.1.221, and behaviour is platform-split: on Linux and WSL2 sandboxed commands read a sentinel copy of the file and the proxy substitutes the real value on egress, while on macOS the file simply cannot be read — no sentinel copy, no substitution, the same effect as deny except that the read block holds even with filesystem isolation off.

nodes.label: Sentinel value
nodes.rationale: The sentinel is the per-session placeholder a sandboxed command sees in place of a masked credential. Verifying a file mask is as simple as running `cat` on the file in a sandboxed command: on Linux and WSL2 the output shows the sentinel, on macOS the read fails instead.

nodes.label: Sandbox proxy
nodes.rationale: Network access is controlled through a proxy server running outside the sandbox: it enforces the domain allowlist from the client-supplied hostname, tunnels allowed connections through any upstream corporate proxy, and — when masking is configured — substitutes real credentials into outbound request contents.

nodes.label: network.tlsTerminate
nodes.rationale: The experimental network.tlsTerminate setting (v2.1.199+) makes the built-in proxy terminate TLS itself, which credential masking requires because the proxy must see request contents to substitute into them. Without it masking fails safely — the command still sees only the sentinel, but the sentinel reaches the server and authentication fails; Claude Code reports the misconfiguration at startup. It does not add content filtering.

nodes.label: injectHosts
nodes.rationale: Each mask entry may list injectHosts, the hosts the real value is allowed to reach; an entry with no injectHosts is substituted on requests to every host in network.allowedDomains. The proxy injects only on connections the domain allowlist admits, so each injectHosts destination must also be reachable through allowedDomains.

nodes.label: IPv6 spelling in injectHosts vs allowedDomains
nodes.rationale: The two lists use different matchers, so an IPv6 destination is spelled differently in each: allowedDomains takes the bracketed form ("[::1]") to admit the connection, while injectHosts takes the bare canonical compressed address ("::1"). A bracketed, zone-ID, or differently compressed spelling in injectHosts never matches, so the proxy silently never injects there.

nodes.label: claude doctor sandbox warnings
nodes.rationale: `claude doctor` surfaces two sandbox configuration defects that are otherwise silent: 'Sandbox credential injectHosts entries can never match their destination' (v2.1.229+) and 'Sandbox network domain entries have unreliable spellings', which names up to three affected entries and counts the rest.

nodes.label: extract pattern
nodes.rationale: `extract` is a regular expression applied across a value or file, replacing only the text captured by group 1 of each match, so structured content — a DATABASE_URL connection string, .netrc, JSON or YAML config such as ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml — still parses inside the sandbox while only the secret becomes a placeholder. The pattern must contain at least one capturing group; without it the whole value or file becomes one sentinel.

nodes.label: onExtractNoMatch
nodes.rationale: onExtractNoMatch decides what happens when matching finds nothing to mask: `warn` (the default) passes the value through unmasked, `deny` unsets the variable or makes the file unreadable, and `error` stops sandbox setup. Claude Code treats deny as error whenever the read block would not be enforced — with filesystem isolation off, or when a filesystem.allowRead entry re-opens the file's path.

nodes.label: decode: "jwt" and maskClaims
nodes.rationale: `decode: "jwt"` (v2.1.224+) verifies the value is a JSON Web Token and replaces it with a structurally valid fake token so code inside the sandbox that decodes it keeps working; `maskClaims` masks only named top-level payload claims and leaves the rest readable. For environment variables decode cannot be combined with extract; for files it may be used instead of or together with extract.

nodes.label: maskDuplicates
nodes.rationale: maskDuplicates (default false) also replaces verbatim copies of each masked value found outside the matched spans, for a secret repeated where matching does not reach. Because it matches raw substrings, a short or common value would be replaced everywhere it appears, so it is reserved for long, high-entropy secrets.

nodes.label: Fallback from mask to deny
nodes.rationale: mask applies to a single file, so each credential file is listed individually. Claude Code falls back to deny for any mask entry it cannot mask safely — a directory path, a glob, a file larger than 8 MiB, or a file that is not UTF-8 text — and the docs advise writing directories as explicit deny entries instead, since only an explicit deny pins filesystem.disabled.

nodes.label: mask is honored only from trusted settings sources
nodes.rationale: Because masking authorizes the proxy to send the real credential to listed hosts, Claude Code honors mask entries, network.tlsTerminate, credentials.allowPlaintextInject, awsPairs and sigv4 only from user settings, managed settings and the --settings CLI flag — never from a repository's .claude/settings.json or settings.local.json. Delivered through server-managed settings, they count as settings that need approval.

nodes.label: AWS SigV4 re-signing at the proxy
nodes.rationale: AWS requests carry SigV4 signatures over the request contents, so AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY must be masked together: the proxy detects a SigV4 request by the access key's sentinel and re-signs it after substituting the real values. Masking the secret alone leaves requests signed with the placeholder and failing at AWS — a case Claude Code warns about at startup, though not when only the key ID is masked.

nodes.label: credentials.awsPairs
nodes.rationale: Claude Code links the conventional AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY / AWS_SESSION_TOKEN variables into one credential automatically; credentials.awsPairs (v2.1.224+) groups differently named variables by hand. Each named variable must be a whole-value mask entry without extract or decode, the proxy re-signs on the hosts in the access key ID entry's injectHosts, and naming any conventional variable in a pair replaces the automatic pairing.

nodes.label: credentials.sigv4 passthrough forms
nodes.rationale: Three AWS request forms carry signatures the proxy cannot recompute — aws-chunked streaming uploads (per-chunk signatures chain off the seed), presigned URLs (the signature is in the URL, with no Authorization header), and SigV4A asymmetric signatures (no shared-key HMAC). By default the proxy fails such a request rather than forwarding a broken signature; credentials.sigv4 (v2.1.224+) can set a form to `passthrough` so the caller receives AWS's own rejection instead of a proxy error.

nodes.label: Network isolation layer
nodes.rationale: Network isolation is the sandbox's second independent layer, controlling which domains sandboxed commands can reach. Its restrictions apply to all scripts, programs and subprocesses spawned by commands, and it keeps working when filesystem isolation is turned off.

nodes.label: network.allowedDomains and deniedDomains
nodes.rationale: Claude Code pre-allows no domains by default; allowedDomains pre-allows hosts so no prompt is needed, and deniedDomains blocks specific domains even when a broader allowedDomains wildcard would otherwise permit them. The sandbox's domain lists are allowedDomains, deniedDomains, and the WebFetch(domain:...) rules that feed them.

nodes.label: First-use network approval prompt
nodes.rationale: The first time a command needs a new domain, Claude Code prompts for approval, or in auto mode sends the request to the classifier. Answering Yes allows the host for the rest of the session; 'Yes, and don't ask again' saves a WebFetch(domain:...) allow rule to local settings so the host stays allowed in future sessions.

nodes.label: network.strictAllowlist
nodes.rationale: Setting strictAllowlist to true in user, managed or CLI --settings makes Claude Code deny sandboxed commands any host outside the allowlist instead of prompting. It applies to sandboxed commands only — in-process tools such as WebFetch still follow their permission rules — has no effect from repository settings, and requires v2.1.219 or later.

nodes.label: allowManagedDomainsOnly
nodes.rationale: When allowManagedDomainsOnly is set in managed settings, non-allowed domains are blocked automatically instead of prompting, and only allowedDomains and WebFetch(domain:...) allow rules from managed settings are honored. It narrows but does not remove the escalation risk of running with filesystem isolation off, because the lock applies only to commands inside the sandbox.

nodes.label: Corporate proxy passthrough
nodes.rationale: When a network requires outbound traffic through a corporate proxy, set HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY in the settings `env` block — so background agents inherit them — or in the launching environment. Claude Code enforces the domain allowlist first and then tunnels allowed connections through that upstream proxy.

nodes.label: WebFetch(domain:...) wildcard forms
nodes.rationale: In a WebFetch(domain:...) rule the sandbox honors only two wildcard forms: a leading `*.` such as `*.example.com`, and a bare `*` (v2.1.186+). A wildcard in any other position, such as `example.*`, still matches fetches but has no effect on sandboxed commands.

nodes.label: Bracketed IPv6 literals in domain lists
nodes.rationale: To match an IPv6 address in a domain list, write the literal in brackets: "[::1]" matches every port and "[::1]:443" only port 443, with the port a number from 1 to 65535 and no leading zeros. The bracketed form requires v2.1.229+; before it, text after the last colon was read as a port. Choosing 'Yes, and don't ask again' saves the rule bracketed.

nodes.label: Conservative handling of ambiguous IPv6 entries
nodes.rationale: An unbracketed entry with two or more colons is ambiguous (`::1:443` is both a complete address and an address plus port), so Claude Code never guesses: on deny lists it blocks every reading the entry parses as, and on allow lists it never allows more than written — rewriting to the host-and-port reading when that parses cleanly, and possibly dropping the entry rather than widening the allowlist.

nodes.label: Sandbox protected paths
nodes.rationale: Inside directories sandboxed commands may write to, the sandbox still denies writes to the files Claude Code loads configuration and code from — .claude settings files, skills/agents/commands/hooks directories, .mcp.json, workflows and scheduled_tasks.json in and above the working directory; shell startup files, .gitconfig, .vscode/.idea and .git's hooks and config in it; files that would make the directory a bare git repo; and most of ~/.claude plus ~/.claude.json and .credentials.json. No allowWrite entry or Edit allow rule can exempt one; only filesystem.disabled turns the protection off, and a symlink appearing at a protected path is denied too.

nodes.label: Git worktree shared .git write exception
nodes.rationale: When the working directory is a linked git worktree, the sandbox also allows writes to the main repository's shared .git directory so commands such as git commit can update refs and the index. Writes to hooks/ and config inside that directory remain denied.

nodes.label: git 'unable to unlink old' failure
nodes.rationale: git merge, git checkout and similar commands fail with 'unable to unlink old' (ending in 'Read-only file system' on Linux/WSL2) when they must replace a file the sandbox denies writes to — a protected path such as .claude/skills, a denyWrite entry, or anything outside the writable directories. The remedy is to approve the unsandboxed retry, run the command in another terminal, or add it to excludedCommands.

nodes.label: @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime
nodes.rationale: The same OS primitives the built-in sandbox uses are available as the standalone @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime package, documented as a separate approach for wrapping the entire Claude Code process. Installing it globally with npm is also how the optional seccomp filter is supplied.

nodes.label: Permission rules
nodes.rationale: Permission rules control which tools Claude Code can use and are evaluated before any tool runs, applying to Bash, Read, Edit, WebFetch, MCP and others. Some of them also shape the sandbox: Edit allow rules grant write access exactly as filesystem.allowWrite does, Read and Edit deny rules block paths, and WebFetch(domain:...) rules control domains — all merged into the final sandbox configuration.

nodes.label: Permission modes
nodes.rationale: /sandbox is not a permission mode: permission modes decide whether a tool call runs and whether you are prompted, while the sandbox restricts what a Bash command can access once it runs. Auto mode replaces the prompt with a classifier, --dangerously-skip-permissions replaces it with nothing and also skips protected-path checks, and the sandbox's auto-allow replaces it with the boundary itself.

nodes.label: Enforcing sandboxing with managed settings
nodes.rationale: Administrators require the sandbox for every developer by delivering the `sandbox` keys through managed settings (an MDM-managed file or server-managed settings on Claude.ai). For boolean keys such as enabled and failIfUnavailable the managed value wins outright; for array keys such as excludedCommands and allowRead every scope merges, so developers can append widening entries unless a managed-only lock is set.

nodes.label: sandbox.failIfUnavailable
nodes.rationale: By default, if the sandbox cannot start because dependencies are missing or the platform is unsupported, Claude Code shows a warning and runs commands unsandboxed. Setting failIfUnavailable to true makes that a hard failure that blocks Claude Code from starting — intended for managed deployments that require sandboxing as a security gate.

nodes.label: allowManagedReadPathsOnly
nodes.rationale: Setting allowManagedReadPathsOnly to true in managed settings honors only the allowRead entries from managed settings, preventing developers from appending entries that widen read access beyond the organization-approved paths.

nodes.label: Custom proxy configuration
nodes.rationale: Organizations needing advanced network security can point Claude Code at their own proxy via sandbox.network.httpProxyPort and socksProxyPort, to decrypt and inspect HTTPS traffic, apply custom filtering, log requests, and integrate with existing security infrastructure. Its CA certificate must be installed inside the sandbox.

nodes.label: Tool incompatibilities inside the sandbox
nodes.rationale: Several tools fail inside the sandbox even though they work outside it: watchman is incompatible so jest hangs unless run with --no-watchman; docker is incompatible and needs `docker *` in excludedCommands; Go-based CLIs such as gh, gcloud and terraform may fail TLS verification under Seatbelt; and host-not-allowed errors are resolved by granting the domain when prompted.

nodes.label: allowAppleEvents (macOS)
nodes.rationale: The macOS sandbox blocks Apple Events by default, so `open`, `osascript` and browser-based auth flows fail with error -600. Setting allowAppleEvents to true (user, managed or CLI settings only — project settings are ignored) lifts the block but removes code-execution isolation: sandboxed commands can then launch other applications unsandboxed with no prompt and send AppleScript to running apps, subject only to macOS TCC consent.

nodes.label: enableWeakerNestedSandbox
nodes.rationale: enableWeakerNestedSandbox makes the inner sandbox bind-mount the container's existing /proc instead of mounting a fresh one, so bubblewrap works inside unprivileged Docker containers or on hosts where unprivileged user namespaces are disabled by sysctl. It exposes process information a fresh /proc would hide and considerably weakens security, so it should only be used when the outer container already provides the isolation boundary.

nodes.label: enableWeakerNetworkIsolation
