nodes.rationale: enableWeakerNetworkIsolation is the alternative to excludedCommands for Go-based CLIs failing TLS verification on macOS: set it to true when using httpProxyPort with a MITM proxy and a custom CA, so those tools can run inside the sandbox.

nodes.label: TLS is not inspected by default (domain fronting)
nodes.rationale: The built-in proxy allows or denies on the client-supplied hostname and by default does not terminate or inspect TLS, so encrypted contents are never examined and code inside the sandbox can potentially use domain fronting to reach hosts outside the allowlist. Allowing broad domains such as github.com can therefore create data-exfiltration paths; stronger TLS-aware isolation is an active area of development.

nodes.label: Privilege escalation via Unix sockets
nodes.rationale: The allowUnixSockets configuration can inadvertently grant access to system services that lead to sandbox bypasses — allowing /var/run/docker.sock, for example, effectively grants access to the host system through the Docker socket. Any Unix socket allowed through the sandbox should be considered carefully.

nodes.label: Filesystem permission escalation
nodes.rationale: Overly broad filesystem write permissions enable privilege-escalation attacks: allowing writes to directories holding executables on $PATH, system configuration directories, or user shell configuration files such as .bashrc or .zshrc can lead to code execution in different security contexts when other users or system processes read them.

nodes.label: Built-in file tools are outside the sandbox
nodes.rationale: Read, Edit and Write use the permission system directly rather than running through the sandbox, and computer use runs on the actual desktop gated by per-app permission prompts rather than in an isolated environment. The sandbox isolates Bash subprocesses only.

nodes.label: Subagents share the parent's sandbox
nodes.rationale: Subagents run in the same process as the parent session and use the same sandbox configuration, so Bash commands inside a subagent are sandboxed whenever sandboxing is enabled in the parent session.

nodes.label: Sandboxed commands inherit the parent environment
nodes.rationale: Sandboxed Bash commands inherit the parent process environment by default, including any credentials set there. Only sandbox.credentials (to unset or mask specific variables) or CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB (for all subprocesses) removes them.

nodes.label: Effective sandboxing needs both layers
nodes.rationale: Effective sandboxing requires both filesystem and network isolation: without network isolation a compromised agent could exfiltrate sensitive files such as SSH keys, and without filesystem isolation it could backdoor system resources to gain network access. When widening defaults, check that an allowWrite path, a broad allowedDomains entry, or an excludedCommands exception does not undo a restriction on the other side.

nodes.label: Merging sandbox arrays across settings scopes
nodes.rationale: When the same filesystem array is defined in multiple settings scopes, Claude Code combines the paths from every scope rather than letting one scope's array replace another's. The same merging applies to credentials deny entries and to array keys such as excludedCommands and allowRead.

nodes.label: Excluding a settings source
nodes.rationale: Excluding a source with --setting-sources on the CLI or settingSources in the Agent SDK (v2.1.246+) makes Claude Code ignore its sandbox.filesystem entries, Edit permission rules and Read deny rules when building the sandbox configuration, and drop all of an excluded project or local source's credentials entries. Excluding user settings still keeps its deny entries and file mask restrictions, but drops its environment variable mask entries.

nodes.label: sandbox.enabled
nodes.rationale: Selecting a mode in /sandbox writes it to the project's .claude/settings.local.json; to enable the sandbox across all projects, set sandbox.enabled to true in user settings at ~/.claude/settings.json, and to enforce it organization-wide deliver it through managed settings.

nodes.label: Self-hosted environment
nodes.rationale: A self-hosted environment runs Claude Code cloud sessions on runners you deploy inside your own network. It is in public beta on Team and Enterprise plans, and in production its sessions execute model-directed code on behalf of everyone who can dispatch a session to it.

nodes.label: Self-hosted runner process
nodes.rationale: The runner is the process that polls Anthropic for work, prepares each session's checkout, runs lifecycle hooks, and starts and supervises session processes. It executes arbitrary model-directed code on your infrastructure.

nodes.label: Session (runner child process)
nodes.rationale: A session is a Claude Code process the runner spawns, plus everything it starts: builds, test suites, package installs, and MCP servers. Sessions, not the runner, are where the load and the untrusted code execution live.

nodes.label: Production hardening checklist
nodes.rationale: A list of items to work through before connecting an environment to production systems, because a runner executes model-directed code on behalf of any organization member who can dispatch a session, plus anyone able to start a Claude Tag channel session routed to the environment.

nodes.label: Ephemeral per-session containers
nodes.rationale: Run each runner process in a fresh container or VM destroyed when the process exits, with --capacity 1 and the default --drain-grace-sec 0, so each container serves exactly one session. Never reuse a filesystem across owners, and only reuse it in the deliberate pre-warmed checkout setup.

nodes.label: --capacity flag
nodes.rationale: --capacity caps how many sessions one runner runs at once, all from the same locked owner. It does not divide CPU or memory between them, and it controls parallelism within one owner's sessions rather than across owners.

nodes.label: No broad credentials in the image
nodes.rationale: Do not bake long-lived SSH keys, cloud credentials, or personal access tokens into the runner image; a credential in the image is available to every session the image runs, whoever started it. Mint push and API tokens per session instead.

nodes.label: Wrapper script credential minting
nodes.rationale: The wrapper script is where a session should obtain its own short-lived, least-scoped credentials, using the session creator's identity decoded from the session JWT, rather than inheriting the host's identity. It can also apply per-session CPU and memory limits.

nodes.label: Environment secret exposure
nodes.rationale: The environment secret can register runners and pick up any session queued on the environment. On a fixed fleet it sits on every runner host where any session's code can read it, so treat that file as readable by every session and rotate it after any suspected session compromise.

nodes.label: On-demand runners
nodes.rationale: With on-demand runners the environment secret stays on an orchestrator host that never runs user code, and each runner receives a single-use work order registering exactly one runner. The orchestrator subcommand polls Anthropic for queued sessions with no runner available and invokes a spawn-runner hook to boot one per session.

nodes.label: Default-deny network egress
nodes.rationale: Deploy runner and session containers in a segment whose outbound traffic is limited to the documented hosts, your git host, and the specific internal services sessions need. The product cannot verify or enforce this, and it applies regardless of permission mode because the default pre-approved tool set already includes Bash.

nodes.label: Least-privilege host IAM
nodes.rationale: The compute identity attached to the runner host, such as an instance profile or node service account, should grant only what the runner itself needs; sessions should obtain their own credentials rather than inheriting the host's.

nodes.label: Block the cloud metadata endpoint
nodes.rationale: Subnet-level egress policies do not intercept link-local metadata traffic, so block 169.254.169.254 inside the session container itself — via IMDSv2 with a hop limit of one, GKE Workload Identity metadata concealment, or an explicit deny in the container's network namespace. The block also applies to wrapper scripts and lifecycle hooks, which share the container.

nodes.label: Session JWT identity
nodes.rationale: The session JWT is what a session presents to your own token service over allowlisted egress to exchange for credentials, replacing host-identity access; a file-based web identity such as IRSA on Amazon EKS is the alternative.

nodes.label: Per-runner filesystem isolation
nodes.rationale: Each runner process gets its own working directory no other process on the host can read or write, and --hooks-dir, the wrapper script, and the host's ~/.claude/ are read-only to the session, either built into the image or mounted read-only.

nodes.label: Dispatch has no per-environment access control
nodes.rationale: Any member of the Anthropic organization can dispatch a session to any of its environments, and if an Owner routes Claude Tag channels there, anyone the Claude Tag access setting admits — by default anyone in the connected Slack workspace — can start sessions on it. Place on a runner host only data all of those people may read.

nodes.label: --lock-to-account
nodes.rationale: --lock-to-account bounds which account's sessions a given host executes but does not narrow who can dispatch into the environment. A pre-locked runner never picks up Claude Tag channel sessions, which is what makes a per-account persistent checkout volume safe.

nodes.label: --confine-repo-settings guard
nodes.rationale: The runner scans each repository's committed settings for grants resolving outside the session's workspace (additionalDirectories, Edit/Write/NotebookEdit allow rules, sandbox.filesystem allowWrite/allowRead), a non-empty env block, and operator-posture overrides such as sandbox.enabled: false. Modes are warn (default, logs and still spawns), enforce (refuses the session), and off; it runs regardless of --trust-workspace and does not cover repository hooks, .mcp.json, or Bash rules.

nodes.label: IP allowlist does not cover runner traffic
nodes.rationale: An organization's IP allowlist does not cover self-hosted runner traffic by default, so it must not be relied on as a network control for runner or session traffic; apply default-deny egress at your own boundary instead and contact your account team for allowlist enforcement.

nodes.label: Always-required egress hosts
nodes.rationale: Two hosts are always required: api.anthropic.com on 443 (runner control plane, session streaming, inference, feature flags, analytics, JWKS fetches, commit signing, the git proxy, and the orchestrator's SCM connector tunnel over WSS) and your git host on 443 or 22 for cloning and pushing, unless --use-anthropic-git-proxy routes git traffic through api.anthropic.com.

nodes.label: Configuration-dependent egress hosts
nodes.rationale: Hosts needed only for some configurations: downloads.claude.ai (native installer and official marketplace plugins), storage.googleapis.com (plugin counts in /plugin), code.claude.com and claude.com (documentation lookups), *.frame.claudeusercontent.com (Artifact tool), registry.npmjs.org (plugin and npx MCP installs), and two Datadog intakes for metrics and error reports, both off unless explicitly enabled.

nodes.label: Hosts the runner does not reach
nodes.rationale: statsig.anthropic.com, *.sentry.io, claude.ai, platform.claude.com and mcp-proxy.anthropic.com appear in older enterprise checklists but are not needed for runner or session traffic: feature flags go to api.anthropic.com and the runner authenticates with the environment secret. Only two host-side flows — the one-line installer and interactive claude auth login — reach claude.ai, so run them from a host whose egress allows it rather than widening session-container egress.

nodes.label: Proxy-Authorization source flags
nodes.rationale: For corporate proxies requiring a Proxy-Authorization header whose token rotates too fast to embed in HTTPS_PROXY, set --proxy-authorization-command (trimmed stdout of a command run on demand) or --proxy-authorization-file (trimmed contents of a file another process rotates). Both require Claude Code v2.1.238 or later.

nodes.label: Proxy-auth start-up refusals
nodes.rationale: Before contacting the proxy or control plane the runner refuses to start in three cases: both flags set (one flag plus the other's environment variable counts), no http:// or https:// URL in HTTPS_PROXY or HTTP_PROXY (ALL_PROXY is not consulted), or either flag passed to the orchestrator subcommand, which does not accept them.

nodes.label: Loopback proxy-auth listener
nodes.rationale: With either proxy-auth flag set the runner starts a forward proxy on 127.0.0.1 before registering (exiting at startup if it cannot), rewrites the proxy variables to point at it, re-reads the token per connection so rotation needs no restart, strips ALL_PROXY and unset proxy spellings from session environments, pins NO_PROXY, and never logs the header value.

nodes.label: --configure-git
nodes.rationale: Starting the runner with --configure-git (or SELF_HOSTED_RUNNER_CONFIGURE_GIT=1) writes global git config at startup: user.name Claude and user.email noreply@anthropic.com, plus SSH-format commit and tag signing through a shim that signs via Anthropic's signing service with the session's own credentials. It does not configure push credentials.

nodes.label: Ship git config in your image
nodes.rationale: The alternative to --configure-git is setting identity and credentials yourself, system-wide in the Dockerfile so they apply regardless of which user the runner runs as. Without an identity git commit fails with 'Please tell me who you are' and sessions cannot make progress; the runner never overrides values you set.

nodes.label: Git version floors on the runner host
nodes.rationale: --configure-git SSH commit signing needs Git 2.34 or newer (checked at startup, the runner exits otherwise), --use-anthropic-git-proxy needs 2.32 or newer, and resuming sessions from branches pushed by --push-outcome-on-release needs 2.29 or newer. Git 2.24 suffices if you omit all three and manage identity yourself.

nodes.label: Anthropic git proxy
nodes.rationale: --use-anthropic-git-proxy (or CLAUDE_RUNNER_USE_GIT_PROXY=1) clones through Anthropic's git proxy using the session creator's GitHub OAuth token, or the organization's GitHub App installation token for bot and agent sessions, so the image needs no git credentials at all. It requires --capacity 1 and git 2.32+, and needs your git host reachable from Anthropic infrastructure.

nodes.label: Non-interactive git and SSH enforcement
nodes.rationale: The runner's built-in clone and fetch disable every prompt: GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, SSH BatchMode=yes appended to any GIT_SSH_COMMAND, GCM_INTERACTIVE=never, and core.askPass cleared (use GIT_ASKPASS instead). Any credential mechanism must therefore work without a prompt or repository preparation fails after a few retries.

nodes.label: safe.directory for mismatched uids
nodes.rationale: If checkout directories are owned by a different uid than the runner process, git refuses to operate on them; add a system-wide safe.directory '*' entry in the image.

nodes.label: Git URL rewrites for private networks
nodes.rationale: Repository URLs arrive from the control plane as HTTPS with your git host's hostname. --git-host-rewrite <from>=<to> handles split-horizon DNS and --git-ssh-rewrite <host> converts HTTPS URLs to SSH form; host rewriting runs first, so name the internal hostname in the SSH rewrite when using both.

nodes.label: checkout lifecycle hook
nodes.rationale: The checkout hook runs before the wrapper script and gives full control over how repositories are fetched; it is the answer for a git host routable only inside your network, and for the initial clone that happens before any wrapper-minted credential exists.

nodes.label: Building the runner image
nodes.rationale: Anthropic publishes no pre-built runner image; you build your own around the claude binary from the standard release URL (linux-x64, arm64, or musl variants), layering in your repositories' toolchains and MCP sidecars, with Claude Code 2.1.224 or later, and can verify the binary against the release's signed manifest.

nodes.label: CPU and memory sizing for sessions
nodes.rationale: Size for the sessions, not the runner: start at 4 GiB memory request and limit (equal, so the scheduler accounts for the full amount, and because hitting the limit kills processes mid-task) and 2 CPU request with a 4 CPU limit so builds can burst — CPU throttles rather than kills. Multiply by --capacity when one container serves several sessions.

nodes.label: /healthz endpoint and poll-age metric
nodes.rationale: The runner serves GET /healthz on port 8080 by default (configurable with --health-port), returning 200 whenever the process is alive. That detects a dead process, not a stuck one, so alert on the last_poll_age_seconds series from /metrics to catch a runner that stopped polling.

nodes.label: Kubernetes Deployment recipe
nodes.rationale: A three-replica Deployment in a claude-runners namespace mounts the environment secret from a Kubernetes Secret read-only, runs --capacity 4, points liveness and readiness probes at /healthz on 8080, and sets terminationGracePeriodSeconds 90. It sets no CPU or memory resources, which you must add for the capacity you run.

nodes.label: Docker Compose recipe
nodes.rationale: The Compose service restarts the runner whenever it exits, covering crashes and the normal post-drain exit, with a file-backed secret and a 90-second stop_grace_period. Because a Docker restart reuses the container's writable layer, the runner comes back on a reused filesystem, so this recipe is for evaluation rather than production.

nodes.label: Shutdown drain path budget
nodes.rationale: On SIGTERM the runner stops taking work, waits up to --drain-wait-sec for in-flight turns, terminates each session's process tree, and runs the post-session hook. The full path needs --session-stop-grace-sec + --drain-wait-sec + --post-session-hook-timeout-sec plus 15 seconds of cleanup and 30 more with --push-outcome-on-release — 80 seconds at defaults, logged at startup; sessions drain in parallel so the total does not grow with capacity, and the runner keeps heartbeating at zero capacity so leases do not expire mid-hook.

nodes.label: --defer-shutdown-max-min
nodes.rationale: This flag (v2.1.238+) makes a restarting runner keep serving its sessions for up to n minutes instead of draining on the first signal, moving through three stages: normal service for n minutes, releasing every held session when they run out, then draining at the end of a 75-second post-release grace. Give the host stop timeout n minutes plus 155 seconds at defaults; a second signal cuts the stages short.

nodes.label: What reaches a running post-session hook
nodes.rationale: The post-session hook and session child run in their own POSIX process groups, so process-group-wide signals miss them while cgroup-wide kills (systemd KillMode=control-group, Kubernetes' SIGKILL at grace expiry) reach everything. A forced exit leaves a mid-run hook unsupervised — its timeout no longer applies and SIGPIPE on the closed log pipe can kill it — which is why the grace period must cover the whole drain path.

nodes.label: Identical --base-dir and --capacity across runners
nodes.rationale: A resumed session's checkout path derives from the picking runner's own --base-dir and --capacity (capacity 1 checks out directly under base-dir, above 1 uses per-session worktrees), so mismatched values make absolute paths the agent recorded point at a location that no longer exists. The base directory defaults to /workspace and the runner exits at startup with 'cannot create or write to base directory' if it cannot write there.

nodes.label: Pre-warmed checkout reuse
nodes.rationale: At --capacity 1 with no checkout hook the runner keeps one canonical clone per repository at <base-dir>/<repo-owner>/<repo> and reuses it: fetch the ref, detach HEAD, hard reset. Supply it by baking the clone into the image or by pointing --base-dir at a persistent volume on a runner pre-locked with --lock-to-account. Any clone shape works, tracked changes reset but untracked files persist because the runner never runs git clean, and git operations are bounded by a 120-second no-progress watchdog and a 30-minute hard cap.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_RUNNER_FETCH_DEPTH
nodes.rationale: CLAUDE_RUNNER_FETCH_DEPTH (full, 0, or a number; default 50) controls only the cold clone the runner makes when no clone exists yet — the runner never passes --depth when fetching into an existing clone, so a full pre-warm keeps full history and a shallow one stays shallow.

nodes.label: Pinning the Claude Code version
nodes.rationale: Each session's child process runs the runner's own binary and the runner disables auto-update inside spawned sessions, so every session runs the version installed on the host or built into the image, and a host-level update takes effect on the next runner start. Plugin marketplaces also do not auto-update unless FORCE_AUTOUPDATE_PLUGINS=1 is set.

nodes.label: Scaling the runner fleet
nodes.rationale: Because of the one-owner-per-runner lock, the minimum replica count is the number of users and Claude Tag agents expected active concurrently. Two approaches exist: a fixed fleet of static replicas scaled on the Prometheus metrics each runner serves, or on-demand runners booted per session by the orchestrator.

nodes.label: Known issues and limitations
nodes.rationale: The release ships with a documented set of limitations, each with a workaround where one exists, covering connector traffic egress, idle accounting, resumed sessions, mid-session repository additions, and connector availability. Issues are reported through your Anthropic account team rather than a public tracker.

nodes.label: Connector traffic leaves your network
nodes.rationale: Anthropic calls connector tools such as GitHub, Slack and Linear from its own infrastructure, so that traffic goes through api.anthropic.com rather than originating inside your network boundary. Filter connectors with allowedMcpServers/deniedMcpServers policy settings — which also apply to Anthropic-delivered connectors — or run equivalent local MCP servers on the runner image.

nodes.label: Sessions that do not count as idle
nodes.rationale: A session holding a never-finishing background task, or waiting on an approval requested from inside a running tool call, does not count as idle, so --release-idle-session-min will not free its slot. Always set --kill-session-after-min alongside it as a hard backstop.

nodes.label: Resumed sessions lose unpushed work
nodes.rationale: A released session resumes on a fresh runner that re-clones from the starting branch, so unpushed work is gone. --push-outcome-on-release best-effort pushes outcome branches first, preserving committed work but not a dirty tree or per-session configuration; before enabling it, restrict who can push to claude/* refs, because the runner fetches the previously pushed branch without verifying who pushed it.

nodes.label: Private repositories cannot be added mid-session
nodes.rationale: A repository added to a session after it has started is not cloned with credentials on a self-hosted runner, so the add fails; select every repository the session needs when creating it.

nodes.label: Connectors missing from self-hosted sessions
nodes.rationale: A connector not yet connected in claude.ai Settings is not listed in a self-hosted session and the session will not prompt to connect it; connect it first and start a fresh session, since adding a connector to a running session does not make its tools available.

nodes.label: self-hosted-runner doctor
nodes.rationale: The doctor subcommand starts an interactive Claude Code session on the runner host with the runner's logs and state attached. Sign in with claude auth login first so it can query the environment, its runners and queued sessions; without that it is limited to the local health endpoint, metrics, and a log it can read only if --log-file was set.

nodes.label: Common runner failure modes
nodes.rationale: The documented set of symptoms and causes: a runner missing from the environment, an unwritable base directory, sessions stuck queued behind owner locks, sessions failing right after pickup on missing git credentials or build tools, proxy-authorization failures answered 502, malformed poll responses, deleted remote branches, slow starts dominated by the initial clone, and pods killed mid-drain.

nodes.label: Runner does not appear in the environment
nodes.rationale: When a runner never registers, confirm the host reaches api.anthropic.com over HTTPS, the environment secret is current, and the host clock is within five minutes of real time — larger skew causes authentication to fail. The runner logs [runner:fatal] with the rejection reason on auth failure.

nodes.label: Malformed poll response from an intercepting proxy
nodes.rationale: 'Poll failed ... rejecting the malformed poll response' means something between the runner and api.anthropic.com — an intercepting proxy or captive portal — answered with its own page. The runner rejects it, counts it under the transport kind of poll_errors_total, retries, and keeps serving live sessions; before v2.1.246 it read such a response as an empty queue, which could end sessions or make it exit.

nodes.label: Runner logging streams
nodes.rationale: Once logging is initialized the runner writes its lifecycle log, including [runner:fatal] lines, to stdout and debug output to stderr as plain text; startup failures print to stderr before that point. Capture both with --log-file, which also lets doctor tail them, and note that each session's child writes its own debug log preserved on failure.

nodes.label: Self-hosted environment end-to-end test recipe
nodes.rationale: The page is a CI test recipe: verify a self-hosted runner image from CI by dispatching a session with the CLI, reading Claude's replies through a Stop hook, and scripting the full loop. It is distinct from the quickstart (setup) and the deploy page (fleet recipes).

nodes.label: Self-hosted environment
nodes.rationale: In a self-hosted environment, Claude Code cloud sessions run on a runner image that the customer builds and maintains, rather than on Anthropic-managed infrastructure.

nodes.label: Public beta on Team and Enterprise plans
nodes.rationale: Self-hosted environments are in public beta on Team and Enterprise plans; the availability-and-limitations section of the self-hosted environments page covers the enablement path.

nodes.label: Smoke-test a runner image before promoting it
nodes.rationale: Before rolling a new image to a production environment, drive a full session against a test environment from a script. That is the shape of a CI smoke test verifying the runner image, git access, and any custom tools before a change is promoted.

nodes.label: Runner co-located with the test script
nodes.rationale: The recipe assumes the CI job starts the runner process on the same host as the test script — the natural setup for testing a new runner image — so the driver can read the hook's output from the local filesystem.

nodes.label: Stop-hook reply capture
nodes.rationale: Read-back works through a Claude Code Stop hook: when Claude finishes a turn the hook receives the final assistant message as last_assistant_message in its stdin JSON and appends it to $E2E_REPLY_DIR/<session_id>.txt. It is installed on the runner host's ~/.claude/, which the runner seeds into every session.

nodes.label: E2E_REPLY_DIR environment variable
nodes.rationale: E2E_REPLY_DIR must be exported to the runner process (systemd unit, pod spec, or CI step) and name an existing directory; the hook is a no-op when the variable is unset or the directory does not exist. The test script requires it too.

nodes.label: Stop hook settings.json block
nodes.rationale: A hooks.Stop entry merged into ~/.claude/settings.json on the runner host registers a command hook with timeout 10 that runs "$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/hooks/e2e-stop-hook-capture.sh".

nodes.label: e2e-stop-hook-capture.sh
nodes.rationale: The capture script is saved as ~/.claude/hooks/e2e-stop-hook-capture.sh on the runner host and made executable. It requires jq, exits 0 in every path so it never fails the turn, and is documented as install-on-the-test-runner-only.

nodes.label: cse_ to session_ id translation
nodes.rationale: CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE_SESSION_ID is exported in cse_... form while the session id the dispatch CLI prints is in session_... form — the same id with a different prefix — so the hook rewrites it with sed 's/^cse_/session_/' before naming the output file.

nodes.label: jq '// empty' guard on last_assistant_message
nodes.rationale: last_assistant_message is absent when the final assistant turn had no text, such as a tool-use-only turn. The jq '// empty' filter makes that case a zero-byte write rather than the literal string "null".

nodes.label: Runner snapshots ~/.claude/ once at startup
nodes.rationale: The runner snapshots ~/.claude/ once at startup, so a hook added to an already-running runner takes effect only after a restart — install the capture hook before starting the runner.

nodes.label: Install the capture hook on test runners only
nodes.rationale: The hook writes every session's final reply to disk whenever E2E_REPLY_DIR exists. That is harmless on a throwaway CI runner but should not be carried into a production-environment runner image where the variable might be set by accident.

nodes.label: Read-back without extra Anthropic API calls
nodes.rationale: Because the Stop hook writes each turn's final reply to a local file the co-located driver reads, the only calls to the Anthropic API in the loop are the two dispatches themselves.

nodes.label: Claude Code v2.1.224 flag floor
nodes.rationale: The --environment and --ref dispatch flags require Claude Code v2.1.224 or later on the machine running the script — the same version floor as the runner itself.

nodes.label: claude -p --environment dispatch
nodes.rationale: claude -p "<prompt>" --environment <environment-id> --output-format json creates a session on the test environment, prints one line of JSON containing session_id plus a link, and exits without waiting for Claude's reply.

nodes.label: --ref checkout pin
nodes.rationale: The optional --ref <branch> flag bases the session's checkout on a named ref instead of local HEAD, pinning what the session works on regardless of the driver host's current checkout.

nodes.label: Repository auto-detection from the origin remote
nodes.rationale: The dispatch must be run from a git checkout so the CLI can auto-detect the repository from the origin remote; that is the repository the created session works in.

nodes.label: --environment outranks remote.defaultEnvironmentId
nodes.rationale: The --environment flag takes precedence over the remote.defaultEnvironmentId setting, so a CI dispatch targets the named test environment regardless of configured defaults.

nodes.label: --environment flag incompatibilities
nodes.rationale: --environment does not support --output-format stream-json and cannot be combined with flags that resume, attach to, or preconfigure a session: --resume, --continue, --teleport, --session-id, or --init-only.

nodes.label: --cloud rejection rules alongside --environment
nodes.rationale: --cloud is rejected when it carries a session ID or URL, and in non-interactive runs when it carries a description; a bare --cloud is treated as absent. From a terminal the task can be passed as the --cloud description instead of a positional prompt.

nodes.label: claude -p --cloud follow-up dispatch
nodes.rationale: claude -p "<message>" --cloud <session_id> --output-format json posts a user event to an already-running session and exits; the example script asserts .ok == true on its JSON response.

nodes.label: Four-step test loop
nodes.rationale: The loop is: create a session on the test environment, wait for its reply to appear in $E2E_REPLY_DIR/<session_id>.txt, send a follow-up with --cloud, then wait for that reply the same way.

nodes.label: Example end-to-end bash driver
nodes.rationale: A set -euo pipefail bash script runs the whole loop against $CLAUDE_TEST_ENVIRONMENT_ID and asserts on a sentinel phrase in each reply. Its prerequisites are a prior claude auth login on the host, jq, a running local runner with the capture hook, and E2E_REPLY_DIR exported.

nodes.label: await_reply 90-second deadline
nodes.rationale: await_reply polls $E2E_REPLY_DIR/<session_id>.txt once a second until it contains the expected sentinel, failing after 90 seconds and dumping the directory listing and file contents. The timeout should be tuned to the environment's cold-start time.

nodes.label: Sentinel-phrase assertions
nodes.rationale: Each turn asks Claude to say an exact phrase and the driver greps for it, e.g. 'ok: custom tools are reachable' and 'ok: follow-up delivered'. The prompts and sentinels are meant to be replaced with whatever exercises the setup, such as running a custom MCP tool and asserting on its output.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_TEST_ENVIRONMENT_ID
nodes.rationale: CLAUDE_TEST_ENVIRONMENT_ID names the test environment's ccpool_... ID, shown in the environment's detail dialog on the admin page or returned by the create-environment call. CLAUDE_TEST_POOL_ID is the legacy spelling the script falls back to.

nodes.label: Remote test runners via HTTP POST
nodes.rationale: When test runners sit on separate infrastructure — such as a persistent Kubernetes fleet the CI job cannot share a filesystem with — the hook's file write is swapped for a curl POST of the reply to $E2E_REPLY_URL/<session_id>.

nodes.label: Driver-side reply endpoint
nodes.rationale: On the driver side, anything that accepts the POST and holds the reply until the test asks for it works — a small HTTP listener inside the CI job or an existing webhook receiver. Because the hook runs on the customer's own infrastructure, the endpoint only needs to be reachable from the runners.

nodes.label: OAuth-only dispatch authentication
nodes.rationale: Both claude -p ... --environment and claude -p ... --cloud authenticate with a claude.ai OAuth token; API keys such as sk-ant-xxxxx are not accepted for either call.

nodes.label: Long-lived CI host login
nodes.rationale: Run claude auth login once interactively on the machine that executes the script, under a dedicated automation account. The token is stored in the OS keychain on macOS or in ~/.claude/.credentials.json on Linux and Windows — and also in that file on a macOS host whose login Keychain cannot be written, as in an SSH session.

nodes.label: 30-day refresh-grant cap
nodes.rationale: The CLI refreshes the short-lived access token on each invocation, but the underlying refresh-token grant is capped at 30 days from the initial login, so claude auth login must be re-run interactively on that host every 30 days.

nodes.label: Ephemeral CI runners have no long-lived token
nodes.rationale: There is no long-lived CI token for this today: the user:sessions:claude_code scope that grants remote-session control is capped server-side at 30 days, so claude setup-token (a one-year inference-only token) does not cover it, and the environment secret only authorizes a runner to register, not to create sessions.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN provisioning
nodes.rationale: To provision a stored login onto an ephemeral runner, set CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN and CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_SCOPES so claude auth login exchanges the token without a browser; the same 30-day refresh cap applies. A machine-identity path not bound to a human account requires contacting the Anthropic account team.

nodes.label: Programmatic per-run test environment
nodes.rationale: Environments can be created and deleted programmatically so each CI run gets a clean one, with the runner the CI job starts registering into the fresh environment. The create and delete calls are the same endpoints the Cloud environments admin page on claude.ai uses.

nodes.label: anthropic-beta: ccr-byoc-2025-07-29 header
nodes.rationale: The environment create and delete endpoints require the anthropic-beta: ccr-byoc-2025-07-29 header, alongside anthropic-version: 2023-06-01.

nodes.label: Owner-role admin OAuth token
nodes.rationale: $ADMIN_TOKEN is a claude.ai OAuth access token for an account holding an Owner role, minted by claude auth login and read fresh from storage each run because the CLI rotates it. It is passed via stdin so it never lands in curl's argument list or the build log.

nodes.label: Create-environment API call
nodes.rationale: POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/code/runners/self-hosted/pools with a JSON name creates the environment; the response yields .pool.pool_id as the environment ID and .pool_secret as the registration secret.

nodes.label: pool_secret must be masked, never echoed
nodes.rationale: pool_secret is a long-lived credential that can register runners into the environment, so the create response must be captured without echoing it: store the secret as a masked CI secret and print only the environment ID.

nodes.label: curl 7.55+ required for -H @-
nodes.rationale: The -H @- form that keeps the token out of the process list requires curl 7.55 or later; older curl treats @- as a literal header and sends the request without authorization.

nodes.label: 403 permission_error until the org allows self-hosted environments
nodes.rationale: Until an Owner turns on 'Allow self-hosted environments' for the organization, the create call fails with a 403 permission_error reading 'self-hosted runners are disabled by your organization's policy'.

nodes.label: SELF_HOSTED_RUNNER_ENVIRONMENT_SECRET
nodes.rationale: After creating the environment, a runner is started on the host with SELF_HOSTED_RUNNER_ENVIRONMENT_SECRET set to the returned environment secret, plus the capture hook and E2E_REPLY_DIR, before the test script runs.

nodes.label: Delete-environment API call
nodes.rationale: DELETE https://api.anthropic.com/v1/code/runners/self-hosted/pools/$ENVIRONMENT_ID removes the environment when the run finishes, so each CI run starts clean.

nodes.label: Server-managed settings
nodes.rationale: Server-managed settings let organization Owners centrally configure Claude Code from the claude.ai admin console without device-management infrastructure. Clients fetch them automatically when the session authenticates with a Team or Enterprise OAuth login, an OAuth token supplied through CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, or a directly configured API key, on supported platforms.

nodes.label: Requirements for server-managed settings
nodes.rationale: Three prerequisites: a Claude for Teams or Claude for Enterprise plan, the Owner or Primary Owner role in the Claude organization to view and edit the configuration, and network access to api.anthropic.com.

nodes.label: Admin Settings > Claude Code > Managed settings console
nodes.rationale: The configuration surface is the Managed settings page under Admin Settings > Claude Code in the claude.ai console. If the link redirects to a different Admin Settings page, the account lacks the required role; Admin and other non-Owner roles cannot view or edit managed settings.

nodes.label: Owner-only access control
nodes.rationale: Only the Primary Owner and Owner roles can manage server-managed settings. The docs advise restricting that access to trusted personnel because a settings change applies to every user in the organization.

nodes.label: Endpoint-managed settings
nodes.rationale: The alternative centralized-configuration approach: settings deployed directly to devices through native OS policies (macOS managed preferences, Windows registry) or managed settings files, rather than fetched from Anthropic's servers. Best for organizations with MDM or endpoint management.

nodes.label: MDM gives stronger enforcement guarantees
nodes.rationale: On devices enrolled in MDM or endpoint management, endpoint-managed settings provide stronger security guarantees because the settings file can be protected from user modification at the OS level.

nodes.label: Cloud sessions need server-managed settings
nodes.rationale: Endpoint-managed settings do not reach cloud sessions in Anthropic-hosted environments, so an organization using Claude Code on the web must configure server-managed settings as well. Sessions in a self-hosted environment do read the managed settings file in the runner image.

nodes.label: The delivered JSON settings payload
nodes.rationale: The configuration is authored as JSON in the console. Every setting available in settings.json is supported except those restricted to OS-level policy delivery, including hooks, environment variables, and managed-only settings such as allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly.

nodes.label: Permission deny-list example
nodes.rationale: The worked example enforces a permissions.deny list (Bash(curl *), Read(./.env), Read(./.env.*), Read(./secrets/**)), sets disableBypassPermissionsMode to "disable", and sets allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly true so only managed-settings permission rules apply.

nodes.label: Managed-only settings keys
nodes.rationale: Most settings keys work in any scope, but a handful are read only from managed settings and have no effect in user or project settings files — the permission and plugin controls. The Scope column of the All settings index lists the full set.

nodes.label: Delivering hooks through managed settings
nodes.rationale: Hooks use the same format as in settings.json; the example runs an audit script via a PostToolUse hook matching Edit|Write across the organization. Because hooks execute shell commands, users in interactive sessions see a security approval dialog before Claude Code applies them.

nodes.label: autoMode classifier configuration block
nodes.rationale: An autoMode block can be delivered the same way to tell the auto-mode classifier which repos, buckets, and domains the organization trusts, using the environment, allow, soft_deny, and hard_deny fields.

nodes.label: Save and deploy propagation
nodes.rationale: After saving in the console, Claude Code clients receive the updated settings on their next startup or on their hourly polling cycle.

nodes.label: Verifying settings delivery
nodes.rationale: To confirm settings are applied, have a user restart Claude Code; if the payload triggers the security approval dialog the user is prompted at the next start or within an hour in a running interactive session. Running /permissions shows the effective permission rules.

nodes.label: claude doctor 'Managed settings (remote)' line
nodes.rationale: On Claude Code v2.1.248 or later, `claude doctor` prints a Managed settings (remote) line reporting one of four outcomes — settings loaded, no server-managed settings configured, the fetch failed (with cause and whether a cached policy still applies), or the fetch was skipped (with reason) — plus an in-progress state.

nodes.label: /status managed-source reporting
nodes.rationale: In a running session /status shows the same Managed settings (remote) line after a failed fetch, and for some skipped-fetch causes such as a third-party provider variable or a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL exported in the user's shell. /status also shows which managed source is currently active.

nodes.label: No per-group configuration
nodes.rationale: A current limitation: server-managed settings apply uniformly to all users in the organization, and per-group configurations are not yet supported.

nodes.label: managed-mcp.json cannot be server-delivered
nodes.rationale: A managed-mcp.json file cannot be distributed through server-managed settings; deliver the allowedMcpServers and deniedMcpServers policy keys instead. Claude Code reads a managed-mcp.json deployed at its system path separately from the managed settings tier, so that file still applies while server-managed settings are in effect.

nodes.label: OS-policy-only settings are not honored
nodes.rationale: Settings restricted to OS-level policy sources, such as policyHelper and wslInheritsWindowsSettings, are not honored when delivered from the server; deploy them through MDM or a system managed-settings.json file instead.

nodes.label: Managed tier tops the settings hierarchy
nodes.rationale: Server-managed and endpoint-managed settings both occupy the highest tier in the Claude Code settings hierarchy. No other settings level can override them, including command line arguments, apart from the documented exceptions to managed settings precedence.

nodes.label: First source delivering a policy key wins
nodes.rationale: Within the managed tier, Claude Code by default uses the first source that delivers at least one policy key, checking server-managed settings first and then endpoint-managed settings. This is a no-merge rule, apart from the documented per-key exceptions.

nodes.label: policyHelper output replaces its source
nodes.rationale: If the selected source is an MDM policy or managed settings file whose policyHelper supplies managed settings, the helper's output replaces that source as the only managed configuration for the run. Claude Code does not consult a policyHelper configured in MDM or file-based settings while server-managed settings deliver a policy key.

nodes.label: Clearing the server config does not fall back immediately
nodes.rationale: Clearing the server-managed configuration to fall back to an endpoint-managed plist or registry policy is not immediate: cached settings persist on client machines until the next successful fetch, and keys that apply only at the next launch, such as model, stay in effect until each client relaunches.

nodes.label: Cross-source lock keys
nodes.rationale: A small set of keys, such as the sandbox allowlist locks, are honored when ANY admin-controlled managed source sets them; the user-writable HKCU registry tier is excluded, and when a policyHelper supplies managed settings its output is the only source these checks read.

nodes.label: The env block merges per key
nodes.rationale: The env block is the second exception to the no-merge rule: it merges per key across admin-controlled sources, the highest-priority source defining a variable wins, and lower admin sources fill in variables higher sources leave unset. Requires v2.1.223 or later; before that, only the selected source's whole env block applies.

nodes.label: Telemetry variables move as one unit
nodes.rationale: The OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_* exporter keys, OTEL_LOG_* content-capture toggles, OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER, ENABLE_BETA_TRACING_DETAILED and BETA_TRACING_ENDPOINT follow the highest source that sets any of them, as a unit. A source delivering otelHeadersHelper claims the unit but lands the variables only when selected, so an exporter endpoint from one source can never pair with credentials from another.

nodes.label: Credential-paired routing variables
nodes.rationale: A source that pairs routing variables with a selected-source-only credential key such as apiKeyHelper or otelHeadersHelper contributes those routing variables only when it wins the slot, rather than through the ordinary per-key env merge.

nodes.label: Startup fetch and hourly polling
nodes.rationale: Claude Code fetches settings from Anthropic's servers at startup and polls for updates hourly during active sessions. Most settings updates apply to running sessions without a restart.

nodes.label: Five-second first-launch fetch wait
nodes.rationale: When a developer signs in at startup with no cache, Claude Code waits up to five seconds for the fetch before opening the session, enforcing the policy from the first screen and showing companyAnnouncements. In any other startup, or once the wait runs out, the session opens while the fetch continues, leaving a brief unenforced window.

nodes.label: Cached settings on subsequent launches
nodes.rationale: On later launches cached settings apply immediately, except the withheld environment variables and a cached modelPricing, while fresh settings are fetched in the background. The cache persists through network failures, and interactive sessions are warned that the cached policy is in effect when the startup fetch fails.

nodes.label: Cached modelPricing waits for confirmation
nodes.rationale: A cached modelPricing value does not apply until the session's fetch confirms the payload; until then the cost figures shown in /usage and the status line are at list price. This hardening requires Claude Code v2.1.242 or later.

nodes.label: Withheld cached environment variables
nodes.rationale: Claude Code withholds several categories of variables in the cached env block until the server confirms the session's payload, so a cached proxy, certificate authority, endpoint, or credential value cannot redirect, intercept, or re-authenticate the very fetch that confirms the payload. Requires v2.1.198 or later and applies only to the server-fetched cache.

nodes.label: The withheld variable categories
nodes.rationale: The withheld categories are proxy and TLS configuration (HTTPS_PROXY, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, CLAUDE_CODE_CLIENT_CERT/KEY), API routing and provider selection (ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK/VERTEX, provider endpoint URLs), authentication credentials (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN), CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, and — from v2.1.223 — federation, profile and OS directory selectors.

nodes.label: Startup-only credential-source selectors
nodes.rationale: Claude Code reads the Workload Identity Federation variables and the ANTHROPIC_PROFILE and ANTHROPIC_CONFIG_DIR selectors only at startup, so a server-delivered value never switches the session's credential source even after the fetch succeeds. To deliver those selectors on v2.1.223 or later, use endpoint-managed settings such as MDM or managed-settings.json.

nodes.label: Reaching api.anthropic.com through a proxy
nodes.rationale: Because the server-delivered proxy value is withheld, a proxy needed to reach api.anthropic.com must come from an endpoint-managed env block (v2.1.223 or later), the shell environment, or user settings. The first launch has no cache at all, so one of those sources is always required for the initial fetch.

nodes.label: Keys that apply only at the next launch
nodes.rationale: Some updates apply only at the next launch rather than to a running session: OpenTelemetry exporter configuration, the model key, and the removal of a variable from the env block.

nodes.label: Tolerant parsing of invalid entries
nodes.rationale: Delivered payloads parse tolerantly with the same rules as other managed sources: when part of a payload fails schema validation, Claude Code surfaces a validation error and applies every remaining valid setting. Requires Claude Code v2.1.169 or later.

nodes.label: ~/.claude/remote-settings.json cache
nodes.rationale: The cache at ~/.claude/remote-settings.json stores the salvaged payload with invalid entries removed, apart from invalid cleanupPeriodDays and desktopSessionCleanupPeriodDays values, which stay in the cached copy and are never applied.

nodes.label: Rejection of an unsalvageable payload
nodes.rationale: When no field in a payload can be salvaged, Claude Code rejects the payload, keeps the last-accepted cached settings, and writes "Remote settings: Settings validation failed - no fields could be salvaged" to the debug log; with forceRemoteSettingsRefresh set, the CLI exits instead.

nodes.label: Debugging delivery with --debug-file
nodes.rationale: To debug delivery issues, run `claude --debug-file <path>` and search the log for "Remote settings". The docs advise validating a payload change with `claude doctor` on a test machine before rolling it out to the organization.

nodes.label: Approval evaluates the salvaged payload
nodes.rationale: The security approval dialog evaluates the salvaged payload rather than the raw one, so an invalid entry that was stripped during validation is never presented for approval and never executes.

nodes.label: forceRemoteSettingsRefresh fail-closed startup
nodes.rationale: Setting forceRemoteSettingsRefresh: true makes the CLI block at startup until remote settings are freshly fetched and exit rather than proceed without the policy if the fetch fails. The setting self-perpetuates: once delivered it is cached locally so later startups enforce the same behavior before the first successful fetch of a new session.

nodes.label: forceRemoteSettingsRefresh is a precedence exception
nodes.rationale: In Claude Code v2.1.191 or later this flag is an exception to the first-source-wins precedence rule: it is honored when set in any admin-controlled managed source even if a cached server-managed payload is present, so an MDM-delivered value is not ignored. The startup check runs before any policyHelper and reads any admin source.

nodes.label: Cache-Control: no-cache on the fetch
nodes.rationale: The settings fetch sends a Cache-Control: no-cache header so intermediate HTTP proxies do not serve a stale response.

nodes.label: claude auth subcommands are exempt
nodes.rationale: The `claude auth` subcommands such as `claude auth login` are exempt from the fail-closed startup check and from the gateway startup exit, so users can re-authenticate when expired credentials are the reason the settings fetch fails.

nodes.label: Connectivity prerequisite for fail-closed mode
nodes.rationale: Before enabling fail-closed startup, network policies must allow connectivity to api.anthropic.com; if that endpoint is unreachable the CLI exits at startup and users cannot start Claude Code at all.

nodes.label: Security approval dialog
nodes.rationale: Certain delivered settings that could pose security risks require explicit user approval before Claude Code applies them in an interactive session. Users see a dialog explaining what is being configured and must approve to proceed; if a user rejects the settings, Claude Code exits.

nodes.label: Settings that trigger the approval dialog
nodes.rationale: Six categories require approval: shell-command settings (apiKeyHelper, statusLine, otelHeadersHelper), sandbox binary settings (sandbox.bwrapPath, socatPath, ripgrep), sandbox network and isolation settings that weaken isolation or let the proxy read/reroute/authenticate traffic, certain delivered env variables, any hook definition, and a managed claudeMd value. A sandbox.credentials block with only deny rules needs no approval; before v2.1.251 the sandbox settings applied without approval.

nodes.label: Approval memory by credential type
nodes.rationale: Claude Code records an approval in the configuration directory (~/.claude unless CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR is set), and what it records depends on the credential the fetch uses: a claude.ai login gives one approval per organization held by the most recent approver; a Claude apps gateway sign-in gives one approval per gateway; any other credential gives one approval for the delivered settings kept with the cached copy.

nodes.label: Re-prompting on account and gateway changes
nodes.rationale: With a saved claude.ai login the dialog is not shown again after sign-out/sign-in or an org switch while the settings are unchanged, unless another account approved them for that org in the same configuration directory in between. Signing in to the same organization with a different account always re-prompts, and that account's approval replaces the previous one. A gateway re-prompts on changed settings, a different gateway, or a new certificate, and a loopback HTTP development gateway saves no approval at all.

nodes.label: When the dialog cannot be shown
nodes.rationale: In an interactive session that cannot show the dialog (v2.1.211+), and when an error closes the dialog before an answer, Claude Code does not apply the delivered settings and keeps the last-approved ones, showing the dialog in the next session that can. `claude install` and `claude update` run with the last-approved settings and defer the dialog, except when the startup fetch is awaited, in which case an install run from a pipe fails.

nodes.label: Non-interactive runs apply settings once
nodes.rationale: A non-interactive run such as `claude -p` or an Agent SDK session cannot show the dialog, so settings requiring approval are applied for that run only: they are not recorded as approved nor written to the local cache, each such run refetches at startup, and the next interactive session shows the dialog. Before v2.1.207 a non-interactive run saved them as approved.

nodes.label: Env variables applied without approval
nodes.rationale: Some delivered env variables apply without the dialog: feature and command toggles, model selection and behavior settings such as ANTHROPIC_MODEL, DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING and CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL, context-window and compaction settings such as DISABLE_AUTO_COMPACT, terminal UI and accessibility options, and numeric limits, budgets and timeouts. A non-empty proxy, base-URL or OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT value always requires approval, and the dialog names the variable.

nodes.label: Value-based approval for privacy toggles
nodes.rationale: For CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC, DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING, DISABLE_TELEMETRY and DO_NOT_TRACK, approval is decided by the delivered VALUE rather than the variable name: a truthy value such as 1 or true only turns tracking or nonessential traffic off and applies without asking, while any other non-empty value shows the dialog. Before v2.1.218 all but DO_NOT_TRACK applied at any value.

nodes.label: API_FORCE_IDLE_TIMEOUT value-based approval
nodes.rationale: API_FORCE_IDLE_TIMEOUT is also judged by value: a truthy value only turns the body idle timeout on and applies without the dialog, while any other non-empty value shows it. Before v2.1.248 any non-empty value triggered the dialog.

nodes.label: ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS approval rules
nodes.rationale: Whether ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS needs approval depends on the value: purely tagging headers such as Accept-Language apply silently, while a line naming a credential, org/tenant selector, routing or host override, or API-behavior header (Authorization, X-Api-Key, Host, anthropic-beta, X-Amzn-Bedrock-*) requires approval, as does an invalid header token or an uncarryable value. The check matches words inside the name, so X-Client-Version requires approval too; before v2.1.251 any value applied without it.

nodes.label: Platform availability and eligible credentials
nodes.rationale: Server-managed settings require a direct connection to api.anthropic.com and a session authenticated with a Team or Enterprise OAuth login, an OAuth token via CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, or a directly configured API key. Keys returned by an apiKeyHelper script do not trigger the settings fetch.

nodes.label: Cowork sessions do not fetch
nodes.rationale: In a Cowork session inside the Claude Desktop app, Claude Code does not fetch server-managed settings from the claude.ai admin console, even when the user signs in with a Team or Enterprise account.

nodes.label: Third-party provider exports skip the fetch
nodes.rationale: Exporting a CLAUDE_CODE_USE_* provider variable or a non-default ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL in the shell makes Claude Code skip the settings fetch. The export cannot be cleared by a server-managed env block, because that block arrives through the very fetch the export prevents, and an endpoint-managed env block does not restore it either since eligibility is checked before managed env blocks are applied.

nodes.label: Restoring skipped delivery
nodes.rationale: To restore server-managed delivery, remove the export from the shell or set the variable to "" in the user settings env block, which applies before the eligibility check. To enforce policy without relying on users to change their shells, deliver the settings through the endpoint-managed channel instead.

nodes.label: Claude apps gateway delivery
nodes.rationale: For Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry and Claude Platform on AWS deployments, a self-hosted Claude apps gateway provides equivalent remote managed-settings delivery: gateway-signed-in clients fetch from the gateway rather than api.anthropic.com, wait for that fetch before the session starts, and exit on a failed startup fetch instead of falling back to cache. The hourly background refresh is fail-open on both channels.

nodes.label: Audit logging of settings changes
nodes.rationale: Audit log events for settings changes are available through the compliance API or audit log export, obtained via the Anthropic account team. Events include the type of action performed, the account and device that performed it, and references to the previous and new values.

nodes.label: A client-side control, not a security boundary
nodes.rationale: Server-managed settings provide centralized policy enforcement but operate as a client-side control, not a security boundary: on unmanaged devices a user does not need admin or sudo access to bypass them.

nodes.label: Documented bypass and failure scenarios
nodes.rationale: The security table enumerates the bypasses: editing the cached settings file (tampered values apply until the next fetch, and next-launch-only keys until relaunch), deleting the cache (first-launch behavior), running a modified binary, running a version predating the feature, API unavailability, authenticating with a different organization, configuring a third-party model provider, and intercepted or redirected network traffic.

nodes.label: ConfigChange hooks and their blind spots
nodes.rationale: ConfigChange hooks log edits to local settings files including managed-settings.json, but Claude Code does not run them when server-managed settings arrive or refresh, or when an MDM profile or registry policy changes, and such a hook cannot block a policy_settings change.

nodes.label: Tenant Restrictions for network-level access control
nodes.rationale: To restrict which organizations users can access with client-supplied credentials, the docs point to network-level Tenant Restrictions in the Claude Help Center; for stronger enforcement guarantees they recommend endpoint-managed settings on MDM-enrolled devices.

nodes.label: Claude Code session
nodes.rationale: A session is a saved conversation tied to a project directory, stored locally by Claude Code as you work so you can resume where you left off, branch to try a different approach, or switch between tasks. The desktop app, Claude Code on the web, and the VS Code extension each maintain their own separate session history; this page covers the CLI.

nodes.label: Session resume entry points
nodes.rationale: Five documented entry points return you to a saved session: `claude --continue`, `claude --resume`, `claude --resume <name>`, `claude --from-pr <number>`, and `/resume` from inside an active session. Sessions are saved continuously to local transcript files as you work, so any of them can be used after exiting or running `/clear`.

nodes.label: claude --continue
nodes.rationale: `claude --continue` resumes the most recent interactive session in the current directory. It skips `claude -p`/Agent SDK sessions, background sessions, and sessions whose first prompt was `/loop`; `claude -p --continue` includes the `-p`, SDK and `/loop` sessions but still skips background sessions.

nodes.label: claude --resume <name>
nodes.rationale: `claude --resume <name>` resumes a named session directly on an exact match, even when it lives in a different worktree of the same repository. When the name is ambiguous it opens the session picker with the name pre-filled as a search term.

nodes.label: Resume by session ID
nodes.rationale: `claude --resume <session-id>` resumes a session by its stored ID and can be run from any directory. If no stored session matches, Claude Code reports `No conversation found with session ID: <session-id>`.

nodes.label: claude --from-pr <number>
nodes.rationale: `claude --from-pr <number>` opens the session picker filtered to sessions linked to that pull request. Because it goes through the picker, the stored permission mode is not restored.

nodes.label: /resume slash command
nodes.rationale: `/resume` switches to a different conversation from inside an active session, opening the picker with no argument. `/resume <name>` resumes an exact match directly and reports an error on an ambiguous name rather than opening the picker.

nodes.label: Headless and SDK sessions excluded from discovery
nodes.rationale: Sessions created with `claude -p` or the Agent SDK are left out of the session picker and out of `claude --continue`. They remain resumable only by passing their session ID explicitly.

nodes.label: Background session
nodes.rationale: Background sessions appear in the session picker for the current worktree marked `bg`, but `claude --continue` skips them — including `claude -p --continue`, which otherwise widens to `-p`, SDK and `/loop` sessions.

nodes.label: Session whose first prompt was /loop
nodes.rationale: A session whose FIRST prompt was a `/loop` command does not appear in the picker and is skipped by `claude --continue`; running `/loop` later in a conversation does not hide the session. Before v2.1.211, a `/loop` run early in a conversation hid the session from the picker permanently.

nodes.label: Cross-project session ID lookup
nodes.rationale: From v2.1.223, `claude --resume <session-id>` looks in the current project directory and its git worktrees first, then in every other project on the machine. The cross-project search resolves the ID only when exactly one other project holds a transcript with messages for it, so a hand-copied duplicate produces a not-found report rather than an arbitrary copy.

nodes.label: State a resumed session restores
nodes.rationale: A resumed session restores the conversation along with the state saved in it: conversation history, model, agent, permission mode, an active goal, and unexpired scheduled tasks. Each of those carries documented exceptions.

nodes.label: Restored conversation history
nodes.rationale: Resuming restores the full conversation history, including tool calls and their results.

nodes.label: Restored model
nodes.rationale: A resumed session continues on the model it was using, except when that model has been retired or is disallowed by `availableModels`, when a `--model` flag or an `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`-family environment variable picks one at launch, or on providers using provider-specific deployment IDs such as Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry.

nodes.label: Restored agent
nodes.rationale: A session started with `--agent` or the `agent` setting continues as that agent, keeping its system prompt, tool restrictions and model. Claude Code looks for the agent in the session's original directory (if that workspace is trusted) and then in the directory you resume from; failing both, the session resumes with default tools and system prompt and shows a warning naming the agent.

nodes.label: Restored permission mode
nodes.rationale: Resuming from a terminal with `claude --continue`, `claude --resume <session-id>`, or an unambiguous `claude --resume <name>` (without `-p`) restores the permission mode the session was in, subject to the exceptions table. `--permission-mode` or `--dangerously-skip-permissions` override the restored mode.

nodes.label: Restored active goal
nodes.rationale: A goal still active when the session ended carries over into the resumed session, but its turn count, timer and token-spend baseline all reset.

nodes.label: Restored scheduled tasks
nodes.rationale: Scheduled tasks that have not expired are restored on resume. Background Bash tasks and monitor tasks are not restored.

nodes.label: Launch flags not restored on resume
nodes.rationale: Not every configuration flag from the original launch is restored: `--mcp-config`, `--settings`, `--plugin-dir`, `--fallback-model`, and `--add-dir` directories must be passed again, and directories added mid-session with `/add-dir` are not restored either (though the picker still uses them to locate the session). Standard settings files such as `settings.json` and `settings.local.json` are re-read at launch and need not be passed again.

nodes.label: Permission mode on resume
nodes.rationale: Which permission mode a resumed session starts in depends on the resume path: terminal, non-interactive `-p`, VS Code, the session picker at launch, or `/resume` inside a session. A `bypassPermissions` or `plan` session resumed in a terminal starts in the mode a NEW session would start in; `auto` is restored only while the account still meets auto-mode requirements; a manual session stays manual unless a settings-file `defaultMode` takes effect. Restoring plan mode on the non-interactive and VS Code paths requires v2.1.246 or later.

nodes.label: Resume in plan mode with -p
nodes.rationale: A `claude -p --resume` or `claude -p --continue` run resumes in plan mode only when all four conditions hold: you pass `--permission-prompt-tool` so the plan can be presented for approval, you pass neither `--permission-mode` nor `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, you do not pass `--fork-session`, and the run is not started through channels.

nodes.label: Resume-from-summary dialog
nodes.rationale: On a Pro or Max plan, resuming a session that has been inactive for more than about an hour and is over 100,000 tokens restores the conversation and then opens a dialog before your first message. Its three options differ in how much of the conversation each carries forward into later requests — a tradeoff between keeping every detail and sending fewer tokens per request.

nodes.label: Resume from summary
nodes.rationale: The 'Resume from summary' option runs `/compact` immediately: one summarization request over the full history, after which the history is replaced by the summary, your most recent exchanges, and up to five recently read files. Later requests carry the summary instead of the full history, costing less per request but losing whatever the summary omitted.

nodes.label: Resume full session as-is
nodes.rationale: 'Resume full session as-is' loads the conversation unchanged; after your first message Claude Code reprocesses and re-caches the full history, then re-reads it from the cache while the cache stays warm. It keeps every detail available at a per-request cost that scales with conversation size.

nodes.label: Don't ask me again
nodes.rationale: The 'Don't ask me again' option resumes the full session and permanently stops the resume-from-summary dialog appearing on all future resumes.

nodes.label: Expired prompt cache on a stale resume
nodes.rationale: By the time the resume-from-summary dialog appears, the session's prompt cache has expired, so the next request processes the full history once no matter which option is chosen. The options differ only in the cost of LATER requests.

nodes.label: Session picker
nodes.rationale: The interactive session picker opens via `/resume` inside a session or `claude --resume` with no arguments. Selecting a session it cannot load prints `Failed to resume the conversation` with a retry command and exits with code 1 from the `claude --resume` picker, while the `/resume` picker reports the failure and leaves your current conversation running.

nodes.label: Default session picker scope
nodes.rationale: Claude Code stores sessions per project directory, so by default the picker shows sessions from the current worktree (including background sessions, marked `bg`) plus sessions started elsewhere that added the current directory with `/add-dir`.

nodes.label: Widening the picker scope
nodes.rationale: `Ctrl+W` widens the picker to all worktrees of the repository (shown only in multi-worktree repositories) and `Ctrl+A` widens to every project on this machine, which also reveals each session's project path. Pressing either again returns to the narrower scope.

nodes.label: /cd relocates a session's storage
nodes.rationale: From v2.1.169, moving a session with `/cd` relocates it into the new directory's project storage so it appears in that directory's picker. As of v2.1.196 a moved session stays out of the old directory's picker even after a crash or forced exit; earlier versions could resurface it there after an unclean exit when the old path contained special characters such as underscores.

nodes.label: Selecting a session from another location
nodes.rationale: Selecting a session from another worktree of the same repository resumes it in place, or in your current directory if that worktree no longer exists. Selecting one from an unrelated project copies a `cd` and resume command to your clipboard instead — unless that project's directory is gone, in which case Claude Code resumes the session in your current directory rather than copying a command that would fail.

nodes.label: Session name resolution
nodes.rationale: Resuming by name resolves across the current repository and its worktrees: both `claude --resume <name>` and `/resume <name>` resume an exact match directly even in a different worktree. On an ambiguous name the CLI form opens the picker pre-filled, while the slash-command form reports an error.

nodes.label: Naming a session
nodes.rationale: Descriptive session names make sessions findable in the picker and resumable by name, which matters most when several tasks run in parallel. Names can be set at startup with `claude -n <name>`, during a session with `/rename`, from the picker with `Ctrl+R`, implicitly by accepting a plan, from claude.ai/Claude app on a Remote Control session (v2.1.221+), or from the desktop app.

nodes.label: /rename
nodes.rationale: `/rename <name>` names the session from inside it; the name also appears on the prompt bar. It is the remedy offered when Claude Code auto-renames a duplicate name and you would rather choose your own.

nodes.label: Duplicate-name auto-suffix
nodes.rationale: When an interactive session starts, resumes, or renames into a name another live session on the machine already uses, Claude Code leaves the name with the session that has it and renames yours to a two-word-suffixed variant such as `auth-refactor-graceful-unicorn`, telling you so. Before v2.1.232 both sessions kept the name. It does not check AI-generated titles or default display names, does not check the `--name` of a background or `-p` session at startup, and cannot rename a session on an earlier Claude Code version.

nodes.label: Default display name
nodes.rationale: Interactive sessions you never name get a default display name at start (v2.1.196+), combining the working directory's name with a two-character suffix, e.g. `my-app-3f`. It identifies the session in listings of running sessions such as agent view and `claude agents --json`, but it is NOT a resume handle — passing it to `claude --resume` or `/resume` finds nothing.

nodes.label: Generated session title
nodes.rationale: An unnamed session gets a generated title: a short summary of the first prompt written by a background request to the small/fast model, normally a Haiku-class model. Accepting a plan replaces it with a plan-based title, which also takes the place of the default display name in running-session listings. Unlike the default display name, either title can be passed to `claude --resume` or `/resume` and resolves like a name you set.

nodes.label: Session picker keyboard shortcuts
nodes.rationale: The picker binds arrows to navigate and expand/collapse groups, `Enter` to resume, `Space` (or `Ctrl+V`) to preview, `Ctrl+R` to rename, `/` or any printable character to search, `Ctrl+A`/`Ctrl+W` to widen scope, `Ctrl+B` to filter to the current git branch, and `Esc` to exit. Pasting a GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, GitLab, or Bitbucket pull/merge request URL into search finds the session that created it.

nodes.label: What a picker row shows
nodes.rationale: Each picker row shows the session name if set, otherwise the AI-generated title, conversation summary, or first prompt, along with time since last activity, git branch and file size. Sessions created with `/branch` or `--fork-session` get their own IDs and appear as separate rows; multiple entries for the same session are grouped under one row that `→` expands.

nodes.label: /branch
nodes.rationale: `/branch [name]` copies the conversation so far and switches you into the copy, leaving the original intact so you can try a different approach without losing the path you were on. Omitting the name names the branch after the conversation's first prompt (from v2.1.198 this also holds after compaction; earlier versions fell back to the literal name `Branched conversation`). The confirmation prints both session IDs, and the unchanged original stays in the picker.

nodes.label: What a branch inherits
nodes.rationale: Because `/branch` copies the transcript and switches the RUNNING process to write to it, the branch inherits conversation history up to the branch point, 'Allow for this session' permission grants, in-flight background subagents and background Bash commands (whose output appears in the new branch, not the original), and a live Remote Control connection that follows you into the branch.

nodes.label: --fork-session
nodes.rationale: From the command line, branching is done by combining `--continue` or `--resume` with `--fork-session`, e.g. `claude --continue --fork-session`. Unlike in-process `/branch`, forking starts a SEPARATE process, so session permission grants do not carry over and must be re-approved there.

nodes.label: Interleaved transcripts from double-resume
nodes.rationale: Resuming the same session in two terminals without forking interleaves messages from both into one transcript. For checkpoint-based rewind within a single session, use Checkpointing instead.

nodes.label: In-session context management
nodes.rationale: Three commands control what is in the context window without leaving the session: `/clear`, `/compact [instructions]`, and `/context`. How compaction interacts with CLAUDE.md, skills and rules is covered by the context window guide, and when to clear versus compact by Best practices.

nodes.label: /clear
nodes.rationale: `/clear` starts fresh with an empty context while SAVING the previous conversation, which is resumable with `/resume` or, in the same process, from the rewind menu's previous-session entry. With no argument the new conversation keeps a name set by `--name` or `/rename` but not an AI-generated title; passing a name as in `/clear release-prep` names the conversation you are leaving and starts the new one unnamed.

nodes.label: /compact
nodes.rationale: `/compact [instructions]` replaces the conversation history with a summary, optionally focused on what you specify. It is also what the 'Resume from summary' dialog option runs immediately on a stale resume.

nodes.label: /context
nodes.rationale: `/context` shows what is currently consuming the context window, without leaving the session.

nodes.label: Exporting and locating session data
nodes.rationale: Session data is reachable three ways: `/export` for a human-readable transcript, four script interfaces for structured data, and the on-disk JSONL transcripts whose location, retention and write behavior are configurable.

nodes.label: /export
