nodes.rationale: A strictPluginOnlyCustomization managed policy and bare mode treat the three customization types differently: a skills lock turns off both .claude/skills/ and .claude/commands/, while .claude/agents/ is governed by the policy's separate 'agents' entry. Bare mode still loads skills but skips commands and every .claude/agents/ folder, and does not watch skill directories at all.

nodes.label: Skills in Cowork and cloud sessions
nodes.rationale: Cowork sessions and cloud sessions, including routines, do not read ~/.claude/skills/ on your machine; both load the skills enabled for your claude.ai account, synced at session start, and cloud sessions additionally load project skills committed to the cloned repository. A skill existing only in ~/.claude/skills/ is reported not found when a routine invokes it, because each routine run is a fresh remote session. Desktop scheduled tasks run locally and load skills like any other local session.

nodes.label: Skills synced from claude.ai
nodes.rationale: Because Claude Code downloads a synced skill from your claude.ai account rather than reading a file you wrote on the machine, it applies rules to synced skills that do not apply to locally stored ones. Synced skills are labelled so their origin is visible: the /skills menu and /context group them under 'claude.ai sync' and the / menu marks them as coming from claude.ai.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_SYNC_SKILLS download flow
nodes.rationale: Outside Cowork and cloud sessions, synced skills load only after being downloaded once by a non-interactive run with the -p flag and CLAUDE_CODE_SYNC_SKILLS=1; the prompt itself does not affect the download. Skills land in ~/.claude/skills/synced/ and persist after the run exits, so later interactive sessions with the same sign-in load them, but changes on claude.ai require running the sync command again. CLAUDE_CODE_SYNC_SKILLS_WAIT_TIMEOUT_MS bounds how long the run waits.

nodes.label: Synced skill name collision handling
nodes.rationale: Claude Code skips a synced skill whose name matches any other command — built-in, bundled skill, local skill at any level, plugin skill, a .claude/commands/ file, or an MCP prompt — and runs that other command instead. Names of built-ins and bundled skills stay reserved even when unavailable in the session. Comparison ignores case, spacing, invisible characters and compatibility forms such as fullwidth letters and dash variants, but a look-alike letter from another alphabet counts as a different name.

nodes.label: Synced skill frontmatter handling
nodes.rationale: Claude Code honors a synced skill's frontmatter in every kind of session, so an allowed-tools grant goes through the normal permission flow. It sanitizes the display text the skill supplies, removing control characters and, in text that reaches Claude such as the description, escaping angle brackets so the text cannot imitate Claude Code's internal formatting.

nodes.label: Synced skill body handling
nodes.rationale: A synced skill's body behaves like a local skill's in a cloud session (isolated container) and in a Cowork desktop session except that every ! command line is replaced with the disableSkillShellExecution placeholder. In any other session on your machine Claude Code does not run ! commands, does not attach files named by @ references, and does not substitute ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} or ${CLAUDE_SESSION_ID}, so all of them reach Claude as literal text.

nodes.label: Removing a skill
nodes.rationale: How a skill is removed depends on its source: delete the directory for a personal or project skill; an administrator deletes it from the managed settings directory for an enterprise skill; disable or uninstall the plugin (then /reload-plugins or restart) for a plugin skill; turn it off for your claude.ai account for a synced skill, since deleting ~/.claude/skills/synced/<name> by hand only causes the next sync to download it again.

nodes.label: Reference content skills
nodes.rationale: Reference content adds knowledge Claude applies to current work — conventions, patterns, style guides, domain knowledge — and runs inline so Claude can use it alongside the conversation context. The doc's example is an api-conventions skill listing RESTful naming, consistent error formats, and request validation.

nodes.label: Task content skills
nodes.rationale: Task content gives Claude step-by-step instructions for a specific action such as a deployment, commit, or code generation — usually invoked directly with /skill-name rather than left to Claude's judgment. Adding disable-model-invocation: true prevents automatic triggering, and context: fork runs the task in its own subagent context.

nodes.label: Keep the skill body concise
nodes.rationale: Once a skill loads its content stays in context across turns, so every line is a recurring token cost. State what to do rather than narrating how or why, and apply the same conciseness test used for CLAUDE.md content. A related tip: keep SKILL.md under 500 lines and move detailed reference material into separate files.

nodes.label: Skill frontmatter reference
nodes.rationale: Skill behavior is configured with YAML frontmatter fields between --- markers: name, description, when_to_use, argument-hint, arguments, disable-model-invocation, user-invocable, allowed-tools, disallowed-tools, model, effort, context, agent, background, hooks, paths, shell, metadata, license, and compatibility. All fields are optional and only description is recommended. Boolean fields accept yes/no/on/off/1/0 in any case as well as true/false; before v2.1.218 only true and false were recognized.

nodes.label: description frontmatter field
nodes.rationale: description states what the skill does and when to use it, and is what Claude uses to decide when to apply the skill; if omitted, the first paragraph of markdown content is used. The name field is only a display label in listings for personal and project skills, since the command comes from the directory name.

nodes.label: 1,536-character description cap
nodes.rationale: when_to_use adds trigger phrases or example requests and is appended to description in the skill listing; the combined text is truncated at 1,536 characters regardless of the listing budget, so the key use case must come first. The cap is configurable with the skillListingMaxDescChars setting.

nodes.label: disable-model-invocation
nodes.rationale: disable-model-invocation: true means only the user can invoke the skill; its description is kept out of context entirely and Claude cannot load it automatically. It also prevents the skill being preloaded into subagents and, as of v2.1.196, prevents it running when a scheduled task fires with the skill as its prompt. Use it for side-effecting workflows such as /commit, /deploy, or /send-slack-message. Default: false.

nodes.label: user-invocable
nodes.rationale: user-invocable: false means only Claude can invoke the skill: it is hidden from the / menu and typing /name does nothing, while its description stays in context. Use it for background knowledge that is not a meaningful user action, such as a legacy-system-context skill. Default: true.

nodes.label: allowed-tools
nodes.rationale: allowed-tools pre-approves the listed tools for the turn that invokes the skill so Claude uses them without prompting; the grant clears with your next message and re-applies on the next invocation. It does not restrict anything — every tool stays callable and permission settings still govern unlisted tools. To pre-approve for a whole session, add allow rules to permission settings instead.

nodes.label: disallowed-tools
nodes.rationale: disallowed-tools removes tools from Claude's available pool while the skill is active — useful for autonomous skills that should never call, for example, AskUserQuestion in a background loop. The restriction clears with your next message and, like deny rules, cannot remove EndConversation while any other tool remains. To block tools across all skills and prompts, use deny rules in permission settings.

nodes.label: model frontmatter field
nodes.rationale: model sets the model while the skill is active; the override lasts the rest of the current turn, is not saved to settings, and the session model resumes on the next prompt. It accepts the same values as /model or 'inherit', a value excluded by an organization's availableModels allowlist is ignored, and with context: fork the value sets the forked subagent's model instead.

nodes.label: effort frontmatter field
nodes.rationale: effort overrides the session effort level while the skill is active, defaulting to inheriting from the session. Options are low, medium, high, xhigh, and max, with available levels depending on the model; the current value is readable in skill content as ${CLAUDE_EFFORT}, where Ultracode reports as xhigh.

nodes.label: context: fork
nodes.rationale: context: fork runs the skill in an isolated forked subagent context: the skill content becomes the prompt driving the subagent, which has no access to the conversation history. It only makes sense for skills with explicit instructions — guidelines with no task give the subagent nothing actionable and it returns without meaningful output.

nodes.label: agent frontmatter field
nodes.rationale: agent names which subagent type executes a context: fork skill, determining model, tools, and permissions. Options include the built-in Explore, Plan, and general-purpose agents or any custom subagent from .claude/agents/; it defaults to general-purpose. Explore and Plan skip CLAUDE.md and git status, so a forked skill using agent: Explore sees only the SKILL.md content and the agent's own system prompt.

nodes.label: background frontmatter field
nodes.rationale: background applies only with context: fork; setting it to false waits for the forked subagent's result in the invoking turn instead of running it in the background. Default is true and it requires v2.1.218 or later — before that, forked skills always blocked the turn.

nodes.label: hooks frontmatter field
nodes.rationale: The hooks field declares hooks that Claude Code registers when the skill is invoked and keeps running for the rest of the session; the hooks documentation's 'Hooks in skills and agents' section carries the configuration format and the 'once' option.

nodes.label: paths frontmatter field
nodes.rationale: paths takes glob patterns (comma-separated string or YAML list) that limit when the skill is activated: with it set, Claude loads the skill automatically only when working with matching files. It uses the same format as path-specific memory rules, and is one of two frontmatter fields Claude Code ignores in a .claude/commands/ file.

nodes.label: shell frontmatter field
nodes.rationale: shell chooses the interpreter for !`command` and ```! blocks in the skill, accepting bash (default) or powershell. Setting powershell runs inline commands via the PowerShell tool, which is on by default on Windows without Git Bash, on by default with Git Bash for claude.ai and Console accounts, and needs CLAUDE_CODE_USE_POWERSHELL_TOOL=1 on Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, macOS, Linux, and WSL.

nodes.label: metadata, license, compatibility fields
nodes.rationale: metadata is a free-form YAML map for your own key-value data read by your own tooling; Claude Code does not act on it and drops a value that is not a map, and frontmatter field names such as paths must not be reused as keys. license and compatibility (a string up to 500 characters) come from the Agent Skills spec and are accepted but not acted on by Claude Code.

nodes.label: Spec-only frontmatter outside Claude Code
nodes.rationale: Claude Code accepts every frontmatter field, but claude.ai skill uploads, the Skills API, and packaging with package_skill.py accept only six: name, description, license, compatibility, metadata, and allowed-tools. Any other field makes packaging or upload fail with a hard 'Unexpected key(s) in SKILL.md frontmatter' error rather than being ignored, and Claude Code-only body features such as dynamic context injection do not function in claude.ai chat or through the API.

nodes.label: How a skill gets its command name
nodes.rationale: The typed command comes from the file location, and for plugin skills also from frontmatter name: a personal or project skill uses its directory name (name is only a display label), a nested skill adds its relative subdirectory path, a .claude/commands/ file uses its file name, a plugin skills/ subdirectory uses name or the directory name under the plugin prefix, and a plugin-root SKILL.md takes its whole final segment from name with the plugin directory name as fallback. From v2.1.246 a name already carrying the plugin prefix is not double-prefixed, as it was from v2.1.216 through v2.1.245.

nodes.label: Available string substitutions
nodes.rationale: Skill content supports $ARGUMENTS, indexed $ARGUMENTS[N] and its $N shorthand, named $name placeholders declared in the arguments frontmatter, and the ${CLAUDE_SESSION_ID}, ${CLAUDE_EFFORT}, ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}, ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}, ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}, and ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} variables. Indexed arguments use shell-style quoting, an indexed placeholder with no argument stays literal, and a named placeholder with no argument expands to an empty string.

nodes.label: ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR} in body and allowed-tools
nodes.rationale: Claude Code substitutes ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR} and ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} (the latter requires v2.1.196+) in two places — the skill's markdown content and Bash rules in allowed-tools — and does the same for ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} and ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} in plugin skills. Using the same variable in both places makes the allow rule match the exact command the body tells Claude to run, so a bundled script executes without a permission prompt.

nodes.label: Argument literal-text and escaping rules
nodes.rationale: An argument value that itself contains $1 or $ARGUMENTS is inserted as literal text and not expanded, though ${CLAUDE_*} variables are still replaced after insertion. To write a literal $ before a digit, ARGUMENTS, or a declared argument name, escape it with one backslash (\$1.00); a doubled backslash leaves both in place and still expands, a backslash before any other $ is left unchanged, and the escape does not apply to ${CLAUDE_*} variables.

nodes.label: Supporting files in a skill directory
nodes.rationale: A skill directory can hold more than SKILL.md — reference.md, examples.md, and scripts/ — so large reference docs, API specifications, and example collections load only when needed rather than every time the skill runs, while scripts are executed rather than loaded. Reference the files from SKILL.md so Claude knows what each contains and when to load it.

nodes.label: Skill content lifecycle
nodes.rationale: An invoked skill's rendered SKILL.md enters the conversation as a single message and stays across later turns; Claude Code never re-reads the file, so guidance meant to apply throughout a task must be written as standing instructions. Re-invoking a skill whose rendered content is identical adds only a short 'already loaded' note, while differing content — new arguments or new dynamic-command output — is appended in full.

nodes.label: Skill re-attachment after compaction
nodes.rationale: Auto-compaction carries invoked skills forward within a token budget: after summarization Claude Code re-attaches the most recent invocation of each skill, keeping the first 5,000 tokens of each within a combined 25,000-token budget filled from the most recently invoked skill, so older skills can be dropped entirely. If a large or long-superseded skill stops influencing behavior, re-invoke it after compaction to restore its full content.

nodes.label: Workspace trust does not gate allowed-tools
nodes.rationale: Claude Code applies a project skill's allowed-tools whenever the skill is invoked, including in a -p run inside a folder never trusted. Because a skill can therefore grant itself broad tool access, review the allowed-tools of skills checked into a repository before running Claude Code there.

nodes.label: Passing arguments to skills
nodes.rationale: Both the user and Claude can pass arguments when invoking a skill, reaching the content through $ARGUMENTS. If no placeholder in the content receives an argument, Claude Code appends 'ARGUMENTS: <your input>' to the end so Claude still sees what was typed; an indexed placeholder with no argument at its position does not count as receiving one, while a named placeholder does because it expands to an empty string.

nodes.label: Stacking skills in one message
nodes.rationale: Several skills can be stacked at the start of one message: /write-tests /fix-issue 123 loads both and passes '123' as $ARGUMENTS to each. Claude Code expands the first skill plus up to five more, stopping at the first token that is not an inline user-invocable skill — a forked-subagent skill such as /code-review (forked from v2.1.218) or one like /loop whose arguments may start with a slash — and that token and everything after become the argument text. Before v2.1.199 only the first skill loaded.

nodes.label: Dynamic context injection
nodes.rationale: The !`<command>` syntax runs shell commands before the skill content reaches Claude, replacing the placeholder with the output so Claude receives actual data. Substitution runs once over the original file and output is not re-scanned, so a command cannot emit a placeholder for a later pass. The inline form is recognized only when ! starts a line or follows whitespace; multi-line commands use a fenced block opened with ```!.

nodes.label: How injected commands run
nodes.rationale: Injected commands run through the Bash tool or the PowerShell tool, except that shell: bash with no bash available fails the invocation outright before any command runs. They execute in the session shell's current working directory (which moves when Claude runs cd), merge stderr into stdout under bash, run under the Bash tool's default 2-minute timeout, and return oversized output as a file path plus a short preview.

nodes.label: When an injected command fails
nodes.rationale: A failed injected command aborts the whole skill invocation, not just its placeholder, and Claude never sees the skill content: the abort shows 'Shell command failed for pattern "..."' with the output under [stderr]. Under bash any non-zero exit fails, except that exit code 1 from listed search and comparison commands is treated as a normal result; append || true to anything else expected to exit non-zero. Injected commands never prompt for permission — a check returning anything but allow, including an ask rule, aborts the invocation.

nodes.label: disableSkillShellExecution setting
nodes.rationale: Setting "disableSkillShellExecution": true replaces each injected command from user, project, plugin, or additional-directory skills and custom commands with '[shell command execution disabled by policy]' instead of running it. Bundled and managed skills are unaffected, and the setting is most useful in managed settings where users cannot override it.

nodes.label: Forked skills run in the background
nodes.rationale: A forked subagent runs in the background — you keep working and its result arrives when it completes. Claude Code waits for the result anyway in non-interactive mode (-p or the Agent SDK), when CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS is 1, when a forked skill is invoked while an earlier invocation of the same skill is still running, and when a scheduled task fires with the skill as its prompt.

nodes.label: Backgrounded forks get a narrower tool set
nodes.rationale: A backgrounded fork runs with the narrower tool set that applies to background subagents, because the skill's subagent is a regular agent type and the exemption for subagents that fork the conversation does not cover it. If the skill's steps depend on a tool outside that set, set background: false to keep the full tool set.

nodes.label: Background forks bypass checkpoints
nodes.rationale: A forked skill running in the background applies its edits outside the session's checkpoints, so /rewind does not undo them; use git to revert them instead.

nodes.label: Restricting Claude's skill access
nodes.rationale: Three ways control which skills Claude can invoke: deny the Skill tool outright in /permissions to disable all skills; allow or deny specific ones with permission rules where Skill(name) is an exact match and Skill(name *) a prefix match with any arguments; or add disable-model-invocation: true to a skill's frontmatter to remove it from Claude's context entirely. A few built-in commands such as /init and /security-review are also reachable through the Skill tool, while others such as /compact are not.

nodes.label: skillOverrides setting
nodes.rationale: skillOverrides controls skill visibility from settings rather than the skill's own frontmatter, for skills whose SKILL.md you do not want to edit. Each key is a skill name with one of four values: "on" (name and description listed, in the / menu), "name-only", "user-invocable-only" (hidden from Claude, still in the menu, labelled user-only), and "off" (hidden everywhere). As of v2.1.199 "off" also hides the skill from Remote Control and Agent SDK command lists. Absent skills are treated as "on", and plugin skills are unaffected.

nodes.label: Baseline comparison for evaluating a skill
nodes.rationale: Seeing a skill trigger only proves Claude found it, so measure two things separately: whether Claude invokes it on the prompts it should, and whether the output matches expectations when it does. The check for both is a baseline comparison — run a few realistic prompts in a fresh session with the skill available and again with it disabled, and compare. A fresh session matters because leftover authoring context masks gaps in the written instructions.

nodes.label: skill-creator plugin eval loop
nodes.rationale: The skill-creator plugin (installed with /plugin install skill-creator@claude-plugins-official) automates the comparison loop: it stores test cases in evals/evals.json, spawns a subagent per case for clean-context isolated runs recording tokens and duration, grades assertions into grading.json, aggregates with-skill versus without-skill pass rate, time and tokens into benchmark.json, runs blind A/B version comparisons, tunes descriptions via should-trigger and should-not-trigger prompts, and opens an HTML review viewer whose qualitative feedback the next iteration reads.

nodes.label: Sharing skills at different scopes
nodes.rationale: Skills are distributed at three scopes depending on audience: project skills by committing .claude/skills/ to version control, plugin skills via a skills/ directory in a plugin, and managed skills deployed organization-wide through managed settings.

nodes.label: Skills that generate visual output
nodes.rationale: Skills can bundle and run scripts in any language, giving Claude capabilities beyond a single prompt — the doc's worked example is a codebase-visualizer whose bundled Python script emits a self-contained interactive HTML tree with a summary sidebar, a file-type bar chart, and collapsible directories. The bundled script does the work while Claude handles orchestration, and the same pattern covers dependency graphs, coverage reports, and schema visualizations.

nodes.label: Troubleshooting a skill that will not trigger
nodes.rationale: If Claude does not use a skill when expected: check the description contains keywords users would naturally say, verify the skill appears in 'What skills are available?', rephrase the request to match the description more closely, and invoke it directly with /skill-name if it is user-invocable. The inverse problem — a skill triggering too often — is fixed by making the description more specific or adding disable-model-invocation: true.

nodes.label: Malformed frontmatter symptoms
nodes.rationale: If a skill's frontmatter YAML is malformed, Claude Code loads the body with empty metadata, so /skill-name still works but Claude has no description to match against. Run with --debug to see the parse error, or run `claude plugin validate` on the skills directory (v2.1.233+) to find SKILL.md files whose frontmatter does not parse.

nodes.label: Skill listing character budget
nodes.rationale: Claude Code loads a listing of skill names and descriptions into context; the listing always contains every name but shortens descriptions to fit a budget of 1% of the model's context window, dropping them starting with the least-invoked skills. /doctor estimates the listing's cost and biggest contributors, an overflow is written to the debug log, and the /context Skills row reports the post-budget size (before v2.1.196 it counted full text). Raise it with skillListingBudgetFraction or SLASH_COMMAND_TOOL_CHAR_BUDGET.

nodes.label: Subagent
nodes.rationale: A subagent is a specialized AI assistant that handles a specific type of task in its own context window, with a custom system prompt, specific tool access, and independent permissions. Claude delegates a matching task to it, and the subagent works independently and returns only its result.

nodes.label: Context isolation
nodes.rationale: The central benefit of a subagent: search results, logs and file contents that would flood the main conversation stay in the subagent's own context, and only the summary returns. Use one when a side task would otherwise fill the main window with material you will never reference again.

nodes.label: description field drives delegation
nodes.rationale: Claude uses each subagent's `description` frontmatter field to decide when to delegate, so the description must be clear and specific enough to route to the right subagent. Phrases like 'use proactively' encourage proactive delegation.

nodes.label: 15,000-token description budget
nodes.rationale: Subagent descriptions consume context. When the combined descriptions of non-built-in subagents exceed 15,000 tokens, Claude Code shows a startup warning with the total token count and still loads every subagent; the remedy is to trim `description` and move detail into the system prompt, which loads only when that subagent runs.

nodes.label: Built-in subagents
nodes.rationale: Claude Code ships subagents that Claude uses automatically when appropriate; each inherits the parent conversation's permissions and most run with a restricted tool set. They are registered by default in interactive sessions.

nodes.label: Explore subagent
nodes.rationale: A fast, read-only built-in agent for file discovery, code search and codebase exploration; Write and Edit are denied. When invoking it Claude specifies a thoroughness level of quick, medium, or very thorough.

nodes.label: Plan subagent
nodes.rationale: A read-only research agent used during plan mode to gather codebase context before presenting a plan. It inherits the main conversation's model and keeps exploration output in a separate context window while the main conversation stays read-only.

nodes.label: General-purpose subagent
nodes.rationale: A capable built-in agent with every tool available to subagents, used for complex multi-step tasks that need both exploration and modification, complex reasoning, or multiple dependent steps.

nodes.label: Other helper agents
nodes.rationale: Claude Code includes additional automatically-invoked helpers: `claude` (a catch-all with every subagent tool, also the default agent for a dispatched background session), `statusline-setup` (Sonnet, for `/statusline`), and `claude-code-guide` (Haiku, for questions about Claude Code features).

nodes.label: Explore inherits the session model, capped at Opus
nodes.rationale: As of v2.1.198 Explore inherits the main conversation's model instead of always running on Haiku; on the Claude API the inherited model is capped at Opus, and on other providers it inherits directly. A user or project subagent named `Explore` overrides the built-in and keeps its own `model` field, so `model: haiku` restores low-cost exploration.

nodes.label: Restricting or disabling built-in subagents
nodes.rationale: Built-ins can be restricted four ways: add a type to `permissions.deny`; deny the `Agent` tool itself to stop all delegation; set `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPLORE_PLAN_AGENTS=1` to remove Explore and Plan (v2.1.198+); or set `CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_DISABLE_BUILTIN_AGENTS=1` in non-interactive mode and the Agent SDK to remove all built-in types.

nodes.label: subagent_type is required error
nodes.rationale: An Agent tool call that omits `subagent_type` fails with `subagent_type is required` when the session has no `general-purpose` subagent left to fall back on.

nodes.label: Subagent file: YAML frontmatter plus Markdown body
nodes.rationale: A subagent is a Markdown file whose YAML frontmatter is its configuration and whose body becomes its system prompt. A subagent receives only that system prompt plus basic environment details such as the working directory, not the Claude Code system prompt. Claude Code watches the agents directories and picks up edits within seconds without a restart.

nodes.label: /agents wizard removed in v2.1.198
nodes.rationale: As of v2.1.198 the `/agents` command no longer opens the interactive creation wizard; it prints a reminder to ask Claude or edit `.claude/agents/` directly. Files, frontmatter fields and directory locations are unchanged — only the terminal wizard was removed.

nodes.label: Subagent scope precedence
nodes.rationale: When several subagents share a name, the higher-priority location wins, in this order: managed settings (1, highest), the `--agents` CLI flag (2), `.claude/agents/` (3), `~/.claude/agents/` (4), and a plugin's `agents/` directory (5, lowest).

nodes.label: Project subagents (.claude/agents/)
nodes.rationale: Subagents in `.claude/agents/` are scoped to one codebase and should be checked into version control so a team can improve them together. They are discovered by walking up from the working directory, and as of v2.1.178 the definition closest to the working directory wins among nested directories.

nodes.label: User subagents (~/.claude/agents/)
nodes.rationale: Personal subagents stored in `~/.claude/agents/` are available in every project on the machine. If Claude cannot find a newly created one, a restart is needed only when that directory did not exist when the session started.

nodes.label: --agents CLI flag (session-only JSON subagents)
nodes.rationale: `claude --agents '<json>'` defines one or more subagents that exist only for that session and are never saved to disk, useful for quick testing or automation. Each top-level key is the agent name (it must not start with `-`), `prompt` supplies the system prompt, and the JSON accepts description, tools, disallowedTools, model, permissionMode, mcpServers, hooks, maxTurns, skills, initialPrompt, memory, effort, background and isolation.

nodes.label: Managed subagents
nodes.rationale: Organization administrators deploy subagents by placing markdown files in `.claude/agents/` inside the managed settings directory, using the same frontmatter format. Managed definitions take precedence over project and user subagents of the same name.

nodes.label: Plugin subagents
nodes.rationale: Subagents from installed plugins load automatically alongside custom ones and appear in the @-mention typeahead under their scoped name. A plugin subagent whose frontmatter has no `name` or does not parse still loads, under its filename.

nodes.label: Plugin-scoped identifier
nodes.rationale: Unlike project and user scopes, a subfolder inside a plugin's `agents/` directory becomes part of the identifier: `agents/review/security.md` in plugin `my-plugin` registers as `my-plugin:review:security`. The colon is reserved for this form, so agent `name` values may not contain one.

nodes.label: Name uniqueness across the agents tree
nodes.rationale: Identity comes only from the `name` frontmatter field, so two files under the same agents directory (including its subfolders) declaring the same name means Claude Code loads only one, chosen by filesystem read order rather than a documented precedence. `/doctor` reports same-directory duplicates and proposes renaming or removing all but one.

nodes.label: Recursive scanning of agents directories
nodes.rationale: Claude Code scans `.claude/agents/`, `~/.claude/agents/` and plugin `agents/` directories recursively, so definitions can be organized into subfolders such as `agents/review/`. For project and user scopes the subdirectory path does not affect how a subagent is identified or invoked.

nodes.label: --add-dir agents directories
nodes.rationale: Adding a directory with `--add-dir` or `/add-dir` also loads its `.claude/agents/` folder alongside project subagents. Those directories are not watched for changes, so edits there need a restart, and a directory outside the trusted workspace's repository needs its own trust entry.

nodes.label: Plugin subagents ignore hooks, mcpServers and permissionMode
nodes.rationale: For security reasons plugin subagents do not support the `hooks`, `mcpServers` or `permissionMode` frontmatter fields; those fields are ignored when an agent loads from a plugin. To use them, copy the agent file into `.claude/agents/` or `~/.claude/agents/`.

nodes.label: Supported frontmatter fields
nodes.rationale: Only `name` and `description` are required. `name` is a lowercase-and-hyphen identifier that hooks receive as `agent_type`, need not match the filename, and may not contain `:` (before v2.1.218 such names were accepted). The optional fields are tools, disallowedTools, model, permissionMode, maxTurns, skills, mcpServers, hooks, memory, background, effort, isolation, color, initialPrompt and experimental.

nodes.label: tools field (allowlist)
nodes.rationale: `tools` is an allowlist naming the tools a subagent can use; omitting it inherits every tool available to subagents. To preload Skills use the `skills` field rather than listing `Skill` here.

nodes.label: disallowedTools field (denylist)
nodes.rationale: `disallowedTools` removes tools from the inherited or specified list, letting a subagent keep everything except, for example, Write and Edit. When both fields are set, `disallowedTools` is applied first and `tools` is then resolved against the remaining pool, so a tool listed in both is removed.

nodes.label: model field
nodes.rationale: `model` accepts an alias (`sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, `fable`), a full model ID such as `claude-opus-5`, or `inherit` to use the main conversation's model. Omitting it makes Claude Code fall through the subagent model order.

nodes.label: permissionMode field and its modes
nodes.rationale: `permissionMode` chooses the mode a subagent runs in: `default` (manual prompting), `acceptEdits`, `auto` (a background classifier reviews commands and protected-directory writes), `dontAsk` (auto-deny prompts), `bypassPermissions`, or `plan`. Left unset, the subagent inherits the main conversation's mode, which starts as auto mode on Pro, Max and Team plans.

nodes.label: bypassPermissions risk and disable switch
nodes.rationale: `bypassPermissions` skips permission prompts and lets the subagent write to sensitive directories such as `.git`, `.claude`, `.vscode` and `.cargo`, though the actions no mode auto-approves still apply. If `permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode` is set, Claude Code ignores the frontmatter mode and runs the subagent with the parent session's mode (v2.1.223+).

nodes.label: Parent permission mode takes precedence
nodes.rationale: If the parent session uses `bypassPermissions` or `acceptEdits`, that takes precedence and cannot be overridden by the subagent. If the parent uses auto mode, the subagent inherits auto mode and its own `permissionMode` is ignored: the classifier evaluates its tool calls with the parent's block and allow rules.

nodes.label: maxTurns field
nodes.rationale: `maxTurns` caps the agentic turns before a subagent stops. On reaching the limit Claude Code returns the output marked as partial (v2.1.246+) and, for subagents that return an agent ID, notes that Claude can message the subagent to continue from where it stopped.

nodes.label: skills field
nodes.rationale: `skills` names Skills to preload into the subagent's context at startup; the full skill content is injected, not just the description. It controls preloading only — without it a subagent can still discover and invoke project, user and plugin skills through the Skill tool.

nodes.label: Preloading skills and its limits
nodes.rationale: Preloading gives a subagent domain knowledge without it having to discover skills at runtime. Skills that set `disable-model-invocation: true` cannot be preloaded, including the bundled `/verify` skill, and a listed skill that is missing or disabled is skipped with a warning in the debug log. To stop a subagent invoking skills at all, omit `Skill` from `tools` or add it to `disallowedTools`.

nodes.label: mcpServers field
nodes.rationale: `mcpServers` scopes MCP servers to a subagent: each entry is either a string naming an already-configured server (which shares the parent session's connection) or an inline definition using the `.mcp.json` schema and the stdio, http, sse or ws types. Defining a server inline here rather than in `.mcp.json` keeps its tool descriptions out of the main conversation's context.

nodes.label: Inline MCP server trust rule
nodes.rationale: Claude Code loads an inline server from a project or `--add-dir` agent file only after the folder that file came from is trusted (v2.1.238+); a parent folder's trust and the automatic trust of a `-p` or SDK session do not count. Until then it skips every inline server in that file and writes the exact `projects["<path>"].hasTrustDialogAccepted` key to the debug log. Name references and inline servers from `~/.claude/agents/`, `--agents`, the SDK, or managed settings load without this check.

nodes.label: Session MCP restrictions cover subagent frontmatter
nodes.rationale: As of v2.1.153, `--strict-mcp-config`, `--bare`, enterprise managed MCP configuration, and `allowedMcpServers`/`deniedMcpServers` policies also cover servers declared in subagent frontmatter; a blocked server is skipped with a warning naming it. Managed-settings restrictions apply to every subagent, while `--strict-mcp-config` does not filter servers passed inline via `--agents` or the SDK, since those are explicit caller input.

nodes.label: hooks field (subagent-scoped lifecycle hooks)
nodes.rationale: Hooks defined in a subagent's frontmatter run only while that subagent is active and are cleaned up when it finishes. All hook events are supported; the common ones are `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, and `Stop`, which is automatically converted to `SubagentStop` when the agent runs as a subagent. Hooks from settings files, managed policy and plugins also fire inside subagents.

nodes.label: Frontmatter hooks need workspace trust
nodes.rationale: A project-level subagent's frontmatter hooks run only after the trust dialog is accepted for the folder containing the agent file; user-level and `--agents` definitions run without this step. Until trusted, the subagent still runs but its frontmatter hooks are skipped and an error is written to the debug log. This is stricter than settings-file hooks: a parent folder's trust is not enough and a `-p` session does not count (v2.1.218+).

nodes.label: PreToolUse conditional validation
nodes.rationale: A `PreToolUse` hook validates operations before they execute, allowing some uses of a tool while blocking others — for example a `db-reader` subagent with Bash whose hook script reads the JSON hook input from stdin, greps the command for SQL write verbs, and exits with code 2 to block it and return the message to the subagent. On macOS and Linux the script must be executable or the hook fails instead of blocking.

nodes.label: memory field
nodes.rationale: `memory` gives a subagent a persistent directory that survives across conversations, scoped `user` (`~/.claude/agent-memory/<name>/`), `project` (`.claude/agent-memory/<name>/`, the recommended default because it is shareable via version control), or `local` (`.claude/agent-memory-local/<name>/`, not checked in).

nodes.label: What enabling memory changes
nodes.rationale: With memory enabled the subagent's system prompt gains instructions for reading and writing the memory directory plus the first 200 lines or 25KB of its `MEMORY.md` (with instructions to curate it beyond that), and Read, Write and Edit are automatically enabled so it can manage its memory files.

nodes.label: Subagent memory depends on auto memory
nodes.rationale: Subagent memory is part of auto memory: turning auto memory off with the `autoMemoryEnabled` setting or `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY` makes the `memory` field have no effect, and the subagent launches without the memory instructions or the memory tool access.

nodes.label: background field
nodes.rationale: Setting `background: true` keeps a subagent in the background even when Claude asks to run it in the foreground. Where fork mode is on, Claude Code already runs the subagents Claude spawns in the background, and Claude Code refuses to spawn an agent-team teammate's subagent whose definition sets it.

nodes.label: effort field
nodes.rationale: `effort` sets the effort level while the subagent is active, overriding the session effort level; it defaults to inheriting from the session and accepts `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` or `max`, with the available levels depending on the model. `/tasks` shows the effort level when the definition or the skill it forked from sets it (v2.1.242+).

nodes.label: isolation: worktree
nodes.rationale: `isolation: worktree` runs the subagent in a temporary git worktree — an isolated copy of the repository branched by default from the default branch rather than the parent session's HEAD, cleaned up automatically if the subagent makes no changes. Its Bash and PowerShell commands run inside that worktree, and a command whose working directory resolves to the main checkout fails (v2.1.203+); for Bash, Claude Code also blocks commands that redirect git into the main checkout or whose shape it cannot verify.

nodes.label: initialPrompt field
nodes.rationale: `initialPrompt` is auto-submitted as the first user turn when the agent runs as the main session agent via `--agent` or the `agent` setting. Commands and skills in it are processed, and it is prepended to any user-provided prompt.

nodes.label: experimental.cacheTtl
nodes.rationale: The `experimental` map's `cacheTtl` key, set to `5m` or `1h`, chooses the prompt cache lifetime for this subagent's requests at the frontmatter's place in the cache lifetime precedence. It must be written inside the `experimental` map rather than at the top level; other values are ignored, `1h` is ignored while the subscription uses usage credits, and the field is read only from subagent files (v2.1.248+).

nodes.label: Subagent files Claude Code skips
nodes.rationale: A file in an agents directory is silently skipped when it has no `name` (treated as documentation), when its opening `---` is not the first line (read as having no frontmatter), when its `name` starts with `-` or contains `:`, when it has a `name` but no `description`, or when its YAML does not parse — the last three also write the reason to the debug log, visible with `--debug`.

nodes.label: claude plugin validate on an agents directory
nodes.rationale: Running `claude plugin validate` against `.claude/agents` or `~/.claude/agents` finds files whose frontmatter does not parse, before a session starts. It checks only the directory named and does not flag a file whose frontmatter parses but has no `name` (v2.1.233+).

nodes.label: Subagent model resolution order
nodes.rationale: Claude Code resolves a subagent's model in this order: the per-invocation `model` parameter, then the definition's `model` frontmatter (where `inherit` selects the main conversation's model), then `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL`, then the main conversation's model. A per-invocation value also applies when the subagent is resumed or messaged (v2.1.211+).

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL
nodes.rationale: This environment variable sits third in the model order and by itself does not change the model the built-in Explore and Plan subagents run on. Before v2.1.251 it came first and overrode both the per-invocation parameter and the frontmatter, including `model: inherit`; setting it to `inherit` is now the same as leaving it unset (before v2.1.196 that value forced subagents onto the main conversation's model).

nodes.label: availableModels allowlist substitution
nodes.rationale: Claude Code checks the per-invocation parameter, frontmatter and environment variable against the organization's `availableModels` allowlist. A blocked family alias such as `opus` runs on the newest permitted version of that family (v2.1.222+); any other blocked value, or a family with no permitted version, falls back to the inherited model. Interactive sessions show a warning naming the requested model and the one actually used.

nodes.label: Subagents inherit extended thinking
nodes.rationale: As of v2.1.198 subagents inherit the main conversation's extended thinking configuration — on if the session has it on, off if not — and there is no per-subagent thinking setting. Before v2.1.198 subagents always ran with extended thinking disabled.

nodes.label: Two-filter subagent tool pool
nodes.rationale: Subagents inherit the main conversation's built-in and MCP tools narrowed by two filters: one removes a fixed list of tools from every subagent, and a second reduces the built-in set for subagents running in the background, which is the default. Forks skip both filters and receive the main conversation's exact tool pool.

nodes.label: Tools removed from every subagent
nodes.rationale: The first filter removes, even when listed in `tools`: `Agent` when the subagent is at the depth limit, `AskUserQuestion`, `EndConversation`, `EnterPlanMode`, `ExitPlanMode` (unless `permissionMode` is `plan`), `ScheduleWakeup`, `TaskOutput`, `WaitForMcpServers` and `Workflow`.

nodes.label: Background subagent built-in tool set
nodes.rationale: A background subagent keeps every MCP tool but only these built-ins: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, PowerShell, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, TodoWrite, Skill, ToolSearch, EnterWorktree, ExitWorktree, Monitor, TaskStop, SendMessage and Artifact. Every other built-in is removed silently, so one definition can resolve to different tools in the foreground and the background. Agent-team teammates additionally keep the task and cron tools.

nodes.label: Agent would be spawned with zero tools
nodes.rationale: When nothing in the `tools` list resolves — every entry misspelled, or naming a tool unavailable to subagents — Claude Code usually refuses to launch the subagent and the Agent tool returns an error naming the unresolved entries. Before v2.1.208 the subagent launched with no tools and could return an empty or confusing result.

nodes.label: MCP server-level tool patterns
nodes.rationale: Both `tools` and `disallowedTools` accept server-level patterns in addition to exact tool names: `mcp__<server>` or `mcp__<server>__*` grants or removes every tool from that server, and in `disallowedTools` the pattern `mcp__*` removes every MCP tool from any server.

nodes.label: Agent(agent_type) spawn allowlist
nodes.rationale: `tools: Agent(worker, researcher)` restricts which subagent types an agent running as the main thread with `claude --agent` may spawn; other types fail and the agent sees only the allowed types. Bare `Agent` allows any type, omitting `Agent` blocks spawning entirely, and in a plain subagent definition the parenthesized type list is ignored. In v2.1.63 the Task tool was renamed Agent, with `Task(...)` still accepted as an alias.

nodes.label: Disable specific subagents with permissions.deny
nodes.rationale: Adding `Agent(<subagent-name>)` entries to the `deny` array in settings, or passing `--disallowedTools "Agent(Explore)"`, stops Claude using that subagent. It works for both built-in and custom subagents, and is the way to block specific agents while allowing all others.

nodes.label: SubagentStart and SubagentStop hooks
nodes.rationale: Hooks configured in `settings.json` respond to subagent lifecycle events in the main session: `SubagentStart` fires when a subagent begins and `SubagentStop` when it completes, both matched on the agent type name.

nodes.label: Matchers are unanchored regular expressions
nodes.rationale: A plugin-scoped matcher name contains a colon and is evaluated as an unanchored regular expression, so it must be anchored as `^my-plugin:db-agent$` to match only that agent. A hyphenated matcher such as `db-agent` matches exactly on v2.1.195 or later; on earlier versions it also fired for names containing it, such as `prod-db-agent`.

nodes.label: Automatic delegation
nodes.rationale: Claude delegates automatically based on the task description in the request, the `description` field in subagent configurations, and current context.

nodes.label: Explicit subagent invocation
nodes.rationale: Three escalating patterns request a subagent yourself: naming it in natural language (Claude decides), an @-mention such as `@"code-reviewer (agent)"` which guarantees that subagent runs for one task, and a session-wide default via `--agent` or the `agent` setting. The @-mention controls which subagent Claude invokes, not the prompt it receives; the manual form is `@agent-<name>`, or `@agent-` plus the scoped name for plugin subagents.

nodes.label: --agent: run the whole session as a subagent
nodes.rationale: `claude --agent <name>` starts a session whose main thread takes on that subagent's system prompt, tool restrictions and model; the prompt replaces the default Claude Code system prompt entirely while CLAUDE.md and project memory still load, and the agent name appears as `@<name>` in the startup header. The choice persists across resume, and `agent` in `.claude/settings.json` makes it the project default, which the CLI flag overrides.

nodes.label: Foreground vs background subagents
nodes.rationale: Foreground subagents block the main conversation and pass permission prompts straight through; background subagents run concurrently. Claude Code picks the mode from the first applicable case: a teammate's subagent runs in the foreground; `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS=1` forces the foreground everywhere; with fork mode on everything runs in the background and Claude cannot ask for the foreground; with fork mode off Claude gets the background by default and the foreground when it needs the result.

nodes.label: Background permission prompts and completion notification
nodes.rationale: A background subagent's permission prompts surface in the main session, naming the subagent asking; Esc denies that one call without stopping the subagent, and an answer that outlasts one call applies to the whole session including the main conversation (before v2.1.186 such calls were auto-denied). Its results reach Claude as a completion notification in a later turn, and Claude waits for it before reporting results (v2.1.211+).

nodes.label: Subagent names make an agent addressable
nodes.rationale: Claude can pass a `name` parameter on the Agent tool call, and may do so on its own without asking. The name makes the subagent addressable so Claude can message or resume it by name after it finishes.

nodes.label: A named subagent can launch as a teammate
nodes.rationale: In an interactive session with agent teams enabled, a subagent Claude spawns from the main conversation with a `name` launches as a teammate instead — unless the call is a fork or passes `isolation` on the call itself. An `isolation` value in the subagent's frontmatter does not prevent it, and the teammate then runs in the main session's working directory.

nodes.label: API errors in subagents
nodes.rationale: As of v2.1.199 a subagent whose run ends on an API error reports the failure rather than returning the error text as findings. In the foreground, a cut-off subagent with text output returns that partial output plus a note it did not finish, while one that produced nothing fails with `Agent terminated early due to an API error`. In the background the subagent is marked failed and the message to Claude names the error and includes its last output.

nodes.label: Fallback model chain keeps a subagent working
nodes.rationale: When a fallback model chain is configured and a subagent hits a failure the chain covers, such as its model being unavailable, Claude Code switches the subagent to the first model in the chain that accepts the request so it keeps working instead of ending on the error.

nodes.label: Subagent output scanning
nodes.rationale: Claude Code scans each subagent's final report before Claude reads it, because the subagent may have read files, pages or command output carrying instructions aimed at the main conversation. The scan removes and rewords nothing; it inserts a backslash into text imitating harness output such as `<system-reminder>` or `Human:`, and prepends a `[harness: subagent output matched instruction-shaped pattern(s):` marker line. It does not judge malice, and tool calls a report leads to still pass through permission checks and sandboxing (v2.1.210+).

nodes.label: Pattern: isolate high-volume operations
nodes.rationale: One of the most effective uses of subagents is isolating operations that produce large output — running tests, fetching documentation, processing logs — so the verbose output stays in the subagent's context and only the relevant summary returns to the main conversation.

nodes.label: Pattern: run parallel research
nodes.rationale: Spawning multiple subagents to investigate independent areas simultaneously works best when the research paths do not depend on each other; Claude then synthesizes the findings. The warning attached: many subagents each returning detailed results can itself consume significant main-conversation context.

nodes.label: Pattern: chain subagents
nodes.rationale: For multi-step workflows, subagents run in sequence: each completes its task and returns results to Claude, which passes the relevant context to the next — for example a code-reviewer finding performance issues followed by an optimizer fixing them.

nodes.label: Choosing between a subagent and the main conversation
nodes.rationale: Use the main conversation for frequent back-and-forth, phases that share significant context, quick targeted changes, and when latency matters since a non-fork subagent starts fresh. Use a subagent for verbose output you do not need, enforced tool restrictions, and self-contained work that can return a summary; consider Skills for reusable workflows in the main context, and `/btw` for a question about what is already in the conversation.

nodes.label: Subagent spawn depth limit
nodes.rationale: By default a subagent can spawn its own subagents up to three layers below the main conversation; at the limit Claude Code withholds the `Agent` tool from every subagent except a fork, whose `Agent` stays listed but returns an error. `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH` changes the limit (`1` turns nesting off). Only the top-level subagent's summary returns to you, and nested subagents appear as a tree in the panel with a `(+N)` descendant count.

nodes.label: Concurrent subagent limit
nodes.rationale: By default, spawning a subagent while 20 are already running fails with `Concurrent subagent limit reached` and the error tells Claude not to retry; `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS` changes it and ultracode sessions are exempt (v2.1.217+). There is no cap on the total spawned over a session. A `/subtask` fork occupies a slot but is never blocked, and resuming a finished subagent takes a fresh slot without checking the limit.

nodes.label: What loads at subagent startup
nodes.rationale: A non-fork subagent's initial context holds its own system prompt plus appended environment details, the delegation task message, every level of the CLAUDE.md hierarchy, a git status snapshot taken at the start of the parent session, the full content of any preloaded skills, and the sibling roster. It does not see the conversation history, previously invoked skills, or files already read.

nodes.label: Sibling roster
nodes.rationale: A system reminder listing `main` and every other named agent in the session, each a valid `to` value for SendMessage (v2.1.206+). It appears only when the subagent's tools include SendMessage and at least one other agent has a name, and it is a snapshot taken at startup, so agents named later do not appear.

nodes.label: Main-conversation state a subagent never receives
nodes.rationale: A non-fork subagent does not receive the session's output style (it runs its own system prompt), the main conversation's auto memory, or the parent's context window size — its window is sized by its own model, so delegating to a smaller-window model gives that subagent the smaller window. Explore and Plan additionally skip CLAUDE.md and git status, with no setting to change which agents skip them.

nodes.label: Resuming subagents
nodes.rationale: Each invocation creates a new instance, but a subagent can be resumed with its full conversation history — previous tool calls, results and reasoning — so it picks up exactly where it stopped. Claude receives an agent ID when a subagent completes; the one-shot Explore and Plan agents return none and cannot be resumed. A completed subagent that receives a SendMessage auto-resumes in the background, and resuming starts a new run under the same ID.

nodes.label: SendMessage tool
nodes.rationale: Claude resumes a subagent with the SendMessage tool, passing the agent's ID or name as `to`. It does not require agent teams to be enabled — only structured team-protocol messages such as `shutdown_request` do — and in sessions with cross-session messaging it can also reach other Claude Code sessions. As of v2.1.199 it verifies a name still refers to the same agent and refuses the send when a newer agent has taken it, reporting which agent the name now reaches.

nodes.label: Subagent transcripts persist separately
nodes.rationale: Subagent transcripts live in `~/.claude/projects/{project}/{sessionId}/subagents/` as `agent-{agentId}.jsonl`. They are unaffected by main-conversation compaction because they are separate files, persist within their session so a subagent can be resumed after restarting Claude Code, and are deleted after the `cleanupPeriodDays` retention period, 30 days by default.

nodes.label: Limits on what an agent message can authorize
nodes.rationale: As of v2.1.198 a subagent treats messages from the agent that launched it as normal task direction, including mid-task course corrections, acting on them within its own permission settings. Two limits hold regardless of sender: no agent message counts as user approval for a pending permission prompt, and no agent message can change a subagent's permission settings, CLAUDE.md, or configuration.

nodes.label: Subagent auto-compaction
nodes.rationale: Subagents compact automatically under the same logic and conditions as the main conversation, and `CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE` applies to them too. Each event is logged in the subagent transcript as a `compact_boundary` system record whose `preTokens` value shows the token count before compaction.

nodes.label: Fork of the current conversation
nodes.rationale: A fork is a subagent that inherits the entire conversation so far — same system prompt, tools, model and message history — instead of starting fresh, dropping the input isolation other subagents provide while keeping its own tool calls out of the main context. Use it when another subagent would need too much background, or to try several approaches in parallel from the same starting point. A fork cannot spawn further forks.

nodes.label: Fork mode
nodes.rationale: Fork mode controls whether Claude may request the `fork` subagent type; it is on by default in interactive sessions (v2.1.232+) and off in `-p` non-interactive mode and the Agent SDK. `CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT` set to `1` or `0` overrides the defaults. With it on, Claude Code runs every spawned subagent in the background and removes the Agent tool's `run_in_background` parameter; an `Agent(fork)` deny rule stops forks while leaving that background behaviour in place.

nodes.label: A fork shares the parent's prompt cache
nodes.rationale: Because a fork's system prompt and tool definitions are identical to the parent's, its first request reuses the parent's prompt cache, making forking cheaper than spawning a fresh subagent for tasks needing the same context. A non-fork subagent has a separate cache.

nodes.label: /subtask and the fork panel
nodes.rationale: `/subtask <task>` starts a fork yourself whether or not fork mode is on (v2.1.212+; the command was `/fork` on v2.1.161–v2.1.211). The fork is named from the first words of the task, runs in the background in a panel below the prompt, and returns its result as a message. Panel keys: arrows move rows, Enter opens a transcript for follow-ups, `x` stops or dismisses a row, Esc returns focus to the prompt.

nodes.label: Subagent design best practices
nodes.rationale: Design focused subagents that each excel at one task; write descriptions specific enough to single out one subagent while staying within the 15,000-token description budget; limit tool access to only what is necessary for security and focus; and check project subagents into version control to share them with the team.

nodes.label: Example: code-reviewer subagent
nodes.rationale: A read-only reviewer with `tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash` and `model: inherit` that excludes Edit and Write. Its prompt tells it to run git diff, focus on modified files, review against a fixed checklist (readability, naming, duplication, error handling, exposed secrets, input validation, test coverage, performance), and return feedback grouped as critical issues, warnings and suggestions with example fixes.

nodes.label: Example: debugger subagent
nodes.rationale: Unlike the code reviewer, this subagent includes Edit because fixing bugs requires modifying code. Its prompt gives a diagnosis-to-verification workflow — capture the error and stack trace, identify reproduction steps, isolate the failure, implement a minimal fix, verify — and asks for root cause, supporting evidence, the fix, a testing approach and prevention recommendations.

nodes.label: Example: data-scientist subagent
nodes.rationale: A domain-specific subagent for SQL and BigQuery analysis with `tools: Bash, Read, Write`, showing how to build subagents for specialized workflows outside typical coding tasks. It explicitly sets `model: sonnet` for more capable analysis and asks for efficient, cost-effective queries with documented assumptions and data-driven next steps.

nodes.label: Example: db-reader with a hook backstop
nodes.rationale: A subagent granted Bash but restricted to read-only SQL by a `PreToolUse` hook, demonstrating validation finer-grained than the `tools` field allows. The system prompt tells it to refuse writes, so the hook is a backstop: if it attempts a write anyway the script exits 2, Claude Code blocks the command, and the subagent sees the blocked message.

nodes.label: Terminal configuration page (symptom-driven)
nodes.rationale: Claude Code works in any terminal without configuration; this page exists only for when something specific misbehaves, and is organized as a list of symptoms (Shift+Enter submitting, dead Option shortcuts, no bell, tmux, Windows Backspace, flicker, Vim keys). Its scope is making the terminal send the right signals to Claude Code, not changing which keys Claude Code responds to.

nodes.label: Universal newline: Ctrl+J or backslash then Enter
nodes.rationale: Enter submits the message. To insert a line break without submitting, press Ctrl+J, or type a backslash and then press Enter. Both work in every terminal with no setup, which makes them the fallback wherever Shift+Enter is unavailable.

nodes.label: Shift+Enter as newline
nodes.rationale: In most terminals Shift+Enter inserts a newline instead of submitting, but whether it works at all depends on the terminal emulator's ability to send a distinguishable Shift+Enter sequence. When it submits instead, that is the terminal's signal, not a Claude Code setting.

nodes.label: Per-terminal Shift+Enter support matrix
nodes.rationale: Three tiers: Ghostty, Kitty, iTerm2, WezTerm, Warp, Apple Terminal and Windows Terminal work without setup; VS Code, Cursor, Devin Desktop, Alacritty and Zed need one run of /terminal-setup; gnome-terminal and JetBrains IDEs such as PyCharm and Android Studio cannot do it at all, leaving Ctrl+J or backslash-Enter.

nodes.label: /terminal-setup
nodes.rationale: /terminal-setup writes a Shift+Enter keybinding into the host terminal's own configuration file, printing a confirmation such as 'Installed VSCode terminal Shift+Enter key binding' and leaving existing bindings in place ('already configured' means no change was made). It must be run directly in the host terminal rather than inside tmux or screen, because it writes to the host terminal's configuration.

nodes.label: Editor settings /terminal-setup changes in VS Code-family editors
nodes.rationale: In VS Code, Cursor and Devin Desktop, /terminal-setup also sets terminal.integrated.gpuAcceleration to "off" to prevent garbled text and adjusts terminal.integrated.mouseWheelScrollSensitivity for smoother fullscreen scrolling. Undo the GPU change by setting it back to "auto" and reloading the window; before v2.1.157 the command left GPU acceleration alone.

nodes.label: Zed keymap.json merge with backup
nodes.rationale: In Zed, /terminal-setup edits keymap.json in place: if the keymap has bindings and none is a Terminal shift-enter, it first writes a backup beside it (e.g. keymap.json.1a2b3c4d.bak) and then merges the binding while keeping other keybindings and comments. If it cannot read, parse, back up, or verify the merged result, it leaves the file unchanged and prints the block for you to add yourself.

nodes.label: chat:newline and chat:submit actions
nodes.rationale: To bind newline to a different key, or to swap behavior so Enter inserts a newline and Shift+Enter submits, map the chat:newline and chat:submit actions in the keybindings file. This is the Claude Code-side remap, as opposed to the terminal-side signal fix.

nodes.label: Option as Meta on macOS
nodes.rationale: Claude Code shortcuts such as Option+Enter (newline) and Option+P (switch models) need the terminal to send Option as a modifier, which most macOS terminals do not do by default, so those shortcuts silently do nothing. The setting is usually labeled 'Use Option as Meta Key' — Meta being the historical Unix name for the key now labeled Option or Alt.

nodes.label: Apple Terminal: Use Option as Meta Key
nodes.rationale: In Apple Terminal, open Settings → Profiles → Keyboard and check 'Use Option as Meta Key'. Accepting Claude Code's first-run terminal setup prompt already does this, because that prompt runs /terminal-setup, which enables Option as Meta and turns off the audible bell in the Apple Terminal profile.

nodes.label: Apple Terminal audible bell and the screen-reader carve-out
nodes.rationale: In screen reader mode, /terminal-setup leaves the Apple Terminal bell setting unchanged so the terminal bell stays audible; before v2.1.211 it turned the bell off even in screen reader mode. If an earlier run silenced it, re-enable it under Settings → Profiles → Advanced → 'Audible bell'.

nodes.label: iTerm2: Option keys set to Esc+
nodes.rationale: In iTerm2, open Settings → Profiles → Keys → General and set both the Left Option key and Right Option key to 'Esc+' so Option is sent as a modifier.

nodes.label: iTerm2 clipboard access for /copy
nodes.rationale: Running /terminal-setup in iTerm2 enables 'Applications in terminal may access clipboard' under Settings → General → Selection so the /copy command can write to the system clipboard. The command detects iTerm2 even when run from inside tmux, and iTerm2 must be restarted for the change to take effect.

nodes.label: VS Code terminal.integrated.macOptionIsMeta
nodes.rationale: In VS Code, add "terminal.integrated.macOptionIsMeta": true to the settings so the integrated terminal sends Option as a modifier. For Ghostty, Kitty and other terminals, look for an Option-as-Alt or Option-as-Meta setting in that terminal's configuration file.

nodes.label: Notification event when Claude finishes or needs input
nodes.rationale: When Claude finishes a task or pauses for a permission prompt and you appear to be away from the terminal, Claude Code fires a notification event; the hooks reference documents the exact timing for each notification type. Surfacing it as a bell or desktop notification is what lets you work elsewhere during a long task.

nodes.label: preferredNotifChannel = terminal_bell
nodes.rationale: In terminals that get no desktop notification, setting preferredNotifChannel to "terminal_bell" in ~/.claude/settings.json rings the terminal bell instead. It is the settings-level alternative to a Notification hook for terminals such as Warp or the VS Code integrated terminal.

nodes.label: Desktop notifications default to Ghostty, Kitty and iTerm2
nodes.rationale: By default Claude Code sends a desktop notification only in Ghostty, Kitty and iTerm2. The notification reaches your local machine over SSH, so a remote session can still alert you; Ghostty and Kitty forward it to the OS notification center without further setup. If notifications never appear, check the terminal app's OS notification permission.

nodes.label: iTerm2 notification forwarding setup
nodes.rationale: Unlike Ghostty and Kitty, iTerm2 requires explicit forwarding: go to Settings → Profiles → Terminal, check 'Notification Center Alerts', then click 'Filter Alerts' and enable 'Send escape sequence-generated alerts'.

nodes.label: Notification hook for a custom sound or command
nodes.rationale: In any terminal a Notification hook in ~/.claude/settings.json can play a sound or run a custom command when Claude needs attention — e.g. {"type": "command", "command": "afplay /System/Library/Sounds/Glass.aiff"} on macOS. Hooks run alongside the built-in notification rather than replacing it, so terminals with no desktop notification (Warp, the VS Code integrated terminal) can use a hook.

nodes.label: tmux passthrough and extended keys
nodes.rationale: Inside tmux two things break by default: Shift+Enter submits instead of inserting a newline, and desktop notifications plus the progress bar never reach the outer terminal. Adding 'set -g allow-passthrough on', 'set -s extended-keys on' and "set -as terminal-features 'xterm*:extkeys'" to ~/.tmux.conf (then tmux source-file ~/.tmux.conf) fixes both: passthrough lets notifications and progress updates through, extended-keys lets tmux distinguish Shift+Enter from Enter.

nodes.label: Windows Backspace read as Ctrl+Backspace
nodes.rationale: On Windows, Claude Code reads a Backspace arriving as ^H as Ctrl+Backspace (delete previous word), except when TERM_PROGRAM is mintty or TERM is cygwin; on macOS and Linux it reads ^H as plain Backspace. Set CLAUDE_CODE_BS_AS_CTRL_BACKSPACE=0 if Backspace deletes a whole word, or =1 on macOS/Linux if Ctrl+Backspace only erases one character.

nodes.label: /theme and auto light/dark detection
nodes.rationale: The /theme command (or the theme picker in /config) chooses a Claude Code theme matching the terminal; the auto option detects the terminal's light or dark background so the theme follows OS appearance changes whenever the terminal does. Claude Code does not control the terminal's own color scheme. /theme also lists custom themes and plugin-contributed themes, with 'New custom theme…' to create one and Ctrl+E to edit a highlighted custom theme.

nodes.label: Custom theme JSON in ~/.claude/themes/
nodes.rationale: Each custom theme is a JSON file in ~/.claude/themes/; the filename without the .json extension is the theme's slug, and selecting it stores 'custom:<slug>' as the theme preference. Example: ~/.claude/themes/dracula.json with name 'Dracula', base 'dark', and overrides for claude, error and success.

nodes.label: Theme fields: name, base, overrides
nodes.rationale: A theme file has three optional fields: name (display label in /theme, defaulting to the filename slug), base (the built-in preset it starts from — dark, light, dark-daltonized, light-daltonized, dark-ansi or light-ansi, defaulting to dark), and overrides (a map of color token names to values, with unlisted tokens falling through to the base preset).

nodes.label: Accepted color value formats
nodes.rationale: Color values accept #rrggbb, #rgb, rgb(r,g,b), ansi256(n), or ansi:<name> where <name> is one of the 16 standard ANSI color names such as red or cyanBright. Unknown tokens and invalid color values are ignored, so a typo cannot break rendering.

nodes.label: Theme directory hot reload
nodes.rationale: Claude Code watches ~/.claude/themes/ and reloads when a file is added or changed, so edits apply to a running session without a restart. The one exception: if the folder did not exist when Claude Code started, restart once after creating the first theme file.

nodes.label: Color token reference groups
nodes.rationale: Overridable tokens are grouped as text/accent (claude, text, inverseText, inactive, subtle, suggestion, permission, remember), status (success, error, warning, merged), input box and mode indicators (promptBorder, planMode, autoAccept, bashBorder, ide, fastMode, effortUltra — the last taking effect on v2.1.239 or later), diff rendering (diffAdded/Removed, their Dimmed and Word variants), fullscreen backgrounds (userMessageBackground, userMessageBackgroundHover, bashMessageBackgroundColor, memoryBackgroundColor, selectionBg), and usage meter/speaker labels (rate_limit_fill, rate_limit_empty, briefLabelYou, briefLabelClaude). The interactive /theme editor shows the same tokens with a live preview plus a few single-purpose accents omitted from the doc.

nodes.label: <color>_FOR_SUBAGENTS_ONLY and rainbow tokens
nodes.rationale: Each subagent and parallel task is drawn in one of eight named colors (red, blue, green, yellow, purple, orange, pink, cyan) via tokens named <color>_FOR_SUBAGENTS_ONLY — a subagent declaring color: blue renders with blue_FOR_SUBAGENTS_ONLY. Separately, the ultrathink keyword is rendered with a seven-color rainbow gradient using rainbow_<color> and rainbow_<color>_shimmer tokens (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet).

nodes.label: Paired shimmer token variants
nodes.rationale: Several tokens have a paired shimmer variant supplying the lighter color in the spinner's animated gradient — claude/claudeShimmer, warning/warningShimmer, permission/permissionShimmer, promptBorder/promptBorderShimmer, inactive/inactiveShimmer, fastMode/fastModeShimmer. Override the shimmer alongside its base token if the animation looks mismatched.

nodes.label: Fullscreen rendering mode
nodes.rationale: If the display flickers or the scroll position jumps while Claude works, switch to fullscreen rendering with /tui fullscreen, which saves the preference — the conversation relaunches intact and future sessions start in fullscreen unless a fullscreen start fails. In this mode you scroll with the mouse or PageUp inside Claude Code rather than the terminal's native scrollback. CLAUDE_CODE_NO_FLICKER=1 can be set as an environment variable or in settings.json env instead.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_FORCE_SYNC_OUTPUT for flicker only
nodes.rationale: If flicker is the only problem and the terminal supports synchronized output but is not auto-detected — Emacs eat is the named example — set CLAUDE_CODE_FORCE_SYNC_OUTPUT=1 to stop the flicker without changing renderers.

nodes.label: Screen reader mode behavior
nodes.rationale: In screen reader mode Claude Code always renders as plain scrolling text except in attached background sessions, and running /tui fullscreen in any other session prints an explanation instead of switching. Screen reader mode also changes /terminal-setup, which then leaves the Apple Terminal bell audible.

nodes.label: Large pastes collapse to a placeholder
nodes.rationale: Pasting more than 800 characters or more than three lines collapses the input to a placeholder such as '[Pasted text #1 +120 lines]' while still sending the full content on submit. In a window shorter than 12 rows the line limit drops — a three-line paste collapses at 11 rows and any multi-line paste at 10 rows or fewer. A word/line delete (Ctrl+W, Ctrl+K) or a vim f/t motion delete reaching into a placeholder removes it whole, and it can be pasted back with Ctrl+Y or with p in NORMAL mode.

nodes.label: ~/.claude/paste-cache/ and its retention sweep
nodes.rationale: Collapsed content is kept under ~/.claude/paste-cache/, so recalling a prompt from command history and resubmitting sends the full pasted content again, even in a later session — until the retention sweep removes the cache file. Claude Code deletes cache files older than cleanupPeriodDays following the retention sweep rules, so a recalled prompt can reference pasted text that no longer exists.

nodes.label: Submitting a prompt whose paste expired
nodes.rationale: Claude Code never sends the literal '[Pasted text #N]' string and shows a notification naming the missing paste. In a plain prompt with text remaining it removes the placeholder and sends the rest; in a shell-mode or / command, where removal would change what runs, and in any prompt the removal would leave empty, it cancels the submission and keeps the original text with the placeholder intact for you to edit.

nodes.label: VS Code integrated terminal drops very large pastes
nodes.rationale: The VS Code integrated terminal can drop characters from very large pastes before they reach Claude Code, so file-based workflows are preferred there. For very large inputs such as entire files or long logs, write the content to a file and ask Claude to read it — this keeps the transcript readable and lets Claude reference the file by path in later turns.

nodes.label: Vim editor mode for the prompt input
nodes.rationale: Claude Code includes a Vim-style editing mode for the prompt input, enabled via /config → Editor mode or by setting editorMode to "vim" in ~/.claude/settings.json (set it back to normal to disable). It supports a subset of NORMAL- and VISUAL-mode motions and operators such as hjkl navigation, v/V selection, and d/c/y with text objects.

nodes.label: vimInsertModeRemaps
nodes.rationale: Vim motions are not remappable through the keybindings file. To map a two-key INSERT-mode sequence such as jj to Escape, set vimInsertModeRemaps in user settings.

nodes.label: Enter still submits in Vim INSERT mode
nodes.rationale: Unlike standard Vim, pressing Enter in INSERT mode still submits the prompt. To insert a newline instead, use o or O in NORMAL mode, or Ctrl+J.

nodes.label: Custom status line
nodes.rationale: To customize what appears at the bottom of the interface, configure a custom status line showing the current model, working directory, git branch, or other context. It is the complement to theming: theme colors the interface, the status line chooses what it reports.

nodes.label: Keybindings file (Claude Code-side remapping)
