nodes.rationale: The keybindings file remaps which keys Claude Code itself responds to, including Enter and Shift+Enter — a different layer from this page, which is about getting the terminal to send the right signals in the first place.

nodes.label: Enterprise deployment overview
nodes.rationale: Organizations can deploy Claude Code either through Anthropic directly or through a cloud provider; this page exists to help an organization choose the right configuration and integrate Claude Code with third-party services and infrastructure to meet enterprise deployment requirements.

nodes.label: Deployment option comparison
nodes.rationale: A six-column table compares Claude for Teams/Enterprise, Anthropic Console, Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud's Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI) and Microsoft Foundry across best-for, billing, regions, prompt caching, authentication, cost tracking, Claude-on-web inclusion and enterprise features. The comparison covers only WHERE MODEL INFERENCE RUNS.

nodes.label: Claude for Teams
nodes.rationale: Claude for Teams is self-service and includes collaboration features, admin tools and billing management, billed at $150/seat (Premium) with pay-as-you-go available. It is described as best for smaller teams that need to get started quickly, with no infrastructure setup required.

nodes.label: Claude for Enterprise
nodes.rationale: Claude for Enterprise adds SSO and domain capture, role-based permissions, compliance API access, and managed policy settings for deploying organization-wide Claude Code configurations. It is aimed at larger organizations with security and compliance requirements, and is priced by contacting sales rather than self-service.

nodes.label: Claude on the web included
nodes.rationale: Only the Claude for Teams/Enterprise option includes Claude on the web: team members get access to both Claude Code and Claude on the web under a single subscription with centralized billing. Anthropic Console, Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry all answer 'No' to that row.

nodes.label: Anthropic Console deployment
nodes.rationale: The Anthropic Console option is described as best for individual developers: pay-as-you-go billing, authentication by API key or a Console sign-in without one, a usage dashboard for cost tracking, and no enterprise features.

nodes.label: Amazon Bedrock deployment
nodes.rationale: Amazon Bedrock is the option for AWS-native deployments: pay-as-you-go billing through AWS across multiple AWS regions, authentication by API key or AWS credentials, cost tracking in AWS Cost Explorer, and enterprise features via IAM policies and CloudTrail.

nodes.label: Claude Platform on AWS
nodes.rationale: Claude Platform on AWS is for organizations that want AWS Marketplace billing while keeping Claude API features: pay-as-you-go through AWS Marketplace, multiple AWS regions, API key or AWS credentials, AWS Cost Explorer, IAM policies and CloudTrail.

nodes.label: Google Cloud's Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI)
nodes.rationale: Google Cloud's Agent Platform, formerly Vertex AI, is the option for GCP-native deployments: pay-as-you-go through GCP across multiple GCP regions, GCP credentials for authentication, GCP Billing for cost tracking, and IAM roles plus Cloud Audit Logs as enterprise features.

nodes.label: Microsoft Foundry deployment
nodes.rationale: Microsoft Foundry is the option for Azure-native deployments: pay-as-you-go through Azure across multiple Azure regions, authentication by API key or Microsoft Entra ID, Azure Cost Management for cost tracking, and RBAC policies plus Azure Monitor as enterprise features.

nodes.label: Claude apps gateway
nodes.rationale: The Claude apps gateway is a self-hosted gateway that adds IdP sign-in in front of Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, or the Anthropic API. It is listed as one of the selectable deployment options with its own setup instructions.

nodes.label: Prompt caching enabled by default
nodes.rationale: Prompt caching is 'Enabled by default' in every one of the six compared deployment options — it is the only row of the comparison table where all providers give the same answer, so it is not a differentiator between deployments.

nodes.label: Per-provider cost tracking
nodes.rationale: Cost tracking follows whichever provider runs inference: a usage dashboard for Claude for Teams/Enterprise and Anthropic Console, AWS Cost Explorer for Amazon Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS, GCP Billing for Google Cloud's Agent Platform, and Azure Cost Management for Microsoft Foundry.

nodes.label: Per-provider authentication
nodes.rationale: Authentication differs per option: Claude.ai SSO or email for Teams/Enterprise; API key or a Console sign-in without one for Anthropic Console; API key or AWS credentials for Amazon Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS; GCP credentials for Google Cloud's Agent Platform; API key or Microsoft Entra ID for Microsoft Foundry.

nodes.label: 3rd-party platform setup wizard
nodes.rationale: For Amazon Bedrock and Google Vertex AI only, you can run `claude` and select '3rd-party platform' at the login prompt to launch an interactive setup wizard instead of configuring the provider by hand.

nodes.label: Self-hosted environments for Claude Code on the web
nodes.rationale: Running Claude Code on the web sessions on compute your organization operates is a separate concern from the inference-location comparison, and is documented under self-hosted environments rather than in the deployment option table.

nodes.label: Feature availability reference
nodes.rationale: The overview table is a summary; a separate Feature availability page carries the feature-by-feature breakdown of what is available on each deployment option.

nodes.label: Corporate proxy
nodes.rationale: A corporate proxy routes Claude Code traffic through an HTTP/HTTPS proxy, for organizations that require all outbound traffic to pass through a proxy server for security monitoring, compliance or network policy enforcement. It is configured with the `HTTPS_PROXY` or `HTTP_PROXY` environment variables.

nodes.label: LLM gateway
nodes.rationale: An LLM gateway is a service that sits between Claude Code and the cloud provider to handle authentication and routing, used for centralized usage tracking across teams, custom rate limiting or budgets, or centralized authentication management. It is configured with `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, `ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_BASE_URL`, `ANTHROPIC_AWS_BASE_URL`, `ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_BASE_URL` or `ANTHROPIC_FOUNDRY_BASE_URL`.

nodes.label: /status provider verification
nodes.rationale: Running `/status` inside Claude Code verifies which provider, base URL, and proxy a session is actually using — the documented way to confirm that gateway and proxy environment variables took effect.

nodes.label: CMEK does not cover gateway-session telemetry
nodes.rationale: If an organization uses customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) and routes Claude Code through an LLM gateway or a custom `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, CMEK does not apply to Claude Code's operational telemetry on those sessions.

nodes.label: DISABLE_TELEMETRY via managed settings
nodes.rationale: To turn telemetry off for every developer in an organization, deliver `DISABLE_TELEMETRY` through managed settings — the documented remedy for the CMEK telemetry gap on gateway-routed or custom-base-URL sessions.

nodes.label: Invest in documentation and memory
nodes.rationale: The strongest organizational recommendation is to invest in documentation so that Claude Code understands the codebase, deploying CLAUDE.md files at multiple levels rather than at one.

nodes.label: Organization-wide CLAUDE.md
nodes.rationale: Company-wide standards are deployed as a CLAUDE.md in system directories: `/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/CLAUDE.md` on macOS, `/etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md` on Linux and WSL, and `C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\CLAUDE.md` on Windows.

nodes.label: Repository-level CLAUDE.md
nodes.rationale: Repository roots should carry a CLAUDE.md containing project architecture, build commands and contribution guidelines, checked into source control so that all users of the repository benefit from it.

nodes.label: One-click install for custom dev environments
nodes.rationale: For organizations with a custom development environment, creating a 'one click' way to install Claude Code is identified as key to growing adoption across the organization.

nodes.label: Start with guided usage
nodes.rationale: New users should start with codebase Q&A or small bug fixes and feature requests, ask Claude Code to make a plan, and check and correct its suggestions; only as users understand the paradigm do they become effective at letting Claude Code run more agentically.

nodes.label: Organization-wide adoption
nodes.rationale: Growing adoption across an organization is the stated goal that the deployment-simplification and guided-usage practices serve; the rollout steps end at sharing installation instructions so team members install Claude Code and authenticate with their own credentials.

nodes.label: Pin model versions for cloud providers
nodes.rationale: Deployments through a cloud provider should pin specific model versions using `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_FABLE_MODEL`, `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL`, `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL` and `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL`, which lets the organization control when its users move to a new model.

nodes.label: Unpinned model aliases lag the newest release
nodes.rationale: Without pinning, model aliases resolve to Claude Code's built-in default for that provider, which can lag the newest release and may not yet be enabled in the organization's account — the failure mode that version pinning exists to prevent.

nodes.label: Managed permission policies
nodes.rationale: Security teams can configure managed permissions defining what Claude Code is and is not allowed to do, and those managed permissions cannot be overwritten by local configuration.

nodes.label: Use MCP for integrations
nodes.rationale: MCP is recommended as the way to give Claude Code more information, such as connecting it to ticket management systems or error logs.

nodes.label: Centrally-owned .mcp.json in the repo
nodes.rationale: The recommended organizational pattern is that ONE central team configures the MCP servers and checks a `.mcp.json` configuration into the codebase, so every user of that codebase benefits without configuring servers individually.

nodes.label: Rollout next steps
nodes.rationale: Once a deployment option is chosen and access configured, the three ordered steps are: roll out to the team (share installation instructions, have members install and authenticate), set up shared configuration via a CLAUDE.md in the repositories, and configure permissions by reviewing the security settings.

nodes.label: Built-in tool catalog
nodes.rationale: The page lists Claude Code's built-in tools with a description and a Permission required column; the tool names are the exact strings used in permission rules, subagent tool lists, and hook matchers.

nodes.label: Tool names are exact strings
nodes.rationale: A tool's name is the literal token used in permission rules, subagent tool lists and hook matchers, so configuration must spell it exactly as the catalog does.

nodes.label: ToolName(specifier) rule format
nodes.rationale: Every configuration surface accepts the same rule format, ToolName(specifier). The specifier depends on the tool, and tools not listed in the format table accept only the bare tool name with no specifier.

nodes.label: Where tool names are referenced
nodes.rationale: Tool names appear in permissions.allow/deny and /permissions, the --allowedTools/--disallowedTools CLI flags, the Agent SDK allowedTools/disallowedTools options, a subagent's tools/disallowedTools frontmatter, a skill's allowed-tools frontmatter, and a hook's if condition.

nodes.label: Shared specifier families
nodes.rationale: Several tools share one specifier format: Bash(npm run *) covers Bash and Monitor; Read(~/secrets/**) covers Read, Grep, Glob and LSP; Edit(/src/**) covers Edit, Write and NotebookEdit; WebSearch takes no specifier at all.

nodes.label: Auto mode classifier decides prompts
nodes.rationale: On Pro, Max and Team plans Claude Code starts sessions in auto mode, where a classifier decides most permission prompts instead of the user; the Permission required column describes Manual mode.

nodes.label: Permission required column semantics
nodes.rationale: The column states whether a tool prompts in Manual mode for paths inside the working directory, not whether it is dangerous in general.

nodes.label: Bash runs read-only commands without prompting
nodes.rationale: Bash is marked Yes in the permission column but still runs a built-in set of read-only commands without prompting.

nodes.label: File tools still prompt outside the working directory
nodes.rationale: File-access tools marked No, including Read, Grep and Glob, still prompt for paths outside the working directory and additional directories.

nodes.label: MCP servers add custom tools
nodes.rationale: Custom tools are added by connecting an MCP server, which is the supported way to introduce a new tool entry.

nodes.label: Skills run through the existing Skill tool
nodes.rationale: A skill extends Claude with a reusable prompt-based workflow but runs through the existing Skill tool rather than adding a new tool entry.

nodes.label: Edit allow rule grants read on the same path
nodes.rationale: An Edit(...) allow rule also grants read access to the same path, so a matching Read(...) rule is unnecessary.

nodes.label: Read deny rule blocks Edit and Write
nodes.rationale: A Read(...) deny rule also blocks the Edit and Write tools on the same path, including creating a new file there, because both tools change content Claude must be able to read back. Requires v2.1.208 on edits and v2.1.228 on writes.

nodes.label: Hook matchers use bare tool names
nodes.rationale: Hook matcher fields take bare tool names, not the parenthesized rule format used by permission rules.

nodes.label: Agent tool
nodes.rationale: The Agent tool spawns a subagent in a separate context window that works autonomously and returns a single text result; the parent never sees the subagent's intermediate tool calls or outputs.

nodes.label: Teammate launch via a name input
nodes.rationale: With agent teams enabled, an Agent call carrying a name launches a teammate instead of a plain subagent, and the teammate reports back through team messages rather than by returning a result.

nodes.label: maxTurns caps a subagent's turns
nodes.rationale: Setting maxTurns in the subagent definition caps how many turns it runs; on reaching the limit Claude Code marks the returned result as partial output and the subagent can be resumed.

nodes.label: Forked subagents inherit the parent conversation
nodes.rationale: The same Agent tool launches forked subagents where fork mode is on; a fork inherits the full parent conversation instead of starting fresh, runs in the background apart from the foreground cases, and still surfaces permission prompts in the terminal.

nodes.label: tools and disallowedTools precedence
nodes.rationale: Neither field set means the subagent inherits every tool available to subagents; tools only grants exactly the listed tools; disallowedTools only grants every parent tool except those listed; with both set disallowedTools wins and a tool in both is removed.

nodes.label: Subagent-available tools are the ceiling
nodes.rationale: The resolved set is always limited to the tools available to subagents: a tool not available to subagents is never granted even when named in tools.

nodes.label: Zero-tools spawn error
nodes.rationale: If every entry in a subagent's tools list fails to match a usable tool, the Agent tool usually returns an error naming the entries instead of launching the subagent.

nodes.label: Where subagent permission prompts appear
nodes.rationale: Launching a subagent does not itself prompt; its own tool calls are checked as it runs. Foreground subagents prompt like the main conversation, and since v2.1.186 background subagents surface prompts in the main session naming which subagent is asking, with Esc denying that one call.

nodes.label: AskUserQuestion tool
nodes.rationale: AskUserQuestion asks multiple-choice questions to gather requirements or clarify ambiguity; the user answers by picking an option or typing text through the Other row or notes field, which Claude Code relays with neutral wording.

nodes.label: Question auto-continue timeout
nodes.rationale: Questions stay open indefinitely unless askUserQuestionTimeout is set to 60s, 5m or 10m; after that idle period the dialog submits any selected options, tells Claude the user may be away, and shows a 20-second countdown that any keypress restarts.

nodes.label: Permission prompts never auto-resolve
nodes.rationale: The auto-continue timeout applies only to AskUserQuestion's multiple-choice questions; permission prompts, including plan approval, never auto-resolve on idle.

nodes.label: Bash tool
nodes.rationale: The Bash tool executes shell commands, running each command in a separate process.

nodes.label: Working directory carry-over and reset
nodes.rationale: A cd in the main session carries over to later Bash commands while it stays inside the project or an additional working directory; landing outside resets to the project directory with a 'Shell cwd was reset to <dir>' note, and CLAUDE_BASH_MAINTAIN_PROJECT_WORKING_DIR=1 disables the carry-over. Subagent sessions never carry it over.

nodes.label: Environment variables do not persist
nodes.rationale: An export in one Bash command is not available in the next; persistence comes from CLAUDE_ENV_FILE or a SessionStart hook, and virtualenv/conda should be activated before launching Claude Code.

nodes.label: Shell startup aliases and functions apply
nodes.rationale: At session start Claude Code sources ~/.zshrc, ~/.bashrc or ~/.profile depending on the shell, captures the resulting aliases, functions and shell options, and applies them to every Bash command.

nodes.label: Bash timeout bounds
nodes.rationale: Claude passes a per-call timeout parameter; BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS is the default when it passes none (two minutes out of the box) and BASH_MAX_TIMEOUT_MS caps what Claude can request, the effective ceiling being the larger of the two, ten minutes out of the box.

nodes.label: Bash output limits and read-back
nodes.rationale: Output streams to a working file and a command whose output passes 5 GB is killed. A valid result reaches Claude inline up to roughly 30,000 characters, then as a saved file path truncated past 64 MiB plus a preview; a failure reaches Claude inline up to roughly 10,000 characters, then as a head-and-tail excerpt with no file path.

nodes.label: Exit code 1 treated as a valid result
nodes.rationale: Exit 1 counts as a valid result only for grep, rg, egrep, fgrep, find, diff, test, [, git diff and git grep. Every other command exiting 1 counts as a failure even when that is benign, such as no matches for pgrep or jq -e, or differing files for cmp.

nodes.label: BASH_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH read-back window
nodes.rationale: BASH_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH sets how many characters are read back from the working file, 30,000 by default up to a hard ceiling of 150,000. Raising it enlarges the read-back window and the window a failure excerpt is cut from, but does not raise the inline ceilings.

nodes.label: Background Bash commands
nodes.rationale: run_in_background: true starts a command as a background task; /tasks lists and stops them. A command started by a foreground subagent ends when that subagent gives its final response, while main-conversation and background-subagent commands keep running, and in -p mode background tasks end shortly after the final result.

nodes.label: Auto-backgrounding at the timeout
nodes.rationale: A command that reaches its timeout without finishing is moved to the background rather than stopped, with a result naming the timeout, the task ID and the output file path; CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS=1 disables it. A cd/pushd/popd/chdir inside a backgrounded command never carries over, and the result says so.

nodes.label: Commands never auto-backgrounded
nodes.rationale: Three kinds of command are stopped at the timeout instead of backgrounded: one starting with sleep, one running git anywhere in it, and a compound command Claude Code cannot fully parse — a parameter expansion such as ${VAR} counts as unparseable.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_TOOL_MEMORY_LIMIT
nodes.rationale: On Linux and WSL this variable caps the memory Bash, PowerShell and Monitor commands can use, counted across the whole session rather than per command, applied with a memory cgroup and held from the first process until relaunch. Requires v2.1.233; before v2.1.246 Monitor ran outside the cap.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_TOOL_MEMORY_CGROUP_EXCLUDE
nodes.rationale: A comma-separated list of process kinds exempt from the memory cap — mcp, lsp, hooks, plugin, helper, agent — with none capping every kind and all-new capping only Bash, PowerShell and Monitor. Unknown names are ignored, and with the variable unset the capped set comes from server-delivered configuration and can change.

nodes.label: Permission-gating hooks are never capped
nodes.rationale: Even with every kind capped, a hook that can block or change the outcome of an action, and any MCP server it calls, is excluded from the memory cap, so the kernel killing such a hook cannot allow the action it was blocking.

nodes.label: Edit tool
nodes.rationale: Edit performs exact string replacement of old_string with new_string, using neither regex nor fuzzy matching.

nodes.label: Match and uniqueness checks
nodes.rationale: old_string must appear in the file exactly as written — one character of whitespace or indentation is enough to miss — and exactly once; otherwise Claude supplies more surrounding context or sets replace_all: true.

nodes.label: Read-before-edit requirement
nodes.rationale: Claude must have read the file in the current conversation before editing it. Opus 4.6, Haiku 4.5 and older models always require the read; newer models can edit an unread file when reading it would not need a permission prompt and the Read tool is available.

nodes.label: Editing a file changed on disk
nodes.rationale: Since v2.1.208 a file changed on disk after the last read can still be edited when old_string matches the current content exactly and unambiguously and the file can be read without prompting; the result notes the other changes. Any other case, such as a stale or ambiguous old_string, forces a re-read first.

nodes.label: Viewing a file with Bash satisfies the read
nodes.rationale: cat, nl, bat, batcat, head, tail, sed -n 'X,Yp', grep, egrep, fgrep or rg on a single file with no pipes or redirects satisfies the read-before-edit requirement; piped output and other commands do not count.

nodes.label: Deny-rule command recognition is a different set
nodes.rationale: Read and Edit deny rules also apply to file commands recognized in Bash such as cat, head, tail, sed and grep, but not to arbitrary subprocesses that read or write files indirectly. That set is not the read-before-edit list: egrep and fgrep count for read-before-edit yet are not checked against Read deny rules.

nodes.label: Sandbox for OS-level enforcement
nodes.rationale: For enforcement that covers every process rather than only recognized commands, the sandbox must be enabled.

nodes.label: EndConversation tool
nodes.rationale: EndConversation ends the current session, used only as a last resort against sustained abusive input after a warning, or when the user explicitly asks to see it demonstrated. Frustration, profanity, a task going badly, or requests for harmful content do not qualify.

nodes.label: Ended sessions lock
nodes.rationale: After the tool runs, the session locks: new prompts return a message to start a new session, and only /clear, /resume, /help, /exit and /feedback still run. The end is recorded in the transcript so resuming restores the lock, and a -p resume errors with exit code 1.

nodes.label: EndConversation cannot be disabled while other tools remain
nodes.rationale: The tool never prompts, PreToolUse hooks do not run for it, and deny or ask rules naming it have no effect, because a safeguard of this kind holds only if the session it applies to cannot turn it off. When deny rules remove every other tool and also match it, such as "*", Claude Code removes it too unless an allow rule names it.

nodes.label: EndConversation availability conditions
nodes.rationale: The tool appears only on v2.1.213+, on Opus 4.8 / Sonnet 5 / Fable 5 or later families, in an interactive terminal session, outside --bare mode, and not on Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry or cloud-gateway sign-ins. Subagents never get it.

nodes.label: Glob tool
nodes.rationale: Glob finds files by name pattern with standard glob syntax including ** for recursive matching; results are sorted by modification time and capped at 100 files, with a truncation flag telling Claude to narrow the pattern.

nodes.label: Glob ignores .gitignore by default
nodes.rationale: Glob does not respect .gitignore by default, so it finds gitignored files alongside tracked ones; CLAUDE_CODE_GLOB_NO_IGNORE=false makes it respect .gitignore.

nodes.label: Grep tool built on ripgrep
nodes.rationale: Grep searches file contents using ripgrep's regex syntax rather than POSIX grep, so metacharacters need escaping — finding interface{} in Go takes the pattern interface\{\}. A rejected pattern, glob or type returns ripgrep's diagnostic so Claude can correct it.

nodes.label: Grep output modes
nodes.rationale: files_with_matches returns file paths only and is the default; content returns matching lines with file and line number; count returns per-file counts plus a total that covers every match even when head_limit or offset truncate the listed entries.

nodes.label: Grep skips gitignored files
nodes.rationale: Grep respects .gitignore, so gitignored files are skipped unless Claude passes the path directly.

nodes.label: LSP tool
nodes.rationale: LSP gives Claude code intelligence from a running language server: it reports type errors and warnings automatically after each file edit, and Claude can call it to jump to definitions, find references, get type information, list or search symbols, find implementations and trace call hierarchies.

nodes.label: LSP requires a code-intelligence plugin
nodes.rationale: The tool stays inactive until a code intelligence plugin for the language is installed, and Claude Code does not start plugin language servers in cloud sessions, so it stays inactive there; the plugin supplies configuration while the server binary is installed by the user.

nodes.label: Monitor tool
nodes.rationale: Monitor runs a command in the background and feeds each output line back to Claude so it can react mid-conversation — tailing logs, polling a PR or CI job, watching a directory, or tracking a long-running script — without pausing the conversation.

nodes.label: Monitor reuses Bash permission rules
nodes.rationale: A Monitor command is checked against the same permission rules as Bash, so Bash allow and deny patterns apply; in auto mode Claude Code sets aside allow rules naming Monitor itself so the classifier reviews Monitor commands like Bash commands.

nodes.label: Monitor WebSocket source
nodes.rationale: Instead of a command, a Monitor call can take a ws input with a url (ws:// or wss://, no embedded credentials or whitespace, ASCII only) and optional protocols. Text messages each become one event, binary messages arrive as a placeholder line, a message over 1 MiB ends the watch, and a socket close ends it with the close code. Requires v2.1.195.

nodes.label: WebSocket destination restrictions
nodes.rationale: Claude Code denies WebSocket URLs pointing at private, link-local or cloud-metadata addresses, including hostnames that resolve to one, hosts in sandbox.network.deniedDomains, and under allowManagedDomainsOnly any host outside the managed allowlist. Opening a socket prompts for approval with no option to skip future prompts for the host.

nodes.label: Monitor availability limits
nodes.rationale: Monitor is unavailable on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry, and also when DISABLE_TELEMETRY or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC is set.

nodes.label: Plugin-declared monitors
nodes.rationale: Plugins can declare monitors that start automatically when the plugin is active, instead of Claude being asked to start them.

nodes.label: NotebookEdit tool
nodes.rationale: NotebookEdit modifies a Jupyter notebook one cell at a time by cell_id rather than by string replacement, with three modes: replace (the default) overwrites the cell source, insert adds a cell after the target (at the start with no cell_id, requiring cell_type code or markdown), and delete removes it. Its permission rules use the Edit(...) path format.

nodes.label: PowerShell tool
nodes.rationale: PowerShell runs commands natively rather than routing through Git Bash on Windows. It is enabled automatically on Windows without Git Bash, on by default for claude.ai and Console accounts on Windows with Git Bash, and opt-in on Linux, macOS and WSL, where it needs PowerShell 7+ with pwsh on PATH.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_USE_POWERSHELL_TOOL
nodes.rationale: Setting CLAUDE_CODE_USE_POWERSHELL_TOOL=1 in the environment or settings.json enables the tool (and 0 turns it off on Windows). When enabled Claude treats PowerShell as the primary shell while Bash stays available for POSIX scripts under Git Bash.

nodes.label: Process-scope execution policy bypass
nodes.rationale: Claude Code spawns PowerShell with -ExecutionPolicy Bypass at process scope only, so .ps1 scripts and module imports work on default Windows installs without changing the machine policy; Group Policy MachinePolicy and UserPolicy still apply, and CLAUDE_CODE_POWERSHELL_RESPECT_EXECUTION_POLICY=1 respects the effective policy instead.

nodes.label: Shell selection in settings, hooks and skills
nodes.rationale: defaultShell: powershell routes interactive ! commands through PowerShell and shell: powershell in skill frontmatter runs !`command` blocks there, both requiring the tool enabled; shell: powershell on a command hook works regardless, because hooks spawn PowerShell directly.

nodes.label: Hooks must match Bash|PowerShell
nodes.rationale: PreToolUse hooks receive the PowerShell command string in tool_input.command with the same fields as Bash, so hooks that inspect shell commands must match Bash|PowerShell rather than Bash alone.

nodes.label: PowerShell exit-code and encoding handling
nodes.rationale: As of v2.1.196 exit 1 from grep, rg, egrep, fgrep, findstr and git grep means no matches and exit 1 from git diff means differences exist, neither reported as a failure, while robocopy exit codes 0-7 are informational and 8+ are failures. v2.1.214 adds UTF-8 redirection on PowerShell 5.1, UTF-8 piped stdin, ANSI-free error capture, EOF for children waiting on stdin, and valid-negative handling of exit 1 from where.exe, fc.exe and diff.exe.

nodes.label: PowerShell preview limitations
nodes.rationale: During the preview PowerShell profiles are not loaded and sandboxing is not supported on Windows.

nodes.label: Read tool
nodes.rationale: Read takes a file path and returns the contents with line numbers; Claude is instructed to always pass absolute paths, and Read reads only files, never directories — a directory listing needs a shell command such as ls.

nodes.label: PARTIAL view and offset/limit errors
nodes.rationale: When a whole-file read exceeds the token limit, Read returns the first page with a PARTIAL view notice saying how much arrived and how to read more with offset and limit; an explicit offset or limit that still exceeds the limit returns an error, and since v2.1.208 an oversized limit is rejected before the range is loaded. Empty files and past-the-end offsets return distinct notices.

nodes.label: Read handles images, PDFs and notebooks
nodes.rationale: Images are returned as visual content, resized and recompressed to the model's limits, and since v2.1.196 an image still over 500KB is re-encoded as reduced-quality JPEG at unchanged pixel dimensions. PDFs over 10 pages are read in ranges with a pages parameter up to 20 pages at a time, and .ipynb files return all cells with outputs but are refused over 100 MB.

nodes.label: Write tool
nodes.rationale: Write creates a new file or overwrites an existing one with the full content provided; it never appends or merges, and partial changes to an existing file use Edit instead.

nodes.label: Read before overwriting an existing file
nodes.rationale: Opus 4.6, Haiku 4.5 and older models always require a read before overwriting an existing file; newer models can overwrite an unread file under the same conditions as read-before-edit. Jupyter notebooks and files read only partially require the read on every model, and new files are exempt. Before v2.1.228 every model required the read.

nodes.label: SendFeedback tool
nodes.rationale: SendFeedback drafts a feedback report about Claude Code — a product problem or Claude's own behavior — when a tool keeps failing, Claude cannot help, a mistake is pointed out or noticed, or the user asks. Drafts are saved under ~/.claude/feedback/drafts/ and nothing reaches Anthropic until the user sends one. Requires v2.1.238.

nodes.label: Feedback draft queue and cards
nodes.rationale: A queued draft shows a card above the prompt with keys to review, send twice-confirmed, or dismiss; at most three cards per session by default, a server-adjustable limit, after which only a count appears in the footer. The queue holds 10 drafts across sessions, the oldest dropped at an eleventh, and a draft expires after 30 days or cleanupPeriodDays if shorter.

nodes.label: What a sent feedback report carries
nodes.rationale: A sent report carries the title, area and details, environment info such as version, OS and model, the IDs of recent API requests, and the conversation transcript only when Send transcript is left at yes in the review screen — sending from the card never includes the transcript. The working directory stays local.

nodes.label: Turning Claude-drafted feedback off
nodes.rationale: Setting Claude-drafted feedback to off in /config writes the feedbackDrafts setting, and CLAUDE_CODE_SEND_FEEDBACK=0 turns it off for one session; feedbackDrafts set to quiet keeps drafting without cards, and administrators can set it in managed settings, which takes precedence.

nodes.label: Sessions without Claude-drafted feedback
nodes.rationale: The tool is left out of non-interactive -p runs and Agent SDK sessions, cloud sessions such as Claude Code on the web, Amazon Bedrock / Claude Platform on AWS / Google Cloud's Agent Platform / Microsoft Foundry sessions, sessions with feedback env vars disabled or feature-flag fetching off, and organizations that turned off product feedback or use zero data retention.

nodes.label: Task tools withheld on newer models
nodes.rationale: In v2.1.233+ TodoWrite, TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskUpdate and TaskList are not available on Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, Fable 5, Mythos 5 or later families unless the user opts in, because those models track multi-step work without a written checklist and the definitions and reminders cost context.

nodes.label: Opting into the Task tools
nodes.rationale: CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1 provides the tools on every model and provider; naming one in --allowedTools or listing them in --tools also restores them, and the Agent SDK's allowedTools and tools options work the same way. Background sessions and Claude Code on the web provide them on every model regardless.

nodes.label: TodoWrite tool
nodes.rationale: TodoWrite manages the session task checklist and is disabled by default in favour of TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskList and TaskUpdate; CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TASKS=0 re-enables it in sessions that have the task-tracking tools.

nodes.label: Subagents inherit the session's task tools
nodes.rationale: A subagent gets the Task tools only when the session has them, even on a different model, and an in-process agent-team teammate follows the session the same way, while a split-pane teammate runs as a separate process whose own model decides. Without them agents coordinate by message rather than the shared task list.

nodes.label: WebFetch tool
nodes.rationale: WebFetch takes a URL and a prompt, fetches the page, converts an HTML response to Markdown, and runs the prompt against the content with a small fast model; for most fetches Claude receives that model's answer rather than the raw page, and the conversion step is not configurable.

nodes.label: WebFetch is lossy by design
nodes.rationale: Because the extraction prompt determines what reaches Claude, a result saying a page does not mention something may only mean the prompt did not ask about it; the remedy is a more specific prompt or curl via Bash for the unprocessed page.

nodes.label: WebFetch response behaviors
nodes.rationale: HTTP URLs are upgraded to HTTPS, large pages are truncated to a fixed character limit, responses are cached 15 minutes by default (tunable with CLAUDE_CODE_WEBFETCH_CACHE_TTL_MS on v2.1.233+), a cross-host redirect returns a text result naming both URLs instead of being followed, and an overloaded extraction API is retried with backoff before returning an error.

nodes.label: WebFetch permission prompt and preapproved domains
nodes.rationale: In Manual and acceptEdits modes WebFetch prompts before fetching except for domains already allowed or denied by rules and a built-in preapproved documentation set, and every fetch first passes the WebFetch domain safety check. The prompt offers approve-once, approve-and-save a WebFetch(domain:...) rule to .claude/settings.local.json (hidden under allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly), or reject.

nodes.label: Explicit domain rules outrank the preapproved set
nodes.rationale: An explicit WebFetch(domain:...) rule in deny, ask or allow takes precedence over the preapproved set, so a preapproved domain can be blocked or made to prompt; auto and bypassPermissions modes skip the prompt except where an explicit ask rule matches, and WebFetch(domain:*) allows every domain.

nodes.label: Sandboxed commands and WebFetch domains
nodes.rationale: Sandboxed commands do not inherit WebFetch's preapproved documentation domains; reaching a domain without a prompt needs it in sandbox allowedDomains or a WebFetch(domain:...) rule, which the sandbox honors. The reverse does not hold — WebFetch never reads the sandbox allowlist.

nodes.label: WebSearch tool
nodes.rationale: WebSearch runs a query against Anthropic's web search backend and returns result titles and URLs without fetching the pages; a single call may issue up to eight backend searches, refining internally before returning. The backend is not configurable — a different provider means an MCP server exposing a search tool.

nodes.label: WebSearch domain scoping
nodes.rationale: Results can be scoped with allowed_domains to include only certain hosts or blocked_domains to exclude them, and the two lists cannot be combined in a single call. WebSearch permission rules take no specifier: a bare WebSearch entry in allow or deny is the only form.

nodes.label: Session cap of 200 WebSearch calls
nodes.rationale: A session may make at most 200 WebSearch calls, counted across the main conversation and every subagent, so parallel research fan-outs share the limit. At the cap further calls return a notice telling Claude to continue with what it has rather than an error inviting retry, invisible to the user. CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION raises but cannot remove the cap; /clear resets the count unless surviving work can still spawn subagents.

nodes.label: WebSearch provider availability
nodes.rationale: WebSearch works on the Claude API and Claude Platform on AWS; on Microsoft Foundry it needs an Anthropic-hosted deployment because Azure-hosted ones do not support server-side tools; on Google Cloud's Agent Platform it works with Claude 4 and later; Amazon Bedrock does not expose the server-side web search tool.

nodes.label: Anthropic-hosted tools are absent on third-party providers
nodes.rationale: Tools whose delivery runs through Anthropic-hosted infrastructure — PushNotification, RemoteTrigger, SendUserFile — are not accessible from Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Microsoft Foundry, and RemoteTrigger additionally requires a paid claude.ai plan.

nodes.label: SendUserFile tool
nodes.rationale: SendUserFile sends session files to the user with an optional caption so a generated report, diagram, screenshot or built artifact reaches their device. Since v2.1.196 the display input chooses render (inline), attach (download card) or client default. It is available when a Remote Control client is connected or in a managed cloud environment.

nodes.label: Artifact tool
nodes.rationale: Artifact publishes an HTML or Markdown file as a private interactive page on claude.ai, shareable by public link or inside an organization on Team and Enterprise plans where an Owner must enable public sharing. It requires a Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan and /login authentication.

nodes.label: Cron scheduling tools
nodes.rationale: CronCreate schedules a recurring or one-shot prompt within the current session, CronDelete cancels one by ID and CronList lists them; tasks are session-scoped and restored on --resume or --continue if unexpired.

nodes.label: ScheduleWakeup tool
nodes.rationale: ScheduleWakeup reschedules the next iteration of a self-paced /loop, called by Claude at the end of each iteration to pick a time between one minute and one hour out, or with stop: true (v2.1.202+) to cancel the pending wakeup; the pending wakeup appears in session_crons in Stop hook input.

nodes.label: EnterWorktree and ExitWorktree
nodes.rationale: EnterWorktree creates an isolated git worktree and switches into it, or switches into an existing one via path; a path outside .claude/worktrees/ prompts for approval since it moves the session's working directory, while new-worktree creation and paths under .claude/worktrees/ do not. Inside a worktree session or a subagent with a pinned working directory, only the path form is available and the target must be under that repository's .claude/worktrees/. ExitWorktree returns to the original directory and is unavailable to subagents that already run in their own directory.

nodes.label: ListAgents and SendMessage
nodes.rationale: ListAgents lists the agents Claude can message — session subagents, agent-team teammates, other local Claude Code sessions and, over Remote Control, web and remote sessions — and SendMessage sends a message to one of them, including a subagent it resumes by ID or name. Both require v2.1.224 and a session with cross-session messaging enabled; SendMessage takes an optional 5-10 word summary truncated past 200 characters.

nodes.label: ToolSearch tool
nodes.rationale: ToolSearch searches for and loads deferred tools when MCP tool search is enabled.

nodes.label: WaitForMcpServers tool
nodes.rationale: WaitForMcpServers waits for MCP servers still connecting in the background so a request can use their tools without restarting the session, and appears only when tool search is disabled, since ToolSearch handles the wait when it is enabled.

nodes.label: ReportFindings tool
nodes.rationale: ReportFindings reports code-review findings as a structured list with a file, summary and failure scenario per finding so Claude Code renders them rather than printing text; Claude calls it when active code-review instructions say to. Requires v2.1.196, and since v2.1.199 a finding may carry an optional category slug.

nodes.label: TaskOutput deprecated in favour of Read
nodes.rationale: TaskOutput retrieves output from a background task but is deprecated in favour of Read on the task's output file path; when no task matches the ID the error lists running background agents by ID and description, which before v2.1.203 named only the missing ID.

nodes.label: TaskStop tool
nodes.rationale: TaskStop stops a running background task by ID and, since v2.1.198, also an agent-team teammate or a named background agent by agent ID or name; since v2.1.203 an unmatched ID lists running background agents including those another agent spawned, which previously could not be identified or stopped from the main conversation.

nodes.label: Workflow tool
nodes.rationale: Workflow runs a dynamic workflow: a script that orchestrates many subagents in the background and returns one consolidated result.

nodes.label: Checking which tools are loaded
nodes.rationale: The exact tool set depends on provider, platform and settings; asking Claude what tools it has access to gives a conversational summary, and /mcp gives exact MCP tool names.

nodes.label: Advisor is a server tool with no referenceable name
nodes.rationale: The advisor tool is a server tool the API runs rather than one Claude Code implements, so it has no name that can be referenced in permission rules or hook matchers.

nodes.label: Find-your-error symptom index
nodes.rationale: The page opens with a lookup table mapping an exact error string or symptom (e.g. `command not found: claude`, `curl: (22) ... 403`, `Killed`, `Illegal instruction`, `OAuth error`) to the section that fixes it. It is the entry point: match the message first, and only work through the diagnostic checks if the symptom is not listed.

nodes.label: Native install script (install.sh / install.ps1 / install.cmd)
nodes.rationale: The recommended install path is the native installer: `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash` on macOS/Linux, `irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex` in PowerShell, and `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.cmd -o install.cmd && install.cmd && del install.cmd` in CMD. It installs a real binary rather than script shims and is the remedy the page repeatedly returns to.

nodes.label: Install directory (~/.local/bin/claude)
nodes.rationale: The installer places the binary at `~/.local/bin/claude` on macOS/Linux and `%USERPROFILE%\.local\bin\claude.exe` on Windows. A native install shows a symlink into `~/.local/share/claude/versions/`; a script or hand-made symlink at that path is a custom launcher that auto-update leaves in place.

nodes.label: downloads.claude.ai release host
nodes.rationale: Claude Code binaries are hosted at `downloads.claude.ai`, and the installer downloads from it. Per-version binaries can also be picked manually from the manifest at `https://downloads.claude.ai/claude-code-releases/{VERSION}/manifest.json`.

nodes.label: Connectivity check (curl -sI against the release host)
nodes.rationale: `curl -sI https://downloads.claude.ai/claude-code-releases/latest` (or `curl.exe` in PowerShell, because PowerShell aliases `curl` to `Invoke-WebRequest` which rejects `-sI`) is the diagnostic probe. A first line showing 200 (`HTTP/2 200`, or `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` from Windows curl.exe) means the server was reached; 403 means proxy/filter or an unsupported region; 5xx is a temporary service issue.

nodes.label: Blocked-network symptoms
nodes.rationale: No output, `Could not resolve host`, or a connection timeout means the network is blocking the connection. Common causes are corporate firewalls or proxies blocking `downloads.claude.ai`, regional network restrictions (try a VPN or another network), and TLS/SSL problems such as outdated CA certificates or a misconfigured `HTTPS_PROXY`.

nodes.label: HTTP_PROXY / HTTPS_PROXY configuration
nodes.rationale: Behind a corporate proxy, export `HTTP_PROXY` and `HTTPS_PROXY` (or set `$env:HTTP_PROXY`/`$env:HTTPS_PROXY` in PowerShell) to the proxy address before running the installer. The proxy URL comes from the IT team or the browser's proxy settings.

nodes.label: PATH verification and repair
nodes.rationale: Check membership with `echo $PATH | tr ':' '\n' | grep -Fx "$HOME/.local/bin"`, or `$env:PATH -split ';' | Select-String '\.local\\bin'` in PowerShell. Fix it by appending `export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"` to `~/.zshrc` or `~/.bashrc`, or by writing the User PATH via `[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable`, then restarting the terminal and confirming with `claude --version`.

nodes.label: command not found: claude
nodes.rationale: After a successful install, `zsh: command not found: claude` (macOS), `bash: claude: command not found` (Linux), `'claude' is not recognized...` (CMD) or `claude : The term 'claude' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet` (PowerShell) all mean the install directory is not in the shell's search path. A freshly-installed shell session also keeps its old PATH, so a new terminal window is often enough.

nodes.label: VS Code extension's private CLI copy
nodes.rationale: The VS Code extension bundles a private copy of the CLI inside the extension directory for its own chat panel; it does not place `claude` at `~/.local/bin/claude` and does not add it to PATH. With only the extension installed, that path will not exist and a standalone install is required to use `claude` from a terminal.

nodes.label: Conflicting installations
nodes.rationale: Multiple Claude Code installations cause version mismatches and unexpected behaviour. Enumerate them with `which -a claude` (or `where.exe claude`) and check the three origins — the native install, the legacy `~/.claude/local/` npm install, and an npm `-g` install — then keep only one, preferring the native install.

nodes.label: Legacy ~/.claude/local npm install
nodes.rationale: `~/.claude/local/` is a legacy local npm install created by older versions of Claude Code. Remove it with `rm -rf ~/.claude/local` (or `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force "$env:USERPROFILE\.claude\local"`). A `No such file or directory` from the `ls` probe is not an error — it just means nothing is installed there.

nodes.label: npm global install (@anthropic-ai/claude-code)
nodes.rationale: A global npm install is detected with `npm -g ls @anthropic-ai/claude-code` and removed with `npm uninstall -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`. It is the source of several distinct failure modes on this page: PowerShell execution-policy blocks, the missing native binary, and ENOTEMPTY on reinstall.

nodes.label: Homebrew cask install
nodes.rationale: `brew install --cask claude-code` is the macOS alternative installer. `Error: Cask 'claude-code' is unavailable` means the local cask index predates publication — run `brew update` first. The `claude-code` cask tracks the stable channel and is typically about a week behind; `claude-code@latest` installs the newest release. Uninstall with `brew uninstall --cask claude-code`.

nodes.label: WinGet install (Anthropic.ClaudeCode)
nodes.rationale: `winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode` is the Windows alternative installer, used when the install script returns HTML or when curl-based downloads fail; it avoids curl entirely, which also sidesteps blocked certificate-revocation checks. Uninstall with `winget uninstall Anthropic.ClaudeCode`.

nodes.label: Directory permissions check
nodes.rationale: The installer needs write access to `~/.local/bin/` and `~/.claude/` on macOS and Linux; probe with `test -w`. If either is not writable, `sudo mkdir -p ~/.local/bin` then `sudo chown -R $(whoami) ~/.local`. On Windows the install location under `%USERPROFILE%` is user-writable by default, so this rarely applies.

nodes.label: Binary verification (exists, executable, links resolve)
nodes.rationale: When `claude --version` prints a version but the binary crashes or hangs, confirm the file with `ls -la "$(command -v claude)"` (or `Get-Command claude | Select-Object Source`), check for unresolved shared libraries on Linux with `ldd "$(command -v claude)" | grep "not found"`, and re-run `claude --version` to confirm it executes.

nodes.label: Install script returns HTML instead of a shell script
nodes.rationale: `bash: line 1: syntax error near unexpected token '<'` / `<!DOCTYPE html>`, PowerShell `iex` parse errors quoting HTML or CSS, and a bare `curl: (22) ... 403` all mean the install URL returned a web page or an error status rather than the script. Downloading with `-OutFile install.ps1` saves the same web page, so it does not help. Causes: unsupported region, a corporate proxy/firewall, regional routing, or a temporary service disruption.

nodes.label: App unavailable in region
nodes.rationale: If the returned HTML page says "App unavailable in region", Claude Code is not available in that country and the fix is the supported-countries list, not a different installer. A 403 status can carry the same meaning, which is why an unexplained 403 is checked against both region and proxy causes.

nodes.label: curl (56)/(23) failure writing output to destination
nodes.rationale: In `curl ... | bash`, exit code 56 means the download itself was interrupted and exit code 23 means curl could not write what it received into the pipe, usually because Bash exited early. Either way Bash did not receive the complete script; re-test connectivity to `downloads.claude.ai` and retry, or use an alternative installer.

nodes.label: TLS/SSL connection errors
nodes.rationale: `curl: (35) TLS connect error`, `schannel: next InitializeSecurityContext failed`, `Could not establish trust relationship for the SSL/TLS secure channel`, `unable to get local issuer certificate` and `SELF_SIGNED_CERT_IN_CHAIN` are TLS handshake failures, commonly caused by stale CA certificates or a corporate proxy performing TLS inspection. On Windows, TLS 1.2 may also need enabling via `[Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol`.

nodes.label: CA certificate update / --cacert
nodes.rationale: Update the system trust store (`sudo apt-get install ca-certificates` on Ubuntu/Debian; on macOS the system curl uses the Keychain trust store, so updating macOS updates the roots), or make the download trust the corporate CA directly with `curl --cacert /path/to/corporate-ca.pem`. The PowerShell installer downloads through .NET and validates against the Windows certificate store, so the proxy CA must be added there instead.

nodes.label: NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS for the installed CLI
nodes.rationale: Fixing the install download's trust is separate from fixing Claude Code's own API requests: set `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/path/to/corporate-ca.pem` (or `$env:NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`) so the installed CLI trusts the same corporate CA bundle.

nodes.label: Blocked certificate-revocation check workaround
nodes.rationale: `CRYPT_E_NO_REVOCATION_CHECK (0x80092012)` and `CRYPT_E_REVOCATION_OFFLINE (0x80092013)` mean curl reached the server but the network blocks the revocation lookup. Re-run the download with `--ssl-revoke-best-effort`, which tolerates an unreachable revocation server while still rejecting a known-revoked certificate. The script retries its own downloads that way automatically, so the flag is only needed on the command you type.

nodes.label: Wrong install command for the Windows shell
nodes.rationale: `'irm' is not recognized` means you are in CMD; `The token '&&' is not valid` means you ran the CMD command in PowerShell; `A parameter cannot be found that matches parameter name 'fsSL'` means you ran the macOS/Linux curl command in PowerShell, where `curl` aliases to `Invoke-WebRequest`; `'bash' is not recognized` means you ran the Unix installer on Windows. If the command merely prints script text, only the download half was run and the `| iex` or `-o install.cmd && install.cmd` part is missing.

nodes.label: PowerShell execution policy blocks npm .ps1 shims
nodes.rationale: `running scripts is disabled on this system` / `PSSecurityException` means PowerShell's execution policy is blocking the `.ps1` launchers npm creates (`npm.ps1`, `claude.ps1`). Remedies: `Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser`, call the `.cmd` launchers instead, or use the PowerShell installer — the policy covers script files, so `irm ... | iex` is unaffected because it runs downloaded text directly.

nodes.label: Downloads folder locked during Windows install
nodes.rationale: `Failed to download binary: The process cannot access the file ... because it is being used by another process` means the installer could not write to `%USERPROFILE%\.claude\downloads`, usually because a previous install is still running or antivirus is scanning a partial download. Close other installer windows, let the scan finish, delete the downloads folder, and rerun the installer.

nodes.label: OOM kill during install (exit code 137)
nodes.rationale: A `Killed` message and `Installation was killed before it could finish (exit code 137)` mean the Linux OOM killer terminated the `claude install` step for lack of free memory — common on small VPS and cloud instances. The install script reports the cause itself and exits 137.

nodes.label: Add swap space
nodes.rationale: Create and enable a 2 GB swap file (`fallocate -l 2G /swapfile`, `chmod 600`, `mkswap`, `swapon`) so disk backs physical RAM and the install completes on a low-memory server, then rerun the install script. Alternatives are closing other processes or moving to a larger instance.

nodes.label: Install and runtime memory requirements
nodes.rationale: Installing needs roughly 512 MB of free memory and running Claude Code needs more; the stated requirement is at least 4 GB of RAM. These figures are what distinguish a genuine resource shortfall from an installer defect.

nodes.label: Install hangs in Docker when run from /
nodes.rationale: Installing as root into `/` inside a Docker container can hang because the installer scans the entire filesystem, causing excessive memory usage. Setting `WORKDIR /tmp` before the `RUN curl ... | bash` limits the scan; raising the Docker Desktop VM memory limit also helps since build containers share that allocation.

nodes.label: Raw mode is not supported during install
nodes.rationale: The approval dialog needs a terminal on stdin, but `curl ... | bash` gives the installer a pipe, so `claude install` fails with `Raw mode is not supported`. Rerunning the installer gets past it in most configurations because the script runs the latest release's `install` command even when installing an older version.

nodes.label: Server-managed settings security-approval dialog
nodes.rationale: When an organization's server-managed settings contain changes needing security approval, Claude Code before v2.1.246 tried to show the approval dialog during `claude install`. v2.1.246 and later defer it to the next interactive session — except when the startup configuration waits for the settings fetch (e.g. `forceRemoteSettingsRefresh`), where the dialog still appears and a piped install still fails.

nodes.label: claude update / claude doctor hang on a directory at a shell-config path
nodes.rationale: Both commands scan `~/.zshrc`, `~/.bashrc`, `~/.config/fish/config.fish` (and on macOS the first existing of `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login`, `~/.profile`; `$ZDOTDIR/.zshrc` when `ZDOTDIR` is set) for an outdated `claude` alias. Before v2.1.214 a directory at one of those paths made both hang and left `/status` System diagnostics blank; find it with `ls -ld` and move it aside, or update to v2.1.214+ by rerunning the install script.

nodes.label: Claude Desktop shadows the claude command on Windows
nodes.rationale: An older Claude Desktop registers a `Claude.exe` in the `WindowsApps` directory that takes PATH priority over the Claude Code CLI, so running `claude` opens the Desktop app instead. Updating Claude Desktop to the latest version fixes it.

nodes.label: Windows requires Git Bash or PowerShell
nodes.rationale: Git for Windows is optional — Claude Code falls back to the PowerShell tool when Git Bash is absent — so the error means neither shell was found. Add `C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\` to PATH or install PowerShell 7 (`pwsh`); installing Git for Windows with "Add to PATH" enables the Bash tool instead.

nodes.label: CLAUDE_CODE_GIT_BASH_PATH resolution rules
nodes.rationale: Unset, Claude Code looks for `bash.exe` in `C:\Program Files\Git` and `C:\Program Files (x86)\Git`, then via the `git` on PATH — skipping a `git` inside the launch directory or under `node_modules`/`.venv`/`env`, so a project cannot plant an executable. Set the variable in settings.json to a file literally named `bash.exe`, `sh.exe`, `bash` or `sh`; any other name (e.g. `git-bash.exe`) or a missing path is ignored with a `--debug` warning. Before v2.1.219 any existing file was used and a missing path aborted startup.

nodes.label: 32-bit Windows / x86 PowerShell entry
nodes.rationale: `Claude Code does not support 32-bit Windows` fires even on 64-bit machines when the Start-menu `Windows PowerShell (x86)` entry is used, because it runs as a 32-bit process. Run `[Environment]::Is64BitOperatingSystem` in the failing window: `True` means reopen the non-x86 PowerShell, `False` means the OS itself is 32-bit and unsupported.

nodes.label: Linux musl/glibc binary mismatch
nodes.rationale: `Error loading shared library libstdc++.so.6` (or `libgcc_s.so.1`) means the wrong libc variant was downloaded — glibc systems carrying musl cross-compilation packages get misdetected as musl. Identify the libc with `ldd --version`; on glibc, reinstall or fetch the right binary from the release manifest and file a GitHub issue; on real musl (Alpine), `apk add libgcc libstdc++ ripgrep`.

nodes.label: Illegal instruction (architecture or AVX)
nodes.rationale: Two distinct causes: an architecture mismatch (check `uname -m` or `$env:PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE`), or a CPU lacking AVX — roughly pre-2013 Intel/AMD parts and VMs whose hypervisor does not pass AVX through (`grep -m1 -ow avx /proc/cpuinfo` returning nothing). There is no native-binary workaround for the AVX case; it is tracked as issue #50384.

nodes.label: dyld cannot load on macOS (version too old)
nodes.rationale: `dyld: Symbol not found` referencing `libicucore`, `dyld: cannot load ... (load command 0x80000034 is unknown)`, or `Abort trap: 6` all mean the macOS version is older than the binary supports. Claude Code requires macOS 13.0 or later; the fix is to update macOS.

nodes.label: Exec format error on WSL1
nodes.rationale: `cannot execute binary file: Exec format error` in WSL is a known native-binary regression on WSL1 (issue #38788) caused by changed program headers WSL1's loader cannot handle. Convert the distro with `wsl --set-version <DistroName> 2`, or stay on WSL1 by wrapping `claude` in a shell function that invokes the binary through `/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`.

nodes.label: npm-in-WSL environment issues
nodes.rationale: WSL importing the Windows PATH causes npm/node/nvm from Windows to win: fix a platform mismatch with `npm config set os linux` then `npm install -g ... --force` (never sudo); fix `exec: node: not found` by installing Linux Node when `which node` shows `/mnt/c/`; fix nvm conflicts by loading nvm in `~/.bashrc` or prepending the Linux node bin. Do not set `appendWindowsPath = false`, which breaks calling Windows executables from WSL.

nodes.label: Error: claude native binary not installed
nodes.rationale: The npm package ships a placeholder script until its postinstall copies the platform binary into place; skipping either the optional-dependency download or the postinstall leaves the placeholder. Rerun `node node_modules/@anthropic-ai/claude-code/install.cjs`, or reinstall without `--ignore-scripts` / `--omit=optional`. On Windows the placeholder is `bin/claude.exe`, so the shell reports it cannot run the file instead of printing the message.

nodes.label: Per-platform optional binary packages
nodes.rationale: The native binary is delivered ONLY as a per-platform optional dependency (e.g. `@anthropic-ai/claude-code-darwin-arm64`), with no JavaScript fallback, for eight targets: darwin-arm64, darwin-x64, linux-x64, linux-arm64, linux-x64-musl, linux-arm64-musl, win32-x64, win32-arm64. `--omit=optional`, `--no-optional`, `--ignore-optional`, `optional=false` in `.npmrc`, or a corporate mirror that omits these packages all break the install.

nodes.label: npm ENOTEMPTY during update or reinstall
nodes.rationale: Reinstalling over an existing global install can fail with `npm error code ENOTEMPTY` while renaming the old package directory. Delete the directory the `npm error path` line names plus any leftover `.claude-code-*` temp directories beside it — using `npm root -g` unless the error's path is outside it (e.g. after an nvm Node switch) — then reinstall and confirm with `claude --version`.

nodes.label: Reset your login
nodes.rationale: When login fails for no obvious reason, a clean re-authentication resolves most cases: `/logout`, close Claude Code, restart with `claude` and sign in again. If the browser does not open, press `c` to copy the OAuth URL and paste it into a browser — which also handles URLs that wrap unclickably in a narrow or SSH terminal.

nodes.label: OAuth error: Invalid code
nodes.rationale: `OAuth error: Invalid code. Please make sure the full code was copied` means the login code expired or was truncated during copy-paste. Retry and complete login quickly, use `c` to copy the full URL, and on a remote/SSH session open the terminal-displayed URL in the local browser because the remote browser opens on the wrong machine.

nodes.label: 403 Forbidden after login
nodes.rationale: `API Error: 403 {"error":{"type":"forbidden","message":"Request not allowed"}}` after a successful login has three checks: Pro/Max users verify the subscription is active at claude.ai/settings; Console users confirm the account holds the "Claude Code" or "Developer" role assigned under Settings → Members; and corporate proxies can interfere with API requests.

nodes.label: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY overrides the subscription
nodes.rationale: `API Error: 400 ... "This organization has been disabled"` despite an active subscription means a stale `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` env var is being used instead of the subscription's OAuth credentials — always so in non-interactive `-p` mode when the key is present. Unset it, strip `export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=` from `~/.zshrc`/`~/.bashrc`/`~/.profile` or the PowerShell `$PROFILE`, and confirm the active method with `/status`.

nodes.label: OAuth login in WSL2, SSH, or containers
nodes.rationale: In WSL2, over SSH, or in a container the browser opens on another host and its redirect cannot reach the local callback server, so the browser shows a login code to paste at the `Paste code here if prompted` prompt. Set `BROWSER` to the Windows browser path if nothing opens; if pasting into the interactive prompt does nothing, use `claude auth login`, which reads the code from standard input.

nodes.label: Token expiry and parallel-session renewal
nodes.rationale: Being prompted to log in again means the OAuth token expired: run `/login`, and if it recurs check the system clock, since token validation depends on correct timestamps. Parallel sessions share a saved login and coordinate renewal so only one process refreshes; before v2.1.211 waking from sleep could make two sessions renew with the same token, revoking the saved login for all of them.

nodes.label: macOS Keychain credential storage and plaintext fallback
nodes.rationale: Claude Code stores credentials in the macOS login Keychain; when the Keychain rejects the write (locked in an SSH session, or its password out of sync with the account password) it falls back to plaintext `~/.claude/.credentials.json`, and Console API-key creation fails. Recovery: `claude doctor` to see the `macOS Keychain is not writable` warning, `security unlock-keychain ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db`, resync the password in Keychain Access, then `/logout` + `/login` — which also clears MCP logins and plugin secrets.

nodes.label: Bedrock / Agent Platform / Foundry credentials not loading
nodes.rationale: `Could not load credentials from any providers` (Bedrock), `Could not load the default credentials` (Google Cloud's Agent Platform) and `ChainedTokenCredential authentication failed` (Microsoft Foundry) mean the provider CLI is not authenticated in the current shell: check `aws sts get-caller-identity`, set `ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_PROJECT_ID`/`CLOUD_ML_REGION` then `gcloud auth application-default login`, or set `ANTHROPIC_FOUNDRY_API_KEY` / run `az login`. If it works in the terminal but not in an IDE, the IDE process did not inherit the shell environment.

nodes.label: claude doctor diagnostic report
nodes.rationale: `claude doctor` produces an automated diagnostic report — used here to check macOS Keychain writability and, in the escalation path, whenever `claude --version` works but something else is wrong. Its own hang on a directory at a shell-config path is a separate documented defect.

nodes.label: Still-stuck escalation path
nodes.rationale: If nothing on the page resolves the issue: check or open a GitHub issue with the OS, the install command and the full error output; run `claude doctor` when the binary works; use `/feedback` from inside a session; and for account-level problems (login loop, unrecognised subscription, disabled organization) contact Anthropic support through claude.ai or platform.claude.com.

nodes.label: Claude Code Desktop app as a no-terminal alternative
nodes.rationale: The Claude Code Desktop app installs and runs Claude Code through a graphical interface, skipping the terminal entirely — downloadable for macOS and Windows, and installable with apt on Linux. It is offered as the escape hatch for anyone who does not want command-line setup at all.

nodes.label: Ultrareview
nodes.rationale: Ultrareview is a deep, multi-agent code review that runs on Claude Code on the web infrastructure: it launches a fleet of reviewer agents in a remote sandbox to find bugs in a branch or pull request before merge.

nodes.label: Research preview status
nodes.rationale: Ultrareview is a research preview feature; the feature, its pricing, and its availability may change based on feedback.

nodes.label: /code-review ultra command
nodes.rationale: `/code-review ultra` is the command that starts an ultrareview from any git repository; where ultrareview is available to the account, `/ultrareview` is an alias for it.

nodes.label: Fleet of reviewer agents
nodes.rationale: A larger fleet of reviewer agents explores the change in parallel, which is what surfaces issues a local review can miss.

nodes.label: Remote cloud sandbox
nodes.rationale: The review runs entirely in a remote sandbox on Claude Code on the web infrastructure, not on the user's machine.

nodes.label: Independently verified findings
nodes.rationale: Every reported ultrareview finding is independently reproduced and verified, so results focus on real bugs rather than style suggestions.

nodes.label: Broader parallel coverage
nodes.rationale: Broader coverage is one of ultrareview's three stated advantages over a local /code-review: parallel exploration surfaces issues a local review can miss.

nodes.label: No local resource use
nodes.rationale: Because the review runs in a remote sandbox, the user's terminal stays free for other work while it runs.

nodes.label: claude.ai authentication requirement
nodes.rationale: Ultrareview requires authentication with a claude.ai account because it runs on Claude Code on the web infrastructure; an API-key-only sign-in must run /login and authenticate with claude.ai first.

nodes.label: Third-party provider and ZDR unavailability
nodes.rationale: Ultrareview is not available with Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry, nor to organizations that have enabled Zero Data Retention.

nodes.label: Local review fallback
nodes.rationale: When ultrareview is not available, `/code-review ultra` runs a local review in the current session instead of refusing.

nodes.label: Default branch-vs-default-branch scope
nodes.rationale: Without arguments, ultrareview reviews the diff between the current branch and the default branch, including uncommitted and staged changes.

nodes.label: Credential-like file upload rules
nodes.rationale: For uncommitted changes to files named like credentials or keys, such as `.env` and `*.tfvars`, Claude Code follows the rules for uploading a local repository to a cloud session.

nodes.label: Branch-mode bundle upload
nodes.rationale: For a branch review, Claude Code bundles the repository state and uploads it to the remote sandbox; in PR mode it uploads nothing from the machine.

nodes.label: Launch confirmation dialog
nodes.rationale: Before launching, Claude Code shows a confirmation dialog with the review scope (file and line count for a branch review), remaining free runs, and the estimated cost; after confirmation the review continues in the background.

nodes.label: Explicit invocation only
nodes.rationale: The command runs only when the user invokes it with `/code-review ultra`; Claude never starts an ultrareview on its own.

nodes.label: Review against a different base
nodes.rationale: Passing a branch name compares against that base instead of the default branch; the base need not exist in the local clone because Claude Code fetches it from origin, and a typo produces a closest-branch-name suggestion.

nodes.label: Pull request review mode
nodes.rationale: Passing a PR number (also `#1234`, `PR 1234`, or a pasted URL pointing at the current repository) reviews a GitHub pull request; the remote sandbox clones the PR directly from the host rather than bundling the local working tree, and works on github.com and connected GitHub Enterprise Server instances.

nodes.label: Connected GitHub account precheck
nodes.rationale: For github.com repositories the sandbox clones with the GitHub account connected to the Claude account, and Claude Code checks read access before creating the cloud session (unless CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC is set), refusing the launch and naming the fix; before v2.1.248 no such precheck existed.

nodes.label: /web-setup connection command
nodes.rationale: Running `/web-setup` connects the GitHub CLI login to the Claude account, which is what the PR-mode account check requires.

nodes.label: Post findings to the pull request
nodes.rationale: On Claude Code v2.1.227 or later, a github.com pull request review can post the finished findings to the PR as a single plain comment from the user's own GitHub account; the comment is not a review or approval and ends with a 'Generated by Claude Code' note.

nodes.label: --no-post is the default
nodes.rationale: Claude Code never posts unless the user chooses to on that run: `--no-post` is the default, and passing both `--post` and `--no-post` results in no post.

nodes.label: Interactive posting choice
nodes.rationale: Interactively, the user selects 'Run and post the findings to the PR as me' in the launch dialog; adding `--post` to the command only preselects that choice and Claude Code still asks before launching.

nodes.label: Non-interactive posting consent
nodes.rationale: Running the `claude ultrareview` subcommand with `--post` is itself the consent, so Claude Code posts without asking; a `claude -p '/code-review ultra'` run exits before findings arrive and posts nothing.

nodes.label: Posting runs through Claude Code on the web
nodes.rationale: Claude Code does not post from the local machine: it sends findings to a Claude Code on the web session, which posts through the connected GitHub account — so posting is unavailable on third-party providers or with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC set.

nodes.label: Session must stay open to post
nodes.rationale: In an interactive session the post starts when findings arrive and the posting choice is kept only in that session; if the session ends before the review finishes, Claude Code posts nothing even if the conversation is resumed later.

nodes.label: Post failure is reported, findings retained
nodes.rationale: When a post cannot start, Claude tells the user nothing went to the PR and why, and the findings stay in the terminal (or on stdout for the subcommand) so they can be posted by hand.

nodes.label: Plain-words request note
nodes.rationale: On v2.1.218 or later the user can describe the work in plain words (e.g. `/code-review ultra check my auth changes`); the scope is still the current branch, and Claude keeps the text as a note shown in the launch dialog and relates the findings to it.

nodes.label: Note vs branch/PR disambiguation
nodes.rationale: Text counts as a note only when it has more than one word and is not a branch name or PR reference; a single word is read as a branch or PR reference, and text mixing a PR reference with other words causes Claude Code to refuse and ask for a rerun with the PR number alone or without the reference.

nodes.label: Too-large repository tip
nodes.rationale: If the repository is too large to bundle, Claude Code prompts the user to use PR mode: push the branch, open a draft PR, and run `/code-review ultra <PR-number>`.

nodes.label: Pre-review diff check
nodes.rationale: Ultrareview checks the diff before any review work runs and tells the user when it cannot review the diff as-is, covering the too-large, nothing-to-review, and no-merge-base cases.

nodes.label: Diff size limits
nodes.rationale: A branch review can include up to 500 changed files and 8,000 changed lines by default; the exact values can change and the refusal names the values in effect, the diff size, and the files with the most changed lines — a too-large pull request is refused the same way but without the per-file breakdown.

nodes.label: Empty diff refusal
nodes.rationale: When the diff against the base is empty, Claude Code says so and suggests staging or committing local edits, or passing a different base.

nodes.label: Whole-repository fallback with no merge base
nodes.rationale: When the branch shares no history with the base branch, Claude Code falls back to reviewing every tracked file in the repository; the fallback requires a full clone and applies the same size limits.

nodes.label: No-branches checkout refusal
nodes.rationale: On a checkout with no branches or other refs — such as a detached HEAD created by checking out FETCH_HEAD after fetching a URL — Claude Code refuses the review and suggests creating a branch first, rather than falling back to the whole repository.

nodes.label: Usage-credits billing
nodes.rationale: Ultrareview is a premium feature that bills against usage credits rather than the plan's included usage; Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise all bill as usage credits once free runs are exhausted.

nodes.label: One-time free runs
nodes.rationale: Pro and Max accounts get 3 free ultrareview runs as a one-time allotment that does not refresh; Team and Enterprise plans get none.

nodes.label: Cost per review
nodes.rationale: After the free runs, a review typically costs $5 to $25 in usage credits depending on the size of the change, matching the estimate shown in the launch dialog.

nodes.label: When a run counts
nodes.rationale: A run counts once the cloud session starts: a review stopped early or that fails to complete still consumes a free run, while a paid review bills only for the portion that ran.

nodes.label: Usage-credits enablement gate
