nodes.rationale: An account or organization must have usage credits turned on before launching a paid review; otherwise Claude Code blocks the launch, linking billing managers to settings and letting Team/Enterprise members without billing access send an admin request from the CLI.

nodes.label: /usage-credits command
nodes.rationale: `/usage-credits` checks or changes the account's usage-credits setting.

nodes.label: Per-conversation billing confirmation
nodes.rationale: Claude Code asks for usage-credits billing confirmation once per conversation, so starting a new conversation (for example with /clear) makes it ask again before the next paid review.

nodes.label: 5 to 10 minute duration
nodes.rationale: An ultrareview typically takes 5 to 10 minutes, against seconds to a few minutes for a local /code-review.

nodes.label: Background task execution
nodes.rationale: The review runs as a background task, so the user can keep working in the session, start other commands, or close the terminal entirely.

nodes.label: /tasks tracking command
nodes.rationale: `/tasks` lists running and completed reviews, opens a review's detail view, or stops an in-progress review; stopping archives the cloud session and returns no partial findings.

nodes.label: Verified findings notification
nodes.rationale: When the review finishes, Claude Code shows the verified findings as a notification in the session; each finding includes a file location and an explanation so Claude can be asked to fix it directly.

nodes.label: claude ultrareview subcommand
nodes.rationale: The `claude ultrareview` subcommand starts an ultrareview from CI or a script without an interactive session; it launches the same review as `/code-review ultra`, blocks until the remote review finishes, and prints findings to stdout, accepting no argument, a PR number, or a base branch.

nodes.label: Subcommand implicit consent
nodes.rationale: Running the subcommand is itself consent to the whole-repository fallback and to the billing and terms prompt, so the run starts without waiting for input.

nodes.label: Non-interactive slash-command launch
nodes.rationale: On v2.1.218 or later, `claude -p '/code-review ultra'` launches the cloud review and prints a tracking link without waiting for findings; when the review would bill usage credits it stops before launching and points to `claude ultrareview`, because the billing confirmation needs an interactive session. Before v2.1.218 it ran a local review.

nodes.label: stdout/stderr separation
nodes.rationale: Progress messages and the live session URL go to stderr so stdout stays parseable for the findings.

nodes.label: Subcommand output and timeout flags
nodes.rationale: `--json` prints the raw bugs.json payload instead of formatted findings; `--timeout <minutes>` caps the wait and defaults to 30; `--post` and `--no-post` control posting and require v2.1.227 or later, with `--post` ignored (and said so) on non-github.com targets.

nodes.label: Subcommand exit codes
nodes.rationale: The subcommand exits 0 when the review completed with or without findings, 1 when it failed to launch or the cloud session errored or the timeout elapsed, and 130 on a Ctrl-C interrupt.

nodes.label: Interrupt leaves the remote review running
nodes.rationale: Interrupting the subcommand does not stop the remote review; the session URL printed to stderr can be followed to watch it in the browser, and nothing is posted when the run fails, times out, or is interrupted.

nodes.label: Local /code-review
nodes.rationale: Local `/code-review` targets a working diff, pull request, branch or path, runs in the session, scales its depth with the effort argument, takes seconds to a few minutes, counts toward normal usage, and is best for quick feedback while iterating.

nodes.label: Pre-merge vs iterative use
nodes.rationale: Both reviews examine code but are used at different workflow stages: /code-review for fast feedback while working or to check a teammate's PR before approving, and /code-review ultra before merging a substantial change when a deeper pass is wanted.

nodes.label: Code Review GitHub integration
nodes.rationale: For automatic reviews on GitHub pull requests, the Code Review product integrates with the repository directly and posts findings as inline PR comments without any CLI step.

nodes.label: Claude Code VS Code extension
nodes.rationale: The VS Code extension provides a native graphical interface for Claude Code integrated directly into the IDE, and is the recommended way to use Claude Code in VS Code. It lets you review and edit Claude's plans before accepting, auto-accept edits, @-mention files with line ranges, access conversation history, and open multiple conversations in separate tabs or windows.

nodes.label: Prerequisites (VS Code 1.94.0+, Anthropic account)
nodes.rationale: Installing requires VS Code 1.94.0 or higher and an Anthropic account: any paid Claude subscription (Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise) or a Claude Console account, with no API key required. Users sign in with that account the first time the extension panel opens.

nodes.label: Extension's bundled CLI copy
nodes.rationale: The extension bundles its own private copy of the CLI to power the chat panel. Installing the extension does not put `claude` on the shell PATH, so the bundled copy cannot be invoked from a terminal.

nodes.label: Standalone CLI install
nodes.rationale: Running `claude` in VS Code's integrated terminal requires the separate standalone CLI install. Running that install once makes commands such as `claude mcp add` and `claude --resume` work in any terminal; if `claude` is still not found afterwards, verify your PATH.

nodes.label: Installation paths (Marketplace, Open VSX, forks)
nodes.rationale: The extension installs via the `vscode:extension/anthropic.claude-code` link, the Extensions view (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+X, search 'Claude Code'), Cursor, or the Open VSX registry for other VS Code forks such as Devin Desktop or Kiro. If an editor cannot install it, install the CLI and run `claude` in that editor's integrated terminal instead.

nodes.label: Spark icon and panel entry points
nodes.rationale: The Spark icon marks Claude Code throughout VS Code; clicking it in the Editor Toolbar is the quickest way to open Claude, but it only appears when a file is open. Other entry points are the Activity Bar sessions list, the Command Palette ('Claude Code' commands), and the Status Bar entry when `preferredLocation` is `sidebar`.

nodes.label: Sign-in flow and shell environment
nodes.rationale: The first panel open shows a sign-in screen completed via browser authorization; a later 'Not logged in · Please run /login' reopens it automatically. If `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is set in the shell but the sign-in prompt still appears, VS Code did not inherit the shell environment — launch it from a terminal with `code .` or sign in with a Claude account.

nodes.label: Permission modes in the prompt box
nodes.rationale: A mode indicator at the bottom of the prompt box shows and switches the permission mode, which determines whether Claude asks before editing. On Pro, Max, and Team plans, Auto is the built-in starting permission mode.

nodes.label: Auto mode
nodes.rationale: In Auto mode a classifier reviews most actions instead of asking the user, and Claude edits most files in the workspace without prompting.

nodes.label: Manual mode
nodes.rationale: In Manual mode Claude asks permission before file edits and most shell commands. `manual` is an alias for the `default` setting value and selects the mode labeled Manual in the indicator.

nodes.label: Plan mode with inline plan comments
nodes.rationale: In Plan mode Claude describes what it will do and waits for approval before changing anything. VS Code automatically opens the plan as a full Markdown document where inline comments can be added as feedback before Claude begins.

nodes.label: Edit automatically mode
nodes.rationale: In Edit automatically mode Claude makes file edits without asking for permission.

nodes.label: Side-by-side diff review of proposed edits
nodes.rationale: In Manual mode a proposed edit is shown as a side-by-side comparison of original and proposed content, which can be accepted, rejected, or redirected. If the user edits the proposed content directly in the diff view before accepting, Claude is told it was modified so it does not assume the file matches its original proposal.

nodes.label: Slash command menu
nodes.rationale: Typing or clicking `/` opens the command menu, offering file attachment, model switching, extended-thinking toggling, `/usage`, and `/remote-control`. Its Customize section reaches MCP servers, hooks, memory, permissions, and plugins; items with a terminal icon open in the integrated terminal.

nodes.label: Focus view
nodes.rationale: Focus view hides tool calls, tool results, and thinking behind expandable rows, leaving prompts and Claude's responses, while keeping the latest to-do list and any pending question text visible. It toggles from the Settings section, with Ctrl+Option+F / Ctrl+Alt+F, or the Command Palette, applies to every open session and persists; it requires Claude Code v2.1.221 or later (to-do visibility requires v2.1.225).

nodes.label: Side questions with /btw
nodes.rationale: Typing `/btw` followed by a question asks about the session without adding to the conversation; the answer opens in a side panel supporting follow-ups and survives window reloads. Claude Code keeps the newest 20 exchanges and expires stored threads on the `cleanupPeriodDays` schedule; requires v2.1.227 or later.

nodes.label: In-extension bug reporting
nodes.rationale: 'Report a problem' in the command menu, or `/bug` / `/feedback` with an optional prefilled description, submits a report to Anthropic when signed in on a first-party connection. On a third-party provider or without Anthropic credentials the dialog opens but submitting shows an error and sends nothing, and unlike the CLI's `/bug` the extension writes no local archive; requires v2.1.229 or later.

nodes.label: Context indicator and compaction
nodes.rationale: The prompt box shows how much of Claude's context window is in use. Claude compacts automatically when needed, and `/compact` triggers it manually.

nodes.label: Extended thinking in the panel
nodes.rationale: Extended thinking lets Claude spend more time reasoning through complex problems and is toggled from the `/` command menu. Reasoning appears as collapsed blocks in the conversation; clicking one expands it, and Ctrl+O expands or collapses every thinking block in the session.

nodes.label: @-mentions of files and folders
nodes.rationale: Typing `@` followed by a file or folder name gives Claude that content as context, with fuzzy matching on partial names and a trailing slash for folders. Files can also be added as attachments by holding Shift while dragging them into the prompt box, and removed with the attachment's X.

nodes.label: Editor selection as automatic context
nodes.rationale: Claude automatically sees text selected in the editor, and the prompt box footer reports how many lines are selected; the selection indicator toggles that visibility, where an eye-slash icon means the selection is hidden. Option+K / Alt+K inserts an @-mention carrying the file path and line range, such as `@app.ts#5-10`.

nodes.label: Reading specific PDF pages
nodes.rationale: For large PDFs, Claude can be asked to read specific pages rather than the whole file — a single page, a bounded range such as pages 1-10, or an open-ended range such as page 3 onward.

nodes.label: Session history and resume
nodes.rationale: The Session history button at the top of the panel opens conversation history, searchable by keyword or browsable by time bucket, and clicking a conversation resumes it with full message history. New sessions get AI-generated titles from the first message, and hovering a session reveals rename and remove actions.

nodes.label: Plan-mode restoration on resume
nodes.rationale: Resuming a conversation that ended in plan mode restores plan mode, requiring Claude Code v2.1.246 or later. It is not restored when the extension picks the starting mode from `claudeCode.initialPermissionMode` or a pick carried over from an earlier conversation, or when `claudeCode.claudeProcessWrapper` is configured.

nodes.label: Resuming Claude.ai cloud sessions
nodes.rationale: Sessions from Claude Code on the web can be resumed in VS Code through the Web tab of the Session history dialog, which requires signing in with a Claude.ai Subscription rather than Anthropic Console. Only web sessions started with a GitHub repository appear, and resuming loads the history locally without syncing changes back to claude.ai.

nodes.label: /usage Account & usage dialog
nodes.rationale: `/usage` opens a dialog showing the signed-in account, plan, and session and weekly usage bars with time until each limit resets. It flags behaviors accounting for 10% or more of recent usage (cache misses, long context, subagent-heavy or highly parallel sessions) with reduction tips, and attributes usage per skill, subagent, plugin and MCP server; figures are approximate, computed from local sessions on this machine only, and it requires v2.1.174 or later.

nodes.label: Repositioning the Claude panel
nodes.rationale: The Claude panel can be dragged by its tab or title bar into the secondary (right) sidebar, the primary (left) sidebar, or the editor area as a tab. Claude remembers the preferred location; the Activity Bar sessions-list icon is always visible and separate from the panel icon, which appears there only when the panel is docked to the left sidebar.

nodes.label: Multiple parallel conversations
nodes.rationale: 'Open in New Tab' or 'Open in New Window' start additional conversations, each keeping its own history and context so different tasks run in parallel. On tabs, a colored dot on the spark icon signals status: blue for a pending permission request, orange for Claude finishing while the tab was hidden.

nodes.label: Session groups in the Activity Bar
nodes.rationale: Sessions in the Activity Bar list can be collected into named, collapsible groups via right-click, with multi-select through Cmd/Ctrl-click or Shift-click; each session belongs to one group at a time and deleting a group returns its sessions to the ungrouped list. Groups are saved per workspace folder, survive window reloads, and searching shows matches in one flat list across groups; requires v2.1.229 or later.

nodes.label: Terminal mode (useTerminal)
nodes.rationale: By default the extension opens a graphical chat panel; checking the Use Terminal setting (`claudeCode.useTerminal`, default false) launches the CLI-style interface instead. The setting is reachable from the settings URI or Extensions → Claude Code.

nodes.label: Graphical plugin management (/plugins)
nodes.rationale: Typing `/plugins` opens a Manage plugins interface with Plugins and Marketplaces tabs: installed plugins carry enable/disable toggles, available marketplace plugins appear below with search and an Install button. Plugin management in VS Code uses the same CLI commands underneath, so plugins and marketplaces configured either way are shared.

nodes.label: Plugin installation scopes
nodes.rationale: Installing a plugin requires choosing a scope: 'Install for you' (user scope, all your projects), 'Install for this project' (project scope, shared with collaborators), or 'Install locally' (local scope, only you and only this repository).

nodes.label: Marketplace sources management
nodes.rationale: The Marketplaces tab adds a plugin source by GitHub repo, URL, or local path, refreshes a marketplace's plugin list, or removes it with the trash icon. After changes a banner prompts a Claude Code restart to apply them.

nodes.label: @browser Chrome automation
nodes.rationale: Typing `@browser` followed by an instruction connects Claude to Chrome to test web apps, read console logs, and automate browser workflows without leaving VS Code; it requires the Claude in Chrome extension version 1.0.36 or higher. Claude opens new tabs for browser tasks and shares the browser's login state, so it can reach any site the user is already signed into.

nodes.label: VS Code commands and keyboard shortcuts
nodes.rationale: The Command Palette exposes the extension's VS Code commands — Focus Input (Cmd/Ctrl+Esc), Open in Side Bar / Terminal / New Tab (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+Esc) / New Window, New Conversation (Cmd/Ctrl+N, gated on `enableNewConversationShortcut`), Reopen Closed Session (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+T), Insert @-Mention (Option/Alt+K), Toggle Focus view, Show Logs, and Logout. Some shortcuts depend on which panel is focused, and Cmd/Ctrl+Esc toggles focus between editor and Claude.

nodes.label: vscode://anthropic.claude-code/open URI handler
nodes.rationale: The extension registers a URI handler at `vscode://anthropic.claude-code/open` so any shell alias, bookmarklet, or script that opens a URL can start a Claude Code tab; it launches VS Code if not running, else opens in the focused window. It accepts two optional query parameters — `prompt` (URL-encoded text pre-filled but not submitted) and `session` (a session ID in the current workspace to resume, falling back to a fresh conversation if not found).

nodes.label: Two settings surfaces: extension vs Claude Code settings
nodes.rationale: The extension has two settings types: VS Code extension settings under Extensions → Claude Code that control in-editor behavior, and Claude Code settings in `~/.claude/settings.json` shared with the CLI for allowed commands, environment variables, hooks and MCP servers. Adding `"$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json"` gives autocomplete and inline validation in VS Code.

nodes.label: initialPermissionMode setting
nodes.rationale: `initialPermissionMode` controls approval prompts for new conversations with values `default`, `plan`, `acceptEdits`, or `bypassPermissions`; left unset, the extension chooses the starting mode itself. VS Code reads it from user settings and ignores workspace values — before v2.1.225 it defaulted to `default` and applied workspace values.

nodes.label: claudeProcessWrapper setting
nodes.rationale: `claudeProcessWrapper` names the executable used to launch the Claude process, receiving the bundled binary path as an argument when present; it is the fix when the extension build has no binary for the platform ('Unsupported platform' at activation). In a wrapped setup conversations start in Manual mode unless `initialPermissionMode` is set or a mode was picked earlier, because the extension skips the settings and built-in-default steps.

nodes.label: Other extension settings (autosave, respectGitIgnore, …)
nodes.rationale: The settings table also covers `preferredLocation` (`panel` default, or `sidebar`), `autosave` (true — save files before Claude reads or writes them), `useCtrlEnterToSend`, `enableNewConversationShortcut`, `enableReopenClosedSessionShortcut`, `hideOnboarding`, `focusView`, `respectGitIgnore` (true — exclude .gitignore patterns from file searches), `usePythonEnvironment` (activate the workspace Python environment, needs the Python extension), `environmentVariables`, and `disableLoginPrompt`.

nodes.label: allowDangerouslySkipPermissions
nodes.rationale: `allowDangerouslySkipPermissions` (default false) adds Bypass permissions to the mode selector. The documentation says to use it only in sandboxes with no internet access.

nodes.label: Screen reader support in the chat panel
nodes.rationale: The chat panel works with screen readers with nothing to turn on and no visual change, and is separate from the CLI's opt-in screen reader mode; it requires Claude Code v2.1.236 or later. It announces completed replies once (silent while streaming), permission requests and questions naming the tool, status changes, errors and model prompts, and gives each turn a visually hidden heading plus a Tab-reachable labeled transcript region; reopening or switching sessions announces nothing until something new happens.

nodes.label: Extension vs CLI feature gap
nodes.rationale: Some features are CLI-only: the extension offers a subset of commands and skills, partial MCP server config (servers are added via CLI, managed with `/mcp`), and no `!` bash shortcut or tab completion, while checkpoints work in both. For a CLI-only feature, run `claude` in VS Code's integrated terminal.

nodes.label: Rewind with checkpoints
nodes.rationale: The extension supports checkpoints that track Claude's file edits and allow rewinding. Hovering a message reveals a rewind button offering three options: fork the conversation from here keeping code changes, rewind code to here keeping conversation history, or fork the conversation and rewind code together.

nodes.label: Running the CLI in VS Code's integrated terminal
nodes.rationale: Opening the integrated terminal (Cmd/Ctrl+`) and running `claude` keeps CLI use inside VS Code, and the CLI automatically integrates with the IDE for diff viewing and diagnostic sharing. From an external terminal, running `/ide` inside Claude Code connects it to VS Code.

nodes.label: Shared conversation history between extension and CLI
nodes.rationale: The extension and CLI share the same conversation history, so an extension conversation continues in the terminal with `claude --resume`, which opens an interactive picker for searching and selecting the conversation.

nodes.label: @terminal:name output references
nodes.rationale: Terminal output can be referenced in prompts with `@terminal:name`, where `name` is the terminal's title, letting Claude see command output, error messages, or logs without copy-pasting.

nodes.label: Limited background-process visibility
nodes.rationale: Visibility for background tasks in the extension is limited compared to the CLI. The documented workaround is to have Claude output the command so it can be run in VS Code's integrated terminal instead.

nodes.label: Adding and managing MCP servers
nodes.rationale: MCP servers are added from the integrated terminal with `claude mcp add` (for example GitHub's remote HTTP server with an Authorization Bearer header), and the command saves configuration without validating credentials, so a placeholder is accepted but the server later fails to connect. Typing `/mcp` in the chat panel verifies status (`connected` vs `failed`) and manages enabling, disabling, reconnecting, and OAuth.

nodes.label: Git workflows from the panel
nodes.rationale: Claude Code integrates with git inside VS Code: it can stage changes, write commit messages, create pull requests, work across branches, and summarize changes on request. Pull request descriptions are generated from the actual code changes and can add context about testing or implementation decisions.

nodes.label: Third-party provider configuration
nodes.rationale: By default Claude Code connects directly to Anthropic's API; organizations using Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry configure the extension for their provider by checking Disable Login Prompt and following the provider setup guide. Those guides configure `~/.claude/settings.json`, which keeps the settings shared between the extension and the CLI.

nodes.label: Risk of Claude editing VS Code config files
nodes.rationale: With auto-edit permissions enabled, Claude Code can modify VS Code configuration files such as `settings.json` or `tasks.json` that VS Code may execute automatically. The recommended mitigations for untrusted code are enabling VS Code Restricted Mode for untrusted workspaces, using Manual mode instead of Edit automatically or Auto, and reviewing changes carefully before accepting.

nodes.label: Code privacy and training
nodes.rationale: Claude Code processes code to provide assistance but does not use it to train models; details on data handling and opting out of logging are in the Data and privacy documentation.

nodes.label: Built-in `ide` MCP server
nodes.rationale: While the extension is active it runs a local MCP server named `ide` that the CLI connects to automatically; it is how the CLI opens diffs in VS Code's native diff viewer, reads the current selection for @-mentions, and asks VS Code to execute Jupyter cells. It is hidden from `/mcp` because there is nothing to configure, but organizations using a `PreToolUse` hook to allowlist MCP tools need to know it exists.

nodes.label: IDE server selection and open-file context
nodes.rationale: While connected, the CLI includes the current editor selection and the active file's path as context on every prompt, shown in the transcript as a `⧉ Selected N lines from <file>` line. Adding a `Read` deny rule for a sensitive path such as `.env` prevents both the selected text and the open-file notice for that file from reaching Claude.

nodes.label: IDE server transport and authentication
nodes.rationale: The `ide` server binds to `127.0.0.1` on a random, non-configurable port in 10000–65535 over unencrypted `ws://`; because the socket is loopback-only, anything able to capture the traffic could also read the token, so TLS would add no protection. Each activation generates a fresh random auth token written to `~/.claude/ide/<port>.lock` (0600 in a 0700 directory, or under `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/ide/`), which the CLI must present as the `X-Claude-Code-Ide-Authorization` header.

nodes.label: IDE tools exposed to the model
nodes.rationale: The `ide` server hosts about a dozen tools but only two reach the model: `mcp__ide__getDiagnostics` (read-only; returns language-server diagnostics from VS Code's Problems panel, optionally scoped to one file) and `mcp__ide__executeCode` (not read-only; runs Python in the active Jupyter kernel). The rest are internal RPC the CLI uses for its own UI and are filtered out before the tool list reaches Claude.

nodes.label: Jupyter execution Quick Pick confirmation
nodes.rationale: `mcp__ide__executeCode` cannot run silently: each call inserts the code as a new cell at the end of the active notebook, scrolls it into view, and asks Execute or Cancel in a native Quick Pick, where cancelling or pressing Esc returns an error and runs nothing. It refuses outright with no active notebook, without the `ms-toolsai.jupyter` extension, or on a non-Python kernel — and this confirmation is separate from `PreToolUse` hooks, whose allowlist only lets Claude propose a run.

nodes.label: Spark icon not visible troubleshooting
nodes.rationale: When the Editor Toolbar Spark icon is missing, the documented checks are: open a file (a folder alone is not enough), confirm VS Code 1.94.0+, reload the window, disable conflicting AI extensions such as Cline or Continue, and check workspace trust because the extension does not work in Restricted Mode. The Status Bar entry or the Command Palette are alternatives that work with no file open.

nodes.label: Cmd+Esc intercepted by macOS Game Overlay
nodes.rationale: On macOS Tahoe and later the system Game Overlay shortcut is bound to Cmd+Esc by default and intercepts the keypress before VS Code sees it. The fixes are clearing the Game Overlay checkbox under System Settings → Keyboard → Keyboard Shortcuts → Game Controllers, or rebinding 'Claude Code: Focus input' in VS Code's Keyboard Shortcuts editor.

nodes.label: Uninstalling and auto-reinstall
nodes.rationale: The extension is uninstalled from the Extensions view, but running `claude` in a VS Code integrated terminal reinstalls it automatically unless 'Auto-install IDE extension' is turned off in `/config`, `autoInstallIdeExtension` is set to `false`, or `CLAUDE_CODE_IDE_SKIP_AUTO_INSTALL` is set to `1`. Removing extension data and resetting settings additionally means deleting the platform-specific `globalStorage/anthropic.claude-code` directory.

nodes.label: Claude Code on the web
nodes.rationale: Claude Code on the web runs on cloud infrastructure instead of the user's machine, Anthropic-managed by default. Tasks are submitted from claude.ai/code in a browser or from the Claude mobile app, with no local setup required.

nodes.label: Research preview availability
nodes.rationale: Claude Code on the web is in research preview for Pro, Max, and Team users, and for Enterprise users with premium seats or Chat + Claude Code seats. Plan tier therefore gates access to the whole feature.

nodes.label: Isolated VM clone of the repository
nodes.rationale: Claude clones the connected GitHub repository into an isolated virtual machine, makes changes there, and pushes a branch for review. The repo is cloned fresh every session, so it never needs to be checked out locally.

nodes.label: Sessions persist across devices
nodes.rationale: Sessions persist across devices: a task started on a laptop is ready to review from a phone later. Session state lives with the cloud service rather than with any one client.

nodes.label: Workloads the web fits well
nodes.rationale: Claude Code on the web works well for parallel independent tasks (each in its own session and branch, without managing worktrees), repos not checked out locally, well-defined tasks that need little steering, and codebase questions or exploration.

nodes.label: Local run or Remote Control for local config
nodes.rationale: For work that needs the user's local config, tools, or environment, running Claude Code locally or using Remote Control is the better fit; a cloud session sees the repo only, not local configuration.

nodes.label: Cloud session lifecycle
nodes.rationale: Submitting a task runs four ordered stages: clone and prepare, configure network, work, and push the branch. The described steps are for Anthropic-hosted sessions.

nodes.label: Stage 1 — clone and prepare
nodes.rationale: The repository is cloned to an Anthropic-managed VM and the environment's setup script runs if one is configured.

nodes.label: Stage 2 — configure network
nodes.rationale: Internet access for the session is set based on the cloud environment's configured access level, so network reachability is a property of the environment rather than of the task.

nodes.label: Stage 3 — work
nodes.rationale: Claude analyzes code, makes changes, runs tests, and checks its work. The user can watch and steer throughout, or step away and return when it is done.

nodes.label: Stage 4 — push the branch
nodes.rationale: When Claude reaches a stopping point it pushes its branch to GitHub, and the user reviews the diff, leaves inline comments, creates a PR, or sends another message to continue.

nodes.label: Session stays open after the push
nodes.rationale: The session does not close when the branch is pushed: PR creation and further edits all happen within the same conversation, and the session stays live after the PR is created.

nodes.label: Self-hosted environment variant
nodes.rationale: In a self-hosted environment the clone and everything after it run on the organization's own runners, where network boundaries, setup, and push behavior are operator-configured rather than Anthropic-managed.

nodes.label: Comparison of ways to run Claude Code
nodes.rationale: Claude Code behaves the same everywhere; what changes across web, Remote Control, terminal CLI and the Desktop app is where code executes and whether local config is available. Only the web surface runs on a cloud VM, uses no local config, requires GitHub, and keeps running after disconnect.

nodes.label: Connect GitHub (one-time step)
nodes.rationale: Connecting GitHub is a one-time step done at claude.ai/code (sign in, authorize on GitHub) or from the terminal with the GitHub CLI. Cloud sessions can reach any repository the connected GitHub account can see.

nodes.label: Admin GitHub connector toggle
nodes.rationale: On Team and Enterprise plans, Sign in with GitHub works only after an Owner turns on the GitHub connector at Admin settings > Connectors; until then the step shows 'GitHub access is required for Claude Code on the web' instead of a sign-in button.

nodes.label: Quick web setup toggle
nodes.rationale: Quick web setup is an optional second toggle at Admin settings > Claude Code, off by default on Team and Enterprise. With it on, /web-setup works and onboarding creates the Default environment for members; with it off, /web-setup is hidden and the browser flow must be used.

nodes.label: Claude GitHub App and Auto-fix
nodes.rationale: Installing the Claude GitHub App on repositories is optional and only enables Auto-fix, which lets Claude respond to CI failures and review comments on pull requests. Sessions can reach the same repositories whether or not the App is installed.

nodes.label: Default cloud environment
nodes.rationale: A cloud environment is the saved configuration controlling what network access Claude has during sessions and what runs when a session starts. Pro and Max onboarding creates one named Default automatically; Team and Enterprise show a 'Create your first cloud environment' form unless Quick web setup is on.

nodes.label: Trusted network access level
nodes.rationale: The Default environment uses Trusted network access: sessions reach common package registries and other allowlisted domains and nothing else through the session's network. Trusted covers most package managers; the None level blocks them all.

nodes.label: Environment setup script
nodes.rationale: A setup script is an optional per-environment script that runs before sessions start, after the clone. It is configured by editing the environment, alongside network access and environment variables.

nodes.label: /web-setup CLI command
nodes.rationale: /web-setup runs inside the Claude Code CLI (not the shell) and sets up Claude Code on the web without a browser: it reads the local gh token, links it to the claude.ai account, and creates a Default cloud environment with Trusted access and no setup script if none exists. On success it prints 'Connected as <your-github-username>' and opens claude.ai/code.

nodes.label: GitHub CLI authentication prerequisite
nodes.rationale: The terminal path requires an authenticated GitHub CLI (`gh auth login`). If the GitHub CLI is not installed or not authenticated, Claude Code opens the browser onboarding flow instead.

nodes.label: claude.ai account sign-in requirement
nodes.rationale: The CLI must be signed in with a claude.ai account via /login; authenticating with an API key or a third-party provider does not count. `/status` shows the Login method row for confirmation, and an expired sign-in produces 'Not signed in to Claude. Run /login first.'

nodes.label: Zero Data Retention blocks cloud sessions
nodes.rationale: Organizations with Zero Data Retention enabled cannot use /web-setup or other cloud session features, and Claude Code on the web is unavailable to them entirely.

nodes.label: gh token missing the workflow scope
nodes.rationale: If /web-setup warns the GitHub CLI token lacks the `workflow` scope, setup can continue but GitHub can reject some pushes made with that token, such as pushes that change GitHub Actions workflow files. The fix is `gh auth refresh -s workflow` then re-running /web-setup.

nodes.label: Repository and branch selection
nodes.rationale: A repository is chosen from the selector below the input box at claude.ai/code or in the mobile app Code tab; each repository has a branch selector so Claude can start from a feature branch instead of the default. Multiple repositories can be added to work across them in one session.

nodes.label: Cloud session permission modes
nodes.rationale: Cloud sessions offer three modes: Auto (a classifier reviews Claude's actions instead of asking, shown when the organization allows it and the model supports it), Accept edits (changes and a branch push without stopping for approval), and Plan (Claude proposes an approach and waits for approval before editing). Manual and Bypass are not offered in cloud sessions.

nodes.label: Write a specific task description
nodes.rationale: Task prompts should name the file or function ('Fix the failing auth test in tests/test_auth.py' beats 'fix tests'), paste any error output, and describe the expected behavior rather than only the symptom.

nodes.label: One session and one branch per task
nodes.rationale: Each submitted task gets its own session and its own branch, so one task need not finish before another is started. This is the mechanism behind the parallel-task use case.

nodes.label: Pre-fill sessions via URL query parameters
nodes.rationale: Adding URL-encoded query parameters to the claude.ai/code URL prefills a new session's prompt, repositories and environment — supporting integrations such as an issue-tracker button that opens Claude Code with the issue description as the prompt.

nodes.label: prompt / prompt_url parameters
nodes.rationale: `prompt` (alias `q`) prefills the input box text. `prompt_url` fetches prompt text from a URL for prompts too long to embed in a query string; that URL must allow cross-origin requests, and `prompt_url` is ignored when `prompt` is also set.

nodes.label: repositories and environment parameters
nodes.rationale: `repositories` (alias `repo`) takes a comma-separated list of `owner/repo` slugs to preselect; `environment` takes the name or ID of a cloud environment to preselect.

nodes.label: Session diff view
nodes.rationale: A diff indicator shows lines added and removed across the session (for example `+42 -18`); selecting it opens the diff view, with a file list on the left and changes on the right.

nodes.label: Queued inline diff comments
nodes.rationale: Selecting a line in the diff and typing feedback queues a comment; queued comments are bundled with the next message, so Claude receives location-anchored feedback such as 'at src/auth.ts:47, don't catch the error here' alongside the main instruction.

nodes.label: Create PR from the diff view
nodes.rationale: Create PR at the top of the diff view opens the change as a full PR, a draft, or jumps to GitHub's compose page with a generated title and description.

nodes.label: Iterating after the PR is open
nodes.rationale: After the PR is created the session stays live: CI failure output or reviewer comments can be pasted into the chat for Claude to address. Auto-fix pull requests is the option for having Claude monitor the PR automatically.

nodes.label: Troubleshooting: no repositories appear
nodes.rationale: Repository visibility follows the connected GitHub account, not the Claude GitHub App installation. If a repo is missing, verify the connected account has access on GitHub; private repositories need the same authorization as public ones.

nodes.label: Troubleshooting: /web-setup hidden or unknown
nodes.rationale: 'No commands match' or 'Unknown command: /web-setup' means a requirement is unmet: usually API-key or third-party authentication instead of a claude.ai subscription, but also Quick web setup being off on Team/Enterprise, an administrator disabling Claude Code on the web, or Zero Data Retention. It is also hidden if typed in the shell rather than inside the CLI.

nodes.label: Troubleshooting: cloud environment creation failure
nodes.rationale: 'Could not create a cloud environment' means automatic creation failed; 'No cloud environment available' means the CLI predates automatic creation. Either way the remedy is running /web-setup or adding an environment from the environment selector at claude.ai/code.

nodes.label: Troubleshooting: setup script failed
nodes.rationale: A non-zero setup-script exit blocks the session from starting. Common causes are a package install blocked by the network access level, a reference to a path absent from a fresh clone, or a command needing a different invocation on Ubuntu. Debug with `set -x` at the top, and append `|| true` to non-critical commands.

nodes.label: Five-minute environment cache time budget
nodes.rationale: Sessions that stall on the setup script step or fail with a generic container error usually exceed the roughly five-minute time budget for building the environment cache — typically from pulling large Docker images, syncing full dependency trees, or downloading model weights.

nodes.label: Trimming the setup script under the budget
nodes.rationale: Three mitigations keep the script under five minutes: run independent installs in parallel with `&` plus a final `wait` instead of serially; move the largest downloads into a SessionStart hook that backgrounds them so the session becomes usable while they finish; and remove long retry sleeps, since a stalled retry loop counts against the budget.

nodes.label: Session survives closing the tab
nodes.rationale: By design, closing the tab or navigating away does not stop the session: it keeps running in the background until Claude finishes the current task, then idles. Sessions can be archived to hide them from the list or deleted to remove them permanently.

nodes.label: --cloud sessions and /schedule routines
nodes.rationale: Once /web-setup completes, cloud sessions can be started from the terminal with `--cloud` and recurring work set up with `/schedule` (Routines). `--cloud` also allows bundling a local repository without GitHub.

nodes.label: Claude mobile app monitoring
nodes.rationale: The Claude mobile app for iOS or Android monitors sessions from a phone, and its Code tab can start tasks. From the Claude Code CLI, `/mobile` shows a QR code for installing it.

nodes.label: Routine
nodes.rationale: A routine is a saved Claude Code configuration — a prompt, one or more repositories, and a set of connectors — packaged once and run automatically. Routines execute on Anthropic-managed cloud infrastructure, or on an organization's self-hosted environment when routed there, so they keep working when the laptop is closed. They are available on Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans.

nodes.label: Research preview status
nodes.rationale: Routines are in research preview: behavior, limits, and the API surface may change. During the preview, GitHub webhook events also carry per-routine and per-account hourly caps.

nodes.label: Trigger
nodes.rationale: A routine starts when one of its triggers matches. Any combination of schedule, API, and GitHub triggers can be attached to the same routine, and triggers can be added or removed at any time from the 'Select a trigger' section of the edit form. For example, one PR review routine can run nightly, fire from a deploy script, and react to every new PR.

nodes.label: Schedule trigger
nodes.rationale: A schedule trigger runs the routine on a recurring cadence — hourly, daily, weekdays, or weekly presets — or once at a specific future time.

nodes.label: API trigger
nodes.rationale: An API trigger gives a routine a dedicated HTTP endpoint; POSTing to it with the routine's bearer token starts a new session and returns a session URL. It is used to wire Claude Code into alerting systems, deploy pipelines, and internal tools. API triggers are added to an existing routine from the web only.

nodes.label: GitHub trigger
nodes.rationale: A GitHub trigger starts a new session automatically when a matching event occurs on a connected repository, such as a pull request or a release. It can be configured from the web UI, or from the CLI on Claude Code v2.1.225 or later.

nodes.label: One-off scheduled run
nodes.rationale: A one-off schedule fires the routine a single time at a specific timestamp; afterwards the routine auto-disables and the web UI marks it as 'Ran'. From the CLI the time can be described in natural language and Claude confirms the absolute timestamp before saving.

nodes.label: Custom cron interval
nodes.rationale: For an interval the presets do not cover, such as every two hours or the first of each month, pick the closest preset in the form and then run `/schedule update` in the CLI to set a specific cron expression. The minimum interval is one hour; more frequent expressions are rejected.

nodes.label: Run stagger
nodes.rationale: Runs may start a few minutes after the scheduled time due to stagger, and the offset is consistent for each routine.

nodes.label: Local-to-UTC schedule conversion
nodes.rationale: Times are entered in the user's local zone and converted automatically, so the routine runs at that wall-clock time regardless of where the cloud infrastructure sits. The same conversion applies to one-off timestamps.

nodes.label: /fire endpoint
nodes.rationale: A routine is triggered by POSTing to its per-routine `/fire` endpoint (`https://api.anthropic.com/v1/claude_code/routines/<id>/fire`) with the bearer token in the `Authorization` header. The endpoint is available to claude.ai users only and is not part of the Claude Platform API surface; a wrong routine ID or token fails with a 401.

nodes.label: Per-routine bearer token
nodes.rationale: Each routine has its own token, scoped to triggering that routine only. The token is shown once when generated and cannot be retrieved later, so it must be stored in a secret store; it is rotated or revoked from the same modal with 'Regenerate' or 'Revoke'. The CLI cannot create or revoke tokens.

nodes.label: Fire `text` field
nodes.rationale: The fire request body accepts an optional `text` field carrying run-specific context such as an alert body or a failing log, passed alongside the routine's saved prompt. The value is freeform and is not parsed: structured JSON sent in it arrives as a literal string.

nodes.label: routine-fire-payload wrapper
nodes.rationale: Fire text never reaches the routine as a bare message: it arrives wrapped in a `<routine-fire-payload>` block that labels it as untrusted data and tells Claude not to follow instructions inside it unless the routine's own prompt says to. The same wrapping applies to text supplied with 'Run now' in the web UI.

nodes.label: Prompt opt-in to fire text
nodes.rationale: Because fire text is wrapped as untrusted data, a routine's saved prompt must opt in to acting on it — for example 'Investigate the alert described in the routine-fire-payload block' — or the routine treats the text as inert context.

nodes.label: Leaked-token fire risk
nodes.rationale: Anyone holding a routine's bearer token can send `text` to its endpoint. The payload wrapper exists so that fire text from a leaked token arrives labeled as untrusted data rather than as direct instructions to the routine.

nodes.label: experimental-cc-routine beta header
nodes.rationale: The `/fire` endpoint ships under the `experimental-cc-routine-2026-04-01` beta header. Request and response shapes, rate limits, and token semantics may change; breaking changes ship behind new dated beta header versions, and the two most recent previous header versions keep working so callers can migrate.

nodes.label: routine_fire response body
nodes.rationale: A successful fire returns JSON of type `routine_fire` with `claude_code_session_id` and `claude_code_session_url`; opening that URL shows the run in real time, allows reviewing changes, or continuing the conversation manually.

nodes.label: Cloud environment
nodes.rationale: Each routine uses a cloud environment that controls network access, environment variables, and setup scripts, and the routine inherits the environment's network policy on every run. A 'Default' environment is provided; changing the policy applies from the next run.

nodes.label: Environment network access
nodes.rationale: Network access sets the level of internet access available during each run — Trusted (default allowlist), Custom (your own allowed domains), or Full (unrestricted). It is edited in the 'Update cloud environment' dialog reached from the routine's environment selector.

nodes.label: Trusted access default allowlist
nodes.rationale: The Default environment uses Trusted network access, which allows only a default allowlist of package registries, cloud provider APIs, container registries, and common development domains. Requests on that path to hosts outside the allowlist fail with `403` and `x-deny-reason: host_not_allowed`.

nodes.label: Custom allowed domains
nodes.rationale: To reach your own services or a domain outside the default list, set Network access to Custom and enter domains in 'Allowed domains'; checking 'Also include default list of common package managers' keeps the default allowlist alongside the custom entries.

nodes.label: API credentials over env vars
nodes.rationale: Keys for APIs Claude calls during a run should be stored as environment API credentials rather than as environment variables, because variables are visible to anyone who uses the environment. The credentials documentation also lists the requests that never get a credential.

nodes.label: Environment variables
nodes.rationale: An environment can provide variables Claude can use during each run, but they are visible to anyone who uses that environment, so they are the wrong place for secrets.

nodes.label: Environment setup script
nodes.rationale: A setup script installs the dependencies and tools the routine needs; its result is cached, so the script does not re-run on every session.

nodes.label: MCP connectors in a routine
nodes.rationale: Routines can use the account's connected MCP connectors to read from and write to external services during each run — for example reading a Slack channel and creating Linear issues. All currently connected connectors are included by default when a routine is created, and any that are not needed should be removed.

nodes.label: Connector traffic via Anthropic servers
nodes.rationale: MCP connector traffic is routed through Anthropic's servers rather than through the session's network path, so connectors added to a routine work without adding their hosts to the environment's Allowed domains.

nodes.label: Local CLI MCP servers are excluded
nodes.rationale: MCP servers added locally in the CLI with `claude mcp add` are stored on the machine rather than the claude.ai account, so they never appear in the connectors list. To use one in a routine, add it as a connector at claude.ai/customize/connectors or declare it in a committed `.mcp.json` inside the cloned repository.

nodes.label: Routine repositories
nodes.rationale: A routine names one or more GitHub repositories, each cloned on every run starting from the default branch unless the prompt says otherwise. Routines need GitHub access to clone; `/schedule` checks whether the account has access to the repository it was run from and adds a setup note naming how to grant it if not.

nodes.label: Branch push rejection rules
nodes.rationale: When a prompt directs Claude to push to a branch other than a `claude/` one, Claude Code checks the push first and rejects it if the branch is protected on GitHub, if someone else has an open pull request from that branch, or if the branch carries commits authored by someone other than you.

nodes.label: claude/-prefixed branches
nodes.rationale: Claude pushes its work to branches prefixed with `claude/`, and those pushes are always accepted.

nodes.label: Autonomous run model
nodes.rationale: Routines run autonomously as full Claude Code cloud sessions: there is no permission-mode picker and no approval prompts during a run. The session can run shell commands, use skills committed to the cloned repository, and call any included connector — including its write tools — without asking.

nodes.label: Scope repos, environment, connectors
nodes.rationale: What a routine can reach is determined by the repositories selected, the environment's network access and variables, and the connectors included — so each of those should be scoped to what the routine actually needs.

nodes.label: Routines belong to one account
nodes.rationale: Routines belong to an individual claude.ai account, are not shared with teammates, and count against that account's daily run allowance.

nodes.label: Actions appear as you
nodes.rationale: Anything a routine does through the connected GitHub identity or connectors appears as the owner: commits and pull requests carry your GitHub user, and Slack messages, Linear tickets, or other connector actions use your linked accounts.

nodes.label: /schedule CLI command
nodes.rationale: `/schedule` (alias `/routines`) creates a scheduled routine conversationally from any session, optionally with a description such as `/schedule daily PR review at 9am`. Claude walks through the same information the web form collects, asking follow-up questions before saving to the account.

nodes.label: CLI routine management
nodes.rationale: `/schedule list` shows all routines, `/schedule update` changes one, and `/schedule run` triggers it immediately. Claude can also explain run history — listing recent runs with status and links, and reading a run's log to report tool errors, permission denials, and the final result (requires v2.1.227 or later).

nodes.label: claude.ai/code/routines web UI
nodes.rationale: The web page at claude.ai/code/routines is where routines are created and managed, where API triggers and tokens are added, and where current consumption and remaining daily routine runs are shown. Routines can be managed there regardless of how the CLI is configured, unless organization policy disables routines or Claude Code on the web.

nodes.label: Three creation surfaces
nodes.rationale: A routine can be created from the web, from the Desktop app's Code tab, or from the CLI. All three surfaces write to the same cloud account, so a routine created in one shows up in the others immediately.

nodes.label: Desktop scheduled task (Local)
nodes.rationale: In the Desktop app, choosing 'Local' instead of 'Cloud' creates a Desktop scheduled task, which runs on your machine with access to local files rather than in the cloud.

nodes.label: Supported GitHub events
nodes.rationale: GitHub triggers subscribe to two event categories: Pull request (opened, closed, assigned, labeled, synchronized, or otherwise updated) and Release (created, published, edited, or deleted). Within a category you can pick a specific action such as `pull_request.opened` or react to all actions.

nodes.label: Pull request filters
nodes.rationale: Filters narrow which pull requests start a session, and all filter conditions must match. Fields are author, title, body, base branch, head branch, labels, is draft, and is merged; each pairs with an operator: equals, contains, starts with, is one of, is not one of, or matches regex.

nodes.label: matches regex is a full-value match
nodes.rationale: The `matches regex` operator tests the entire field value, not a substring: matching any title containing `hotfix` requires `.*hotfix.*`, since bare `hotfix` matches only a title that is exactly that. For literal substring matching, use `contains` instead.

nodes.label: GitHub webhook hourly caps
nodes.rationale: During the research preview, GitHub webhook events are subject to per-routine and per-account hourly caps; events beyond the limit are dropped until the window resets. Current limits are shown at claude.ai/code/routines.

nodes.label: Claude GitHub App requirement
nodes.rationale: The Claude GitHub App must be installed on the repository being subscribed to, whichever surface the trigger is configured from. The web UI prompts to install it when missing; from the CLI it must be installed from the GitHub App page first.

nodes.label: /web-setup does not enable webhooks
nodes.rationale: Running `/web-setup` in the CLI grants repository access for cloning, but it does not install the Claude GitHub App and does not enable webhook delivery.

nodes.label: One session per event
nodes.rationale: Claude Code does not reuse sessions across GitHub events, so two updates to the same pull request produce two independent sessions.

nodes.label: Run session
nodes.rationale: Each run creates a new session alongside your other sessions where you can see what Claude did, review changes, and create a pull request. Run sessions behave like any other session and can be renamed, archived, or deleted; past sessions survive deleting the routine.

nodes.label: Green status is not task success
nodes.rationale: A green status in the run list means only that the session started and exited without an infrastructure error — not that the task in the prompt succeeded. Blocked network requests, missing connector tools, and task-level failures surface in the transcript rather than in the status indicator.

nodes.label: Run now
nodes.rationale: 'Run now' on the routine's detail page starts a run immediately without waiting for the next scheduled time, and can optionally supply run-specific text that reaches the routine the same way as the API trigger's `text` field.

nodes.label: Pause and resume a schedule
nodes.rationale: The toggle in the 'Repeats' section pauses or resumes the schedule; paused routines keep their configuration but do not run until re-enabled.

nodes.label: Routine detail page controls
nodes.rationale: The detail page shows a routine's repositories, connectors, prompt, schedule, API tokens, GitHub triggers, and past runs, and offers Run now, pause/resume, the pencil icon to edit name, prompt, repositories, environment, connectors and triggers, and a delete icon.

nodes.label: Daily routine run cap
nodes.rationale: Routines draw down subscription usage like interactive sessions, and additionally have a daily cap on how many runs can start per account. Consumption and remaining daily runs are visible at claude.ai/code/routines or claude.ai/settings/usage.

nodes.label: Usage credits / metered overage
nodes.rationale: When a routine hits the daily cap or the subscription usage limit, organizations with usage credits turned on can keep running routines on metered overage; without credits, additional runs are rejected until the window resets. Admins enable them for Team and Enterprise organizations.

nodes.label: Routine prompt
nodes.rationale: The saved prompt is what Claude runs each time a trigger fires and is described as the most important part of the routine.

nodes.label: Self-contained prompt requirement
nodes.rationale: Because the routine runs autonomously with no one to answer questions, the prompt must be self-contained and explicit about what to do and what success looks like.

nodes.label: Saved prompt is an assigned task
nodes.rationale: When a trigger fires, the session receives the saved prompt as its assigned task rather than as untrusted content arriving mid-conversation. The trigger attests only that the prompt was stored ahead of time by an authorized session, so the fired prompt is not live user input and cannot act as approval or consent during the run; content fetched during the run keeps its normal handling. Before v2.1.213 the prompt was framed as an untrusted background notification and Claude could refuse to act on it.

nodes.label: Per-routine model selector
nodes.rationale: The prompt input includes a model selector, and Claude uses the selected model on every run of that routine.

nodes.label: Organization Routines toggle
nodes.rationale: Team and Enterprise Owners can disable routines for all members with the Routines toggle in admin settings; when disabled, existing routines stop running and members cannot create new ones. It is a server-side organization setting that cannot be overridden locally, and on v2.1.227 or later it also hides `/schedule` in the CLI.

nodes.label: /schedule 'Unknown command'
nodes.rationale: The CLI hides `/schedule` when a requirement is unmet, showing 'No commands match' while typing and 'Unknown command: /schedule' on submit. Causes include a Console API key or Anthropic profile/federation credential, a cloud-provider login (Bedrock, Google Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry), being inside a Claude Code on the web session, org policy disabling Claude Code on the web, or an Owner having turned routines off.

nodes.label: claude.ai subscription login requirement
nodes.rationale: `/schedule` requires a claude.ai subscription login; API accounts are not supported for routines. `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, an `apiKeyHelper` in settings.json, or a profile/federation credential take precedence over a claude.ai login and must be removed or switched off first, then `/login`.

nodes.label: Example routine use cases
nodes.rationale: Routines suit unattended, repeatable work tied to a clear outcome: nightly backlog maintenance via a tracker connector, alert triage fired by a monitoring tool's API call, bespoke code review on `pull_request.opened`, deploy verification called by a CD pipeline, weekly docs-drift PRs, and porting a merged SDK change to a parallel SDK repository.

nodes.label: Week 34 digest (Aug 17-21, 2026)
nodes.rationale: The Claude Code what's-new digest for Week 34 (August 17-21, 2026) covering three headline features plus a list of smaller wins: draft editable UI artboards with the /design skill, set the Concise output style, and start a Claude Code session on your machine from your phone.

nodes.label: Releases v2.1.234 -> v2.1.239
nodes.rationale: The week's changes span Claude Code releases v2.1.234 through v2.1.239, with a link to the full changelog for that range.

nodes.label: /design skill (research preview)
nodes.rationale: The /design skill, shipped as a research preview, brings Claude Design's artboard workflow into the Claude Code CLI and Claude Code Desktop. You run it with a brief (e.g. `/design redesign the composer based on what people actually use it for`), Claude prints a link to a published canvas, and you pick an artboard for Claude to implement.

nodes.label: Published canvas of editable artboards
nodes.rationale: Running /design makes Claude publish a canvas of editable artboards for your UI. Claude prints a link to that canvas; you open it, tweak an artboard, then tell Claude which option to implement.

nodes.label: Artifacts as the /design foundation
nodes.rationale: The /design artboard workflow is built on artifacts, so where the canvas can be published follows artifact availability; the digest links to the artifacts availability documentation.

nodes.label: /design availability and version floor
nodes.rationale: The /design skill is available on Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans and requires Claude Code v2.1.234 or later.

nodes.label: Concise output style (v2.1.237)
nodes.rationale: Concise is a new built-in output style shipped in v2.1.237: Claude leads with the result and skips preamble and narration while doing the work as thoroughly as in the Default style, and answers in full when you ask for an explanation or more detail.

nodes.label: Concise style content carve-outs
nodes.rationale: Under the Concise output style, error reports, security warnings, and confirmations for destructive actions keep their complete content rather than being shortened.

nodes.label: Setting the output style
nodes.rationale: Concise is turned on under Output style in /config, or by setting `"outputStyle": "Concise"` in ~/.claude/settings.json; running /clear or starting a new session makes replies lead with the result.

nodes.label: Remote Control (`claude remote-control`)
nodes.rationale: Running `claude remote-control` on a machine makes it reachable from the Claude app, so a session can be started on that machine from a phone. It is the transport behind the device card and the phone-side session controls described this week.

nodes.label: Remote Control out of research preview
nodes.rationale: Remote Control graduated out of research preview during Week 34, alongside the new device-card entry point in the Claude app.

nodes.label: Device card in the Code tab
nodes.rationale: Any machine running `claude remote-control` now appears as a device card at the top of the Code tab in the Claude mobile app; tapping it lets you pick a directory and start a session there.

nodes.label: Other wins list
nodes.rationale: Beyond the three headline features, the Week 34 digest lists a grid of smaller improvements spanning usage-limit continuation, prompt input, GitLab, Remote Control, permissions, /goal, model defaults, cross-session messaging, keybindings, and self-hosted runners.

nodes.label: Auto-continue at usage-limit reset
nodes.rationale: Claude Code now continues your session automatically when a claude.ai usage limit resets; it can be turned off from the 'Continue automatically at usage limit' row in /config.

nodes.label: spellcheck setting
nodes.rationale: The optional `spellcheck` setting underlines misspelled words in the prompt input as you type.

nodes.label: aspell / hunspell / ispell backends
nodes.rationale: Spellchecking in the prompt input uses your own installed `aspell`, `hunspell`, or `ispell` binary rather than a bundled dictionary.

nodes.label: GitLab `MR !N` footer badge
nodes.rationale: On a branch with an open GitLab merge request, the footer shows an `MR !N` badge colored by whether the merge request is a draft, open, or mergeable.

nodes.label: Authenticated `glab` CLI
nodes.rationale: The GitLab merge-request badge depends on the `glab` CLI being authenticated through `glab auth login`.

nodes.label: Effort level and permission mode from a connected device
nodes.rationale: Changing the effort level from your phone or claude.ai/code applies to the session running on your machine; Remote Control sessions hosted by Desktop or VS Code also show connected devices the session's current permission mode.

nodes.label: /permissions and /add-dir mid-turn
nodes.rationale: You can open /permissions or run `/add-dir <path>` while Claude is working, and permission rule changes apply to the rest of the current turn.

nodes.label: /goal background-task check-ins
nodes.rationale: When background tasks keep a /goal waiting, Claude checks in on them after 30 minutes instead of waiting indefinitely and keeps checking in at longer intervals while the session sits idle; setting CLAUDE_CODE_GOAL_CHECKIN_MINUTES=0 opts out.

nodes.label: Markdown rendering for your own prompts
nodes.rationale: Your own prompts now render markdown in the transcript — highlighted code blocks, inline code, and lists — the same way Claude's replies do.

nodes.label: ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL
nodes.rationale: The new ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL environment variable sets the model new sessions start on; an explicit /model pick still overrides it and persists across restarts.

nodes.label: Cross-session messaging
nodes.rationale: Claude Code sessions on the same machine can message each other with SendMessage and find each other with ListAgents; Week 34 extends both the mechanism's inputs and the platforms it runs on.

nodes.label: notify_when_idle on SendMessage
nodes.rationale: With the `notify_when_idle` input on SendMessage, Claude can ask another Claude Code session on the same machine to send one notice when it next goes idle.

nodes.label: Cross-session messaging on native Windows
nodes.rationale: On native Windows, Claude Code sessions can now message each other with SendMessage and find each other with ListAgents, as they already could on macOS and Linux.

nodes.label: keybindingFlavor: readline
nodes.rationale: Setting `keybindingFlavor` to `"readline"` makes Ctrl+W in the prompt delete back to the previous whitespace, as Bash does, instead of stopping at punctuation such as `/`.

nodes.label: Self-hosted runner deployment flags
nodes.rationale: Self-hosted runners gained two new deployment flags in Week 34, one governing drain behaviour after SIGTERM and one supplying credentials to an egress proxy.

nodes.label: --defer-shutdown-max-min
nodes.rationale: Self-hosted runners accept `--defer-shutdown-max-min`, which keeps serving attached sessions for a set number of minutes after SIGTERM instead of draining on the first signal.

nodes.label: --proxy-authorization-command / --proxy-authorization-file
nodes.rationale: Self-hosted runners accept `--proxy-authorization-command` or `--proxy-authorization-file` to supply a fresh `Proxy-Authorization` header for egress proxies that require one.

nodes.label: Dynamic workflow
nodes.rationale: A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates many subagents at once: Claude writes the script for the task you describe, and a runtime executes it in the background while your session stays responsive. Reach for one when a task needs more agents than one conversation can coordinate, or when you want the orchestration codified as a script you can read and rerun.

nodes.label: Plan and platform availability
nodes.rationale: Dynamic workflows are available on all paid plans, with Anthropic API access, and on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry. On Pro they must be turned on from the Dynamic workflows row in /config.

nodes.label: Who holds the plan (primitive comparison)
nodes.rationale: Subagents, skills, agent teams and workflows can all run a multi-step task; the difference is who holds the plan, where intermediate results live, what is repeatable, the scale, and what an interruption does. With the first three Claude is the orchestrator deciding turn by turn; with a workflow the script decides.

nodes.label: Subagents
nodes.rationale: A subagent is a worker Claude spawns; Claude decides turn by turn what runs next, intermediate results land in Claude's context window, the worker definition is what is repeatable, scale is a few delegated tasks per turn, and an interruption restarts the turn. Subagents are the worker primitive that workflows orchestrate.

nodes.label: Skills as an orchestration primitive
nodes.rationale: A skill is instructions Claude follows: Claude decides what runs next by following the prompt, results live in Claude's context window, the instructions are what is repeatable, scale matches subagents, and an interruption restarts the turn.

nodes.label: Agent teams
nodes.rationale: An agent team is a lead agent supervising peer sessions: the lead decides turn by turn, intermediate results live in a shared task list, the team definition is what is repeatable, scale is a handful of long-running peers, and teammates keep running through an interruption.

nodes.label: The plan moves into code
nodes.rationale: A workflow script holds the loop, the branching, and the intermediate results itself, so Claude's context holds only the final answer. That is the structural difference from subagents, skills and agent teams, where every result lands in a context window.

nodes.label: Repeatable quality pattern
nodes.rationale: Moving the plan into code lets a workflow apply a repeatable quality pattern, not just run more agents: independent agents can adversarially review each other's findings before they are reported, or draft a plan from several angles and weigh them against each other, giving a more trustworthy result than a single pass.

nodes.label: /deep-research bundled workflow
nodes.rationale: /deep-research is the built-in workflow Claude Code ships: it fans out web searches on a question across several angles, fetches and cross-checks the sources it finds, votes on each claim, and returns a cited report with claims that did not survive cross-checking filtered out. It requires the WebSearch tool to be available and runs only when explicitly invoked.

nodes.label: Unverified vs refuted claims
nodes.rationale: When the verifier agents cannot check a claim — for example after a rate limit or an API error — the report lists that claim as unverified instead of counting it as refuted. A failure to ask is reported distinctly from an answered no.

nodes.label: /workflows run manager
nodes.rationale: Running /workflows at any time lists running and completed workflows; selecting one with the arrow keys and pressing Enter opens its progress view. It is also where a run is paused, resumed, stopped, and where a run's script is saved as a command.

nodes.label: Run progress view
nodes.rationale: The progress view shows each phase with its agent count, token total, and elapsed time, and lets you drill into a phase to see its agents and what each one found. It also surfaces a warning naming both the requested and the substituted model when an allowlist blocks a script-requested model.

nodes.label: Progress view keybindings
nodes.rationale: Arrows select a phase or agent, Enter or the right arrow drills in, Esc or the left arrow backs out, j/k scroll agent detail, f cycles a status filter, p pauses or resumes the run, x stops the selected agent or the whole workflow, r restarts a running agent, and s saves the run's script as a command. In v2.1.203 through v2.1.205 the left arrow did not step back out, so Esc is required on those versions.

nodes.label: Task panel progress line
nodes.rationale: A one-line progress summary for a running workflow appears in the task panel below the input box; the down arrow focuses it and Enter expands it. A run can also be managed from there instead of from /workflows.

nodes.label: ultracode keyword opt-in
nodes.rationale: Including the keyword `ultracode` in a prompt runs that single task as a workflow without changing the session's effort level; asking in your own words ("use a workflow") counts as the same opt-in. Before v2.1.160 the literal trigger keyword was `workflow`, while natural-language requests work in both versions.

nodes.label: Keyword changes structure, not permissions
nodes.rationale: The keyword only chooses how Claude structures the work: the agents' tool calls receive the same permission checks and sandboxing as any other tool call in the session.

nodes.label: Dismiss or disable the keyword
nodes.rationale: An unintended trigger is dismissed for the current prompt with Option+W on macOS or Alt+W on Windows and Linux, or by pressing backspace with the cursor right after the highlighted keyword. Turning off the Ultracode keyword trigger in /config stops it firing at all.

nodes.label: Keyword works only on human-typed input
nodes.rationale: The keyword is an opt-in only in a prompt you type yourself — the interactive prompt, an IDE extension panel, a Remote Control client, or an Agent SDK application that stamps the input's origin as { kind: "human" }. It does not start a workflow from a -p prompt, an unstamped SDK prompt, a scheduled task, or a webhook payload or pull request comment relayed into the conversation; before v2.1.210 all of those routes did trigger it.

nodes.label: ultracode effort level
nodes.rationale: Ultracode combines xhigh reasoning effort with automatic workflow orchestration, so Claude plans a workflow for each substantive task instead of waiting to be asked, and a single request can turn into several workflows in a row. Set it with /effort ultracode (session-scoped), claude --effort ultracode, the /model picker's effort slider, or the persistent `ultracode` setting; it requires v2.1.203 or later and only appears on models that support xhigh effort.

nodes.label: Per-run approval prompt
nodes.rationale: In the CLI the per-run prompt shows the planned phases with four options: run it, run it and don't ask again for that named workflow in that project, view the raw script, or cancel. Ctrl+G opens the script in your editor and Tab lets you adjust the prompt before the run starts; the don't-ask-again option is offered only for a bundled, saved or plugin workflow invoked by name, not for a script Claude wrote for the current task.

nodes.label: Prompting by permission mode
nodes.rationale: Auto mode prompts on first launch only, records any Yes as consent in user settings, and skips the prompt entirely when ultracode is on. Manual and accept-edits prompt on every run unless don't-ask-again was chosen for that workflow in that project, while bypass-permissions mode, claude -p and the Agent SDK never prompt.

nodes.label: Headless and SDK permission evaluation
nodes.rationale: In claude -p and the Agent SDK the Workflow tool call goes through the same permission evaluation as every other tool call, so deny rules, ask rules and dontAsk mode apply to the launch. A workflow can be allowed to start there by a `Workflow` or `Workflow(<name>)` allow rule, auto permission mode's classifier, bypass-permissions mode, a PreToolUse hook returning allow, or the host via --permission-prompt-tool, a canUseTool callback, or a PermissionRequest hook.

nodes.label: Desktop approval card
nodes.rationale: In the Desktop app an approval card shows the workflow name, the phase list, and a token-usage caution, with Once, Always and Deny actions; the run's progress view then appears in the Background tasks side pane.

nodes.label: Permissions of spawned workflow agents
nodes.rationale: The subagents a workflow spawns use your permission rules, and Claude Code picks their permission mode by the ordinary subagent rules. Adding the tools those agents need to your allow rules before starting avoids prompts on a long run.

nodes.label: Save a run's script as a command
nodes.rationale: Running /workflows, selecting a run and pressing s saves that run's script as a command; Tab toggles between the project location .claude/workflows/ (shared with everyone who clones the repo) and the personal ~/.claude/workflows/ (every project, visible only to you, relocated by CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR). The saved workflow then runs as /<name> in future sessions and appears in / autocomplete alongside bundled ones.

nodes.label: Symlink check on save
nodes.rationale: Claude Code checks the save location for symlinks and errors rather than writing through one: for the project location it refuses if .claude, .claude/workflows, or the target file is a symlink; for the personal location only if the target file itself is, so a dotfiles-managed ~/.claude still works. Before v2.1.216 it followed the link, which could place the file outside the chosen location.

nodes.label: Monorepo workflow resolution
nodes.rationale: As of v2.1.178, saving to the project location writes to the closest existing .claude/workflows/ between the working directory and the repository root, or to the repository root if none exists. Project workflows load from every .claude/workflows/ along that path, the one closest to the working directory wins on a name collision, and a project workflow beats a personal workflow of the same name.

nodes.label: Distribute a workflow in a plugin
nodes.rationale: To share a workflow across teams or repositories, include it in a plugin: place the script in a workflows/ directory at the plugin root, or point elsewhere with the plugin manifest's `workflows` field. Plugin workflows are namespaced by plugin name, so a script whose meta.name is release-audit inside plugin acme-tools runs as /acme-tools:release-audit.

nodes.label: args input to a saved workflow
nodes.rationale: A saved workflow accepts input through the `args` parameter, read inside the script as a global named `args`, so a research question, a list of target paths, or a configuration object is supplied at invocation time instead of by editing the script. Claude passes the value as structured data usable directly with array and object methods, and the global is undefined when args is omitted.

nodes.label: Example workflow prompt shapes
nodes.rationale: A workflow fits best when a task is larger than one agent can hold in context or the same step must run across many items. The documented shapes are: audit many files for one issue with adversarial verification, keep fixing until a check passes, migrate many files in parallel, review every changed file then merge findings into one ranked summary, research a topic across many sources, and search in rounds until the finding list stops growing.

nodes.label: Per-file isolated copies in a migration
nodes.rationale: A parallel migration workflow discovers the files to migrate, transforms each one in an isolated copy so concurrent edits do not conflict, and verifies each result.

nodes.label: Convergence stop condition
