nodes.rationale: Iterative workflow prompts carry an explicit termination rule rather than looping forever: keep fixing until the type check passes or two rounds in a row make no progress, and keep searching in rounds until two rounds in a row turn up nothing new.

nodes.label: Saved script shape
nodes.rationale: A saved workflow file in .claude/workflows/ holds an `export const meta` block with a name and description, followed by a script body of plain JavaScript with top-level await that orchestrates subagents and returns a result.

nodes.label: agent(), pipeline(), parallel()
nodes.rationale: The script body's orchestration primitives are agent(), which spawns one subagent and can take an output schema and a label; pipeline(), which runs one agent per item in a list; and parallel(), which runs a set of agent tasks at the same time and waits for all of them.

nodes.label: agent() resolves null on stop or fatal error
nodes.rationale: An agent() call resolves to null if you stop it mid-run or it hits an unrecoverable API error, and pipeline() keeps that null in its results array — which is why the documented example ends with .filter(Boolean) to drop those entries.

nodes.label: /workflow-authoring skill
nodes.rationale: Before editing a saved workflow or asking Claude to change one, run the bundled /workflow-authoring skill to load the script-writing reference Claude works from; it requires Claude Code v2.1.248 or later. To run an edited version in the current session, /reload-skills re-reads the workflow directories before running /<name> again.

nodes.label: meta block rules
nodes.rationale: `export const meta` must be the first statement and a plain object literal carrying a name and a description. If it contains anything other than literal values — a variable, a function call, a spread — Claude Code drops /<name> from / autocomplete.

nodes.label: Script body rules
nodes.rationale: Besides agent(), pipeline() and parallel(), the body may call phase() to group the agents that follow under a title in the progress view, log() to show a message above the phases, and read the args global. A syntax error in the body is reported when the workflow is run.

nodes.label: phases entries must match phase() titles
nodes.rationale: If phases are listed in meta, each entry must carry exactly the title passed to phase(); a phase() title with no matching entry gets a progress group of its own.

nodes.label: Timestamps and randomness throw
nodes.rationale: Claude Code makes Date.now(), Math.random() and a no-argument new Date() throw inside a workflow script, so that a relaunched run repeats the same agent() calls. A timestamp a script needs must be passed in through args.

nodes.label: Isolated workflow runtime
nodes.rationale: The workflow runtime executes the script in an isolated environment, separate from the conversation, with intermediate results staying in script variables instead of landing in Claude's context. It also enforces the run's behavioural constraints and tracks each agent's result as the run progresses.

nodes.label: Per-run script file
nodes.rationale: Every run writes its script to a file under the session's directory in ~/.claude/projects/, and Claude receives the path when the run starts, so the file can be read, diffed against a previous run's script, or edited and relaunched from.

nodes.label: Script must be readable by the session
nodes.rationale: Claude can start a workflow only from a script file the session is already allowed to read; running a script kept outside the working directory requires adding its directory with /add-dir or granting a Read allow rule first.

nodes.label: Per-agent result tracking
nodes.rationale: The runtime tracks each agent's result as the run progresses, and that saved-result record is what makes a run resumable within the same session.

nodes.label: Shared prompt cache across fan-out agents
nodes.rationale: Agents in the same run can read each other's prompt cache: two agents sharing model, effort level, agent type, tools, output schema and working directory build the same tools-and-system-prompt prefix, so an agent starting after a matching sibling's response has begun reads that sibling's cache on its first request.

nodes.label: Workflow agent cache TTL
nodes.rationale: A workflow agent's requests fall outside the main conversation's cache TTL bucket, so its cache holds for five minutes by default, including on a Claude subscription. Setting subagentPromptCacheTtl to 1h keeps it for an hour, and the API bills 1-hour cache writes at a higher rate.

nodes.label: Fan-out prefix stagger
nodes.rationale: When a fan-out starts several matching agents at once, Claude Code holds all but the first until the first agent's response begins, then releases the held agents together so their first requests read the shared prefix instead of each processing it uncached. The hold is capped by CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_PREFIX_STAGGER_MS, 5000 ms by default, and 0 disables it.

nodes.label: No mid-run user input
nodes.rationale: A run takes no mid-run user input; only agent permission prompts can pause it. For sign-off between stages, each stage must be run as its own workflow.

nodes.label: No direct filesystem or shell access
nodes.rationale: The workflow script itself has no direct filesystem or shell access: agents read, write and run commands, while the script only coordinates the agents.

nodes.label: No module loading
nodes.rationale: A script containing import() fails before the run starts: the body is plain JavaScript with no module loading, so work that needs a library belongs inside an agent's task.

nodes.label: 16 concurrent agents
nodes.rationale: The runtime allows up to 16 concurrent agents, and fewer when Claude Code has fewer CPUs available, including inside a CPU-limited container. The cap exists to bound local resource use.

nodes.label: 4,096 items per parallel/pipeline call
nodes.rationale: A single parallel() or pipeline() call accepts at most 4,096 items and the runtime rejects a longer list with an error, because a silent cap would drop part of the workload without telling the script.

nodes.label: 1,000 agents per run
nodes.rationale: A single run may spawn at most 1,000 agents in total, a cap that prevents runaway loops and bounds the cost of a runaway script.

nodes.label: Resume and replay semantics
nodes.rationale: On relaunch Claude Code replays the run in the order agents started: a completed agent returns its saved result, but the first agent whose prompt differs from the previous run re-runs and so does every agent after it; an agent still running when you stopped starts over; a failed agent re-runs along with everything that started after it, and stopping one agent alone counts as failing. So a mid-fan-out failure reruns work that already finished.

nodes.label: Leaving the session with a run in flight
nodes.rationale: Backgrounding the session replays and continues the run in the background session; exiting with agent view on offers 'Move to background and exit' which carries the run over, while 'Exit and stop tasks' (or no such option) stops the run with the session. Saved results are kept under that session's directory in ~/.claude/projects/, so a session resumed with claude --resume can replay them while a fresh session has nothing to replay and starts the workflow over.

nodes.label: Workflow cost
nodes.rationale: A workflow spawns many agents, so a single run can use meaningfully more tokens than working through the same task in conversation, and runs count toward the plan's usage and rate limits like any other session. To gauge spend before a large task, run the workflow on a small slice first; the /workflows view shows each agent's token usage and the run can be stopped there, usually without losing completed work.

nodes.label: Large workflow warning
nodes.rationale: When a workflow schedules more than 25 agents, or its projected token total passes 1.5 million, its progress line in the task panel shows a 'Large workflow' warning pointing to /workflows. The warning is advisory and neither pauses nor limits the run; a chosen size guideline's agent count replaces the 25-agent threshold, and ultracode sessions do not show it at all.

nodes.label: Workflow agent model selection
nodes.rationale: Claude Code picks each workflow agent's model in the same order it uses for subagents, with a model the script names for a stage counting as the per-invocation model and the session's model used when nothing else assigns one. When an organization's availableModels allowlist blocks a requested model, the agent runs on a substituted model and the progress view warns, naming both.

nodes.label: Dynamic workflow size guideline
nodes.rationale: The size guideline tells Claude how many agents to aim for when writing a workflow — unrestricted, small (<5), medium (<15), large (<50) — and is sent as advice, not a cap, so a prompt calling for a different scale overrides it. The default is medium (v2.1.219+; earlier versions default to unrestricted), it is set in /config, via /config workflowSizeGuideline=small, or by the workflowSizeGuideline settings key which takes precedence and hides the /config row, and changes take effect on the next prompt.

nodes.label: Turning workflows off
nodes.rationale: Workflows are disabled for yourself by toggling Dynamic workflows off in /config, setting "disableWorkflows": true in ~/.claude/settings.json, or setting CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_WORKFLOWS=1 (read at startup); organization-wide it is the same key in managed settings or the admin settings toggle. When disabled, the bundled workflow commands and the /workflow-authoring skill are unavailable, the ultracode keyword no longer triggers a run, and ultracode is removed from the /effort menu.

nodes.label: Surfaces where workflows run
nodes.rationale: Workflows are available in the CLI, the Desktop app, the IDE extensions, non-interactive mode with claude -p, and the Agent SDK, and the same disable settings apply on every surface.

nodes.label: Zero Data Retention (ZDR)
nodes.rationale: Zero Data Retention for Claude Code means prompts and model responses generated during Claude Code sessions are processed in real time and not stored by Anthropic after the response is returned, except where needed to comply with law or combat misuse.

nodes.label: Claude for Enterprise plan
nodes.rationale: Claude for Enterprise is the plan on which ZDR for Claude Code is offered to qualified accounts. ZDR is not part of the standard Claude for Enterprise plan and cannot be turned on from admin settings.

nodes.label: Separate enablement by Anthropic
nodes.rationale: ZDR is available only to qualified accounts and requires separate enablement by Anthropic; an organization that requires ZDR must contact sales or its Anthropic account team to confirm eligibility.

nodes.label: Administrative capabilities under ZDR
nodes.rationale: ZDR on Claude for Enterprise gives customers zero data retention plus administrative capabilities: per-user cost controls, the Analytics dashboard, server-managed settings, and audit logs.

nodes.label: Anthropic direct platform only
nodes.rationale: ZDR for Claude Code on Claude for Enterprise applies only to Anthropic's direct platform. Deployments on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry are governed by those platforms' own data retention policies.

nodes.label: ZDR scope
nodes.rationale: The scope of ZDR is Claude Code inference on Claude for Enterprise: which requests, which organizations, and which platform surfaces the guarantee reaches.

nodes.label: Per-organization enablement
nodes.rationale: ZDR is enabled on a per-organization basis and does not automatically apply to new organizations created under the same account; each new organization must be enabled separately by the Anthropic account team.

nodes.label: Routing traffic to the ZDR organization
nodes.rationale: ZDR applies only to requests that authenticate into a ZDR-enabled organization. Sessions where a developer signs in with a personal account, or with an API key from a different organization, are not covered.

nodes.label: forceLoginMethod and forceLoginOrgUUID managed settings
nodes.rationale: Deploying the forceLoginMethod and forceLoginOrgUUID managed settings is how an admin requires developers' claude.ai logins to belong to the ZDR organization, per the Restrict login to your organization guidance.

nodes.label: Covered: Claude Code model inference
nodes.rationale: ZDR covers model inference calls made through Claude Code on Claude for Enterprise: prompts sent from the terminal and the responses Claude generates are not retained, across every model available to the ZDR organization.

nodes.label: Surfaces ZDR does not cover
nodes.rationale: Even for ZDR-enabled organizations, a defined set of surfaces stays outside ZDR and continues to follow standard data retention policies.

nodes.label: Chat on claude.ai (not covered)
nodes.rationale: Chat conversations held through the Claude for Enterprise web interface are not covered by ZDR.

nodes.label: Cowork sessions (not covered)
nodes.rationale: Cowork sessions are not covered by ZDR and fall under standard data retention policies.

nodes.label: Claude Code Analytics metadata
nodes.rationale: Claude Code Analytics stores no prompts or model responses but does collect productivity metadata such as account emails and usage statistics. Contribution metrics are unavailable for ZDR organizations, so the dashboard shows usage metrics only.

nodes.label: User and seat management data
nodes.rationale: Administrative data such as account emails and seat assignments is retained under standard policies rather than under ZDR.

nodes.label: Third-party integrations and MCP servers
nodes.rationale: Data processed by third-party tools, MCP servers, or other external integrations is not covered by ZDR; those services' data-handling practices must be reviewed independently.

nodes.label: Standard data retention policies
nodes.rationale: The standard Anthropic data retention policies are the fallback regime that governs every surface ZDR does not cover, even inside a ZDR-enabled organization.

nodes.label: Features disabled under ZDR
nodes.rationale: When ZDR is enabled for a Claude Code organization, features that require storing prompts or completions are automatically disabled at the backend level; future features may be disabled on the same criterion.

nodes.label: Claude Code on the Web (disabled)
nodes.rationale: Claude Code on the Web is disabled under ZDR because it requires server-side storage of conversation history.

nodes.label: Desktop cloud sessions (disabled)
nodes.rationale: Cloud sessions launched from the Desktop app are disabled under ZDR because they require persistent session data that includes prompts and completions.

nodes.label: Claude Tag (disabled)
nodes.rationale: Claude Tag is disabled under ZDR because it retains channel memory and session transcripts.

nodes.label: Artifacts (disabled)
nodes.rationale: Artifacts are disabled under ZDR because publishing one requires storing the published page content on Anthropic-operated infrastructure.

nodes.label: Feedback submission (/feedback, /bug, /share)
nodes.rationale: The /feedback, /bug and /share commands are disabled under ZDR because submitting feedback sends conversation data to Anthropic.

nodes.label: Remote Control (disabled)
nodes.rationale: Remote Control is disabled under ZDR because it stores the session transcript on Anthropic servers in order to sync the conversation across devices.

nodes.label: Backend enforcement regardless of client display
nodes.rationale: Disabled features are blocked in the backend regardless of client-side display: a feature may still appear in the Claude Code terminal at startup, and using it returns an error saying the organization's policies do not allow that action.

nodes.label: Requirement to store prompts or completions
nodes.rationale: Needing to store prompts or completions is the single criterion that decides which features are disabled under ZDR — conversation history, persistent session data, transcripts, published pages, or submitted conversation data.

nodes.label: Covered Models (Fable 5.1 and Fable 5)
nodes.rationale: Claude Fable 5.1 and Fable 5 are Covered Models that require data retention by default; whether a ZDR organization or workspace may use them is governed by the Covered Models policies rather than by Claude Code. Where they cannot be used they are absent or disabled in the /model picker and the server rejects requests for them regardless of client configuration.

nodes.label: 'best' alias falls back to Opus
nodes.rationale: Other models remain available under ZDR, Fable models are not the default, and the 'best' alias — which resolves to the latest Fable model where available — resolves to Opus for organizations where Fable is not available.

nodes.label: Retention for policy violations
nodes.rationale: Even with ZDR enabled, Anthropic may retain data where required by law or to address Usage Policy violations; a session flagged for a policy violation may have its inputs and outputs retained for up to 2 years, consistent with Anthropic's standard ZDR policy.

nodes.label: Requesting ZDR
nodes.rationale: To request ZDR, contact sales or the Anthropic account team; the account team submits the request internally and Anthropic reviews and enables ZDR on the organization after confirming eligibility. All enablement actions are audit-logged.

nodes.label: Migrating from pay-as-you-go API-key ZDR
nodes.rationale: An organization already using ZDR for Claude Code via pay-as-you-go API keys can transition to Claude for Enterprise to gain the administrative features while keeping ZDR; the account team coordinates that migration.

nodes.label: scan-loader agent
nodes.rationale: `scan-loader` is a restricted read-only loader subagent shipped with the Claude Security plugin. Its entire job is to return one candidates file from a scan run directory, and it is explicitly not meant for direct invocation.

nodes.label: Claude Security scan workflow
nodes.rationale: The Claude Security scan workflow is the only sanctioned caller: it dispatches scan-loader to fetch one candidates file from the run directory. An earlier stage of that same scan wrote the file's content.

nodes.label: One-directory-one-file dispatch contract
nodes.rationale: The dispatch names exactly one directory and one file name; the agent reads `<directory>/<file name>` and nothing else. The path is assembled from the two dispatch parameters rather than chosen by the agent.

nodes.label: Candidates file (JSON scan output)
nodes.rationale: The candidates file lives in the scan run directory and holds JSON content written by an earlier stage of the scan. It is the single artifact scan-loader exists to fetch and hand back.

nodes.label: Verbatim JSON pass-through
nodes.rationale: The JSON content must be returned exactly as the file has it — every row and every field, with nothing added, dropped or reworded. The agent is a transport, not a summarizer, so no LLM paraphrase can corrupt the scan's data.

nodes.label: Structured output return channel
nodes.rationale: The file's content is returned through the agent's structured output rather than as free prose, which is what makes a machine-checkable exact pass-through possible.

nodes.label: Loaded content is data, not instructions
nodes.rationale: The agent is told explicitly that the file's content is data an earlier stage of the scan wrote, not instructions to it. This is a prompt-injection defense: scan findings can quote attacker-controlled source text, so the loader must never obey what it reads.

nodes.label: Read-only tool grant
nodes.rationale: The agent's frontmatter grants exactly one tool, `Read`. With no write, edit, or execution tool available, a compromised or misled loader has no capability to act on injected instructions.

nodes.label: Read nothing else, do nothing else
nodes.rationale: The prompt closes with an absolute scope bound: read nothing else and do nothing else. It converts the tool grant's capability ceiling into an explicit behavioral floor for the one tool the agent does hold.

nodes.label: Sonnet at low effort
nodes.rationale: The frontmatter pins `model: sonnet` and `effort: low` (with `color: cyan`). A pure file-fetch task needs no reasoning budget, so the cheapest viable tier is declared rather than inherited.

nodes.label: Not for direct invocation
nodes.rationale: The description states the agent is not for direct invocation. It has no standalone value: without a dispatch naming a run directory and file it has nothing to read, so the description doubles as a routing hint that keeps the model from selecting it on its own.

nodes.label: Message Batches API (C#)
nodes.rationale: The C# Anthropic SDK exposes the Message Batches API under client.Messages.Batches, with Create, Retrieve and Results members. It is the surface for submitting many message requests as one batch instead of individual calls.

nodes.label: client.Messages.Batches.Create
nodes.rationale: A batch is submitted with `await client.Messages.Batches.Create(new() { Requests = [...] })`. The call is awaited and returns a batch object carrying an ID used by the later polling and results calls.

nodes.label: Requests collection
nodes.rationale: The Create call takes a `Requests` collection, each element being one queued message request. This collection is what makes a batch a batch rather than a single Messages call.

nodes.label: CustomID per request
nodes.rationale: Each entry in the Requests collection carries a caller-supplied `CustomID` (e.g. "req-1"). It is the caller's own label for a request within the batch.

nodes.label: Per-request Params
nodes.rationale: Every batch request entry carries a `Params` object holding the ordinary Messages parameters — `Model`, `MaxTokens` and `Messages` — so each request in the batch is fully specified on its own.

nodes.label: Model "claude-opus-5"
nodes.rationale: The example names `claude-opus-5` as the Model on a batched request, alongside `MaxTokens = 1024`. The model id is set per request inside Params, not once for the whole batch.

nodes.label: batch.ID
nodes.rationale: Create returns a batch whose `ID` is the handle passed to both `Batches.Retrieve(batch.ID)` and `Batches.Results(batch.ID)`. Without holding that ID the batch cannot be polled or read back.

nodes.label: Polling Batches.Retrieve
nodes.rationale: The documented flow is to poll `client.Messages.Batches.Retrieve(batch.ID)` repeatedly until the batch reaches a terminal state. Batches are asynchronous, so the caller waits by polling rather than by awaiting a single completion.

nodes.label: ProcessingStatus == "ended"
nodes.rationale: `ProcessingStatus == "ended"` is the terminal condition that stops the polling loop. It is the signal that the batch's results are ready to be iterated.

nodes.label: Iterating Batches.Results
nodes.rationale: Once processing has ended, the caller iterates `client.Messages.Batches.Results(batch.ID)` to read each request's outcome. Results are consumed as a sequence, one per submitted request.

nodes.label: Files API (C# SDK)
nodes.rationale: The Anthropic C# SDK exposes a Files API for uploading files and referencing them from message requests. In the version this page documents, files live under client.Beta.Files rather than the stable client.Files surface.

nodes.label: Files API out of beta
nodes.rationale: The Files API is out of beta. In current SDKs client.Beta.Files carries breaking shape changes from previous versions, so that its shape now matches the stable client.Files.

nodes.label: Migrate per live-sources.md
nodes.rationale: Callers are told to migrate according to the Files API row in shared/live-sources.md, which is the authoritative pointer for the current shape rather than this page.

nodes.label: Examples predate the change
nodes.rationale: The page states outright that the code examples below the notice predate the out-of-beta shape change, so the sample code is known-stale relative to current SDKs.

nodes.label: client.Beta.Files namespace
nodes.rationale: Files live under client.Beta.Files, whose types come from the namespace Anthropic.Models.Beta.Files. Examples also import Anthropic.Models.Beta.Messages to reference the uploaded file.

nodes.label: BinaryContent implicit conversion
nodes.rationale: BinaryContent implicit-converts from Stream and from byte[], which is why File.OpenRead("doc.pdf") can be assigned directly to the File property of the upload parameters with no explicit wrapping.

nodes.label: client.Beta.Files.Upload
nodes.rationale: await client.Beta.Files.Upload(new FileUploadParams { File = File.OpenRead("doc.pdf") }) uploads a file and returns a FileMetadata instance. FileUploadParams carries the File property that holds the binary content.

nodes.label: FileMetadata.ID
nodes.rationale: Upload returns a FileMetadata whose ID is the file identifier later passed as FileID when referencing the uploaded file from a message document block.

nodes.label: BetaRequestDocumentBlock + BetaFileDocumentSource
nodes.rationale: Referencing an uploaded file requires Beta message types: a BetaRequestDocumentBlock whose Source is a BetaFileDocumentSource carrying FileID = meta.ID.

nodes.label: Non-beta DocumentBlockParamSource has no file-ID variant
nodes.rationale: The non-beta DocumentBlockParamSource union has no file-ID variant, so a file reference cannot be expressed through the stable message types at all.

nodes.label: client.Beta.Messages.Create() required
nodes.rationale: Because the non-beta source union lacks a file-ID variant, file references need client.Beta.Messages.Create() rather than the stable messages entry point.

nodes.label: C# streaming with the Anthropic SDK
nodes.rationale: The C# Anthropic SDK streams a message by building a MessageCreateParams and iterating the events returned by client.Messages.CreateStreaming, printing text as it arrives. The documented example streams a haiku from Model.ClaudeOpus4_8 with MaxTokens 64000.

nodes.label: MessageCreateParams
nodes.rationale: MessageCreateParams (from Anthropic.Models.Messages) is the request object for a streaming call: it carries Model, MaxTokens and a Messages collection of role/content pairs, e.g. Model.ClaudeOpus4_8, MaxTokens = 64000 and a single Role.User message.

nodes.label: client.Messages.CreateStreaming
nodes.rationale: client.Messages.CreateStreaming(parameters) is the entry point for streaming in C#: it takes a MessageCreateParams and returns an async sequence of RawMessageStreamEvent values consumed with await foreach.

nodes.label: await foreach consumption loop
nodes.rationale: The stream is consumed with `await foreach (RawMessageStreamEvent streamEvent in client.Messages.CreateStreaming(parameters))`, so each event is handled as it arrives rather than after the full response completes.

nodes.label: RawMessageStreamEvent
nodes.rationale: RawMessageStreamEvent is the element type yielded by CreateStreaming — a union-like event whose specific variant is unwrapped through TryPick methods rather than by casting.

nodes.label: TryPick method set
nodes.rationale: RawMessageStreamEvent exposes TryPickStart, TryPickDelta, TryPickStop, TryPickContentBlockStart, TryPickContentBlockDelta and TryPickContentBlockStop; each attempts to unwrap the event into a specific variant and reports success as a bool.

nodes.label: TryPick naming drops the Message/Raw prefix
nodes.rationale: The TryPick method names deliberately drop the `Message`/`Raw` prefix carried by the underlying event type names, so the wire event `message_start` is picked with TryPickStart rather than TryPickMessageStart.

nodes.label: No TryPickMessageStop exists
nodes.rationale: There is no TryPickMessageStop method; the documentation states explicitly that TryPickStop is what detects the message-stop event. This is the named pitfall of the prefix-dropping convention.

nodes.label: Extracting text from a content-block delta
nodes.rationale: Incremental text is obtained with a two-step unwrap: streamEvent.TryPickContentBlockDelta(out var delta) followed by delta.Delta.TryPickText(out var text), after which text.Text is written to the console.

nodes.label: Anthropic.Models.Messages namespace
nodes.rationale: The example opens with `using Anthropic.Models.Messages;`, the namespace supplying the streaming message types used in the snippet (MessageCreateParams, Model, Role, RawMessageStreamEvent).

nodes.label: Files API (Go SDK)
nodes.rationale: The Anthropic Go SDK's Files API reference: how to upload a file, which client namespace and parameter struct to use, and which other file operations exist.

nodes.label: Files API out of beta — breaking shape change
nodes.rationale: The Files API is out of beta. In current SDKs `client.Beta.Files` carries breaking shape changes from previous versions so that it matches the stable `client.Files`; the code examples on this page predate that change.

nodes.label: Migrate per the live-sources Files API row
nodes.rationale: The doc directs readers to migrate according to the Files API row in `shared/live-sources.md`, which is the authoritative pointer for the current shape rather than the examples inline here.

nodes.label: client.Beta.Files namespace
nodes.rationale: File operations in the Go SDK live under `client.Beta.Files`. Its shape in current SDKs matches the stable `client.Files`.

nodes.label: Stable client.Files
nodes.rationale: `client.Files` is the stable (non-beta) Files namespace; the breaking changes to `client.Beta.Files` exist precisely to make the beta namespace match it.

nodes.label: Upload method (not New/Create)
nodes.rationale: The upload call is `client.Beta.Files.Upload(ctx, params)` — the method is named `Upload`, explicitly NOT `New` or `Create` as other Go SDK resources are.

nodes.label: BetaFileUploadParams
nodes.rationale: `anthropic.BetaFileUploadParams` is the parameter struct passed to `Upload`; it carries the `File` field and the `Betas` list.

nodes.label: File field takes an io.Reader
nodes.rationale: The `File` field of `BetaFileUploadParams` accepts an `io.Reader`, so an opened `*os.File` (e.g. from `os.Open("./upload_me.txt")`) can be handed to it directly.

nodes.label: anthropic.File() multipart helper
nodes.rationale: `anthropic.File(reader, filename, contentType)` wraps the reader so the multipart encoding carries a filename and content type, e.g. `anthropic.File(f, "upload_me.txt", "text/plain")`.

nodes.label: Betas: AnthropicBetaFilesAPI2025_04_14
nodes.rationale: The example passes `Betas: []anthropic.AnthropicBeta{anthropic.AnthropicBetaFilesAPI2025_04_14}` on the upload params to opt the request into the Files API beta.

nodes.label: meta.ID is the file_id
nodes.rationale: `Upload` returns metadata whose `ID` field is the `file_id` to reference in subsequent message requests — that identifier is the point of the upload.

nodes.label: List, Delete, Download, GetMetadata
nodes.rationale: Beyond `Upload`, the `Beta.Files` namespace exposes `List`, `Delete`, `Download` and `GetMetadata`.

nodes.label: Streaming - Go (Claude API skill)
nodes.rationale: A Go-language reference page of the claude-api skill showing how to stream a Claude message response with the Anthropic Go SDK: open a streaming call, iterate events, switch on delta variants, check the stream error, and accumulate the final message.

nodes.label: client.Messages.NewStreaming
nodes.rationale: The Go SDK entry point for a streamed message: `stream := client.Messages.NewStreaming(context.Background(), anthropic.MessageNewParams{...})`. It takes a context and the same MessageNewParams used for non-streaming calls, and returns a stream object rather than a completed message.

nodes.label: anthropic.MessageNewParams
nodes.rationale: The request parameter struct passed to NewStreaming. The example fills Model (anthropic.ModelClaudeOpus4_8), MaxTokens (64000), and Messages built with anthropic.NewUserMessage(anthropic.NewTextBlock("Write a haiku")).

nodes.label: stream.Next() / stream.Current() iteration
nodes.rationale: Go consumes the stream with a `for stream.Next() { event := stream.Current() ... }` loop: Next advances to the following event and Current returns it. This iterator shape, not a callback or channel, is the documented consumption pattern.

nodes.label: event.AsAny() type switch
nodes.rationale: Each streamed event is discriminated with `switch eventVariant := event.AsAny().(type)`. AsAny converts the union event into a concrete Go type so a normal type switch can select the variant of interest.

nodes.label: anthropic.ContentBlockDeltaEvent
nodes.rationale: The event variant carrying incremental content. The example matches `case anthropic.ContentBlockDeltaEvent` and then performs a second type switch on `eventVariant.Delta.AsAny()` to find the delta kind.

nodes.label: anthropic.TextDelta
nodes.rationale: The delta variant holding a text fragment; the example prints it with `fmt.Print(deltaVariant.Text)`, which is how incremental output reaches the terminal as the model generates.

nodes.label: stream.Err() after the loop
nodes.rationale: Errors are not returned per iteration: after the loop ends the code must check `if err := stream.Err(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }`. Both examples on the page repeat this check, making it the documented way to detect a failed stream.

nodes.label: message.Accumulate(stream.Current())
nodes.rationale: To rebuild the full response in Go you start from an empty `anthropic.Message{}` and call `message.Accumulate(stream.Current())` for every event; after the loop `message.Content` holds the complete response.

nodes.label: No GetFinalMessage() on the Go stream
nodes.rationale: The page states explicitly that there is no `GetFinalMessage()` on the Go stream, unlike SDKs that expose one. Manual accumulation is therefore the only documented way to obtain the finished message.

nodes.label: Files API (Java SDK)
nodes.rationale: The Anthropic Java SDK's Files API lets a client upload a file once and then reference it by file ID from a message, instead of inlining the document bytes. The doc covers the upload call, the document-block reference shape, and the remaining file management methods.

nodes.label: client.beta().files()
nodes.rationale: In the examples shown, the Files API lives under `client.beta().files()` — upload and the other file methods are reached through that beta namespace rather than through the top-level client.

nodes.label: client.files() (stable)
nodes.rationale: `client.files()` is the stable, out-of-beta Files API surface. In current SDKs the beta namespace's shape has been changed to match it, so the stable surface is the migration target.

nodes.label: Out-of-beta breaking shape change
nodes.rationale: The Files API is out of beta: in current SDKs `client.beta().files()` carries breaking shape changes from previous versions, now matching the stable `client.files()`. Readers are told to migrate per the Files API row in `shared/live-sources.md`, because the examples on this page predate the change.

nodes.label: Examples predate the change
nodes.rationale: The page states outright that the code examples it shows predate the out-of-beta migration, so the snippets are a historical shape rather than the current one and must be reconciled against `shared/live-sources.md` before use.

nodes.label: File references need beta message types
nodes.rationale: Referencing an uploaded file from a message requires the beta message types. The non-beta message classes cannot express a file-ID reference at all, so the beta types are mandatory for this flow.

nodes.label: Non-beta DocumentBlockParam.Source has no file-ID variant
nodes.rationale: The non-beta `DocumentBlockParam.Source` type exposes no file-ID variant. That gap is the stated reason a file reference must be built with the beta message types instead.

nodes.label: FileUploadParams
nodes.rationale: `FileUploadParams.builder().file(...).build()` is the argument passed to `client.beta().files().upload(...)`. It is imported from `com.anthropic.models.beta.files.FileUploadParams`.

nodes.label: Three file input forms
nodes.rationale: The `.file(...)` setter accepts a `java.nio.file.Path` (e.g. `Paths.get("/path/to/doc.pdf")`), an `InputStream`, or a `byte[]`, so the caller may upload from disk, a stream, or memory.

nodes.label: FileMetadata
nodes.rationale: `upload(...)` returns a `FileMetadata`, whose `id()` is the file ID used to reference the uploaded document in a later message.

nodes.label: BetaFileDocumentSource
nodes.rationale: `BetaFileDocumentSource.builder().fileId(meta.id()).build()` is the document source that carries a file ID. It is the beta-only variant that the non-beta source type lacks.

nodes.label: BetaRequestDocumentBlock
nodes.rationale: `BetaRequestDocumentBlock.builder().source(...)` is the message content block that carries an uploaded document into a beta message request.

nodes.label: list / delete / download / retrieveMetadata
nodes.rationale: Besides upload, the Files API exposes `.list()`, `.delete(String fileId)`, `.download(String fileId)` and `.retrieveMetadata(String fileId)` — the rest of the file lifecycle, all keyed by file ID.

nodes.label: Streaming with the Java Claude SDK
nodes.rationale: The document is a Java reference snippet for streaming a Claude message response: build MessageCreateParams, call client.messages().createStreaming(params), and consume the resulting event stream incrementally rather than waiting for a complete message.

nodes.label: client.messages().createStreaming(params)
nodes.rationale: The streaming entry point in the Java SDK is client.messages().createStreaming(params), which takes a MessageCreateParams and returns a StreamResponse instead of a single completed Message.

nodes.label: StreamResponse<RawMessageStreamEvent>
nodes.rationale: createStreaming returns com.anthropic.core.http.StreamResponse parameterised by RawMessageStreamEvent; its stream() method exposes the events as a Java Stream for functional consumption.

nodes.label: try-with-resources around the stream
nodes.rationale: The example declares the StreamResponse inside a try-with-resources block, so the underlying HTTP stream is closed deterministically once consumption finishes or throws.

nodes.label: RawMessageStreamEvent
nodes.rationale: com.anthropic.models.messages.RawMessageStreamEvent is the element type carried by the stream; each event is one server-sent chunk of the message being generated, and the caller narrows it to the variant it cares about.

nodes.label: MessageCreateParams builder
nodes.rationale: The request is assembled with MessageCreateParams.builder(), which takes the model, a max-tokens limit and the conversation messages before .build() produces the immutable params object passed to createStreaming.

nodes.label: Model.CLAUDE_OPUS_4_8
nodes.rationale: The example selects the model through the typed constant Model.CLAUDE_OPUS_4_8 rather than a raw model-id string, so the SDK's enum carries the identifier.

nodes.label: maxTokens(64000L)
nodes.rationale: maxTokens is a required builder field and is set to the long literal 64000L, bounding how many output tokens the streamed response may produce.

nodes.label: addUserMessage("Write a haiku")
nodes.rationale: addUserMessage is the builder convenience that appends a plain-text user turn to the conversation; here the prompt is "Write a haiku".

nodes.label: Filtering to contentBlockDelta events
nodes.rationale: The consumer calls .flatMap(event -> event.contentBlockDelta().stream()), using Optional-to-Stream flatMapping to keep only the content_block_delta events and silently drop every other event variant.

nodes.label: Extracting the text delta
nodes.rationale: A second flatMap, deltaEvent -> deltaEvent.delta().text().stream(), narrows each content-block delta to its text variant, so non-text deltas (such as tool-input JSON deltas) are excluded.

nodes.label: Incremental printing of text chunks
nodes.rationale: The terminal operation .forEach(textDelta -> System.out.print(textDelta.text())) writes each text fragment as it arrives, which is what makes the output appear progressively instead of all at once.

nodes.label: Message Batches API (PHP)
nodes.rationale: The PHP Claude SDK exposes the Message Batches API as $client->messages->batches, with create, retrieve and results methods for submitting many message requests as one batch job.

nodes.label: batches->create(requests: [...])
nodes.rationale: A batch is submitted with $client->messages->batches->create(requests: [...]), where requests is an array of per-request entries; the call returns a $batch object.

nodes.label: Per-request customId
nodes.rationale: Each entry in the requests array carries a 'customId' key (e.g. 'req-1', 'req-2') that identifies that individual request within the batch.

nodes.label: Per-request params (model, maxTokens, messages)
nodes.rationale: Each batch entry carries a 'params' key holding the ordinary Messages request fields — the example shows 'model' => 'claude-opus-5', 'maxTokens' => 1024 and 'messages'.

nodes.label: $batch->id handle
nodes.rationale: The object returned by create carries an id ($batch->id) which is the handle passed to both retrieve() and results().

nodes.label: Polling batches->retrieve()
nodes.rationale: Batch completion is detected by polling $client->messages->batches->retrieve($batch->id) repeatedly until the returned processingStatus reports the batch has ended.

nodes.label: processingStatus === 'ended'
nodes.rationale: 'ended' is the terminal value of the batch's processingStatus field; the poll loop stops when processingStatus === 'ended', which is the signal that results may be read.

nodes.label: Iterating batches->results()
nodes.rationale: Once the batch has ended, its outputs are read by iterating $client->messages->batches->results($batch->id).

nodes.label: Files API (PHP SDK)
nodes.rationale: The Claude Files API as surfaced by the PHP SDK: files are uploaded through the client's files accessor and the resulting file id is then referenced from a message create call.

nodes.label: Files API is out of beta
nodes.rationale: The doc states the Files API is out of beta, which is the status change that motivates the SDK shape change and the migration note attached to it.

nodes.label: Breaking shape change in $client->beta->files
nodes.rationale: In current SDKs `$client->beta->files` carries breaking shape changes relative to previous versions; the new shape matches the stable `$client->files`.

nodes.label: Stable $client->files accessor
nodes.rationale: `$client->files` is the stable, non-beta accessor for the Files API in the PHP SDK, and is the shape the beta accessor now matches.

nodes.label: Migrate per the Files API row in shared/live-sources.md
nodes.rationale: The doc directs readers to migrate according to the Files API row in `shared/live-sources.md` rather than restating the migration steps inline.

nodes.label: files->upload() with a file handle
nodes.rationale: The PHP example uploads by calling `$client->beta->files->upload(file: fopen('upload_me.txt', 'r'), ...)` — the file argument is a PHP stream resource opened with fopen.

nodes.label: betas: ['files-api-2025-04-14']
nodes.rationale: The example passes the beta opt-in `betas: ['files-api-2025-04-14']` to the upload call, which is what the beta accessor required before the API left beta.

nodes.label: $file->id as a file content block
nodes.rationale: The upload returns a file object whose `id` is the handle used downstream: it is referenced as a file content block inside a message request.

nodes.label: beta->messages->create() consuming a file
nodes.rationale: `$client->beta->messages->create()` is where an uploaded file is consumed — the uploaded file's id is passed to it as a file content block.

nodes.label: Example predates the shape change
nodes.rationale: The doc explicitly warns that the PHP snippet shown predates the out-of-beta shape change, so the sample is stale relative to current SDKs and must not be copied verbatim without migrating.

nodes.label: PHP streaming with the Anthropic SDK
nodes.rationale: Streaming a Claude Messages response in PHP is done with the official Anthropic PHP SDK: the client exposes a streaming message call whose return value is iterated event by event. The documented example streams a haiku from claude-opus-5.

nodes.label: $client->messages->createStream()
nodes.rationale: `$client->messages->createStream(...)` is the entry point for streaming in the PHP SDK. It is called with named parameters (model, maxTokens, messages) and returns a stream object that can be iterated with foreach.

nodes.label: Named-parameter call style
nodes.rationale: The documented call passes PHP named arguments — `model:`, `maxTokens:`, `messages:` — rather than a single associative array. SDK v0.4.0 and earlier accepted only a single `$params` array, so a named-parameter call against those versions throws `Unknown named parameter $model`.

nodes.label: Requires SDK v0.5.0+
nodes.rationale: The snippet is explicitly marked as requiring anthropic-ai/sdk v0.5.0 or later. Versions v0.4.0 and earlier used a single `$params` array API and cannot run this code.

nodes.label: composer require "anthropic-ai/sdk:^0.7"
nodes.rationale: The documented remedy for the pre-0.5.0 named-parameter error is to upgrade the dependency with `composer require "anthropic-ai/sdk:^0.7"`.

nodes.label: Unknown named parameter $model
nodes.rationale: Calling the SDK with named parameters on v0.4.0 or earlier throws `Unknown named parameter $model`. The error is a version-mismatch signature, not a bad argument name.

nodes.label: foreach over the stream events
nodes.rationale: The stream returned by createStream is consumed with a plain `foreach ($stream as $event)` loop; each iteration yields one typed streaming event object that the caller inspects.

nodes.label: RawContentBlockDeltaEvent
nodes.rationale: `Anthropic\Messages\RawContentBlockDeltaEvent` is the streaming event class that carries incremental content-block updates. The example filters the event loop with `$event instanceof RawContentBlockDeltaEvent` before touching its delta.

nodes.label: TextDelta
nodes.rationale: `Anthropic\Messages\TextDelta` is the delta payload carrying incremental text; the example checks `$event->delta instanceof TextDelta` and then echoes `$event->delta->text`. A delta of another type is skipped.

nodes.label: instanceof type guards on events and deltas
nodes.rationale: The documented consumption pattern is a double `instanceof` guard: first that the event is a RawContentBlockDeltaEvent, then that its delta is a TextDelta. Only when both hold is the text emitted.

nodes.label: Streaming request parameters
nodes.rationale: The example passes `model: 'claude-opus-5'`, `maxTokens: 64000`, and a `messages` array holding one user turn with content 'Write a haiku'.

nodes.label: Streaming in Ruby
nodes.rationale: The Ruby Claude API skill documents streaming as a single pattern: create a stream from the client's messages resource, then iterate over the streamed text as it arrives rather than waiting for a complete response.

nodes.label: client.messages.stream
nodes.rationale: `client.messages.stream(...)` is the Ruby entry point for a streamed message request; it returns a stream object that is assigned to a local variable (`stream`) before any output is consumed.

nodes.label: stream.text.each
nodes.rationale: Streamed output is consumed with `stream.text.each { |text| print(text) }` — an enumerable of text fragments over which a block prints each piece as it arrives.

nodes.label: model: :"claude-opus-5"
nodes.rationale: The streaming example names the model as a Ruby symbol, `model: :"claude-opus-5"`, using the quoted-symbol form required because the model id contains hyphens.

nodes.label: max_tokens: 64000
nodes.rationale: The example passes `max_tokens: 64000`, bounding the length of the streamed response; it is supplied on the streaming call exactly as on a non-streaming message request.

nodes.label: messages array
nodes.rationale: The conversation is passed as `messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Write a haiku" }]` — an array of role/content hashes, the same shape as a non-streaming request.

nodes.label: Ruby SDK tool use
nodes.rationale: The Anthropic Ruby SDK supports tool use in two ways: via raw JSON schema tool definitions, and via a beta tool runner that executes tools automatically.

nodes.label: Raw JSON schema tool definitions
nodes.rationale: One of the two supported paths in Ruby is declaring tools as raw JSON schema definitions, the same tool definition format described in the shared tool-use concepts document.

nodes.label: Tool runner (beta)
nodes.rationale: The Ruby SDK provides a beta tool runner, reached as client.beta.messages.tool_runner, which performs automatic tool execution rather than requiring the caller to drive the loop.

nodes.label: Anthropic::BaseTool subclass
nodes.rationale: A runner tool is a class inheriting Anthropic::BaseTool that declares a `doc` description ("Get the current weather for a location"), names its `input_schema`, and implements `call(input)` returning the tool result string.

nodes.label: Anthropic::BaseModel input schema
nodes.rationale: The tool's input is typed by a class inheriting Anthropic::BaseModel, e.g. GetWeatherInput declaring `required :location, String, doc: "City and state, e.g. San Francisco, CA"`; that class is passed to the tool's `input_schema`.

nodes.label: Tool #call implementation
nodes.rationale: The tool body is `def call(input)`, which receives the parsed input object and reads its typed fields (`input.location`) to produce the result the runner returns to the model.

nodes.label: tool_runner invocation parameters
nodes.rationale: The example calls tool_runner with model: :"claude-opus-5", max_tokens: 16000, tools: [GetWeather.new] (tool instances, not classes), and a messages array with a user turn.

nodes.label: each_message iteration
nodes.rationale: The runner's result is iterated with `.each_message do |message| ... end`, so the caller consumes each message of the automatically-executed tool conversation as it is produced.

nodes.label: Manual agentic loop
nodes.rationale: The alternative to the runner is a manual loop; this page defers its tool definition format and agentic loop pattern entirely to the shared tool-use concepts document rather than restating them.

nodes.label: Shared tool-use concepts doc
nodes.rationale: The conceptual overview — tool definitions, tool choice, and tips — lives in the language-agnostic shared/tool-use-concepts.md, which this Ruby page links to twice instead of duplicating.

nodes.label: Anthropic CLI (ant)
nodes.rationale: The `ant` CLI exposes every Claude API resource as a shell subcommand, with the shape `ant <resource>[:<subresource>] <action> [flags]`. `ant --help` lists resources and appending `--help` to any subcommand shows its flags.

nodes.label: Ergonomics over hand-written curl
nodes.rationale: Compared to curl, `ant` builds request bodies from typed flags or piped YAML instead of hand-written JSON, inlines file contents with `@path`, extracts fields with a GJSON `--transform` (no jq), auto-paginates list endpoints, and auto-sets the right `anthropic-beta` header via the `beta:` prefix.

nodes.label: Control plane belongs to ant
nodes.rationale: Agents, environments, skills, vaults and files are relatively static control-plane resources defined, configured and debugged with `ant`: YAML checked into the repo, applied from CI, inspected from a terminal, with typical calls `create < agent.yaml`, `update --version N`, `list`, `retrieve`, `archive`, `--debug`.

nodes.label: Data plane belongs to the SDK
nodes.rationale: Sessions and events are dynamic and driven by the application through the SDK — created per task, streamed, reacted to on every turn — via calls like `sessions.create()`, `events.stream()` and `events.send()`. Both surfaces hit the same API; the split is about where the call lives, not what is possible.

nodes.label: Install methods
nodes.rationale: Three install paths: Homebrew (`brew install anthropics/tap/ant`, then `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine` on the binary), a Linux/WSL release tarball extracted into /usr/local/bin, or `go install github.com/anthropics/anthropic-cli/cmd/ant@latest` with Go 1.22+.

nodes.label: Credential resolution order
nodes.rationale: The CLI resolves credentials exactly as the SDKs do, first match wins: explicit flags, then ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, then ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, then the ANTHROPIC_PROFILE-selected or active profile, then Workload Identity Federation env vars, then the default profile on disk. The host is overridden with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL or --base-url.

nodes.label: API key authentication
nodes.rationale: The simplest authentication is a static API key set as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the environment; it occupies a higher precedence slot than any stored profile.

nodes.label: OAuth profile login
nodes.rationale: `ant auth login` opens a browser, exchanges for a short-lived token and stores a profile, so no static key is managed. Subsequent `ant` and SDK calls pick it up automatically — a bare `Anthropic()` client works after login, but scripts reading ANTHROPIC_API_KEY directly do not. Claude Code and the Claude Agent SDK honor the same profile resolution; `ant auth logout` clears the active profile (`--all` for every profile).

nodes.label: ANTHROPIC_CONFIG_DIR layout
nodes.rationale: Profiles live under $ANTHROPIC_CONFIG_DIR — by default ~/.config/anthropic/ on Linux/macOS and %APPDATA%\Anthropic on Windows — with `configs/<profile>.json` holding settings and `credentials/<profile>.json` holding tokens.

nodes.label: ant auth status
nodes.rationale: `ant auth status` reports which credential source and profile won, the active workspace, and the scopes the active token carries. It reports status only — the doc warns not to script against its exit code as a health check.

nodes.label: Headless --no-browser login
nodes.rationale: On a remote host with no browser, `ant auth login --no-browser` prints the authorize URL and accepts the returned code back in the terminal.

nodes.label: Workload Identity Federation for CI
nodes.rationale: Interactive login is for development on your own machine; non-interactive workloads (CI, servers, containers) should use Workload Identity Federation instead, documented via the authentication docs referenced in shared/live-sources.md.

nodes.label: The #1 auth trap: a stale API key
nodes.rationale: Profiles are only consulted when no API key is set, so a stale exported ANTHROPIC_API_KEY silently overrides every profile and requests hit whatever org/workspace that key is scoped to. The remedy is to unset the key, or run one command with `env -u ANTHROPIC_API_KEY ant ...`.

nodes.label: Empty API key still wins
nodes.rationale: The key must be truly unset: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=""` still wins its precedence slot and authenticates with an empty key rather than falling through to the profile.

nodes.label: Claude Code profile conflict
nodes.rationale: The same shadowing applies in reverse to Claude Code: after `ant auth login`, Claude Code may warn about an auth conflict between the profile and its own /login credential. Keep exactly one — use the profile and /logout in Claude Code, or `ant auth logout` to keep Claude Code's own login.

nodes.label: Named profiles, one per workspace
nodes.rationale: Multi-workspace work means one profile per workspace: `ant auth login --profile <name>` (optionally `--workspace-id` to skip the picker), `ant profile activate <name>` to switch the default, `ant --profile <name> ...` or ANTHROPIC_PROFILE for one-offs, and `ant profile list` to inspect.

nodes.label: Workspace-scoped resource visibility
nodes.rationale: An interactive-login token is bound to a single org+workspace and the API only shows resources belonging to that workspace, so when an agent, session or file appears to 'disappear' the usual cause is a token scoped to a different workspace than the one that created it.

nodes.label: ant profile set edits config only
nodes.rationale: `ant profile set` edits an existing profile's config keys (workspace_id, base_url, organization_id, scope, ...). It never creates a profile and it does not rebind already-issued credentials — a fresh `ant auth login` under that profile is required to mint a token for the new target.

nodes.label: A missing profile is an error, not a fall-through
nodes.rationale: Pointing ANTHROPIC_PROFILE at a profile that does not exist is an error, not a silent fall-through to the default profile.

nodes.label: Refresh tokens hard-expire
nodes.rationale: Refresh tokens eventually hard-expire and do not slide with use, so when a previously working profile starts failing auth the first move is to re-run `ant auth login` before debugging anything else.

nodes.label: OAuth scope set on a profile
nodes.rationale: A profile's OAuth scope set is requested at login with `--scope` and persists on the profile (scope is also a `profile set` config key, and changing it requires a fresh login). Privileged scopes such as `org:admin` are not in the default set — pass the full set explicitly, and the server grants a privileged scope only if your role actually has it.

nodes.label: Dedicated privileged profile
nodes.rationale: Because the scope set rides on every token a profile mints, privileged work belongs on a dedicated profile (`admin` vs `default`) with day-to-day inference on the unprivileged one, switching with --profile or ANTHROPIC_PROFILE.

nodes.label: ant auth print-credentials
nodes.rationale: `ant auth print-credentials` hands the active credential to a subprocess or raw-HTTP script: `--access-token` emits the bare token for an Authorization header, and `--env` emits bare KEY=value lines setting ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN (and ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL if the profile has one), so `set -a; eval "$(...)"; set +a` is needed to export them. It refreshes the token if needed, but the token passed via env var is short-lived and not auto-refreshed.

nodes.label: print-credentials with no flags
nodes.rationale: A documented foot-gun: with no flags, `ant auth print-credentials` prints the entire credentials JSON rather than the bare token, which in an Authorization header yields an empty response or an HTTP/2 protocol error. Always use `--access-token` for headers; a set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY does not override credential printing.

nodes.label: OAuth needs Bearer plus a beta header
nodes.rationale: OAuth tokens go on `Authorization: Bearer` (not `x-api-key:`) plus the `anthropic-beta: oauth-2025-04-20` header — converting a raw curl/httpx script from an API key is a header change, not a key swap. The beta header requirement is endpoint-dependent (/v1/messages requires it), so always send it.

nodes.label: Both key and token set is rejected
nodes.rationale: If both ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN are set, the SDKs send both and the API rejects the request — so ANTHROPIC_API_KEY must be unset before eval'ing the `--env` output of print-credentials.

nodes.label: Command structure
nodes.rationale: Every invocation follows `ant <resource>[:<subresource>] <action> [flags]`, e.g. `ant models list`, `ant beta:agents retrieve --agent-id agent_01...`, `ant beta:sessions:events list --session-id session_01...`.

nodes.label: beta: resource prefix
nodes.rationale: Beta resources — agents, sessions, environments, deployments, skills, vaults, memory stores — live under the `beta:` prefix, and the CLI auto-sends the correct anthropic-beta header, so callers should not pass it themselves unless overriding with `--beta <header>`.

nodes.label: Self-hosted worker commands
nodes.rationale: For self-hosted environments, `ant beta:worker poll/run` and `ant beta:environments:work stats/stop` drive and monitor the work queue, documented further in shared/managed-agents-self-hosted-sandboxes.md.

nodes.label: --format
nodes.rationale: `--format` selects the output rendering: `auto` (pretty on a TTY, compact when piped), plus `json`, `jsonl`, `yaml`, `pretty`, `raw`, and `explore` for an interactive TUI.

nodes.label: --transform (GJSON path)
nodes.rationale: `--transform` applies a GJSON path to the response and, on list endpoints, runs per item rather than on the envelope — e.g. `ant beta:agents list --transform '{id,name,model}' --format jsonl`. It is not applied when `--format raw` is used.

nodes.label: -r / --raw-output
nodes.rationale: `-r`/`--raw-output` prints a transformed string result without quotes, jq-style, and is paired with `--transform` for scalar capture — e.g. `AGENT_ID=$(ant beta:agents create ... --transform id -r)`.

nodes.label: --max-items versus --limit
nodes.rationale: List endpoints auto-paginate; `--max-items N` caps the total number of results returned, which is distinct from `--limit`, which only sets the server page size.

nodes.label: --format-error / --transform-error
nodes.rationale: Error shaping mirrors the success path: `--format-error` and `--transform-error` apply to error responses. `-r` does not apply to the error path, so `--format-error yaml` is how an unquoted error scalar is obtained.

nodes.label: --debug
nodes.rationale: `--debug` prints the full HTTP request and response to stderr with the API key redacted, which is the terminal-side debugging affordance for control-plane work.

nodes.label: Flag input with relaxed YAML
nodes.rationale: Scalar fields map directly to flags; structured fields accept relaxed YAML (unquoted keys) or strict JSON; and repeatable flags build arrays — each `--tool`, `--event` or `--message` appends one element.

nodes.label: Stdin body and merge semantics
nodes.rationale: A full JSON or YAML body can be piped on stdin and is merged with flags, with flags winning on conflict; for array fields any flag replaces the stdin array entirely rather than appending. Heredoc delimiters should be quoted (<<'YAML') to disable shell expansion inside the body.

nodes.label: @file references
nodes.rationale: `@path` inlines a file's contents into any string-valued field; inside structured flag values the path is quoted. Binary files are auto-base64'd (forceable with `@file://` for text or `@data://` for base64), a literal leading @ is escaped as \@, and flags that natively take a path (like `--file` on beta:files upload) accept a bare path without @.

nodes.label: Version-controlled resource YAML
nodes.rationale: The recommended flow for Managed Agents resources is to check a `*.agent.yaml` / `env.yaml` into the repo and sync it with `create` the first time and `update` thereafter, capturing the returned ID once with `--transform id -r`.

nodes.label: --version optimistic lock on update
nodes.rationale: Updating a resource from CI needs both the resource ID and its current version — `ant beta:agents update --agent-id "$AGENT_ID" --version 1 < summarizer.agent.yaml` — where `--version` acts as an optimistic lock.

nodes.label: Session create and events
nodes.rationale: With an agent ID and an environment ID, `ant beta:sessions create --agent ... --environment-id ...` starts a session, then `beta:sessions:events send`, `events list` and `events stream` post to and read from it.

nodes.label: Stream-before-send loop
nodes.rationale: `ant beta:sessions:events stream` only delivers events emitted after the stream opens, so the stream must be opened before the kickoff message is sent. The documented shell pattern holds the stream on a file descriptor via process substitution, sends the event, then reads until `session.status_idle` or `session.error`.

nodes.label: SDK for real application event loops
nodes.rationale: The shell stream loop is for interactive exploration and demos only; application code that must react to agent.tool_use / agent.custom_tool_use events, reconnect after drops, or dedup against events.list should use the SDK (shared/managed-agents-client-patterns.md).

nodes.label: Scripting composition patterns
nodes.rationale: `--transform id -r` on a list endpoint emits one bare ID per line for composition with xargs, and `--max-items N` bounds the result set without piping through `head` — e.g. capturing the first agent ID and then listing its versions as jsonl.

nodes.label: Shell completion
nodes.rationale: Shell completion is generated with `ant @completion {zsh|bash|fish|powershell}`.

nodes.label: Live sources for the full reference
nodes.rationale: This page is a summary: for the full, always-current reference including per-endpoint flags, the reader is told to WebFetch the Anthropic CLI URL listed in shared/live-sources.md.

nodes.label: count_tokens endpoint
nodes.rationale: The `count_tokens` endpoint (`POST /v1/messages/count_tokens`) is the sanctioned way to get accurate token counts against Claude models. It is the single authority the doc points every counting surface at.

nodes.label: Token counts are model-specific
nodes.rationale: Token counts are model-specific: you must pass the same model ID you will use for inference. A count taken against a different model ID does not describe the request you will actually send.

nodes.label: Do not use tiktoken for Claude
nodes.rationale: `tiktoken` is OpenAI's tokenizer and undercounts Claude tokens by roughly 15-20% on typical text, and by much more on code or non-English input. Any estimate from `tiktoken`, `gpt-tokenizer`, or similar is wrong for Claude.

nodes.label: input_tokens response field
nodes.rationale: The count is returned as `input_tokens` on the response. Every documented surface — Python, TypeScript, and the `ant` CLI — reads that same field to obtain the number.

nodes.label: Python SDK count_tokens call
nodes.rationale: In Python, `Anthropic().messages.count_tokens(model=..., messages=[...])` counts a file or string, and the result is read from `resp.input_tokens`. The doc's example passes the contents of `CLAUDE.md` as a single user message.

nodes.label: TypeScript SDK countTokens call
nodes.rationale: In TypeScript the call is `await client.messages.countTokens({model, messages})`, whose result exposes `.input_tokens`. Other SDKs are covered by `{lang}/claude-api/README.md`.

nodes.label: ant CLI count-tokens command
nodes.rationale: From the shell: `ant messages count-tokens --model claude-opus-5 --message '{role: user, content: "@./CLAUDE.md"}' --transform input_tokens -r`. The `@./path` form inlines a file and `--transform input_tokens -r` prints the raw count.

nodes.label: The endpoint is stateless
nodes.rationale: The count_tokens endpoint is stateless: it holds no memory of a previous count, so it cannot itself report a delta between two versions of a document.

nodes.label: Diffing a file across two versions
nodes.rationale: To measure how many tokens an edit added, count each version separately and subtract. The worked example reads the old text with `git show HEAD:CLAUDE.md`, the new text from disk, and prints `count(after) - count(before)`.

nodes.label: Full docs in shared/live-sources.md
nodes.rationale: This page is a summary; the authoritative full documentation is reached via the Token Counting entry in `shared/live-sources.md`.

nodes.label: Message Batches API
nodes.rationale: The Batches API (POST /v1/messages/batches) processes Messages API requests asynchronously at 50% of standard prices. It is the batch-processing entry point documented here for the TypeScript SDK.

nodes.label: Messages API
nodes.rationale: The synchronous Messages API whose requests the Batches API packages and processes asynchronously. Every request inside a batch is an ordinary Messages API request expressed as a params object.

nodes.label: 50% batch discount
nodes.rationale: Batch processing applies a 50% cost reduction on all token usage relative to standard Messages API prices. It is the economic reason to accept asynchronous latency.

nodes.label: Batch size limits
nodes.rationale: A single batch holds up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever limit is reached first.

nodes.label: Completion window
nodes.rationale: Most batches complete within 1 hour, with a maximum of 24 hours. That bound is the latency a caller trades away in exchange for the discount.

nodes.label: 29-day results retention
nodes.rationale: Batch results remain available for 29 days after the batch is created, after which they can no longer be retrieved.

nodes.label: Full Messages feature support
nodes.rationale: All Messages API features are supported inside a batch, including vision, tools and prompt caching. Batching is therefore a billing/latency mode, not a reduced feature set.

nodes.label: Anthropic TypeScript client
nodes.rationale: The batch calls are made through `new Anthropic()` from the `@anthropic-ai/sdk` package, which exposes the batch surface at `client.messages.batches`.

nodes.label: batches.create
nodes.rationale: `client.messages.batches.create({ requests: [...] })` submits the batch and returns an object carrying `id` and `processing_status`. Each element of `requests` pairs a `custom_id` with a `params` payload.

nodes.label: custom_id
nodes.rationale: Every request in a batch carries a caller-chosen `custom_id` (e.g. "request-1"), and each returned result echoes it back as `result.custom_id` so outputs can be matched to inputs.

nodes.label: Per-request params
nodes.rationale: Each batch entry's `params` is an ordinary Messages request body — `model` (e.g. "claude-opus-5"), `max_tokens` (16000 in the example) and a `messages` array.

nodes.label: Polling for completion
nodes.rationale: Completion is detected by looping on `client.messages.batches.retrieve(id)` until `processing_status === "ended"`, sleeping 60 seconds between polls.

nodes.label: processing_status
nodes.rationale: The batch-level state field. "ended" is the terminal value the poll loop waits for; a cancelled batch reports "canceling".

nodes.label: request_counts
nodes.rationale: A per-batch tally exposing `processing`, `succeeded` and `errored`, read during polling for progress and after the batch ends for a pass/fail summary.

nodes.label: batches.results streaming
nodes.rationale: Results are consumed with `for await (const result of await client.messages.batches.results(id))`, an async iterator yielding one entry per request rather than a single materialised array.

nodes.label: succeeded result
nodes.rationale: `result.result.type === "succeeded"` carries the completed message at `result.result.message`, whose `content[0].text` holds the model output.

nodes.label: errored result
nodes.rationale: `result.result.type === "errored"` exposes `result.result.error.type`, which distinguishes an `invalid_request` from a server-side error.

nodes.label: expired result
nodes.rationale: `result.result.type === "expired"` marks a request that was never completed within the batch window; the documented handling is to resubmit it.

nodes.label: Per-result retry triage
nodes.rationale: The result type decides the remedy: an `invalid_request` error must be fixed before retrying, any other server error is safe to retry as-is, and an expired request is simply resubmitted.

nodes.label: batches.cancel
nodes.rationale: `client.messages.batches.cancel(id)` requests cancellation and returns a batch whose `processing_status` is "canceling" — cancellation is acknowledged as in-progress, not instantaneous.

nodes.label: Files API (TypeScript)
nodes.rationale: The Files API uploads files for use in Messages API requests. Uploaded files are then referenced from message content blocks rather than being re-sent with each call.

nodes.label: file_id content-block reference
nodes.rationale: Files are referenced inside Messages API content blocks via a `file_id`, e.g. `source: { type: "file", file_id: uploaded.id }`. The id is returned as `uploaded.id` by the upload call.

nodes.label: Avoiding re-uploads across API calls
nodes.rationale: The stated purpose of referencing a file by `file_id` is to avoid re-uploading the same content across multiple API calls.

nodes.label: Files API out of beta — breaking shape change
nodes.rationale: The Files API is out of beta. In current SDKs `client.beta.files` has breaking shape changes from previous versions, now matching the stable `client.files`; callers migrate per the Files API row in `shared/live-sources.md`. The examples in this document predate that change.

nodes.label: Maximum file size: 500 MB
nodes.rationale: A single uploaded file may be at most 500 MB.

nodes.label: Organization storage: 100 GB
nodes.rationale: Total Files API storage is capped at 100 GB per organization.

nodes.label: Files persist until deleted
nodes.rationale: Uploaded files have no expiry: they persist until they are explicitly deleted.

nodes.label: Free file operations, billed message content
nodes.rationale: File operations — upload, list, delete — are free. What is billed is the file content once it is used in a message, charged as input tokens.

nodes.label: Not on Bedrock or Vertex AI
nodes.rationale: The Files API is not available on Amazon Bedrock or Google Vertex AI — it is a first-party Anthropic API surface only.

nodes.label: Anthropic TypeScript client
nodes.rationale: All examples run against a client constructed as `const client = new Anthropic()` from `@anthropic-ai/sdk`; file operations hang off `client.beta.files` and messages off `client.beta.messages`.

nodes.label: toFile() SDK helper
nodes.rationale: `toFile`, exported from `@anthropic-ai/sdk`, wraps a Node read stream into an uploadable file: `await toFile(fs.createReadStream("report.pdf"), undefined, { type: "application/pdf" })`, where the third argument carries the MIME type.

nodes.label: betas: ["files-api-2025-04-14"]
nodes.rationale: Every example call — upload, message create, list, delete, download — passes `betas: ["files-api-2025-04-14"]`, the beta opt-in flag the pre-GA shape of the API required.

nodes.label: Upload a file
nodes.rationale: `client.beta.files.upload({ file, betas })` returns an object exposing `id` (the file id used later) and `size_bytes`.

nodes.label: document content block with file source
nodes.rationale: A PDF or text document is used in a message via a content block `{ type: "document", source: { type: "file", file_id }, title, citations }` alongside an ordinary text block in the same user message.

nodes.label: citations: { enabled: true }
nodes.rationale: The document content block can turn on citations with `citations: { enabled: true }`, shown together with a human-readable `title` such as "Q4 Report".

nodes.label: List files
nodes.rationale: `client.beta.files.list({ betas })` returns a page whose `data` array holds entries carrying `id`, `filename` and `size_bytes`.

nodes.label: Delete a file
nodes.rationale: `client.beta.files.delete(fileId, { betas })` removes a stored file, taking the file id as a positional argument.

nodes.label: Download a file
nodes.rationale: `client.beta.files.download(fileId, { betas })` returns a response whose `arrayBuffer()` is wrapped with `Buffer.from` and written to disk with `fs.promises.writeFile`.

nodes.label: Log out of all active sessions
nodes.rationale: A global sign-out that signs a user out of their Claude account across all devices at once. It is performed through Settings > Account on the web version of Claude.

nodes.label: Settings > Account page on claude.ai
nodes.rationale: The Account section of claude.ai settings (https://claude.ai/settings/account), reached from the user's initials in the lower left corner. It hosts the 'Log Out' button that ends every active session.

nodes.label: Not available in iOS/Android apps
nodes.rationale: The global log-out option is not currently available in the Claude mobile apps for iOS or Android; it must be triggered from a web browser.

nodes.label: 28-day web session duration
nodes.rationale: Logging in via claude.ai creates a session with a duration of 28 days, which determines how long a user stays logged in while inactive on the web app.

nodes.label: Hourly session refresh on activity
nodes.rationale: Any action on claude.ai, such as reloading the page, causes the session to be automatically refreshed every hour to 28 days from that point in time.

nodes.label: Seven-step log-out procedure
nodes.rationale: The documented steps: visit claude.ai in a browser, sign in, click your initials in the lower left corner, select Settings, navigate to Account, click 'Log Out', and confirm when prompted.

nodes.label: Immediate sign-out across all devices
nodes.rationale: Confirming the log-out immediately signs the account out on every device where it was previously logged in, including web browsers, mobile devices and desktop applications.

nodes.label: Re-authentication after global log-out
nodes.rationale: To regain access on any device after a global log-out, the user must authenticate again using either Google login or a login link sent to their email address.

nodes.label: Logging out of Claude Code via token removal
nodes.rationale: If a Claude account was used to authenticate into Claude Code, authorization tokens are managed at Settings > Claude Code (https://claude.ai/settings/claude-code); clicking the trash can icon removes a token and logs out of Claude Code.

nodes.label: Claude Code authorization token
nodes.rationale: The credential issued when a Claude account authenticates Claude Code. Tokens are listed and individually removable from the Settings > Claude Code page.

nodes.label: Shared device or unauthorized access risk
nodes.rationale: The situations the feature exists for: having forgotten to log out on a shared device, or suspecting unauthorized access to the account.

nodes.label: Unable to sign in to the account
nodes.rationale: The failure case where a user cannot sign in to their account at all, and therefore cannot reach Settings > Account to log out of all sessions.

nodes.label: Support team contact fallback
nodes.rationale: When self-service log-out is impossible, the documented escalation is to contact the Support team via the message icon in the bottom right of any Help Center page, per the 'How to get support' article.

nodes.label: Claude Console organization deletion
nodes.rationale: Deleting a Claude Console account means deleting the whole Console organization from Console settings. The article explains how a Console Admin performs that deletion and notes it impacts all members of the organization.

nodes.label: Console Admin-only permission
nodes.rationale: Only Console Admins can request deletion of a Console organization. The deletion flow therefore begins with logging in to a Console Admin account.

nodes.label: Claude Console Roles and Permissions article
nodes.rationale: The article points readers to 'Claude Console Roles and Permissions' (support.claude.com article 10186004) for a full overview of what each Console role can do.

nodes.label: Organization-wide impact of deletion
nodes.rationale: Deletion affects every user within the Console organization, not just the admin who requests it, so all members should be notified before it happens.

nodes.label: Before-deletion checklist
nodes.rationale: Before deleting, the admin should confirm which specific Console organization is to be deleted, notify all affected users, and back up any necessary data because the action cannot be reversed after seven days.

nodes.label: Seven-day irreversibility window
nodes.rationale: Account data can be restored by Support within seven days of deletion; after seven days the action cannot be reversed, which is why backing up data beforehand is advised.
