nodes.label: Six-step self-service deletion flow
nodes.rationale: The documented flow is six steps: log in as Console Admin, go to Settings > Organization, click the red 'Delete organization' button, acknowledge and continue in the modal, type the confirmation phrase and click 'Delete this organization', then see the 'Organization deleted' confirmation.

nodes.label: Settings > Organization page
nodes.rationale: Deletion is initiated from the Console's Settings > Organization page at platform.claude.com/settings/organization.

nodes.label: Red 'Delete organization' button
nodes.rationale: The red 'Delete organization' button on the Settings > Organization page opens the deletion modal.

nodes.label: Type-to-confirm deletion modal
nodes.rationale: A 'Delete [your org name]' modal requires clicking 'Acknowledge & continue' and then typing 'delete [your org name]' before the 'Delete this organization' button becomes clickable.

nodes.label: 'Organization deleted' confirmation
nodes.rationale: After the final confirmation, an 'Organization deleted' message appears in the upper right corner of the screen, signalling the deletion succeeded.

nodes.label: Accidental-deletion recovery
nodes.rationale: An organization deleted by mistake can be reverted: the Support team can restore the account data within seven days of deletion if contacted.

nodes.label: Contacting the Support team
nodes.rationale: Support (reachable via the 'how to get support' article) is the escalation channel both for restoring an accidentally deleted organization and for deletions that cannot go through the self-service pathway.

nodes.label: Outstanding balance blocks deletion
nodes.rationale: If the organization has an outstanding balance, the deletion flow shows a message prompting payment first and routes the admin to Settings > Billing; the balance must be paid before deletion can proceed.

nodes.label: Settings > Billing page
nodes.rationale: Settings > Billing (platform.claude.com/settings/billing) is where an admin pays an outstanding balance that is blocking organization deletion.

nodes.label: Self-service pathway unavailable
nodes.rationale: In some scenarios the deletion flow displays a message telling the admin to contact the team; that message means the Console organization cannot be deleted through the self-service pathway.

nodes.label: Organization feedback settings control
nodes.rationale: An organization-level administrative control that governs whether members of a Team or Enterprise organization may submit feedback to Anthropic. It is exercised from the organization's settings rather than per user.

nodes.label: Primary Owner or Owner role
nodes.rationale: Only a Primary Owner or an Owner of the plan is entitled to manage the organization's user-feedback setting. The doc states the capability in terms of that role, so ordinary members cannot change it.

nodes.label: Team and Enterprise plans
nodes.rationale: The plan tiers on which this feedback control exists. The article scopes the whole procedure to Team and Enterprise plans, so the setting is a property of those organizational plans.

nodes.label: Thumbs up / thumbs down feedback submission
nodes.rationale: The member-facing action being governed: submitting feedback to Anthropic via thumbs up / thumbs down on a chat. Whether organization members can do this at all is what the admin toggle decides.

nodes.label: Rate chats toggle
nodes.rationale: The named setting, 'Rate chats', changed with a toggle for the whole organization. It is the concrete UI control that turns member feedback submission on or off.

nodes.label: Organization settings > Data and Privacy
nodes.rationale: The admin location where the setting lives: Organization settings > Data and Privacy, at claude.ai/admin-settings/data-privacy-controls. Step 1 of the procedure is navigating there.

nodes.label: Feedback data collection, use and storage
nodes.rationale: How Anthropic collects, uses and stores feedback data is documented separately in the Privacy Center article 'How long do you store my organization's data?'. The support article defers the retention question to that page rather than answering it.

nodes.label: User feedback settings (Claude Console)
nodes.rationale: An organization-level Claude Console setting that governs whether members of the organization may submit feedback to Anthropic. It is managed from the Console rather than per user.

nodes.label: Claude Console Admin
nodes.rationale: The Admin role on a Claude Console account is the role authorized to manage whether organization members can submit feedback to Anthropic. Only an Admin can change this control.

nodes.label: Thumbs up / thumbs down feedback
nodes.rationale: The feedback mechanism being governed: organization members submit feedback to Anthropic via a thumbs up / thumbs down control. Enabling or disabling the setting determines whether members can use it.

nodes.label: Organization members
nodes.rationale: The members of a Console organization are the subjects of the setting: their ability to submit feedback to Anthropic is what the Admin turns on or off.

nodes.label: Settings > Privacy controls page
nodes.rationale: The Console location where feedback is managed: Settings > Privacy controls, at https://platform.claude.com/settings/privacy. Step 1 of the procedure is navigating there.

nodes.label: Feedback toggle switch
nodes.rationale: The single control that implements the setting: a switch on the Privacy controls page that the Admin toggles on or off. Step 2 of the procedure is toggling it.

nodes.label: Feedback data collection, use and storage
nodes.rationale: How Anthropic collects, uses and stores feedback data is documented separately in the Privacy Center article "How long do you store my organization's data?", not in this article.

nodes.label: Anthropic Privacy Center
nodes.rationale: The external reference surface (privacy.claude.com) that holds the authoritative detail on organization data retention, linked from this article for anyone needing more than the toggle procedure.

nodes.label: Claude LTI integration for Canvas LMS
nodes.rationale: The Claude LTI integration connects Claude for Education to Canvas LMS by Instructure. Enabling it takes three stages: creating an LTI 1.3 developer key in Canvas, installing Claude LTI as an app by Client ID, and turning the Canvas connector on in Claude for Education organization settings.

nodes.label: Intended audience: Claude for Education and LMS administrators
nodes.rationale: The setup steps are intended for Claude for Education administrators and Learning Management System (LMS) administrators, not for individual instructors or students. Both Canvas admin access and Claude for Education admin access are needed to complete the flow.

nodes.label: Creating the Claude LTI developer key in Canvas
nodes.rationale: Signed in as a Canvas administrator, go to Admin -> Developer Keys and click '+ Developer Key' then '+ LTI Key'. Name it 'Claude LTI', fill in the LTI 1.3 endpoint fields, save, and toggle the key's state to On.

nodes.label: LTI 1.3 endpoint fields for the developer key
nodes.rationale: The LTI key is configured with a Key Name and Title of 'Claude LTI', a short description of the LTI 1.3 app, plus four Claude-hosted URLs: Redirect URIs, Target Link URI, OpenID Connect Initiation Url, and JWK method.

nodes.label: Launch URI https://claude.ai/lti/launch
nodes.rationale: Both the Redirect URIs field and the Target Link URI field are set to https://claude.ai/lti/launch — the endpoint Canvas sends the LTI launch to.

nodes.label: OpenID Connect Initiation Url https://claude.ai/api/lti/login
nodes.rationale: The OpenID Connect Initiation Url is https://claude.ai/api/lti/login, the endpoint that begins the OIDC login handshake for an LTI 1.3 launch.

nodes.label: JWK method https://claude.ai/api/lti/keys
nodes.rationale: The JWK method field points at https://claude.ai/api/lti/keys, the public key set Canvas uses to verify signatures from the Claude LTI tool.

nodes.label: Privacy Level set to Public
nodes.rationale: Under Additional Settings on the developer key, the Privacy Level toggle must be set to Public so that user information is passed to the Claude LTI tool on launch.

nodes.label: Recommended placements: Course Navigation and Assignment Edit
nodes.rationale: Under Placements, the recommendation is to remove the default placements and add only 'Course Navigation' and 'Assignment Edit', which controls where Claude appears inside Canvas.

nodes.label: Toggling the developer key state to On
nodes.rationale: After saving the LTI key, its state must be toggled to On. A saved-but-off developer key does not make the tool usable in Canvas.

nodes.label: Installing Claude LTI as an app by Client ID
nodes.rationale: In Canvas go to Admin -> Settings -> Apps, click 'View App Configurations' then '+ App', choose Configuration Type 'By Client ID', input the Client ID generated for the developer key, click Install and refresh the course page.

nodes.label: Client ID
nodes.rationale: The Client ID is generated by Canvas when the Claude LTI developer key is saved, and is found again under Canvas Admin -> Developer Keys. It identifies the tool both when installing the app and when configuring the Claude for Education connector.

nodes.label: Deployment ID
nodes.rationale: The Deployment ID is read from Canvas Admin -> Settings -> Apps -> View App Configurations -> Claude LTI Settings Button -> Deployment ID, and is one of the three values the Claude for Education connector modal requires.

nodes.label: Canvas Domain
nodes.rationale: The Canvas Domain identifies the institution's Canvas instance and is entered in the Claude for Education connector settings modal alongside the Client ID and Deployment ID.

nodes.label: Enabling the Canvas connector in Claude for Education settings
nodes.rationale: Signed in to Claude for Education as an administrator, go to Organization settings > Connectors (https://claude.ai/admin-settings/connectors), find Canvas, click Enable, fill in the settings modal, and click Save Changes; the integration then shows as enabled.

nodes.label: Questions go to the university's administrators
nodes.rationale: Questions about a Claude for Education plan account or the Claude LTI are directed to the university's own administrator(s) rather than to a general support channel.

nodes.label: Payment method verification
nodes.rationale: Claude accounts may be required to verify the payment method on file. The support article's answer to 'why am I being asked to verify my payment method' is that the verification is requested at login and must be completed by the account holder.

nodes.label: Login verification pop-up (modal)
nodes.rationale: The verification request surfaces as a pop-up modal shown when logging in to a Claude account. It is the only surface the article describes for starting or deferring payment-method verification.

nodes.label: "Verify now" button
nodes.rationale: The article's instruction is explicit: if the pop-up appears at login, you need to click the 'Verify now' button to verify your payment method. It is the affirmative action in the modal.

nodes.label: "Remind me later" dismissal
nodes.rationale: The deferral option in the modal. Clicking 'Remind me later' dismisses the verification modal for 24 hours rather than cancelling the verification requirement.

nodes.label: 24-hour re-prompt
nodes.rationale: Dismissal is time-boxed: after the 24-hour window elapses, the user is prompted again to verify the payment method. The prompt therefore recurs until verification is actually completed.

nodes.label: Monthly-to-annual Team plan switch
nodes.rationale: A self-service flow that converts an existing Team plan on a monthly subscription to an annual subscription. It is performed in Claude's billing UI and completes in six steps, ending with an immediately active annual plan.

nodes.label: Owner / Primary Owner eligibility
nodes.rationale: Only Owners and Primary Owners of a Team plan with a monthly subscription can perform the switch to annual billing. The role gate is stated as the precondition for the whole procedure.

nodes.label: Monthly Team subscription
nodes.rationale: The starting state: a Team plan billed monthly. It is the subscription the switch replaces, and its unused remaining time is what gets credited back.

nodes.label: Annual Team plan
nodes.rationale: The target state: the same Team plan billed annually. The document treats the move from monthly to annual as an upgrade with a single displayed total cost.

nodes.label: Organization settings > Billing entry point
nodes.rationale: One of the two starting places for the switch: Organization settings > Billing at claude.ai/admin-settings/billing, where a banner confirms the current monthly plan and offers a 'Switch to Annual' button.

nodes.label: claude.ai/upgrade entry point
nodes.rationale: The alternative starting place: claude.ai/upgrade (the /upgrade page), which exposes a 'Switch to Annual plan' button instead of the billing-settings banner.

nodes.label: Current monthly plan banner
nodes.rationale: In Billing settings a banner confirms the organization's current monthly plan; it is the surface that carries the 'Switch to Annual' button.

nodes.label: 'Switch to Annual' button
nodes.rationale: The control that starts the conversion, labelled 'Switch to Annual' in Billing settings and 'Switch to Annual plan' on /upgrade. Clicking it leads to the confirmation screen.

nodes.label: Upgrade confirmation screen
nodes.rationale: The screen shown after clicking the switch control. It displays the total cost of upgrading from monthly to annual billing before anything is charged.

nodes.label: Total upgrade cost display
nodes.rationale: The total amount for moving from monthly to annual billing, presented on the confirmation screen so the owner sees the cost before confirming.

nodes.label: 'Confirm subscription' step
nodes.rationale: The final commit action: clicking 'Confirm subscription' on the confirmation screen. It is what actually converts the subscription to annual billing.

nodes.label: Immediate annual plan start
nodes.rationale: After confirmation the new annual Team plan starts immediately — there is no wait until the end of the current monthly billing period.

nodes.label: Credit for unused monthly time
nodes.rationale: Because the annual plan starts immediately, the organization is credited for any unused time remaining on the previous monthly plan, so switching mid-cycle forfeits nothing.

nodes.label: Incognito chats
nodes.rationale: Incognito chats are temporary Claude conversations that are not saved to the user's chat history and are not written to Claude's memory. The article states they differ from regular chats in several specific ways covering training, retention, search, memory and recap.

nodes.label: Availability on every plan
nodes.rationale: Incognito chats are available to all Claude users on the Free, Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise plans. Availability is not a paid-tier feature, though some of its consequences (custom retention, Compliance API) are Enterprise-only.

nodes.label: Regular chats
nodes.rationale: Regular (non-incognito) chats are the default mode: they are saved to chat history, feed Claude's memory, are searchable as previous conversations, and appear in the monthly recap. The article defines incognito chats by their differences from this baseline.

nodes.label: Not saved to chat history
nodes.rationale: An incognito chat is never written to the user's chat history and cannot be saved to it. This is the defining property from which the search, memory and recap exclusions follow.

nodes.label: Excluded from model training
nodes.rationale: Incognito chats are not used for model training. The article defers the full policy to two Privacy Center articles, one for Free/Pro/Max plans and one for Team/Enterprise plans.

nodes.label: 30-day default retention
nodes.rationale: Although an incognito chat is not saved to chat history, it is still retained for 30 days by default. On Team and Enterprise plans the article states this retention is specifically for safety purposes.

nodes.label: Organization custom data retention
nodes.rationale: An organization's custom data retention setting, available for Enterprise plans, can hold incognito chats longer than the 30-day default. The organization's policy, not the incognito flag, decides the upper bound.

nodes.label: Excluded from previous-conversation search
nodes.rationale: Claude will not pull information from incognito chats when it searches previous conversations. Content discussed incognito cannot resurface in a later ordinary chat through chat search.

nodes.label: Two-way memory isolation
nodes.rationale: Memory isolation runs in both directions: starting an incognito chat will not use Claude's existing memory, and the incognito chat will not be included in future memory entries. Neither reading nor writing of memory happens.

nodes.label: Excluded from monthly recap
nodes.rationale: Incognito chats are not included in the user's monthly recap. The recap summarizes ordinary usage only.

nodes.label: Ghost icon entry point
nodes.rationale: When starting a new chat outside of a project, a ghost icon appears in the upper right corner of the screen; clicking it enables incognito mode. The icon is the only documented way to start an incognito chat.

nodes.label: Black border and Incognito chat label
nodes.rationale: Once incognito mode is enabled the interface shows a black border and an 'Incognito chat' label in the upper left corner. This is the visible confirmation that the session is incognito before the user begins typing.

nodes.label: Closing an incognito chat
nodes.rationale: The documented way to end an incognito chat is to click the 'x' in the upper right corner when finished. This is step 4 of the start-to-finish flow.

nodes.label: Closure is irreversible
nodes.rationale: Once closed, an incognito chat cannot be reopened, including after an accidental close. The article advises saving any important information before ending the session.

nodes.label: Organizational data exports
nodes.rationale: On Team and Enterprise plans, incognito chats are included in the organizational data exports available to account Owners. Incognito hides a chat from the user's own history, not from the organization's administrators.

nodes.label: Compliance API
nodes.rationale: Incognito chats are included in the Compliance API, which is available for Enterprise plans. This is a second administrative surface on which incognito content remains visible.

nodes.label: Profile information stays available
nodes.rationale: Claude can still access profile information such as custom styles and personal preferences inside an incognito chat. Incognito suppresses history and memory, not the user's profile settings.

nodes.label: No conversion to a regular chat
nodes.rationale: Once an incognito chat is started it cannot be converted to a regular chat or saved to history. The mode is chosen at the start of the conversation and is not switchable mid-conversation.

nodes.label: Unavailable inside projects
nodes.rationale: Incognito mode is currently only available for chats outside of projects; no ghost icon appears when starting a chat within a project. This is stated as a current limitation rather than a permanent design.

nodes.label: Claude in Xcode
nodes.rationale: Claude in Xcode brings AI-powered coding assistance directly into Apple's IDE. It is delivered through Claude Sonnet 4 running inside Xcode 26 and powers both a conversational coding assistant and a set of inline coding tools.

nodes.label: Plan eligibility (Pro, Max, premium Team/Enterprise seats)
nodes.rationale: Claude in Xcode is available to individuals on Pro and Max plans, and to users holding premium seats on Team and Enterprise plans. Access is therefore gated on the subscription tier of the account signed in.

nodes.label: Claude Sonnet 4 as the model
nodes.rationale: Claude Sonnet 4 is the model made available in Xcode 26, and it is what powers the coding intelligence features described in this article.

nodes.label: Xcode 26
nodes.rationale: Xcode 26 is the Apple IDE version that hosts Claude. It is downloaded from the Mac App Store and is the required host application for every feature in this article.

nodes.label: Coding assistant (conversational)
nodes.rationale: The coding assistant answers natural-language questions about your code, helping with debugging, improving code structure, and developing new features.

nodes.label: Project context and conversation memory
nodes.rationale: Claude understands the project's context and remembers the conversation as you work, so the assistant is stateful across a working session rather than answering each question in isolation.

nodes.label: File attachment
nodes.rationale: Users can attach files to the conversation with the coding assistant, supplying material beyond whatever project context Claude already has.

nodes.label: Coding tools
nodes.rationale: Beside the conversational assistant, Claude in Xcode exposes a set of discrete coding tools: documentation generation, explanation of highlighted code, SwiftUI previews and playgrounds, inline edits, and automatic fixing of warnings and errors.

nodes.label: Generate documentation
nodes.rationale: One of the coding tools generates documentation for your code.

nodes.label: Explain highlighted code
nodes.rationale: A coding tool returns explanations of highlighted sections of code in the editor.

nodes.label: SwiftUI previews and playgrounds
nodes.rationale: A coding tool creates SwiftUI previews and playgrounds, which are Apple-platform-specific artifacts for previewing and experimenting with code.

nodes.label: Inline code changes in the editor
nodes.rationale: A coding tool makes inline code changes directly in the Xcode editor, rather than only proposing code in a chat pane.

nodes.label: Automatically fix warnings and errors
nodes.rationale: A coding tool automatically fixes compiler warnings and errors surfaced by Xcode.

nodes.label: Getting-started setup flow
nodes.rationale: Setup is a three-step flow: download Xcode 26 from the Mac App Store, open Xcode preferences and navigate to the Intelligence settings, then log in with a Claude account.

nodes.label: Step 1 — download Xcode 26 from the Mac App Store
nodes.rationale: The first setup step is downloading Xcode 26 from the Mac App Store.

nodes.label: Step 2 — Xcode Intelligence settings
nodes.rationale: The Intelligence settings pane inside Xcode preferences is where Claude is configured; the second setup step is navigating there.

nodes.label: Step 3 — log in with a Claude account
nodes.rationale: The final setup step is logging in with a Claude account, which is what binds the IDE session to the user's subscription and its usage limits.

nodes.label: Usage limits shared across all platforms
nodes.rationale: Claude usage limits are shared across all platforms: chats with Claude and coding work in Xcode draw from the same pool, so IDE work consumes the same allowance as ordinary conversations.

nodes.label: Five-hour reset period
nodes.rationale: The shared limit pool resets on a five-hour period, which is the short-window component of the limit scheme.

nodes.label: Weekly usage limits
nodes.rationale: Xcode coding work also counts towards the weekly usage limits, the longer-window component that sits alongside the five-hour reset.

nodes.label: Rate-limit message
nodes.rationale: On reaching either the five-hour or the weekly limit the user sees the message "You've reached your rate limit, please try again later." — the single observable signal for both limit types.

nodes.label: Session duration controls
nodes.rationale: Session duration controls let Enterprise and Console Admins set a maximum session length for every user in their organization. When enabled, users must sign in again after the specified period even if they have been actively using Claude.

nodes.label: Admin/Owner eligibility
nodes.rationale: The feature is available only to Admins and Owners of Enterprise plans and to Console Admins. Enabling it requires logging in with an Admin-or-above role in the relevant organization or Console account.

nodes.label: Compromised session validity window
nodes.rationale: The threat the control addresses: a compromised session that stays valid indefinitely. Bounding session length limits how long such a session could remain usable, which is the stated protection for the organization.

nodes.label: Session security settings section
nodes.rationale: The 'Session security' section is the settings block that both Enterprise Admins and Console Admins locate on the Organization and access page, and it is where the Shortened session length control lives.

nodes.label: Shortened session length setting
nodes.rationale: 'Shortened session length' is the named control inside Session security. An admin clicks Enable next to it, selects a duration from a dropdown, and confirms the selection by clicking Enable again.

nodes.label: Enterprise duration options (1/7/14/28 days)
nodes.rationale: In an Enterprise organization the dropdown offers four durations: 1 day, 7 days, 14 days, or 28 days.

nodes.label: Console duration options (1/3/7 days)
nodes.rationale: In the Console the dropdown offers three durations: 1 day, 3 days, or 7 days — a shorter and smaller set than the Enterprise organization dropdown.

nodes.label: Organization settings > Organization and access
nodes.rationale: Enterprise Admins reach the control at Organization settings > Organization and access (https://claude.ai/admin-settings/organization).

nodes.label: Console Settings > Organization and access
nodes.rationale: Console Admins reach the control at Settings > Organization and access (http://platform.claude.com/settings/organization).

nodes.label: Enterprise Admin enable flow
nodes.rationale: The five-step Enterprise procedure: log in as Admin or above, navigate to Organization settings > Organization and access, locate Session security, click Enable next to Shortened session length and pick a duration, then confirm by clicking Enable.

nodes.label: Console Admin enable flow
nodes.rationale: The five-step Console procedure: log in to the Console account as an Admin, navigate to Settings > Organization and access, locate Session security, click Enable next to Shortened session length and pick a duration, then confirm by clicking Enable.

nodes.label: Expiry behavior after enabling
nodes.rationale: Once shortened session length is enabled, existing sessions older than the selected duration expire immediately, and all other active sessions expire no later than the selected duration.

nodes.label: Forced re-sign-in
nodes.rationale: Users whose sessions expire are directed to sign in again; re-authentication is the user-visible consequence of the expiry rules.

nodes.label: Updating the session duration
nodes.rationale: An admin can change the session duration at any time from the dropdown. Selecting a shorter duration expires sessions older than the new duration immediately and shortens the expiration of sessions scheduled to expire beyond it.

nodes.label: Disabling shortened session length
nodes.rationale: Selecting 'Disable' next to Shortened session length turns the control off. Existing active sessions still expire at their already-scheduled time; only new sessions revert to default behavior.

nodes.label: Default session behavior
nodes.rationale: By default, with no shortened session length configured, sessions remain active for as long as the user stays active — there is no fixed maximum session length.

nodes.label: Shortest-duration rule across organizations
nodes.rationale: When a user belongs to multiple organizations with different session duration settings, the shortest duration wins. A member of Organization A (7-day limit) and Organization B (28-day limit) has sessions expire after seven days.

nodes.label: One session shared across organizations
nodes.rationale: A single session is used across all of a user's organizations. Because one session cannot hold two lifetimes, the most restrictive organization setting takes precedence.

nodes.label: IP allowlisting
nodes.rationale: IP allowlisting lets Enterprise plan administrators control which IP addresses can access Claude through their organization, so requests can only be made from approved network locations.

nodes.label: Enterprise-plan-only availability
nodes.rationale: IP allowlisting is available for Enterprise plans only; it is an administrator-facing control scoped to an Enterprise organization's account.

nodes.label: Source IP validation of authenticated requests
nodes.rationale: When the feature is enabled, Anthropic validates the source IP address of every authenticated request against the organization's configured allowlist.

nodes.label: Blocked request from a non-allowlisted IP
nodes.rationale: Requests from IP addresses that were not added to the allowlist are blocked; when a request originates from an address outside the allowlist, access is denied.

nodes.label: CIDR range support
nodes.rationale: The allowlist accepts CIDR ranges rather than only single addresses, covering both IPv4 and IPv6 — the doc's example is `10.0.0.0/8, 2001:db8::/32`.

nodes.label: Compiled CIDR range inventory
nodes.rationale: Before enabling the feature an organization must compile a list of all necessary CIDR ranges, including office locations, VPN exit points, and any other approved access points.

nodes.label: Allowlist configuration request
nodes.rationale: Enabling the allowlist is not self-service: the organization shares its list of CIDR ranges with Anthropic, who add them to the account's allowlist to turn the feature on.

nodes.label: Anthropic Contact or Support team
nodes.rationale: The configuration channel is an organization's Anthropic Contact or the Anthropic Support team, who receive the CIDR list and apply it to the account.

nodes.label: User lockout from omitted CIDR ranges
nodes.rationale: Omitting required CIDR ranges from the submitted list could result in users being locked out of Claude — the failure mode of an incomplete allowlist is denial of legitimate access.

nodes.label: IT administrator escalation for wrongful blocks
nodes.rationale: Users who believe they are being blocked in error should contact their own IT administrator, not Anthropic — remediation happens on the customer side by amending the allowlist.

nodes.label: Additional layer of security
nodes.rationale: Network-location restriction is positioned as an additional layer of security on top of authentication, not a replacement for it — the check applies to requests that are already authenticated.

nodes.label: Account management FAQs
nodes.rationale: A Claude support FAQ covering account administration for Team and Enterprise plans: renaming a team, changing a member's name, creating multiple teams, viewing the member list, and viewing/adding/removing allowed email domains.

nodes.label: Owner role
nodes.rationale: The Owner is the highest-privilege role on a Team or Enterprise plan. Owners can update the team name, view the member list, and add or remove allowed email domains.

nodes.label: Admin role
nodes.rationale: Admins can view a list of all members on a team via Organization settings. The FAQ grants Admins no team-rename or domain-management capability; those are stated for Owners only.

nodes.label: Organization settings > Organization
nodes.rationale: The admin console page at claude.ai/admin-settings/organization. It is where the team name is updated and where the full team member list is viewed.

nodes.label: Updating the team name
nodes.rationale: Owners update the team name by navigating to Organization settings > Organization, clicking "Update" under the current team name, typing a new name, and clicking "Save".

nodes.label: Members edit their own name only
nodes.rationale: It is not possible to change another user's name on their behalf. A user edits their own name by logging in, going to Settings > General, editing the "Full name" field, and clicking "Save changes".

nodes.label: Settings > General
nodes.rationale: The per-user settings page at claude.ai/settings/general, which holds the "Full name" field a user edits for their own account.

nodes.label: Multiple teams via multiple Team plans
nodes.rationale: On Team plans you can create multiple teams by purchasing multiple Team plans; a new Team plan is created by going to the team creation page and naming the team. Self-serve, no sales contact required.

nodes.label: Multiple Enterprise plans via Sales
nodes.rationale: Purchasing multiple Enterprise plans is not self-serve: the FAQ directs interested customers to contact the Sales team at claude.com/contact-sales.

nodes.label: Viewing all team members
nodes.rationale: Admins and Owners can view a list of all members on a team by navigating to Organization settings > Organization.

nodes.label: Allowed email domains
nodes.rationale: The set of email domains team members may use. By default it is the single domain used to create the Team or Enterprise organization; Owners may extend or trim that set after account creation.

nodes.label: Domain capture
nodes.rationale: An organization configuration that gates the self-serve domain workflow: only Owners of organizations that are NOT using domain capture can add additional allowed email domains.

nodes.label: Organization settings > Identity and access
nodes.rationale: The admin console page at claude.ai/admin-settings/identity holding the Domains section and the "Add or edit domains" control, which opens the "Update organization email domains" modal.

nodes.label: Adding an allowed domain
nodes.rationale: Owners add a domain by going to Organization settings > Identity and access, clicking "Add or edit domains" under Domains, entering the new domain in the "Update organization email domains" modal, clicking the "+" button, then clicking "Save".

nodes.label: Removing an allowed domain
nodes.rationale: Owners remove a domain by opening the same "Update organization email domains" modal and clicking the trash can icon to the right of the domain.

nodes.label: Account creator must use a business email
nodes.rationale: The person creating the organization must sign up with a business email address; public consumer domains are not acceptable for the account creator.

nodes.label: Public domains allowed for other members
nodes.rationale: Public domains such as @gmail.com, @yahoo.com and @hotmail.com can be added as allowed domains for other members of the organization, even though the creator's own address cannot be one.

nodes.label: Console appearance settings
nodes.rationale: The Console exposes user-customizable appearance settings, of which the documented one is the color mode. Customizing them is a self-service action performed from within a logged-in Console account.

nodes.label: Color mode
nodes.rationale: Color mode is the appearance setting that controls the Console's light/dark presentation. It is chosen under the 'Color mode' control on the Appearance settings page and offers exactly three options: Light, System, and Dark.

nodes.label: Console account login
nodes.rationale: Step 1 of the procedure is logging in to your Console account. The appearance settings are per-account, so the change is reached only from an authenticated session.

nodes.label: Settings > Appearance page
nodes.rationale: Step 2 is navigating to Settings > Appearance at https://platform.claude.com/settings/appearance. That page is where the Color mode control lives.

nodes.label: Light color mode
nodes.rationale: Light is one of the three selectable values under Color mode, pinning the Console to a light presentation regardless of the operating system's setting.

nodes.label: System color mode
nodes.rationale: System is one of the three selectable values under Color mode. Unlike the two explicit choices it defers the light/dark decision rather than fixing it.

nodes.label: Dark color mode
nodes.rationale: Dark is one of the three selectable values under Color mode, pinning the Console to a dark presentation regardless of the operating system's setting.

nodes.label: Model knowledge cutoff
nodes.rationale: Every Claude model has a knowledge cutoff: the date up to which its training data extends. The cutoff is per-model, so different models in the family have different cutoffs.

nodes.label: Continuous updating of Claude's data
nodes.rationale: Anthropic states it is constantly updating Claude's data. That ongoing update effort does not remove the per-model cutoff: an already-trained model stays fixed at the date its training data ended.

nodes.label: Claude Fable 5.1 — June 2026
nodes.rationale: Claude Fable 5.1 was trained on data up until June 2026 — the most recent cutoff listed in this article.

nodes.label: Claude Opus 5 — May 2026
nodes.rationale: Claude Opus 5 was trained on data up until May 2026.

nodes.label: Claude Sonnet 5 — January 2026
nodes.rationale: Claude Sonnet 5 was trained on data up until January 2026.

nodes.label: Claude Fable 5 — January 2026
nodes.rationale: Claude Fable 5 was trained on data up until January 2026 — five months behind its 5.1 successor.

nodes.label: Claude Opus 4.8 — January 2026
nodes.rationale: Claude Opus 4.8 was trained on data up until January 2026.

nodes.label: Claude Opus 4.7 — January 2026
nodes.rationale: Claude Opus 4.7 was trained on data up until January 2026.

nodes.label: Claude Sonnet 4.6 — August 2025
nodes.rationale: Claude Sonnet 4.6 was trained on data up until August 2025.

nodes.label: Claude Opus 4.6 — August 2025
nodes.rationale: Claude Opus 4.6 was trained on data up until August 2025.

nodes.label: Claude Haiku 4.5 — July 2025
nodes.rationale: Claude Haiku 4.5 was trained on data up until July 2025.

nodes.label: Claude Opus 3 — August 2023
nodes.rationale: Claude Opus 3 was trained on data up until August 2023 — the oldest cutoff listed, nearly three years behind the newest model in the same list.

nodes.label: Post-cutoff unawareness
nodes.rationale: Models may not be aware of events or information that occurred after their respective cutoff dates; asked about more recent events, a model may not have accurate information.

nodes.label: Models overview documentation
nodes.rationale: The article points readers to the Models overview page in the Claude Docs (docs.claude.com/en/docs/about-claude/models/overview) for more detailed information about the models than this cutoff list provides.

nodes.label: Context window size on paid Claude plans
nodes.rationale: There is no single context window size on a paid Claude plan: the limit depends jointly on the model and on the surface being used (chat with Claude, Claude Code, or Claude Cowork). The article answers the question by enumerating the per-model limits for each of those three surfaces.

nodes.label: Context windows when chatting with Claude
nodes.rationale: For ordinary chat with Claude on a paid plan the window falls into three tiers by model: 1M tokens, 500K tokens, or a 200K default for every model outside those two lists.

nodes.label: 1M-token chat models (Fable 5.1, Opus 5, Sonnet 5)
nodes.rationale: Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5, and Sonnet 5 support a 1M token context window on all paid plans when chatting with Claude.

nodes.label: 500K-token chat models (Opus 4.8/4.7/4.6, Sonnet 4.6)
nodes.rationale: Claude Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.6, and Sonnet 4.6 support a 500K token context window on all paid plans when chatting with Claude.

nodes.label: 200K default context window
nodes.rationale: Outside the 1M and 500K model lists, the context window on a paid Claude plan is 200K tokens, which the article characterises as ingesting 200K+ tokens or about 500 pages of text or more.

nodes.label: Context windows in Claude Code
nodes.rationale: Claude Code on a Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise plan has its own model list and its own credit conditions, distinct from ordinary chat: several models that are capped at 500K in chat reach 1M tokens here.

nodes.label: 1M-token Claude Code models
nodes.rationale: In Claude Code, Claude Fable 5.1, Sonnet 5, Fable 5, Opus 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7, and Opus 4.6 support a 1M token context window on Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans. Pro users must enable usage credits to reach 1M on the Opus models.

nodes.label: Usage-credit enablement for 1M windows
nodes.rationale: Some 1M-token windows in Claude Code are gated behind enabling usage credits rather than behind the plan alone: Pro users need credits enabled for the Opus models, and Sonnet 4.6 needs them on every paid plan except usage-based Enterprise plans.

nodes.label: Sonnet 4.6 1M window in Claude Code
nodes.rationale: Sonnet 4.6 also supports a 1M context window on Claude Code for all paid Claude plans, but usage credits must be enabled to access it, except on usage-based Enterprise plans.

nodes.label: Context windows in Claude Cowork
nodes.rationale: Claude Cowork on a Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise plan has a third model list, in which some models get 1M tokens, one auto-compacts partway, and others are held at 200K.

nodes.label: 1M-token Cowork models
nodes.rationale: In Claude Cowork, Claude Fable 5.1, Fable 5, Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8, and Opus 4.7 support a 1M token context window on Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans.

nodes.label: Sonnet 5 auto-compaction at 500K in Cowork
nodes.rationale: Claude Sonnet 5 automatically compacts the conversation at 500K tokens in Cowork, so its nominal 1M window is not a flat 1M of retained conversation.

nodes.label: 200K-token Cowork models
nodes.rationale: Claude Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.6, and Haiku 4.5 support a 200K token context window in Cowork, notably lower than the same models get on other surfaces.

nodes.label: Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans
nodes.rationale: The paid plan tiers named as the precondition for the Claude Code and Cowork context windows are Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise; usage-based Enterprise plans are called out separately as exempt from the Sonnet 4.6 credit requirement.

nodes.label: Automatic context management
nodes.rationale: For users on paid plans with code execution enabled, Claude automatically manages conversation context: as the conversation approaches the window limit it summarizes earlier messages to make room, allowing conversations to continue indefinitely in most cases. Users may notice this as Claude organizing its thoughts during long conversations.

nodes.label: Summarization of earlier messages
nodes.rationale: The mechanism behind automatic context management is summarization: when the conversation approaches the context window limit, Claude summarizes earlier messages to make room for new content.

nodes.label: Summarization does not count toward usage limits
nodes.rationale: The automatic summarization performed by context management does not count towards the user's usage limit, which is what makes indefinitely long conversations affordable.

nodes.label: Full chat history preservation
nodes.rationale: Summarizing is not deletion: the full chat history is preserved so Claude can still reference it even after earlier portions have been summarized out of the active window.

nodes.label: Code execution must be enabled
nodes.rationale: Automatic context management only works when code execution is enabled; without it, the conversation is not automatically summarized and the raw window limit applies.

nodes.label: Residual context-limit edge cases
nodes.rationale: Even with automatic context management active, rare edge cases such as a very large first message or a system error can still make a user hit the context window limit.

nodes.label: Maximizing your context window
nodes.rationale: Even though context is managed automatically for most conversations, the article recommends three user-side optimizations of available context space: use projects, keep project instructions concise, and manage active tools and connectors.

nodes.label: Projects and retrieval-augmented generation
nodes.rationale: Projects use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which lets Claude work with larger amounts of information than the window holds by loading only the relevant content into the context window.

nodes.label: Concise project instructions
nodes.rationale: Project instructions should be kept concise: Claude performs best when they carry general context about the project, key guidelines, and Claude's role, rather than bulk content.

nodes.label: Managing active tools and connectors
nodes.rationale: Tools and connectors are token-intensive features, so being mindful of how many are active at once helps maximize the context space available for the conversation itself.

nodes.label: Settings > Appearance page
nodes.rationale: The Settings > Appearance page at https://claude.ai/settings/appearance is where a Claude account's visual preferences are changed. Both the color mode and the chat font controls live on this one page.

nodes.label: Account menu navigation to settings
nodes.rationale: To reach the appearance settings you log in to your account and click your initials or name in the lower left corner, then navigate to Settings > Appearance. This click target is the documented entry point to the settings area.

nodes.label: Color mode setting
nodes.rationale: Color mode is the appearance control that switches between light and dark presentation. It offers three selections: Light, Match System, and Dark.

nodes.label: Switching between light and dark mode
nodes.rationale: The documented procedure for switching light/dark is three steps: log in and click your initials or name in the lower left corner, navigate to Settings > Appearance, then select Light, Match System, or Dark under Color mode.

nodes.label: Chat font setting
nodes.rationale: Chat font is the appearance control that changes the typeface used in chats. It is found in Settings > Appearance and offers Default, Match System, and Dyslexic Friendly.

nodes.label: Match System option
nodes.rationale: Match System is offered as a selectable value on both appearance controls — it appears among Light/Match System/Dark for Color mode and among Default/Match System/Dyslexic Friendly for Chat font — deferring the choice to the operating system's own preference.

nodes.label: Dyslexic Friendly font
nodes.rationale: Dyslexic Friendly is one of the three Chat font selections, alongside Default and Match System. It is the accessibility-oriented typeface choice exposed on the appearance settings page.

nodes.label: Sidebar cannot be fully disabled
nodes.rationale: The documented answer to "Can I disable the sidebar?" is no: it is not currently possible to completely disable the sidebar. This is a stated product limitation, not an appearance setting.

nodes.label: Sidebar open/close button
nodes.rationale: A button at the top right of the sidebar opens or closes it. Collapsing the sidebar with that button is the only available control over its visibility.

nodes.label: Disable public projects (org setting)
nodes.rationale: An organization-level setting that lets Team and Enterprise owners restrict the creation of public projects across their organization while maintaining internal sharing capabilities.

nodes.label: Primary Owner / Owner on Team or Enterprise
nodes.rationale: The feature is available only to Primary Owners and Owners on Team and Enterprise plans; it is not exposed to ordinary members or to other plan tiers.

nodes.label: Public projects toggle in Data and privacy settings
nodes.rationale: The control lives at Organization settings > Data and privacy (claude.ai/admin-settings/data-privacy-controls): find 'Public projects' and toggle it off.

nodes.label: Public projects enabled by default
nodes.rationale: By default, public projects are enabled for all Team and Enterprise plans, so disabling them is an opt-out action rather than an opt-in one.

nodes.label: Existing public projects converted to private
nodes.rationale: When public projects are disabled, all existing public projects are converted to private projects. This conversion is not undone by re-enabling the feature later.

nodes.label: Creation of new public projects blocked
nodes.rationale: With the setting off, users are prevented from creating new public projects anywhere in the organization.

nodes.label: Private projects still shareable with individuals
nodes.rationale: After disabling public projects, users can still share private projects with individual users inside the organization, and any private projects already shared with individuals retain their shared settings.

nodes.label: Internal project sharing capabilities
nodes.rationale: The bundle of sharing and collaboration features available to Team and Enterprise users inside the organization, which disabling public projects explicitly does not affect.

nodes.label: Individual project sharing by email invitation
nodes.rationale: Users can still share projects with specific team members using email-based invitations after public projects are disabled.

nodes.label: Organization-wide project sharing
nodes.rationale: Projects can still be shared across the entire organization where permissions allow, even with public projects disabled.

nodes.label: View and edit permission levels
nodes.rationale: All view and edit permission levels remain available for internal sharing after the change.

nodes.label: Shared with me tab and collaboration features
nodes.rationale: The 'Shared with me' tab and other collaborative features continue to function as expected once public projects are disabled.

nodes.label: Scope: external public sharing only
nodes.rationale: The setting specifically controls external public sharing while preserving all internal collaboration functionality — that boundary is what defines its blast radius.

nodes.label: Re-enabling public projects
nodes.rationale: Turning the setting back on restores the ability to create new public projects, but is not a rollback: projects converted during the disable stay private and internal sharing settings and permissions are unchanged.
